Tomb Raider: Chronicles started off so promising, so well set up. The opening cutscene had me hooked. Is Lara really dead? Who knows? Winston finally gets a role other than cannon/freezer fodder, opting to recount Lara's past expeditions around the globe to Father Patrick Dunstan, after a memorial service for her is held. Meanwhile, Werner von Croy, Lara's mentor and rival, continues excavating the Temple of Horus in hopes of finding her after the events of The Last Revelation.
But after the opening cutscene, I've made a stunning revelation myself: this game is utterly soulless, lazy and devoid of heart. In my reviews of Tomb Raider II and III, I made comments addressing that I found them to be more effective as expansion packs rather than sequels, but still good games. Chronicles, however, feels more like a map pack created by someone who had the Tomb Raider concept hastily explained to them in 2 minutes.
There's only 13 levels this time around. To boot, a lot of them are incredibly short. The amount of puzzles has been reduced, an addition that I really loved from the Last Revelation, instead opting to return to key, switch, door and backtracking from Tomb Raiders I-III. The levels are also annoyingly easy, except for the final level, which is ridiculously hard and total change of pace from the previous 12. Here's a breakdown of the levels:
1-4: Reskinned Venice levels from Tomb Raider II with a hint of the Greece levels from Tomb Raider I.
5-7: Painfully unoriginal snowy Russian base and submarine levels. Cause that's never been done before.
8-10: Okayish levels pretty much stolen from Shadow Man/Medievil. Seriously.
11-13: Why is Lara Croft stuck in the Matrix now? Why didn't you take the blue pill?!
Lara's new techniques include: tightrope walking and swinging from horizontal bars. As usual, these additions are barely noticeable as they appear about 3 times each throughout the entire game. Because the level system jumps around to different time periods, Lara's inventory is reset at the beginning of each set, which is actually a pretty good addition. Secrets have been replaced by golden roses which, upon collecting them all, unlocks an artwork menu (yay). If you miss one, you miss out, but it really doesn't matter. It's not worth it. There's also no vehicle sections either, other than a crappy underwater mission which is irritatingly short (literally 2 minutes).
Not to mention that it's filled with some irritating bugs as well. Using hotkeys for medkits depletes your supply, but doesn't actually heal you half the time. Weapon hotkeys don't work anymore. A couple of times Lara just refused to draw her weapons, whether I used the draw key or equipped it from the inventory menu. Saving also screws up for a lot of people, but thankfully I never encountered this issue. The final level is ghastly in its bugginess.
Plotwise, well, what plot? It's four completely random episodes thrown together. This entire game is totally unnecessary in the overarching plot from Tomb Raider through to The Angel of Darkness. The concept is good, but it's executed so poorly that it's just sad. The only connection that Chronicles has to past entries is, at the end of the game, Werner von Croy finds Lara's backpack. It would be a spoiler, but come on, we know she's still alive, and playing through this dreck really isn't worth such an equally pitiful ending.
The sound is just average. I don't know what happened to Peter Connelly's great soundtrack from The Last Revelation. Most of the music is gutted, reused or remixed from previous entries. Egyptian-themed music from The Last Revelation is used, for example, in the depths of water beneath a Russian submarine. It doesn't flow and it's just freaking lazy. Voice acting is just bad all around. Stereotypical Americans, Frenchmen, and Russians flood the cutscenes, of which there are inexplicably many, consistently interrupting the little gameplay that there is. Voice volume is also far too low, leading to important dialogue, such as hints given by Zip in the final 3 levels, being missed.
Oh, and the camera! My God, the camera. The fixed angles are revolting, obscuring your view and disabling the use of the look function. Meaning that, unlike in previous entries, if you wanted to return to your normal view, you just pressed look or draw weapon. Here, nope! Enjoy this beautiful tilt while you fall to your death, or this stunning pan while you get the♥♥♥♥♥♥shot out of you by  a helicopter!
The game somehow looks worse than The Last Revelation. Lara's model remains unchanged from the previous year, and only a small amount of levels actually take place inside a tomb, the rest of which are cities, military bases or submarines. I'm all for variety, but it is called TOMB Raider. Why the sudden aversion to one of the core (no pun intended) elements of the game? Human models other than Lara look downright awful, especially Father Patrick's. Time Crisis on PS1 had better models than this game. The only above-standard thing about this game is the pre-rendered cutscenes, and even they aren't up to scratch with other games released in the same period.
I suppose one other good point about the game is its disappointing length, which means that it's over quickly, even though it feels like an eternity. I passed Tomb Raider: Chronicles in five hours. FIVE HOURS. It's one of the most disappointing games I've ever played. And if you're afraid of missing out on some plot details, don't be. This game is worthless in every aspect.

The Witcher 2 is a game with memorable characters, beautiful towns and landscapes, and a story filled with political intrigue. It's rare to come across a game with choices which feel impactful while avoiding typical 'black and white' or 'good and evil' situations. What lacks in gameplay is made up through the narrative.
The gameplay is sub-par. Geralt of Rivia is equipped with two swords: one for human-slaying and one for monster-slaying. With magic-like abilities called signs to go along with his swordplay, Geralt is a force to be reckoned with. Dodging and parrying are two important aspects of the combat system. Geralt can die in a moment's notice if the player isn't careful, so it's vital to know when to be aggressive or defensive. However, The combat feels sluggish. The tab-targeting feels unresponsive at times, dodging does not always go the way the players want it to, and contact with enemy units does not feel responsive. A huge plus though is the way a player has to prepare for each encounter. Geralt cannot use potions during combat, only when he is meditating, which a player can do at anytime outside of combat. Potions range from boosting his recovery rates to increasing his attributes and resistances. It's a fairly comprehensive system and adds a layer often missing from other games.
To level up, the player is given a 'skill tree' to add attribute points to four different categories, each composing of their own active and passive skills: Training, Alchemy, Signs, and Swordsmanship. The leveling up system is not complicated, but the choices you make are important. Geralt can level up to 35, which for example can fill up  the Training Tree and one other. So the player is given the choice of specializing in a certain tree, or become a jack-of-all-trades, balancing their skills points across all areas. It's a simple system which relies on player choice as a main driving force.
The story is interesting enough to continue unraveling its many mysteries. Geralt meets friends, foes, and backstabbers along the way. What's great is that each character has a sensible motive to their actions. Voice-acting is great and the writing is well-done. The cutscenes do not offer much in terms of action, but the dialogue options and the strive to know more about the characters is enough to justify the more static encounters.
Visually the game is absolutely beautiful. The lighting was and still is the best in the gaming industry. It benefits to take a second and marvel at the scenery surrounding Geralt. The forest around Flotsam, the first town Geralt encounters, is stunning. It helps make the world come alive, and like Mass Effect, creates a very convincing world, as if there's a lot more going on than what Geralt sees in his eyes. The character models, although great, could use some variety. It was common to come across the same character models across various parts of the game.
If you are a fan of mature-themed RPG adventure, this game ranks among the best of them. It comes highly recommended.

Tomb Raider Chronicles is a great memorial to the legendary Lara Croft after the events of the last game. We learnt she wanted some of Harry Potter's Philosophers Stone, a trip on a Russian sub, flashbacking to grim Ireland to talk to the demons with a priest who treats exorcism like a tea party and she spites old Von Croy in a wheelchair in the good ol' US and A in his own company HQ! We globetrot with our favorite female icon through stories told by old friends sitting around a fireplace after the memorial, getting steadily drunker.
It's a gentle and perhaps thankfully easier pick up and play title after the titanic epic of The Last Revelation and a breather from the relentless TR3, perfect for novices or those who want to breeze through the game without too much difficultly. That said, although the difficulty isn't too high, it boasts the hardest (and buggiest) final level to date; the perhaps ironically named Red Alert.
Highlights for me are the Italian levels with their lovely visuals and beautiful scenery injected with some good humor from series stalwards Larson and Pierre from TR1, now a bumbling comic duo that set to try and thwart our heroine but fail horribly! The Russian levels are very tense, particularly in the Deepsea Dive and Sinking Submarine levels. Ireland does well with the grim, macabre setting to instil a creepy atmosphere (Labyrinth gets props for being eerie) and as Lara is unarmed, it adds to the drama! The final stages are very hi-tech, a huge contrast to the rest of the game act as a thrilling hi-octane conclusion!
I recommend you play this after you play the first four so you get a good feel for the Core Design era before Angel of Darkness plunged it into....uh darkness. Such a shame they rushed AoD, it would have been interesting to see what future installments that could have been. But to fully live the Core Design era, start at the beginning and have yourself a TR marathon.
TRC has a special place in my heart even to this day!

If you're reading this, you have probably already tried at least one of the other Tomb Raider games, and are wondering, "How will I react to Tomb Raider 5: Chronicles compared to the other Tomb Raider game(s) I have played?". I will try to review Chronicles based on its quality relative to the other classic games in the series (i.e. the ones developed by Core).
Compared to the first four classic games, Chronicles is fairly short and (for me) probably the easiest out of the five "Core classics". I enjoyed the varied settings in the game's 13 levels, and I think the developers did a great job in creating a suspenseful atmosphere despite a dated graphics engine relative to that time period of PC gaming. To support this atmosphere, there are plenty of varied puzzles (although they are nowhere near as difficult as Tomb Raider 3's puzzles), good use of ambient sound effects to set the mood, an emphasis on exploration and, for a number of levels, a fun avoidance/stealth-based mechanic where the clunky combat is non-existent.
Chronicles is split into four locations and unfortunately I feel that only the first location (Rome) has that traditional tomb-raiding feel which I so dearly love. I don’t mind the occasional “modern-day” level; however I felt that Chronicles was a bit too heavy on modern-day exploration (more than half of the levels are in modern-day settings). This is a matter of taste, but one of the things I really appreciated about some of the older Tomb Raider games was getting immersed in the lore of Ancient or lost civilizations. So, while the atmosphere of Chronicles is overall still suspenseful and well-crafted, I felt that the game lacked that “epic feeling” that certain levels of previous Tomb Raider games provided (I’m looking at you, Temple Ruins of Tomb Raider 3 and St. Francis’ Folly of Tomb Raider 1).
TLDR: Chronicles is a decent “classic” Tomb Raider game, despite it being relatively short and easy, and lacking a certain epic atmosphere that all 4 previous games possessed. I would only recommend it if you have played some of the other classics (i.e. 1-4) and are just looking to add to your collection for a very cheap cost ($6.99 for approximately 10 hours of gameplay). If you’re completely new to the series and are looking to start your Tomb Raider experience, start with Tomb Raider 1, or, if you can’t tolerate the outdated graphics of the Core classics, start with Tomb Raider: Legend developed by Crystal Dynamics.
Just for reference, here’s how I would rate Tomb Raider 5: Chronicles relative to the other classic Tomb Raider games I have played, from best to worst:

A delightful little gem.

The core gameplay is X-COM like. The terrain/objectives are diverse (though thematically unified). The gameplay outside combat is (though visually identical) asstoundingly diverse. Some maps focused on prospecting, others on trade and survival, others on gambling/theft, others on locating relics. The game really feels like a number of vingettes that share common elements and combat mechanics -- and this was delightful.
As for the core gameplay -- the perk system, available weapons, and item loadouts, taken together with inherent character differences make for very satisfying experience. Despite a visual simalarity to the levels/enemies, the game offers a variety of combat experiences.
This was a hidden gem for me. If you're into this style of game, and you're willing to forgive a lack of polish in some places, you will really enjoy this one.

The camera takes a bit of getting used to, but with some practice all of the controls and knowing what buttons to press and when becomes second nature. I would definitely recommend Spintires to anyone interested in buying it.

The first installment of Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos is, when taken as a whole, a very solid experience.  The art and music are well crafted at pretty much every juncture, and the story picks up a lot after the first half hour.  It does however, stumble a little bit coming out of the gate.  Initially, the game's protagonist, Winter Harrison, comes across as both incredibly naïve and needlessly childish for a 14 year old.  This, along with the weird, veiled flirting that seems to pass between Winter and her mentor, Cyrus, felt very inauthentic and made me cringe more than a couple of times.  To the game’s credit though, as the story progresses into the climax and the extended epilogue, the dialogue improves substantially, becoming far more naturalistic and believable.
Despite some problems with characterization and dialogue, the story of Learning to Manage Chaos really delivers by developing a strong, tight plotline.  Everything that happens feels like it occurs as a very natural consequence of the events that happened in previous scenes, and the events culminate in a pretty exciting finale.  The climax may feel like it came from out of left field to those who didn't take the time to read through the provided codex, but given how interesting most of the entries are, I don’t think any blame for this lies with the developer.
Some final notes to keep in mind.  This story is short, probably only an hour and a half or two in length, depending on how fast you rush through it and there’s not much in the way of replay value.  Most of the choices come in rapid fire right before the story’s finale.  If you're not the type who’s willing to shell out a few bucks for only a couple of hours of entertainment, definitely look elsewhere.  I'll also say that there are points where it feels like some corners were cut.  For example, the epilogue, which makes up maybe a quarter or so of the story's running time, is shot from a single point of view, showing only Winter and her roommate.  This wouldn't necessarily be a problem, however it’s very noticeable when three people come to the room, and all three remain distinctly off screen.  This isn’t a sticking point for me, nothing else about the game looks or feels cheap and I know that it can be tough balancing your budget as small developer, but it is something I’d keep in mind.
Overall, I’d definitely say dive in.  It’s a fun little Visual Novel with a pretty nifty science fiction premise and nice, well-paced plot.  Thumbs Up.

Overview: I loved the original concepts and the storyline, but the actual gameplay could use a bit of work.
Broken Age features a split storyline - a provincial girl with a fiery spirit, and a boy who grew up an only child on a "spaceship". I'll skip over the spoilers and just comment on the game style. Very few games have more than one hero, making this one more interesting than your standard video game. The characters and conversations are engaging and largely realistic, addressing issues like cults, misjudging people, blind obedience to "how it's always been done", and basic human decency.
The game is primarily linear, but allows a lot of wiggle room to complete parts of an objective in any order. (Eg: Finding the parts to fix a ship can be done in any order, but they must all be found before the story will progress.) Some of these objectives are, as others have noted, nearly impossible to complete without cheating. The most notable example is rewiring the hexipal - who would know to decode a picture sitting in the background of the other character's adventure?
There's a question of sexual references. As far as I can tell, they're so obscure that anyone who understands them already has experience from elsewhere. Raising a teenager and a younger child myself, I can confidently say this game is family-friendly.
But would they WANT to play it? Only if they have a walkthrough. Most of the time it's fun and easy, but some of the puzzles are just too frustrating to bother playing through, and I'm no intellectual slouch. (Btw, kudos to the authors of those walkthroughs!)
Recommended as a good story and an interesting experience. As noted above, the actual gameplay needs work. Classic Double-fine product.

First  and foremost, this game isn't bad in the least bit. I just wouldn't reccomend buying it unless your computer can ♥♥♥♥ing decimate any next gen game because all hanger 13 did with this game is copy and paste a console port. Optimization needs SERIOUS help, like I know my specs aren't that good but I shouldn't be getting the frames I'm getting. Now, let's get into the game itself, Mafia 3 is a gritty story of revenge and it does a damn fine job of doing this. The side missions are a bit repetitive, but you'll be overall entertained with the gameplay. The soundtrack is AMAZING. (Listening to All Along the Watchtower by Jimi Hendrix as I write this review). This game does NOT shy away from the topic of racism in any way, and this just adds to the amazing story this game has to tell. The animations are pretty good but sometimes can be disruptive to the flow of the game. The brutal takedowns are awesome but can be way too overpowered, come on, who wants to have a gunfight when you can just charge at the mobsters and ♥♥♥♥ing execute them effortlessly. This brings me to Lincoln Clay, who in case you didn't know, is the game's main protagonist. He is a no-nonsense orphan turned Vietnam vet that will do anything for family. Him along with every other character are very interesting and it is even more interesting how they progress throughout the story. I love the added fact that he was a skilled soldier during the war, seeing as how you can anally destroy groups of mobsters using only your trusty combat knife. Overall Mafia 3 is an amazing story within an absolutely amazing portrayal of a 1968 New Orleans that is extremely volatile and unoptimized for pc at the moment. While this is a very good game that I would reccomend to anyone who has console handy, I would not get this game on PC at the moment because it is PLAGUED with graphical bugs, upscaled resolutions, and sometimes ugly textures.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I waited forever to buy this game because of the doubt caused by all the terrible reviews about part 2. Finally, it came in a bundle with games I defintely wanted so I decided, why not give it a try.
And, my initial reaction was something like: screw this game with it's dumb puzzles and stupid story.
Which was not entirely fair.
First of all, the art is very beautiful, cute and just sort of calming to look at (probably because of the colour scheme).
Second of all, the voice acting was very good, and the writing was decent as well.
Act 1 started off brilliantly, I loved the story, and the intrigue and all the questions that started to pop up that needed answers, and I got really excited.
Most of the puzzles in act 1 were fine, not difficult, not extremely illogical or annoying.
Act 2 also started out oke, it still could go anywhere. But it didn't. The story felt extremely rushed, and I felt like they skipped over some built-up from act 1 and left some stuff hanging while kinda dumbing down the story (In my opinion).
But, It was still an ok story, could have been more maybe, but It was not terrible. Which I decided on after some post-hoc consideration.
However, a lot of puzzles in act 2 I really hated. First of all they do the same one like 4-5 times, exactly the same thing, which feels lazy. Also, some of these puzzles you need information from the one character to use for the second character, which takes away a bit from the immersion (how does this character know this information). So after I guess half of act 2 I just asked google what to do because i got way to frustrated and did not enjoy the game anymore.
So, since there is no neutral option for reviews it's a hard decision. But in the end, besides the extremely annoying puzzles, and slightly dissapointing story progression, I still decided to finish it. And I'd like to think that when I at least finish it, it was worth my time.

Another fun installment in the series. This one has some of the best puzzles yet, a bit less monotonous than the thematic puzzles of the "Water's Edge". Also, the mini-games are much more interesting, and they offer a nod to any Euro-style board game fans out there.
The dialog is great, with Lukas playing the part of Rentaro, this episode's cut-up. The accents can be a bit painful, but it's still well written.
The flow of the plot is a bit less smooth than the prior games, though. There is one puzzles that you can get all the clues to solve, but the solution doesn't work until the game "knows" you have the solution by doing things in a certain order. Also, there are lots of dialog blocks to progression that only unlock if specific things are found - which is normal stuff, but there are so many of these elements, there can be long stretches of wandering around looking for the thing you missed that will unlock a dialog you don't know you need to advance the plot.
All in all a good P&C mystery, though.

The first time I played Captive Curse, I was absolutely terrified.
Though the game firmly keeps with being family friendly, it does an excellent job of conveying the castle and its array of characters fear. From the dark atomsphere to the animal skull in the dungeon to the monster lurking outside the castle walls, replaying it gave me the shivers!
If you'd like to play a spookier Nancy Drew game, this one makes for a great choice.
♥ Love the mini games.
Usually I tend to skip the mini games unless they're directly related to clearing a task or two. Playing Raid? Killing cows in search of the hidden monster? Loved them! The two mini games added a great amount of replay value to the game. Admittedly I wouldn't mind if they made more of the mini games as fun as those two!
♥ Her Interactive stays true.
No matter how updated the graphics become or how much the budget expands, I always admire how Her Interactive keeps the Nancy Drew games with the spirit of the books. Only once have I ever felt that the game was without heart, without spirit, thankfully not with this title.
The Captive Curse is for sure fitting with Nancy Drew!
✘ Danger music while ... shopping?
I rarely play games with the audio enabled however Nancy Drew is an exception. The one trait of all Nancy Drew games I wish Her Interactive would change is music playing in the most unfitting scenes. Music can do a wonderful job of influencing a player's mood however danger music while in the gift shop? A heightened heart beat while making a phone call to Ned?
It always makes me laugh yet I do wish they would adjust it to play in sync with the proper scenes.
✘ Ned.
Is it only me or are others tired of the drawn out drama between Ned and Nancy? If Her Interactive wants to add a bit of emotional spice in Nancy's life, couldn't they involve Hannah, her father, Bes, George, or even the Hardy boys?
Ned feeling neglected is getting a bit stale. Toss the bread out!
✘ The layout is confusing.
It's a bit of a puzzle in itself to find your way around the castle & woods. Not only was it difficult to remember the way through ever twisting hallways, it turned into a major annoyance, especially since it took my time away from focusing on tasks and the actual story.
Overall Nancy Drew: The Captive Curse is a wonderful addition to the series and would settle in well in your Steam library! ~

TR5 is the last oldschool Tomb Raider game. It features the same visuals as Tomb Raider 4 and also includes some new moves.
Chronicles tells us four stories about Lara's previous adventures (the events before The Last Revelation). The Rome is set before Tomb Raider 1 (1996), Russia is somewhere in the middle, Ireland when Lara was 16 (same age as in TR4's Cambodia levels), New York (when she decided to steal Cambodia's Iris from Von Croy).
The game is somewhat notably shorter than the previous parts, but it features some variety. Rome was similar to TR2's Venice style adventures. Russian submarine was similar to TR3's modern vibe. Ireland is quite a unique experience, you could even tag it as survival horror. VCI headquarters is more similar to The Angel of Darkness concept of modern Tomb Raiding.
Unlike TR4 the TR5 is completely linear, you can't go back between the levels and on top of that each time you finish a chapter (on of four) all your items are gone. On the bright side that prevents item hoarding. The game has 36 secrets. Collecting all unlocks game's concept art.
TR5 has native widescreen support. There's no need to patch it.

If you're reading this review, you probably want to know if this game is worth the money, and time. Assuming you're into rpg's (otherwise i don't see any reason you're here), and want to get your mind blown away, then this game is for you. I can't possibly describe how fantastic Witcher 2 is. While the "general" story might not be something outstanding, the way you progress through it, the way you interact with people completely engulfs you into the experience, and you won't even realize when it's already 5 am, and you've been playing for 12 hours at least. This is partly because of the side missions. Unlike other rpg's where they are mediocre at best, and mainly consist of something like "Get to point B, Talk to someone, Return, ????, PROFIT", side missions in Witcher 2 are self contained stories, some of them being more enjoyable than the main game itself. And of course if you don't want to do them for whatever reason, you'll miss A LOT.
Another thing at which Witcher 2 excels is the combat. While at low difficulty you should be able to complete the game by "pressing X to win", other difficulty settings require knowledge, thinking, and tactical aproach. You'll have to create mixtures, craft weapons and armor, find or buy herbs and recipes, just in order to be able to survive. While this might be confusing, and hard, trust me that it's not. It's understandable, it's logical, and requires just a little bit of initial effort.
At this point you're probably thinking "Yeah, cool, i'll go buy it", and you won't be wrong in any way. BUT, be advised that while this is a great looking game, it isn't particulary well optimised,  and you may find yourself struggling even at minimum settings if your PC isn't powerful enough.
So what is my score for the game? Definitely 10/10. I really do think it's such a good game.

First, i need to say: When i firstly played this game, i found it pretty good. But by the time i've played it i was way younger. Today, my opinion as changed a bit. Let's go to the topics.
Graphics: This game uses the same engine from Tomb Raider 4: The Last Revelation, with a little improvement over the textures. Overall, they're pretty good to look at and does it job for a Tomb Raider game.
Soundtrack: Overall, pretty forgetable. The only music i could remember was the menu music. And that's it. And i really mean it. Music is almost not present on gameplay, most of time you will only hear ambient sounds, like in the previous game. But at least i felt that in the previous title, it felt more present. The only times i heard music were during the cutscenes, but most of them were "suspense music" and not really catchy. Witch let me down since Tomb Raider is a game known for it's orchestred music track.
Gameplay: It pretty much remained the same from the fourth title, it only added a few new moves. Lara could run, jump, climb almost everywhere, and fall down through vents while crouched and looking forward (In the old game, you could only do that if you rotated 360).
Gunplay is the same from the fourth title, featuring the manual aim from the combination of Revolver + Laser Sight. But not only it. As the game tried to bring new weps, guess what...DESERT EAGLE IS BACK! Yeah! After a whole game without it, i can't express how i missed it so much. It kills enemies with one shoot, holy mackina. Finally.
Also, many other new guns were introtuced, especially at the VCI levels. And in these levels, were present a stealth mode. For the very first time in a Tomb Raider game, you could only kill enemies without being detected (Because you lost you weapons at these levels). Different from other levels were you got no weps, you could at least make your way to kill all the enemies.
New enemies were introduteced, as well a new level of teen Lara. Everything works fine and it's well constructed. This game is more puzzle-like than the fourth one. But if i can say something from this game is that its SHORT.
It could be bigger and i will tell you why at the end of the review.
Also: Secrets are back. But finding them is a pain. Because your statistcs are not per stage, but global. You can't know witch stage has a secret neither how many one level has. If this game wasn't that short, it would be a pain getting it all.
I can't remember if TR 4 was like that, so i can't say anything about it.
Cheats in this game are a little different from the fourth one and harder to do. But they still exist.
A stage consists of getting to point A to B or completing certain tasks to do so, not many problems. There are mini bosses throught some stages and they aren't that challenging. No real boss at the end tough (Trapping him feels the same as trapping Seth), witch felt a bit empty.
There are a few unlockables at this game as you find the secrets, they all had screenshoots of the next gen of Tomb Raider witch was...TRAOD. Damn, it just ain't worth when you already know the finished product.
Story: Here was the weakest point of this game. At least, for me. The CANON MAIN TIMELINE of Tomb Raider pretty much remains UNTOUCHED. The only thing revealed at the end of the game, surprise, surprise, Lara is still alive. In the CANON NOT MAIN TIMELINE, pretty much nothing is explored from Lara's past, except for the young stage. But even there, not much is explored. It just feels that they put Lara's on random adventures with an excuse. And this game also has a big hole conection between him and TRAOD. Vernom was the one who discovered Lara was alive, searching for her all the days of many months. But when you start TRAOD, Lara says: "You left me on Egypt". HOW?! Damn. Another thing that's never explained is how Lara survived from the TR4 ending. At least in the game. In the book series, there's one book that explain how. I never read it, so i can't say anything, but it's there.
Focusing on the adventures on Lara's "chronicles", it divided in four acts.
The first one, Lara is looking for the phylosophy stone, with a little "help" of Pierre and Larson. The only strange thing on this chapter is the Pierre fall. How the hell did he survived it? We already knew in Tomb Raider 1 that Lara knew Larson and Pierre from a long time before, that matches. But Pierre falling to his death...What the hell?!
The second one, Lara is in a russian ship looking for the spear of destiny. See what they are doing? Random stories. The only good thing at this chapter was the ship's captain. I felt bad for him at the end. Damn.
The third one, is the young stage. Lara sneaks into a Winston's friend boat to uncover a secret from a cursed island. Even if the premises looks idiot, this one has the most well constructed atmosphere, mostly because of you being without your weapons, like a true adventurer.
The fourth and last one was about how Lara stealed Iris from Van Croy. It was the mostly overrated stage and it was all worth it. It was so shorth tough that i felt bad when i was about to end it. Damn. Really.
The Level Editor: This is where this game could've been a lot more revolutionary. You see, random stories for random levels with random enemies. Sounds like a thing you do while doing mods or maps for some game, doesn't it?
The PC version got a exclusive Level Editor that allowed the players to make their own levels and even full games. If you acess a site called "Lara's Level Base" you will see there's a lot of levels made by players. And they are still being made until today. Why is it bad? Read again: PLAYERS.
Players made the community, players made their site for their levels/new items for the engine (Witch you could add) and players made this whole "Let's make a Tomb Raider game ourselfs" worth.
The devs couldn't see how much the community could have used this more. There was no real support for the Level Editor and after its launch, there were no patchs whatsoever. If the player base din't kept it alive, nobody would be using. But if the devs gave the right attention to it, it could've been something BIG and NEW. Nobody ever tough of making his own Tomb Raider adventures, and that would bring something new. Mostly because the engine is not hard like Unreal or Source (And not easy as Portal 2 PTI i might say) and, for its time, it was still a good engine. They missed a big oportunity here. The game was rather sort and they din't even bothered giving a extended lifetime, at least on PC. When they launched the Level Editor for free, they pretty much gave up. Because you CAN use the engine to PLAY ALL THE LEVELS made by players WITHOUT NEEDING TO OWN THE GAME!
I guess for today, this is fine. But, the engine was released for free in the same day that the game came out. Jesus.
I remember the purple "Level Editor" disk that came with my original TR 5 CD, i felt so special by having something like that at my hand and was sad to see it was free on the new. Legaly. With a manual too. Jesus, why?
Overall, TR: Chronicles is the mostly forgetable Tomb Raider and the shortest of all, but it was a fun game to play...While it lasted.
Getting all the secrets and playing with the Level Editor will keep youself busy more than the game itself, sadly. But it's not bad, it could've been better. They just missed a good oportunity here. Only if they gave more support to the level editor...
If you want to play this game, be preapared for fun and disapointment, at the same time.
PS: Why did these "Next Gen Screens" looked so promising back there? Damn.

Tomb Raider Chronicles received mixed reviews and was criticized for the fact that "it started becoming more of the same" and I agree; both this and TR4 utilize the same game engine and TR2 and 3 utilized a similar engine, this is very easy to notice in game. Although I agree with this, I will be reviewing Chronicles as a game in its own respective right and disregard its predecessors.
The game on the whole acts as a memorial tribute to Lara Croft who is presumed dead (after the events of TR4). The game is comprised of 13 levels which are split into 4 "acts". Each act tells a story of one of Lara's many past adventures, reminisced by her butler and past friends. Her adventures vary from her quest in search of the Philosopher's stone in Rome to infilrating a high-security tower block in New York to steal the Iris. There is a fair amount of variety in the game that stops it from getting bland and boring.
The vital, important aspect that's always held up well in the Tomb Raider games are the puzzles in them; whilst the puzzles in Chronicles aren't as complex and mind-boggling as the puzzles in the previous games (especially TR4) there are still there and keeps you constantly thinking and questioning in the game.
In terms of the graphics in the game, there isn't much to say, as mentioned it utilizes the same engine as TR4 and therefore looks exactly the same in terms of graphic detail. For a 2000 game, it really doesn't look that bad.
Sound was another aspect of Chronicles that was criticized, with it being viewed as mediocre; I personally slightly agree with this, the sound in Chronicles doesn't exactly stand out, it is very ambient and takes the "back seat" for the majority of the game, only in particular flybys or boss fights that there is distinctive music. A lot of music has also been reused from The Last Revelation, which is slightly disappointing.
The game itself is very short compared to the previous games, it took me only 5 hours to beat however I have played the game countless times in the past (I grew up around this game) so it may take a new player slightly longer. Is there a lot of replay value in the game? Not really, there are secrets in each level which are quite hard to find/gain access to and finding all of them will unlock some special features from the menu. However, finding all secrets would require you to play through the entire game again if you miss one as there is no level select and finding them all only unlocks concept and cinematic art, so is it really worth it?
Despite the mediocre sound and shortness of the game, I would recommend this game. Is it my nostalgia recommending it? Yes and no; I believe new players will find the game engaging and puzzling from start to finish there's quite a bit of variety and challenge in the game, don't be expected to just gun the bosses down, there is some challenge involved and skill needed and I feel that makes it worthy of the £4.99 that it costs.

In this game you play 4 different Lara's adventures: her search for the Philosopher's Stone in Rome, her hunt for the Spear of Destiny (imo, this is the best level of Chronicles), her adventure on the Black Isle (only puzzles on this one, 'cause you play with a younger Lara who doesn't use guns yet) and the final level is her infiltration on Werney Von Croy's high-tech complex to retrieve the Iris Artefact (the one you see at the beginning of The Last Revelation).
Even though TR: Chronicles isn't as good as its predecessors, it still is a great game. Chronicles uses the same engine from The Last Revelation, which improved Lara's movements, making it much easier to play, but the graphics are still the same (not a bad thing, it's really good for a PS1-era game). The variety of the scenarios got my attention here: you go from the Coloseum to the deep of the ocean to the island of Lost, among others. I highly recommend this if you're a fan of the series, but if you're just starting to play the old TR games, check out TR 2 and The Last Revelation first (I know some people don't like TLR, but it was my first TR game so it has a special place in my heart). The only really bad thing is the save bug on the last minutes of the game, so make sure you don't save only on one slot and search on the internet where the bug starts to cause problems and you'll be good to go.

A highly complicated mulitplayer game that utilises the mechanics of RTS and FPS games alike.
The game revolves around the commander, who controls the upgrades and tactical positioning of defenses, and the other players, units who either help build and take control off the map from the other team. Each team is trying to destroy all the command post of the other team to win. (although they are also other community maps with a variety of mods and goals available). Throughout the map resource points are scattered in each area, providing necessary resource points for upgrades and the purchasing of upgraded weapons and evolutions.
The game is made of 2 sides, Marines and Aliens.
Marines utilise military weapons (mostly guns) and mechs (exo suits) to fight against the Aliens. The Aliens on the other hand use unique evolution traits to provide advantages in speed, stealth and even shockwaves for more damage. The upgrades that each commander make can decide the tides of battle and the personal skill of the unit players themselves are also a factor for winning.
The NS2 community although small is very friendly with different servers marked out for beginners or veterens.
TLDR: A very good game with heaps of teamwork , depth and skill. The good graphics are also a big plus.

This game has a lot of great things going for it, but those great things come with some weird design choices that seem to only be there to limit your fun.
The Good:
- Very cool setting that puts you in an old west that's haunted by the supernatural
- Well done turn based combat system with all the usuals - cover, height bonus, etc, as well as some new ideas.
- The Luck system removes RNG dependancy from the game - If your hit chance is higher than an enemy's luck, you hit and give him a luck boost. If your hit chance is lower than his luck, you miss and subtruct your hit chance from his current luck. Shots that you know will miss can still be worth taking to damage an enemy's luck and allow a higher damage shot to connect.
- The Ricochet skill is freakin' awesome
- Good sountrack by Marcin Przybyłowicz, the man behind the Witcher games' soundtrack
The Bad:
- The story is nice but doesn't fully use the potential that the setting allows. Some story threads just fall apart and lead nowhere
- The "world map" phase in scenarios is horrible. It's slow, it's not fun, and it actually expects you to read everything that happens so just clicking through it is not an option. It feels like they couldn't find a good way to connect all the cool missions together so they just rushed a jumbled mess of a system and said "yeah whatever"
- Skills rely on Luck to use (even weird skills that don't seem to have anything to do with luck), which is a problem because Luck doesn't replenish unless you get hit. Results in sometimes not being able to use skills for an entire mission, rendering a lot of them quite useless.
- No "Overwatch" option (Overwatch being the skill from X-COM that refelxively shoots enemies that step out of cover). Basically this means if an enemy decides to run out of cover, get behind you and shoot you in the face there's nothing you can do about it. If you try to do it though, enemies shoot you reflexively if you get too close. What the hell game?
- That being said, the AI is stupid. Best strategy is to keep your distance and let them run towards you like idiots
The Ugly:
- Demons
- That one character that has syphilis
Overall verdit is - Worth it when on sale. Not the best game out there, but I would love to see a more refined Hard West 2 some day.

Juniper's Knot is another game created by the same people that made Dysfunctional Systems, and is legally free to download for Windows, Mac, Linux, and iOS at
. It's pretty short, and should give you a good idea whether or not you'll actually enjoy this game.
You'll probably notice that there was no sort of interactivity involved in playing Juniper's Knot, aside from clicking to progress to the next line of text. This is more or less how Dysfunctional Systems plays, except this game actually has moments where you get to choose from a short list of options what you (Winter) should do. However, there aren't many times you actually get to do this, and it is actually possible to play through the entire story by only making a single decision. All of the choice moments in the game are placed together around half-way through the game, and they only lead to two endings. The ending you get is determined entirely by whether or not you can convince your mentor (Cyrus) to listen to what you have to say, and not do what he initially decides he should do in order to solve the problem he's given. I wouldn't consider either ending to be a "good ending", but I suppose that's why this is only the first episode in the series.
As for how the game looks and sounds, the artstyle is similar to Juniper's Knot's, and you can listen to the ost on YouTube, so you can decide for yourself if you like those parts before you buy the game. If you really like the sountrack, you can find all 18 tracks in both flac and mp3 format in the game's files.
This game is short. I'm not a fast reader, but I played through this the first time in only about two and a half hours, then about another hour to get the second ending. You can get more playtime by going through all the routes for the achievements for a little extra replayability, but there's a guide on the game's community hub that'll tell you exactly what routes you need to go through to unlock all the achievements.
After a successful
, episode 2 of Dysfunctional Systems is planned to be released by September later this year, and episode 3 by March 2015. Until these episodes are finished and released to the public, the story in this game is incomplete. If you're looking for a complete story, then you should at least wait until the next two episodes come out.
EDIT: Yeah, Dysfunctional Systems is dead.
that caused the devs to stop working on episodes 2 and 3. The prequel will be released, but other than that, it's not certain if we will ever see more from this series. Because of this, if you're going to buy this game, know that you probably will never be able to get the full story that was planned out for this game, and what is available isn't all that much.

~ I'D GIVE SOMETHING LIKE... ~
~ #1 - Alan Wake ~
=STORY=
Alan Wake is the story of a despicable popular writter who wants to take a break from the celebrity of being a writter.
It is as hipster and cringe worthy as it sounds.
In love with a dumb*** woman who's scared of the dark, Alan has to take care of her everytime a fu**ing light turns off somewhere.
And also every nights, for obvious reasons.
Lights shutting down in the evening is enough to make her :jarate: herself.
Every day must be a stressful event where she's more anxious the more the time goes.
Blinking and closing her eyes must be a constant ~Nightmare~.
Getting to the end of episode one, I realised that this game was made to be similar to a TV show, just like many episodic games such as TWD.
The thing is, the story in the former is absolutely ret-/-/- while the one in the later is actually good.
The story tries to go for this dark and grim tone, like a psychological thriller with some kind of deep and complexe paradox...
but every dialogues are a reminder of how absurd the story and characters are.
IDGSL : 3/10
=GAMEPLAY=
The idea behind the gameplay mechanics is interesting, casting light with your flashlight to break some kind of darkness shield and shoot the enemies when unvulnerable.
The fact that it's pushed aside for a dumb TV-like story is pretty sad. But I'm not over yet.
The game was obviously made for consoles with auto-aiming in mind. If you're looking for any kind of real skill requirement, this isn't the game for you.
Without auto-aim, the game would be a chore, pretty much like Resident Evil 4 actually is.
My despise for the Over-The-Shoulder view is beyond and above and every game using this broken third-person view confirms my hatred towards it.
Even though the auto-aim makes shooting somewhat fun, the fact that you need to break the darkness shield of other enemies makes it a hassle.
You will often shoot at an enemy that is not unvulnerable, wasting ammo in the process.
The enemies are fast and taking the time to reload after wasting ammos will often get you hit and most probably killed
Fortunatly, batteries for the flashlight and ammos are abundent in game and you will respawn to the closest checkpoint when you die, which makes the game feel easy, even if you die.
Playing the game at an harder difficulty obviously won't fix these things that are simply balanced to be unbalanced. Less Ammo, Less HP and staring from further awaydoesn't make a game more enjoyable.
It just makes it more annoying and frustrating to play.
IDGSL : 4/10
=GRAPHICS=
The graphics are alright, the shadings and lightnings are a wonder but the facial expressions of the main character are just laughable sometimes (at times).
The animations aren't the best we've ever seen, it's working from far away but the closer you get, the more you see the uncanny valley of their expressions.
Shading & light : 9/10
Character design : 9/10
Animations : 5/10
IDGSL : 6/10
=SOUNDTRACK=
While not memorable, the soundtrack fits well with the story-telling in overall. It isn't annoying, it isn't pleasing, it's just bland and neutral.
The music played at the end of the first episode is absolutely ridicoulus for the dark and grimy theme the game and story is aiming at. This wasn't good at all.
The sound effects are alright, nothing special, it get's the job done. I've got nothing more to say about them other than that the revolver's sound feels great.
IDGSL : 5/10
=LAST NOTE=
As the timer goes up, I'm actually writting this review instead of playing the game.
And it's the second time I'm trying to get into it. I think it says a lot about my feeling toward it.
I really liked the dark aspects of the game but the clunkyness of the gameplay, the awful story and the annoying protagonist and his wife makes me wonder if I really want to go further than the first episode.
As a TOTAL, IDGSL : 35/100

Short review: Don't waste your money. Even if it's on sale, there are better hidden object games.
Details: There are several puzzles that are "do these things in the correct order." (Remove stones, select books, etc.) The order is random - pick on one to start; if it's correct, it stays in place, and if not, it slides back to where it started. Pick on the next... if it's correct, both stay removed; if not, both slide back into the starting position. There are no clues or logic to the correct order; it's all guesswork.
The translations for the HO scenes have problems; some objects are poorly translated into English. Also, several scenes have multiple items that could fit the description. (Nut, Bow, etc.) Since there are achievements for HO scenes with no misclicks, this is really annoying. Also, every HO scene has parts that change - e.g. a number 6 that shifts to a 9 and back again every few seconds; a rooster that turns into a hen and back again - and you're supposed to click on one of those. When it's the one you need, it's clear in your HO list; when it's not, it shows "shaded" in the list, like an item that's in a drawer. As far as I can figure, the purpose of this is to increase the chance of misclicks if you don't catch it in time.
Many of the gather-items-and-use-them steps make no sense, and some of the puzzles are frustratingly time-consuming. (At least two puzzles where you have to spin multiple wheels and align pieces that all move with each spin. After fifteen minutes of move one wheel clockwise, move another counterclockwise, move the first two steps to the right, move the center wheel back... I gave up.)
The plot, as others have mentioned, is weak. I'd expect this whole game's plot to be Part 1 of a longer game. The voice acting is laughable, and often doesn't match the transcription.
If this had been one of the first HOGs I'd played, I'd've given up on the genre entirely.

This is another in the series of hidden objects games published by Artifex Mundi and it plays largely the same as their other titles. The game is divided into five or so portions, each containing a handful of different screens to explore. You go from screen to screen, picking up items and solving various puzzles and hidden object scenes from time to time. You also have a fairy at your disposal for some reason the game developers apparently knew but never decided to share with us. You get it at the beginning of the game and I sort of assumed it would talk to you along the way like a creepier, even more annoying version of Navi. But, no, she just sort of chills in your back pocket most of the game eating all your loose jelly beans. There’s a handful of times in the game where something is up high and your character goes “I CAN’T REACH IT IF ONLY I HAD SOMETHING THAT COULD LIKE A FAIRY HINT HINT” and then you use your fairy and that’s it. It is basically just an occasional extra step in the puzzle solving process, and this magical fairy with super powers basically serves the role of a medium sized stick.

The main aspect of the gameplay, other than “compulsive hoarder that keeps on picking up what they find on the street” is the hidden object scenes. The scenes themselves are fairly standard sorts of things, the kind you’d expect from this genre. They aren’t really that interesting to look at, and most of the items are easy enough to find right away. These might be suitable for diehard enthusiasts of hidden object games, but there needs to be more creativity here to make these appealing to everyone else.

I will say this for Queen’s Quest - the puzzles here aren’t completely mindless like they were in the other games I’ve played by Artifex Mundi. These still aren’t really on par with what you would expect for a puzzle game, still, but a handful of them actually will require you to sit and think for a couple seconds. These still aren’t quite as challenging as they should be and there were not enough in them to save the game, but for once there was actually some little part of the game I actually enjoyed.  Usually these games just like to slowly drag their nails across a chalkboard while it refuses to break eye contact with me, so anything that isn’t totally awful is definitely worth noting.

Unfortunately, a lot of my complaints I’ve had about their past titles applies here as well. There aren’t enough hidden object scenes and the ones that are here get reused a couple of times in a blatant cost saving measure. There is too much needless backtracking because you need to go back to these scenes to get some important item, but the game never really tells you when or where so you just go back to every screen you can and hope you don’t waste too much time wandering around for the right one. The voice acting is so atrocious that the game is best played on mute and the voice actors need to all be gathered up and sent back in time to the 1800’s, a time where voice acting wasn’t a thing and they can’t hurt anyone else’s ears. And on and on it goes. This is the same game Artifex Mundi always puts out, with minor changes here and there so they can hurk up another monstrosity on the marketplace and con their audience into buying the same game they just bought three months ago.

Something slightly different worth mentioning is the art, which went from its usual level of boring to so bad it’s creepy. The backdrops are fine, although they look like they were copy-pasted from the “generic fantasy background” asset pack . The people though couldn’t be animated worse if they were trying. I don’t know what’s happening, but their skin doesn’t always seem to be connecting to their face, and portions of it tend to move on its own like it is trying to escape their skull. When they talk, it looks like they’re wearing a mask of human flesh, and moving that around with their hands to get the mouth to move. I have no idea how much it cost for them to hire an animator for this game, but I am nearly positive the currency they used to pay them with was goat’s blood.

Sadly, this was actually probably one of the better hidden object titles I’ve played by Artifex Mundi. Sure, the story is so bad I think it was likely written by someone that had an actual grudge against the English language, and this game makes almost all of the same mistakes every single other game published by Artifex Mundi makes, but at least the puzzles here are just a bit above “can be solved by someone after their lobotomy” level of difficulty. I still can’t recommend this to most gamers, but if you’re a huge fun of hidden object games and don’t mind terrible plots featuring weird potato humans, then you could certainly find worse ones than Queen’s Quest: Tower of Darkness on the market. I’d know. I’ve played them.

Excellent game. Just finished and bought the DLC. There are lot of gripes about lack of saves and the luck system. Firstly, the a quick save option has been enabled, though I rarely used it. The missions are short and playing through without save gives you a sense of narrative journey. It isnt an issue at all. The luck system is a bit new, and hence some may find it unfamiliar. Luck is a combination of mana and shield. You need luck to activate special skills (or spells) and hence is similar to mana. You luck is depleted if your opponent's shot misses you (hence like a shield). Luck can be regenerated by munching on mandrake, or killing opponents or over time (you need to enable a special mod before the start of scenario).
This is similar to XCOM in terms of gameplay, but also significantly different. Its not battle oriented like XCOM, and XCOM2 (or LW2) players may feel it a bit underwhelming. The strength of the game is the excellent narrative. The meticulous graphic designs gives a very retro feel and you feel transported into the wild west. You identify with the fate of the characters. A very enjoyable turn based tactical combat game that vividly captures the aura of the wild west. 8/10. Again, dont bother about the complaints on lack of good save and luck. You wont need the saves and the luck dynamics is a fresh new layer of strategy.

Wasteland 2 is a flawed gem.
I'll start with the bad:
-A lot of the weapon classes are downright useless. Pistols and submachine guns aren't worth bothering with period. Shotguns are alright, but you only really need one party member proficient in it for when you're in close quarters with a lot of enemies bunched together. Energy wepons are only useful against enemies with high armor ratings, so they really only come into play mid to late game. The only three weapon classes worth focusing on are Heavy Weapons, Assault Rifles, and Sniper Rifles. Even then, Heavy Weapons guzzle ammo like there's no tomorrow, which isn't terrible late-game when you have a ton or resources saved up, but they aren't practical early on. The only melee skill worth taking is Blunt Weapons because its high armor penetration keeps it relevent through to the end-game.
-On normal difficulty, the combat is very challenging until mid-way through. You really feel like you have to conserve ammo and resources, and every move counts. But unless you intentially build your party to suck, everything gets pretty easy by end-game. I had more money and supplies than I knew what to do with.
-I experienced huge performance issues in certain areas even on my 970. It was smooth sailing for the most part, but it's pretty clear the game isn't terribly well optimized. Being a turn-based game, FPS drops aren't a huge concern, but it shouldn't be a problem on a rig that far exceeds the recommended specs.
Now onto the good:
- The story is good and the writing is solid. The mains story, while not mind-blowingly amazing, is good enough to keep you ineterested, though it is suprisingly linear. The side quests are far more interesting, I think, and they offer much more freedom to approach it how you want. Almost every encounter has multiple outcomes depending on what choices you make, and the game does a good job of giving you the sense that these chioces actually matter. Many of the characters have rich backstories and opinions to offer. You will run into a lot of messy situations that you can choose to help resolve through diplomacy or violance or ignore altogether. At the end of the game, you are rewarded with a little slide show (à la Fallout) that goes into detail about all the characters and situations you ran into throughout your travels, which is a nice touch.
- Inventory management. It took me around 55 hours to complete this game. I reckon I spend at least 10 of those hours in my inventory screen. If you're a freak like me, and you actually enjoy inventory management, this game is a treat. It is extremely easy to move items between party members, quickly see all their stats, and compare equipment to what you have equipped. It even tells you the average damage output per action point a given weapon will deal, which I think is pretty sweet.
-Combat. No, it isn't a diverse and interesting as something like XCOM, but it does a good job of scrating that turn-based strategy itch. A lot of people have complained that the combat essentially boils down to "shoot stuff until it dies," and, that's pretty much true. Unlike XCOM, there aren't any speicial abilities, and you won't find nearly as much cover to hide behind. Wasteland does offer a greater host of enemies and weapons, though, which keeps things interesting enough, espeially late game when your enemies start using energy weapons and suddenly your heavily armored super-soldier who could normally tank round after round of enemy fire suddenly loses half his health from a single hit.
All-in-all, Wasteland 2 is a great turn-based roleplaying game that isn't without its flaws. If the forthcoming Director's editions addresses some of these, I think Wasteland 2 could be a truly fantastic RPG.

The Captive Curse is the 24th (of 31 as of December 2014) installment within the Nancy Drew point and click adventure game series. Within this game you assume the role of amaranthine sleuth Nancy Drew and investigate rumors of a mythical monster that has terrorized German grounds, specifically Castle Finster, for as long as many residents can remember. Recently the monster has emerged from the castle woods with a penchant for destruction; causing fires and destroying private property. Markus the castle’s owner has pleaded with Nancy to step in and find out the truth behind the creature before the castle is closed for good.
Nancy Drew adventure games are not your typical triple “A” open world RPG or FPS. As the genre mentions it is a “point and click adventure game” where one searches for clues, solves puzzles, questions suspects, and unravels a larger mystery through deductive reasoning. The game is not designed to be an engrossing universe or narrative, but rather for me, is designed as a light-hearted story for anyone of all ages. It serves as a nice break from larger games and is easy to simply kick back to, relax, and enjoy. The plot-line of these games typically takes about 7-12 hours to unravel, depending on your sleuthing skills.
This game in particular had a great Germanic atmosphere, weaving tales from Grimm’s fairytales and mythical folklore into an intriguing plot. However, its dialogue, scripting, and voice acting falls a little bit flat for me. If this is your first time looking at the Nancy Drew game series, I tend to recommend some of the more classic titles, which are in my opinion, of higher quality and contain better narratives (keep in mind though that their graphics and game engines may be a bit more dated, being from the earlier 2000s). To understand if you might like these games I recommend checking out the more iconic titles: The Curse of Blackmoor Manor, Ghost Dogs of Moon Lake, or Treasure in the Royal Tower. During the summer or holiday sales these games are easily $2-$5 on Steam so just wait until then and you can check out these games as a nice cheap break from the usual. Happy sleuthing.

First and foremost, I enjoyed this game and played it to completion. But I do have some issues with this game.
The story behind it isn't strong and no means compelling but more than enough for what I think any gamer would like as long as they don't want anything to engrossing. I really like the idea behind Lincoln and they do a really cool one or two hour setup to the actual game as such. It touches on the 1960s in a general way from the racial discrimination, the culture, mobs and lastly the music. My god, the soundtrack they put into this game is something of a delight for me.
The different districts stand out and the people that run the different districts differ somewhat too. If I felt like I could sink more into the game I'd really feel the 1960s vibe to it.
Performance wise, I have to admit I had no major issues but does performed a bit on the poor side.
I've got a Intel 5960x and two GTX 980s but at this time there is no sli support. Which I don't mind, that seems to be the ongoing trend. But to keep it at a stable 60fps wasn't going to happen at 1920x1080 and quite frankly anything under the highest settings looks somewhat garbage compared to what I'm used to. So I believe they do need to do some optimisation. Regarding the graphical settings, at this time there's very little in the way of options and I hope they expand this.
I did however experience the odd crash to desktop with no explanation as to why, never really got any idea as to what caused it either. I also encountered playing over time it would make the PC chug as the FPS seem to decline. They really do need to include a borderless windowed mode, so in general there's a lot of PC options that have been somewhat "standard" and they just seem to be missing.
The grievances I have for the game are the following:
- It's very rinse and repeat. Which for me in this case was fine I enjoyed it, mostly...
- The AI doesn't ever change, it's very much the same. Crouch behind wall or crate brutal kill guys until you get discovered and then start laying into them with bullets. They always seem to have the same pattern of one after another coming through the same door way even though there are different ways to flank me and there was never any reason for me to try a different tactic or experiment with different guns.
- Not much in the way of side missions apart for unfortunately more rinse and repeat, which I did but if you were hoping there was more of a excuse to keep running around New Bordeaux you may be quite disappointed, unless you really like being a completionist and collecting.

I tried.  I honest-to-God, really, REALLY tried to like this game, twice, but I can't.  I just can't.  Everywhere I see, this game has nothing but positive reviews, and I'm honestly wondering if Steam somehow pranked me into giving me a version from an alternate reality in which the game was bad.
Alan Wake is a supernatural-themed game from the makers of Max Payne, dealing with the subject of dreams and darkness.  It tells the story of a writer named Alan Wake (get it?  A. Wake?  GET IT?!?), who suffers from writer's block so he goes on vacation with his wife to try and find some peace, but it turns out it's all just an excuse for her to try to give him some inspiration.  His wife, who suffers from fear of darkness, and apparently lives in a world where therapy doesn't exist, gets kidnapped by an unseen force and Alan wakes (tee hee) missing a week and finding the line between reality and fiction blurred, as he's suddenly haunted by people who are vulnerable to light and finds scattered pages he doesn't remember having written literally laying out the plot of the game for him.
Now, I realize I made the game sound far more interesting than it actually is.  The game itself is REALLY dull, and it suffers from a personality disorder.  It's not sure if it wants to be a graphic adventure, a shooter, a survival horror or an interactive movie.  And instead of focusing on a genre and developing it, it half-asses all of them.  The graphic adventure part is slow and cumbersome, because Alan handles like molasses, with nary a puzzle in sight.  The shooter part is annoying because the only way to defeat enemies is by shining a flashlight on them to turn them vulnerable before shooting them.  You'll recognize this as "shooting, only slightly more annoying".  There's nothing clever about this mechanic, and you'd get the same result by having guns with smaller magazines, so you'd have to see the reloading animation more often.  Also, sometimes you're forced to run from enemies, but either Alan suffers from asthma or he's a wimp, because he runs for a couple of seconds and he already can't take it anymore.  Hell, *I* suffer from ashtma, and I can run longer without getting tired.
The survival horror part is dead because this game's "horror" depends exclusively on jump scares, and we should all stop pretending surprise is the same as terror.  Also, children and Alan's wife believe darkness is scary, but other people don't.  At least not when the game botches is so early by showing all its cards right from the beginning.  And then there's the interactive movie part.  I tried to play this game close at launch and now, and I don't remember having ever be impressed by its ridiculous facial animations, so I don't think it's a problem of holding up.  They were always blow-up-doll-like laughable.  And technology is not the problem, the Playstation 2 could easily handle facial expressions much better.  But the real problem are the story, which is full of cliches, and the characters, who range from "meh" to unlikable.  Specially the main character, whose story arc seems to actually be going from one to the other, in that order.  This has nothing, though, on the fact that the plot is constantly spoiled literally minutes before it happens because of those manuscript pages.  Who thought that was anything even close to a good idea?
I'm leaving the game now, for good.  If memory serves right, it will be at pretty much the same point I left it the first time I tried to play it.  Maybe it gets better later, but when a game can't ever pique my interest after more than an hour of playtime, I call it a lost cause.  I play games for instant entertainment, I have real life for when I want to slog through boredom to get to the good stuff.  According to other reviews, gameplay never changes, so I'm confident that I'm making the right decision.  I honestly don't get it.  Is everyone liking this game ironically?  Will I ever make someone's life so miserable that they'll go back in time to make this game just to annoy me?  I mean, I understand why people like other games I don't like, but this one is legitimately puzzling me, and probably not the way the developers intended.

Middle-earth(TM): Shadow of War(TM) is the tragic tale of a man who just wants to do parkour but cannot walk through a bush without getting stuck. Our brave lad learns with the assistance of colourful orc friends like "edgy mcdarkface", "the big Russian one" and "the funny one you're actually here for". Under their tough-but-fair tutleage, Talion learns to run, mantle, and leap. He still gets stuck in ankle-high bushes.
Also there's a war and a spider lady and stuff but who cares
Oh no is this the bit where I do the informative review after the joke review here goes.
If you liked the first one, this is the same but more. More maps, more parkour, a LOT more orcs of various strikes. I'm gonna start with the cons this time because there's a big one preying on my mind:
CONS
-- The game doesn't seem to understand why people are playing it. I'm sure there ARE huge fans of the Silmarillion who are super excited to play out the history of Middle-Earth but most folks are here for all that orcy goodness and the game witholds it for a loooong time. Blasting through the plot, skipping cutscenes, it took four hours to get to the point where you start collecting orcs.
-- Way too many DARK & EDGY orcs, not enough fun orcs. I've started autoshaming them in a desperate attempt to make them more interesting.
-- Microtransactions are not particularly obtrusive but man do they feel forced in and they reinforce the idea the devs thought collecting the orcs was a chore while listening to Shelob was the big draw. "You hate the whole main bulk of the game, right? Well you can skip it by giving us money!"
-- Assassin's Creed happened a decade ago, guys. The contextual movement controls were pretty revolutionary at the time but things have moved on. These aren't even particularly good movement controls: Talion's #1 cause of death is getting stuck on a surface sliiiiightly higher than the one next to it and being unable to move between them. Adding to that problem, there's invisible walls everywhere.
PROS
-- goddam, I remember why I loved Shadow of Mordor so much. There's no other game that makes it feel so PERSONAL. The Nemesis System is expanded and refined. Storytime:
After getting destroyed by the same orc four times in a row (including having all three bodyguards betray him), the fifth fight was going awfully. The killing blow sync animation cued up aaaaand ... my favourite orc, Dush the Poet, came sailing in outta nowhere and 1-shot the unkillable marauder shrack. It was the first savior kill I'd seen, and it's still the only one. I stood up and cheered. This is not internet hyperbole where you say you did a thing IRL to show strong emotion: I literally LITERALLY (actually, with my body) stood up and cheered. I haven't had an emotional reaction like that to a video game in years. When the fortress fell, I made Dush overlord and he goddam earned it.
On the other hand, there was an Olog called Ar-Henok the Guardian. He had a cool hat, so I wanted to recruit him (I'm a simple man). He had an iron will, so I shamed him. He started hunting me down, and I shamed him again and again but his will wouldn't break. Eventually, he was lvl1 and tried to jump me during another mission. My bodyguard cut off his head. A few hours later, Ar-Henok was back as Ar-Henok the Stitch, with his head crudely sewn back on and still iron-willed. I shamed him again and he became a maniac. Now he's lvl49, covered in stitches and burns, screaming indiscriminantly and coming outta nowhere to 1-shot Talion like a goddam stitched-up meat freight train. You can hear him screaming from miles away and if I hear those screams, I give the area a wide berth. It helps, but he still loves to ambush and I have no idea how to deal with him. I took some random olog and accidentally made a monster. The game keeps throwing dudes covered in maggots at me and they've got nothing in Ar-Henok, because I DID THAT.
Oh man guys the Nemesis System is SO GOOD.
IN SUMMARY
Shadow of War is a deeply flawed game whose core mechanics often don't work and whose devs don't seem to understand why people want to play it. It is also incredible and I can't stop playing it.

Story: So far havent finished this but the story is indeed rich but it is seriously undermined by the missions in which you complete to achieve this great scenarios. Anyone who plays a Ubisoft game would understand that misisons are basically, kill the target, tail this guy, interrogate this guy. Throughout this game, it is 80% the same missions. Tail these guys, kill this leader, kill/recruit this rackeeter, assassinate the final leader. This is completely fine, but severely repetetive, Some of these missions like the final boss killings actually have a variety of content in them as you attempt to kill them.
In short, general missions blow, occassionaly a great mission, repetitive.
Graphics: At this time, the graphics don't capture what 2K can produce. Look at Bioshock and compare the stunning visuals to this game. Two thumbs up up up! Hard West is best summarized as a turn-based tactical RPG, similar in game mechanics to X-Com. The story takes place in chapters, during which there is no opportunity to perma-save, so it can be a slight pain to leave it should you have, you know, a life.
The narrator and music track work together to create an eerie sense of the strange, which is most appropriate for the story considering it's definitely in the much-too-small Weird West category. You work to properly equip your chapter's characters with the best arms, usable items, and artifacts. This will require buying, bartering, and flat-out murder on occaision, and a nice feature they've implemented is to allow you to purchase the special items from the previous chapters that you wouldn't normally be able to access in later chapters. Many of the decisions the game forces you to make between tactical engagements cannot be intuited, as being moral will not always reward you, nor will being the bad guy every time. Thankfully the newest patch implemented a quicksave/quickload feature which allows you to save your gain temporarily and go forward into these blind decisions with more confidence since you can unscrew yourself if you screw yourself. :)
Gameplay features some pretty tight squad-based tactical shootouts, which the options give you the opportunity to change to make more difficult, easier, or just plain weird. It's not nearly as long as X-Com, nor nearly as in-depth in terms of gear, scenery, or cut scenes, but if you're a fan of the core gameplay then you'll like Hard West.
The only real nitpick is that when you start out your enemies will open fire if you enter their personnal space. Essentially they've got an Overwatch mode. But nowhere in the game does there seem to be an Overwatch mode for your own team of shootists. And that can get pretty annoying. But since they patched in a save mode, I expect to see them remedy the problem before too long.
