I only just learned of the upcomming DLC so this is likely too late, but whiule the game is very good, it has some glaring drive-me-insane issues, and it sounds like the directors cut is not addressing them.  The changes made to directors cut I have read about, while nice do not sound like thery fix these issues.
1) random and innacurate weapon behavior.  Someone appears to have assumed that the older a weapon is the worse it's performance.  While this is true in IT, it is NOT true of any weaponry made after about 1930, when powder technology matured the way cpu technology did in around 2008.  improvements are incremental.
What changes is the method of warfare, and therefore you have weapons tailored to different types of combat.  If the type of combat gotten into is of an older fashoin newer weapons often UNDER PERFORM older ones.  The type of round fired is much more important to performance than gun design.
The various weapons have names of current models, but they do not follow the actual properties of these weapons at all.
The M2 is not a small bore machine gun. it fires .50bmg not 22cal ammunititon.  You could fit the intore barrel of a >5.56mm weapon inside the bore of a 12mm gun like the m2.
this is actually a pretty easy fix.  A renaming and a new description are all that are required.  You could modify an m2 very easily to fire small bore ammunition.  It's a straight blowback weapon with huge pieces.  making stuff smaller is much easier than adding metal, so it could concievelably be a normal conversion for 50cals with worn out parts.
It was designed origionally as an anti tank weapon, and cannot even be fired from a light vehicle without risking tipping the thing over.  It should be at the top of the food chain rather than the bottom, and have an incredibly high strength requirement.
the 5.56 is actually a very powerful high pressure round.  Using it as a base ammo is a bit silly.  remington 223 is similar but lower pressure and civilian weapons like hunting rifles designed for 223 are often incapable of firing 5.56, though generally a 5.56 gun is capable of firing 223.
meanwhile the easiest to produce, most common longest produced round in existance which DOES fit the characteristics of the low end weapons is the .22 long rifle round.  There ARE assault type rifles that use it, by far the most common in the US where the game is set being the ruger 10/22.  it si effectively identical to the m14 so the same models could be used.
Meanwhile the m1 garand is not a 5.56mm weapon but 30.06 or 7.62 weapon, and is really a fast firing sniper rifle.
2) The game's randomisztion and travel sytem requires huge amounts of reloading and downtime to play.
Loot in theis game is massively random.  to the point that game difficulty is more dependant on random chest results than difficulty level or player ability.  As a result, the only effective way to play the game is saving/reloading on chests.  repeatedly.  I would say I spend 80% of playtime repeatedly opening the same chest, or digging the same hole.  also, spending 20 minutes following a tortise?!  There must be someone on staff who treasures the unparraleed joy of rush hour traffic or something.

It's good, but you have to know what you're getting into.
For example, one of the first levels is you rescuing your girlfriend from some bandits. This is used as a tutorial for the 'subdue' mechanic, and stealth as a whole, having you sneak around a base and 'subdue' enemies repeatedly, preventing them from starting combat, giving them a countdown till they raise the alarm and start shooting. You can subdue multiple people at once, and move from one to another to juggle 'subdue' commands between enemies so they never run out.
The problem is this: you're holding a gun to them, rendering them defenseless, and you make no effort to disarm them of their weapons while you do so. So you just point a gun at a guy, scaring him, and then you run off, allowing him to eventually chase after you and fire shots at you. Not just that, but when you finally get the key and then unlock the door to your girlfriend's cell, every enemy immediately begins their combat turns, regardless of whether they were subdued and how much of a subdue countdown they had remaining. So effectively all subduing accomplishes in this instance is to ensure that you are completely surrounded and out in the open, with no cover, when combat suddenly starts. The game's stealth tutorial tells you with its mechanics, "Stealth is stupid in this game, you should probably just go and kill everyone instead." which directly contradict the game's prompts telling you how useful stealth can be.
So it's a game of good ideas that weren't completely thought out. There are worse sins, and this is manageable given that you can replay a level at any point during it, but it is rather annoying. My expectations were higher than this.

Я не думаю, что многие люди не видят ценность в Горе, и когда люди делают, они стремятся просто усложнить игру так, как она есть. Это не значит, что это «игра». Разработчики игры целенаправленно говорят об этом изначально: «Оставьте это открытым - оно предназначено для работы на периферии вашей жизни. Только взаимодействуйте с ним, когда вам хочется. Вы можете играть в гору, играя в другие игры. Если вы не играете Он, он будет играть сам. ". Снова гора просто означает оставаться открытой, и вы можете вернуться к ней, когда захотите. Возможно, вы не сразу заметите его внешний вид, но вы можете найти его позже ... надеюсь. Но опять же, каковы стандарты «игры»? Должны ли мы просто отделять гору просто потому, что это возможно вне нормы? Напротив! Различный опыт приводит к различным точкам зрения, которые делают вас более открытыми. Так могут люди действительно заявить, что Гора - не игра, а скринсейвер? Существует множество способов просмотра горы и ее просмотра, поскольку скринсейвер - одна из наиболее популярных деморализованных точек зрения, к которым многие так привыкли. Поэтому можно рассматривать гору просто как автономную, а не сравнивать ее с более современными проблемами. Или можно сравнить, но тем самым теряешь номинал самой игры. Я думаю, что теперь я решил, что эта «игра» может быть скринсейвером или просто не «игрой» вообще.
С другой стороны, разработчики заявили следующее: «Если у вас неприятный шторм или скучная ночь, сыграйте мелодию (используя клавиатуру), и время ускорится». Гора там для вас, когда вы решите вернуться к ней и сыграть ее. Я думаю, что это распространенное заблуждение. Это не столько игра для вас, сколько вспомогательная и поддерживающая игра рядом с вами. Тем не менее, есть много способов увидеть Горы, как с любой формой проблемы в жизни. Но Путь Гора был построен, порой непривлекательный для глаз, позволяет ему показать вам другой путь и, возможно, тот, который вы, возможно, не видели раньше.
Но вам не нужно следить за тем, что говорят разработчики. «Игра» должна воспроизводиться в зависимости от того, как вам это нравится. Если вы чувствуете, что вас обманули, купив эту игру, тогда сделайте два шага назад и подумайте об аспектах этой «игры» и элементов. Возможно, вы начинаете замечать замечательный окружающий звук, который играет среди ночи, или, может быть, вы влюблены в то, как полосы солнца касаются вашей Горы. Но вам может не понравиться все это, чтобы по-настоящему насладиться игрой. Возможно, у вас есть все эти игры, и у вас появилась любовь к игре. Или, может быть, вы пытаетесь насмехаться над игрой, но в свою очередь вы уже привыкли к игре. Я, например, не могу ответить на этот вопрос о том, понравится ли геймеру это или нет, но все зависит от того, кто его покупает, и готов ли он открыть свое сердце и ум.
Теперь Гора действительно ваша гора и ваша собственная собственность? Я думаю, что в концепции только геймера для геймера можно составить представление о том, действительно ли Гора является само воплощением, или игрок действительно управляет Горой. Гора не говорит с нами и не рассказывает нам о ее мыслях? Или это передача скрытого сообщения туда, где мы могли бы быть его собственным порождением, и это - мастер. Каким бы способом вы не сочли нужным, существует достаточно много способов увидеть гору, как в любой игре. В горах может не быть сюжетной линии, не стрельбы, не любовного треугольника (если только вы не начнете что-то делать между вещами, Горой и небом, и в этом случае вы, возможно, пошли слишком далеко), но в Горе есть Момент одиночества, в котором вы можете заметить вещи в играх, которые могут повторяться в горах. Возможно, Гора может содержать все эти элементы, в которых вы создаете историю. Гора всегда может быть сюжетной линией, в которой вы, геймер, идете по дорожке с Горой к месту назначения в ваше подсознание. В горах многое предстоит сделать, и ваше воображение будет блокировано, а логика только помешает этому. Но если вы так решите сделать это, вы не обидели никого, кроме себя, в отрицании возможных сил в самой игре. Этот обзор не может показать мой нейтралитет по отношению к игре, но я только хочу объяснить геймеру, что гора может быть акцентирована только игроком.

I have played this game for a long time, even before release, and never posted a review. Do keep in mind when you see the play time for reviews that many people did/do play KSP outside of steam. I only have about 130 hours logged, but I've played close to 1k hours in this game outside of steam since alpha.
If you learned to play this game before the recent changes, you may need to relearn the launch physics, and take the old youtube videos with a grain of salt.
However, this is one of the best games I have ever played. It pulls you into HOURS and HOURS of engineering fun.
You build a ship. It looks amazing. It does everything. You are proud of yourself.
You move your ship to the launch pad. It ascends into the heavens. But then it spins out, and everybody dies.
You make a tiny change. Launch it again. Failure. Tiny change. Failure. Repeat for hours.
Finally, a tiny change and you're in space!
Next time, you build the ship, and it gets into space your first attempt. Now you have to learn to orbit. Once you're orbiting, you have to learn to rendevous. Once you rendevous (or before) you learn to land on other celestial bodies.
You build the perfect ship. It escaped Kerbin. You approach the mun, and prepare to burn retrograde.
But you forgot to extend your solar panels and your ship runs out of power!
So here you are, floating towards the moon, gaining speed with a full tank of fuel, and no way to light your engines. You crash into the moon, and do it all again. This time will be different.

I started playing this game in between bouts of Starcraft. It was my go-to game for a more casual, relaxed experience. Two months later, I still haven't finished the game and find myself increasingly frustrated by that fact.
It's a Zelda-like dungeon crawler but randomized to the hilt. Don't expect to be able to unlock every chest as the developers have put plenty of dead ends in the game. Also, don't expect to get that favorite item every playthrough because there are plenty of randomized rooms with various types of weapons. The art style is grotesque and cartoonish. It's macabre in a light way.
Upgrades include the following: Number one, a tear drop that gives you yellow pee shots; stem cells, an affix to your head in the form of a siamese like twin that increases your health; mom's high heels, giving you increased range and upgraded speed. The story is inconsequential, but basically, Mom is a religious nut who locks you in the basement...with your worst nightmares!
The game is easily enjoyed in 1/2 hour playthroughs in between your games that require more time investment, which isn't to say that you won't be putting your time into this game. And don't forget: it may say casual under the category, but this game is about as hardcore as they come.

Spintires is a Russian game about teaching trucks to swim.
After the post-communist years many Russian trucks found themselves without meaningful work. In order to boost the economy, and show the world that Russia is still as stronk as ever, you have been given the job of teaching these aging Soviet vehicles a new art and thus giving them a new lease on life.
The game starts easily. The trucks have a high morale and are eager to learn. The basic lessons include swimming in creeks and puddles. Graduates of these lessons move onto more advanced courses: mud and rivers. Eventually you will test your students by loading them with heavy weights such as timber or oversized equipment. You will lose a few students on the way. Sergei C-255 was one of my most promising students. Unfortunately Aleksey E-7310 was unable to reach his tow-cable in time. RIP in piece, Sergei.
A select few students who survive their trials and tribulations are able to master the forbidden art handed down by the KGB special trainer and learn the technique called, "Spetsnatz Underwater Submersible Assault Transformation" in which the trucks (overcoming their fear of drowning) are able to truly become one with the Eath and emerge victorious on the other bank.
Levels include "That muddy one", "The one with that giant river in the middle" and "That goddamned volcano".

Skip it. Too short, awful characters, paper-thin plot, haphazard HOGs, limited locations, pathetic bonus chapter (more than usual for the genre). Not worth your time or the asking price.
I didn't go into this expecting much, but I was still let down nonetheless. Queen's Quest offers very little by way of satisfying gameplay or story, and it falls short on almost everything that should make a hidden object adventure fun.
Paper-thin is an understatement. The entirety of the storyline is even more basic than something a rambling 5-year-old child might come up with. The child's version would probably be more interesting, too.
You're the queen of Generic Kingdomland, marry Generic Prince Charming, have a baby a year later (which is also somehow the baby's 1st birthday, so I guess there was some nookie going on before marriage or something), and a Generic Evil Wizard arrives to kidnap your child and turn hubby into stone. You then spend the entire game doing very un-queenly things to help absurdly-helpless people so you can reach the Generic Dark Wizard Tower and get your baby back before he performs a Generic Time Sensitive Evil Ritual Requiring A Baby As A Component. You save your baby via Generic Deus Ex Machina, and return home to completely forget about also saving your husband. The End.
The bonus chapter does resolve the husband bit, but it's even more shallow, rushed, and derpy, and contains a confusing "misplaced hint" bug when looking for the 3 balls of yarn (the hint will circle one spot when the yarn is in an entirely different location).
There's a "twist" of a sort in the main chapter regarding your husband's past, awkwardly presented in the form of a stage puppet minigame, but it's blander than stone soup and has zero influence on anybody's actions (even though one would assume the queen would be at least mildly indignant about it). It may as well not be in the story at all.
Clunky and awkward. Certain actions are just bizarre, like needing to burn down a potted plant with a "flamethrower" medallion to get to a locked box, when any other HOPA would have you searching for a pair of garden shears.
One of the main things that bothered me was the fact that parts of the story or specific objectives make no sense unless you remember to read your diary (which gives no indication when new entries are added). Instead of explaining the basics in dialogue or flavor text, you get oddly vague comments, like a pirate who complains his "friend" is missing, but you wouldn't know he's talking about a parrot until you read your notes.
There's an even more frustrating part in the bonus chapter. You find what appears to be a mirror, but it doesn't show up in your inventory. I was convinced that was a game-breaking bug until I noticed it appeared on the toolbar, but I had no idea what I was supposed to do with it because there was no tooltip or comment about what it was for. Apparently it's not a mirror but a magnifying glass, and you need to use it like a UV light to find invisible balls of yarn in the scene (which, again, you wouldn't even know you're supposed to look for unless you read your diary). Not even the hint button is helpful, because it just highlights the bottom of the screen, which looks like it wants you to move backwards one location, then when you do it tells you to move forward again. I finally fumbled around enough to figure out that it was hinting at the entirely wrong spot.
In the main chapter you have a Barbie-meets-Tinkerbell fairy buddy that helps you reach certain places to take or place objects, but the whole mechanic feels forced and unnecessary.
Hidden Object scenes are boring. Items are easy to find because of odd scale or placement.
The puzzles are a mixed bag of too easy, unnecessarily difficult, or "this solution makes no goddamn sense". Like the board with knights and dragons you have to arrange. It's basically a form of the chess puzzle where you have to position certain pieces so they don't occupy the same row or column, but with the logic part thrown out the window. The only layout that worked DID have knights and dragons in the same row/column/diagonal in multiple locations, so what was the point in declaring those rules?
The location backgrounds are kind of nice (with the exception of HO scenes), but the character art is ghastly. Everyone looks creepily deformed, and the queen and king are Uncanny Valley incarnate. The fairy is also rendered in stiff 3D for some reason, which doesn't fit with the rest of the aesthetic.
The complete package of annoying SFX, forgettable music, and pathetic voiceovers. VOs also don't match the text in quite a few places.
If you're itching for a quality HOPA, this is like using poison ivy as a back scratcher. I'm actually surprised Artifex Mundi is even affiliated with this title, because it has none of the positives I usually associate with them as developers/publishers. Queens Quest is easily one of the crappiest games they've put their name to, right alongside Emerald Maiden. It's a quick 100% for achievement hunters, but that's about the only thing going for it. Otherwise, avoid.

It's a bit watered down X-Com. I had mixed feelings about Hard West. I think the premise and setup is incredibly interesting. It's a really fresh concept, and I enjoyed the story beats quite a bit. The game also captures the X-Com style combat very well in a basic way with a few twists.
And there lies the problem. The game is very basic. There's no real enemy variety from what I've seen. The majority of enemies I encountered through much of the game were people with guns and a certain number of HP. I even came across missions with specific "bosses" that needed to be killed as part of the mission, but even those designated enemies were nothing more than a person with a gun. The combat is interesting in some ways via tha cards system, which adds some variety to the mission. However, the gun and gear loadouts seemed very shallow with no real "progression" to them.
All that said, it's not fair to consider the game a bad game because it didn't measure up bit to bit with a AAA title with probably 4-5x the development team. This game does a lot of cool things from the narrative and mechanics perspectives. Playing Hard West makes the next game from Creative Forge exciting because of the possibilities. I think it's worth the entry point, just don't expect the same level of depth as with the X-Com games. It scratches the same itch, though.

Queen’s Quest is made up of a standard story, great visuals, some fairly unimaginative puzzles, and a bunch of really fun hidden object scenes; all wrapped into a roughly 3-hour-long game.
Queen’s Quest: Tower of Darkness is almost a poster child for a standard hidden object game, as it doesn’t have one single original element, nothing we haven’t seen plenty of times already in other HOGs. But to its credit, it mixes these old elements well together.
The advantage of building from known blocks is that there are no surprises, we already know every little element. This includes the story of a young queen, whose newborn baby gets kidnapped by an evil wizard, so she travels through a set of the standard castle–forest– wizard lair backdrops to save her. (And her husband too, in one of the shortest sorry excuses of a bonus chapters ever seen.)
Gameplay is similarly predictable: all puzzles have been featured elsewhere and the point ‘n’ click parts use the safest, time-tested tasks. On the upside, the hidden object scenes are fantastic, so, in the end, the game can earn its place in a HOG player’s collection.

Wasteland 2 isn't Fallout (although if you look into the history of the game franchise you might see where I was going with my awkward intro story and how I got to this point on my caffeine-fueled gushfest) but according to my buddy, it "should be." According to him, this would be Fallout 3 just in a different package. Like New Coke if New Coke was made by the people who orignally worked on Coke, then left the company and made something else. Only then they went back to...you know what, I lost myself in my ramble.
Wasteland 2 is a top-down, turn-based tactical RPG. While the graphics aren't as spectucular as those of say, X-Com, they aren't the main selling point of the game anyway. The selling point of this game is the fact that it lets you custom tailor a team of 4 starting Rangers to fit your own play style and then pick up some pre-generated recruits along the way to flesh out the rest of your team. Hell, they even have a pre-made B team that sits at the front gate picking their noses until you come back and sign one up after scraping one of your hand-crafted wasteland survivors off the asphault with a spatula after a fight gone horribly wrong.
If you want a game that has a lot of voice-overs and flashy graphics, this isn't going to be the game for you.
If you like post-apocalypic games where you can min-max stats and gear, then I would definitely recommend it. Hell, I know I have sunk a lot more hours into it than I'm proud of.
This game is suprisingly good, but be aware it has a steep learning curve. If you have the time to put into it, it's totally worth it.

When I first came across this game, I thought "hey, what an interesting concept for an adventure game". As it turns out, it's much more than an adventure with one special mechanics - the story, the atmosphere, it's all very captivating. This is one of those games, where you might find yourself playing for 2-3 hours straight and really wanting to continue (getting up for work in 5 hours? Oh come on!).
If you enjoy slower-paced games with an emphasis on the story, if you are not looking for another shooter and if you are prepared to face the consequences of your decisions (believe me, the smallest things might have consequences here - even watering your houseplant!), this just might be the game for you. You will sit through a lot of dialogues, sometimes with little to no interaction, often you will be faced with possibility to examine literally dozen of little things in your surroundings. You might be temped to skip that, but that would be mistake - you might later find out you missed a critical detail and that will have the gravest consequences ("Spoilers!" as River Song would say :-) ). And even if that's not the case, Max (the protagonist) often makes more or less humorous quips that might conjure a smile on your face.
It might not fit everybody, but I would happily nominate this as one of the best adventure games I have ever played. And unlike Telltale adventure games, here I felt like my actions really influence the course of the story...

Gameplay wise, Shadow of War takes everything Shadow of Mordor did right, and improves upon it. Nemesis system (hierarchy of Orc bosses) has been expanded upon, but it can get a little predictable sometimes (a captain that killed you many times will usually cheat death, etc.). But it still adds a lot to the open world experience.
As for micro transactions, they're seriously completely avoidable, and just play the game for you honestly. The end-game is only grindy if you're trash at the game (I started on highest difficulty) and are dependent on your orcs to defend the base instead of defending it yourself. People boycott this game as if this is the first offender in a 60$ game but there are so many other offenders that they're doing a huge disservice to this game.
If you like the Arkham (not really as stealthy as AC) games or the LoTR universe, this is a pretty justified purchase.

Much has been written about the steep difficulty spike of the game's second half (and I would be lying if I didn't admit to using a walkthrough through the rewiring and knot-tying sections), but this is pretty typical for these sorts of games. However, I also think the narrative becomes a little too rushed, opaque, and clumsily told in this section (there's far too much "tell" and not enough "show"). The endless fetch-quests also become a little tedious after a while. I still really liked this, despite its flaws. It could have reached the upper echelons of adventure gaming... but as it stands, it is an entertaining (if flawed) b-side.

Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos might be the beginning of something pretty good, but on its own I don't think that I would recommend it on its own. It is a visual novel, essentially a choose-your-own-adventure game on your computer. It has plenty of good points: the art is good, the premise is interesting, the setting is introduced nicely, and I found the characters entertaining. The problem with Dysfunctional Systems is that it does not have many interaction points, at least not in the path that I took. Along the path that I selected, I was able to branch the story only twice. I can understand that as the first episode in what seems to be a planned series Dysfunctional Systems wants to keep its possible end states manageable, but the game would have been vastly improved by adding a few more interaction points, even if they did not actually impact the story.
As it stands, Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos would probably have been better served by being a graphic novel than a game. If the premise interests you, then by all means buy it. It is an interesting story, but its gameplay value, at least at this point, is limited.

What i love best about this title is the main character's OCD. Her baby was just kidnapped by a dragon-wielding Dark Wizard and yet she'd rather search the castle for half an hour for something to apply glue with, rather than just spread it on with her finger. She is not strong enough (or is too stubborn) to push the curtains aside, and resolves to build some scissors to cut them in half instead.
Of course, such are the tribulations of HOPA protagonists. OCD in the extreme. They cannot pick up an item until they find all other pieces of it and assemble it in the place where the initially found it (as opposed to carrying it around (btw: a barrel is too heavy for her to shove aside, but she'll not hesitate to stuff a stone column(!!!) in her pocket for later use... on a high ledge(!!!)).
But without OCD, they wouldn't be the star of a HOPA game, so it kinda goes with the territory. "HOPA protagonist must be OCD or have similar disorders which prohibit them from, e.g., simply breaking a window to get at an object on the other side (instead they are forced _insist_ on finding a glass cutter)." It's a simple fact.
One true complaint so far: the "knights and dragons" puzzle's description is so far removed from the solution that one can accurately call the puzzle's rules a bald-faced lie. i eventually gave up on it, tapped Skip, and was appalled at the solution which was revealed - it violated the description text at least 5 times.
And one minor complaint: ambiguous words in HO scenes upset me. One scene wants you to find a "bow" and has both a ribbon-bow and a violin bow (right next to each other, too). Aaarrggg.
Taken with a grain of salt, and a hefty dose of mocking the protagonist for her odd ways, this journey is turning out every bit as fun a romp as most of Artifex Mundi's works. i'm liking it better than their Demon Hunter title, but not finding it as engrossing as the newer Enigmatis 2 and Eventide titles (both of which set new standards for this genre, IMO). Somewhere in between Demon Hunter and Eventide/Enigmatis. Graphically excellent. Music is... unmemorable, apparently, as i can't recall a single note of it. The voice-overs are actually quite good. The subtitles to the voice-overs have a few very minor grammatic problems, but nothing terribly distracting (look who's OCD now!).
There are some colorful characters here, like Mr. and Mrs. Piggy Bank, and some grumpy dwarves who accept the protagonist as their Sovereign Queen, yet refuse to give her the items she's searching for until she performs favors for them. As mentioned above - take such with a grain of salt, because a HOPA isn't a HOPA if NPCs simply hand you everything you need.
i had to laugh my butt off when the protagonist put her baby in her inventory. Just classic.
Oh, and having a little fairy in your inventory, useful to access certain out-of-reach places, is pretty cool.
i've gotta thumb this one up.
PS: my greatest thanks to the devs for their continued support for Linux. All of their titles i've tried (about 6 or 8 of them) have worked flawlessly on my system (currently Mint Linux 17.3).

Pros:
-Low price for a high quality game - $25 normally, but frequently goes on Steam sales at 90% off.
-Has not resorted to DLC and such - all updates (including some huge ones that really spiced up the game) has been free so far, and looks to continue to be free in future updates. Players can optionally donate money to the developers to support their efforts.
-Unique, fun FPS/RTS hybridd, featuring mainly first person perspectives and top-down perspectives for commanders
-Very asymmetrical gameplay that is balanced and entertaining.
-Gameplay is all about teamwork and communication, for those who are seeking that kind of gameplay.
-Both sides have enough variety to keep things from getting too stale. Flamethrowers, jetpacks, mech suits, different alien lifeforms, etc.
-Surprisingly very good community. Hostilities are kept to a minimum, there are plenty of "rookie" servers, emphasis on teamwork means players have no room to brag and lone wolf it.
-Male and female gender choices as marines - and the females are armoured just as well!
-Steam workshop, mod support, and trading cards round out the goodies.
Cons:
-Tutorial/training is very basic, you'll need to learn everything from real matches
-Commander user interface is not bad, but definitely could use improvements to make it feel smoother like an RTS game
-Commanding is very tough and will take lots of practice. Due to their large influence, 'bad' commanders are often blamed for losses, and unfortunately do contribute to snowballing defeats.
Natural Selection 2 is a fairly fun game with a unique spin that separates it from most first person shooters - the game is basically an interesting blend between FPS/RTS. The closest comparison would be if Counter-Strike and Starcraft were merged as one. This comparison is very accurate from both gameplay anad thematic perspectives - the sci fi setting and many game mechanics will definitely remind players of Starcraft.
The game is essentially aliens vs marines. Both sides play in first person mode, shooting if you're a marine and clawing/biting/spitting/whatever as the aliens. However, one player on both sides can assume the role of commander, which gives them a top down perspective. The commander is a complex role not suited for new players, but once you get the hang of it it basically plays as it would in an RTS, except your units are actually players.
The objective is to eliminate all hives or commander stations. Spread throughout the map are resource nodes that are fought for control in order to bring precious resources flowing to your side instead of the enemies. The commander has a major influence of the flow of battle, as they decide what to research/upgrade and what to build. They can also issue orders (best done with a mic of course) to their fellow players, utilizing their 'eye in the sky' perspective to their advantage. The vast majority of the players meanwhile, fight in first person mode.
The asymetricality of the game is well balanced, and keeps things fresh. The marines are very standard, playing like any other FPS, although they can eventually gain access to some neat weapons like flamethrowers and even mech suits. The aliens on the other hand are very novel, featuring different lifeforms that translates to different roles and abilities. From Skulks whom are like Zerglings, rushing with great speed and climbing on any surface (ceilings, walls, you name it), to the massive Onos, a rampaging organism of destruction, there's plenty of variety here.
Unlike most games, NS2 is a game that's VERY much about teamwork. Communication and teamwork is necessary to win matches. Any marine or alien walking about on their own is simply too vulnerable - it absolutely pays to work in groups to accomplish goals. In addition variety is needed to succeed - each weapon and lifeform has their weaknesses that require teamwork to compensate for. For example, simply being in a mech suit or as an Onos does not mean you've won the game - they too can easily be killed without support.
The commander in particular has a lot of influence here, as good commanders will take charge of the team to really lead them, ordering where to go and informing their fellow players what's going on.
The unique FPS/RTS blend really separates this game from most FPS's. It can be quite satisfying to lead actual human players from an RTS perspective as a commander, or to develop comraderie and teamwork when playing as the soldiers of either side. In short, this game is novel yet entertaining and holds its own against many other games out there. If you get this for 90% off, I'm willing to say it's one of your best Steam purchases ever and you won't regret it if you're even just barely a fan of FPS games.

Most of the game's puzzles are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them. Some of these puzzles can be played over again in the extra section.
Since this game is a collector's edition, it comes with extra contents, "Wallpapers;" "Concept Arts;" "Music;" "Bonus Chapter."

This game caught my eye a few months back, but the negative reviews scared me off. recently went on sale for 5 bucks and figured I'd check it out. Really glad I did. I'm a long time Isometric player from Baldur's gate to X-com, to Pillars of Eternity and Tyranny, to Shadowrun. Of all the tactical isos I've played, this has been the least RNG based, or at least Iv'e felt it's been the least RNG based.
A lot of the negative reviews talk about mechanics in the game and poorly represent them. This game isn't not like your typical turn based tactical isometric, It's not too far off from X-COM in the way the campaign is handled, but even there it's pretty different. here are the features that originalyl had me weary:
Luck: Luck is not what it usualyl is. it's more of a shield that is also your resource pool. when a character attacks, they first have tog et through the attacked character's shield, or luck, and then they can hit their HP. This makes deciding whether to use an ability that consumes luck or not a critical decision. I read somewhere that luck affects hit chance, I can say with certanty it doesn't. Hit chance is affected by range, cover, your base aim, your gun's bonus or penalty, and the character being attacked's defense.
Not saving: The way this was expresse din the reviews was super misleading. Let me explain.
Instead of walking around and so forth, the game's campaign is broken into chapter, and each chapter is set up more like a game board. You move your peice to a location, and a scenario plays out. Sometimes the scenario is a mission (combat) sometimes it's decision time, sometimes it's a trader, sometimes it's a conversation leading to other locations. The game auto saves after each scenario. You can't save during combat, which I assume is to prevent save scumming.
Enemies getting reaction shots when they see you: This mechanic can be turned off if it doesn't appeal to you. I personally turned it off.
in fact, the game has a bunch of modifiers that can be turned on/off to fit the experience you want. I'd recommend checkign this out as many of the negatives I was weary about were addressed in the modifier section.
All in all I'm on chapter three and very happy I picked this up, it's different from any other tactical Isometric I've played, the writing is realyl solid, and old west themes are very hard to come by in gaming in general. If you're curious about this game, I'd say check it out, you'll know very quickly if it's for you or not and can get a refund before you hit that 2 hour mark if it's not.

So it's been a while since I initially picked up Wasteland 2 on a whim. I'm not a stark supporter or against the idea of the game. I wasn't a kickstart supporter, nor was I one who got swept away in the hype before the game came out. Comeing back to the game, I've had time to mull over my choices, as well as the game in general. I believe, without a doubt, that this was one of the best RPG games I've ever played.
Don't get me wrong, it's not open-ended or loose with the story. You can't just run around and do what you want. You are on rails with the story for most main segments of the game. Where it shines, however, is in just how powerful the game's willpower is in letting you choose what happens. Most games have their "in order to get the best outcome, you have to do this" situation that I always feel pushed towards. In Skyrim, for example, they always pushed you towards one side. If you were on the rebel's side, you were always pushed towards one stock ending for that story ark. Wasteland 2, weather by misfortune or by choice, allows your mistakes to shape the story. If you kill innosents along the way through saving a city, you'll most likely find the city upset about who you killed, or at least less happy about your intervention of their problem. It's not "do X to get Y response" but instead every X you have to do can yield various Y responces.
This is the real way that Wasteland 2 shines. I do wish more morality issues came up that weren't isolated insodents. Many a time missions would either be "large strings of missions with a resolution" or "little one-off missions" and very little between it. It's a small gripe, as well as my wish for combat to be a tad easier at the start. This game really is a trial-by-fire game and causals won't find it easy.
This game easily gets a 9.5/10 for me,  only lowered by the slight anoience I have when re-playing certain segments I wish were more open-ended.

As I am not really experienced in writing reviews, but since I just completed the game, l would like to share my experience with others whom are still deciding to buy it or not. I am dividing it in several stages: Character Building, Storyline, Combat and Gear.
==
Character Building
==
I found it really challenging to build a team that would last me through the whole game, just because there are too many skills to choose from for only 4 characters of your team. I had to make a new game 3 times to find out that it's actually better to leave a couple of skills out, which you will find on other followers (even better progressed) later on in the game. - Rose for example has a really high computer skill and handgun skill.-  Apart from the skills I think there are limited but reasonably enough faces and clothing to choose from to make a pretty random team.
EDIT: After I made new game on highest difficulty, it came to my surprise that I could use me old rangers again, still having all the skills and abilities from my previous end-game. Knowing this I can reccomend new players to start and complete an easier difficulty and then use the same experienced (veteran) rangers on higher difficulty to make it easier! Changed my rating from 7/10 to 8.5 after knowing this.
Rating 8.5/10
==
Storyline
==
Depending on the choices you make, the storyline will change in many, many ways. Sometimes it doesn't turn out the way you want, and you can't do anything about it because of one of your previous choices. I quite liked this because it makes making choices more difficult and you will have to think ahead to make sure everything turns out ... o.k.
Dialogues are sometimes crazy long, and very tiring to read it all. You will be clicking a lot. Mind you, read carefully. Sometimes you will need information in order to make the right choice. Having an advanced speech skill will also come in handy to unlock several special dialogues which will help you get things easier.
The main story takes you and your team into the wasteland of Arizona to plant a couple of radio repeaters on several radio towers and re-establish broadcast range for your fellow rangers at the Citadel. During this mission you will stumble upon a lot of people whom need your help... or do they? You decide.
After going through a lot of trouble to get the radio going again, you will fly to Los Angeles, where you will have to clear the name of the Rangers and bring good to the people of LA. You will soon notice that you're not the only one trying to gain power in LA and find yourself in conflict with several organizations that will stop for nothing until they have it. Make the right choices to make the right alliances and save the world from extinction.
Rating 9/10
==
Combat
==
Combat is pretty much the same throughout the whole game.. this doesn't mean that it’s boring though. You will have a limited amount of action points per character, depending on your skills. Both moving and shooting will cost action points so use them wisely. Some combat phases can be really challenging because of the environment you're in. Gain advantage by seeking higher ground and make sure that you get a lot of cover, it will definitely save your life multiple times. A higher combat initiative allows your team to act more often in a battle and will surely come in handy when you fight 10 baddies at once.
Rating 6/10
==
Gear
==
You will be happy to know that you will be able to choose from a lot of weapon types to use. And you can even put modifications on them! A big variety of weapons and weaponmods allow you to create your own personal weapons of mass destruction. The only thing I found disappointing was that you will be using the same weapon for a long time until you proceed into a new area. They are also pretty expensive in the shop. Make sure that you make the right decision on bringing the guns you find with you, or turn them into scrap metal to sell.
There is also a lot of clothing to be found in the wasteland. You will stumble across the weirdest hats, shirts and pants which together make an even weirder outfit. Make sure you try everything on!
Rating 8/10
-------------------------------
So after having said all of this, I would very much like to recommend this game to people who like a game full of adventure, mystery and action with a lot of choices and plot twists. The overall rating of this game for me concludes:
7,9/10
A few extra tips:
* Save a lot!!
* Always reload before battle!!
* Stock up on ammo!!
* Take cover!!
* ENJOY!!

When I first saw this on Steam, I thought it was a♥♥♥♥♥♥platformer with ducks. I could not have been further from the truth.
What happens if you mash together crazy physics interactions, intense one-hit-kill sidescrolling combat, and dozens of excellently designed maps switching at a breakneck pace? You get Duck Game. This game is multiplayer crack.
Here's how it works: you and three other ducks get dropped into an arena randomly selected out of a large list. You start with no weapons and have about one second to look over the map, see the various weapon pickups and formulate a plan. After that, it's go time, the fight usually lasts around 10-25 seconds, the last duck standing scores a point and off to the next map you go! Conditions are constantly changing: last map you were shooting eachother with sniper rifles across the map, now you're fighting with freezeguns above an instant death pit, and next time you'll all be racing to grab the minigun at the top platform, or locked in a tiny room where the only available weapon is grenades, or shooting through a series of connected portals, or...
The combat is easy to learn but hard to master. There are only two buttons: pick up/throw and attack. What makes it interesting is the weapons. Each weapon has a place in this game, there are many tricks to using them and they all provide advantages and disadvantages. Pistols fire quick and precise, but quickly run out of ammo and can't be reloaded. Shotguns cover a large cone, but have limited range and have to be pumped after each shot (very easy to forget in the heat of battle!), magnets can steal enemy weapons, mind control ray has short range but lets you control your foe off a cliff, swords can be thrown. Grenades have a large kill radius, but you have to remember to pull the pin first (and then remember to throw it!). Even nerf guns can be useful, to push enemies off platforms and away from that one sniper rifle spawn... Every map has spawns for only certain kinds of weapons, ammo runs out quick, you have to be precise, fast and able to grab and use the first thing you come across to push back, block, disarm or kill your opponents.
There's a high skill ceiling for hardcore players to reach, and plenty of whacky situations for the casual player to have a good laugh: all four players shot eachother within the first 3 seconds of the match? You accidentally dropped your sword on a spring and it killed everyone else? Last duck standing ran into his own mine before he could score? The guy with a rocket launcher chasing you slipped on a banana peel and fell off the edge of the map? That's Duck Game in a nutshell.
Lightning-fast, competitive and laugh-out-loud funny, this game is a masterpiece.
If there is one criticism I could give it, it's that the singleplayer is pretty boring. It mostly consists of timed obstacle and shooting courses, and doesn't hold a candle to the multiplayer. Luckily, there's plenty of multiplayer games going on, so what the hell are you waiting for?! You NEED this game in your life. NOW!
P.S. I have only played this with an Xbox controller, I can't vouch that it plays well with kb&m.

I wrote a review once before on this game and gave it negative review because of the flaws I saw within the game, and said "I would never finish this game."   Well I decided I needed to finish it, so I did.
The Good:
The graphics are super cool especially the lighting effects for everything it's done well.
The story is the strongest point of this game it made me forget about a lot of the flaws I saw and honestly kept me on the edge of my seat begging for more.  It is quite a unique story as well being the only game I can think of that makes you"live the story,"
The Enemies while they aren't anything too new just people taken over by a powerful force and every once in a while there is the poltergeist.  Where it gets interesting is the combat.
The second most unique thing about this game by far is the combat.  This games combat relies heavily on the use of the flashlight.  Let me explain,  every enemy has a shield that must be dropped in order to kill them, in order to drop this shield you need to "focus" the flashlight on them.  Then you can finish them off with the regualr weapons.  The poltergeist is an interesting entity it possesses objects around you and tosses the item at you, similar to the "Taken" (As the game refers to them.)  You just have to shine your flashlight on them.  One of the most interesting weapons are actually spotlights you find in certain areas in the game that acts as a turret so to speak.   There are a few weapons beyond just the flashlight.  Pretty standard stuff for the most part, shotgun,Revolver,hunting rifle.  However, there are a couple of weapons that shake things up such as; flares, flaashbangs, and a flaregun.  The flares act as more of a shield in a sense you can drop them to give yourself a little bit of breathing room.  The flashbang acts as frag grenade here and just wrecks anything that is unlucky enough to be caught in its blast radius.  The flaregun is like a grenade launcher insanely powerful.
The Bad:
Dodging & Sprinting: Oh god, the dodging in this game feels so clunky it's unreal.  The dev's decided it would be an amazing idea to bind the sprint key and the dodge key to the same buttton.  It seemed like when I was trying to run away from something I just ended up dodging first and getting hit from behind only to be gang ♥♥♥♥ed by the enemies. Another thing is Alan can't run for a long time he seems to get tired pretty much instantly after even starting to sprint, so if you have a relatively fast enemy you are trying to get away from they WILL catch up and kill you no way around it except to ice them.  I also found it odd in platforming segments because I was trying to jump a gap and just ended up dodging right into the hole I was trying to jump over and ended up dying.  This is by far the killer of this game to me, this was the primary reason I stopped playing, it was just impossible to get used to.  This is coming from a guy whole literally just beat Onimusha one of the most confusing games when it comes to control.
TL;DR- I would say I give this game like 6 out of 10, it's a hard score to give because I liked the story so much but the     dodging is unforgivable.  I will say pick this game up if it ever goes on sale, definetly worth $10.

Th	The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a must have game on any RPG and fantasy lover’s list. Assassins of Kings is a heavily narrative driven video game filled with compelling character’s and mature themes. The combat is fluid and has been designed so that it is easily learnt but difficult to master. Aspects that usually feel tedious and annoying in other RPG’s such as collecting and crafting items has been implemented so it is now a simple and enjoyable task that becomes crucial to your success in the tougher battles.

Graphic is an improvement from previous installment but still glitchy and the lighting implementation is weird. Story, characters and voice acting are good. World is pretty lifeless and linear, not much to do (normal for Mafia series, dont expect a GTA bustling and lively world).
The missions are reminding me of the very first Assassin Creed, go to new area, do the exact same thing as previous area (taking out rackets using exactly the same method), kill the boss of the area, rinse and repeat. The side missions to improve your weapons, stats, etc are full of fetching quests, i.e. go to this swampy area, clean up enemies, drive the vehicle all the way to the respective racket, it's simply time consuming, very boring and intended to jack up the playing time.
So, I feel that the only redeeming thing is the story and characters. I can't help but feel sick of boredom after playing for 1 hour for each gaming session due to how repetitive the missions are.

Honestly, this is an amazing game; great voice acting, story, puzzles, and writing. However, I'm still not done (I'm at the knot puzzle in act 2 which is a pain) so my opinion is subject to change, but I doubt it.
It's a just a simple point and click game similar to Day of the tentacle or Monkey island; well it is made by Tim Schafer. The puzzles start off rather simple but then spike in complexity in Act 2, but doable nonetheless.A lot of the puzzles aren't straightforward and require a good deal of thought and time.
The game mechanics aren't bad and I don't really see why other people are complaining. Literally, you point at an object and click. The cursor changes shape  when you can interact with an object/person. In the inventory bar you can combine items. You can pick an item for your inventory and use it to interact with other objects or people in the overworld. Really, just basic funtctions thats in any other point and click game.
The writing is filled with a lot of sexual innuendos (or maybe I'm just a really sexual person, I don't know) and satirizes hipsters a lot (All I'm saying is that Wil Wheaton's role in this game is better than his role in TNG, because in this game he actually contributes to the story in a meaningful way). The plot, without spoliers, starts off simple: Vella is preparing for a festival and Shay is a Space captain. The actual story shifts between two main characters: Shay and Vella, and you can between them at any point throughout the game and sometimes it proves beneficial to jump (Hint: The Toy Puzzle).  Eventually the two do merge in an unexpected manner ( well at least I didn't expect it) and it becomes epic as well as a bit more difficult. .
The music for this game is amazing and fits in exceptionally well. Every location and scene comes with complimentary music.
Some reviewers who complain already have some experience with Tim Schafer games and can attest to the quality with respect to Schafer's other games; I, however, can't, so sorry for the lack of greater detail in this review.
So all in all, an excellent game, a bit pricey, but well worth the play so I recommend you get this game when it's on sale.
[update]
So I finished, and well the puzzles only get more difficult in Act 2 (there are only 2 acts in case you didn't know). Story wise it becomes more vague as in we never really get a fleshed out motive for the enemy. Dialog options with any character no longer provide us with insight into that character as much as the options are there to tell us how to progress on with the game. Even then the dialog doesn't help much. Act 2 essentially becomes lackadaisical towards the end.
The actual ending (without spoiling anything) is very similar to a Studio Ghibli film, I can't really explain in but it just is. If you know what I mean then great if not then well you'll see. I, personally liked the ending and felt satisfied with it; however, others didn't since it doesn't so much wrap the story up.
Some fans are asking for an Act 3 to tie any loose knots, but I doubt there will be another installment considering the way it ended. Don't get me wrong it would be awesome to see another but with what we have now I'm happy with.
Finally, my overall outlook on the game is still the same: I really recommend it !!

DISCLAIMER: THIS IS NOT A CRITIQUE OR MEANT TO BE WELL WRITTEN/ENTERTAINING REVIEW, IT"S JUST ME EXPLAINING AND RECCOMENDING IT.
Duck Game is an Ouya game ported to Steam, published by Adultswim. It's a 4 player sideview 2d Deathmatch game. 2 vs 2 is also possible. Similar to towerfall, players die in one hit and then go to the next level when everyone is dead.
First when starting it up you'll notice the great sega genesis style soundtrack.
Second, you'll notice presenation is great. For example the main menu is navigated by actually walking to the options, and it is a nice looking menu.
When you start the game, you'll be thrown into a little waiting lobby that also explains the controls. You can change your profile here, and pick what hat you want to wear. You have to destroy the glass next to you to step into a beam and start floating in it. When you get into the beam you can either find a multiplayer game or play or, play the single player arcade missions. If another person is there, you can play locally instead.
The gameplay of Duck Game is simple. 4 people get thrown into a level, and in that level weapons and items are scattered throughout the map quake style, or hidden in blocks which you have to jump into like in Mario. The objective is ofcourse to kill eachother with these weapons. Everything is a one hit kill. When everyone is dead the person who survives gets a point and the next map loads. When 1 person has 10 points the game ends. The controls are simple. You move with the directional keys, and you have a jump and a shoot button. If you press down you can slide, which you can use to slide under small places. Unique to Duck Game is a dedicated button to pick the weapons up. When weapons or items are picked up, the player can throw them with the same button. These throwing physics are very well implemented. The movement speed is fast, and you're in pretty much full control of your jumps. If you jump and let go of the right or left button you'll almost immidiately fall. If you jump, and hold the jump button in mid air you'll slowly descent to the ground. There's also a feign death button, not sure what it's for but it's nice.
Oh, and there's a dedicated quack button, to, well, just make a quack sound.
The game is fast paced, chaotic fun. It's very easy to pick up and play. There's always funny moments to be had. People accidentally suiciding in the most stupid way right after winning and thus not awarded a point for example.
Most weapons are bullet based, and have a bit of a random spread. You also often can't see the ammo you have left. With some guns there's knockback, which gets higher when you crouch. They kind of work like incredibly fast projectiles, and the range varies. What you'll notice is that seemingly, you can only shoot sideways. On the surface it seems like Duck Game has no depth to it and is just casual fun. However, when playing for a while you'll notice there's quite a few things to get good at. First of all, many weapons have their own unique little quirks. A small thing is that many weapons require the button to be pressed again to for example eject shells before they can be shot again. You can mostly just shoot left and right, but aiming can actually be more skillfull then you think for a 2d game like this. You can walk through enemies, and when standing in an enemy the gun often can't hit that person, which happens a lot because of the fast movement. When you throw a weapon hard enough at your enemy, the enemy's weapon drops.
When you jump and hold down the jump button in mid air, not only will you slowly descent, but your weapon will point upwards, so you actually can shoot up. Not only can you do this, but you can actually shoot up diagonally. Since the gun doesn't point up immidiately, if hold the jump button and almost immidiately press the shoot button right after, you'll shoot diagonally.
The revolver has kickback, so if you keep shooting you can shoot diagonally with the recoil.
For the grenades you press the shoot button to take the pin off, and then you can throw it in any direction with the other button, and the physics (and the ease of killing yourself) of it make it a skillful weapon to use.
The grenade launcher not just arcs and then explodes on contact, but when you hold it down it goes up, so you can aim it. The longer you hold the button the more upward it aims.
The chainsaw has to be activated by pressing shoot twice, and after, you can do all kinds of crazy movements with it.
With the hammer you can also effect your movement but in a different way, and since it's heavy you can kill someone by dropping it.
There's an net gun that has a fast arcing projectile which traps your enemy, and then you can pick your enemy up and throw him out of the map.
There's a flamethrower and flame gun that can be extinguished by fire extinguishers, and the nerf gun ammunition catches on fire when shot at the flamethrower.
And there's more. 2 shotguns (with 1 you can see your ammo left on the gun itself), a few pistol's,  a minigun, a sword you can also throw kill people with (and slash downwards in the air), lasers that bounce off of walls, a small laser gun you can charge up, a gun you can charge up for a HUGE laser, the mooninites gun from Aqua Teen Hunger force that shoots a really slow moving square and has a big knockback effect when shot, a magnet gun to push people off the map, a gun that turns people into you, a rocket launcher that destroys terrain, a sniper rifle, a rifle with a really long reload time, some thing powerful that I forgot, a flaregun, mines, an uzi type thing and an earthworm jim type gun, and a suicide gun. I think I got most of them. There's enough vereity in weapons to be had here, although I'd love there to be more interesting projectile weapons.
Aside from weapons, There's sometimes jetpacks and grappling hooks to find for movement, and there's body armor, a helmet and shoes(against spikes).
as far as the levels themselves go, you can pick up blocks in certain levels that you can use to drop on people's heads. There's other blocks you can use to block doors with. There's keys you can pick up to open certain doors with better weapons. There's hazards such as spikes. There's oil drums you can shoot to make all the oil come out. There's windows that can be broken open when pressing down or shooting on them. In a few levels there's teleporters you can actually shoot in and the nyour bullets come out of the other portal. What's cool is that there's a level editor, but an issue is that you can't play these online yet. Otherwise there's some crashes, and there's no game browser to speak of, only automatic matchmaking.
The singleplayer arcade missions are not that special, but they're a nice addition. Some of them are pretty fun. They're missions such as shoot as many targets as you can in a certain amount of time, or finish an obstacle course as quickly as possible, etc. You can either get a bronze, silver, golden or blue medal, and the better the medal the more tickets you get to spend on a few gameplay modifiers and hats.

I have played the game through, nearly to the end, and after investing a couple dozen hours into the game have decided that (at least in it's current state) while playable, it has real problems.
First, there's a plethora of bugs, specifically regarding the different ways to solve assorted missions. I am officially stuck in the second area, unable to complete the mission to bring peace between two waring factions (names left vague to avoid spoilers for readers) but because I put one guy on one side in charge first, I am unable to complete the quest. It is not a main story quest, but half the fun of games such as this are the side quests.
Second, prepare to spend a lot of time... watching your team do the same thing 20 times. See that toaster you want to repair? Save first, you're going to have to try five times and if you critically fail you will have to reload. Almost more annoying, you have to sit there and fail over and over just waiting for the one lucky chance that you will succeed. You really do spend a good portion of the game either randomly moving around the wastes (which just takes a long time) or attempting to unlock / hack / disarm things.
- It would be profoundly helpful if the developers had figured out either a more engaging way to do these things or just made them instant pass / fail tests so you could sit and spam attempts until they work.
Third, there really is a 'winning party', you will have to have one person with essentially every skill to be successful in this game. Which is fine, except that there are more skills than you end up with characters able to have them. It is nearly impossible to do a good chunk of the game if no one has lock picking / demolitions / field medic, and at the point where they are essentially required skills to win, why not at least tell people when they start building their party?
Going past that, I really do question the effectiveness of their random number generator. It can be really strange watching someone with a 95% in a skill fail 20 times in a row. I realize that is in fact the nature of an RNG, but it leaves me questioning how they did their seeding.
That all said and done, the game is strangely graphics intensive for how simplistic the graphics are. They really do need to do some optimization to help the game either run more smoothly or look better, a game with graphics this old should not be struggling on most modern PC's.
All in all, the game had a ton of potential, but the execution leaves a lot lacking and other games of the same approach (Shadowrun for example) have done a better job at engaging players and keeping them involved with minimal bugs.

Paladins is a fantasy sci-fi Overwatch clone that fais to capture the feeling of the award winning team based shooter. It does, however, provide interesting gameplay that keeps you coming back time and time again.
I was a bit scared to download Paladins at first, as it looked like a competitive shooter that would wreck me. I downloaded it after recommendation from my friend, BrainSushi. I loved the graphics right away. It's a colorful, vibrant world that gives me the sense of adventure and exploration. However, this is not a adventure game that gives you the chance to explore. It's a team based shooter about meeting a certain objective to win the match. The atmosphere just did not match for me. Sure, it's fun and entertaining as a shooter, but it does not use many original gameplay mechanics for it's characters.
The characters' main gameplay is ripped from Overwatch. Half the cast 20+ characters they give you have the same mechanics as Overwatch Heroes. Makoa is Roadhog, Pip is D.VA, Viktor is Soldier 76, and Maeve is Genji. There are more, but I'm not about to waste my time naming everyone. Only a few characters feel more original than the others. Also, the charcters don't feel like characters. Sure, you can have a main, but the characters lack personality. Overwatch's heroes have origins, ages, countires in the real world that they're from, personality, lines of dialogue, relationships with other heroes. Paladins lacks character and personality. Every character I play as in this game feel like a shell that I put myself in. They are not their own person or being. They're not relatable because they have no indicators of origin, backstory, and a place to come from. They have a name, weapons, and an over the top outfit.
The gameplay is this. Shoot, meet the objective, pull off a few ultimates now and then. It's simple yet complex at the same time, which keeps me hooked, with all the various moves and techniques to use on enemies. It feels good to get streaks and pull off the play of the game, or get recognizied at the end for Best flank, or Best damage. I give Paladins props for this.
Customization is sort of diverse. There are complete skins you can buy on the store with gems, but the skins you build for your own character through chests you get for leveling up inculde headpieces and armor of 5-6 different colors. Yaaaaaaaaaaay.......
To talk about all of it's flaws and strengths would take me so much more time, and I'm a bit tired so I'll leave you with this.
6.5-Okay
+Simple Yet Complex gameplay
+Colorful vibrant Graphics
+Variety in Character Gameplay
-Atmosphere is a bit Confusing
-Characters lack depth and personality
- Rip-Offs of Overwatch heroes
-Wonky Customization
-Few Game Modes
Paladins, as an Overwatch clone, fails pathetically. As it's own game, it's an entertaining, colorful experience that prepares you for Overwatch in a preview sort of way. As of the time this review is out, I have yet to play Overwatch, which is why I cut the game a little slack. I recommend it for no other reason that it's as good game to blow an hour or so on a vacation day. I cut the game slack because it's in a beta phase, and when the full game is released, I'm sure we'll have something special.

I usually don't bother or wish to share my opinion on much of anything, but I feel this particular game warrants it, considering the impact it had on me. One of my all time favorite games, all the episodes included in that statement. I might make a more in depth review later, but suffice to say, this game will lift you up; it will make you happy, or at times calm and tranquil. And then, not to spoil anything, it will drag you to places that will show you how sensitive you are to emotional trauma. Also, don't be fooled as I was initially. I thought it was going to be just another indie-esque walking simulator with some choices here and there, not that that is a bad thing necessarily, but I had lower expectations than I should have had. It does indeed keep you on a general linear path, with some minor exploration and collectible stuff spread throughout, as well as plenty of dialogue and choices therein with a variety of different characters and personalities, but the part of it that I was not expecting, was that this game is like a good detective story or show. You can barrel through the plot and not pay much attention, and then suffer consequences as you go, or you can choose to play it more slow, and carefully review clues you encounter as you progress, thereby influencing how you approach certain choices. They even have a clue that I initially missed that hints at one of the biggest twists in the story, and it's an easy one to miss. One tip for any person considering this game, don't make assumptions about the people present in this story; a rule that should be applied to real life certainly, but it is law in this game. Also, for the love of all that is good, avoid spoilers for this one until you are finished with it, there are ones that could potentially destroy your whole experience, or at least heavily dampen the impact of certain in game events. Overall, I would give this game the rating of a masterpiece, a 10/10, with the caveat that it is not in the same vein as other games like Fallout New Vegas or Witcher 3, at least in terms of gameplay, but I feel that the story for this one goes beyond that, as it was the reason I couldn't put this one down until I had finished it, even when I tried to space it out and give myself time between episodes.

In Alan Wake, you play the titular Alan Wake, a successful writer from New York with the rather mysterious sounding name of Alan Wake. Secretly, Alan is a superhero. A Guardian of the Light. When he's asleep, he enters a parallel dimension where he roams the galaxy fighting megalomanical demi-gods and insane zealots with his trusty companions; a talking raccoon and a sentient tree. When he hears his name in the real world "Alan... Wake... Alan... Wake...", he wakes up and returns to the real world. Unfortunately, none of this is in the game.
At the beginning of the game, Alan is on a vacation with his wife Alice MacGuffin in a Pacific Northwest town named Mystic Falls. It just so happens that Mystic Falls has a history of strange goings-on dating back hundreds of years; like the time when the town was infested by vampires and the townsfolk trapped them all under a church. More recently, there was that incident where Mr. Muldoon, the groundskeeper of the local school, dressed as a ghost as part of an elaborate scam in cahoots with a crooked property developer, but was foiled by a bunch of meddling kids and a talking dog.
Seeking some peace and solitude, Alan rents an old dilapidated cabin on a tiny island at a nearby haunted lake named Lake Placid. According to the tourist brochure, the lake is used by the military as a dumping ground for failed genetic experiments and is full of weaponised piranhas, giant crocodiles, and Miley Cyrus. Even worse, it's also where Microsoft dumped all their unsold Microsoft Zunes. On a cloudless night, one can see entire shoals of Microsoft Zunes gently bobbing on the waves, a shroud of failure covering the entire lake, as far as the eye can see.
However, just when Alan thought he could relax, he suddenly wakes up in a car crash with absolutely no memory of the event whatsoever. He's in a car he can't remember driving, next to an empty bottle of Vodka he can't remember drinking. When he goes looking for help, random strangers try to kill him. This is normal in New York City but unheard of in the Pacific Northwest. Even stranger still, he starts finding pages from a manuscript that he's absolutely sure he wrote but doesn't remember writing. One of them was titled "Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets". Harry, Hogwarts, and Dumbledore... it all felt terribly familiar to Alan.
To top it all off, Alan's wife Alice disappears under mysterious circumstances. The only clue Alan could find was Alice's phone. All it contained was a digital receipt for a one-way plane ticket to Vegas and salacious text messages to a muscular Yoga instructor named Julio. Apparently Alice loved doing the Downward Dog with Julio. Other than that, it was a complete mystery. Not deterred, Alan decides to go look for Alice. By blundering around the forest at night, in the dark, yelling her name.
For some reason, a bunch of people known as 'The Taken' want to kill Alan. Why they would name themselves after a Liam Neeson movie is a mystery that's never explained. Fortunately, Alan is not totally defenceless. He's actually quite handy with flashlights. Sometimes he puts it under his chin and tells scary stories. He also waves it around and makes Lightsabre noises. But most of his fights involve him shining light in peoples faces until they get mad and try to kill him. Then he runs like a sissy girl for the next checkpoint.
At this point, the line between fantasy and reality begins to blur and the storytelling takes on a surreal quality. Some guy named Billy Zane tries to help Alan. "Alan, you're not a kid anymore, you could get hurt out there," said Billy Zane helpfully. Then there was a Walk-Off and David Bowie was there and some guy pulled his underpants out without removing his pants. It was all hazy to Alan. So many mysteries, so little explanation. That's why Alan Wake is so good.
Clearly inspired by authors like Stephen King and Dean Koontz, the storyline and characters are typically clichéd, but nevertheless entertaining. The plucky overweight comedy relief sidekick, feisty female sheriff, sleazy doctor, fruity FBI Agent, and kidnapped wife are all there. There's even a television program in the game named Night Springs that's clearly a parody of, or perhaps a tribute to, creepy television serials such as Twilight Zone, X-Files, and Yo Gabba Gabba. The Pacific Northwest environment, on the other hand, is very well modelled. Some of the background panoramic vistas are breathtaking and complements the storytelling perfectly.
The weakest aspect of Alan Wake is the combat. While it's nowhere as good or as satisfying as similar games like Resident Evil 4, it's not terrible either. But it does get repetitive. Weapon selection is limited to revolver, rifle and shotguns. Alan also gets Flares that act as temporary 'Taken Repellant', Flash Bangs that kill anything nearby like grenades, and the smart bomb Flare Gun that's best saved for boss fights.
During combat, the Taken are surrounded by shadows that make them impervious to conventional weaponry. Before Alan can hurt them, he has to 'burn away' the shadows with his flashlight. This exhausts the batteries of the flashlight. He has to do this with every single Taken and there are lots of them. Managing two combat resources, batteries and ammo, can get annoying. However, flashlight energy does regenerate slowly over time when not used in combat. The game is also fairly generous with ammo, with boxes of unlimited ammo conveniently placed near some boss encounters.
What is most annoying is the lack of a melee ability. If Alan runs out of ammo he's basically screwed. You'd think being from New York City he would have at least picked up some rudimentary street-fighting skills since hailing a cab usually involves some hand-to-hand combat. To even the odds, Alan has an evasion ability that allows him to dodge melee attacks, but it's flaky and unreliable. Dodging is basically just spamming the dodge action key and hoping that it works.
Overall, Alan Wake is a good game with its strength being in the narrative. A nice touch is the episodic synopsis that plays before the game begins, "Previously, on Alan Wake...", so you won't forget who Alan Wake is. There's also lots of extra content like the 2 free DLCs, good music, and an in-game commentary. Highly recommended for those who like their mystery spiced with some action.
TL;DR
A mediocre mystery writer battles supernatural evil in the dark using the world's worst flashlight.

I simply could not get past the revamped controls/HUD and combat mechanics as compared to those from The Witcher 1. Indeed, unlike the original which was only released for the PC this game was also released on consoles and I firmly believe that the controls and combat mechanics greatly suffered from this desire for potentially greater exposure and sales. By this I mean that the logical and deep control system from the 1st game was modified (i.e. watered-down) into something that works best with a game controller. You can no longer click around to find and select things, you have to orient the cumbersome camera towards your point of interest and physically move the witcher over before you can identify items in the environments. This is further compounded by the fact that while movement and combat is best achieved through use of a gamepad, maneuvering through the menu and crafting system is a pain in the butt without a keyboard so you'll find yourself constantly switching back and forth between both modes of input.
This wouldn't be such a point of contention if they also hadn't 'dumbed' down the combat: no more light/medium/heavy awesome combos that are geared towards specific types of mobs, both in nature and in number. No parries or blocking, no chaining of attacks, no coup de grace when you stun an enemy. Since you can neither block nor parry you have to resort to continuous dodges (i.e. rolling on the ground) to avoid attacks aimed your way and mash the attack button when you can, or try to lure enemies into your traps as you frantically toss bombs, knives and signs their way while desperately trying to stay alive and not get overwhelmed.
This is further exacerbated when you play on the harder difficulty levels as 1-3 hits can kill you and even though you can position yourself so that you're facing 2-3 opponents your hugeass broadsword is incapable of hitting more than 1 mob at a time (unlike in "The Witcher 1", yet again). This makes combat unenjoyable as you're supposed to be this badass witcher and yet you find yourself constantly running away from groups of enemies as you try to position them to your advantage or lure them into your traps as opposed to being able to take them down toe-to-toe like a proper master swordsman. It's sad when you can beat a game of this nature by only using 2 buttons in combat: dodge/roll and your attack button.
In sum, despite the great story and characters I couldn't play more than 10 hours or so due to the boring and uninspired combat: it isn't enough for a game to have a fantastic story (and characters), it also has to have solid gameplay or people will get frustrated and stop playing.
