Wasteland 2 is a decent CRPG, Game is worth playing especially if you loved the old Fallout games and wish Van Buren was real.
The character creation is intimidating at first, but the manual will explain things. For the most part it avoids having any single attribute as a dump stat, although charisma and luck come close. The skill system could use some work. Three dialogue skills is two too many, and a lot of non-combat skills are just various ways to open loot crates, although there are several cases where high repair or demolitions are needed to progress in a quest. Strangely, your attributes only affect your derived stats - the majority of which are sadly hidden from you - but have no effect on your skills.
Combat is a huge part of this game, and while it is fun it's also rather simple. It uses a turn based system similar to Fallout, but you get control of each member of your party. There's an ambush attack similar to overwatch from XCOM which is pretty useful, but there aren't any aimed shots except for headshots, which are pretty boring. The weapons are seriously imbalanced, with assault rifles becoming really good about 1/3 of the way through, and godlike in the end-game.
The quest design is decent; there are a handful of major quests in both areas of the game that are pretty complex and fulfilling to solve but the majority of them are short and combat focused. The quests in the first half are more polished while the back half feels rushed and incomplete.
PROS
The game successfully incorporates tips and training pointers as you progress early on in the game. Rather than have to go through boring tutorials, you learn along the way.
Absolutely loving the Ambush option available when you encounter enemies. Makes for excellent strategy and placement and forces you to consider approaches for maximum benefits as you encounter enemies later on.
The Unity Engine is nice looking, with details in landscapes.
The game is realistic in that you need to be prepared to take on encounters by having clear lines of fire along with readied weapons. Shooting an enemy who's in front of another friend isn't a good idea...
A planned approach with players who have specific perks like lockpicking, etc are beyond valuable early on in the game.
The devs have a wicked sense of humour with very colourful language all-around in the game...
CONS
-When you are investigating in real-time an area, I find the map option lacking. There is no map function already built into your display. You can alternate to the map by pressing 'm' but I'd rather have it as part of the overall picture itself as you move your characters around.
-Some of the penalities associated with shooting are not realistic. I have one merc crouched while another one behind him is standing up firing with a rifle and he still manages to friendly fire the guy in front of him. Stupid, and the devs should have taken this into account.
-Some of the shooting mechanics are way off. I have a merc with a rifile crouched who cannot take a shot at an enemy who is diagonally across from me.
-The AP for rabbits is ridiculously overgenerous. They can scamper across half the screen and still carry out an attack.
-The enemy AI seems to have crazy high AP...
-No regional Pricing for India I need to wait for a year to buy at suitable price.

This is a fork of the open source freeware game Pioneer, which is in itself a remake of Elite II. Try Pioneer for free and then of you enjoy it, buy this, as it looks and sounds a lot better.
The graphics have been massively improved as has the soundtrack. The game goes for a retro 80's feel (right down to the Cold War In Space scenario) and the optional filters that make it look like a 80's sci fi film or its being played on a cathode monitor!
The universe and the individual planets look wonderful and there is a plethora of stuff to do. As with the original elite, the intial progress in the game is extremely slow, but once you gain traction there is a fantastic and absorbing range of activities, you can be a pirate, an interstellar taxi driver, a trader or fight for one of the factions. There's no overarching plot as such, but your imagination can build your own as you play.
For the price, this represents better value for money than E:D by a long chalk (and you can land on fantastically rendered planets NOW).
The only problem is that it is still a little bit buggy. I cannot load a saved game from the start page, I have to begin a new game, play for 10-15 minutes and then load my older saved game which is a bit of a pain. There's the occasional CTD to, and the graphics can lag a bit when you don't expect them to (and likewise be extramely smooth when there's a lot going on)
The game is soon to be updated, hopefully to iron out the glitches and push it closer to beta. If you like space trading games, this is definitely one of the better ones that I have tried.

Only scratched the surface with this game with 12 hrs under my belt, but with Jagged Alliance 2 and Fallout as all time favourites, I come in with high expectations.
So far, the verdict is "meh". The story is beginning to grind and the repetitive gameplay is a letdown. This game came out with massive hype and after 12 hrs I find myself getting bored.
PROS
The game successfully incorporates tips and training pointers as you progress early on in the game. Rather than have to go through boring tutorials, you learn along the way.
Absolutely loving the Ambush option available when you encounter enemies. Makes for excellent strategy and placement and forces you to consider approaches for maximum benefits as you encounter enemies later on.
The Unity Engine is nice looking, with details in landscapes.
The music that plays in the background during the game suits the theme. Reminds me of Borderlands a bit.
The game is realistic in that you need to be prepared to take on encounters by having clear lines of fire along with readied weapons. Shooting an enemy who's in front of another friend isn't a good idea...
A planned approach with players who have specific perks like lockpicking, etc are beyond valuable early on in the game.
The devs have a wicked sense of humour with very colourful language all-around in the game...
CONS
-When you are investigating in real-time an area, I find the map option lacking. There is no map function already built into your display. You can alternate to the map by pressing 'm' but I'd rather have it as part of the overall picture itself as you move your characters around.
- I couldn't find a quick quest button that I could hit and view my current quests.
-Some of the penalities associated with shooting are not realistic. I have one merc crouched while another one behind him is standing up firing with a rifle and he still manages to friendly fire the guy in front of him. Stupid, and the devs should have taken this into account.
-Some of the shooting mechanics are way off. I have a merc with a rifile crouched who cannot take a shot at an enemy who is diagonally across from me.
-The AP for rabbits is ridiculously overgenerous. They can scamper across half the screen and still carry out an attack.
-The enemy AI seems to have crazy high AP at times.
- Now 12 hours into the game, the combat is getting repetitive. Most of the enemies I face have underpowered weapons, like a handgun while I have long range guns. The recipe of 'ambush/send in snipers first' first proved a success and is now kind of boring.
- The shotgun is a useless weapon so far. You need to have an enemy directly next to you in order for it to work, it seems.
- After a while the story starts appearing convoluted with far too many subplots to keep track. Going from one area with plants overruning the joint to another that has tribal warfare between different clans, I sort of tuned out at one point.
- A lot of plot is demonstrated through clicking NPCs which becomes a bit tedious after a while.
- The voice acting is alright but the quality sounds a bit amateurish at times, as if the recordings were done on the cheap. As well, it's obvious that actors were recycled among characters.
- At its current price level, it isn't worth it. Around 20$ I'd consider buying it.
-I've had one crash so far when exiting and hope this isn't something that happens again...
Verdict so far? With its current price tag, this game doesn't offer much out of the way of other games. The gameplay is proving a bit tedious and keeping up with the objectives and story is beginning to prove boring. Unless it's 20$ on sale, consider skipping this.

A western themed turn-based strategy title by CreativeForge Games, Hard West was released during the latter months of 2015. Originally funded on Kickstarter, this title surpassed the goal of $70,000 CAD and reached over $90,000 by the end of the campaign. The nearly 4,500 backers were not disappointed by the game that they helped fund, and to this day Hard West has been an overall success despite some outcry about the reaction shot, a feature that replaces the overwatch mechanic from XCOM, which has been the only real controversy surrounding the title.
Taking place in a heavily fictionalized American Old West setting, the story of Hard West is one that's completely unique to the title itself, and also one that takes a strange turn at the very beginning. Starting off, the player will find themselves playing the father of Warren, who is just a boy at the time, as him and his family set off down the Oregon Trail. As misfortune would have it, the family hits a series of hardships that take Warren's mother from him early, and leaves his father understandably distraught. Soon, Warren grows up, his father becomes stricken with a mysterious curse that seems permanent and as such he abandons his son, believing that he will have better fortune without him. Of course, this is not the case, and Warren finds himself in the middle of bloody battles between outlaws and demonic forces.
The story has its up and down moments, as it not only follows the adventures of Warren, but also his father and a few other characters as the scenarios branch off in different directions. This is really a take-it-or-leave-it feature, although the game is split into 8 total scenarios with 40 some odd missions that lay within them. The title would fair better by sticking to one or two storylines, rather than trying to weave in the tales of various characters that Warren interacts with throughout his campaign; the result ends up with a story that's more convoluted than it needs to be, and players may see themselves losing interest during the latter half of the game.
Not only told through comic-styled cutscenes, the story unfolds through a lot of reading material within the main portion of the game. Players will travel around a base map, where various locations can be revealed and visited; some will lead to fights, some will have you mining for gold or looking for treasure, some places are weapon shops or supply stores, and some are just there to add depth to the campaigns. Overall, the writing is very well done and completely immersing, and it never feels like a chore to visit all of the locations, although it's not a requirement. When the player gets into the heart of a battle, the map changes to a standard turn-based strategy overhead view of the player and AI characters. Each battle map is highly detailed, with tons of blood, gore, satanic rituals, and plenty of buildings and obstacles to remind you that you're still in the American Old West.
If you've played XCOM: Enemy Unknown, then the mechanics in Hard West will be familiar to you. At any given time, you will control 1-4 characters, each with their own health bar, luck bar, and action points to use for movement and fighting. The gameplay relies heavily on cover, some trial and error, as well as some tactical thinking. The difficulty isn't as high as what's present in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, but with that being said do not be misled into believing that Hard West is an easy turn-based strategy title; especially if you turn on Ironman Mode, which sees to it that you restart a scenario instead of returning to the previous checkpoint if your main character, or entire party, dies. The good thing here is that there are hardly any crazy critical hit chances, unlike in XCOM, which makes the gameplay more fair.
On the flip-side, the gameplay can be extremely slow and at times even tedious. This is due to the fact that you must wait for each character, whether player or AI controlled, to finish their entire animation before being able to flip to another character, or perform another action; whether it's shooting, reloading, moving, or consuming an item. Once you've reached your 7th-ish hour, these small seconds end up feeling like small eternities, especially during the AI's turn. It should also be mentioned here that Hard West has a habit of freezing during the pre-battle menu, where you outfit your crew with guns, consumables, relics, and cards; the latter being another unique feature to the game that gives each member of your posse various perks, abilities, and stat increases, depending on the five cards you select for them. In my experience, during the later parts of the campaign the framerates also took a huge dive, going from a smooth, consistent 144 FPS down to 20-40 FPS.
Despite the numerous flaws that it does have, Hard West is still a solid turn-based strategy title with a unique plot and premise that anyone who enjoys twisted westerns should give a chance. There are a total of three difficulties per scenario, Ironman mode, Injury mode, and a ton of modifiers that can be enabled to spice up the gameplay even further. The battle maps are absolutely wonderful to look at, some are brimming with fire, blood, and occult rituals, while others house large wooden buildings, cacti, sand, and many other items that are standard in western type games. Although sometimes tedious and frustrating due to its slow nature, the gameplay is still fun and addictive. Where Hard West really shines though, is within its fantastic storyline and deep dialogue. Did I also mention that the twangy, memorable soundtrack is also absolutely incredible?

Tactical gem with some flaws. I'd recommend everyone with a slight interest in tactical games to check this moderate priced game.
: Hard West plays in a dirty, gritty, and gruesome wild west setting with steampunk attitude and a supernatural twist. It starts bad for your character, and turns worse. There is no reason to be optimistic here, the question is not whether to die or not, it's how long you have left to live. The story is divided in 8 (nonlinear) chapters, 4 of which comprise the "main" story, 1 is a prequel and 3 tell the stories of alternative chars you encounter during your journey. This is without a doubt the excelling feature of the game, underlined by:
: The cel shading/graphic novel look is absolutely masterful and sets the tone for the experience. Absolutely serviceable and nothing to not like. Call of Juarez comes to mind, not the worst reference i guess. The voice acting and cutscenes are top notch, and nobody expects a wide array of sound effects in a game which revolves around shooting i guess.
: There are two levels of gameplay, the world map and the tactical encounters. World map plays roguelike, with your decisions having immediate and permanent consequences. There is no way to save in this game, except the autosave at the beginning and the end of an encounter.
There is very little randomness involved, and very little room for errors. "Luck", instead, is a ressource. Bullets always hit, unless the target's "luck" is bigger than the shooter's chance to hit (unless it's 100% of course), which in turns leads to luck being depleted accordingly, and recovering luck is very hard or painful (gettig hit restores character's luck).  Cover is of utmost importance (reduces enemies' CtH and damage), standing in the open and allowing the enemy to flank you ends in certain defeat, at least in "hard" mode. Every turn has to be planned carefully with the knowledge that the same rules apply to the enemy as well. If you manage to surround the enemy without exposing your vulnerable back yourselves, you win. Make a mistake, and you have to restart the encounter. In Ironman Mode, death of a "essential" character makes you start the chapter from scratch. Surviving a difficult encounter is very rewarding, and defeat turns into "i won't make this mistake again".
Every character can use two weapons at the same time, which can be swapped without penalties. Ammunition is endless, but reloading uses up 1 action point (each character has 2). Furthermore each character can use 2 consumables (healing items or "increases aim at the cost of max health" etc.), and ONE talisman, which is an item with a strong passive bonus (+10 aim and +4 sight for example). Every chapter has three "trinkets" to unlock (weapons, talismans or consumables), which can be bought at the "Fate Trader" in every other chapter afterwards.
Difficulty is very well tuned, and since there is very little randomness, the outcome is always depending on your tactical expertise. There are several built in mods that can customize it to your liking, such as "replenish a little luck each turn" or "every hit with at least 2 damage causes a wound".
There is little to no progression in the game. Every chapter requires you to manage your gold and your inventory, and an additional ressource, which differs from chapter to chapter. There is no experience, HOWEVER beating an encounter unlocks an additional slot for "cards". Cards are found at random during your journey and are mostly randomized. Like characters, they don't carry over between chapters. Every card has an inherent bonus ("+2 movement" or "+5 aim"), and a unique passive or active skill (like "deal 5 damage to a character not protected by sunlight"). Active skills use luck as a ressource as well. If you manage to gather cards according to a good poker hand (4 of a kind, royal flush etc.) you unlock a powerful set bonus.
Loading screens are rare and very fast, however, as others have described here, sometimes opening a menu, a trade screen or the card interface leads to increasingly long freezes, sometimes up to a few minutes, probably due to a memory hole, which can turn into an annoyance since you can't save at will.
Post Scriptum: The DLC is absolutely worth its money as well. It ramps up difficulty a lot (modifiers don't apply here), i nearly f**ked up, confident as i was, after starting the scenario on Ironman and with Injuries enabled. The card system has been replaced by a body parts system, which is basically the same, with the exception that there is no randomness involved, all body parts can be bought or unlocked through decisions on the world map. Set bonuses are a little less transparent, though, since you have to search a little to assemble "4 of a kind" since the static passive bonuses are spread instead of tied to a column or row. There are 4 "golem" recipes, each needing 5 specific body parts to unlock their powerful set bonuses. You probably won't be able to assemble them in your first playthrough, since it needs careful planning which specific recipe to aim for.
The length of the DLC is ~1,5- 2 of the "old" scenarios, there are about 7 or 8 tactical encounters in it, some of which are optional, but this increases the difficulty of the ironman mode a lot. Also, there is no accessible Fate Trader, every playthrough you start from scratch, there are no permanent unlocks.
The story is a mixture of Frankenstein and slave liberation, the main protagonists are the aptly named "Libertee", a wounded ex-slave, and the doctor that turns her into his "monster". Perspective changes multiple times between the two which makes ressource-, inventory- and card management very hard. The scenario starts at the end of the story with the final encounter in the quarry, and then tells the two earlier sub plots culminating in the grand finale. Everyone who liked Hard Wets will almost certainly enjoy "Scars of Freedom" as well.

Fun game: atractive setting, great voice-over, ok graphics and sound. In almost every aspect, this game is like a simplified version of a couple of genres, particularly squad focused turn-based games.
You play Hard West in chapters, so progression is not something you should focus on (don't get attached to that loot). That is bad from a classic RPG perspective, but is a decision that also keeps thing simpler.
The game divides itself between turn-based combat and a "choose your own adventure" exploration of the map. The latter one comes with a different mechanic attached to each chapter, but nothing really innovative enough for you to remember. Sooner than later, that mechanic becomes a little chore you do while waiting for the next combat (or looking for the special items hidden in each chapter).
The combat is fun, you have a lot of different guns and items to try, some amazing abilities (that you add to the gunslingers via poker cards you get in the game, allowing you to mix and match with gusto), and a "luck system" that you will either hate or love (luck equals mana, you needed it for the abilities but is also depleted when enemies miss you).
Difficulty wise, you have three options, plus ironman. I found normal to be too easy, but hard, with ironman mode enabled, was rage inducing. Sadly, the sweet spot might lie somewhere in the middle.
I would recommend Hard West to anyone wishing to try turn-based "X-Com lite" (very lite) combat, in a very nice Wild West setting.

I don’t think Tim Schafer needs much introduction as his brilliant works speak for him. But can Broken Age be put among his best creations? In my humble opinion, it definitely can. All the characteristic features are present: captivating storyline, original setting, interesting (and many quite absurd) characters, dialogues filled with humour, top-notch voice acting, good music…
Broken Age is a story of a girl and a boy, each one with unique circumstances, that try to escape from their destiny, but the way this story is told is unlike any other you may have ever read. I don’t want to spoil the game by revealing the details, but, if you like the games of Double Fine Productions or good adventure games in general, I can pretty much guarantee you won’t be disappointed. I, for one, have barely noticed how I’ve spent 20 hours playing, reading, laughing, solving puzzles and, most of all, enjoying the ride.	Surely, if you want to, you will likely find some weak points in Broken Age, but as it never was my intention, I can truthfully say that those 20 hours were like a breath of fresh air.
Highly recommended. Period.

TL;DR If you love turn based combat games, and a little RNG doesn’t bother you, this game is a must!
Pros:
+ Sound design (truly blown away by the music, sound effects)
+ Great voice acting (narrorator only)
+ Interesting and engaging plot
Cons:
+ Tedious non-combat sections
+ No overwatch
+ Frustrating/unpredictable RNG luck system (explained below)
Hard West is a turn based combat game with a little bit of resource management thrown in. To avoid any spoilers, I won’t reveal any of the plot, but trust me, it’s engaging and good. The sound design in the game completely floored me. From the beautiful almost LOTR-esque music for the epic moments, to the sounds of the various weapons, it’s all masterfully done. I even turned the volume up louder in my headphones just to enjoy the atmosphere of the game. Also, if you thought the narrorator in Bastion was good, give this guy a try, he's brilliant.
The parts of the game outside of combat are relatively engaging, but I found myself rushing to complete them to read more of the story or get back to combat. The core game mechanics were pretty disinteresting in these sections and it felt a bit tedious at times with one mission in particular, and less worthwhile. Example: In Xcom researching and building facilities can add ways you can find more combat areas, or give you things to use in combat. This is not so much the case in Hard West. (aside from being able to purchase or occasionally being awarded a strong gun or other equipable)
The one thing these sections do have going for them, is the “loadout” page(s). It’s not under detailed, not over detailed, it’s just right. At no point did I think it took too long to build my characters to the exact specs I wanted, nor did I feel like there weren’t enough options for me. Additionally, there’s a unique buff system that gives different buffs depending on what cards you give your characters. They can even get a bonus buff if the cards you give your character form a poker hand (pair, straight, flush). It’s a pretty cool addition.
Combat is great in this game with ONE relatively major caveat; luck system. The luck system determines how likely your character will be missed when fired upon (among other things), and is honestly extremely unpredictable and can be frustrating. I should also note that there is no overwatch, or way to have your character fire automatically when an enemy approaches too closely. For the most part, neither of these problems will really bother you as long as you are careful with your character placements. As with any turn based combat game, over extending and getting caught will suck really hard for you.
All in all, I would highly recommend this game, even at full price. The frustrations that can be caused by the slow/tedious non-combat sections, luck system, and no overwatch, are blown away by the sound aesthetics, great plot, and solid turn based combat. You can buy it or not buy it, “Either way, you’re as good as dead.”
Happy gaming!

Alan Wake is a game that is easily recommendable, even after all those many years since release. For one the game still looks gorgeous and the dense atmosphere is going to murder you ;)
In Alan Wake you are taking on the role of the titular "hero". The gameplay consists of you running around in 3rd person, lighting up enemies with your trusty flashlight and then shooting them till they disappear. That's pretty much it. The game is strictly linear, there is no open world, there is little room to explore (but enough in my opinion) and the path is always clear. The gameplay will be the same for the whole duration more or less. You get different guns and stuff, but the core gameplay always revolves around light and darkness and your boomsticks. I just wish you could disable the slow mo camera swings when you avoid an attack. These happen way too frequently. Combat in general is probably also the greatest weakness of Alan Wake, it is pretty repetitive and some people will be bothered by that. However, I think that this is not a game you play because of its great combat mechanics, this is a game you play because of the story and the atmosphere.
The game consists of episodes. Each episode can be brute-forced and completed pretty quickly if you don't die. If you take the time to explore, however, you can find secret staches, manuscript pages and other collectibles like TV shows or radio broadcasts. Those are especially worth it. The game just oozes atmosphere and is set up like an episodic thriller that leans heavily on novels, which makes sense, since Alan Wake is a writer. It's dark, it's mysterious and full of surprises and really, really good story telling and voice over. It's rare to find a game that has so much charme. It just feels like the devs were really into this as well. The attention to detail is testament to that. Alan Wake invites you on an emotional, psychological suspense/horror trip, but does not rely on cheap jump scares to make you feel uneasy.
What's also great is that you can watch and listen to any cutscenes or cellectibles you've found from the main menu after you've encountered them.
If you like great stories and thrillers in particular, pick this one up, as it's absolutely unique.

50% soundtrack, 50% gameplay. An addictively enjoyable psycho-murder simulator. I think without the music this would still be a great game, but with it it's hypnotically captivating when playing and inevitably replaying stages over and over, while you absolutely, positively, gotta kill every motherf*cker in the room (accept no substitutes) without dying.
For the most part if you get hit once you die, so reflexes and timing are essential in making it through alive. Occasionally if a guy shoots you who is far away you might survive if he hits you in the arm, later on you get a mask that allows you  to take a hit before you die. In fact there are a ton of masks which you unlock that grant you special abilities, like being able to kill people with one punch, or that make the enemies unable to hear your gunshots if they are in another room (really useful).
Later on the levels have 2 or 3 areas to clear, but if you die after clearing the first area you will restart at the beginning of the second area so you don’t have to restart the whole level over again, which could have become really tedious to the player.
A few things that are annoying are  sometimes the enemies get stuck in doors or bug out and start spinning around in one spot. Also all the boss fights are really annoying, you will die (a lot).
The story is interesting while also being kinda pretentious and ambiguous. The second game fixes some of this with more backstory and details into what may be going on. I don’t imagine that many people are playing through for the story though.
If you enjoy good music or killing a metric f*ckton of bad guy pixels in increasingly gory ways,  then you should hit this up and imagine you’re Ryan Gosling in a chicken mask.

Blackwell Deception finally kicks it production quality up to the level the series deserves. Audio and art are significantly improved and the story preps for a grand finale. To spoil the review, it is a great game.
In the previous three games in the series, Joey’s voice actor sounded like he was speaking into a tin can.  It was the biggest glaring flaw in an otherwise great series.  No more, Joey’s voice is now clear and audible. No more issues with weird audio, everything, even background music, comes through clearly. Voicing acting issues are somewhat diminished with characterization that is now more suitable for the actors. Yes, it is kind of like nailing the hammer, but it works.
Story plotting continues to improve as well.  We are not just randomly running into characters that lead to a case, every interaction is purposeful. Theming is well founded as the story now relates lost souls to people trying to find themselves.  Moreover, the lore and mythos in the game builds further without overwhelming the story too much.  Sidekick Joey takes on an even larger role than before and is not just a source of sardonic whit.  His character’s past is hinted at but the details are not overworked, you understand the character with just few lines and that’s enough.  Previously, Rosangela was motivated by threat of insanity, now the story has developed in a way to motivate and give her a personal interest in the cases. She no longer feels like someone you are dragging along, but takes on a proper protagonist role.
Overall, there are no longer any outstanding flaws requiring justification for a recommendation.  The games formula works and is well written and produced.  At this point, the only reason a point and click adventure fan should not play this game is because they still need to play the previous games in the series.

My review is about the entire Blackwell series, not about a specific episode.
TL;DR - highly recommended if you're looking for good quest games.
Although being quest series, the Blackwell series isn't difficult comparing to other games in that genre as there aren't logic puzzles to solve. However, the games don't suffer from one flaw that exists in many quests, and that is excessive use of items. In some quest games you usually stack up a lot of items and end up trying every combination of item and something clickable on the screen until you find that absurd combination that makes you progress. The Blackwell series doesn't have that flaw as items aren't the main part of the game. Also, when places become irrelevant you can't access them anymore, which also prevents having to go back and try to find something useful in every place that you've been through at the endgame.
The progression in the game is made by combining the abilities of Rosa (or Lauren in Blackwell Unbound) and Joey, which complete each other. Joey can enter locked rooms but cannot interact with anything, and Rosa can do the opposite. Only by combining their abilities you will make progress. There's also a built in search engine inside a game in which you have to use in order to progress, which makes you feel that you're doing detective work and not just trying to figure out how to use your inventory.
The plot becomes "bigger" in each episode and ends with a grand finale in Blackwell Epiphany, so you don't feel like you're doing that same thing in each game.
I really enjoyed the series and I highly recommend it.

I heartily recommend this game.  It deserves far better than a "Mostly Positive" rating, as it's an absolute hidden gem.
For those that enjoy tactical strategy games like X-com, Blackguards, or the old Fallout games, this is a treat.
The game's setting is thoroughly enjoyable.  Standard spaghetti-western meets the demon invasion from Doom.  The game's structure is both a strength and a weakness.  It's split up into 8 different scenarios (9 with the DLC).  On the plus side, you never risk working yourself into a corner that you can't come back from, and the game has the luxury of throwing all sorts of varied battles, team members, equipment and storylines at you on a consistent basis so you are never bored.  But this stop-start approach means you never get a chance to become too invested in your characters or their struggles, and it doesn't matter how much time or effort you pour into fine tuning your setup, as after another couple of battles the characters are gone and you start from scratch again in the next scenario.  There is a little bit of carryover between scenarios, as you can unlock equipment that is available in each subsequent scenario's Fate Trader merchant.  But nothing beyond that.  Also the way the scenario's are laid out is odd as well.  I ended up accidentally finishing the main path via 4 of the scenarios and blazed through the really hard final battle and got the end credits before I realised I should have tried the other scenarios first.
This structure also limits the usefulness of the injury system the game has.  Basically if your character is wounded in combat (if enabled in-combat using settings, or on the strategic map, more on this later), and you get them to survive the next couple of encounters, they'll end up stronger going forward.  But because of this structure your time to capitalise on these healed injuries is practically nil.  But overall, it was probably the best choice to ensure balance across the game.
The game is split between the tactical battles and a simple strategic map phase, where you explore the countryside, gather supplies and crew, and wind up in different text-exposition encounters where often you must make choices that influence your teams health and wealth.  It's not terribly in-depth, but the different scenario's throw a different mechanism at you constantly so it never seems repetitive.  The writing must be commended as well, baring a liberal sprinkling of spelling and grammar mistakes.
Before each encounter you make sure your team is equipped with up to 2 weapons, 2 consumables, and a trinket.  But even more interesting than that is a "poker-cards" system where you equip each member with up to a full hand (5) of cards, each with different stat boosts and either passive abilities or ones that must be activated in battle.  And you should try to pair up the cards, which each have a suit and a rank (nine, ten, jack, queen, king or joker) and you should try and build the best hand possible to receive additional bonuses.
In battle you expend "luck" to activate these card abilities.  But be careful, as your luck is eroded as you take fire from the enemy.  Though whenever you get hit and loose health, you regain luck.  So this presents all sorts of interesting scenarios where you could move a lucky character out into an exposed position, and although he'll take lots of fire, he likely won't get hit and he can get in a killing blow or two.  In the game there exists cover, either full or half, with half absorbing less damage if the enemy lands a hit.  Although sometimes the cover system would show up some oddities with its pathological pedanticness on line of sight.  Basically you could be outflanking the enemy but you're still slightly in front of them, and your chance to hit is the same as if you were attacking them straight on.  But then as soon as you move slightly over so you're firing directly into their flank or from behind and suddenly your chance to hit shoots up.  A little unrealistic but the rest of the tactical combat is solid.
The difficulty is spot on, with a noticeable bump up in the Scars of Freedom DLC.  I strongly recommend you play on hard with the combat injuries turned on.  I would have went Iron-Man mode, where the death of a main character means you must restart the scenario (not just the battle!) but I'm not that much of a masochist!
So in summary, a solid tactical strategy game, with a grim, demonic setting and plenty of bloody shootouts.  Get it, you won't be disappointed!

I'm a big fan of Fallout 1 & 2 and similar games. When I first started playing Wasteland 2, I enjoyed it. It had a similar feel. Unfortunately, as the game progressed, it just aggravated me. I found myself spending all my time performing useless actions rather than actually playing a game.
There are crates/boxes strewn about everywhere, and nearly every single one is locked/trapped, so you spend a lot of time using skills to open them (which takes several seconds each attempt), having to reload multiple times because the difficulty of each lock/trap seems to be random. They pretty much never have anything useful, so you've just wasted your time. Also, you have to run across the same areas you've already cleared, just to exit the map. Then run BACK across just to turn in a minor quest.
The areas are sprawling, but VERY repetitive. There's relatively little NPC interaction, and most of those are the same, too. I don't know how many times I've gone to a town where they complain about a disease, had to find the local doctor who magically can cure it, but he needs you to go get a specific item to save the day. It creates the illusion of a sandbox as you explore the open world, but most places won't appear on the map until you hit that point in the storyline, no matter how many times you walk over it.
Even the fights got boring quickly. Weapon variety seemed decent at first, but ultimately felt pointless. And the "friendly fire" is ridiculous. I don't mind friendly fire, but it seems almost guaranteed to hit your friend if he's between you and the opponent, even if it doesn't make sense (like if the friend is in a crouched position right in front of the firer, who is standing, and you're firing at someone at a higher elevation).
I got to a point where I thought the game was almost over, and I was excited. Then I discovered I was only about halfway through and got depressed. I considered quitting the game right then, but hoped it would get better in the second half. I should've stopped playing.
Nothing that we haven't already seen before. Some sloppy optimization and graphic design too. Reminds me of Quake Wars: Enemy Territory. Just as boring too, don't waste time with this one.

This atmosphere filled game is a great surprise! I grabbed it at May's "Frontier" Humble Bundle, and I haven't touched any other games yet. I would characterize this game with three words : coherent, atmosphere and engaging.
It's basically a tactical game, à la Final Fantasy Tactics. You can take cover to increase your defense, ricochet bullets off of metallic objects throughout the map, use dark forces to injure enemies, use ruse to surprise the target. The inventivity of this game runs deep, from the mechanisms to the loots you can get.
The campaign makes you move around a map to get useful information on the current scenario. Sometimes, you can interact by buying items, offering bottle of liquor to get precious information, ravage places to weaken the enemy, kill people to increase your bounty... The possibilities are numerous and well inserted in the scenario. In the case where you encounter enemies, you will have to switch to a tactical map, where you'll have to either position yourself silently before engaging the enemies, or accomplish objectives. I was surprised by the variety of those, and how they don't feel generic, like many other games out there. All the objectives are tied to the scenario and make sense. They don't feel like someone threw ideas and tried to make it fit.
You can collect different items, namely cards (giving you bonuses), weapons (with different ranges, ammos and damage), potions, bombs and special bonus items. Some special items are to be collected by using the bonuses cards gives you (one allows you to loot rare weapons on dead bodies, but you tend to lose them after the fight), or by completing hidden tasks throughout the campaign map.
I completed 4 or 5 scenarios in 7 hours, in hard mode. This is about halfway through and I wasn't bored one moment. The art is candy to the eyes and a bit grim, dark.

This is a great indie game. In hell of a lot aspects! If you like RPGs, Tactics or Strategies, if you like rich story with choices that matter, if you like westerns, or clever incorporation of folklore with historic realism and a bit of gore, if you like balanced gameplay with decent challenge, or if you like very well detailed setting and characters, you must play Hard West.
Especially I want to note that mechanics and gameplay are very balanced compared to modern games in general, while having a lot of different features and cherries on cake. Each scenario incorporates a global map to explore, with some special constraints making gameplay a bit different. Locations are waiting to be explored in an old good text-based way with choices. From time to time, battle occurs.
Battles are implemented as a turn-based tactics, where all the characters have 2 action points, up to 2 weapons and some inventory items. While this looks like a straight nostalgic tribute to older games of the genre(s), this is customizable quite a lot with cards, assigned to characters, providing boosts and skills. Here I must warn you - while players are free NOT to use any 'cherries', it is up to us to take the best we can. Thus, I want to specifically point that cards must be carefully set up with weapons, equipment and consumables to create powerful character 'builds' providing more fun and great epic moments during the gunfigts.
For example there is a card that allows a character to perform ricochet shots, using metal objects, cozily distributed over every map. This means, that only 1 character from the posse will be able to perform these shots, and there is not much opportunities to use them often, especially to advantage over normal shot. At first you may wonder - why implementing such a [cool] feature and making it used quite rarely? But playing this game a lot, you may feel that amount of usage of ricochet is just about the perfect, not to make it overpowered, boring or silly; especially when you learn how to use this not only by opportunity, but to make from fighting environment a theatre of massacre of YOUR choice and cunning design.
Another thing that I love a lot - is how carefully lore of Wild West is collected and merged into a fine story with interconnected characters, where historical realism is naturally combined with mystics. Game setting is so realistic, that this alone creates a driving force to explore and enjoy more. I like how some pieces of art bring to the surface, through stories of supernatural characters, naked real human motives. This game succeeds in this, too.
Every small detail and aspect of gameplay fits perfectly, also graphics and music are nice, you will not find much things that could ruin the whole atmosphere and impression. I see here a great work on development side.
This was more than a game for me. I didn't like much westerns before, but now I can reconsider this. Generally I love history and historic games, and knew not so little about Wild West, probably this is why I can appreciate, with what kind of emphasis and warmth had developers created this game. There was even a circus a la Carnivale!
Game has really awoken my interest and old thoughts of everything that happened before and during European expansion there. So overwhelming. People need to know the history, especially violent, cruel and unjust, not to make the same mistakes and to be openminded. Our world is so interesting place to learn about and to draw inspiration from.

'Interrogating' informants? Nah, just shoot them in the head. No need to 'chase' them down. Just shoot them and they'll kneel in place waiting to spill the beans.

50% soundtrack, 50% gameplay. An addictively enjoyable psycho-murder simulator. I think without the music this would still be a great game, but with it it's hypnotically captivating when playing and inevitably replaying stages over and over, while you absolutely, positively, gotta kill every motherf*cker in the room (accept no substitutes) without dying.
For the most part if you get hit once you die, so reflexes and timing are essential in making it through alive. Occasionally if a guy shoots you who is far away you might survive if he hits you in the arm, later on you get a mask that allows you  to take a hit before you die. In fact there are a ton of masks which you unlock that grant you special abilities, like being able to kill people with one punch, or that make the enemies unable to hear your gunshots if they are in another room (really useful).
Later on the levels have 2 or 3 areas to clear, but if you die after clearing the first area you will restart at the beginning of the second area so you don’t have to restart the whole level over again, which could have become really tedious to the player.
A few things that are annoying are  sometimes the enemies get stuck in doors or bug out and start spinning around in one spot. Also all the boss fights are really annoying, you will die (a lot).
The story is interesting while also being kinda pretentious and ambiguous. The second game fixes some of this with more backstory and details into what may be going on. I don’t imagine that many people are playing through for the story though.
If you enjoy good music or killing a metric f*ckton of bad guy pixels in increasingly gory ways,  then you should hit this up and imagine you’re Ryan Gosling in a chicken mask.

UPDATED REVIEW (OSX): This game will not launch in OSX as of January 28, 2017. This issue has been around a while (according to others in the forum) and the developers haven't made any updates to fix it. The development team seems to be on-again-off-again, working on this project now and then rather than consistently. The Windows version is OK, but if you're on Mac, don't waste your money.
OLD REVIEW: This game has made leaps and bounds since the last time I played! The developers have clearly been putting a lot of work into this, and it shows. The game loads much quicker and plays much smoother than ever before. This is a fantastic improvement!
However, there are still a few minor problems. I wasn't able to get my XBox 360 controller to work with the game. The triggers don't work as buttons, so I can't map triggers to weapons and bumpers to yaw/roll. And when I tried to clear one of the joystick axis options, the game crashed  outright.
These are minor bugs, though, and overall the gameplay is quite good. I was a little dissappointed that the "fast travel" mechanism simply blacked out the screen and showed a loading screen. I recall the autopilot actually piloting while you watched your ship travel. I miss that. But I guess I can just as easily fly by myself; the piloting controls are pretty good.
Great job, everyone! I hope a few of these little bugs can be ironed out, but I'm a happy customer regardless.

- Excellent story and design. I loved how you have to choose right away between two different areas and it completely changes the story based on which one you pick.
- Extensive character customization. This may well be the first game set on Earth that actually lets you choose both your nationality and religion. Dunno if that actually DOES anything, but its neat.
- Crafting, modding, and so on is ready from the word go (provided one of your guys is a weaponsmith) and you can immediately use any mods you get.
Cons:
- The combat is horribly stacked against you even on the lowest difficutly. Here's a quick rundown of the issues I had with it:
- I want it to be a rule in games like this that if you have ranged combat, whether its guns or bows or whatever, that your BASIC ammo is unlimited. Especially, and I mean ESPECIALLY, when one of the first areas you go to has zombies that explode upon death and plants that burst the second you get near them. The only way to get past those without getting hurt was to shoot them, which eats up ammo very quickly.
- Some of the fights are so stacked against you it's painful. I get that people want a good fight, but when my four guys are up against four raiders with assault rifles, two throwing dynamite, two more with pistols, and one big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a machine gun in the same fight I might begin to think that this game's difficulty needs to be adjusted a bit. Yes it does come with difficulty settings but here's the thing: I WAS PLAYING ON ROOKIE WHEN THIS HAPPENED! I'm not asking for a free ride here, but for ♥♥♥♥'s sake I did that fight three times and each time my entire team got wiped out within a few rounds because our half of the battlefield is narrow and, again, TWO GUYS THROW BOMBS AT US!
- It seems like my guys miss a hell of a lot. My team had one guy who specialized in energy weapons, one who was good with pistols, another who used shotguns, and a melee specialist. No matter what though, even with crouching, I could sometimes only get about 50% hit chance even at point blank range and this was with them having most of their points in that weapon type.
- Status effects for everyone! This involves combat too, but also those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t plants I mentioned and others. It is way too easy for the enemy to stack up damage over time effects on you. Poisons, bleeding, and other debuffs cause severe difficulty in and out of combat, especially when my healer girl would run out of medkits to keep my crew alive. Yes I get that if you got shot several times its very realistic for you to bleed... but in a game where I fight pod people, giant mutant rabbits, and maggots the size of dogs realism can kiss my big fat♥♥♥♥♥
Overall: Fans of classic 'crush your balls' difficult CRPGs like the original Fallout will enjoy it, but in the end I found it too frustrating to keep going. By all means have some difficult fights, but when every fight is one that can kill the hell out of your team and I wind up resorting to save scumming just to get past them it doesn't exactly make me feel like the heroic lawman of the wastelands. Go the fantasy route and give Pillars of Eternity or Divinity: Original Sin a try instead.

First off, I like this game.

Later, you got even more puzzles that had that "What do I do? What effect did this action have on ANYTHING?" feel. Some puzzles flat-out made no sense. Shay had to rewire a robot using a clue you found on Vella's side of the story. Literally how would Shay know what diagram Vella is seeing? And vice versa? The story felt like it had no real conclusion. It gave no real feelings about the antagonist(s), because they were hardly there. There wasn't even really an end to the game, but rather, the "ending" was told through pictures in the credits with no words. A draw your own conclusion thing, I guess?
Pros:

Cons:
- Act Two

- Backtracking
- No real resolution/conclusion
TL;DR
- Act One good
- Act Two bad
Might be worth it if you use a guide for the puzzles for Act Two, but I don't care enough to replay and find out.

Can I recommend a game that is half good and half bad? No
The story of Broken Age revolves around two children Shay and Vella. Shay is trapped in a spaceship with an overbearing and supressive computer. Vella is trying to fight a monster who the people in town sacrifice maidens to (which includes her). The stories seem disconnected at first but they come together in the second half and blend together. However, I think they work better separately almost. Shay’s story especially is interesting because how the plot implies that he is supressed. He is forced to repeat the same 4 missions twice to learn how he has no agency in his life and, being a kid, he wants to escape and adventure. Vella on the other hand, fights with the villages she encounters almost as much as the monster. She has to convince the people that ANYONE should be sacrificed. Plus, it’s creative as it brings up characters that I remember for their characters rather than simply “person x”.
However, the game really breaks apart as the stories combine and I think it loses a lot of steam. There is a whole backstory revealed dealing with pretty much Hitler (I’m not joking) and it gets just super complicated and unfocused. The first part was about the characters and the surroundings but the second half tries way to hard to make the mystery big and super interesting while I liked it fine as it was.
It’s an adventure game so the story revolves around talking to characters, collecting puzzle pieces, and solving puzzles. Again, the first half of the game does this well. There is a puzzle before you. You have like 3 things. Go and get the thing. Some might say easy but they were logical.
You need an egg.
Where is it? In a nest.
You can’t reach it. Where can you do?
Get a ladder. It keeps falling.
What to do? Put floating shoes on it.
Bam. Done.

The second half ♥♥♥♥ed that up by giving you contrived solutions to WTF puzzles.
You need a metal thingy
Get a schematic and give it to a guy who knows about sand
Put it in front of a tree
Make the tree throw up sap to harden it
Use that as a mold for the metal guy
What the ♥♥♥♥? What sort of ♥♥♥♥ing logic is that? And each person is in a different ♥♥♥♥ing room so you backtrack not knowing what step is next. A lot of the dialogue doesn’t activate until you actually get a specific item so then you have to go talk to everyone again hoping to find the one person that can solve your♥♥♥♥♥♥ It worked in the first half because of it’s simplicity and logic but they lost it in the second half.

Broken age is the game that really got kickstarter started for games. While it's not the first game, it helped opening the floodgates. And a lot of great games have come out of kickstarter. So, how does Broken Age hold up?
Let me just start this review with saying that no, I've not actually beaten the game.. And I don't feel like doing so, despite having less than 1/3 of it left. That's probably saying a lot about the game.
Broken Age has a very distinct art style. While it might not have the most advanced graphics on the market, it has its own visual identity. If it looks good or not, well that's up to each and every one of us to decide, but the screenshots are representative. The game looks like it does in the screenshots. Personally, I'm a fan of it, I think it's a very pleasing art style. Some of the animations do look a bit off though, and the character models sometimes look like they're not really a part of the world, but overlayed on it. For the most part though, it looks good.
One can't talk about Broken Age without mentioning the voice acting. It's excellent. The voice actors all convey the personalities of the characters really well, and it does not sound phoned in. Looking at the list of voice actors this is not surprising though, these are veteran voice actors. The soundtrack is no slouch either, and while it's unlikely to be remembered as one of the all time greatest, it works well with the game, and actually sounds really good.
Broken age follows two different characters, Vella & Shay, who live very different lives. Vella grew up in a colourful fantasy world, terrorized by a big beast who demands a sacrifice of maidens (and she is one of the maidens who's going to be sacrificed), while Shay lives on board a space ship that caters to his every needs. And never the two shall meet. Or so it feels at least, during half the game. The two characters are entirely separate, and their stories don't seem to relate in any meaningful way. And this, I feel, was a mistake. As the two stories are so disconnected from each other, it's easy to just focus on one character at a time and ignoring the other. The stories do of course end up crossing each other, but then they split again.
I found Vella to both have a more compelling story, and to be a more interesting character. Shay just felt a bit bland, where when I was playing through Vella's story I found the game interesting and it motivated me to push forward.
This is a traditional adventure game, in the vein of the games made by Lucas Arts in the mid 90's. Puzzles are mostly inventory based. Find the item that goes with the other item or character, which gives you an item that you then can use to solve a puzzle that gives you another item. It's all very traditional, and there's nothing wrong with that. The issue are with the puzzles. During the first half of the game you're mostly confined to small areas with few items, so even if you can't figure out a logical way for the items to fit together, you don't have many combinations to worry about, so brute-forcing puzzles is easy. During the second half the puzzles gets more involved, but they also don't make much sense. Even after having solved some puzzles, I don't know how I was supposed to know what to do. Moon logic is often used to describe puzzles like these, puzzles that don't make much logical sense, and there's a good amount of moon logic in Broken Age. The worst offenders are the puzzles that require you to use one character in order to find hints on how to solve puzzles for the other character, where the two characters have no way of communicating with each other. It does not make much sense to switch to another character in order to solve a puzzle when they have no way of interacting. The game also does not communicate that you should do this, and in the first half of the game it teaches you that you don't need to switch characters to solve puzzles.
While Broken Age is by no means terrible, I feel that I can't recommend it. The moon logic puzzles in the second act and a story where only one half feels compelling just killed it for me. Had the stories been more intertwined and the puzzles better, this game could have been a winner, but as it stands, it just feels like wasted potential.

Brilliant game if you like a gritty, demonic-themed Western setting and turn-based combat.
Has a "strategic map" (where you make story choices and collect equipment and team members) and a tactical combat level that is remotely reminiscent of "XCOM" (which is why this is popping up so often in reviews - but that's like comparing every RTS to "Command&Conquer").
The game has a few entirely new game mechanics that are nicely designed to fit the setting (such as "luck" as a defense mechanism, and collecting cards and combining them into poker hands to give your characters new abilities).
Also, there's great story writing - this is not an RPG where one is endlessly leveling up one's character, but one is rather following a well-written story with different main characters.
The only downside is the various Linux bugs that require workarounds - I assume the game is not really being maintained on Linux.  So if you want to play on Linux I suggest to have a look at the "Known Issues" topic in the Forum before you buy to see if you think these are going to work for you.

IMO best turn based tactics game on the market.
Theme and narrative are fantastic; weird west is underused and this is an excellent take on it.
Combat is a great take on the standard formula. Difficult to explain but the system they use is much less RNG based than other such games. Special abilities are useful but there aren't overmany, items and weapons are varied with perhaps a little too many objectively better/worse weapons but seeing all these cool old-timey guns is worth the small bother of selling superfluous items.
One thing to bear in mind is that there is a bug (I think it's a memory leak but don't quote me) whereby the longer you play the longer it takes to load, up to the point where opening the inventory screen takes a second instead of instantaneously. Restarting fixes this but it is annoying and would have stopped me playing were this not such a compelling game.
Aside from the combat there are text adventure segments with consequences as to how that chapter plays out - these are Fighting Fantasy type choose your own adventure which have a different mechanic in each chapter. E.g. in Chapter 1 text is used to follow your mining venture and determines how much money you'll get; in the Inquisitor side chapter, the text choices determine how bloody a path you carve and the fights you take while in others it'll be how many soldiers you lose, how insane your character becomes, how and when to use mind powers.
One last point, the DLC is completely worth it if you like the main game, one extra chapter about one and a half times as long as most of the others. This game has me wishing there was more.

Wow.  Rarely has a game started so promisingly and ended so poorly.  Like many games in this era, Hard West seeks "hard, but fair" gameplay that encourages careful decision making.  They nailed the "hard" part, but I guess "fair" got lost along the way.
The game's combat system revolves around classic cover mechanics, and a new luck mechanic.  It works like this: if you're in cover, you'll be harder to hit, and will take less damage when you get it.  If someone tries to shoot you and you have enough luck, your luck gets spent and the shot misses.
It works well for the first sccenario (mini-campaign), but then you get introduced to new scenarios and something fundamentally breaks.  Here's an example.  You spot an enemy in the distance.  It's the last one on the board of dozens brought down, and you've already killed the vicious boss of the level.  You carefully move your hero with the most hitpoints and luck into cover halfway across the map from the enemy.  The game has taught you that even if your hero gets hit, this cover will prevent substantial damage and you can take out this one last enemy without too much trouble.  In response, the enemy does not try to flank you or otherwise act tactically. I can only recommend this game under the condition that it actually starts, but when it does, it's a romp, but the style isn't the same as some other games of this genre.
Firstly, you have to really know what role you've assigned for yourself.  As a tank, you're not as fast (duh!) as the others, but have armor up the ying yang.  That being said, it's still easy for assassin-types to get a backstab on you, killing you instantly at full health (which I find BS, but whatever).  I can understand that to a point, but it's a little too frequent for my taste.  Still, it's survivable if you have a team that's willing to stay by your side.
That aside, this is REALLY BASED ON TEAM EFFORT and NOT ON INDIVIDUAL EFFORT!   I can't stress this enough.  My first (and as of this writing) only experience in this game wasn't pleasent.  My entire team didn't know the importance of objectives AND sticking close together.  All they seemed to care about were ganks and nothing else.
Respawns don't take that long, which is a plus and a negative.  WHy negative?  Well, if the enemy has a lead, it's very hard to recover without some sort of cooperation from your team.
Still, the game is fairly fast-paced and the action is actually okay, if you can ever get into a game, that is.  The matchmaking system needs improvement, especially for new players.  The tutorial offers a gateway into how to play, but it's limited and lacking in a few areas.  This is easily solved as there's a coop mode vs AI that I found when you hit play (just click the right arrow when selecting the ONLY ARENAS available and you'll see it).
The game is still lacking other modes of play, but it's still young, so I'm expecting to see more varients come alive soon.
All in all, a good game if you can find a good group of friends you can trust to watch your tanky♥♥♥♥♥  Otherwise, struggle with some working mechanics and hope you don't get matched up with people who feel ganks = win all the time.  Also a good game if you can get it to actually connect to the server.

This game has literally no flow. It's stiff beyond belief and they don't seem to have fixed that judging by the trailer. (No way I am downloading it again to see if they improved it if the trailer looks basically the same)
They don't seem to have improved the UI either, which is attrocious. It blocks about 2/5 of your view just to show your abilities and meters, which could have been at the bottom of the screen or in the corners. It's way harder to follow your UI like that. Some people have compared it to WoW add-ons, and even then it was just the health and mana meters along with possible class specific resources, not your damn abilities that you have to keep a track of. Plus you don't really need to be pixel specific in WoW either, there is a permanent lock on there.
Oh well, maybe the UI is just a nitpick and the rest of the game is good, right? No...
As I mentioned, it feels incredibly stiff and they didn't improve that one bit. Animation quality isn't terrible honestly, for the most part since most since all characters kind of float around when they try to sprint. That was a nitpick though. What isn't a nitpick is how hard it is to hit people. You have to be incredibly precise with your targeting, timing and position. Looking and running around are also extremely slow and heavy that I would end up feeling heavy on my actual shoulders after playing.
Another thing is the flow of the game, or should I say the breaks the game wants you to take while playing. There are combos that you can execute on melee characters mostly that take a while to master and are not easy to learn either, kind of like a fighting game but without weird and complicated button combinations, just hard to execute combos due to the reasons mentioned above. It could take a while to perfectly execute a combo on a standing, motionless AI opponent that only gets up. Okay, you executed a combo, was it satisfying though? Naaah, the combos are also incredibly stiff and don't feel like combos at all. Connecting light punches and light kicks in Tekken 3 was more satisfying and less stiff than this. Why is that? Well, most of the combos end up with your opponent dead in two-three hits so OP character or your opponent on the floor where they are untouchable by most attacks, can't get up fast so both your opponent and you have to wait for the character to get up (which takes forever) and then having to repeat that process.
There are ranged characters as well, but they manage to be even more boring than the rest. Throwing your abilities and bullets around is boring and you can't kite since turning is stiff on all characters anyway. Shoot and run? Might as well forget about it unless your opponents are either new or brain dead. Also the targeting is hard for them as well.
The maps are generic, so nothing to complain or praise them for. Well, technically if something is generic it's not good, but whatever.
Finally, my biggest problem despite all that is the idea of wanting to make it more like a MOBA and adding Fog of War in the mix, which just doesn't work in a third, or first person game. Surely you must know that, right? Even actual third person MOBAs like SMITE know that and its view distance is huge compared to this.
First of all, it looks like terrible popping, which asthetically is hideous. Next on the list, it's so short that you have to be kissing your opponents to keep an eye on them. Combined with that comes the fact that you can shoot out of it if you are playing a sniper but nobody can see you if there is no one nearby, so you freely stay invisible and too far away to get caught in time since everyone moves slowly. And finally, it's not just the snipers that can take advantage of it but everyone. There isn't any temporary lock or something, they can come and go as they please, effectively going invisible even if there is nothing between you and them. If they had removed the Fog of War I might have given this game another chance even if it's not that great, but it's just the icing on the cake really. The reason why instead of giving it another try and learning it you just throw it into the trash.

Broken Age is the genre where a lot of the founding members of Double Fine started: point-&-click adventure games like Monkey Island so I was expecting good things. And that is what I got. It's hard to complete, but is a wonderful world to spend racking your brain for the solution.
There are two story lines, one of  girl who decides she'd rather not be sacrificed a princess-eating monster, the other a boy who is bored of being molly-coddled on a ship after his planet began to die when he was a baby. Both rebel with varrying levels of catastrophy & that's "Act 1"
Act 2 is where the stories start to intertwine & the only way to explain it is to explain the whole thing so I won't. Like Psychonauts, Double Fine's previous game, the difficulty curve can be mind bendingly steep; I often found myself sitting & scratching my head as to what the blazes I was supposed to be doing. Tthere's a nice inventory system that I suspect is there to throw you off slightly; some items need using immediately, some you have for AGES before needing them, but everything is always there but doesn't get in the way of the visuals.
The best is that, also like Psychonauts, the NPC's are interesting, engaging & fun, the look & feel of the graphics suit the game perfectly & the plot is curious & weird enough that you want to keep playing just to work out where it's al going & how it'll end.

I just beat this game tonight, so I feel like this review will be looking on it with the freshest eyes possible.
It's strange to me how torn the comments are from: "This is the best thing ever" to: "This game is the worst point and click adventure game I've ever played."
I found myself somewhere in between, and I did like it and would recommend it to people who like point and click adventure games, I got it on sale, but, I don't know for sure if I could say I would pay full price for this. So the story focuses on two characters who's seemingly very different lives are about to sort of, collide? *wink wink*
I liked the art style a lot, and thought it had really nice visuals, and I really appreciate the voice work, it's really nice, the story as it begins is very easy to quickly get sucked into, as you learn more about each characters life, it leaves you wanting to know more about where you will be going next. As for the story, I  didn't find it that predictable and bad, I wasn't expecting the twist I'll admit, and while the ending could have a little more too it, I think the overall story wrapped itself up and tied together well.
I feel like another thing the game isn't getting credit for is it's sense of humor, I kind of am a sucker for sillyness and funny bits in my adventure games, and I thought the whole thing was really well written too.
The puzzles:
In my book, an adventure game needs to be able to help the player along, and the story should be told in a way so that the player can figure out what to do and where to go, using a little bit of imagination. There is a fine line between, working to figure it out, and REALLY stretching your imagination, then reaching into desperation to figure it out.
The first half, I think successfully does that, it has pretty fair puzzles and guides you along without making it a piece of cake (hah, because vella likes to bake? get it?.. sorry :/)
I'm gonna have to agree with everyone else, that the second half of the game is chocked full of really mundane, frustrating puzzles that will leave you not only asking yourself "what do i do" but screaming in frustration "HOW WAS I SUPPOSED TO KNOW THAT" when you give up and read the walkthrough. I swear I have as many notes on this game then I do on my college history class..
I'm not actually very good at these types of games to be fair, but there are certain puzzles.. *cough* robots... that left me really irritated to the point of having to take a break from the game. The puzzles aren't just hard if they don't tell the player what to do or how to figure them out, they are downright unfair.
So unless you are a psychic, or the game developer, (or maybe just, the king of point and click adventure games) get your walkthrough out and ready.
One more thing I should mention, is this game didn't quite leave me with the satisfaction of world exploration that most adventure games usually do, I know the game is linear and moving in one direction, but in a sense, it almost made me feel unsatisfied, like I wanted to know more about the world around Vella and Shay before the game ended. That's not to say that what you do see isn't interesting though.
Not my favorite point and click, but it has great artistic flair, writing and voicework. I'd say check it out if you can.

The game starts great - many people find it annoying, but I loved how brutal was the game to a newbie who doesn't know how to optimize the characters. Yes, you are unable to open a lot of locks, and you often can't talk the crooks out of doing bad stuff, but it's more realistic this way, and I never got the feeling I was stuck. It only made me want to play again to see the things I've missed. There are other ways to accomplish a goal even if you think you're too low on resources to do it. Combat feels right even if it's less tactical than, say, Jagged Alliance's, and the scarcity of ammo only adds to the atmosphere.
On the other hand, the base story is kinda flat, and the game is slightly buggy and unpolished in some places, but there are still enough details to distract from it, so it didn't bother me most of the time. More problematic is the lack of cues for completing side quests, and it's easy to miss important locations/people, or do things in a wrong order. The end is probably the most disappointing part, as the final battles are quite anticlimatic (the badass scorpion robot on the start screen looks like a plush toy and does about as much damage to well-equipped characters). Still, the rest of the game was enjoyable enough to be worth my time.

Some people might think it's similar to Overwatch, I played Paladin before Overwatch because I wanted to try something that looked alike. I think they both take inspiration from TF2,  but they have a complete different feel.  The maps are smaller and designed around the concept abstract level design, which makes it both like chess and easy to navigate (Those hallways that lead nowhere in Overwatch!) This means that it feels more like a MOBA than a FPS, because the time it takes to get from one point to another is small, which encourages team fights even more. The cards makes it possible to customize your champion by giving passives to the skills you have and boosting their effectiveness. It is also easier to aim in Paladin than it is in Overwatch, the battles take a bit more time and management.
The game mode that makes it worthwhile for me is the Siege game mode, as I find it quite unique in respect to other games. There is a payload in the center of the map. Capturing the payload gives you one point,then you have to push the payload in the enemy base which gives you another point. Should the enemy stop the push, they get one point. Whoever gets 4 points wins. This makes for interesting battles.
I'll try the game again to see what is going on with the new reviews about the update and P2W/grind status and update the review. Regardless, the game is still a lot of fun if you pick it up
