I just finished the first campaign in Hard West a task which took around three hours and I feel that I have seen enough of the game to give it a thorough review.
Hard West is a Tactical, Turn Based, Psuedo-RPG game that takes place in the gritty, low magic, low fantasy and rough and rowdy Wild West. I call it a Psuedo-RPG because while it does have some RPG elements, the campaigns are short and the only leveling you do is through the use of a playing card system that allows you to customize your characters special attacks and abilities. It becomes a moot point because while each campaign unlocks the next, your characters change for each one so you do not retain the cards from your previous campaign
Graphics  - 8/10
The game has a beautiful, realism based graphics model, that is as resource efficient as it is lovely. I have no problem with cranking the game up to maximum settings, on my 10 year old custom built gaming PC. It is obvious that a lot of love and patience were put into the characters and environments in Hard West, each one feels alive and organic.
Audio - 8/10
The audio in this game is amazing and really sets the mood during storytelling and combat phases. The voice acting while limited, is top notch and extremely immersive. The sound effects and music are all in par with what I would expect from a game that was set in the Wild West and have the same gritty and somewhat spooky vibe that is present through the whole entire game.
Gameplay/Combat - 8/10
The campaigns in Hard West are played in two phases, the world map phase and the combat phase.
World Map Phase
This phase takes place on a small, but vibrant and detailed open world map. At the start of the campaign, only a few locations are unlocked, but as you progress through the campaign and make decisions, new locations appear. There are no random combat encounters on the world map and travel between unlocked locations is quick. The locations vary in purpose from mining camps and claims, to trading posts and mining skill trainers, to combat locales and random events which can be both positive and negative in nature. All encounters aside from Combat encounters take place in the form of a pop up window, which gives you a short, gritty narrative and allows you to choose how to react. The choices you make during these interactions, have a direct effect on which locations pop up next as well as having potential implications to your characters. The whole system ends up feeling a lot like those old Choose Your Own Adventure Novels I used to read, I found it very charming and it adds a ton of replay value to each campaign.
Combat Phase - 9/10
This is where the game earns it's stripes at and while the combat encounters are short on quantity, the quality as well as the challenge each one provides, makes the experience plenty memorable. I fought around 4-5 battles over my first playthrough of the first campaign on medium difficulty and I had to replay each one at least 2 times and a few, 4-5 times and don't expect any epic gear to save your♥♥♥♥♥ The maps are all brilliantly implicated and masterfully crafted with multi-story buildings, 1/2 & full cover items and areas and other really neat tactical elements like the possibility to stage some of the maps prior to combat, spaghetti western style as well as character abilities like Ricochet shots. If you fail to use your brain, your character will die and die hardsauce and if the character that dies is a main character, you are forced to restart the encounter. It does feel like the hit percentages are in your favor more often than not, but this doesnt ruin the experience, like it does in other similar games.
Writing & Storyline 6/10
In the same way the game focused on quality over quantity in the area of combat, the writing focused on quality over quantity, but unlike the Combat, the writing was not so well done that it overarched the lack of quantity. I found the stories to be somewhat unique to video games, but not unique in general and since there are not many similar video games set in the time and period of Hard West, I had to give it a lower rating on writing and storyline.
Overall, this game is totally worth your money, even at full asking price it would be even more so if it had more content but I understand that these smaller studios have to get their foot in the door and earn some money before they can begin creation of larger and more intricate RPG or Tactical Epics so in light of the effort they made with quality, I can forgive the overall lack of quantity. I am a tough customer to please, a grizzly old gaming vet if you might and I  am very satisfied with my purchase.

Cons

The game is worth a buy, I would wait until they release Patch 1.02 which is unknown when, probably soon though as forums are crying with problems. Only bug I have noticed is the random crashes, other than that I haven't experienced any bugs that stop me from continuing quests etc.
The game is a hit and miss, its not your typical Mafia game. Research it more, watch gameplay footage, do what you will. 2hrs won't show you much of the game incase you want to refund it with the 2hr refund policy.
Since there isn't another option for recommending the game other than "yes" or "no". I would recommend this game, ONLY if you do your research, understand this isn't your typical Mafia game. Remember this is in a time where black people were targetted and a lot of racism was going around. And the devs have clearly gone all out for an experience into the way people lived back then, and showing what people still, to this day, get treated. For that, I applaud them, they weren't scared in censoring anything. You will hear the N word constantly, you're targetted from cops, just because you're black, constantly being called the N word and other nasty stuff. So keep that in mind.
I rate this game a solid 7/10 - Decent game, needs a new patch to allow Shade + SweetFX and open up modding for the community so we can do what devs won't do, such as increase texture resolution.
Don't watch the Steam videos or pictures as they are somewhat misleading, their using rendered cutscenes and footage. Watch You Tube videos on Mafia 3 so you can see for yourself, but a good Shade + sweetFX can make the game look more beautiful and remove some of the ugly.
EDIT: The game is MUCH better and runs beautifully. Even all the hate I put above. Its a good game. Is it Mafia 2? no. You must use a Reshade to make the game look nicer still. But I would recommend this game.

tl;dr: If you crave early-90s LucasArts-style adventures, get this whole series. You won't regret it.
These games were a VERY pleasant surprise and this is both the best and longest of the series up through the fourth (though I recommend playing them in order, because there are continuing elements). The first four games had been sitting in my Steam collection for a couple of years before the urge to play an early-90s-style adventure game came over me, but when it did these games satisfied that urge almost perfectly. They're designed according to the rules that Ron Gilbert and other designers worked out at LucasArts in the late 80s -- you can't die, you can't find yourself in an unwinnable position -- as opposed to the inexplicably popular Sierra adventure games, where you could die from simply examining an object and frequently needed to restore to old saved games to pick up an object you needed. (The Sierra games improved with the Gabriel Knight series.) The puzzles in The Blackwell Deception are challenging but generally fair, though occasionally you need to stumble around until you accidentally find a solution. At least the solutions tend to make sense in retrospect and you probably could solve almost all of them with a lot of thought if you have the patience. The main characters, a medium and her wiseass spirit guide, are charming and the voice acting is top notch. In fact, these are the only games I've seen that not only credit the voice actors at the end but show pictures of each actor next to a picture of the character they played, so you'll want to stay for the credits. This will take several hours to play and you'll feel you got your money's worth, especially with the way prices have dropped. I can't wait to play the fifth game, which I've already bought.
10/10 - I can't recommend this game and the earlier ones enough.

I have not played the last in the series yet, but out of all the four previous, Deception ratchets up the quirky concepts the series introduced in the first three games, by attaching some weighted stake and intrigue. Overall, this has piqued my interest for Epiphany, and has brought my lukewarm opinion of the series to a considerable simmer.

The fourth installment of the Blackwell series stumbles a bit visually. A new pixel artist was chosen for this game, so the slowly improving character designs have taken a few steps back. This issue is usually easy to ignore thanks to the much more attractive character portraits and the series' general aesthetic of leaning more on its sound than its visuals. Finer details, however, can be downright inscrutable which adds unnecessary difficulty in a genre that relies on a close examination of one's surroundings. Confusing graphics don't result in impassable obstacles though as anything that can be interacted with does have its own hover text.
Thankfully, the mechanics of this game have continued the pattern of the refinement of the past three games. Physically combining clues to come to new conclusions has returned from its absence in Convergence and has been moved to Rosangela's new smartphone. Additionally the smartphone has taken over the email and web search functions, which not only streamlines a process previously marked by constant location hopping, but also gives our modern heroine and her older spirit guide something to banter over. Convergence may have seen Rosa and Joey starting to get along, but by Deception the two have really hit their stride together. They seem more like partners now as opposed to the unwilling allies they were before.
Deception stands on its own better than the previous three games. The story is strong from end to end, picking up on the momentum from the last game and carrying that through this game to its own resolution. This time, the need to play the next Blackwell game isn't fueled by a desire to learn more but by an eagerness to experience more.

Well what could be better than wanting to explore an entire galaxy of stars and planets (and even moons)? Not much this observer thinks but then what if you add space stations and cities or spaceports into the mix? It's not illusion in paragon, it's all there and that concept alone is the basis of a game with plenty of depth. But of course i'm not just reviewing one side but all and so far the plot, as an avid sci-fi fan myself, is very interesting but still has much development. It is curently based in the not so distant future, around the 22nd century if i'm not mistaken, in a world where the Cold War doesnt end!
So far however, this plot has yet to be implemented fully and more technical issues have to be solved around how such a massive procedurally generated galaxy can be kept stable and in working order. I take my hat off to the devs who are attempting this task because from what i've seen already if these technical issues, minor and major, can be handled I honestly believe this could be one hell of an adventure.
With regards to the depth of the game, this is also something that is wanting but from the hammer and sickle on the space stations to maps of various aligned and non-aligned planets it seems the basis is there to create a universe of mixed politics and motives. Its one thing to play an rpg or free roaming games based in some distant land or with compulsory missions to weigh you down, but to have free reign to go about your business and make a name for yourself? That doesnt sound too bad and the potential is there.
As it is you can fly around, see the sights, get a feel for how the game would work and with enough imagination have some idea of the end product but it is a long way off and despite my enthusiasm it has to be said that getting involved with an early access program with massive scope is not for the faint of heart and so only those of patience (and a definite love for sci-fi) should apply now, otherwise give it time!

The fourth Blackwell game is also the best. (I have not played the last game yet, however.) Everything about the design and style feels right. It is more streamlined, more visually stunning, and almost twice as long as any of the previous games. It advances the main storyline of the game, although after a long detour, and the storytelling is more action-packed and compelling than before. All of the side-characters have meaningful and complex backstories that the player can sympathize with, and the open-ended nature of your investigations (since you can complete the cases in any order you prefer) makes the game feel bigger than it actually is. Even the last act of the game is very satistfying.
The voice-acting is more professional than before, although the writing still suffers from occasionally low-quality and cheesy dialogue. The soundtrack, too, follows the high bar set by the composer across the previous three entries.
Overall, there is very little to complain about, aside from the occasional adventure game clichés and frustrations. (The in-game hint system, which certainly is a requisite in any self-conscious adventure game, is mostly good, but sadly unreliable at points.) Almost everything else, from the gameplay to the story, just flows very smoothly, and is a pleasure to play though (AND a second time with the commentary track turned on.) This feels like the Blackwell game that always should have been. That said, I HIGHLY recommend playing through all the 5 Blackwell games in the order of their release.

I believe Natural Selection 2 is a masterpiece of a game, that represents the perfect blend of FPS and RTS game play. It is one of the few games where teamwork and individual skill are highly rewarded. On top of that, the community is accepting of new players and offers a friendly hand to educate those who are new.
Due to the fact that Natural Selection 2 is a hybrid of FPS and RTS game play, it allows for very competitive play in that the deciding factor of victory and defeat involves the long term decisions of a commander and/or the quick reactions and overall skill of the individual combatants (whether shooting aliens, or stalking marines). Due to this style of game play, games can very well last over an hour and yet feel very "tight" throughout the entire match.
However, as of now, there is a lack of a ranked match system. The fact that the average game easily lasts over 20 minutes, and longer games tend to last for at least an hour, a very serious deciding factor of the winner is simply how many players leave and join the game. I understand that this is not really a game breaking problem, however due to the fact that players do not have much "loyalty" to their respective team, and the fact that the average match is rather lengthy, if a number of "pro" players join or leave the match during the middle of the game, it could drastically change the fate of the match instantly. I believe that having a sort of ranked match system, like that in Counter Strike: Global Offensive, will serve a very competitive game like Natural Selection 2 justice. Having ranked matches will also remove the occasional "newb stomping" matches, where there is a skill-based team stack.
The game features asymmetrical teams with very different game play styles. This provides for a different style of FPS game play, and not the traditional shooter vs shooter like in most FPS games. I believe that because of this asymmetry, it expands the average gamer's experiences about FPS games in general. However, in Natural Selection 2, because it is also an RTS hybrid, a player could choose from essentially four game play experiences within one match alone which highly increases the game's overall learning curve. These four game play "roles" are: Marine commander, Marine player, Alien commander, and Alien player. Each type of "role" presents new strategies and information upon which the player has to know, and ultimately, having a sense of all the 4 roles is the minimum requirement for being "decent" in the game. Overall, having asymmetrical teams can interest those who are tired of the same-old shooter vs shooter, and because Natural Selection 2 is an asymmetrical FPS/RTS hybrid, such game play increases the overall learning curve to become fully understanding of every aspect, tactics and counter-tactics within the game.
Do not let the lack of a ranked match system and rather difficult learning curve stop you from playing this game however. The lack of a ranked match system simply means that Natural Selection 2 is always going to be played on a "casual" game play setting, which many FPS games have. The difficult learning curve is also easily passed if one simply spends about a good 2 hours playing in a sandbox training server by themselves, learning all of the abilities, techniques, tech-trees, map-knowledge, weapons, and life forms to get that "full" understanding of the 4 game play "roles" I mentioned earlier. Furthermore, if you still need further clarification and help, the overall community in Natural Selection 2 servers are kind, vocal, and willing to help those who ask.
I believe that Natural Selection 2 marks the standard for all asymmetrical and even symmetrical FPS/RTS hybrid games in the future. I would highly recommend this game to anyone, especially those with a background in playing other FPS and RTS games as they could easily apply their knowledge of both game genres into their Natural Selection 2 game play.

TL;DR: HARD WEST IS A FUN IF FLAWED GAME.
The reviews on this game are mixed not because Hard West is a bad game, but because there's too many flaws to call it a great game. If you like turn-based tactics, you'll enjoy it to some degree, if not you might not stick with it.
As a Tactics buff, Hard West scratches that turn-based itch, and throws in elements I didn't expect as well. The supernatural stories and hard-boiled characters are engrossing, the Card-perk system is clever, the luck mechanic that serves as both armor and a mana of sorts is new and different, the persistant injuries that become buffs over time are challanging but good, managing loadouts and abilities is never tedious, a solid VO makes a great anchor, and a narritive overworld that encourages you to not only make hard choices, but live with them as opposed to save-scumming to get the best result. All of these come together to make the game a worthwhile purchase.
But there are some major flaws, things that should have been ironed out by taking a look at XCOM 2: the UI is unpolished, menus could be better, the animations are just a little too slow, the visuals are uninspiring, there's ambiguity regarding things like cover, the repetitive music, and other little problems that hold it back. However, In my oppinion, Hard West's stronger points hold it together and make sure its still a FUN game, and to me that's the most important thing.
I bought Hard West and its DLC, Scars of Freedom, for $13. At that price, I can highly reccomend this game for strategy and Tactics players. I dont think this game deserves as many negitive reviews as it does.

Lets get this out of the way first: I hate Turn-based games. I think theyre amazingly boring and a waste of time. So why the positive review for this game you may ask. Well, its complicated and Im not too bright. So lets try and keep this simple and slowly count to potato. While this is turn-based it also doea a very good job of being a visual novel with "choose your own adventure" qualities. Youre free to make poor decisions that seem to affect the story and how your characters will develop and/or what inventory items they will acquire. It might not be the most moral thing to let a murderer go free but you may get something of value out of it. After all, this is the wild west. Every man for himself. And every man that has more than a nickel to his name could find themselves targeted.
As far as game play it seems to handle all of the stats and modifiers very well. The interface is simple and straight-forward. Your character gets and activates different cards taht are numbered and suited like a regular poke deck. If the character is holding a good poker hand a benefit will be added to your base stats. The nice part about this is that it uses a well-known and almost universally understood platform to play with. We all know that four of a kind is better than a pair. Put 4 of a kind into your characters inventory and youll get a better buffer than just holding a pair. Put a flush into your hand and get even better buffs for that character.
Overall design is nice done with cell animation. And thats a deal-clincher for me. When done right I think that animation looks great for games. Maybe its nostalgia, but when I was a kid and saw Dragon's Lair in the arcade I had always thoguht playing a cartoon was the coolest concept Id ever seen. So any game suing this type of art is hard for me to ignore, even if its a genre I hate like turn-based strategy games.
I think its jsut a good blend of strategy and story-telling. The bits of the story are brief; another major bonus since having to read page after page of dialogue in between actual playing is a major turn-off. The small stories interlaced into the game are so brief that they literally take seconds to read but will (and do) impact the gameplay and the course of the story. Maybe turn-based and RTS geeks might think this is too simple or doesnt do the genre justice. But thats not who I am and I dont care what they think. Those are the people that CosPlay and like frosted Pop-Tarts. We should allow them to park handicap and attempt to isolate them from the rest of us. Sooner is better than later.

I have to say, I was pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoyed this game.  Well, actually, story with puzzles.  I liked that most puzzles were not too difficult, but enough to make it fun. (Remember the wiring!  That will make sense the first time you play and realize you paid no attention.)
The story was deeper than I thought it would be and, happily, longer than I thought it would be.  Don't let the unusual art work deter you.  It is more sophisticated than it seems from the previews.  It fits well with the story and I enjoyed this.
As for playability, I've played through once so this is from a one-time play-through perspective.  Let me put it this way, if you enjoy reading a story, setting it aside for awhile and then reading it again, you could replay and enjoy it. If, however, you are a person who reads a book once and never reads it again, you may not enjoy playing it again.  But I bet you enjoy playing it at least once.
Though the story seems to be set, the fact that you are allowed to solve the problems in your own time, and some interaction is done differently, I think you could play it more than once.
I definitely recommend it.

I've played the game now for a total of 6.7hrs. And after the initial 30 fps lock, which they promptly released a patch allowing users to switch from 30, 60, unlimited FPS it has made the game that more tolerable. Performance wise, after the unlock has been near perfect, I get a constant 60 fps (when locked to 60 fps).
For me though, Mafia 3 isn't really a "Mafia" game, where you "work" hand in hand for the mafia. You're a lone guy killing off  gangs + Mafia bosses to exact revenge. Personally, I don't mind it, but if you're looking for a Mafia 1 or 2 type game, you won't find it here. Its more along side Mad Max / GTA. Driving in the game is beautifully done, probably the best i've seen in an open world game to date, I think even better than GTA, Not all cars drive the same, some are faster, slower, can turn quicker, can do burn outs or not do burnouts etc.
Pros
- 30, 60, unlimited FPS settings
- fun gameplay
- amazing soundtrack
- amazing voice acting
- good story
- gunplay and cover system is good
- good variety of guns
- mods for your weapons
- mods for your car
- AI is ok (nothing spectactular)
Cons
- shaky launch
- low res textures (fixed with Shade + SweetFX..somewhat)
- can't store cars that you wish to keep in a garage
- A few bugs, most big one, constant random crashing (probably due to the game not liking Shade + SweetFX)
The game is worth a buy, I would wait until they release Patch 1.02 which is unknown when, probably soon though as forums are crying with problems. Only bug I have noticed is the random crashes, other than that I haven't experienced any bugs that stop me from continuing quests etc.
The game is a hit and miss, its not your typical Mafia game. Research it more, watch gameplay footage, do what you will. 2hrs won't show you much of the game incase you want to refund it with the 2hr refund policy.
Since there isn't another option for recommending the game other than "yes" or "no". I would recommend this game, ONLY if you do your research, understand this isn't your typical Mafia game. Remember this is in a time where black people were targetted and a lot of racism was going around. And the devs have clearly gone all out for an experience into the way people lived back then, and showing what people still, to this day, get treated. For that, I applaud them, they weren't scared in censoring anything. You will hear the N word constantly, you're targetted from cops, just because you're black, constantly being called the N word and other nasty stuff. So keep that in mind.
I rate this game a solid 7/10 - Decent game, needs a new patch to allow Shade + SweetFX and open up modding for the community so we can do what devs won't do, such as increase texture resolution.
Don't watch the Steam videos or pictures as they are somewhat misleading, their using rendered cutscenes and footage. Watch You Tube videos on Mafia 3 so you can see for yourself, but a good Shade + sweetFX can make the game look more beautiful and remove some of the ugly.
EDIT: The game is MUCH better and runs beautifully. Even all the hate I put above. Its a good game. Is it Mafia 2? no. You must use a Reshade to make the game look nicer still. But I would recommend this game.

A gritty, sophisticated, and intelligent adventure RPG.
I'm not usually into the genre, but this grabbed me, and held my attantion, and still does. The Witcher 2 throws you right into the heart of momentous events that have gravity, and you're instantly made an integral part of the game from the very start.
I felt drawn into the Witcher world, and involved in a way that I don't often experience with games.
The game is also unforgiving. It's not infuriating, at least I didn't think so, but it's demanding in that you actually need to use combat tactics in real time.
You have to dodge and evade attacks, block, parry, and riposte. Dangerous/malicious forest creatures can kill you quite easily if you try a hack-and-slash approach. You have to put some forethought into the items you take along.
It's also a visually stimulating game. The design is oh so intricate!...
The only downside to this amazing game is that it's quite demanding in terms of hardware.
At the time of posting this review, I'm running it on an end of 2009 model laptop, with one of the core2 duo chips from just prior to the i-series release. It barely meets specs.
It's still very playable, but far from seamless. Other than a good processor, you'll need a decent graphic card. I have an ATI Mobility Radeon HD 4650 1GB, and it runs.
It's hard to find that out if you're trawling through forums and query-posts, but it runs. Laptop version too, so less powerful.
One of the more engaging games I've played for a good while now, and complete fun. A joy to play and to look at, 9/10.
(Only for the high hardware requirements meaning you really need a top end system to bring out it's full potential.)
Well worth it, especially at steam's almost obscenely cheap discount-sale price!

"Life is Strange" is an emo point-and-click adventure with an inventive gimmick at its heart. The gimmick is reminiscent of "The Sands of Time", but this version is far more compelling and will definitely haunt you. "Life is Strange" quickly finds its footing as a detective thriller full of real consequences and hard decisions.
While the overall drearyiness of this world may not appeal to everyone, the game's mechanics draw players in anyway. The drama of highschool is the story's primary focus, but our heronine's powers turn out to be worth exploring even in such an everyday context. The stakes are far higher than you realize, as a true serial killer may be on the loose....
Frankly, this game is brilliant in its simplicity and absolutely profound in its execution. Yes, it's one of my contenders for 2015 Game of the Year. Everyone should try "Life is Strange" (and Ep.1 is free, so do it).

Overall, this game is a lot of fun and I think it's a worthwhile purchase. I've almost completed it and am around 70 hours in, so it hits the $1:1hr ratio I hope for with most games.
First off, the graphics are incredible. I'm playing with the high resolution texture pack and the detail / character models are very well done. The display options are also great, supporting custom display resolutions (ultrawide) and even resolution scaling (up/down) which is a really great thing to see in games these days. The performance is also very good, with the resolution scaling at 1:1, graphic settings at high, at 3440x1440 res, with a CPU/GPU of i7-3820/GTX-980, I was able to achieve a very good and stable framerate given the graphical fidelity. Good stuff.
The gameplay is a lot of fun. The skills you have allow you to freely navigate the world and rightly feel like a badass. There have been many moments where I said to myself "wow that was so cool" after I did it, even up through the 60th hour I had fresh moments like this. Like flying a drake, dismounting to shoot an arrow at someone in slomo, then remounting the drake without touching the ground. Way cool. The game is filled with moments like this because there are so many ways to approach situations (like completing missions full stealth instead of charging in). The skills you unlock really support different approaches and offers a lot of fun and interesting tools to the player. The Nemesis system is VERY cool, and the game was able to make me very angry about a couple orcs, and as a result finally dealing with them was very gratifying.
The world was really well done. It features five main areas that feel very big (if you're not flying on a drake), and the varying scenery in each is great. I was very impressed in this respect. It's not important but I did want to mention that the world map that the game uses, where you can look around all of Mordor and see where each of the areas is was a great idea on someone's part. Without it, the game would feel like five very disconnected areas, but the map allows you to get a feel for where each place is in relationship to one another. A lot of players probably don't realize how important it is to get a proper sense of continuity.
Progression is meh. It's very easy in the beginning, I got through Acts I-III no problem, but Act IV (the final one) is proving to be somewhat of a challenge. To clarify, everything in the game is tied to your level. The gear you get, the max level of your followers, etc. And with the lack of possible quests to complete (the main source of EXP) by the time you're in Act IV, it's quite tough to compensate. I think it's feasible, but I'm a little annoyed by it and may YouTube the rest of the game because I don't want to spend time getting to the point I likely need to be at. For the record, spending money on the microtransactions for followers / gear is definitely not necesssary to progress (at least up to Act IV). I didn't spend an extra cent on the game.
As a final recap, the progression in the game is the only sucky part, and that's really only due to the situation I found myself in come Act IV. The rest of the game was phenomenal and I had a ton of fun playing it, the gameplay definitely sells this game for me. What got me interested was the sieges (I'm a Mount and Blade butter nut), but that's not a *huge* part of the game and I had a lot of fun just slaying orcs and finishing quests. This game is a good buy, even at the full 60$ price tag.

This is one of the best adventure games I ever played. Very good storyline and game mechanics. It kept me up late at night several times because I just wanted to know how the story ended. The only bad thing I can say about it, is that the story ended after part five. But that is probably a good thing because you do not want to ruin a good story by stretching it thin.
You play this adventure with two main characters: Rosangela Blackwell and Joey Malone. Part two is kind of a prequel in which Rosangela is replaced by her Aunt Lauren Blackwell.
Rosangela and Lauren are mediums and Joey Malone is their spirit guide. Together they help the souls of dead people (ghosts) that are stuck in this world to move on. Doing so they encounter a number of persons/ghosts who play an important role in the story later on.
Joey is a ghost himself so he can reach places that Rosangela cannot, but he cannot wander off too far because he is bound to Rosangela. He also cannot touch anything so he needs Rosangela for this. This poses some interesting situations in which Joey needs to get Rosangela into locked rooms/buildings.
A very interesting game mechanic is that you have to cross-reference pieces of information. By cross-referencing the right information you will learn new things which will help you to further progress into the game. Some information you have to lookup on the internet (in game) and emails play an important role too in this game.
The Blackwell series consists of five separate parts:
1. The Blackwell Legacy
2. Blackwell Unbound
3. Blackwell Convergence
4. Blackwell Deception
5. Blackwell Epiphany
Be sure to play them in that order because it is in fact one big story divided over five parts.

I pre-ordered this and I really really wanted to like it. Unfortunately there is not a lot to love. I know with the onset of roguelike RPG's there seems to be a consumer market for old-school difficult games but there is a fundamental difference between difficult and inconvenient. Wasteland 2 isn't that difficult it is just extremely inconvenient. Spammy and monotonous battles on the main map, no useful fast travel for getting from one area to another, and writing that, while definitely serviceable (sometimes funny), just doesn't stack up against other major RPGs. The combat is boring as hell, the upgrades system is weak and uninteresting, and there is little depth (though they can be interesting) to the few characters you can pick up that do have characterization (the main group you use is a blank slate with zero characterization). When you compare this to Kickstarter RPG's such as Pillars of Eternity there is just no comparison. Pillars of Eternity (which I am using as a comparison because it is also a kickstarter) is just a fundamentally better game.  Sure the graphics are crap (what do you expect from a kickstarter game?) but the plot, characters, upgrade system and combat is infinitely (haha pun) better. This is not a horrible way to kill time but there are just a lot better ways to kill it.

It's fun, it's fast paced, it's hectic, and it's crazy.  Skill does make a difference, although strategy and randomness (and the quick nature of the game) means it usually feels pretty balanced.  The weapons and stages are varied, and where the mechanics end the shear oddness of the game picks up (There is, after all, a dedicated quack button).
What I like the most is the game is mostly meat.  You press start and within 30 second you can be in a full area fighting.  The transitions between stages can be so fast as to be easily missed and the game has already started again.  There is a brief stop after a few matches to show the scores, and then it's right back to the mayhem.  There is a single player challenge mode to train up certain skills (more an unobtrusive tutorial really) and to unlock new hats.  After the solid and consistent mechanics, the plain oddness of the game never stops being fun.  Again, a dedicated quack button, also a ragdoll button.  When ragdolled other players can pick you up, so you can pick up the dead bodies of your opponents and walk around with them.  Lots of hats and masks that pop off when you die, so you can also pick up and wear the heads of defeated ducks.  There are some levels with drum sets, others with old-timey muskets that reload in an old-timey way.  I don't know if I've seen a game with this much personality in a long time.
I only have two major complaints.  I do love the condensed nature of the game, meaning you can have a fulfilling in about half a hour.  But the game is so hectic and intense that after 30 min it becomes a little jarring, forcing a break.  While it is mostly meat, it's also kind of one note.  I'm hoping some other game modes might get added eventually to mix up the play some.
It's worth it at full price.
Small disclaimer:  My hours played is misleading.  There is currently a glitch (about to be fixed) that doesn't close the game after quitting.  So thought I've played quite a lot, I haven't played that much.

This game has come a long way since it was initially released upon the public and made quite an impact for being a terrible game. At the time of it's release this game was clearly a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and unfinished game with uncountable amounts of bugs, only 2 or 3 maps and about 3 types of dinosaurs. This is all the past now, and though this may not be a perfect game it is a fun arcade style shooter to play with your friends.
The game now sports about a dozen different game modes and maps, a nice selection of weapons and powerups, a working progression system with 3 class types, over 200 Steam achievements and most bugs have been fixed. If you have a couple of friends with you and you just want to mess around and have a fun time on a game with a silly premise and don't mind mediocre graphics and audio then this is absolutely for you, if on the otherhand you like to play a serious survival game then this might not be for you.

The game runs very smoothly for the most part with a couple of graphical artifacts here and there but nothing I've found gamebreaking yet, and there are lag spikes when waves end on survival.
Taking a little step away from the technical problems of this game and looking into the gameplay though is where this game is great, it's perfectly fun to play for an hour or two every now and then prefferably with friends and just have a blast shooting dinosaurs with handcannons, shotguns, gatling guns, sniper rifles, lasers, flamethrowers, rocket launchers and so much more. I picked up this game a while ago, considering it among the many other great games I had in mind, but I still decided to experiment, and I spent my money on it. I was slightly wary of this purchase though, as I have made bad choices in games in the past, but I decided it was worth a shot. I started it up, and as soon as I joined my first lobby, immediately loved it. The game concept is great, merging a sort of warped MOBA with an First person shooter. Throw some aliens in there and basiclly sums it up.
The game in essence is a moba, with two teams going at eachother, trying to destroy a immoble structure, but its so much more complicated then that. At the begining of the game, a commander is chosen for each team, a commander for the marines, and the "Queen" for the aliens. To win, the marine must destroy the Aliens "Hive" structure, where the Queen operates, and the aliens must destroy the Marines Command Station. Basiclly, the Commander/Queen is like Battlefield 4's Conquest mode, where either team's commander can virtually call in support, ping key points on map, research new weapons or technologies, and generally advise the team.
Resources are important to either team. They are gained from building extractors, and can be used to buy upgrades, and weapons.
However, the Marines are arguably as important, if not moree, then the commander. While commander can call in buildings, it takes the Marines to actually construct them. The marines also do all the fighting, their arsenal consisting of a medium range assault rifle, pistol secondary, and combat hatchet. (God I love that unholster animation) The Commander can research new weapons to add to the arsenal, including shotguns, landmines, and a range of grenades. Mid-to-late game, the Commander can order a lab drop, which lets you buy (with enough resources,) flame throwers, or exo-suits. Marines expand their territory by building facilities, such as power generators, then extractors, and so forth. If Marines can get multiple bases running, they can build teleports, which let you sweep across the map faster.
For the Aliens, the game is very similar, yet so different. The "Queen" (Alien's commander) gets a skyhigh view of the map from her hive. She can ping areas, advise the team, and spread the infestation across the area. The aliens are very diverse.
The default alien is a skulk. It appears to be some sort of hybrid of a crab, and a hyena or something. They run much faster then marines, can scale walls, or even crawl across the ceiling, even using vents to their advantage. Their default melee can kill a Marine in 2 or 3 hits. It also has a far weaker range, called Parasite.
The second alien, and cheapest to evolve into, is the Gorge It generally resembles a turtle/hippo, with a swollen belly. It's attacks are all range, and involve it spitting up on Marines. But the Gorge's main purpose is to support. It can build Infestations, which cover rooms with swells of green goo. It's primary attack can also heal allies.
Lerks are the third cheapest alien evolutions. They resemble pterodactyls, and flies around, quickly striking down Marines at close combat, or picking them off with their ranged spikes. Very agile and hard to hit, Lerk's are a fresh pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for Marines.
The second most expensive evolution is the fade, the Fade is virtually an alien assassin, that can leap, teleport, and fade itself into invisiblity. Leaves Marines Wondering what hit them.
The biggest evolution there is, usually a mid-to-late game version, is the Onos. Basiclly the alien equivalent of an exosuit, this thing appears to be a huge rhino, dinosaur mother hubbard that charges its way through enemy lines. It absorbs damage in its shell, and excels at smashing Marine structures to pieces.
The game is amazingly fun to play, and much more diverse then the average moba. Unfortunately, there are a few cons. There is literally no progression systems. Of course, good Mobas really don't need them, as progression is'nt the point of the game. (Unless you play LoL, and your spending twenty bucks on a revealing outfit for your female champion.) But there are not even leaderboards, apart from some server's fanmade versions.
The other problem I have with this game is its rarely updated. Currently there is 4 maps, but I believe there is definetely room for more. Of course, the way most of the game is already is pretty balanced, and trying to change the roots of it would not be good, but this game needs some DLC. Some kind or reskin, weapon modifications, anything.
Overall this game deservers 8, or even 9 out of 10. It is one of my favorite games, and I hope to enjoy this game for many more years.

The Bad:
- Glitches: Shoddy programming makes enemy and player movement very glitchy.  The issue occurs when a character ends their movement and the game engine tries to determine how the character should be standing in that square.  It'll often enter an endless loop where the character is jittering around in that square.  The only way to resolve this is to restart the mission, as there is no mid-game saving.  Missions can often be very long and you will be forced to repeat hours of progress.
- No Overwatch: Enemies have an overwatch skill when you enter their small field of vision that allows them to immediately take a suprise shot at you.  You and your allies do not have the same reaction and enemies are permited to run up to you and shoot point blank without penalty.  It was a poor design choice that forces difficulty for difficulty sake.
- Luck System: All characters have a pool of Luck points that swings an attacker's chance to hit in favor of the defender.  If the game tells you that you have a 95% chance to hit, it's a lie.  Luck is great in games.  But when it's as swing-y as the way Hard West implements it, you'll be more frustrated than having fun.

This is a pretty unique tactical strategy game. The gameplay is similar in some basic ways to X-COM and the many clones of it, but with substantial differences. What really sets this game apart is the goth-western setting, complete with atmospheric music and dark storytelling. Each scenario contains several missions, but also a sort of text adventure map format--and each scenario's adventure map has its own rules and quirks.
You play by the point of view of several characters, most of them unsavory, who are all tied to the devil in the old west. The DLC gives you another scenario in the same setting but a whole new storyline.
If you're a fan of X-COM-style games and also like the gothic atmosphere of games like Darkest Dungeon, and would like to occasionally break from the usual Tolkienesque and sci-fi settings, this game is well worth your time.
I've played through every scenario, including the DLC, on Normal in about 30 hours. There is some replayability in that many missions and scenarios can be pulled off different ways. The final scenario and the DLC also appear to have alternate endings.

Spintires has to be the most frustratring games ever to be made for the PC!
The graphics are beautiful, the way the terrain deforms and the mud and earth pile up when your trucks tyres displace it is a wonder to behold! The trees look fantastic and small ones can be flatten in front of your truck as you make your way to the objective.
Even the trucks models look brillient with the way their tyres actually deform as you make your way across rocks and the occasional tarmac. The exhustive effects give a real sense of an old diesel engine.
The game play is unique, I've never played a game with vehicles which didn't involve a timer of some sorts which is refreshing and allows a relaxed and unrushed approach to achieve your objective, you're fighting the terrain not the clock. The objectives themselves are normally to take an amount of lumber (wooden logs) from a logging camp to a specfic location. To do this you have to search for and unlock other vehicles. The maps are clouded by a 'fog of war' type of affair but instead of becoming unvieled as you travel you instead have to make your way to a specific location in order to reveal a map section. Which itself adds sort of a sub-objective as these locations are often in hard to reach places you'd never dream of actually navigating to to achieve your mission.
In short there are a lot of great things about this game, it's been very well thought out. Except for two important elements. Firstly, no first person view inside the cab. Well I can understand if the designer wants you to mavel at all the deforming terrain etc you can't see all his hard work. I still would like a cabin view though. But even the third person view and the way it's connected to your truck defies any sort of logic or sensible thinking. I can't only suggest it was designed especially to obscure your view of anything you'd actually want to see at all times...or at least make it difficult to get the camera into a position where you can see. And this is where the frustration begins.
I must have re-started the same level 50+ times because I end up in a position (normally with all wheels pointing skywards) because I couldn't see enough ahead. I have literally driven off the edge of cliffs and steep hills to my doom simply because I can't get the camera into a position to see where I'm going, which seems ridiculous for a driving game! Truck is at the bottom of a valley, damaged and can't be driven, oh and lack of savings means you can't track back. Progess lost, start again! I'd say after 2hrs of of play I've seen about 5% of 1 map. Not because they are so large, but because I've been playing the same bit over and over again.
Not making progress and failing at what should be simply tasks (like crossing a small bridge) just makes you head for the Exit button and reach for the valium! I even got stuck in the mud in the 'safety' of my own garage not 1 minute into a game and couldn't do a thing about it (no trees to attach the winch to). Stuck AT MY OWN GARAGE! Seems ridiculous (again)?
The second frustration are the controls. There is no support for steering wheels game-controllers. Controlling ANY car or truck in ANY game is a pain with a keyboard and when your main enemy is the terrain about you control over your vehicle is a must! If you put these two main points of frustration togther and try and 'decompile' the intial planning process of the devs, then it must have been something like this:
"Lets made a driving game! But we won't add the two main things you'd actually expect in a driving game. 1.Using a steering wheel, 2. A view from the actual position you be in real life. Leaving out these two naturally expected features will give our game an edge over any other driving game on the market"
Would I recommend this game? Overall I've got to say yes, saying no would suggest it's a bad game, which it isn't. It's just missing what is small but import piece of the puzzle. Being able to see out of the front of the vehicle and control it. If you can wait then I'd suggest adding to your Wish List and wait for a sale, add it to your library and hope that there will be a future patch to add the lacking features.

PC Version Review
The Good:
1. The world - New Bordeaux is a great mix of all sorts of landscapes and urban layouts with plenty of flavour of New Orleans, though I've never been so I could wrong but it's a rich tapestry to be sure. It's actually nice to just drive through and take in the sights or just stand around and look at the world laid out before you. The weather also varies much more also with an increase of differences in lighting compared to previous games. The weather also appears to be connected to progress within the game to make story missions more atmospheric.
2. The main story - It's a good tried and true, organised crime revenge story set in a turbulent time in the 60's when there were big shifts/upheavals in society, economics and politics around the globe. In the US a loss of innocence and shock return to reality from the golden age of the 50’s. The game does interesting flash forwards in time to supporting characters giving documentary style interviews about the history of the main story, giving background and lining things up for the next episode of the story. Your actions do have an impact on the outcomes in the game and they hold true to the Mafia franchise style.
3. The characters - very colourful and diverse, well thought out with a good range of supporting characters and the return of our friend Vito Scaletta as a supporting character. Great voice acting and realistic facial expressions, movements and small details makes sure to do the characters justice. All characters have suffered trauma in one way or another due to local and world events and face internal struggles with their own personal demons.
4. The Cars - A good mix of cars of the era, the end of the fins and the rise of the muscle car with some late 40's throwbacks for good measure. Each car, like in previous mafias, is a conglomeration pieced together from a number of real life makes and models with some being a mix of several models or more easily recognisable examples altered slightly. Cars styling span from GM, Ford, Chrysler, Desoto, AMCs, Jeeps, Kaisers etc. and to even the ol Checker Cab. There are also exotics, Italian, German, English and Japanese inspired/combination cars. Lots of detail and choice.
5. The details - Things like dash lights, windscreen wipers, puddles, gators who will and do bite, a larger array of weather, clouds and lighting effects. The rectangular speedo, the zoom in and shake when braking violently and the rear vision mirror at the top of the screen. Rain is also multi directional and causes lighting and reflection changes. More character movement in car even tapping the wheel with the music.
6. The music - a great soundtrack of the era with three stations to choose from, helps with the atmosphere. The music also changes over the course of the game so you get new songs.
The Bad:
1. The graphics - Even after the frame rate unlock patch there are still graphic issues with some blurry, soft or washed out looking elements and reports of low frame rates with high end systems, indicating poor optimisation for PC. There are a few visual glitches with floating objects, items not quite lined up and NPCS and cars doing odd things. The detail/lighting effects of your car when driving is never as good as other cars be they moving or stopped.
2. Loss of unique elements - You could argue that the good/unique elements that attract you to a franchise should be kept or evolved with each new game, Mafia III however has lost a fair number of these. Elements I always enjoyed and was hoping to see back have been removed. Things like refuelling, getting caught running a red light or speeding, the speed limiter to stop from speeding, eating at a diner, drinking in a club, and the ability to buy clothes. There was also much reduced original music score which in previous games was used to increase atmospheric feel to great effect at specific points in the game. The “garage” from previous games where you could keep a stable of cars and modify them is gone, you can only choose a number of select vehicles which have to be unlocked.
3. Change of game style – This has changed from being a much more cinematic, linear game with a smaller detailed map, to a fully open world game that is being compared to GTA , Watchdogs etc. Mafia III can’t compete against most of them because it’s still trying to provide the storytelling cinematic experience and be open world. It’s pretty much impossible to do this without seriously effecting one these factors. This is something that games like LA Noire suffered from but could be forgiven given the large array of unique elements they included in the game. I don’t know if they did this to try and keep old fans whilst also trying to attract new fans. The problem is you can’t take an existing franchise and change its’ style in big leaps because you can lose your original fan base and disappoint new fans who are expecting a different type of game.
Though the game has gained a lot of open world elements few of them are new and/or unique to the Mafia franchise. There’s a good argument for franchises undergo some changes to keep them fresh, but if those changes are already “par for the course” in other games it just comes across as content filler. A lot of the new elements are standard open world “grind” achievements that are all too common in many games simply to utilise the large map.
4. The cars – While good they aren't quite in proportion to the world size wise compared to their real world models they’re based on. So your player and other people driving can look a bit strange driving some vehicles. Other times it’s almost like the people get smaller when they get into a car and get a bit bigger when outside. I think this was done simply to make driving easier, the roads smaller and allow for more traffic. Car damage is more generic and requires much more violent crashes before a car shows damage or finally gives out. Cars, while well detailed, just simply aren’t as carefully detailed as they were in previous games and the change of the game developer from being solely Czech 2K probably has a lot to do with this.
5. Little details - There is no "jump" movement which can be annoying, e.g. when moving from a jetty to a boat you have to fall into the water first before getting in. The integration of the news announcer who announces topical/historic news events at feels a bit tacked on. Sometimes the smaller supporting character's expression changes like flicking on a switch, the more major supporting characters don't have this issue but it is noticeable. Inability to put the top up or down on convertibles or switch car engines/lights on or off. The camera angle while driving always resets even if you've adjusted it with the mouse to a view that's more comfortable.
Overall:
If I had the choice I'd certainly buy the game again, the world, main story, characters and cars were enough to keep me playing. There are some beautiful aspects to the game and some wonderful cinematic elements and storytelling. The voice acting is top notch, social commentary element of the times and environmental details are great. The only disappointments I had were to do with the pc graphics, the removal of certain elements unique to the Mafia franchise, use of stock standard open world elements and an overall feel that the game could’ve done with a bit more polish before being released.
Switching to an “Open world” type game I believe has made this game the shaky link in the franchise because in the past you never compared Mafia I or Mafia II with any open world game as it was a linear cinematic storytelling experience in a small but detailed world. Mafia III suffers from the loss of that becomes a little bit of a pale shadow of other open world games.
All in all I'd give it around 70 out of 100, if the graphics weren't an issue I'd have given it 80.

Writing a review about a rather old game? Hmm, well, why not. After all I really enjoyed playing this game. It's not awesome, but good and solid. It's got descent graphics and an even more descent story which is most highly Stephen King inspired. King was my most favourite writer when I was a teen so I appreciate a good story of that kind. What keeps this game from being epic? Well, it has it's flaws. Game and story are very intensive for the first couple hours. It feels like playing a real awesome and eerie movie. Fantastic opening. The long middle part however dumps all the things that made the opening great, turning the game into a rather repetitive action packed experience that feels rather stretched and quite stressy, but not at all eerie no more. Then, to the end however, Alan Wake goes back to it's roots and presents you a both thrilling and totally Stephen King like finish. A few aspects are rather annoying. Ammo is quite rare, and Alan sure takes his time reloading his guns. All the batteries that Alan finds for his flashlight are sucked empty after seconds. Why?! Even though Alan seems better in shape than me myself, he is entirely exhausted after ten meters of running. I tell you, I'm not into sports really, but if I had a bunch of chainsaw-armed monsters on my tail, I WOULD RUN! Not so Allan.. okay but that's actually all that I got to complain about. The game is fun, it looks and sounds fantastic, so even though it's old, I say give it a try.

In this game you play as New York Times best selling author Dean Koontz. Finding himself at the end of his wits from writer's block the past 2 years, he goes to a quiet Washington mountain town with his smokin' hot wife Alice, in hopes of finding some desparate source of inspiration. Little did he know the town was in the midst of preparing for a major annual festival, since Dean couldn't find the peace and quiet to write his next big hit, he eventually loses his mind and the line between what is good and evil slowly dissolves.
Dean Koontz, still depressed, realizes that he'll never be a great author like his Uncle Stephen King develops a severe addiction to coffee in the hopes it might improve his writing. You are then tasked to go about the town collecting miscellaneous coffee thermoses and misplaced manuscript pages that he lost during his caffeine fueled frenzy.
After a brief stay at a mental health clinic for deranged artists, Mr. Koontz breaks free and finally sits down and writes his new hit book "The DaVinci Code".
Final Verdict:
Story is alright, but not amazing.
Too much emphasis on finding collectables.
Unique concept for combat.
Verizon and Energizer product placement is really annoying throughout.
Please don't buy this game for full price. It's a fun way to kill a few hours if you buy it on sale.

I think this game can best be described as a roguelike retooled as a casual game. Not casual in the "Cawwadoody is for casuals!" sense, casual like Tetris: challenging but addictive and meant to be played in short bursts. It's not a game you play hoping to win; it's a game you pick up because you're bored and feel like shooting some dudes. You can quit whenever you're tired of losing, and pick it up again when you feel like shooting some more dudes. Going up against the same enemies and learning what powerups do what means you gradually get better, while the randomization and the new items you keep unlocking keep it from feeling repetitive.

This games review is going to be much like my review of Blackwell Convergence. The reason being the games were both very similar in nature. As I stated before, the Blackwell Series is an interesting one and as each game progresses, the storyline becomes more and more polished, the art gets better and better, and the puzzles and clue finding get more interesting. In the fourth installment holds true to Unbound and Convergence, but its real strength comes from the best puzzles of the four games. Here are some of the pro's and con's of the game.
Pro's: The storyline is evolving into a rather interesting and mysterious one. Rosa and Joeys relationship is fully developed by this point and is quite hilarious. Many more puzzles than the other games and a bit more involved than just left click this object and see what Rosa/Joey will do. I also enjoyed the music and the length much more in this game from the the first two games, it was comparible to the third installment.
Con's: I still hate the art. It is definitely not my style and they just keep changing it from game to game. Consistancy please! And the consistancy between the games is also a little headache. But most of the changes seem to enhance the new game and make you wish they did it with the previous games (Potential Spoilers but not too much: I loved when they allowed the swapping).
I've yet to play Epiphany, but here are my scores of the games.
Blackwell Legacy: 6/10
Blackwell Unbound: 8/10
Blackwell Convergence: 7.6/10
Blackwell Deception: 8.2/10
Blackwell Series: 7.8/10

I paid $10 for it and I feel ripped off.  Your 95% to hit is really about 40%, and the levelling system is ponderous at best. As others have said, the voice acting is atrocious.  The game plays better without it, but that doesn't help all that much because the text is boring to read.  The movement is slow and lanky.  It really ruins immersion when I'm bored and watching my guys move ponderously slow.  This game has too many serious flaws to be worth playing.
The levelling system is seriously just painfully bad. You get 23 attribute points, and you get 2-5 skill points depending on how many of your attribute points you put into Intelligence.  You can't raise your attributes later on.  So if you put half your attributes into intelligence, then you cripple your combat skills so you can get enough survival skills end-game.
First skill level takes 1 point, 2nd takes 2, 3rd takes 3, etc. You have 4 characters and you can get an npc.  You will need to level 10 non-combat skills to open doors, see traps, upgrade weapons, etc.  Another few skills if you want to get good use out of your medical supplies.
If you're a big fan of games like these, check out the Avernum line of games or X-COM: Enemy Unknown.     You can get Avernum on sale for $1-3  and it is far superior.

I gotta say Paragon is not a mod nor a port of Pioneer (which in itself is a remake of Elite II: Frontier) but at this point just a blatant reskinning. Virtually everything is identical to Pioneer expect for slightly higher quality graphics with a bit of post processing. Though I was keenly aware of the similarities before I bought this game the promotional videos and info I had read about the game on their site beforehand made it seem that  -even at this early alpha state- they had improved  on some of the base features of Pioneer. Sadly that is not the case at all (at least not as of now).
In fact they managed to screw up some basic mundane things that were already working well in Pioneer. For instance, simple things like word wrapping in menus and UI. A large part of Pioneer's and subsequently Paragon's gameplay has you pouring through resource lists, menus and just general text. At HD resolution (1920x1080) the font is oversived, janky, somewhat fuzzy and in certain areas words or phases overlap making it a puzzle to decipher if you aren't already familar with what it is supposed to say. That's a big part of the game and if that's not formatted properly well that certainly degrades the experience.
Another simple thing - In Pioneer when you visit various stations and or cities on planets throughout the universe the station personnel is represented by dynamically generated character pictures, made from snippets of male and female facial features of varying ethnicities and...silly mismatched sci-fi type gear. There are like 10 distinct facial features that are aslo mismatched to make somewhat unique (if not sometimes terrifying and creepy O.O) variations of characters to "interact" (they are just photos with text underneath them but use your imagination) with. Did Paragon improve upon this aspect at all? No, in fact they replaced that quirky dynamic character generating system with a very boring single, all encompassing male or female faceless avatar. I mean really? Maybe that's something that will be changed in the future but who knows.
These may seem like little things but if they can't get these things right, well you get the picture.
I personally regret the purchase and would rather just support Pioneer which is free and open-source. It's kind of shameful in my opinion that the Paragon devs are even making money off essentially a straight forward clone of a free game. Maybe in the future they will be able to develop enough unique content as to separate their game from Pioneer but as of now it is a mirror image of Pioneer with just an extra bit of visual polish.
If I am somehow woefully misinformed and Paragon was intended to be a visual upgrade mod of Pioneer then my question is how did it get Greenlit on Steam? I seriously would like to know what is happening here.

Having read the mixed reviews, I hesitated for quite a long time before finally getting Wasteland 2. I do like old-school RPGs, but I was not sure if the reported flaws would not kill all the fun.
They didn't. I enjoyed playing Wasteland 2 so much that I finished within just 2 weeks time, during which I played it for a total 82 hours.
Yes, the fights could have more strategic depth. Yes, the missions could be a bit more transparent. Yes, the character design could have been a bit more detailed. Yes, it would not have hurt to give every NPC an own artwork.
And yes, the skill system could be described a little better, so that you don't have to start over after a few hours, when you realize that your party just isn't gonna cut it.
With all these flaws removed, Wasteland 2 could have been an outstanding RPG. But even with the flaws, it still is a very good one.
So if you are unsure, give it a try. There is a good chance you won't regret it.

A very cute yet flawed point and click adventure from Double Fine.
----
+ Great art
+ Great music
+ Excellent, funny dialogue
+ A slew of really interesting ideas
- Obscure, immersion breaking puzzles at the end
- Suffers a little bit from "point and click nonsense"
----
So, if you don't already know, Double Fine have a bit of a reputation for making really interesting games full of unique ideas which are unfortunately either technically or mechanically flawed in some way. Does this one follow that trend? Absolutely.
First off, fair warning - it's a point and click game and as such it comes with the traditional "point and click nonsense", i.e. tons of backtracking, some obscurity and just a touch of pixel hunting, though admittedly none of this affected my experience too badly except for the obscure ending (which i'll get to in a minute).
Broken Age is split into two acts, the first of which I found to be quite excellent. You're introduced to two very different scenarios that you can swap between at will or complete in order, both of which are incredibly imaginative. The puzzles that exist aren't too difficult, but more importantly they MAKE SENSE (at least, in the strange context of the two settings). You will meet a ton of interesting, funny and downright strange characters and generally have a pretty good time.
Unfortunately the second act let's the whole thing down a bit. The story remains interesting but gets increasingly bogged down by some awfully obscure puzzle design. The last few puzzles - aside from being almost unreasonably complicated - rely completely on immersion breaking player knowledge instead of what each of the two protagonists could reasonably know, which really pulls you out of the story and leaves a sour taste in your mouth for the ending.
Overall, I'd say that if you like the point and click genre or Double Fine's other games then Broken Age is definately worth at least a look. The first half is exquisite, but being a Double Fine game it unfortunately falls short of perfection due to some very dodgy and quite frustrating puzzle design towards the end.
This is the "Lost" of point and click adventures, though sadly without the dreamy Sawyer.

As one of the backers fromtye original Kickstarter campaign, I ought to be really cross and take my annoyance out on the game in this review. But I won't, for the simple reason that it was never a factor to begin with. Even as I was finding the game my then computer was in no shape to run it, so had it been released sooner I still wouldn't have been able to enjoy it before now. Therefore, this will be a more objective look, removed from the drama.
The first thing I wanna say is just how nice it is to have a point and click adventure that I can control with my wireless 360 controller. I know that's odd but the way it's set up using the mouse to drag by default is just awkward; I know you can change it but I got so used to the controller it felt nice. In a way, the game feels optimized for controllers, especially when you factor in that ludicrous 1 hour achievement - but more on that later.
Visually and audibly the game is wonderful. I love the seemingly hand drawn art style, although I can't actually say if it is or merely simulating it. The voice acting is great and the music was always fitting and pleasant. I'm not sure the game NEEDED to have top o' the line voices actors like Elijah Wood, but their talent adds to the presentation.
The gameplay is... It's a Point & Click adventure game, you would expect nothing more than inventory management and some puzzles of various natures. Instead we get a couple of really awkward timing/reflex puzzles and one that is completely awful due to two things: solutions being unique per run and needless trial & error. There's another that some people feel is in the same vein but that just takes a little imagination for the interpretations to make sense. By and large, though, the puzzles are actually fairly clever and all have logical solutions. Even if one DOES kinda make you wish you had a notepad.
I'm giving this a recommended because I really did enjoy the game and felt I got my money's worth out of that initial crowdfunding attempt. A couple of bad puzzles just mean I'd take it down to 4 stars instead of 5 on my Backloggery.
Incidentally, about that achievement... Who the hell puts a "beat the game lightning fast" objective for a point and click. That's like telling someone to finish a visual novel in an hour; it's DOABLE, but there's absolutely no enjoyment anywhere to be found. Unlike a VA, though, there's little room for error here. I actually got it, but it made me put off wanting to replay it for a while.

Excellent game. The atmosphere is grim. The story is a classic tale of the devil playing his schemes on mankind. It's up to you to play along or foil his plan. Gameplay is solid. Graphics are nice. I have finished the main questline in about 15 hours and got several side campaigns left to play. The game happens on a map. You will disover locations here to advance the story or do some side quests or just bargain for stuff or heal your characters from injuries suffered during the combat missions. The quests on the map are unspectacular: click here, move there, make a decision, continue. The obvious main part of the game is doing the combat missions. Those are quite fun, very bloody and entertaining. I particularly liked the poker mechanics for the skill cards giving you bonuses beyond the individual skills.
However, the game is also quite buggy. You would think they have fixed all bugs by now, but right on the first map there is a bug where your gold mining goes crazy and you'll end up with either no money or thousands of dollars. Likewise, the game reliably crashes on me when I try to move the game window to my other screen the first time. On second attempt it works. And I had another bug where the map wouldn't show which forced me to replay the campaign. Also, I found it somewhat annoying that I cannot have separate save games, which forces me to replay entire campaigns. Likewise, there is lots of slow loading dialogues and clicking. For instance, there is no option to feed all your chars at once, so the game asks you which char to feed, you pick one, then it asks you again, pick another, rinse and repeat for all four chars.
Nevertheless, I very much enjoyed the game, despite the apparent shortcomings.

It's fun, it's fast paced, it's hectic, and it's crazy.  Skill does make a difference, although strategy and randomness (and the quick nature of the game) means it usually feels pretty balanced.  The weapons and stages are varied, and where the mechanics end the shear oddness of the game picks up (There is, after all, a dedicated quack button).
What I like the most is the game is mostly meat.  You press start and within 30 second you can be in a full area fighting.  The transitions between stages can be so fast as to be easily missed and the game has already started again.  There is a brief stop after a few matches to show the scores, and then it's right back to the mayhem.  There is a single player challenge mode to train up certain skills (more an unobtrusive tutorial really) and to unlock new hats.  After the solid and consistent mechanics, the plain oddness of the game never stops being fun.  Again, a dedicated quack button, also a ragdoll button.  When ragdolled other players can pick you up, so you can pick up the dead bodies of your opponents and walk around with them.  Lots of hats and masks that pop off when you die, so you can also pick up and wear the heads of defeated ducks.  There are some levels with drum sets, others with old-timey muskets that reload in an old-timey way.  I don't know if I've seen a game with this much personality in a long time.
I only have two major complaints.  I do love the condensed nature of the game, meaning you can have a fulfilling in about half a hour.  But the game is so hectic and intense that after 30 min it becomes a little jarring, forcing a break.  While it is mostly meat, it's also kind of one note.  I'm hoping some other game modes might get added eventually to mix up the play some.
It's worth it at full price.
Small disclaimer:  My hours played is misleading.  There is currently a glitch (about to be fixed) that doesn't close the game after quitting.  So thought I've played quite a lot, I haven't played that much.

This is easily the best game I have played this year in the action category.
Let me start by saying that I haven't played as much of this game as I would like to have. So if I am missing out major things then I apologize.
Story is very good, but I don't think it follows the lore of the books at all if that bothers you. It bothers me every now and then as they throw some weird stuff in to make the story make sense but if you let that go its great.
The level system is very good. Can customize exactly how you want to play the game. Also the gear system is satisfying as well. Makes it so there is more stuff to work for.
The star of the show is the nemesis system. Its awesome. I have never played a game which has got me so into getting revenge on a randomly created urak. Each urak has meaning and some can be a proper pain in the backside. I started the game on the highest difficulty to try and get as much time as I could with it. This meant that the urak bosses could easily kill me if I messed up with meant I then started creating my own personal revenge movies to get back at them. One Urak was called Ratbag. He killed me 3 times each time he gets harder and levels up. I finally managed to beat him even though he manged to recruit a caragor party. I was so happy it was unreal. Until i load the game up the next time and I found out he has cheated death and come back harder as Ratbag the machine. I was angry, shocked, scared but most of all pumped for round 2. Taking him down a second time was even more pleasing! This is just a small insight into the nemesis system. There are tonnes of different types of orcs each requiring you to kill them in a unique way. I would be here forever explaining it all but just let me tell you its worth buying the game for.
I really enjoy the combat. A lot of players say its a copy of the Arkham style games which it is but that's not a bad thing. The combat it smooth and very enjoyable. After leveling up a bit you have a lot of moves to keep the combat interesting and fresh in my opinion.
There seems to be a lot of talk about the micro transactions. I haven't played a lot however I have found absolutely no need to use the micro transaction system at all. Legendary gear is really quite simple to get your hands on. Once you have unlocked and ability called death threat. Use it on a high level urak and he will boost his level and give you legendary gear. Kill him and you get the gear. So I don't see why you need to use micro transactions. Nothing is technically locked away from you so all its for is for getting better gear to make the game easier. I like a challenge so I will never use it. As far as I am aware there is no PVP element so there no pay to win against other players. I agree micro transactions in a full price game is a scummy♥♥♥♥♥♥move but if you don't need to use it then its not necessarily a problem.
