I find it strange that I like this game as much as I do. After all I get easily frustrated and angry when I get my car stuck in the snow. But I find SPINTIRES delightful and satisfying from how much hard work it forces you to put into it.
SPINTIRES is a game that puts you in the middle of some isolated forest or marsh, and your goal is to deliver logs from the lumber yard to the mill. Sounds straightforward.
However, the terrain will prove to be your biggest obstacle. Most 'roads' are nothing more than muddy trenches, destinations sit at the top of steep hills, and it will become necessary to haul logs and trailers through rivers...which may end in disaster. Fortunately, you have some pretty hefty trucks at your disposal, a couple of which can barrel over smaller trees with no problem.
The aforementioned satisfaction comes from trudging through the mud and reaching your destination with your load intact. There's a wonderful sense of accomplishment when you get your vehicle stuck and manage to winch yourself to a tree and pull yourself out.
The physics SPINTIRES is something to boast about. The terrain changes under your tires, depending on the vehicle you're operating; mud gets kicked up, roads get chewed up, small bridges might collapse under your weight.
You can play more casually by respawning your vehicle to an unlocked garage or not have to worry about shifting gears manually. But there is a hardcore mode where respawning is disabled, providing a more realistic experience; if your vehicle is stuck submerged in a river, you need a bigger truck to pull it out.
Even so, at the start of each level your traveller's map will be covered in black spots. To uncover these, for better or for worse, you need to drive to the source of these spots to remove the cloaking. This promotes more aggressive exploration, though this is more of a negative than a positive for some players, as there is no option to have the entire map visible.
There is a multiplayer option in SPINTIRES as well as steering wheel support, though there are many people who have had issues with both lately. Briefly glancing through forums, there might be some fixes that can clear up these issues, but hopefully the developers will look into the problems quickly and patch them out.
All in all, I highly recommend SPINTIRES. I've sunk a lot of hours into delivering logs across a marsh and walked away feeling satisfied and very entertained. Sounds strange, but, if you give it a try, you might be surprised at how fun it can be.

Fettuccine Alfredo began as regular fettuccine al burro until the Roman restaurateur Alfredo di Lelio enriched it with a double and a triple dose of butter for his pregnant wife, who could not keep anything down. The dish was so delicious he kept it on the menu of his restaurant, Alfredo all Scrofa, in Rome. Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks had it during their 1920 honeymoon trip to Rome, loved it, brought the recipe back, and served it to their friends when they returned to Hollywood. And so another Italian came to America. Fettuccine Alfredo has most certainly been eaten more in the States than in Italy since then. The dish is used as the base for many different versions, topped with shrimp, broccoli, asparagus, and more. Since butter separated readily when heated, cream is added to make the sauce creamier. In this version, I also add a few leaves of sage, since sage and butter are a marriage made in heaven.

Ingredients 1 teaspoon kosher salt, plus more for pasta pot
1 pound dried fettuccine
2 cups heavy cream, or half-and-half
4 tablespoons unsalted butter
10 fresh sage leaves
½ cup grated Grana Padano, (or Parmigiano-Reggiano)
Directions Bring a large pot of salted water to boil for pasta. When you are ready to begin the sauce, slip the fettuccine into the water.
Combine the cream, 1 cup pasta cooking water, the butter, sage, and half of the grated cheese in a large skillet over medium heat. Stir to melt the butter and bring just a simmer. Let simmer lightly for a minute or two, so the cream infuses the sage leaves.
When the fettuccine is al dente, transfer it directly to the skillet with the simmering sauce. Season with the salt and return to a simmer. Simmer, tossing with the tongs, just until the sauce begins to coat the pasts, another minute or two. Remove from heat, sprinkle with the remaining grated cheese, and toss. Serve immediately.

Easily one of my all time favs!  Alan Wake has a whole bunch of three of my most coveted things: woods, darkness and flashlights.
Synopsis: A vacation in the charming little mountain town of Bright Falls was supposed to be a much needed break from the hectic city life of New York and  the stress of insomnia paired with a classic case of writer's block for our crime thriller author protagonist, Alan Wake. Little did he or his wife know that a dark presence was once again stirring beneath Cauldron Lake and the island cabin they were supposed to be staying at during their trip.  Next thing you know, Wake's wife Alice goes missing and so does a week's worth of time as Alan awakens in the wreck of their car not fully able to remember how  everything transpired up to that moment.  Thus begins his dark journey to find his wife and to discover what's been taking over the town's people and twisting them into what is known as the Taken.
This game is heavy on narrative and the superb voice acting makes for an unforgettable mystery/thriller gaming experience. There's a lot of exploration if you choose to track down the collectibles, most prominent among those being the manuscript pages from a missing novel you didn't realize you were working on which actually reveals much of the backstory of the townspeople and what's really been going on.  The use of light/dark, namely burning the darkness off of the Taken so that they become vulnerable to attack is a very satisfying gameplay mechanic and the two bonus episodes are very well done. Also, the graphics are really good and truly make you feel what it is to run around a mountainous forest at night while being pursued by darkness. Thankfully this game contains more batteries than have ever been manufactured in the real world.  You're gonna need them!!
Don't wait for a sale if you're contemplating getting this game - you'll be glad you bought it.

CroNix is an Arena fighting game that has tactical aspects to it.  The characters are very unique and the fighting is pretty epic.  There are people complaining about getting juggled to death but that isn't very common unless you let it happen to you.  When you get up after being knocked down you are invulnerable for the duration of standing up and .5 seconds after so letting yourself get chain-cced is purely the players' fault.
Your character will feel slow and clunky but I feel this is how it is intended.  The gameplay is fairly slowpaced overall due to character running speed and how long the matches can last. (10-20 minutes)
I have played the 5v5 and 3v3 game types. The 7v7 gametype does not appear to have many people queueing for it so I cannot try it.
5v5 is basically a team deathmatch (first to 50 points) with 2 points where you must grab an item and bring it to the middle. When you get the item to the point it gives your team a 10-15 second random buff ranging from damage to damage reduction. If you get 4 of the items onto the point then you gain a point bonus which is extremely helpful for teams that are losing by a bit.
3v3 is a best of 5 team deathmatch where both teams have 5 lives. Each death will lower your team life count by 1 so try to keep your team mates alive as much as you can and do your best to minimize your deaths.
In terms of equipment there are items called "Cards" and "Tonics."  Cards are basically used to customize your skills of a certain character to better match your play-style and have good and bad effects that balance out.
Tonics are like potions that you can use several times a game. There's 4 different types that you can bring in: Recovery, Offense, Defense, and Special. Recovery/Offense/Defense are pretty much self explanatory but Specials have a variety such as Move speed and detection.
Both of these types of items are obtainable by just playing games and using ingame or premium currency to get packs which give you a random card/tonic.
[Tonics] Recently I have found out there is a very limited pay to win feature. Some of the Tonics obtainable via their premium currency packs are extremely strong for what they are almost tripling the effect of beginning/low level tonics. I'm hoping the developers see this and make sure it does not get out of hand.

Right now this game is the most realistic and affordable firefighter simulation available to the public, that being said it does need a fair bit of work to make it truly shine. I'll cut to the chase now and say that if you're interested in fire/emergency services (especially from Germany) and love simulation games you should definitely pick it up, especially on sale!
That being said there are a lot of bugs such as the AI getting stuck during a task making missions unable to complete without a restart (e.g. AI failing to assemble the hose and just standing around, tasks failing to update, not receiving any new tasks etc.)
One of the aspects I find most disappointing currently is that the game (outside of the firefighting aspect) is pretty lifeless in it's current state. There is limited civilian traffic, no pedestrians on the street, no onlookers watching the fire and so on. The devs have spent a lot of time creating a world that is true to detail, the station and surrounding areas are meticulously modelled. At some times the game looks and feels pretty real, but you're pulled right out of it by the empty feeling world.
All that aside, if the devs keep improving the game and listening to the community I can see Notruf 112 becoming a great product, and perhaps the best firefighter sim available to date. Please keep up the good work and don't abandon this game!
Pros:
+ Realistic vehicles and equipment that you can actually use
+ Good fire physics that keep being improved with each update
+ Good mission variety - dumpster fire, alarm call, traffic collisions/vehicle fires etc.
+ Randomised mission locations with enterable buildings
+ Varied roles & tasks (e.g. command vehicle, water tanker etc.)
+ Realistic feel (getting the callout and responding to the scene feels amazing at times)
+ Pretty decent graphics for a game of its kind
Cons:
- The world feels empty in it's current state
- AI needs to be vastly improved
- Many important sounds (such as the engines, hose etc.) need reworking
- Saving system needs to be reworked
- Lack of ambient sounds
- Opening the menu doesn't pause the game
What devs could improve on:
- Character models (overall appearance, more variety, uniform improvements etc.)
- Ambient sounds (add in mission dialogue instead of just displaying on screen, ambient radio chatter, communication between firefighters etc.)
- Make the world more life-like (add more traffic & improve variety of vehicles, include some pedestrians on the street or at least add a chance for civilians to gather around the scene of a large emergency)
- Improve animations for the player and NPCs (e.g. getting into and out of vehicles, putting on SCBA etc.)
- AI improvements

There are certain animated children's movies that strike an emotional chord, which compel adults to keep watching them over and over again.  This game manages to capture that emotional chord.  I'm sure kids will love it, but there's something special about the story that will draw in adults and make you feel something.

Reading some of the negative reviews, I'm surprised how much dislike there is for part two.  Personally, I really enjoyed getting to revisit locations as they change and watching the two main characters get to know each other indirectly.  The puzzles got harder in part two, but given how easy they are in part one, that's not a bad thing.  You get to see all the characters you've met earlier change, develope, and grow.
In terms of plot, the one thing I wish would have been changed was part one.  I felt like there wasn't really time to establish Vella's character the way there was for Shay.  I had a very strong sense of who Shay was as a person in part one, but since Vella's story was so driven by her adversity to the obstacles around her, it wasn't really until part two that I began to get a sense of her personality beyond being willing to stand up for herself.  It would have been nice to have her do some small puzzle unconnected to the maiden's feast to define her personality to the player, before her adventure started.
I'll admit also I bought this on sale, so I didn't mind so much that it was short.  (I took my time and it lasted about 14 hours.)  Never the less, I will definitly be replaying this game, just like I rewatch Toy Story and the Iron Giant.

Wow......people say this isn't like Fallout. Of course it's not, but it certainly, without a doubt feels just like it. I felt the nostalgia all over me playing this.
If you take Fallout and put it in a bed with Divinity: Original Sin or Pillars of Eternity, well, this is the result.
Now to the break down.
The Good:
Combat(8.7/10)- Combat is smooth, feels so much like XCOM, a favorite of mine, and is strategically rewarding. It has a good amount of gore and the animations are done fantastically. There are a lot of weapons to use and each weapon is made accordingly making strategic planning and placement crucial.
Gameplay(9.6/10)- I couldn't exit the game. I didn't want to. I wanted to keep playing. It has that perfect feel of "Whats around this corner, whats in this box, whats in that cave" you dont want to leave your screen. The voice acting, holy hell the voice acting, it's a work of beauty. And the graphics, the graphics fit perfectly, backgrounds and non-enterable areas are drawn out and made so beautifully.
Story(8.5/10)- The story so far, is quite interesting as there is interesting plot changes, eerie coms messages and decisions in each and every corner of the game to question, explore, and discover. The gears in your mind turn and you keep wanting to find out more and more.
Character(8.9/10)- I was immediately attached to my characters after I spent about 10 minutes creating my 4 custom squad-mates. I had Bill my strong charismatic Desert Ranger look. Kit, my hard♥♥♥♥♥big-mouthed spy-sniper chick. Liam, my Australian drugged mechanic, and Rico, the young suck-up, Combat medic from the Marines. The level of detail is amazing, the designs and amount of combinations are extreme.
The Decent:
AI(6.8/10)- The AI is OK. It's not that hard, but it's not that easy either. It has strategies, and tries it's best to use cover and enemy types use their weapons accordingly.
Pathfinding(7.3/10)- Pathfinding, I have had a few issues with. In combat and walking around. Some party members stray off at times, and in combat some of them take odd directions when I told them not to take that direction. It's a rare annoyance but is very very nagging when it comes around.
The downright terrible♥♥♥♥♥♥
Saving(1.6/10)- There is no autosave. Simple. Well, there is one, but it's non-existant. My last autosave from my most recent manual save is 45 minutes ago. 45 MINUTES. That is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Terrible. And in a game like this there needs to be a working autosave.
Combat UI(4.6/10)- The Combat UI is near useless. It skips out on basic features that you have to use your Inventory to view like how much ammo one person has on them, and how much armor before that person begins taking real damage. Also, the only health-bar you see is when you hover over that person. It's annoying, when a person is low on health, I will RARELY know that until they die. That leaves you constantly wasting a minute or 2 checking health and seeing how many med-packs you have left.
OVERALL VERDICT (8.7/10):
Wasteland 2 is a welcoming game that if you're new, you will quickly get the hang of it, and at the same time can be a brutal experience. It is fun, heart racing, and definitely a "What's around the next corner" game that I can easily, easily, sink 80 hours into.
If these few nagging bugs can be fixed, it will make the experience a whole lot smoother. And with these issues fixed the verdict is an easy 9.3/10

First of all, I must say I feel a bit cheated. The game runs natively in 640x480 resolution, but other than the title screen and one unused background mentioned in the commentary mode, all art is point resampled from 320x240. It shows and is such a pity, especially given that the background art used ingame is pre-rendered, so it should be a cinch to up-res it natively.
Also, the whole medium/psychic bashing was extremely heavy handed. I'm all for social commentary, but there's a fine line between this and irrational bashing and I feel this game crosses it at times. Yes, mediums are con artists. This does not mean they feast on child flesh, drink human blood for breakfast, etc, etc.
Speaking of crossing the line - Joey has been getting meaner and meaner with each game and some of his lines here are downright abusive. Not sure how to feel about that.
Other than that, another improvement from previous game. Really loved the implementation of commentary mode, and it actually had some good insights into development this time instead of n-th musing about how Dave Gilbert met this or that voice artist. Being able to use phone to look up clues was amazing, since you had to travel to PC apartment to do that in previous games, killing pacing in the process.
Some nice, simple puzzles - nothing akin to Donkey Cart puzzle in Discworld or Cat's Mustache from Gabriel Knight 3, everything was really logical. A few conversation puzzles as well, and few instances of needing to combine clues. Good hint system if you ever get stuck, although I still had to look some things online once or twice - though take it with a grain of salt, since I never was good with actual adventure game 'gameplay' - I play them mostly for story/conversations.
Personal 'not feeling ripped off' price point: $5

Like Space? Like Green, Cube headed alien people? Well then this game is for you, trust me, it's awsome. If you're afraid to get the game because you think you won't understand it, don't worry because the game has very good tutorials and you'll understand it all in some time. this game has 3 main gamemodes to it, Sandbox, Science, and Career, Sandbox is just as it sounds, all parts and features are available to you right from the start and you're free to build whatever you want. Career starts you off with a very low budget space center and you have to complete missions ( they're mostly random each time ) to earn funds, science, and reputation to unlock new parts, abilities, and station upgrades. You also manage everything in Career mode. ( Sandbox and Science have certain features disabled. ) Science is basically Career mode, but without missions, funds, and reputation, Science being the only thing you can earn. Other than that, it's the same as Career. All these gamemodes are unlocked right from the start and i recommend spending plenty of time in Sandbox before heading to Career or Science so you can get a proper feel of the game. That's basically it, physics are incredible, art style and models are all charming and pretty to look at, and i can't explain the satisfaction you'll feel when you complete a goal you've been going at. and never fear, if all else fails for your plans, just use the cheat menu! ( fn alt f12. )

I'm rewriting my review to give a more indepth look at CroNix.
PROS: Very rarely do I find a game where I can say it is truely all skill dependant and does not rely on gear or some other gimick to determine how good of a player you are, and for that CroNix does well.
CroNix has a very unique roster of currently playable characters with unique skill sets and different skill caps associated with them.
Objective based mechanics for the larger scale maps is a really nice touch for making teamplay a priority over just mobbing and ganking everyone on the map.
CroNix sort of eliminates the idea of "1 Fed person can carry a whole team." Individual skill does matter as a player in CroNix but 1 person can only do so much on their own, so teamplay is essential and helps grow the community to be more accostumed to working together.
CONS:
And for the not so good......
The overall gameplay of CroNix feels super clunky at the moment, the inability to auto and move on melee characters puts them at an extreme disadvantage to the ranged counter parts who can.
The UI isn't the most intuitive UI I have ever seen and yes its a bit messy but that isn't where my concern lies in the UI. My concern with the UI is the lack of information when it comes to the being affected by status effects and how hidden some of the things are like your SP gauge and you buffs at the bottom of the screen.
A major concern I'm having with Cronix is the server instability I can't neccesarily blame them because it is beta but the inconsistency without warning is the true issue. There is never any warnings or indications of when you will or will not be dropped. Your ping doesn't directly effect when you're going to be dropped and it isn't like theres a massive amount of players stressing out the servers. Which brings me to my next concern.
Matching making is terrible, between the lack of players and not appearing to have a solid MMR system in place you will see new players get stomped by more experienced players which inturn leaves a bad taste in their mouths. Those very same people then leave the game upset because they have no idea what happened to them give and a bad review. Its hard to grow your community when majority of players aren't having fun, because of inexperience or ridiciously long que times. At the moment in it's current state CroNix has quite a few issues that need to be adressed but with time I believe it could grow into a nice competitive game.
Thats all for now I will update this at a future time, but if you're interested in helping both this game and its community grow download it and play. :3

CroNix just released but I am already enjoying it. It is an action game at heart, but 3D fighting is also a genre I would consider it for.  You play by selecting character class to play, you can change class each for each respawn similar to TF2, thats a definite plus for team work. there are tons of classes and most of them are fun to play. I have probably spent most my time playing the healer class so far, but there is a good variety of classes to chose from.  As it is now there are only 3 maps and each is tied to a game mode. If CroNix ends up successful though I would bet we get more.
The negative I have for this game are clear to me even after a little bit of playing. The biggest is probably the matchmaking. Its pretty terrible. I know the game is new but matchmaking needs work. I also really hope they add the ability to join a game in progress, having leavers cripple a team like that is just a shame, and its pretty unnecessary. My second complaint is probably class balance. I understand it will be hard to balance out all these classes, but its definitely something that will need a lot of work in the future.
I dont have much else to say as it stands. The game is just released in open beta early access so there is not much more content than that to talk about. I enjoyed my time playing even if I dont plan on dedicating myself to following it all through development.  I do however recommend you guys try it if you get the chance.  I am sure ill be back playing it again in a few months time if it ends up continuing development. That is something I hope happens after all.

I got this as a gift a while back, had to wait for it to be released.
I'm like 8 hours in. The PC port is kinda bad. The graphics aren't that great, and it runs pretty slow even post 30fps patch. It looks worse than GTA V, plus it's a lot smaller, so there's no excuse for it to run with roughly half the fps I get for GTA.
Story's alright, though. Playing a big scary black man in 1968/69 is interesting. People in white neighborhoods don't trust you and cops flat-out hate you. Though the latter thing is always true for open world games. It's fun that you're some kinda scary special forces Vietnam veteran. Basically a Rambo who also used to torture people.
Gameplay's pretty standard, though it has a higher emphasis on stealth than most open world games. Sneaking is often preferable, and it fits your character since you're supposed to be some kinda highly trained black-ops assassin dude. Not that you're subtle, since knife kills are especially brutal. It looks more like a damn machete than a knife, and the protagonist seems to be especially fond of aiming it for mobsters' throats.
Gunplay's standard cover-based shooting. It's cool how enemies don't just ragdoll instantly (unless headshot). They usually live for a long time after being perforated, though they're too heavily wounded to stay in the fight. Makes it seem realistic.
Conclusion: it's an alright game so far, worth a recommendation. Though it's best if you wait for a decent sale and wait for more patches, since the performance really needs to be improved.

Rating: 6/10
Recommendation: Buy at reduced price (if at all).
I had fun playing this game and enjoyed the story. Despite that, in retrospective mostly neagtive things stand out. In part because the game could have been so much better. Some might consider it weird that I posted this as a recommendation (considering that I mostly criticse the game in the review below), but I had enough fun while playing Mafia III that I would buy it again - albeit at a cheaper price once it is on sale.
What strikes me most about this game is the missed potential. There are tracks for trains and streetcars, but no trains or streetcars. There is police, who supposedly react to traffic violations, but rarely do anything if you barrel past them at 120 mph on the wrong side of the road. Even if they react, they are easy to outrun - if you make it past the blue search zone, you are safe, even if you stand right next to a police officer with the stolen car that the police were searching for in the first place. And during the few times it gets tough to get away from them you can just go for the next body of water and outswim them - they don't have boats to follow you on water and seem to shortsighted to discover you even in daylight floating in some river. The AI is stupid and easy to beat, you can dispatch an unsuspecting enemy with your knife and another enemy five feet away wont notice unless he looks directly at you.
There are some options to customise guns and cars, but they don't go beyond clicking on "Improved Accuracy" or "Faster Speed" (or whatever that's actually called in-game). You can't individually modify guns or cars and options of visual modification of your cars or clothing are non-existant. A free DLC to intrudce visual customisation has been announced, but in my opinion this should have been included from the start.
Well, time to get to what the game actually does feature. Some of the gameplay is fun, the storyline is interesting and the voice acting and mocap/facial animation are superb. The radio stations and soundtrack are also very well done. Unfortunately for most of the game the storyline missions require you to grind through a repetetive type of mission: you have to take rackets and districts from your enemies and assign them to your own underbosses. There are various types of rackets, but taking them over always follows the same basic formula. At first this is fun, but later on it becomes boring.
New Bordeaux looks nice and the graphics are fine, but in some ways the city felt bland. You can listen to some conversations, but then the people will just finish speaking their part and remain standing in a group silently. There are various shops and bars, but aside from robbing their cash register, there is not as lot you can do there.
There are a couple of optional side missions, but these too are repetetive (deliver drugs/alcohol etc. with a boat and/or truck from A to B) and take ages to complete. The locations of the trucks are in the middle of nowhere and especially at the end of the game require you to drive across almost the entire map to deliver them.
Weirdly enough, I still enjoyed the game and had fun playing it. What I enjoyed most about Mafia III were the cutscenes/story, while the missions were at time more of a distraction than an interesting part of the game. I would wait for the content of the free DLCs to arrive and the price to drop if I were to buy it again.

Overall a great concept.  Being in the public safety field for over 20 years, I can relate to almost all duties performed in-game, either from experience or from being able to observe it first hand.  That said, I'm in the United States, this is set in Germany (I think).  Regardless, it does not take away from the playability of the game.  All of the in-game text is in English, so there's no issue there.
That said, the nitpicky part...
Not much ambient sound, maybe some crackling of the fire, or radio chatter (as another reviewer stated) would add to the game a bit, but all-in-all does not affect the playability of the game.
It's a bit confusing at first when you've got to figure out on you're own, but after about 10-15 minutes you kinda catch on to it.   After that it's much more enjoyable.
You start out in station, get an assignment, have to find your assigned vehicle, either as a driver or passenger, enter the vehicle, then either drive or ride to the fire.  Once you get there, your mission leader will give you a briefing and you go from there.  Basically you havet o procure a water source from an underground hydrant, attach hose to that and supply the engine, then pull the hose off the engine into the fire.  Then you can swap firefighters and either take on a different duty, or take the attack nozzle and go to work.  After the fire is out, you've got to clean up!  Nice touch... But like in real life, it must be done.
The game could use a bit more polishing, but it's very playable and enjoyable.  Would love to have some of the audio in English, or at least English sub-titles.  Some more ambient sounds.   I have no doubt that as long as the developers continue to make improvements, this game can only get better.

Where to start with this one? I've asked myself this question for a couple of hours before starting to type.
I suppose the easiest way to start is at the beginning. Notruf 112 (or emergency call 112 as the english version will be called) is a firefighting simulator made in cooperation with the professional Fire department of the German town of Mulheim an der Ruhr. It means you start a firestation and are assigned to an engine, a pumper or a laddertruck. Next door, but still within the building, are the paramedics with their ambulances. But these are currently just set dressing and not a subject of this review.
Unfortunately there isn't really much to do at the fire station. There's a small area where you can train in knocking down a small fire, connecting a hose and working with some of the rescue tools. You can also go to the engine bay and check out the usable gear on the available engines. Unfortunately not all the gear is apparently ready to be used yet nor are there call outs available where said gear, like the motor saw or the chain saw, can be used.
On the other hand, it still is kind of interesting to check out the ingame fire station. The posters that show the fire engines of the Mulheim Fire Brigade through the ages are a nice touch. And, the equipment containers at the back of the station perhaps also hold promise of bigger things to come. If so interested you can always try to load a container on the back of the carrier vehicle and unload it somewhere else. The containers and the gear installed on them however do not work.
In the meantime whilst you were busy checking out the gear on the fire engines or exploring the station, perhaps you might have had a call out.This could be anything, ranging from a traffic accident with persons trapped to an appartment fire and yes, even a false alarm or two.
Remember how i said that you can check out the gear on the engines? Well, now you can go up to your assigned engine or pumper, open the hatch(es) and take out hoses to fight that appartment fire. You can also help and build a supply line to the engine and prepare extra hose lines for an interior attack on that appartment fire. It's here however that you run into one of the games major shortcomings.
The ai
The ai is such that it can actually do a lot of tasks for you and thereby take a lot of work of your hands. This in itsself is a boon as it prevents you from having to do a lot of work yourself. HOWEVER, the ai is also still a bit finicky with regards to its pathfinding and the chores it has to do. I've experienced more then one case where I as a player had apparently done something the ai was supposed to do. This in turn caused the ai to lock up and literally do nothing.
I would say that in a game about firefighting you'd also wonder about the modeling of the fire and the way it would spread. Unfortunately, I can't really comment on this as I haven't really seen fire spread yet.It's another shortcoming and I suppose that the devs are working on it, as they have by releasing 5 patches (so far) on to the separate BETA branch.
There is still a lot of work to be done on this game and yes, the developers are aware of it. All in all however, despite the developmental shortcomings,  Notruf 112 is an enjoyable game which has definetly raised the bar for firefighting games (if you compare it to games like the ff2014 game) but it's not quite there yet. Time will tell if it will get there, or not.
Wheter you want to buy it or not, the choice is entirely up to you.

I got about 17 hours into the game and I can say beyond a doubt that it is a fun yet incomplete game as compared to Mafia 2 wich gets a higher score from me! They left so many elements and mechanics out of Mafia 3 that actually are in Mafia 2 that made the game so much fun and unique, all those little things! In this 3rd instalment of Mafia you don't realy have realistic driving (even on simulator driving mode)! The driving and shooting are a step down from Mafia 2 (although still acceptable it feels as a downgrade), there is no car tuning in garages (atleast not that I have seen) cars no longer need fuel (like they do in Mafia 1 & 2) The tire smoke from wheelspin is much less visible and unimpressive in this 3rd part! The damage models for destroyed and damaged vehicles are realy appalingly bad and an utter insult to Mafia 2 wich did a much much better job with the damage models! (even Mafia 1 has better damage models!) The skybox and clouds look very bad, pixely and unnatural in the evening hours and at night time! (ingame day/night cycle)
Also melee combat has unfortunately been downgraded and over-simplyfied! Car stealing can only be done by smashing a window in this 3rd part where as in Mafia 2 you had the choice to either bust a window or use the clean non damaging method with the lockpick! Frankly the only thing Mafia 3 has got going for itself as of right now and where it certainly does shine and does not dissapoint is in the storyline and in its unbelievably awesome licenced soundtracks! The music in this game is (like in Mafia 2) again absolutely fantastic and magnificent and true to the time period! I had Buddy Holly with "Rave On" blasting from the cars in Mafia 2, and now I have CCR with "Fortunate Son" blasting from the cars in Mafia 3! I remember finding the music so fantastic that I would most of the time remain seated in the car until the song finished before I got out to do a mission! lol ***** 5 stars for the music!
If you're a fan of open world 3rd person action adventure games then this is a great game for you. Yet Mafia 1 & 2 veterans (such as myself) might find this 3rd part in the Mafia franchise somewhat lacking and a bit incomplete! This game has got great potential with some more polishing, better porting and some more optimization! on a scale from 1 to 10 I give this game a solid 7! Though Mafia 2 scores a solid 9! :)

If you like Turn Based Tactical (XCom for example), this is a very nice game, I would say that "this game is a must" (especially if you will find it on sale).
From the point of view of time needed playing it, you may finish the game in 15-20 hours of play.
The atmosphere in the game is really nice. The story has a meaning and the choices you make are influencing what options you will have, at least in the latest part of the game. For example, in the last part, if you accept to take with you the inquisitor in certain conditions, you will not receive the quest to have a native indian in your posse.
There are 2 quests to which you must pay a bit of attention (the 4 brothers, Tzompantli), there are some easier quests (the broken skull bear and others). The quests part could have been richer but I am not complaining, for a "short game" it is quite OK. You may solve the quests and riddles without any hint from internet, just be patient and search and interpret correctly the information. For the 4 brothers, Tzompantli, I had to write on paper the information to find the solution - it is not difficult, it just requires some attention and some trial and error (English language and text interpretation are needed). I am saying this after searching on the internet how to solve Tzompantli, I realized that it is logical. After Tzompantli riddle, the 4 brothers was so simple and so clear: it is logical and I have been very happy to find the answer without any help.
I do not see too much replay value for this game, it is a "one story game", you may choose different solutions but in the end the path is the same. For me one time is enough, I do understand that some people would like to replay it a few times.
Do I recommend the game? Absolutely. It is a very good game.
And if you will watch the ending and see the number of people who participated to create it, it will make you understand how much effort is involved into creating a very good game.

I had a craving for some more gritty western lore, and the Steam Store just so happened to advertise this gem of a game to me.  I couldn't buy it fast enough.  No regrets.  It plays just like XCOM so if you are a fan of turn based, squad style SRPG, this game is great.  The content is very dark and I probably wouldn't recommend it for young kids, but I found the story to be unpredictable and interesting.
Even on the hardest mode, it scales a bit on the easy side.  Individual characters are only somewhat customizable via limited gear (two guns and a defensive trinket + expendable items) and playing cards acquired throughout a scenario.  Each card has a minor boost, and a skill, and when combined to form a poker hand have added bonuses as well.  I had fun doing unique things like boosting one character's Movement through the roof and letting him tear up the map, so the customization is adequate, it just doesn't have much in the way of leveling up.
All in all I estimate the game to be a solid 30 hour investment.  The original game could be longer, but there is DLC with added scenarios as well too.
The game has some nice features but is not ready for sale. A lot of bugs and crashes happen during the game. I also think this game is not worth the price!

Broken Age is a click and point game that is about the perspective of two young protagonists name Shay and Vella. Where Shay lived on a spaceship  for his entire life  while Vella lives in a village where she is seleceted (or more as a sacrfice) as a young maidan to the monster Chothra. Furthermore the game is broken down into  two acts.
The first act of the game is very enjoyable, even though it can be challenging from someone who hasn't played a lot of click and point games. However, the first act is not overly difficult as one can get through the first act until the very end without a walkthrough. For the story of the first act, the ending has an unique twist that is compelling and interesting.
The second act is where it gets the most criticism because while in the first act you explore the beautiful visual world. The second act is repetition as instead of exploring you end having to backtrack a lot in the game. For the puzzles, the second act is way more difficult as some gamers may use a walkthrough as there isn't any logic with the puzzles.
That being said, I found some of the characters likeable and funny with actors like Jack Black being a voice actor for one of the characters in the game and Elijah Wood being the VA for Shay. However, some people may have found that there should have been more character development with Shay and Vella due to different upbringings of the two characters.
If you are a fan of click and point games then I definitely would recommand this game to you. If you are not then perhaps you might want to avoid this game. I give this game a 7.3/10.

Not a bad game at all. The soundtrack is neat, though the choral parts during the demon battles gets a little annoying after a while. The game's battle mechanics are on par with XCom: Enemy Unknown with enough tweeks and changes to it that makes it different. The story is told mostly through dialogue and text as you traverse an overworld that gives you many choices on how to approach many of the conflicts you find yourself in. Though the main scenario and the side scenarios can be blazed through in about 16 hours (assuming you do everything there is to do in each scenario) you will beat it in about 16 hours.
The story itself is mostly what one would expect out of a Western Themed game with a delicious side dish of Satan. It has a very dark enviornment and the manner in which you can go about dealing with things can make it even darker. The side stories are also quite interesting and give insight to small off shoots of the main plot, and are somewhat interesting in light of the main storyline. Replayability is only here for story and difficulty, as the game itself is only a good challenge on hard mode with battle wounds enabled.
Fans of tactical games in the style of X-Com: Enemy Unknown will probably love this game's take on the combat system. With many parallels the system itself lacks any need to overly micromanage characters prior to battle and does a lot to ensure that combatants can have different skills and abilities to set up per combat based on an inventory system and special ability poker hands system. You primarily get stronger as you find better guns, consumables, relics, and playing cards.
I think people of tactical games, in the same style as XCOM: Enemy Unknown, will enjoy this game on the medium or hard setting for sure, the easy setting is far too easy and detracts from the strong points of the battle system. There is also an ironman mode for the diehard gamers to tackle and the game also has an available expansion I have yet to check out.
The game is easily worth the cost they ask for at 20 bucks. If you're short on cash try to pick it up on a steam sale and you will most likely will enjoy this game for it's dark western themes, decent music, and decent tactical combat system.

I’m playing Life is Strange, the stunning episodic game from DONTNOD Entertainment. I think I knew I was going to love it from the opening credits, as the protagonist steps into her high school hallway, sighs momentarily, and drowns out the gossip and hubbub with exactly the right indie song. Her internal dialog runs over the smooth lyrics and burbling guitar as she makes her way through the flowing river of students.
Back in the day, games were always about the gameplay. A game was good if it had fun combat or interesting mechanics. Gaming itself was still fresh and new, and the process of interacting with a computer and overcoming challenges was entertaining in its own right. Lately, though, that hasn’t been enough for me. A shooter where the plot only exists to keep you moving down the path towards the end of the game while both your gear and the enemies incrementally improve… it feels stale at this point. More and more, I’ve been moving towards games that skip the ‘action’ entirely in favor of the story.
The central mechanic of Life is Strange is a key reason it works so well. Max, the hero, gains the ability to rewind time in short bursts. Most games would use this as a way to liven up a combat system or to create intricate puzzles to navigate, but in Life is Strange, you use it to make choices. Everyday, normal decisions, at first — should you raise your hand with the correct answer in class or not? You see people’s immediate reactions, and if you don’t like them, you can go back and pick another option. Once your choice is locked in, though, there’s no going back.
This isn’t Fallout 4 — it soon becomes very clear that your choices have large and growing impacts on the world around you. Friendships and romances begin and end, lives are threatened, and you start to learn more about the characters, the world, and your powers. The ability to rewind time and change your choices leads to long moments of contemplation, exploring all of the options and carefully considering the ramifications, but other than your movement and the decisions, the game plays like an interactive movie. The perfectly selected indie rock soundtrack adds depth and feeling to the scenes and the voice acting is spot on. It takes place in a fictional town in Oregon, and it feels so much like the Pacific Northwest that it’s making me homesick.
I’m only a few hours into the game, and I’ve already completely screwed everything up. I was trying to save someone, but I just couldn’t make it happen. All my decisions have come home to roost. The haunting sound of Jose Gonzalez’s Crosses plays in my ears as the results of my decisions play out on the screen. I’m powerless to stop it.
It’s one of the few times a game has made me roll back in my chair and just sit, staring blankly at the screen and feeling the sick, sinking sensation of every poor choice I’ve made piling up on me, my good intentions useless in the face of what’s unfolding.
And, suddenly, the game isn’t about the game anymore. I’m transported back through my own life, reliving my pivotal decisions: dropping out of college, moving to Costa Rica on a whim, moving to Japan on another. The branching path of the choices that have shaped my life has never been as apparent to me as it is right now. I’m not distraught because of what’s happening in the plot. I’m mourning for all the other versions of me that I’m not — the ones who bounced down a different path because of an offhand decision, a minor, momentary, careless impulse that sent them spiraling off in another direction. The ones who worked harder, the ones who took more chances, the ones who played it safer…
I shake my head, jarring myself out of my reverie. I chase it away for good with the rest of the glass, the smooth burn searing my throat as I pull myself back into position, enthralled, gutted. All I can do is keep going.
Written by
Mark "Markzi" Olsen

An old-style RPG, almost to a fault. I will say, it very much does feel like the logical extension of the original Wasteland/Fallout, had Fallout not gone the way of Elder Scrolls.
There's some nice tactical turn-based combat here, but it's not especially deep. Similarly, the story is certianly inoffensive as far as quality, but it didn't really grab me, either. I got some nice nostalgia jolts from the presence of dialogue trees and inventories, but there's also plenty of clunky interfaces and awkward questlines.
This is a game that feels out-of-time. It's not pushing anything forward, but it does play more or less like you'd expect a game from 1998 to play. As such, I think I appreciate it more in idea than in execution. And I'll say this much, if you're looking for an RPG that's long like old RPGs used to be, then buddy you will not be dissappointed.
With Steam's binary scale, I think this one is more on the "recommend" side, but I'd throw in the caveat of "fourty dollars is perhaps a bit high." I liked it, but I didn't love it.

I have over 2k hours logged in steam for KSP, and probably another 2k outside of steam. It's my all-time most-played game.
The thing you have to know about KSP is that you learn by failing. This is true of most games, really, but it's especially and most spectacularly true with KSP. You try something, explode, try something else.
If you can just enjoy the explosions and learn your lessons and try again, this is absolutely the game for you. If failing a few dozen times (even in amusing ways) before succeeding is something that would frustrate you, I guess pick another game.
You don't have to be a rocket scientist to play, but you do have to aspire to rocket science. The simulation isn't perfect, but it's close enough to require that you develop some understanding of orbital mechanics to play. You don't need to understand all that stuff to start with; but you need to be willing to learn as you progress.
Heavy math is not required; there are mods that add displays for all the most commonly used data so you don't have to pull out a calculator. I recommend Kerbal Engineer Redux; other people use MechJeb, and some people spurn the mods and actually do use calculators. But that's a preference issue.
I've purchased KSP both on steam and on GoG, and purchased gift copies for six or seven people across both platforms too. If you consider it on a hours-of-fun-per-monetary-unit basis, it's the most cost effective purchase you will ever make.

Heyo folks, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for Auto Age: Standoff by Phantom Compass.
Auto Age Standoff is an 80’s themed vehicular combat game that plays similarly to Twisted Metal. There’s no story so it’s main focus is on it’s multiplayer based battles.
The game currently features 8 game modes including Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Elimination, Team Elimination, Point Capture, Cube Command, Team Cube Command, and Horde Mode.
Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch are pretty standard game modes where you mainly focus on destroying each other or the opposing team. Elimination and Team Elimination is probably the quickest game mode where you knock out opposing players by destroying them. Point Capture is one of my favorites and is sort of like King of the Hill where each team tries to capture a point in the map. The team that manages to hit 100% captured wins the match. Cube Command and Team Cube Command is another favorite. In this game mode players must capture and hold onto a cube in the game world to gain points. The cube damages you over time though so a heavy vehicle is recommended for the most amount of points. Finally, Horde Mode is a survival based game mode for multiple players where you take down waves of the opposing team. The enemies you encounter increase in strength as you progress through each wave as well.
Currently the game features only 7 maps and you can play through them pretty quickly. Maps include Crossroads, Hot Dam, Ghost Town, Eagle’s Nest, Core Sample, Eagle’s Fall, and Aerie. Each map is unique and has a different theme. My personal favorites are Hot Dam and Ghost Town.
You can also adjust various parameters when setting up a game, like player count, the inclusion of bots, timed or score based gameplay, and allowing unbalanced teams.
The game can be played online, in offline single player or in a splitscreen environment. I will admit that the game currently has a small fanbase so it can sometimes be difficult to find games to play with other players but I hope that more people will wind up discovering the game to allow for more multiplayer mayhem.
You can also customize the many vehicles that the game has to offer to suit your play style. You can choose from weapons, rams, missile launchers, rear utilities and bonus additions like armor and more health.
Overall, Auto Age Standoff is a very fun game that exudes the 80’s, from its artstyle to it’s 80’s anime style theme song. The game’s multiple game modes are a lot of fun as well but I will admit that you can burn through the available content pretty quickly. On the plus side the game is update pretty frequently and they had just recently released version 1.3 which added a ton of new stuff. The game is expanding and if you enjoy vehicular combat games as much as I do then you’re sure to have a lot of fun with auto age standoff.

I absolutely LOVE this game. Although it may have its rough spots, I definitely recommend it.
It has many downsides and many upsides.... if that's a word. One big downside is that the stock plane cockpits lack severely in quality. You can't even use half of the buttons whereas you can in X-Plane 11. Also, they didn't even take the time to model the switches or knobs to even look remotely circular. I'm not trying to play minecraft, I'm trying to play FSX! On the plus side, the interface is very easy to use and the game is just easy to understand. I learned almost everything I needed to know to play the game well, except from flying IFR. Another cool thing is that there are like 40,000 airports to choose from. Recently I've done and IFR flight from KATL-KMIA, then KMIA-KATL. I just got back from flying a shared cockpit online session with my friend from SVMT to TNCM. In the other hand, this game needs add-ons to be enjoyable. Like I mentioned earlier about the stock aircraft, I need something more. After I got the PMDG 737, 747 and 777 I was pretty satisfied, but something still lacked. I eventually ended up buying many texture packs for it to be fully enjoyable. Lastly, another good thing is that the game is just so fun. From realism to messing around, this game provides hours of fun day-to-day. I have about 230 hours at the time of writing this review and I've enjoyed every second of it. Another thing I love is the curveballs it throws at you. For example, I was flying from heathrow to Atlanta and and end up circling the airport because of how much traffic was there.
In conclusion, I absolutely love the game and I think you totally need it. Definitely great for someone starting in aviation, or even if you've flown to the International Space Station and back and have tens of thousands of hours of flight time under your belt. Fun to play for anyone.

For what it's worth, this game is a lot different than any other game out there, the game that most relates to this would be something like Archeblade. There's no other game out there(Other than Archeblade) that allows you to just pick a character and just go in and fight, and nothing but pure skill matters.
That being said, even though this game closely resembles Archeblade, and some others may say Smite, there is still a hefty amount of getting used to when trying this game out. One thing to keep in mind is that this is a team game. For you Archeblade players: You have the ability to kill everyone in the game with any character you wish if you really try, that is definitely not the case for this game. You will need to rely on your team in this game, and forming parties with friends and voice chatting will get you pretty far if you are all decent at the game.
The game has a pretty steep learning curve if you're coming from Archeblade, but if you actually take the time to see the game for what it is worth, and not play it like AB and leave it because it is just not "Archeblade enough", you would actually be able to see that this is a much more in depth game, enough to even say that it's completely different.
Archeblade is a good game in my opinion, as well as CroNix, CroNix differs from Archeblade so much that I'm willing to call it a completely different game, the combat is just not the same, regardless of what anyone says, which is why so many people leave the game after comparing it to Archeblade; they don't like change. So instead of listening to what your friend says about Archeblade being better, at least give this a try before you decide not to play it.
TL;DR: If you're an Archeblade fan, at least give this a try for more than 5 minutes/1 match, go to practice and find out who you like.

As far as storytelling and production values go (aside from low-res cut scenes) Alan Wake is great. The story is interesting and will keep you guessing and resolves itself admirably. Unfortunately, the game play can't keep up.
Alan Wake isn't your typical third person shooter. You have a very limited amount of supplies to deal with what seem like impossible odds. While it's possible to overcome these odds in this game, it usually comes at the cost of constant trial and error and dealing with some seriously clunky movement and aiming mechanics. The worst offender are platforming sections which have NO place in a game of this kind other than to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the player with cheap deaths. The jumping mechanic is simply horrendous and you sometimes never end up where you wanted to.
As far as getting all the achievements this one had a few tough ones. The toughest come in the form of "complete x part of the story without restarting a checkpoint." This being the PC release we get all the DLC and there are two of these (one for each piece of DLC) there and one in the main story. Aside from that there is a ridiculous number of collectibles for the single player campaign. Fortunately, most of these can be picked up using chapter select but some achievements require collecting all items in that set in a full play through (which isn't that bad considering you'll likely play through the whole game twice for the difficulty achievements).
Overall I recommend this game to people who love a good mystery or good storytelling in games in general. Just be forewarned about the controls and the combat. They can be quite a pain.

The first couple hours of this game were great. The story was interesting, there were a bunch of twists and turns, and the environments were decently varied.
I am now 7 hours into the game and find myself having trouble just staying awake while playing this game.
It's become the game equivalent of an iTunes preview of a nursery rhyme stuck on loop.
Pros:
- Interesting story (at the beginning)
- Graphics are nice, with forest areas looking especially good.
Cons:
- One of those games that isn't hard so to speak, but you find yourself dying constantly
- Almost always taking place at night, in a forest, with blue color grading
- Some plot explanations are weak and overly simple
- One  of those games that tries to be both a TV show and a game at the same time, while completely misunderstanding the purpose of each medium and why they should never be "combined".
- Game treats you like a complete idiot with "hints" to help guide you across completely linear paths in an almost insulting manner
- Alan explains every bit of environmental story-telling you come across
- Fighting possessed objects by shining a light at them... why
- Practically impossible to run from any combat scenario (don't run out of bullets)
- Enemies that throw hammers at the speed of sound
- Clunky driving segments
- Combat that is tedious, repetetive, and unsatisfying
- 95% of combat encounters begin with a "spooky" chord and the camera moving to show you a group of the same 3 guys you fight throughout the whole game advancing on your position
- Alan's manager guy is commonly found saying things that directly conflict with the current mood
- Incredible amounts of walking in straight lines through blue forests
- Enemies that are supposed to be scary say the dumbest♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes
- Unlike the beginning, the plot later begins to slow down almost to a hault, making it hard to be driven by the story to continue
- If using mouse/keyboard, camera always stays to one side of Alan (good), but if using controller, camera is not locked to a specific side and moves between sides as you turn the camera (bad)
- Puzzles are just easy time wasters
- Lots of custscenes
- Game dumps exposition about the town on you, which would be fine if the information mattered and wasn't just filler
- Alan talks to himself CONSTANTLY
Overall I'd say the game is highly overrated and there are much better alternatives.

The very first thought that came to my mind when I initially heard of this game was 'Please don't be another Firefighters 2014'.  Anyone who has played that game knows what I mean.  I watched a few Youtube videos to figure out if it was something I wanted to dive into, and finally I went for it.  My oh my is Notruf 112 vastly better than FF14.  Notruf 112 was released on November 10th, and while it does have its fair share of bugs, the developers are actively working on the game.  As of right now, there is a beta update available to test out.  At first I had issues with the game crashing, but I discovered I was missing something crucial for the game.  Once I got that installed, the game has worked.  I do get the occasional random hard crashing, and I think I may have one idea as to why, which I'll include later.
Notruff 112 does the character options in a nice, unique way in that you're not limited to one person per play through.  You can switch between the firefighters/battalion on the spot.  One second you're driving the ladder truck, the next it's the water tender.  If you prefer driving to the scene and then switching to a firefighter who is going into a building, you can, and it's a seamless transition.  There's no loading screen, no pause in the game.  This mechanic, geared by the fact that it's so smooth, is a huge plus.  I really love being able to decide each shift what I want to do.  It really lets me get a better understanding for each firefighter and his task.
The game does keep a task list that tells you what to do in the event you have no clue.  I'm quite pleased with this, but it has also led to an issue where if I do something on my own, for example just grab a hose and go after the fire (and not take the time to set up a supply line), the game breaks.  It does not like you doing things out of order.  I kinda understand wanting things in order, but if I can just grab a hose from the truck and put out the fire, I'm saving us a lot of time.  Would be nice if the game acknowledged that we skipped ahead.
Moving onto the AI, I must say I'm impressed.  If you choose to be a passenger in the firetruck, the AI will drive the truck for you.  This, in itself, is amazing.  Obviously, because it's not perfect, the AI will make mistakes.  Thus far,
is the only time the AI has crashed the rig.  To be fair, I
.  So it's not just the AI that makes mistakes.  Notruf 112 provides an experiences you don't often get in simulator games: riding as a passenger.  There is something so awesome about sitting in the back of the fire truck in first person as you respond code 3.  As I said, the AI does make mistakes while driving, but overall, it's really not that bad or an issue.  As per the actual AI civilians....well, what do you expect.  They somewhat mimic real life in that they can screw you over in a heart beat if they choose.  Thankfully, even with lights on, they do pull over and recognize you're there.   Finally, with the AI, and this ties into the previous character selection, the AI actually do work.  If you're the driver of the fire truck, you operate the truck only.  The AI partners will open the compartment doors, and get out the tools for the hose as needed.  If you're the attack squad leader, you'll wait for the team to get the hose ready for you and then you'll fight the fire.  Quick note, I am still learning here, so maybe it's not the leader that fights the fire, but it's someone. >_>  Point is, the AI isn't
useless.  I say entirely because once on scene, the only people who do anything is either the ones with the water tender or the engine.  Battalion, paramedics, ladder, don't do anything.  To my knowledge, I don't believe there are any calls yet that require the use of the ladder truck.  It just responds for aesthetics.  (It's still fun to set up the ladder and have it against a building.)  Driving wise, I'm using KB/mouse, and its as about as you'd expect - poor.  I do have a controller, but haven't tried it, as I personally don't feel the need for it.  The trucks do feel heavy when driving them, and while the handling may not be spot on, it's close enough.
As I mentioned above, I do get the occasional crashing, and I think it has something to do with switching between characters mid-mission.  The couple times I've hard crashed is when we're driving back to base and I'm a passenger.  Normally, I drive there and let the AI drive back.  I'm wondering if the game is getting a little confused as to whom is actually driving.  I'm not sure, just my thoughts.
Another mechanic I really like in the game is that if you get in a car crash while responding, the call ends immediately.  I really like that they punish you for not being a safe driver when responding.  Yes, it only does this when responding. (at least for me.)  This has led to me raging a bit at stupid drivers, which is what I do in real life anyway. :P
Lets step into fire animations.  A lot of people are probably going to get picky about this, as the fire animations look like a cheap effect you get from those free photo editing websites.  It's not beautiful or realistic (looks wise), and I'm 100% okay with this.  In FF14, a huge issue was that the water did nothing.  The fires wouldn't dissipate, and you'd spend a half hour fighting this and then realize it's pointless.  In this game, the fire does get extinguished, and as long as it does this, the fire can look as cheap as it would like.  I'd rather have a functioning, poorly looking fire than one that doesn't work and is gorgeous.  There is fire spread, and while it may not be entirely realistic, it gets the job done.  If you extinguish a table, and move onto a cupboard, that table can catch on fire again after a bit of time.
Finally, as I was told, there is procedural generation for each call, so there will always be something different.  I still believe that it may, at times, send you to the exact same place.  As long as it doesn't do it all the time, I'm fine with this.  Obviously they can't make every single call something new/different.  They can try, but it will always get to a point where you're going to the same places.  Besides, as a firefighter, you are doing the same thing over and over again, so it's unfair to think 'I do this a lot! I want a new call'.
All in all, this is a huge improvement to other previous games, and I quite enjoy playing it.

TL;DR: It's good.
13 years as FF/EMT and this is by far the best firefighting simulator out there. It's not quite polished but they claim they're still developing it. It's not the prettiest (though it's not bad, and the apparatus are amazingly detailed). Fire effects are about as close as you can get in a simulator at this time without killing performance. I've got a higher end machine but it doesn't even blink. I'd imagine mid-grade machines would do ok. The tools are as close to correct as I can tell (I'm an FF/EMT in the US, not Germany, and there are some differences between how we store hoses and connect to hydrants, etc. but most of the equipment I am very familiar with and recognize). The game is relatively stable. Had a few events of CTD but it's usually if you do something the game doesn't like and you usually realize quickly what it is you did. I haven't experienced any random CTD. The Traffic AI is very good. They actually move out of the way and form an emergency lane for you (now if only I could get real people to do that when actually driving a fire truck or ambulance...)
You definitely need to read the manual and even then things aren't very straightforward. The AI firefighters tend to do stupid things and I've had a few UI issues where I can't pick up objects but manage to work around them ok. There's also a few times where the task list doesn't tell you what to do next and you have to figure it out yourself. Sort of annoying but considering the complexity of the simulation I'm willing to overlook that at the moment. There are some visual disturbances too but they don't really destroy the gameplay.
Pros:
-Looks good for what it is.
-Most realistic firefighting simulator currently commerically available.
-Doesn't seem to stutter on a higher end machine.
-Generally quite stable.
-Good traffic AI.
Cons:
-Could use a few tutorials. Definitely need to glance over the manual.
-Firefighter AI can do weird things from time to time
-Visual Disturbances
-UI freaks out on occasion
-No save game yet (There's a button for it so I imagine they'll implement it)
Overall I'm pleased considering how awful I thought it was going to be. Again definitely beats all the other firefighitng simulators available to the general public. This would be really cool with multiplayer but not sure how they'd do it.
7/10 would play this before going back to the fire academy again

Hard West as you'll hear is "XCOM with Cowboys", there's definitely some truth in that but Hard West is still a fun game on it's own merits, particulary I found the Story telling engaging and was thoroughly compelled throughout to read each bit of text as it told me a little more each time about the surrounding area and the possibility of opening up new places for me to visit and plunder via dialogue options.
The combat is very much in the like of XCOM as you take control of a character in each of the main scenarios and a few extra companions along the way, taking turns to move, shoot and take cover as you try to find the best way to kill enemies with your Rifles, Six Shooters and Double Barreled Shotguns. In the same vein as most games, there's some customisation in what arsenal of items and weapons you can take and also extra boosts to stats in the form of playing Cards, one thing that it does well is that it's not overbearing with tons of options and neither underwhelming with too few at the same time.
The aesthetic and feel of the scenarios of overworld map give a decent impression of a small landscape out in the middle of the Wild West, not only this but it adds an extra dark layer on top that there's something more sinister afoot in the lands, which I enjoyed a lot especially in the cut scenes at the start of each scenario and the great voiceover, selling the tales of each character.
It's a definitely possibility that the Gameplay maybe doesn't sell the Characters as well as the Cut Scenes do, I didn't feel the most engaging when actually playing out the attacking missions, in comparison to XCOM this is where the game does feel a little bare, the Sounds of the Guns, Enemies dying and the Animations of the characters are lacking in visual feedback, this is a small gripe and obviously for an smaller indie title it's nothing to fret over.
Overall I would really recommend this game to anyone who likes the Turn Based Tactical style game, the Wild West aesthetic was enjoyable and engrossed me into each of the scenarios really ewasily. One more point about the scenarios from my playthrough is that I tended to play for an Hour or 2 here and there complete a Scenario, then come back to the Game and start a brand new one a few days later and wouldn't be lost trying to remember what my characters did.
I purchased the game with the DLC, I would heartily recommend you get it along with the game, I definitely felt like I'd gotten my moneys worth and could easily see myself possibly going for a second playthrough to 100% it.

As someone who grew up playing a lot of point-and-click adventures, with the Monkey Island series being my first foray into video/PC gaming as a young child, I've always felt these sort of games resonated deeply with me.  There's a fun story filled with colorful characters, heaps of dialog to read and choose from (making it a great excuse to be educational too!), and a bevy of inventory items - paired with verbal commands like push/talk/give - that become an intuitive solution to any given puzzle or challenge.  Sometimes the solutions aren't so straight-forward either (as who would expect a rubber chicken could be so useful), but they often have a sort of cartoony logic behind every action/reaction that takes place.  Essentially:  If you're paying attention to the game and not skipping dialog, you'll know exactly what needs to be done and have an idea of what tools are needed to accomplish any given task.
So when I heard Tim Schafer and Double Fine were working on a new traditional point-and-click adventure, I jumped at the opportunity to dive in!
Now at the time of my initial purchase it was only partially finished, and despite this I still enjoyed the first half of the experience...with some reservations...
The puzzles were easy, but still relied on some casual problem-solving.  The 2D art style was colorful and full of texture.  The voice-over work was well done too, with some A-listers thrown in among the veteran voice-over talent.  If you got bored of playing one character, you also had the option to switch over to the other character's seemingly unrelated story, but it didn't really matter much at this point - play until you finish and switch over to do the same.  Maybe not worth half the cost of the full asking price of $25, but there was still a second act to follow, so my hopes were high.
A little over a year later now and i've finally found a moment to finish the second act, and sadly to say i'm let down.
Without being too verbose (have I already?) and giving away too many spoilers, I found a lot of what was originally setup in terms of pacing and puzzle-solving completely abandoned.  A few solutions felt a little too random, and I found myself sometimes clicking on any given character with all of the items in my inventory until I got the required reaction (ex. the guy who licks the icing off your cupcake...).
Even going against my own gaming habits, I found myself peeking at guides when I had no clue what was needed from me...because how was I supposed to know that an established feature of the game - switching characters - would actually become a tool to solve puzzles in the second half of the game?!?  If this was established early on it would have been less of an issue, but it still felt like it ruined any immersion since I couldn't understand how the two characters could share such information between eachother.  Am I some sort of psychic figure that bonds and leads these two heroes?  I don't know.  Just play until you dont know what you're doing and switch characters to see if the other person knows something that the other one doesn't.  How neat!
The story also felt far too rushed and tied-together by the end.  A lot of people complain that not enough was explained, but the real issue is that it's all kind of dumped on you with some rushed exposition at a few moments near the finale.  Okay.  Now we sort of understand what's been going on here, but oops - now it's over.  The End.
Hopefully I can revisit this game one day and judge it based on its other merits.  A game like The Secret of Monkey Island is no longer a challenge as I've memorized it's ins-and-outs, so I'm able to bask in the other aspects without worrying about a puzzle that brings all pacing to a halt.

I purchased Blackwell Deception as part of the Indie Royale Bundle and to be honest, I didn't know the game beforehand. It's an old school Point and Click graphic adventure, a genre that's lacking nowadays. No need to say it far exceeded my expectations. I hadn't played a P n' C Adventure this good since the Chzo Mythos collection by Ben "Yahtzee" Croshaw. Surely there are other great recent games like the Secret of Monkey Island HD remakes, Sam & Max: The Devil's Playhouse or Hector: Badge of Carnage but they're nothing new. On the other hand, Blackwell Deception is a breeze of fresh air. If I had to describe it I'd say it is a mixture between The Secret of Monkey Island (the boat segment is clearly inspired by the Pirate LeChuck), Maniac Mansion (the supernatural part of the game), Broken Sword (the ambience) and Beneath a Steel Sky (the gadgets Rosa uses, the disco scenario).
The characters are well built and the side dialogues make you know them better if you give the effort. By the end of the game you will really care about what happens to the protagonists (hint on a sequel) .
The puzzles are inventive and well thought-out even though I would have liked to see more item combinations. The "switch character" system can become a little confusing in the not so obvious bits because you'll need to analyze the effect Rosangela and her "spiritual guide" have in each single object to figure out a solution. There's one particular puzzle where you'll need to click the same object for an indetermined amount of times until you succeed, it's kind of random so you might get stuck in that part for some minutes, but it's really nothing serious.
The soundtrack is excellent, the trumpet songs reminded me of Dire Straits final studio album On Every Street.
The game has some replay value, you will probably miss 2 achievements during the first playthrough and then you still have the commentary mode to finish.
I got BD for about 4€ with 3 other games (AVSEQ, Oil Rush and To The Moon) so I consider it was a hell of a deal. Unfortunately I started playing the Blackwell saga from the fourth chapter so I didn't know much about characters' backgrounds/side stories but that's not the game's fault.
I've bought The Blackwell Bundle from Steam since then. I'd recommend this saga to any Graphic Adventure enthusiast.

Imagine that your task is to describe a Commodore 64 game in an alternate reality where every single Commodore 64 game was purged from existence. Now imagine that, instead of spending an hour writing a bunch of words that people will willfully misinterpret, or filming a tedious hour-long Youtube vlog that nobody is going to watch, you get on your Steam client, navigate to Flag N Frag, and launch it.
Imagine your audience experiencing the incredible music, the blocky yet colorful and functional graphics, the gameplay that is vaguely similar to modern gaming yet at the same time odd and vestigial, and the fact that this game is not nearly as fun as you'd imagine, infer, or remember, as the case may be.
Congratulations. You've done it. Because this game is the very archetype of a C-64 game. The music is absolutely incredible, it's just a pity that the game itself completely falls apart due to its reliance on a "battle mode" that's far too fast-paced and chaotic for a human to do well at, and far too simple for the computer AI. Imagine Pong played at ten times the speed, and you have to hit a button in order to actually deflect the ball. Even against another human it'd be more "goofy button mashing" than an out-and-out competition, but against a computer? Forget it, it's not even remotely fun.
