Broken Age is a beautifuly crafted point & click adventure that challenges you to use a long lost tool vital to all human beings; logic. The absolutely stunning hand painted art style accompanied by whimsical and inspiring orchestrated music easily sets this game apart from many other adventure games within it's genre. Without a doubt, I would recommend this game to anyone who has the ability to think for themselves, and are yearning for a challenging game that won't hold your hand throughout the play-though.
I also feel that I have to address the negative reviews that are slowly encroaching upon this wonderful game's reputation.
A: I would have to agree that the second act is slightly lacking in the overwhelming epiphany department, in terms of the awe struck feeling it leaves you with at the end of act one, however, that shouldn't warrant people throwing the entire project under the proverbial bus as a result.
B: As I previously stated in the introduction to my review, this game heavily relies on the players ability to utilize their personal logic and problem solving skills throughout the duration of the game. If you read the negative reviews, you will encounter a plethora of individuals complaining about the difficulty of particular puzzles, with which they defeated the purpose of the game by selling their own intelect short and merely looked up the answers. Once again, this game will not hold your hand, and assumes that YOU the player, actually has the ability to think for yourself via deduction and analysis of your surroundings.
C: Many gamers within the playerbase of this project constantly complain about plot holes and "unexplained" circumstances of intuition between Vella and Shay, as well as their overall importance to the Thrush. Within the second act, it's my personal opinion that players were too busy looking for things to hate about it, rather than actually paying any bit of noteable attention to conversational clues; albeit rather vague, but clues nevertheless. Tim Schafer himself has even explained some of these things within a post on the DoubleFine Forums, which you can read for yourself on this link:
-- 6 posts down.
In conclusion,  everything is up to the player to decide, if you actually have the capacity to decide for yourself.

Great first act, not quite as good second act, terrible ending (imo).
Really becomes apparent that they ran out of money.
First act is gorgeous and well written, a lot of fun to play.  The art style is amazing and the high quality voiceovers contribute greatly to the game.  The second act starts to fall apart as they reuse nearly all assets and locations from the first act, and resort to simple item swapping puzzles (fetch quests, effectively) across multiple characters and NPCs to stretch the length (seemingly).  The end of the second act, if you can even call it that, is about 5 minutes long and consists of several scenes of exposition and a fairly poorly explained 'ending', where you get little to no actual information about what is going on, just a brief explanation and then credits.
The villain provides little to no motivation outside from one sentence as to why he is doing what he is doing, and even then, never explains at all why he has chosen the specific path he took to complete his action.  He exists almost solely as diabolus ex machina for the plot.  His motivation is unclear until the very end, and even then it seems completely weakly written.
Save your $ unless this becomes extremely cheap.  There is no real pay-off at the end, you spend a lot of time getting excited about a few things that you never end up seeing and that never get explained, only to get a really short throwaway ending that exists solely to tie up one or two plot threads while leaving many, many others dangling.

Remember PAWNGAME? Remember Stick Arena Online? Introducing Duck Game: The new "coffee break MMO shooter" that falls in line with these previous two classics.
Duck Game is a silly hyper-blast-processing shooter that takes place over several rounds. The goal is simple- shoot everyone else, don't die. Play saxaphone. Quack.
There is a ton of guns, stages, crazy unlockables, hats, more hats, and hilarious situations to dig yourself into.
The controls are simple: There's a button to pick up a weapon, a button to shoot the weapon, and jumping and moving. The controls are so simple in fact that the developers decided to make basically almost all the remaining buttons on your controller do absolutely useless things that increase the PVP experience, in a style similar to gestures in "Dark Souls". You have a dedicated quacking button, you have a pressure sensitive button that changes the pitch of your quack, even a button that makes you ragdoll on the ground (actually useful sometimes)
It's kind of hard to say more about Duck Game. I'm not sure how active the online will be, but I think it'll be a game that's more fun with friends anyways. If you like fast paced shooters that aren't serious at all, pick this up ASAP.

Short Review:
Weird choice of breaking the campaign into different mechanics, some were more compelling than others. It's probably the weakest thing about the game, a lot of stopping and starting.
Another fault is that the mechanics aren't explained fully, so there is a lot of guessing at the start, there are some good gameplay guides on steam for answers.
Characters were good, gameplay is excellent (it really feels like a ol' western shoot-out), good storytelling and puzzling.
Music is great, narration is great.
The horror elements didn't really punch me as hard as they could, most of the time it was the out of place demon that ate a hail of bullets.
Guns are as weird and wild as the game is, but some are much worse than others and you'll end up trading them fast.
Interesting abilities mechanic, mixed with poker hands, the salve +1hp (straight) should be the (royal flush) not +3 hp.
Probably a touch short compared to other turn based tactic games, I finished everything in 18.9 hrs and that's with seeing everything possible (hitting every clickable map option) in one play through.
If you like TBS(turn based strategy) western/horror cross genre, this pretty much nails it on the head. But you have been warned about the dicey campaign direction that doesn't really flow.

A good old friend suggested me to buy this game, telling me some good stuff about it. Well, on the Autumn Sale I gave it a try, and I'm glad I did. This Kickstarter project that I wasn't even aware of it's existence is actually quite a great game! However that doesn't mean at all that it's safe from faults, and I actually did find a few things that made my playthrough be weirder than the weird west. As usual, I'm gonna talk and warn you first about the issues you might find on it, then move up to it's stronger points.
First and foremost, the difficulty. I can understand why they added some of these features, but I don't think they added them properly. First is the lack of any kind of save feature. If you screw up on a battle, you gotta start from the beginning (unless you're playing on Ironman, which means restart the whole chapter). I understand they want to stop people from save-scumming the game, however removing saves all together isn't the best way. I believe the developers should have taken an approach similar to Hitman, and limit the amount of saves by the difficulty settings. Play it on easy, you can save 3 times, play on normal, 2, play in hard, 1. Some of the battles can actually be a bit long and being forced to repeat them over and over because of one little mistake is way too harsh.
Another factor on this is Overwatch. You know how in XCOM you can put your soldiers in guard instead of shooting, and firing on anyone that moves? Well, it's here, but only the enemies have it. The game and even the tutorial tell you how great is to flank enemies, but then avoids telling you about this overwatch mechanic completely. The way it works is that if you get near an enemy, you get shot. That makes flanking enemies a pain in some situations, and I do not like the way it's been put. I'd say that if the game ever gets a sequel, remove this overwatch mechanic completely.
Lastly about the difficulty is how enemies are usually around the dozens and you will never have above 4 characters. That along with the fact that any character that's relevant to the story CAN'T die or you get an instant game over makes things way too tough at times. I think the game needed less enemies, but make them tougher.
Leaving the difficulty asside, there's really not much else that's bad on the game, just a few odd things and bugs. The inventory menus seem to not work well, could be because my screen is kinda small for today's standards but most if the time some items would appear under the lowest area of the scrolling item list, and I had to mess around with them to make the item I wanted to select appear and equip it. Something that was also kinda weird is the AI in some stages, which seems either brain-dead or bugged. I ended up abusing that a little, gotta be honest, by just sitting at the extreme opposite of the map and firing at them with long range weapons; for some reason they wouldn't fire back or try to get out and chase me. Even worse, some enemies would just move in and out of a building, never firing and I could just sit back and pick them up without a single problem. Lastly, I've found twice on the game multiple NPC's appearing on the same spot during Setup stages, and I even got witnesses and a screenshot of that sh#t, as I was streaming through Steam.
All of that being said, what do we got left on Hard West? A different take on XCOM's style with a really good Western setting.
The biggest point in favor of this game is the story. Do you know XCOM or XCOM 2? Sure they got a story, but it's nowhere near being the biggest point on it. There's not much development on it and it's sure as hell not it's selling point. That's the complete opposite here, Hard West does offer a really good storyline that branches all over the place and is fun from start to finish... If you ignore the stuff I talked about before. Took me around 24 hours to finish all of the scenarios on Hard Difficulty with Combat Injuries on, and I'll gladly play some of those again with Ironman as well just to see the things I've missed, that's how much I liked it.
The combat and gameplay is also well implemented. The game has a TON of different weapons, usable items and wearable items that all fit perfectly with the setting of the game and work wonders in a gameplay standpoint. There's enough of them to fit pretty much any playstyle, and further more, as you play along you might discover unique items which will then be available on ALL other scenarios on the Fate Traders shops, something I do love as it gives more meaning to go back to it after you've played it once.
The map itself also offers different gameplay from what you could be used on XCOM and XCOM 2, and also offers different gameplay on all scenarios, which is great! In one scenario you're mining for gold, in others you're trying to form an expedition into the unknown, all of them with their own gameplay.
The sound department is something I usually hold high on games and reviews always seem to ignore for some damn reason. And you know what? This game delivers pretty well on this regard. The voices (or rather, the only voice who truly speaks, the narrator) and the music fit PERFECTLY with the game, and make the game feels way more alive.
And then come the different difficulty options. Sure there's Easy, Normal and Hard, but there's also two other options you can choose: Ironman mode, which means if an important character for the story dies, you gotta start not the battle fron the start but the entire scenario, and then another really interesting mode, Combat Injuries. This means that some enemies might be able to cause additional random injuries on you after hitting, from a f#cked up eye that will reduce your aim to a big wound that's gushing blood and reduces your max HP by a lot. Then you have two different ways to handle this: if you go to a doctor and pay to get those wounds healed, the negative debuffs dissapear forever, If you don't, however, and play two battles with them, the wounds become scars, giving a less damaging debuff but also giving another strong buff to you. For example, going from having a f#cked up eye to just having one will still reduce your Max HP a little, but will make the other eye give you way more sight and aim. It's a really good idea and I love it.
Then comes the Luck stat. I bet the developers played the crap out of XCOM too, as it clearly shows. Each character, allied or enemy has a luck stat, usually being around 100. If you shoot at someone and your chances of hitting do not go over his remaining luck, the shot misses, but the luck is reduced by the chances of that shot. This needs to be in more games.
The game also has a shadow mechanic that I wish it appears in other games such as this. In sunny battles, everything makes a shadow, and that is used very well here. If you see someone's shadow but not him, you can try and aim through soft stuff that's blocking your view and try getting to him that way. Then there's special skills that work better when the sun ain't bothering as well too, which brings me to my last point...
The card system. I f#cking love it. It's ideal. As you play through the game, you'll be getting cards, and each character can have a max of 5 cards equiped, all giving extra skills. From here you can choose to pick cards that give different stat bonuses or pick cards that combined give a passive extra buff to yourself.
In the end, the positive parts of the game outweight the negatives by a large margin. It's a great game and if you liked XCOM, you'll love it. Be wary of it's difficulty and problems, I don't suggest playing it on Hard from the start like I did. On a sale, it's a safe purchase.
TL;DR Edition: Similar to XCOM with a ton of unique features. Kinda hard but fun as hell. Lovable narrator and music. Totally recommended on a sale, it's 15-20 hours of hellish fun.

7 Things not to do when you are making a video game.
1. Dumb collectables. If you are going to make people collect something in a game, give them a reason to do so. Don't make collectables for the sake of making them. It is unimmersive and stupid.
2. Bad voice acting. You can't convince people to take the story seriously if the voice actings for the majority of characters are cringy as hell.
3. Inconsistent gameplay. I like many multi-genre games, but this is getting stupid. What is this game even trying to be? Is it an action horror game or third person puzzle platformer? Why are there several jumping puzzles and what do they add to this game?
4. Not horrifying horror elements. No, "Absurd" does not equal to "Scary". Corny lines are not intimidating; they are corny.
5. Arena-styled level design. Don't ever make "this is obviously an arena, therefore you are going to have a big battle" type of level in every goddamn episodes. This is the most "gamey" thing you can ever achieve.
6. Bad driving mechanics. Here's a general rule: either make a good driving mechanics, or don't make a long driving section if you don't have a good mechanics for it. Cars in this game remind me of MAKO in Mass Effect, and that is not a compliment.
7. Walking Simulator gameplay before cutscenes. Why would you force players to follow a slowly moving, crippled npc just to have a cutscene to play afterward? What is the point of this lack of gameplay? Does this achieve anything? Why not just make a cutscene of those characters walking then? At least, that will save players from pressing W for like 20 minutes.
Other than these, story is mildly interesting but nothing mind blowing or new. Graphics is mediocre. Gameplay is somewhat satisfying, but dodging mechanics is annoyingly unresponsive.

A good X-Com styled tactical RPG that's greater than the sum of its parts. While it lacks the long term progression of other games in the same genre, the bite sized chapters means you don't get bogged down with agonizing over optimal gear and stats. Good storytelling, setting, atmosphere, and sound design allow this game to trade blows with its peers.
The luck system is an interesting break from the bog-standard mana or energy for skill usage, and the cards are quite brilliant allowing you to tailor each party member between missions. Any given character can be a fragile sniper in one mission and a close range agile shotgunner in the next. The game also has a decent ammount of built in "gameplay mods" that allow you to tweak things to your liking. Some examples are disabling enemy reaction shots (if you move a character within a certain radius of an enemy they get a free potshot), extra skills for enemies, and luck regeneration on kill.
Also no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like missing 3 times in a row when you supposedly have a 95% chance to hit. Always a plus.

First of all, I'll begin with the fact I never played this genre of Turn-Based RPG, it was my first time and I regret nothing, that's because Wasteland 2 is awesome from the start to the end!
You play as one team of the famous Desert Rangers, as the newbies, you will receive your first assignment, to attach a "repeater unit" to one radio tower, that will expand the Desert Rangers signal on Arizona... At same time you will search clues to know what happened to Ranger Ace. And then you will progress to the next tasks.
This game have a well written story, that makes you focused to the lore, the feels of being the law in a chaotic world, this is a game where every decision has consequences, and the impact is big! So big that you have fear to do a simple mistake! I love that!
The gameplay is easy to domain, its beautiful how you control you party into combat (which is well, investing in their skills so they wont miss any shot! After all, its a bad turn if you burn your AP (Action Points) on a missed shot. I love how you can upgrade your weapons with scopes, silencers, etc. Enemies have weaknesses (like robots and their weakness to energy weapons), so you need to equip your party in every detail to combat.
There is a lot to explore, even side quests are interesting, some items that can be found and linked to another quest in the other corner of the map. Wasteland 2 have a lot of details and easter eggs, and a lot of mystery places and persons, its a great game to explore, where the psychopaths rules the world, enslave innocents and only you can make the difference.
Wasteland 2 have open me the door for the isometric RPG's, I really recommend this game!

An amazing remake of the classic post-apocalyptic RPG of the same name, Wasteland 2 truly delivers when it comes to content.  Honestly, with all the crowdfunding games that under deliver, WL2 actually caught me by surprise with simply how much many locations and situations there are to discover.  This is a complete and well thought out game.

Story wise, there are a lot of choices to be made among the ruins of the old world and the game excels at showing you the consequences of those decisions.  There is a location that became so story rich, I had to actually stop and think about the multi-layers of intrigue before acting on anyone’s request for help because the ramifications affected so many other characters.  (to be fair, this section was so involved that I found my trigger-finger itching for some combat but it was well worth it when it came)
I also found the game mechanics deep and leveling characters was very satisfying.  There’s a ton of skills and your characters become focused on specific builds – one will be your safecrack/lockpick/alarm disabler and another might be your expert in assault rifles and demolitions – but I never felt limited when customizing.  What is equally surprising is that all skills come into play at some point and you are never required (mostly) to have a certain skill to progress through the main storyline; you always have options.
All in all, a great time.  Be warned: it's a time gobbler.

Where's the rich story-driven experience I bought the game for?
I keep slogging trough it hoping and waiting to get an experience similar to Mafia 2, but it just feels like all I'm being given is more and more busywork.
To get the most out of your story missions, you've gotta wiretap the districts you do the missions in. There's what, 10-ish districts? I'm too lazy to count. Anyway, each have like 8 boxes you need to wiretap, that's 80 times you need to do the wiretap picklocking minigame... But no, that's not all! For each wiretap you need to collect 3 electronic parts, so that's 240 times of getting out of your car, walking over to a part, picking it up, getting back into your car... Are you kidding me? How does this contribute to playing -and enjoying- the game?
The main storyline missions are 90% of the same with only 10% of the missions actually being unique and having a lot of dialogue. All the side quests for each 'boss' are pretty much the same as well.
The few story elements that the game does have are good, satisfying. Surprisingly intricate too. I gave one racket to Cassandra and another to Vito when I took over my first district, then when the time came to appoint either one to have it all, I chose Vito. And Cassandra gave unique dialogue on having a racket 'taken from her' after I called her in to protect it ect ect and it was refreshing and good. But there's just not enough of these story missions to justify all the busywork this game makes you do.
Mechanically the game is okay. The driving feels decent, the shooting is actually fun. It looks fine graphically as well. Not much to say there. There's just not enough story in the game to keep my interest, just endless busywork between the few fun missions there are.

While the game has been consistantly bombarded with criticism for having micro-transactions, they're barely even noticible. The only time this is even somewhat noticible is in online conquest (The equivalent of multiplayer in this game) when an enemy might have every buff in the game. The game never shoves the micro-transactions in your face and yells "Buy it!"
You'll also see a large quantity of complaints about how the end game is a massive slog, and to that I say a few things. The final phase of the game is often considered a grind. This is completely false. The "grindy" phase of the game only took me 3 hours to beat with no microtransactions, glitches, or exploits.
Now that we've gotten past the major complaints, (Congratulations for getting through that rant) there are a ton of good things about the game. The combat is very similar to the previous game (Shadow of Mordor) and thusly similar to the Arkham series. However, with the addition of varying perk modifiers, you can modify your playstyle in a variety of ways, from an unkillable swordsman, to a near invisible stealth character who si never seen. This also causes you to create unconventional playstyles, such as someone who deliberately gets their health low to do bonus damage, or using health for attacks.
The new loot system also compliments the variety of play styles by adding various bonuses based on what you wear. While theirs only about 4 different armor styles, the details on the armor reflect the character of the armor and who it came from.
The nemesis system has been further improved, allowing for new encounters and adds a lot of character to otherwise bland NPC's that act as enemies in other games. This also enforces varying playstyles as an enemy may be immune to your playstyle.
Now for my perosnal complaints. The way you can give your followers obscene amounts of bonuses with "Training orders" you can get from the market make it a bit ridiculous to fight a fortress when everyone is immune to everything and is superbuffed by doing anything that he isnt immune to. This is the only time I ever feel like it wants you to go with the market, countering micro-transactions with other micro-transactions.
***MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD! BEWARE!***
The game has a ton of lore breaks, such as Shelob choosing the form she does, mainly due to that likely helping marketing. A few other4s being Celebrimbor forging ALL the rings (Though thats a matter for debate), Isildur being a necromancer for somereason, Talion being effectively imbued with Isildur by putting on his ring, Isildur and Hammerhand even being Nazgul, and how Shelob had a "relationship" with Sauron before she went full spider bent on revenge.
***SPOILERS END HERE!***
Overall, despite the constant battering on it because it simply has microtransactions and its sometimes pay to win online mode, the game still has tons to offer despite these problems. Whether it be the intriguing nemisis system, or the fluent combat, this game still remains a great game with a great deal of effort put into it.

It's a really fun driving simulator that combines the fun of driving and the fun of large trucks with the mix of planning, careful approaches and control of off road driving while attempting to explore the map and deliver various items to the objectives.
Anyone who likes driving simulators might like it, and anyone who likes trucks and/or has driven off road or surplus type trucks should love it and can immediately visualize all the creaks and rattles these things have. The game is great co-op, you and a friend can explore these fantastic maps and mess around with an off road sandbox. Sure, it's not like the usual driving games with a dozen different cab over trucks that are hard to visually tell apart or fast cars on roads, these are big trucks made of steel with winches, possible wood paneled beds, many with more than four tires, all wheel drive and locking diffs. These things are old, slow brutes with usually massive wheels and horrible turning circles. There is no carbon fiber or aluminum here and no racing lines or three digit top speeds. Despite that, for anyone who likes vehicles the game delivers this immense satisfaction as you winch your eight wheel drive truck up a muddy hill at single digit speeds as you head out to rescue your friend in co-op in their stuck truck with a full load of logs on the back. The feeling alone as you're trundling trough mud and winching around, and then the diffs get locked and you pull it into the right spot, everything catches and the engine noise changes and the beast lumbers forward again is glorious.
That being said, I have my complaints. The fact that the cloaked parts of the map all return when you start on a new map is annoying, as you have to find the cloak item and eliminate the cloak to be able to see the roads, and after spending a while driving around the map finding all of them, getting stuck, winching and repeating ad nauseum, the last thing you really want when you go to play that map again is to spend all the time finding the cloaks again, and driving blind is just as unappealing. It would be better if unlocked vehicles, removed cloaks and unlocked areas remained persistent on the map so future plays or multiplayer plays could just be able doing the objectives or playing around in the mud and on the trails, as chasing the cloaks gets really repetitive after the first clearing of the map. Having to go back and do it takes it from a great tool for exploration (and it is a great mechanic to force exploration of the map) to a chore that has to be done before you can do the objective.
The introductory how to play section of the game is lacking, to say the least. It's essentially a single slide of a presentation with labels pointing at everything. You get to memorize that at the start and that's it for you. You can look at the controls later on in the controls menu, but the introduction to things is poor. The game would greatly benefit from a tutorial level introducing the various vehicles and attachments and their controls one at a time, making things a lot easier when you start the full game.
The final complaint is when the game updates, you lose your save file. It seems the version may be coded into the save file itself, so it can be annoying to lose work on a map where you have the final load almost there and then the game updates and you have to start all over.
All those complaints aside, you get to drive huge trucks off road and haul logs, ford rivers, smash trees and drive a wrecker and recover crashed vehicles you or your friend crashed. The fun is worth the price, although the presistent cloaks and non-storage of found vehicles and locations make a lot of the gameplay feel like a chore, even though the hauling objectives don't feel as chore-like. The game is full of awesome fun trucks that lumber around and over things, if you love vehicles it's easy to imagine the noises and rattles and shakes they have. Playing this game for long enough somehow results in the idea of "I should buy a truck" making sense.
Personally I like this game, it doesn't have a lot to offer but it's focused onto the aspect of fast-paced FPS games with it's own focus for it's mode.

Imagine if Stephen King wrote a season of Twin Peaks.
Alan Wake is a frustrated writer taking a break with his wife to the small, secluded town of Bright Falls. All is not as it seems as there is an undefinable evil hiding in the woods, stalking townspeople and turning them into crazed monsters known as "taken". When Alan's wife dissapears, he must venture into the woods to find her and piece together what happened using pages from a book he doesn't remember writing.
Alan Wake is a tense, forboding horror game. The most notable feature is the "fight with light" mechanic, where the taken are invulnerable to regular weapons until you burn out their protective aura using your torch, flares and flashbangs, as well as stationary light sources. Combat is a close quarters affair, as your dodge mechanic lets you evade slashes by the skin of your teeth. There isn't really any boss fights but there are occasional poltergeists (inanimate objects infused with the darkness and act as missiles) as well as some great set pieces to add variety to the combat.
Remedy's use of light and shadow in Alan Wake is outstanding, helping to create an incredible sense of dread. Seening a quick fog come screaming through the trees and catching glimpses of taken watching you from the distance is quite unsettling.
The story is quite good, even if it does contrive reasons for Alan to be out in the woods every night. The game is divided up into six episodes (8 if you include the DLC), each with their own recap and credits making you very much feel like you're playing a t'v show, even if the lip-synching is pretty poor.
All in all, Alan Wake is an excellant game. I wouldn't call it survival-horror as you're usually kept reasonably stocked up on ammo but more as psychological horror, as you are constantly asking yourself what's real and what's not. Alan Wake stays with your for a long time.

Alan Wake's developer Remedy have long tried to innovate with all of their games.  For better or for worse, Remedy tries to shake up the formula of gaming with each release, pushing the boundaries of interactive entertainment.  Alan Wake is a result of that attempt at innovation, rooted in not only the ideas and philosophies of fiction itself, but also in telling a unique story using unique gameplay mechanics and ideas.
Alan Wake takes place in the Pacific Northwest of the United States, with our titular protagonist Alan Wake arriving the small fishing town of Bright Falls with his wife.  There on vacation to get away from the stresses of their lives and help clear Alan of his writer's block, Alan's Wife goes missing at their island cabin, and Alan is forced into combating dark forces that have begun to take hold of the local residents.
While the story of a man searching for his missing wife is nothing new, it's the gameplay mechanics, the thematic narrative of fiction itself, and the game's dark atmosphere that set it apart from its contemporaries.  The gameplay primarily revolves around the idea of illumination, with light as Alan's primary weapon, both literally and figuratively.  The enemies in the game are surrounded by darkness, and cannot be harmed until the darkness has been burned away using light.  To this end, Alan has numerous tools at his disposal to aid him in this.  His primary weapon is a flashlight, but he can also find items such as flares, flashbang grenades and even environmental items such as lamps and searchlights that can be used against the hordes of Taken that Alan contends with throughout the game, in addition to a small array of firearms.
The style of gameplay is most similar to survival horror, requiring constant scrounging for ammunition, batteries to power Alan's flashlight and other items while avoiding constant attack by enemies in the darkness of the woods.  The game also rewards exploration as items and collectibles are hidden everywhere in the game.  Enemies can appear literally from nowhere, however, and the player is rarely safe in the dark forests that make up most of the game's environments.

Combat in the game involves a balance between burning away the darkness from enemies, shooting them when they are vulnerable, and dodging their attacks.  Most every attack in the game can be dodged as long as the player does so just before it connects.  However, the game's foes tend to flank Alan and appear behind him, requiring the player to be vigilante and keep a constant watch to ensure that no enemies are attacking from outside his sight.
The idea of illumination also plays into the health system in the game.  Alan will regenerate health, but very slowly.  However, standing in bright light will restore it almost immediately, and it is only in these bright lights that Alan is safe from attack.
The game is based very heavily in weird fiction.  Lovecraft is a particular influence, as is Stephen King, both of whom get name dropped (King gets name dropped several times.  In fact the first words in the game are 'Stephen King').  The ideas of weird fiction, the creepy, small town atmosphere, the strangeness of many of its inhabitants, and the way the game tends not to explain many things helps to build the feel of an place that is just not quite right.  It's a tone in games that I love, though many will not.  If you're the kind of player who needs straight answers from your stories, this is probably not the game for you.
The narrative revolves around the foundations of fiction and art in general, and the implicaitons of how fiction affects the world around us.  It delves into the structure of stories and the creation of artistic works, the ramifications of creation and its impact.  In doing so, the developer is attempting to shed light on not only the impact of fictional works such as the game itself, but also how taxing and destructive any creative work can be, on both the creator, those around them, and the audience itself.  The metanarrative revolving around the ideas are fascinating when paired with the interactive nature of games, in which not only the developer but also the players are involved in making the story happen.
These themes and ideas, along with the game's illumination mechanics informing the titular character's actions, and the actions of the players themselves, creates a unique gameplay experience that deconstructs the ideas of game creation itself.  Both figuratively and literally, the game is shedding light on the ramifications of artistic creation.
In general, the game is very well designed.  It's environments are at once gorgeous, giving us incredible scenery in the form of America's Pacific Northwest, and ominous and terrifying, with the environments becoming dark and twisted in the night.  The combat flows well, and the gameplay and set pieces are used to drive the story forward, instead of merely relying on cutscenes constantly.  By and large, it's an excellently designed game with a superb narrative.
It is not without its flaws, though, some fairly severe.  Though the combat is well designed, the variations of enemies to be found are very small, and just two chapters in the player has seen almost every foe they will face throughout the game, with virtually no variation from then on out.  It can occasionally be tedious to fight the same foes over and over again throughout the game.
The voicework and dialogue are generally fine, but for a game about writing it can occasionally screw up hard, particularly in the case of Alan's wife Alice.   Her dialogue is atrocious, virtually unforgivable in its cliched awfulness.  Her voice acting is not good, but then I'm not sure what anyone could have done with the tripe she was given.
Speaking of Alice, let's talk about the facial animations.  They were awful upon release, and they look even worse now.  Alan's facial animations are decently done for the most part, but almost everyone else in the game looks terrible, with Alice looking particularly awful.  Her lips don't sync up, barely moving at all, and her expression barely changes throughout the game, no matter the circumstances.
I do have a few other gripes here and there, such as some of the collectibles never showing up again after you've found them but some do, making it hard to find them all using a guide, or the game's lack of variations in combat and environments.  These things, however, are not dealbreakers for me, and I love the unique narrative and gameplay styles that we haven't seen before or since.
My final verdict is that Alan Wake is an excellent game that tried to push the ideas of interactive narrative forward, and I'd definitely recommend at least checking it out.  It's not going to be for everybody, but it's most certainly an experience you can't get anywhere else.

I wanted to like Broken Age, I really did. The first half of the game, released all the way back in January 2014, is absolutely incredible. Sure, the puzzles were a tad easy at times, but I'd rather have that than the ridiculously obtuse "adventure game logic" based puzzles that the genre had been plagued with. For me at least, point and click adventure games have always been about telling a story. And the story of Broken Age Act I was absolutely brimming with promise. It took on universal coming of age themes in a clever, lighthearted way, with a quirky cast of characters and a healthy dose of humor to round out the mix.
Unfortunately, it was too good to last. Act II, released in April 2015, fell short in almost every area Act I had previously succeeded in. The art and music remained as good as ever, but the story became a cliche ridden mess that abandoned many of the first act's thematic elements in favor of a much simpler resolution. The puzzle quality took a massive hit as well. Adventure game logic is back in full force here, locking the (increasingly disappointing) story progression behind a gauntlet of infuriating mind-twisters. I'm not terribly good at adventure games, so I often find myself having to consult walkthroughs even for well designed ones. However, I can tell when my inability to solve a puzzle is due to my own shortcomings (as was the case with much of Gemini Rue, for example), and when the puzzle itself is just plain stupid (as was the case with Broken Age Act II).
I've seen a lot of stories, across many mediums, that fall short of their original promise in the later acts. However, Broken Age takes that to an absolutely mind-boggling level. It went from one of the best games I'd ever played to one of the worst just past the halfway point. If you're curious about the premise, picking it up on sale might be worth it just for the amazing first act. However, under no circumstances should you pay full price for what is ultimately a huge letdown.

SPOILER FREE REVIEW:
I was part of the kickstarter for this game. I am only writing a review now because Psychonauts 2 reached its kickstarter goal and I see all this chatter about Tim again. This title is on sale and naturally interest will regain, but people need to know what they are getting into!
This game STILL suffers from gameplay problems that adventure games like grim fandango and full throttle etc had. Those games are some of my favorites, but they are not perfect games. Many often puzzles are solved not by logic, not by paying attention, not even by the games own rules but by completely nonsensical choices you have to make. These fantasy worlds, no matter how fantastical, still need to be grounded within rules, rules the gamer learns, and iterates on especially as those rules are expanded upon. That's ultimately what gameplay is about! No matter how you dress the world, no matter what the setting is, who your characters are, if your gameplay sucks, if your puzzles make no sense, it isn't fun. This game suffers from that greatly and I think even WORST than it plagued those original, classic titles. There certain twists that make absolutely no sense. There is no natural progression - in other words, it isn't a twist if some random event out of left field happens to spin the story that direction.
tl;dr this game has good art, good voice acting, but nonsensical solutions to puzzles that can only be solved by trying everything.

I have just finished Wasteland 2, and thought this the perfect time to write a review.
Honestly, I was very close to marking this game as not recommended, and I will explain this first. The game boasts that every player has a unique gaming experience but I truthfully do not believe this, quests and side quests are so linear that it is very easy to predict their result and I have never played a game where you gain a huge chunk of experience every 5-10 minutes, it is very easy to level up. The level cap is 50, my characters finished on level 48, levels 38 onwards are useless as there are not enough quests to warrant the skills needed from levelling. Finally, and most importantly I was really really disappointed by the last 5-10 hours of the game, it was hugely rushed and it was so blindly obvious as to what was going to happen.
Now onto the good bits, and why I have decided to recommend this game. The world of Wasteland 2 is very open and after completing the first quest you are very much able to just wander off and find your feet. The biggest perk to me was building my own team of 4 very contrasting rangers, but as others have said honestly most weapon types are useless by the end game, I had 2 assault rifle users and 3 snipers including an NPC. The inhabitants of Wateland 2 are lovingly built and the game does have alot of dry humour which I found quite refreshing, and once again as others have stated, all NPCS are very down to earth and honest - most people are dead, life is♥♥♥♥♥♥ everybody is fending for themselves, they hate rangers regardless of what you decide to do. Dont pick up this game expecting to be some end game hero of the world like BG1 and 2. You will always be jerks according to most of the population.
This is what I loved so much about Wasteland. It is a very honest game and for this reason, very realistic. You can craft weapons, if you are not strong enough for body armour you are useless in a fight, you have to reload your weaons or you go in to the next fight with empty magazines, weapons jam and bullets are expensive, barter skills do not help significantly, I could go on. These are just a few parts which I loved. This game does not hand feed you, it kicks you out of the door and if you can't disarm that bomb or unlock that door or patch up that wound then you don't get some silly perk to be able to do it, you have to come back when you are stronger.
I could write paragraphs and paragraphs, but in the end Wasteland 2 is very realistic and the story line is gritty and substantial. The graphics are not great but this is more than made up for by the amount of in game material to keep you busy. Overall? 7/10.

Art, choice, content and caring.. I detect all those things in this game :) With the recent explosion of "roguelike" games, I've came across /many/ terrible, terrible games.
I don't want to only be able to equip body armor, a helmet, a ring, and a weapon.
I don't like character tiles that stand up beyond a single tile's size (lookin' at you, Dredmor!)
I don't like simplified /anything/..
I dislike cartoony, goofy graphics, for the most part (now lookin' at you, Battlepaths.. and a bit of Dredmor)
Worst of all, I can't stand a "rogue" that doesn't try to kill you (unfairly, hopefully)..
This game.. is clear for all the above :) As far as it having phone/tablet roots, I was unaware and unable to detect that myself in my mighty 13 minutes played.. Controls seemed solid and very usable.. At the very least it has the 1-9 hotkeys and full numpad support, which means the devs put some decent work in when porting it over.. I think the biggest problem with "phone games" is that 90% of them are built to be small, casual games from Day 1.. This game doesn't share any family lineage with Flappy Bird :) The 'cutscene' art style (on some of the cards, too), reminds me of Monster Hunter and a couple Legend of Zelda games (quality stuff :> )
Anyway, from my 13 minutes played, I'll say that this game is very good. I've played ADOM, Angband (ZAngband, Kangband, Oangband, -band so-forth-and-so-on), DC:SS, Dwarf Fort adv mode, Brogue, Nethack, Ivan, Ragnarok, Valhalla, ProspectorRL, Incursion, and a hundred others..  I've also played rogue-versions of Doom, Mass Effect, Grand Theft Auto, Diablo, XCOM, Dungeon Keeper and Dark Souls.. Now that I've name-dropped, I'd say that unless you are a current and avid player of Stone Soup or equivalent, then this is a good middle-ground between content and polish.. The hard part about competing with the Stone Soup is how long the soup has been cooking (same thing with Dwarf Fort vs Gnomoria.. Gnomoria is /great/, unless you're an avid, current DF player.. but if you've never played DF then Gnomoria will blow you away..)
Its good! If the devs kept at sinking new features and content in this game could turn into a "Easily worth 15-20 dollars!!" game.. then again, that goes for /a lot/ of games out there ;)

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is probably one of the best story driven RPG's of the past few years in my honest opinion, and I'll be telling you why. The game is set in a world that is similar to the world of the 'A Song of Ice and Fire' book series by George RR Martin, which has also been made a show on HBO titled 'Game of Thrones', with more High-Fantasy elements like, Elves, Dwarves (With beards), mages, monsters, and mutants that are called Witchers. The lore of the world is just fantastic, with all of the wars and such, and just overall every creature in the game. The gameplay is another great thing about this game, as it's very similar to the Dark Souls gameplay in the sense of controls and combat, but without the proper lock on strafing system that I am used to, but hey it's fun killing a few enemies at once and cutting people's arms and heads off during a battle. And the thing that literally shines is the graphics, because they are some of the best graphics I've seen in an RPG other than Skyrim, which with mods can look like the original Crysis at max settings, and without mods just looks magnificent in general. The story of the game is one of the most captivating stories I've seen in an RPG ever, hands down... *SPOILER ALERT, MAYBE* The concept of the story is of the current King of Temeria, King Foltest being assassinated by a man who has killed a number of Kings in the world,  and has reached Foltest, killing him before Geralt of Rivia, the King's bodyguard, a Witcher, can stop him, before guards arrive and find Geralt kneeling next to the King's body, jailing him. Now, you must find a way to clear your name and face dangers that could lead to a whole other thing entirely. This is where your adventure begins.
I give The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings, a perfect score: 10/10!

IF you liked the Mad Max game, then yes.
IF you hated the Mad max game, then no.
IF you are somewhere in between, then hold of for now and wait for more patches and a discount.
I compare it to Mad Max because the core gameplay (shooting, running, melee, stealth, driving) is actually very very good, BUT that is all you actually do, over and over, even in the main story quests. Now don't get me wrong the game has a great story, great characters and the best voice acting and cutscenes in any game other then the witcher, but that is a much smaller part of the game. The original game was developed as a mod that worked through the Halflife Engine as a standalone multiplayer game that incorporated RTS functions - something I loved and played to death during my college days. The developers worked tirelessly to bring a worthy sequel that brings back the elements of the original game plus adding a few new features that make a gorgeous and thouroughly engrossing game - no matter which side you play.  The aliens and their hives have an eery mystique about them that sometimes makes just sitting still and observing the surroundings as much fun as it is to go on a rampage biting the marines to death, or grabbing a pulse machine gun and letting loose on the alien swarm from the end of a narrow hallway. This game puts heavy emphasis on teamwork and cooperation to achieve the goals of team expansion and research for better effectiveness against the other team. As a result, most players will likely find themselves more than content to just log in and play as a humble foot soldier, communicating with their fellow teammates as they clear the rooms and hallways.
For the players who find themselves wishing they could command the team better and give them clearer instructions and objectives, theres also an option to play as the team's "commander," and work with an RTS overlay of the game map. As the commander your objective is to guide your team to victory through sound tactical planning and feedback with your teammates in order to bear down on the other team and destroy their base/hive, while investing your team's resources into tech-trees that research everything from weapon upgrades, to armor and even better alien life forms or marine technology.
From start to finish, no single game ever seems to play out exactly the same, as map starting positions are (depending on the map) variable for each team and as a result each game feels fresh and exciting to explore and scout out the positions of the other team. Guaranteed to keep you on your feet and coming back to experience the variability in strategy and tactical planning between each team, this is a title that I recommend whole-heartedly and hope you get a chance to pick up!

is an extremely enjoyable third person action-adventure/survival game with a very story-driven experience and the theme of a psychological thriller. It is a very cinematic game, with a lot of dialogue and cutscenes. So if you need constant action, you won’t find it here; but if you enjoy games that feel a lot like movies-you-control, this is a great pickup.
The backbone of this game is the excellent narrative, which is well-executed and well-acted. The main story arc is mysterious, intriguing, and suspenseful.  And the voice acting is quite convincing, which is critical for a game this heavily story-driven. But my personal favorite aspect of
is the development of the various characters. Video games sometimes have great stories, but often they lack the depth of character development one may find in other mediums of storytelling, like books, TV, or movies. The way this game was produced, though, it is easy to feel the connection with the characters and immerse yourself in their personalities.
The graphics, animations, effects, and soundscape all work in concert to create an extremely engaging atmosphere that reinforces the strong narrative. The gameworld looks great and you can feel the heavy atmosphere of the creepy little village that acts as the story’s setting.  This vivid and intense setting allows the entirety of the game to be entertaining; even slow plot points remain amusing due to the immersive ambiance.  If you are into immersion,
is definitely the kind of game you want to play with headphones on, lights off, and no interruptions.
But looking past the engaging narrative and atmosphere, you will find that the actual gameplay is also pretty decent. The controls are mostly solid, albeit a little clunky— but it is the kind of clunky that is purposefully imposed to adhere to the paradigm of the scary/survival genre.   And there is an interesting dynamic involving shadows and illumination from which all action/combat is derived and that affords the game a charming uniqueness. There are also a lot of collectibles that provide further lore/backstory and add an additional dynamic to the total gameplay. Be warned however: the collectibles system can break the immersion of the game at times because you’ll have to sidetrack to find them during intense moments in the storyline.
In short,
is a great experience.  It may not appeal to those who want constant action from their games, but for those who enjoy cinematic, narrative-driven games, then this will be great to consider trying if you haven’t yet.  The dark psychological-thriller theme is easy to find intriguing and the gameplay, while not innovative, has a unique charm that is gratifying to experience.

Dungeon-crawling has always been a favorite past-time of mine. Scavenging every inch of some forgotten tomb in hopes of finding treasure that might help me scavenge even deeper. Rogue-likes are also a passion. Permadeath really keeps one on his toes. Combining these two together seems like the perfect marriage, I’ve been screaming for games like this, with such amazing replayability, since I was a child, and developers have answered my cries in absolute droves. The quirky Dungeons of Dredmor, the mathematical Desktop Dungeons, the daring Spelunky… All amazing games that, while similar, have been able to carve out their own niche. Is 1Quest able to do the same? I found it came quite close, but it’s surely not without it’s shortcomings. Without further adieu, let’s take a look at 1Quest.
1Quest has a more realistic look than most of its competitors, and it captures the dark story and serious nature of the game quite well. With a story centering around a demonic sacrifice, this ain’t your grandma’s RPG. If she even plays RPGs. She seems more like an FPS gal… Erm, anyways… It is a turn-based RPG, but moves fluidly without a move-counter. Enemies will pursue when you move, but if you stop and go AFK, they will politely wait for you to get back. You can select between 5 races and (currently) 4 classes. There is some obvious synergy, such as the Orc Warrior, but if you feel the need to step up the difficulty, nobody is going to tell you not to roll an Orc Priest. The classes feel quite different during play and will require different strategies to complete the same tasks, which is great for aforementioned replayability. The UI is quite intuitive, but the default control scheme seems like a total mess for the way I tend to place my hands… Luckily you are able to rebind everything to your liking.
There are a multitude of different dungeons, offering their own buffs, creatures, and traps… All of which you will become uncomfortably familiar with. You have seven days to cross the map, if you don’t want to lose any children, and completing it in that time will give you one of two “good” endings. If you go past the seven days, a child will die each day until the 9th and final child. This gives you 5 chances to get to the final castle, (for those doing the math) so you must choose your path wisely. If you get completely bamboozled by a dungeon, it is possible to change your course, but it may be wise to try and complete the dungeon you picked, since it will be rerandomized upon your return… And since the clock is ticking to keep those kids from being sacrificed, and blazing a new trail can cost precious days. Overall a very fun game if you enjoy scraping stats together while racing against the clock to beat the big baddie.
On the downside to this game, the music and sound effects don’t do a thing for me. Generic, bland, and maybe even kinda grating after a while. Many of the enemies are simply reskinned instead of being something completely different to match the new dungeons you delve into. The enemies are still quite varied though, and the hero sprite is quite lovely. Different races and classes are represented with the equipment given to them. Because everyone knows RPGs are about 20% fashion-show… Give or take. Still, might be nice to see a bit more love shown to the critters you’ll be beating on for the entire game.Getting used to the keypad/spacebar combo doesn’t quite feel right to me, but is the most efficient way to move diagonal, which has nothing to do with the game and is just a personal gripe. The game doesn’t do much that its predecessors haven’t, and struggles to really create an identity, but the timed aspect is engaging and the core mechanics are there, and done nicely. There is a lot to love about this game, but it’s likely for the more hardcore fans of the genre.
Summary: A dungeon-delving roguelike with an intense difficulty curve.
Final Score: 6/10 for gameplay and replayability. 8/10 with better keybindings, music/SFX, enemy sprites.

Most AAA releases are extremely polarizing these days. Shadow of War has a big hill to climb based upon the novelty of the first installment and the prepurchase expectations of "bigger and better" sequel that goes along with a $60 price tag.
That all said, Shadow of War is a great game. There are some new features, but largely it is the same game. For me this isn't a negative, I really enjoyed the first game, and if you know that going in, you wont expect a complete overhaul. The improvements that are made are well done IMO.
Is it worth $60? For me, yes, others may want to purchase when on sale. I expect to play the game for 50-60 hours+, and 1$ per hour is worth it to me.
There are some negative reviews regarding the microtransactions that have become a part of so many games now. While I wont debate the gaming ethics of $60 AAA games (or $100+ with DLC) including microtransactions in games, I can state that I have not been affected by the inclusion of microtransactions in Shadow of War. I haven't completed the game yet and have seen reviews about a "true" ending that is difficult to achieve without "paying" for gear to help you through the final battle. In any event, after 36+ hours I have not felt the need or felt disadvantaged by not purchasing "loot" chests. As others have noted, they are there, they are not "in your face" and you can easily ignore them. Should you avoid this game because of microtransactions? ABSOLUTELY NOT. Whether this game is fun and appealing to you is a different matter, but the microtransaction issue alone should not stop you from purchasing the game if you had intended to.
TL;DR - great game that is a continuation of the first with minor tweaks. Worth purchase if you liked the first, microtransactions are not really an issue

Simply and plainly one of the best FPS/RTS hybrid games available on the market.
Where other games of this genre are lacking Natural selection 2 makes up for with unique a symetrical combat versus a vile alien race. Unlike most games of this type fighting against an enemy team of a COMPLETELY different makeup and abilities to your own makes quite interesting and pulse pounding games. Often ending is a very real struggle on both sides with team work, almost inherently making even the most random and public of games competitive.
On top of this Natural Selection 2 is one of the few PC games that remains open source, coming with everything from the level designer to a PDF file explaining the dynamics of map making and how to make one that is balanced, the same PDF i assume Unknown worlds gives to their employees. Natural Selection 2 is a gem for its time, one of the last PC games to still embrace the community as PC games used to do.

--Played on Hard 70 hours. No spoilers--
Not only is Shadow of War just as fun, or even moreso, than its predecessor, but it even has a level of self-awareness--about war, and fascism, and its own characters--that I was not expecting. 90% of the game is just dumb fun about orc slaughter and domination, but it definitely has some clever and charming moments.
Shadow of War can be a bit of a grind, especially toward the end. If you don't find enjoyment in repeating the basics of the game--of killing orcs you don't like and dominating orcs you do--then I probably wouldn't recommend this game for you. I do feel like the last stage of the game could have ended one or two steps sooner. But I also got some of my most fun, natural moments with strong nemesis orcs during this stage.
Some reviews seem to express that the grindiness is to push people toward resorting to loot boxes. I disagree in my experience. You earn loot boxes for free. You earn currency for some of the loot boxes for free. It's fairly easy to get good gear for your level. I never paid a cent extra, and I never felt underpowered in terms of gear. I hit the level cap about where I feel like I should have. I hate the idea of microtransactions; they're the main reason I didn't get Dead Space 3, and I absolutely loved the first 2 games. But I don't find them troublesome here.
Although there are a lot of orc introduction voicelines that are quite good, you will eventually hear them all. And you can't skip them. Even if you're hearing the orc who was consumed by warm wriggling maggots for the fifth time. Even if you were mid-killing blow on another captain. And often once the intro is over, orc inputs seem to have priority, as a little in-game time had passed during the voiceline. Can cause some frustrating injuries and deaths.
The skill upgrades are not very well balanced. On the surface they look like playstyle choices, but some hardly do a thing or work infrequently while others are pretty much necessary. Dominating orcs is also a skill upgrade, and in order to try the other two options you have to turn off the ability to dominate--a core mechanic of the game. Seems like a silly decision.
Everything else about the game is great. The orcs, the sieges, the gameplay. All super fun. If you think you can deal with the minor annoyances I listed above, I would highly recommend Shadow of War.

It was a good game, and it plays like a Stephen King novel. The graphics are a little dated; but, the story is what holds this game together.

It seems like some of the segments including the multiple driving sequences and the times when you are dodging The Darkness' poltergeist objects went on too long. Also, in multiple instances throughout the game, I smirked at the amount of advertisements that are in the game. Specifically, I'm referring to the fact that Alan uses a Verizon cellphone, there are Verizon billboards, and a recurring Lincoln MKX SUV with Microsoft's Sync displayed on the car's radio screen.
All in all, 7.5/10. Good for a playthrough, and maybe a collectibles run on the Nightmare difficulty, but this is definitely one I'd pick up on sale.

Alan Wake has a really interesting story and a main character that is flawed enough not to be a Hollywood style bad♥♥♥♥♥♥hero, but motivated enough to press on in the face of adversity. You might find the plot difficult to follow, but give it a chance. It's smooth and creamy and goes down easy, like dipping your sack in melted butter, but it's not your sack, it's your brain.
The combat system is pretty clever. While the "Over the shoulder shooting" style game isn't an original idea, the way the enemies are made vulnerable is both relevant to the plot and smart enough that it creates tension without having to have foes burst out of air ducts every 5 seconds, using shock to replace fear. It's challenging and frightening in a story driven way, like a good novel, but it's not a novel, it's a game.
Go on, give it a go. It's no doubt much cheaper these days and it still holds up, even after all these years. The whole thing is very refreshing, like jumping into a cool lake. Only it's not a lake, it's an ocean.

At first glance, 1Quest seems like a fairly simplistic, but brutally hard, roguelike. Part of that impression is because the lack of a tutorial leaves you to discover the game's intricacies on your own. The more time you spend playing and examining the GUI however, the more depth you'll find. 1Quest takes the standard RPG method of character building, combines it with the random item collecting of Diablo, the skill trees of Fable, and adds a bit of turn-based strategy to create a complex game that, unlike most roguelikes these days, can be played countless times with a different feel each time.
The gist of the plot is this: Bad Guy has captured several children and the princess. Take too long to find and kill him (hopefully, your princess is not in another castle!), and those children begin to die. Thankfully, the game gives you extra days (one per child) to complete your task, but you'll really need to dig into the mechanics to achieve your goal.  Take too long, and eventually Bad Guy will come to
and then...well, you know. Might as well just quit and hit the "New Game" button.
Paths to Bad Guy's castle are branching, although, as each map along the way is procedurally generated, this really serves no purpose other than to give you a spurious sense of choice. Killing mobs gives you experience points that you can spend on core traits or skills, and different class skills can be combined to make, for example, a Battlemage, or an Arcane Archer. The possibilities are dang-near endless. Adding to the challenge is that only one of your class skills can be activated (even if it's passive in nature) at any given time. As a Rogue, do you increase your defenses via your combat stats, or add armor piercing capabilities to your weapons? As a Mage, do you reduce the cost of your spells, or increase their range? It's the
choices like these that make this game incredibly flexible and provide near-unlimited replayability.
The main complaint I see online is that the game's dungeon generating process is unfair (or "done poorly," as one Youtuber put it), and, because of this, it's just too hard. I believe that to be false. First off, because I see those same players rushing headlong into the middle of an area before even taking the time to see what's there, ignoring heart (health) drops, making premature and incorrect assumptions about class skills (yes, rogues really
detect and avoid traps), and leaving valuable items on the floor. At that point, it's not the game's fault you've been surrounded and defeated, it's yours. Second, surviving a ton of  mobs is completely possible; you're just not going to
on your first time through the game. So many Roguelike players are used to just bashing their way through a battlefield and healing after, that the thought of strategic gameplay seems almost foreign. Make that mistake while playing 1Quest, and you will die. A

In defense of the complainers, though: The game gives you no help (other than mouseover, contextual tips), so this attitude really is, in part, the developer's fault. Players are used to simple games; 1Quest appears to be simple, so most will assume it is "unfair" and move on. Give those people a public forum, and there goes the chance of the game finding the right audience. In the case of 1Quest, this would be a very sad thing for Roguelike lovers, indeed. If you are at all interested in buying a copy, be prepared to spend a fair amount of time just exploring the various buttons and figuring out what everything does.
As for the rest: The graphics are average at best, and the music, while serviceable, will grow tiring pretty quickly. There is so much goodness in the actual gameplay however, that, were they to improve the A/V and add a tutorial, I would happily drop $20 US on this. As it stands now, as long as you are aware of what this is going into it, 1Quest is easily worth the current list price of $6.99 (and I'd still recommend it as a value up to the $12 mark).
And, as an additional incentive, the dev has recently

.)

Fallout Shelter is a good fun little game where you manage the development of a fallout shelter.
The cartoon-style drawings are nicely done.
The general structure of this game seems to have been well thought out.
You acquire resources to expand the size of your base, recruit people, and send out some hardy adventurers on quests.
The requirements for food, water, and power seem to be balanced.
The emergency incidents that occur have not seemed to be out of proportion to the resources at hand (so far, at least).
Fallout Shelter is essentially a management game.
However, in some ways it is almost like a clicker game, albeit quite an advanced one. You have to keep on going back and forth between production units to keep the resources flowing. And there are long waits for the completion of quests, and the production of some resources and skill levels, to encourage players to get impatient and purchase upgrades (microtransactions).
Sending Vault-dwellers out on quests can take a long time, unless you use your bottles of "Nuka-Cola Quantum" (which speeds up the journeying), but such bottles are few and far between  unless you feel like spending some real-life money on buying some more (yes, there's the catch).
Your questers engage in battles versus enemies in various buildings, but it's action of just a very basic nature (no first person shooting happens in the game).
The fate of those people who go out into the Wasteland, to explore, is relayed to you via lines of text; you don't actually see them in action, unless they go into a quest building (which you have to authorise).
Mostly the game is about managing the resources of your base, or "Vault".
I quite like Fallout Shelter. From my point of view, the pros far outweigh the cons.
Be warned that you will need a goodly store of patience to play this game (which brings to mind the old prayer, "God grant me patience, but hurry up about it!"); so, if you aren't a patient person, you might want to let this one pass by; but, if patience is one of your virtues, then this might just be the game for you.
If you're a patient person who enjoys a bit of post-apocalyptic fun, then I recommend that you give this game a try.
*********************
P.S. People should be aware that there is a major problem with this game, although it is easily overcome.
If your game crashes, or your computer crashes, then you can lose your entire game (apparently it's something to do with it then not synchronising with the Steam cloud).
This drama has happened to many people, whereby they have lost all of their many hours of game progress.
You need to back up your game.

First and foremost, let me be clear, I have been a massive fan of the Mafia series ever since the first installment, it was amazing and the realism/immersion was incredible with the speed limit, indicators, fuel, stuff like that, so you can understand I was VERY excited when I heard about this game.
Now, lets skip forward to just a few days ago when I finally got the game I was so eager to play... to say I was disappointed would be an understatement. I am VERY unhappy with how Hangar 13 has failed in keeping up with the quality and attention to detail we came to love in Mafia 2.
I also apologise if my review is "TL:DR" but details are important in a review.
The following are the reasons why I don't recommend Mafia 3.
1: No fuel. The Fuel system in the previous Mafia games added a level of immersion that we hadn't seen before, it was what made it different from other similar games.
2: No speed limit. Previous Mafia games had an enforced speed limit, if the cops saw you going too fast they came after you lights and all, but in Mafia 3 you can buzz past the police as fast as you want and they won't even bat an eyelid.
3: No Indicators. This isn't a HUGE feature but it added immersion and that is very important in a game like Mafia. Previous Mafia games you used the indicator by holding left or right while in a vehicle, but none of that in Mafia 3.
4: Graphic issues. You will frequently see that the transition from day to night is VERY quick, sometimes its instant you just see it go from dark to light in seconds. The skybox at sunset and dawn is U.G.L.Y, it just looks horrible.
5: Car Flipping. Just like in GTA if your car rolls over you can just roll it back over and drive off, in the previous Mafia games you could not do that, you had to get a new car which is FAR better and much MUCH more immersive.
6: Combat. In Mafia 3 it feels as if you are fighting the same fight over and over again, much of the buildings are simply copy/pasted and it gets very boring. Especially when all you have to do is hide, whistle and stab, thats it.
7: Weather. Mafia 3 has no real weather. Yes it rains, but thats it, either rain or sun, no snow, no ice, no fog, nothing, I understand its New Orleans but it still snows in New Orleans. Especially when it comes to driving, Mafia 2 has snow and ice and that affected how your car handled, even NPC's slipped and fell over on the ice.
There are plenty other small things that made the previous Mafia games so much better than Mafia 3.
Such as, shooting hub caps, repairing engines, customising car in garage, random NPC, actual MAFIA not this Haitian bullsh*t, Can't interact with phonebooths, Police are nerfed in Mafia 3, No car wash, Can't use car trunk and finally NO BLOODY FOOTPRINTS!!  (You also can't interact with the small things like sinks, toilets, lights, fridges and windows like you could in the previous games).
So I think I have made my point, Mafia 3 is NOT a Mafia game. Yes it has the name and the same devs, but I refuse to believe THIS heap of sh*t is what they had in mind after all these years.

Okay. Like the Alien Trilogy? Like actual teamwork. Want an actually friendly community? Like the sound of xenomorphic teeth ripping through space marine armor? Like feeling like like the STATE OF THE BADASS ART? GET THIS GAME.
Down to its core, NS2 is a game of teamwork. Two asymetrical teams fight to the death for the future of their species. This isn't an average FPS. Both teams, the human Frontiersman and the alien Kharaa, have radical differences in playstyle, but also some striking similarities. The largest similarity, is the presesne of a player acting as a commander for the team. Being a commander compared to being a soldier or a skulk on the front lines is radically different as well. You have to act as the coordinator of your team. You are responsible for keeping an eye on the map, and telling your teammates what needs to be done. NS2 is like an armsrace, where both teams compete to outdamage, outgrow, and eventually overwhelm the other. Playing as a marine, you experience an almost completely different game than as an alien. And because each and every game populated by soley players, no two games are alike. NS2 is not a "spunk-gargle-weewee 360 noscope FPS". NS2 is a game of tactics.
Natural Selection looks beautiful. The sci-fi maps, the Darwinism-on-steroids aesthetics of the Kharaa, the sounds, the effects... These all give NS2 this amazing and unique appearance. I have felt true fear when the aliens cut the lights and forced me to engage them in near pitch dark. I have felt the pride swell at being a part of a sucessful push into enemy territory. I have felt the joys of victory, the humility of defeat, and also respect for the enemy team when they manage to outmaneouver us.
The community of Natural Selection 2 is generally friendly and helpful. While there might be a few bad examples here and there, the players are consistantly nice. So long as you're not a caustic individual, you find the community to be one of the strongest aspects of this game.
Get this game. As a fan of the Alien series, this is the game I never recieved. As a fan of deeper games, NS2 has more depth than any probably any other online shooter out there. Thats why I recommend this game. Because this was the kind of game I was always looking for.
