TL;DR: Alan Wake is a well-constructed and interesting game, with great atmospheric environments that work well with an interesting combat mechanic. With this is a clever story line and charming but somewhat poorly animated characters; this game is great for anyone looking for a solid thriller game.
In Alan wake there is a dark and twisted world where light and dark are prominent in both environment and tone. The graphics still hold up today and work beautifully with the lighting mechanics to build an intense experience. The atmosphere in Alan Wake is excellent; walking through dark woods in the night with your flashlight and weapon is rather creepy and with the light based combat mechanic manages to scare and reward. While at times the environment may seem repetitive the game does break up its action with puzzle sections and slightly dodgy driving segments.
Positive features:
-Fantastic atmosphere
-Different combat mechanic with array of weapons
-Beautiful graphics and lighting
-A well put together story line
-DLC comes included
Negative features:
-Occasionally repetitive areas
-Cut scenes are dated with poor character models and lip syncing
-Sudden physics related glitches on more than one occasion
To conclude Alan Wake is a solid all-round game; while not perfect and debatable in terms of its "horror" tag the whole experience is one that is well worth your time with replay ability for completionsists and DLC that adds to the game and story.

After watching the documentary, I get that a lot of blood, sweat and tears went into making this game.  Unfortunately, part 2 does not deliver on what part 1 set up.  I totally empathize with what they went through, but I have to be honest here.  I was extremely let down by this  game.
I feel like we got the outline of an interesting story.  The two main character's worlds are explained fairly well.  Unfortunately the antagonist's isnt, and instead is simply summarized through dialog...and even then it's still not explained very well.  Imagine if a character is on a journey to a destination, and when they finally get there, the only thing you get to see is an exterior shot and nothing else.  That pretty much sums it up.  There were some major, "Hey!  What about the so and so's trapped in the you know where?" type of plotholes that were never resolved.
There's also an extremely frame-breaking puzzle mechanic introduced in part 2.  Characters A and B are completely separated with no way to communicate.  Yet Character A has puzzles with solutions that only Character B has information about.  So when Character B looks at an inventory item, you have to use information about that item so Character A can solve the puzzle.  I was literally stumped for a couple of hours because I didn't think Tim would actually break that kind of rule.  It made absolutely zero sense in the story so why should it be possible?  When I finally gave in and used walkthrough to find an answer, I literally put the game away for a few months.  I was suddenly disinterested because it's cheating the story just to make the puzzle harder.
Anyways, after I finished watching the documentary, I decided to start over and finish Broken Age.  I was even more excited now that I got a glimpse at how it was made!   Maybe I was wrong.  Maybe that was just one puzzle that was bad.  Well, it turns out several puzzles break the narrative.  The end of this game has two characters coordinating an attack who aren't in communication at all!  Seriously!  It felt like I was playing an old Sierra puzzle game called Gobliiins.  Get these characters in the right places and push the buttons and pull the levers to continue.  Couldn't Tim just put some sort of communication device in the story that allowed them to communicate in some fashion?  I think it would have led to better story telling as our characters actually got to know each other.
I'm even more disappointed after seeing so many likeable people put a lot of time and energy into this and to come up with something that feels 77% complete.  The art and the music are superb.  The voice acting is top notch.  Unfortunately the part two's puzzle felt like busy work (seriously, once I demonstrate I get the gist of it, I shouldn't have to go through all the steps over and over again) and felt like they focussed more energy on making puzzles harder and less time developing the story.
So I cannot recommend this game at full price.  I'd definitely wait for it to go on sale.  I never thought I'd say that about a Tim Schafer game...

2D action platformer with 100 levels. The quality of level design is excellent and imaginative, along with tight, responsive controls. There is no settings menu but everything is already set up exactly as you would want it. Steam/Xbox controllers 'just work', the sound volume is set just right and it starts in fullscreen. Alt-Enter to switch to windowed and you can stretch it to any size you like. Controller X button to zoom the level view in/out, Y to toggle music (which is very good). The whole playing experience feels comfortable and satisfying. Other devs could learn a thing or two from this.
Overall I highly recommend Pinkman, and at this price it's just plain rude not to buy it. I do wish I could play it on Linux though.

I personally purchased this game. I reviewed it for my 99 Cent Gaming series.
Wow...I think there has been a gold standard set when it comes to games I've reviewed on my show. Ladies and gentlemen I present to you Pinkman, a very fun masochistic platformer that is in the same vein of Super Meat Boy, N+, and those before it.
There is so much going for this title that being priced at a cool .99 (and cheaper if you get it during the first week) makes it almost criminal to not recommend. Everything from the controls to the gradual increase in difficulty to the introductions of new mechanics and obsticals are all done in a way to only help the player understand what exactly brought them their doom.
Like many platformers of this kind, Pinkman offers very simple controls that support both keyboard and controller. I used controller in this case and the character handled very well and never felt too sensitive or weighty. In addition to moving and jumping you can utilize a jetpack (or "fart" if you perfer) to give an extra boost when trying to make up to other platforms or trying to avoid an explosive death.
Never once did I feel like a death was cheap or unavoidable, something that could have easily been done to make players try over and over again to pad out play time. Every level I had played through for my review (1-35) felt fair, difficult, and fun which only made me want to keep playing once the video was over.
Altough the graphics are very simplistic, they also help the player to keep focused on the obstacles at hand. There's never a distraction thrown at you from how it's designed. The sound is also amazing and it kept my adrenaline going even when I suffered a round of deaths on a few levels.
If I had to nitpick, I wish there were options for recording how fast you beat a level. Games like this are a speed runners dream, and the lack of a time keeping mechanic just baffles me. Hopefully in a future update this can get added.
I have more to save in the video below, but overall this was a joy to not only discover but to review. Controls were on point, everything seemed polished, and it felt like a game with a purpose. Was this worth the .99 cents: absolutely! In fact, I was in doubt I'd ever find a gold standard when it came to games around this price point. Now I hope that I'll find other games that can reach this level of 99 cent enjoyment. Definitely give this developer your support.

I don't usually write reviews but I just had to for Broken Age, mainly also because number of negative reviews here.
In a short Broken Age is a "traditional" point and click adventure set in an interesting worlds. You controll two main charactes with possibility to switch between them any time, sometimes it is even necessary to find out a solution to puzzle in other character's "world". Main charactes are Vella, young girl which escapes her fate of a sacrifice for giant monster and Shay, a growing-up boy trying to escape his over-caring space ship. Plot is really interesting and I was hooked to see how will the two story lines cross or join.
As for the puzzles, I have to say they are mostly fair. You are given an overall clear idea (or multiple goals) what has to be done and it is up to you to come up with the execution. Many people complain that some puzzles in Act II are unfair because you had to look for the answer with other character in his/hers world. I found it interesting and smart, requiring you to think outside of the box or pay attention to details. Kind of reminded me the old days of Day of the Tentacle.
The art style and animation in game is beautiful, voice acting is excellent and dialogues are quite funny, I especially enjoyed Vella's interaction with "hipster" woodcutter. Not only because I like poop jokes :)
What I didn't like so much is the harsh conclusion of the story. There was potential for Act III, it is shame that authors didn't extend the last part of the game to its own Act.

The fact that you don't do anything and just look at it and listen to the sounds is oddly entertaining. Really helps with stress/anxiety
/seriousreview

Wasteland 2 is an incredibly fun post-apocalyptic RPG. I came into this series with this entry (although I own the first one from a bundle), and although some of the nuances of this world's narrative are lost on me I have little difficulty becoming immersed in the world and its stories.
This game has very dense RPG elements to it, and I think that is a very good thing. There are an incredible number of skills that could fall under various traditional RPG roles (tank, rogue, healer, etc), and even within one of those major categories there's plenty of room for variation. I find this a fun aspect of the game, because the four characters (which I created completely from scratch, from their appearance to their skills to their religion and the brand of cigarettes they smoke) can be completely different from each other and are able to support each other well in combat, trading, persuading, and other tasks in which they find themselves.
I will definitely work my way through the entire storyline in this game at least once, and it's entirely likely that I'll go through several more times because, with this wide variety of character traits to choose from, I don't see myself playing the game the same way twice.

After playing the original, I must say that I really think this game is an improvement in almost every way. The open world is bigger, there is more dialogue between characters, and the orcs have way more personality and character. This game is by no means perfect lore wise but stays on track for most of the game, so long as you can get past Shelob and mistakes like that. I was able to get past that because I can see what they wanted to do and I recognized the story they wanted to tell, and I think they pulled off that vision pretty well. The game mainly revolves around the concept of "absolute power corrupts absolutely" and I think this was a good choice, not just because it was a central theme for Tolkien in many of his works, but also because I like the tension between Talion and Celebrimbor and the framing of their story. The gameplay is great just like in the original just with a few added flares like the double jump that makes movement all the more fluid and enjoyable. I also really like the concept of forging a new ring of power. Not only does it raise the stakes but it gives us a great excuse to go completely overboard with Talion's powers which is always nice for a fantasy video game.
As far as the microtransactions go I was not thrilled when they announced them but they are not to invasive and I never actually bought one. This was even after completing the Shadow Wars and seeing the true ending, which I found to be beautiful and keeping perfectly with the source material. In conclusion this is a great game marred by unnecessary controversy that deserves to be played, and enjoyed for what it is.

I bought this game during it's early access period and tried it, thinking it was a confusing mess, uninstalled it and left it for 6 months. I then saw a multitude of Scott Manley's youtube videos on the game, some of which were tutorials and decided the game looked like fun, so I reinstalled it and haven't removed it since.
(Although my steam counter only says I currently have 220hrs in this game, outside of steam with mods installed I estimate I've got around 1000hrs in this game, which may be the first time I've reached that time with any game.)
I'm not going to lie, it takes people who want to play the game seriously a fair bit of effort to get into it, but after a week or two I felt competent enough to play it, every day, in fact most hours that I had free were spent playing KSP.
For fans of contemporary space sims there is nothing better, nothing more emersive. Don't let the cartoony little green guys fool you, this game is serious when it comes to simulating space exploration and it does it in a way I find fun and even educational, at time when I don't even feel like I'm learning anything I will then look back and realise I'd just inadvertently experienced space flight and physics phenomena first hand that I never would have if not for this game.
The game is a stand alone great, but is made even more amazing and addictive with mods which are relatively easy to install and learn.
The developers have never stopped working on updates, most of which are generous in their content and always improve gameplay and often stability especially since updating to the newer version of Unity.
My only concern for the future of this game is that as I understand it, Take Two Interactive have purchased the game and as a lot of the KSP community seem to already be aware, this publisher doesn't have a great reputation when it comes to the long term health of the games it owns, or respect for it's consumers.
That said, Squad (the devs) are amazing and the game it's self at the moment only seems to be getting better and better.

I'm amazed by how well written and developed this game turned out to be. If you love games that focus on story, unbelievably likeable and dislikeable characters, and difficult choices that affect the game's ending, BUY THIS GAME!
Starting out, it's pretty mundane. You take on the role of Max Caulfield, a teenager attending a prestigious art school. You spend the beginning of the game just exploring the setting and being introduced to other characters. You also learn how to use Max's mysterious gift of manipulating time. There's a great sense of nostalgia as if you've stepped back in time to high school. You've got the different cliques and teenage drama all wrapped with a sense of naivety.
Once you've gone through the first major encounter involving Max using her power, the game really steps it up. Your choices affect relationships with other characters which in turn affect which ending you'll see at the conclusion of the game (Episode 5). If you don't like how an encounter turned out, just use Max's gift to rewind time and you can do it all over again to your heart's content. Certain encounters in the game require you to use Max's gift in order to progress. As you progress deeper into the game, you'll inevitably be enthralled by the story and the various characters which is this game's strength. The songs used in the game do an amazing job in provoking the feels. Whenever I got the chance in-game to sit, I did and just let the music and visuals wash over me with nostalgia.
By the end of the game, I was simply stunned. The characters felt real and distinct with their own personalities. There were those I didn't care for and those I grew attached and wish I knew in real life. Despite how black and white the decisions I made were, watching how events play out and what Max has to grow through really made me shed a tear. The animations suffer a bit towards the end of the game but the amazing voice acting and music really drive home the emotions this game manages to provoke.
If you're ready for a feels trip where by the end of the game you're second guessing yourself, BUY THIS GAME!

Review after about 20 hours playing
Pros -
- Open world is well made, districts have their own personalities and varied police presence.
- Music is fantastic
- Some of the animations are really well done, shooting guns then moving for example
- Story is really well made and the use of flashbacks adds more depth
- Driving (on simulation) feels great, the cars are weighty and its much harder driving fast in rain or mud roads
- Evening and night time the atmosphere looks and feels really good
- Little details like enemies flipping you off as they die or mini-stories you hear as you eavesdrop on patrolling guards talking to each other
Cons -
- Game is FULL of bugs and glitches, boats having seizures and flying around, bodies glitching through objects, story missions needing to be reset and some missions being bugged and unable to be completed. No word from the dev's about them working on any of these even though the forums are filled with people unable to continue or play.

Alan Wake is a linear third-person shooter whose atmosphere and story attempt to redeem the frankly clunky combat. The game proceeds in six episodes (with two additional DLC episodes that are now included for free). Worth a purchase on sale if you enjoy a combat-driven interactive movie, but there's not much replayability (unless you're a collectibles and achievements fanatic).
You can
.
Installed size on hard drive (all DLC and extras): 11.2 GB
Alan's wife, Alice, gets “taken” by a mysterious “dark presence.” The entire game is spent trying to release her from its power. Alan is frequently lost, operating on whim, and not really sure of how to proceed. A writer himself, he begins researching old legends of Cauldron Lake and the power that words written there seem to possess. This is really the best part of the game, as the labyrinth of creation and created and how to balance what is desired with what is needed leads Alan down an increasingly dark path (pun intended). As he discovers, he is not alone in his knowledge of the lake's mysterious power, nor the first to suffer from it. The supporting cast are varied and colorful characters, several of whom have their own history with Cauldron Lake.
The atmosphere is suitably dark and fog-swept at times. Most of the game happens at night, so turn down your room lights and crank the audio to catch the ambiance (the sound design is superb). The setting is a unique one: the woods and small town atmosphere of the Pacific Northwest. The ambiance is captured nicely, and the woods have thick foliage and dark shadows. Old logging and mining gear abounds, providing just the right touch of historical nostalgia and rusty menace. The buildings and architecture are a mix of rustic, country-style structures (built sturdy to withstand the harsh winters) other more attractive, modern structures designed to impress tourists (Cauldron Lake Lodge). The superb music score is the icing on the atmospheric cake: moody but melodic, it catches the feeling of solitude at night-time haunted by the supernatural.
A supernatural that is made perhaps more terrifying by the clunky combat. Shine a light at enemies to burn away the darkness, then shoot them with whatever weapon you have to hand. It works well enough, but feels loose and sloppy. The weapons are few, but do feel different: revolver, shotgun (regular and pump-action), flare gun, hunting rifle, flares, and flash-bangs. That's it. They're not all available at the same time, and at the beginning of each episode, Alan only has a flashlight and a revolver. So, no matter how good you were with saving up your gear, thinking there might be a big battle coming up, once the episode ends, you'll lose it all anyway. The enemies offer little variety. You've got the standard hatchet-throwing “taken”, the big “taken”, the fast “taken”, and random flocks of crows that fly out of the sky and attack Alan. Sometimes random objects (like cars, tires, dumpsters) will become possessed and attack Alan. With so many creatures that dwell in the woods of the Pacific Northwest, I expected there might be a boss fight with a bear or a pack of coyotes, but no.
None of these drawbacks would matter if the total experience offered by Alan Wake were more than the sum of its parts. Unfortunately, it isn't. I enjoy it because when I first played it years ago I had no idea that video games could handle narrative in this fashion. I'll always have a nostalgic appreciation for it and it just kills me to provide a mixed recommendation. But if you want more than story and atmosphere, look elsewhere, because you'll be sorely disappointed by everything else. If story and atmosphere suffice, though, get Alan Wake right away.

I have just finish the game and I have honestly review it.
I would recommend it to anyone who likes true RPG (choices that matter, not just character development) and post-apocalitpic mood.
(+) The single strongest advantage of the game is giving player many choices, small and large regarding people and communities player run across in the wasteland. Very ofteb there are more that two possible solutions, so everyone should find the one they like the most, it is usually support faction A or B, kill them both, or make peace between them. Sometimes you will have to chose side as peace is not always possible. Such choices are give to the player not only about the very end-game (how most games nowdays deliver), but from the start to the end, from small signel quests to whole communities future.
So I often had a chance to ask myself, what do I think that matter? What would I do in such situation? Should I pick side or let them fight each other?
Regarding end-game player also has bad and good ending to chose from.
Now regarding other stuff.
(-) Game is unfortunately poorly made, even after all the patches it still crashes like hell. I had to play in window mode and lowest graphics (apparently my bugs were about graphics).
(-) Graphics in general are poor compared to modern game standards, I would even say that they are from the times of Fallout.
(-) Combat is this game is not tactical by comparing for example to XCOM. Most often best solution is to engage from as far as possible and wait as close range enemies will charge you so you can shoot them like on firing range. Cover is not well done and AI somehow always find right angle to hit my troops. Line of sight is even worse, very often enemies and my team were shooting through walls, rocks etc that usually blocks like of sight.
(-) Equipment is poorly delivered, there are few weapon categories, however few such as Heavy Weapons and Handguns are made useless because there are much better alternatives. Assault Rifles are kings of battlefield. Approach to armor and armor penetration is in favour to armor penetration, so wearing any kind of armor (except the one with value of 10, which slows to down to a crawl) is useless as enemies most likely have enough armor penetration.
(+) However developers shown us new approach to energy weapons, instead of competing with ordinary bullets, energy guns deal more damage the higher target armor and minimum damage to low armor.
At the end few more good points.
(+) Story of the game is well told. It is interesting, engaging, full of choices. There are a lot of dialogs in the game, however not that much to make you tired. Some stuff, solutions, ways to solve problems are a bit hidden or not plain obvious.
(+) Regarding end of the story I had my suspicions, but I was never the less plesently suprised by how it all played.
I managed to find a computer in the game with Wasteland 3 on it, so I hope that inXile will deliver us the third part of the story in some near future after new Plancescape.

Very cool take on a western themed turn-based strategy with some occult stuff thrown in. The level design is great and there is a huge amount of weapons and items available.
The only downsides i can think of is that the game often hangs when opening inventory/trade menus, and that the framerate droppes occasionally for no apparent reason.

The astounding collection of familiar voice actors and quirky art style makes this game feel more like a movie at times, but it still plays for the most part like a classic point and click.
I have to agree with former reviewers that the writers didn't lead the story to an end that fully showcased the premise's potential, but the ending wasn't disappointing either, simply fitting.
Overall Broken Age is a cute game to play when you want to test your mind and enjoy a unique story in order to kill time. Most of the puzzles are too easy, and a select few are more esoteric by comparison.
The games biggest flaw is that when it requires you towards the end to switch between characters for information, it doesn't give you any context as to how the characters themselves are supposed to know whatever info it is you got from the other side. You're less playing as a character and more controlling one.
Regardless, I enjoyed Broken Age, although it's admittably not a groundbreakingly memorable game.

The game is more about surviving the stuff thrown at you than it is about killing everything in your path; which is a nice departure from most games. It means that sometimes the best plan really is do dodge attacks and get to safety rather than fight.
The story definitely keeps you guessing the whole time and confused for a lot of it. It does all become more clear later in the game and seems to me to be more of the focus of the game above combat and such which is always good in my book.

One of the best cinematic experiences comes from a game. Ironic, right? But it's true, and it tells a lot about the game.
Virginia is comparable to a movie, even in its lenght (about 2 hours, depending on how you play it: straight-forward or searching for clues/easter-eggs). There aren't choices. No real-time events. No enemies to kill. You can barely move out of your own free will, so I'm a little reluctant to call Virginia a game. It feels more like an interactive movie. However, a really good one at that.
It's hard to recommend this game. I, for one, won't even say its name to none of my friends. Nonetheless, there are people out there that may enjoy movies just as much as me (especially David Lynch) and would love to dive into a surreal cinematic experience. For those, I recommend this game with no restraints.
All the aspects I could analize in a movie are here in this "game", and I can say it excels in every single one of them.
Even the lack of dialogue can be portrayed as something meaningful about the story, and I must resalve how risky that is: They could have messed up with the voice actors, however, with none, how do you fill the void? With music, that is. And that's the risky part. But worry not, Virginia has one of the best soundtracks I've heard.
For what it is, this game is the best. Those who don't enjoy it, are playing the wrong type of game. If this is your thing, you'll love it. It's just that simple, so, go on, buy Virginia.

I remember playing Chuck Yeager's Advanced Flight Trainer on my C>= 64 as a teen and thinking to myself: it's sims like this that keep the dream alive. Years have gone by and many simualation games have come and gone. Almost anything by Microprose (and "Wild Bill" Stealy). Elite. Jane's Aviation series. Sid Meier's Civilization. Chris Sawyer's Transport Tycoon. Third Wire Wings series Falcon 3.0. Microsoft Space Sim. X-Wing. Elite: Frontier. Deuteros. They all seemed to catch onto something related to the human spirit and the drive to fly, explore or expand like shining like beacons on a barren landscape. Every once in a while such games tickle the keys of our primal need to fly, explore and expand. Elite Dangerous certainly is one such mammoth if you want to be there after the explosion of space exploration has been unleashed.
For those Efram Cochrane's out there yearning to invent the technology from scratch to get us to the planets and then finally the stars, figuring it out all the way there's Kerbal Space Program.
If you want to walk in the shoes of NASA (Never Afraid Of Seeking Adventure), the CSA (Canadian Space Agency or Can't Stop Aerospace) or the ESA (European Space Agency or Everyone's Search For Answers) then Kerbal Space Program is for you. You have to play it to understand though don't come here looking for an action FPS. Come here looking for tinkering, strategy, curiosity, aventure and exploration that is addictive with a great campaign and even a sandbox mode.
Manage your own space program just like NASA, CSA, ESA, Elon Musk or Guy Laliberté (of Cirque Du Kerbal fame). There's something mystical about this game and I'd recommend it to just about anyone though certainly to students, youth and children who want a physically accurate rocketry playground to let their creativity run amok. It's games like this that inspire the next generation of Aerospace Engineers. So what are you waiting for?

is an Old West-themed tactical roleplaying game.
The player assumes the roles of various protagonists
in a series of compelling, disparate chapters that eventually weave together to form a tapestry of love, loss, heroism, despair, vengeance, and salvation.
The game looks and sounds great - in particular, the environments are rich and detailed without getting in the way, the soundtrack features a selection of appropriately twangy Western themes from inspiring to anxiety-enhancing to spooky, and the narration of key events is absolutely perfect. I experienced a little flickering of the visual overlays on Linux (
), but otherwise everything ran well.
In terms of gameplay, the player explores a world map, gradually revealing the story by participating in choose-your-own-adventure-style interactions, recruiting her posse, trading for supplies and weapons, and engaging in tense stealth missions and bloody firefights. Although combat uses traditional cover-based mechanics, it features several unique touches: shooters' accuracy is opposed by the targets' luck, which is drained when a shot misses and replenished when one hits; areas in which combat takes place are often multilevel labyrinths of run-down buildings; out-of-sight enemies can sometimes be heard or detected by their shadows; and savvy gunslingers can ricochet shots off of environmental objects to literally circumvent their enemies' cover. There's an additional clever mechanic where the player accumulates playing cards that can be distributed among her posse to award special powers - if the player uses these to form poker hands, she can bestow additional bonuses inversely proportional to each hand's probability.
Hard West gives the player plenty of room to shape the story. The player can rescue posse members or sacrifice them; she can take advantage of down-on-their-luck settlers or deal squarely with them; she can respect native customs or desecrate them; she can deal with the devil or spit in his face. Most choices affect the story in larger or smaller ways, but often not in the expected manner, since only a portion of events are under the player's control.
I spent about 20 hours playing through the main campaign, which included retrying a few battles - I'll likely play through it again in order to explore the boundaries of the story in different directions.
If you're a fan of tactical RPGs, Call of Cthulhu, Mansions of Madness, or Shadows of Brimstone, try Hard West NOW.

I liked it from the beginning... it should however be noted that this game is a slow burner.
Fallout 2 was one of my favs as a child, so I'll use it as a comparison despite the fact that WL2 isn't a Fallout game.
I like the Wastland 2 soundtrack, though it maybe a bit avant-garde. It makes more use of ambiance, instruments that embody complex harmonics and lean arrangement, then it'll juxtapose those tunes with some driving electronic music for combat sections. FO2 had the same thing going for it music wise and even the newer Fallout games employ some very non-traditional music when the radio isn't on. I don't think there were any original pieces in the FO series that you would hear the mailman whistling.
Also, if you haven't seen it, watch the movie The Stand. I think a lot of the original music from that movie, particularly the slide guitar portions, directly influence a few tracks for the Wasteland and Fallout games.
Combat, if we're comparing this to older Fallout titles, is an improvement overall. It's not as much as an improvement to as say Pillars of Eternity made upon the formula of games like Baldur's Gate, but Wasteland 2 is still less clunky and requires less fuss than the FO 1 or 2. Combat can get extremely intense though. You will be confronted with situations that require tactical engagement and that might get you through threadbare.
The real draw of the game for me is the story. There is a sense of intrigue from the beginning and you're there to hunt down answers. Along the way you meet some characters and the interactions feel meaningful. Also, a lot of areas of the game are chockful of macabre grim darkness and despair, which appeal to me greatly.
I say give it chance. Some of the things about the game are hella sketch especially those godawful 3D character models and the optimization is poor for what the game is, but it's got a great aesthetic and the story should keep you wandering the wastes to solve the mystery.

Holy crap is this game an unexpected diamond! I like turn-based strategy, but only when it's not boring. This game constantly surprises me with the interesting choices I have to make, doling out its interesting story one choice at a time.
In the larger meta-game, I have to pick where I mine, how I mine, and how I deal with the various problems that crop up along the way. That gold I mine can be traded for better weapons, items, and other goodies that help me in the tactical combat portion of the game, which I can't long avoid.
And said tactical combat is awesome! I haven't had so much fun in a western setting since playing Boot Hill on pen and paper with my friends decades ago. It was a little tricky to grasp how to handle things at first, and the luck system still continues to stymie me at times, but I haven't felt this good about a turn-based strategy combat system in a LONG time.
And then there's the ambiance and overall plot direction, both of which I absolutely LOVE. If you have even an inkling of interest in the western setting, if you have even the barest fraction of appreciation for turn-based strategy, I'd say this is a bloody MUST BUY game.
I have no idea how this slipped under my radar for so long, but I'm glad I've found it.

A wonderful, deep, pretty, funny, and extremely long game - I clock 252 hours at the time I'm writing this, and this is my first playthrough which is quite a bit from finished (I restarted maybe a few hours in, and must have kept the game on a few times while not playing, but I doubt this accounts for even 50 hours). You can certainly finish faster, but if you try to obsessively find and do everything (and which true RPG fan doesn't?), I doubt by much if you read all dialogue and such.
I'm an RPG, and more generally fantasy old-timer. I've played D&D all night through each Saturday back in the mid 80s, and later the Baldur's Gate series, etc. Strangely, while I owned it, I never finished or even progressed much into Fallout, but from the first steps into this game, this felt like the real deal from 20 years back with a very attractive new chassis.
While the game allows for much optional questing and is largely open-world, it also guides you along nicely, so you rarely have to wonder what you could do next, which I appreciate. The character animations are awesome, with special shoutouts to enemies in wheel chairs, or those whose legs you chopped off sometimes still crawling for a few seconds before collapsing. :) Voice acting is excellent, and plentyful; and by the end of the game, you had enough background text to read that it amounts to almost a short book. The UI is great and allows for easy access to really everything, with little gimmicks such as the game allowing for automatic intelligent loot sharing (but, in line with RPGamers being OCD, who would want that? :)). The skill system truly matters, and you'll miss out on a lot if you don't cover ALL skills among your team (which you can, by and large - I skipped two somewhat useless skills only).
And so much of the dialogue really cracks me up...my favorite is probably the leader of the robotic faction who keeps advertising on air with demented marketing such as to not follow another leader who'll just enslave you, while he'll kill you prganic vermin as free men! Another recent favorite was the third prize in a lottery organized by a gang leader which was described along the lines of "you'll get to work on my farm...which used to be your farm."
I'm playing on normal. On this difficulty, the game is somewhat easy after the first few levels. I personally like that as for the first playthough, I focus on story; and as there are two higher difficulty levels, I assume those looking for a challenge can find it too.
Looking for something to criticize, I find:
(1) Occasional in-fight freezing - not the game, but the camera, which means typically that you can no longer use your team and need to re-load. It's very rare though. I've noticed a few other small bugs as well; none even close to game-breaking
(2) Occasional un-finished scripting (e.g., if in a Cali town you act like the usual good guy and kill the "Leather Jerks" (Tom of Finland type men all wearing fashionable chastity belts), a lot of the dialogue and such that follows doesn't quite fit what really happened
(3) Weapons are very unbalanced. That is NO negative for me (it's single-player, so who cares?), but might be for some
(4) Attribute 'intelligence' is WAY too important. You'll be a fool to not have an entire team of brainiacs, all with maximum intelligence of 10
(5) The team doesn't grow too much on you, as you have no inter-character dialogue
But this is really a game that I expect anyone who likes classic RPGs will not like, but adore (if you're a WoW PvPer, sorry, you're not an RPG fan. I'm talking about those being in it more than anything for story, setting, and atmosphere).
Get it if you haven't yet!

What is Alan Wake? Summed up: Luigi's Mansion meets Twin Peaks meets Deadly Premonition and with a small serving of early '90s slasher/action flick on the side.
For some of the flaws and missteps it takes, Alan Wake is an enjoyable experience, especially for those with a penchant for creative writing. The titular character, Alan, acts as an avatar of sorts for writers and players and for those inclined, both. He takes a vacation in the sleepy town of Bright Falls, located somewhere in the state of Washington. It is here he finds out - rather harshly - that there are dark forces at work, and with it, unveiling a mystery that engulfs the town.
Don't be fooled, however; this is not a traditional horror game. It has more in common with action-adventure games such as Uncharted and Alone in the Dark 2 than it does with more cerebral games like Silent Hill and Sanitarium. The game plays with a behind the shoulder perspective and your crosshair, so to speak, is provided by a flashlight. Even so, the game controls rather well and Alan's movements and responsive and crisp. There are a few parts where the rather solid movement can make jumping from one platform to the next a little cumbersome, but those are a minor gripe. As for the graphics, they do the job. Often times, you can notice artifacts or little quirks, such as questionable facial animations, but if Fallout 4 can get a free pass for that, so can Alan Wake.
The game's biggest flaw (outside of icy driving controls) is the fact that you cannot explore the town of Bright Falls, as the game is incredibly linear in its direction. You cannot hang out at a local joint like you can in Deadly Premonition or talk to random strangers and get a feel for the town. The reason why I note this is that the characters and dialogue, and by extension writing, are all quite wonderful. All the characters are vibrants with their quirks and personalities. A no-nonsense sheriff, a trigger-happy agent, a disturbingly unfettered doctor, they all stand out vividly. The gameplay itself is nothing to write home about, but it keeps you on your toes and some might find it repetitive at times. But the scenery and massive levels are more than enough to keep you engaged.
[On that note, getting the game with the DLC is highly recommended. You get two full-length episodes (~2 hours of gameplay) that continue the story straight from the ending. They are quite fantastic and switch up the formula nicely.]
Oh, and the soundtrack? ♥♥♥♥ing incredible.
Conclusion: Get the game when it's on sale, you won't regret it.
8/10.

Hard West is an interesting game, in that it's basically Wild West X-COM with some supernatural drop-ins like demons, a bit of magic and curses, etc. It fundamentally works very well, and has great music, but it suffers from a few flaws.
Firstly, the difficulty is very much down to you, the player, because of how customizable it is. You can make it grindingly painful, or you can make it a simple breeze.
Secondly, every single scenario has its own little sub-mechanics(like managing decay for a group of frankensteins in Scars of Freedom, managing food and people in a scenario about an archeological dig, etc.), and none of these sub-mechanics are painful... but they never re-occur. So it keeps feeling like you're being given a tutorial for each mechanic before they're about to launch you into the real game...
But then said scenario ends after ~5 tactical missions and said mechanics are never re-visited. The game really would've benefited from longer individual scenarios, so your resource managing in that scenario, and the scars accrued, the damage taken, given, the choices made, etc. would have had longer to matter.
Ultimately it comes off feeling a bit like a tech demo for modders to grab and run with. And I'd say said modders would have a LOT of fun stuff to play with, don't mistake me there, but it feels a bit rough around the edges.
Either way, I had fun playing it and don't regret Kickstarting it. If you're jonesing for some X-COM-esque gameplay, give it a shot.

I might be in the minority when I say this but I really didn't like this game. First off I didn't really know what to expect when I purchased this title on sale only that it had nice atmospheric graphics and good reviews. I thought it was going to be a survival horror type game but I was sadly dissapointed. What kind of game is it? I have no clue. I think what the developers were trying to aim for was a "Indigo Prophecy"/"Heavy Rain" experience but falls short in terms of story and character development. You play as Alan Wake who's a reporter on vacation with his wife and she goes missing. He tries to hunt down her kidnapper while strange things occur in the small town.
Sounds like a promising start but there are a few problems. The main character narrates the events happening around him and how he feels as if he was reading from one of his novels. The way the story is told feels artificial and poorly written as if you were reading a short story from a kid in high school. Constantly having to hear what he's thinking plus reading the "manuscript" pages he finds which explains things we've already seen gets really annoying. It also sounds like a cliche plot which ends up having you think the whole thing he's going through is fabricated in his crazy mind.
The characters don't have well...any character. They're so hollow. Your wife goes missing, so what? I only knew her in the game for like 10 mins. The main guy Alan Wake has the dumbest robotic look on his face and his voice sounds whiny. The other NPCs have about 2 or 3 lines and when the town goes crazy with paranormal events you don't really care about what happens to them.
Gameplay is just as bad. You walk around, talk to people then nightmare world. In nightmare world shadow figures chase you. You shine a flashlight in their face then shoot them when their defenses are down. Rinse and repeat. The combat (if you can call it that) is robotic as Alan Wake's face and not very exciting after the second encounter. Don't get me started on Alan Wake's cardio. I think the writers forgot to explain in the game how he smokes 10 packs a day as he can't run for more then 3 seconds before getting gassed.

The positives: I like the aesthetic, the soundtrack was great, it was very short, I was okay with the lack of any words.
Everything else though, ehh. I didn't connect with the story, so I had no emotional involvement. I'm a simple man and often I don't pick up on symbolism, which didn't help me, but even so there seemed to be barely a story to tell, it felt at times more like a case of the developers patting themselves on the back for how clever they were. It also felt very much like staring at an unassuming piece of modern art and seeing whatever you wanted to see - and that's backed-up by the lead dev saying (in an article I just read) that it was very much open to interpretation. Indeed, he said the actual interpretation of the ending (in his mind) was very melancholic and he was surprised to see how many theories had an optimistic end.
It makes me think of the end of Inception and Nolan's refusal to say whether the top was going to fall or not. In that example I was happy to have the ending I wanted to believe (rather than the one the director told me was true) because the film had earned it through my bonding with the characters; here, the frequent jump cuts, changes of perspective, dream states etc just meant I didn't feel I was following an underlying narrative. Is it about Lucas? Halerpin? The FBI? It's all of them and none of them really and, in such a short space of time, none of those things have much meat on the bones and I felt I needed to know more.
I don't really know why it was a game, rather than an animated short. The interactivity feels largely like an effort to pad things out, because unless you are going for the pointless achievements there's no exploration to be rewarded, it really is a case of doing a quick scan around whatever environment you are in to find the bit to press A on and then going there.
Ultimately it won't put me off trying these things in future, but this was disappointing after the critical acclaim it got.

Virginia is a first person walk 'em up narrative. It does not entail tedious rummaging like Gone Home, elaborate puzzles like The Witness, or patronising quick time events like The Walking Dead.
I find nothing wrong with the formula per se, but when it comes to recommending this game to friends, I just didn't enjoy the story enough. I played it with a friend and I'm not joking, we both literally went for a nap half way through.
The designers made the decision to have no dialogue at all, and to rely on character emotes to fill the void. This may have negatively impacted my engagement. It may have also negatively impacted the pace.
When it comes to pace, there's no particularly slow scenes, which is at certain times a positive or a negative. The game is always time-lapsing in order to hold your attention. I would rather if they made the story more engaging to hold my attention.
There's some moments of surrealism and atmospheric tension which I enjoyed. What I liked most are some hints of chemistry between the main characters. There's  also some emotional hardship which pulled at my heartstrings. But most of these were only vague feelings which failed to fully grasp me.
Also, I didn't really understand what happened towards the end. I'm sure I could go read the forums to find out, like I did in for Twin Peaks, but unlike Twin Peaks, I just don't care.
I commend the team for trying something arty and new. I hope it influences future works.

Plenty of games get qualified as "cinematic," but I've yet to see a game that manages to be such without following a summer blockbuster formula--Battlefield and Call of Duty could easily have been written by Michael Bay or John Woo. That changed when I played Virginia. This game feels more like an Oscar bait type, and seems especially reminiscent of Silence of the Lambs, with its premise, main character, at once soaring and somber score, and meticulous environments as reminiscent as one can be of the cinematography Demme's Magnum Opus without taking the camera out of the player's hands entirely. I also see this game compared to Lynch's work, possibly because of some of the surreal imagery in the dream sequences and the game's conclusion.
This is a "walking sim," and a strictly linear one, and plays out much more like a movie than a game. If that's a no-go for you, fair enough--but I don't mind movies, or games, or intersections on the spectrum thereof. The runtime is about the length of a movie as well, so you won't be stuck to your seat for too long.

I've noticed that the overall reviews for this game put it under a mixed evaluation which I find honestly unfair. Virginia is honesly unlike most games out there in that the story is told predominantly through animations and text, without the characters uttering a single word and with a heavy Twin Peaks inspiration.
My main gripe with the game is that it tends to lead you by the nose. I loathe the negative connotation that "walking simulators" have and you are required some input along your journey, though it's usually restricted to actions you're locked into in order to progress. Which is certainly a curious decision, since the story doesn't hold your hand, only the gameplay does that.
Aside from that, Virginia has a striking art style that is often gorgeous, animations that succeed in conveyed the personality of the characters and an absolutely phenomenal soundtrack that is worth the price of admission alone.
All in all, if you enjoyed watching Twin Peaks, if you enjoyed games such as Edith Finch and Gone Home and you don't mind the extremely linear nature of the game (with some infuriating achievements, though the game itself shouldn't be faulted for them), then I absolutely recommend Virginia. You're in for a wild ride.

I wanted this game to be good.  I really did!  It's inspiring to see new games, in a overly saturated genre, by an indie developer.  There's so much potential for a dev to bring new ideas to the table that can reignite the joy of playing a first-person shooter.  If there's anything this genre needs it's a new game that pulls away from the Call of Duty, Battlefield, and Counter-Strike mentality.  The problem is; Warmode doesn't do any of that.
Before I begin to complain, hats off to the devs for making their game a free-to-play.  It's very easy to lose money rather than make it when your game is free.  But, so far, that is the only good thing about the game.  It just isn't fun, new, or even exciting.  I'm sorry, but why should I play your overly generic game when there are so many others too choose from?  I understand that your game is in early-access and that you plan so much more content, but will it be enough?  You need to ask yourself "Why would someone play my FPS game rather than Counter-Strike?  Or even other free-to-plays like Team Fortress, Dirty Bomb, or Warframe?"
Frankly there's nothing special about Warmode.  It's not bad, it's just not good either.  The game is pretty solid, it's just not fun to play.  There's nothing here for me to harp on or compliment.  Unless the devs focus on making their new title stand out from other games, it will die and join all the other generic fps, that attempted to make a life on Steam, in the depths of Steams free-to-play section.
Devs, I wish you the best of luck.  I hope that one day I will return to this game and be able to recommend it.

FSX has a huge reputation in the civillian flight sim community and has been very well regarded for a few years now and this is the point at which I'll probably receive the wrath of the dedicated fans: If you're new to FSX, don't be suckered in by the pretty screenshots on the steam store. This is ultimately an old game and these images are only representative of the visual fidelity in a few cherry-picked areas. Outside of these areas (about 99% of the rest of the world), your scenery will be generic, flat, empty and barely recognisable as anything that you might know.
If you want visuals that won't make your eyes bleed and might actually represent places with which you're familiar,  be prepared to spend a lot of money on terrain files and imagery to bring things up to anything approaching an acceptable level. In fact, in FSX generally, expect to spend a lot of money on third-party addons if you want to flesh things out. I can't give a personal opinion, but if you're in the market for a new flight simulator I have seen a lot of people enthusing about X-Plane 11.
Don't get me wrong, I don't have a massive downer on FSX and I'm not saying there is inherently bad about it.... I just don't believe that this game/simulator is the product that it appears to be on the steam store page. FSX had its day a few years ago now. Shinier, more modern alternatives are definitely available
tl;dr If you're new to flight sims and don't already have FSX, don't bother.

Wasteland 2 is an isometric party-based role-playing game set in a post-apocalyptic southeastern United States.
The Great:
- Deep and expansive story that starts quickly and expands out in numerous branching paths
- Real player choices that change both the progression of the story and how gameplay mechanics play out (can avoid combat using conversation)
- Incredible amount of quality content as the story expands to tremendous length and allows for deep exploration
The Good:
- The combat system is of good quality and gives much variety and satisfactory tactical options
The Bad:
- RPG progression skills and traits are locked once selected which can cause significant potential problems for new/inexperienced players
- Some of the areas are notably barren or seemingly unfinished (e.g. all the random encounters that are nearly exact repeats of each other)
Conclusion:
Wasteland 2 should be on everyone's short list for engrossing stories in RPGs.

I personally tried very hard to like Hard West (pun not intended), but the major turn off is the overhead map. 90% of the time you're there, running around doing uninteresting things with uninteresting characters, while 10% of the time you're in actual turn based combat. It's really a chore.
They also keep switching up the mechanics from one scenario to another. In one, you're recruiting tens of peons which you put to work at points of interest around the map. These are actions which consume rations and leave the peons prone to injury or death (watch out for the jaguars when hunting for food). In another, it's just your posse which you have to keep fed after every day (morning, noon, evening, night) and perform fetch quests.
It's also annoying when posse members decide to leave randomly, usually right after I set up their gear.
The combat I mostly like, but that's because it's borrowed heavily from XCOM. Exceptions are the nonsensical luck system and the fact that there isn't much differentiation between weapons. Stealth sections are also pretty silly because it looks you're running around in plain sight, when in fact enemies are very near-sighted. This is normal difficulty.
I've seen other people complain about the save system - there are no in-mission checkpoints, you have to restart from scratch if you fail - but most of the time the combat is too easy.
So yeah, I can't really recommend the game at this point, but I'd still be excited for a sequel if it manages to address most of my complaints.

XCOM was a big favourite for me, so I was looking for similar turn-based tactical games. Wasteland 2 was a disappointment for me, mainly because the combat is very boring to several reasons:
- map is not properly designed for the combat, not enough cover (or something which looks like a cover turns out not to be a cover once the game turns into turn-based) in many cases simple open area
- enemies have terrible AI, they just keep running towards you, until they are in firing range, then they start shooting someone randomly
- melee is useless, most efficient is assault/sniper
- no way to properly prepare for a battle, you cannot position your soldiers, because you don't know what is cover, and how the grid layout looks like (that only becomes visible when the game switches to turn-based)
So after a while I realized that the most efficient is to use only weapons with long range (sniper/assault/heavy), and being defensive, just wait until they come close enough, and shoot them. Many of the combats was just going into position with the group, crouch everyone, shoot something with the sniper to initiate the battle, then keep shooting the closest enemy with everyone, without moving at all. No tactics, boring like hell. I was really trying to be more offensive, but it doesn't work.
Story is OK, but the character progress is boring, you pick a few skills for each character at the beginning, and then just put skill points on those as the character levels up. Lots of the skills are just to open boxes for loot. Graphic could also be better.
I played most of the time in offline more, so I played way more than just 0.3 hours.

This was my first point and click adventure game so this review is coming from fresh eyes for these things.
I very much enjoyed the game. So much so I binged it in 11 hours because I wanted to know more about the story, world, characters and the puzzles. I particularly wanted to play this game due to the Double Fine Adventure documentary posted on Youtube. Watching parts of that and then getting to play the game really made me feel more connected with the people who made this game and all the work they put into it.
The Story and Dialogue is what sets this game apart. It's infinitely witty, humourous and charming. I found myself smiling, lauging and gasping at surprising moments. The creativity in this game oozes out of your screen and makes you want to keep going just a little bit longer. I have not played a game in a while that got me so invested in the story and characters that I couldn't sleep.
The two 'acts' show a definite shift in difficulty in terms of puzzles and I found mself having to consult a walkthrough on the second act. However difficult it was to me, that did not ditract from me enjoying the game as I was more invested with the story than the puzzles and gameplay.
I have only two criticisms. Often times the art style made it difficult to tell what was a clickable object and what was part of the scenery. I guess it's an adventure trope to have to go clicking around the screen but to me that's not enjoyable. The art is gorgeous and I wouldn't want it to be done in any other way, it just overall made it harder to tell what I should be doing in a certain area.
The second criticism was in the second act you have to switch back and forth between the two characters not having done this at all in the earlier part of the game. One of the characters hints in a dialouge that you should do that, but the other did not when I needed it because I didn't expect that to happen as it hadn't happened at all in the earlier part of the game. Gameplay wise I really like the idea, story wise it doesn't make any sense and I would have preffered a more clear connection to when characters should and should not know something the other knows.
Other than these very minor issues I really enjoyed this game and highly recommend it for anyone interested in getting into the adventure game genre. I really wanted to support Double Fine in this (even though it's been a while since release) because as a game company they put their heart and soul into every game they make and I want to see them make more. I'm definitely going to play Grim Fandago remastered because of this game and I think you should all check it out! (Broken Age that is)

A very well put together RTS/FPS Hybrid in a sci-fi setting with 3D-printed people, railguns and one hell of a bacterial infection.
The game features asymmetrical combat between the more traditional marines who play as you would expect with typical shooter fare such as LMGs (the defauilt gun), shotguns and grenades. Reliant upon squad tactics and logistical support the marines may be more familiar, but require solid aim and awareness.
The alien infestation are worlds apart, with a mix of disposable skulks, dog like aliens very similar in play to runner aliens from the early AvP games; through to Fades and Onoses, much more specialised lifeforms that are important to keep alive. The aliens are build around hit an run tactics and guerilla warfare; breaking supply and picking off isolated pockets to keep the marines on the defensive.
The RTS aspect is really what makes the game special, there is macro and micro required. Commanders (limited to one lucky person per side) placing Resource Towers to allow marines to get new weapons and upgrades and aliens to evolve, and also being able to provide more direct help to his footsoldiers by dropping medpacks, ammo and scans.
The game is very slick without being dumbed down, and is based on team work and strong tactics without being clunky. The game looks beautiful, but that has not been at the expense of gameplay.
The one thing I cannot account for is the community, whilst I have had mostly positive experiences the game relies upon teamwork; thus, people not working as part of the team or following the commander's suggestions will be dead weight, something that will get on everybody's nerves. Rokkies are flagged up, and the developers have tried to encourage a forgiving environment, but trust me when I say there is one golden rule...
Do as you are asked: you will have a lot more fun that way.

This game is a stripped down version of the modern Fallout games.  I've played for a few weeks on ther version from the Windows store, and the Steam version has just a bit more menu options compared to that (stress on "a bit").
What I like about it:
1.  Fallout vintage vibe to look and sounds
2.  Levelling up of dwellers
3.  Earning caps, crafting, and exploring like the other fallout games
4.  Sending Dwellers on missions, etc.
And now for what sucks....
1.  You are limited to one vault with a maximum of 200 dwellers
2.  it takes Dwellers ages to return back to the vault...unless you want to use up (or pay for) Nuka Colas to speed that along.
2.  You have to click on each dweller when they are ready to be leveled up - no "master button" for doing all at once.
3.  You have to click on each room when it finished collecting it's given resource (water, food, whatever) - no master button for that either.  Adding a Mr Handy can help there, but you pretty much have to buy those with real money
4.  It's too easy to accidentally drag dwellers to the wrong place when scanning around the vault.
3.  Children are completely usesless until they grow up.  Why not be able to assign them to the classroom and have a random SPECIAL attribute be higher than the rest?
4.  Microtransactions - get rid of them and just allow a one time payment for the game
5.  Allow for turrets to be posted by the vault door to help fight off attackers, and allow them to be upgradable.  The Vault door can be breached even after 3 upgrades and you can only post 2 dwellers there which is pretty useless when the Deathclaws start attacking.
6.  Need to be able to better swap weapons between dwellers or at least be able to better find the ones with key equipment so you can send them on missions
7.  The rushes on rooms gets tedious, and there should be more variations as to what happens when they fail - fires and critter infestations get boring quickly
8.  There should be more things for the dwellers to do besides work, train, fight, or f*ck.  No resting or sleeping?
9.  Add more variety to the Mysterious Stranger character.  Right now, he is the "Where's Waldo"of the game and gets nearly impossible to find later on.
10.  Dwellers should be able to either auto heal/remove rads or allow for a one click button to do it to all of them (do you see a theme here?)
11.  The game really has no end - after you reach 200 dwellers and do the missions....ehh, then what?
I'll recommend it because it's in the Fallout world, but it needs some tweaking to make it very good.

A visceral and fast paced multiplayer shooter combined with real time strategy make for Natural Selection's strengths. Gameplay involves either being on the ground or in the commander's seat, fusing beautifully the first person shooter and the real time strategy genres.
Numerous weapons and classes are available for both the Marines and the Kharaa, this allows for diverse play and keeps the game interesting. From the humble skulk, running on the ceilings and dropping in on unsuspecting victims. To the gargantuan and brutish Onos, smashing everything in it's path and reducing Marine machines to their component parts in seconds. There's a class for all kinds of players on both sides. Want to run around fearing for your life? Stick with your bog-standard infantryman. Want to go crazy and toe-to-toe with an Onos? Get yourself a mech and be feared by the Kharaa.
WIth hours of replayability, servers up 24/7, and a well balanced system of play. Natural Selection 2 is by far one of my favourite games of all time. Go ahead, buy it. I'll be waiting on the ceiling round the corner.

While I really enjoyed this game and recommend it, this is one of those games were you should make sure it's the right game for you before spending money on it as it's definitely not for everyone. Despite the massive critical acclaim this game has recieved I never really knew how difficult it was before diving into it. I knew it would be hard, but I wasn't expecting this.
This is one of the most unforgiving shooters I've ever played. One false step can mean death in an instant and the game doesn't wait too long to throw you into this punishing difficulty. That though is where the game really shines for me. It's hard but that makes the game super satisfying to progress through. If you enjoy the adrenaline of playing a fast and brutal game, the satisfaction of killing an annoying enemy, or the high of finally completing a level then you will love this game.
You could look at it like the Super Meat Boy equivalent to the top down shooter genre; really difficult yet short levels meaning that every time you die you think to yourself "this time I think I can make it" and that drives you right through the whole game, despite how many times the game likes to tell you "You are Dead". I think with enough persistance you would eventually beat it but how good you are might make you rage quit and never touch the game again. I personally kept going until I beat the story which took me about 4 hours, that's probably terrible compared to a lot of players, but the game kept me hooked brilliantly.
If however your idea of a good payoff for a difficult game is a satisfying story conclusion then I think you should look somewhere else. I've seen some people praise the story but I find it became such an incomprehensible mess by the end of the game that I started to ignore the story, and the "explanation" at the end for all the events of the game is pathetic. Perhaps that was the point? but that's still a negative in my eyes. Some people seem to be enjoying it though so perhaps you'll see something I don't.
The only other problem I have with the game is that it didn't seem very stable. In the 4 hours it took me to complete the story it crashed on 3 seperate occasions. I checked around and apparently it was due to a recent update shortly before I bought the game that hasn't yet been fixed. There are various work arounds supposedly so you might be ok.
I had a lot of fun with this game and I'll absoultley try the second game, which I also bought along with this one. Do I recommend it at full price though? I bought both games on sale for 3 pounds so I clearly got my moneys worth, but is this game alone worth the full price of 7 pounds? This again I think comes down to personal preference. If this is the kind of game you enjoy, brutal yet satisfying shooters, then I do think it's worth that price, just. If you are a very casual gamer who doesn't like gameplay that'll make you want to pull your hair out then I would try it at sale price, or pass on it.
Overall though a very well designed and original Indie game that I'm glad to have in my library.

Hard West. Turn based, squad sized tactical fights mixed with some elements of the text games, some, even if a bit rigid, RPG fragments, and many, many parts of grim and horror. Lovecraftian way.
It all together tastes just like multicomponent special cocktail, with multiple layers of taste and rather ambiguous aftertaste. This comparison is kind of warning - most probably, you will not like it, if you don't ready to take shots, not only making them. Taste of bitterness will be the most persistent in the gameplay. It is even stronger there than in the recent Mad Max game, without gasoline, adrenaline and other distractions. Bitter and sorrow, the story of the man in so dire straits, that even Mephisto himself feels lesser evil.
What's it looks like? Well, right from the beggining, you'll see fighting mechanic, almost similar to one in the Firaxis XCom titles. You're either move two times, or move and shoot, or just shoot, and also there are some items to use and some special skills to perform during the combat. But I said - almost similar. That distinction is about Luck system. Every man usually starts the fight with the full health and luck bars. The health is usually between 4-8 points, that means 1-2 direct shots to death. System of covers is the same as in the XCom game - only take a note that almost all covers are wooden. Which means they're not that safe, as one may hope. Luck is another bar, with usual digits somewhere between 70-150. It is both your mana points to perform some special actions - and your shield. If you stand in the plain site, with 100 points of luck, and someone shoots at you - there are good chances that you'll survive the first shot, for the price of huge luck depletion. If you're hiding behind something, and take shots - again, you'll be losing some luck points until some bullet finally will find you, and do some (reduced) damage. Enemies also have luck levels, so everything said applies to them as well.
Okay, I know, it sounds a bit complex, and not fair, maybe. Everyone hates missing with 70-95 hit percentage. It happens - even in the real world - but it is always sucks to miss an enemy standing right next to you, 'cause that means he will likely shoot you now... But in the end, luck system works, and works good in given setting. Once you'll learn the pattern, that will be your equalizer, as you're always outnumbered and outgunned in games like this.
Apart from battle system, by other components Hard West is closer to bizarre projects like Space Rangers, using all those texts just like in the ancient by now Interactive fiction stories.
One of the most questionable game features is that every scenario works separately from others. Yes, they are lined by the story events, but every new scenario, basically, every new chapter, you're bound to start with the very beginning, without money, collected inventory pieces and so on. That approach has some pro points by the way the story goes (you know, pause in narrative like "x years passed"), and some of the previously collected rare items can be recollected during the next scenario... But as of the pace of the game, that approach is decreasing interest to the game sometimes below the level of acceptance. Especially if you're trying to play it "ironman" style, where every random death of the main character in the scenario means you have to start it all over again.
Also, one of the noted downsides of this game is enemies AI behavior, most precisely, group movements. Most of the enemies are using quite the same algorithm in battle, which means they tend to use same routes, same covers... So if you're having the shotgun and/or bombs, you can make quite big killstreak, with just one-two moves. Now, I know the cowboys are not basically trained soldiers, and there are, in fact, some different algorithms to randomize enemies behavior. Yet, the challenge is mostly fixed to the "ironman" condition, and not for really-tough-to-beat combat collisions.
So, do I recommend the game? Yes. But I know for sure that it is not for the wide audience. Too bitter, too fixed in RPG elements for real empathy to game's characters. And even combat, while quite good in depicting the end of the 19th century western topic, is not absolutely brilliant, to vouch for the game carelessly, like I did in cases of "7.62" or some other facinating TurnBased Squad Tactical type of games. Still, it's solid 7.5/10 in my book. Interesting elements of game mechanic, heartfelt scent of western, well-styled horror "Lovecraft style". And even decent visuals, for an indie project.

Do you enjoy Tactical Turn Based Strategy games?
Do you enjoy a Supernatural Wild West setting similar to that of the table top cult-hit Deadlands?
If so then this is the game for you. Gameplay is similar to XCom, thus making Hard West an enjoyable game. Tactics and strategy win out over brute force in this title.
The setting is perhaps the game's best selling point. It has notions of supernatural horror within a Wild West setting complete with some of the conventions of both genres. The setting helps to hold the game together where it's story may feel like it is lacking.
Graphics-wise, Hard West is a decent looking game. It won't make you say 'wow,' but the presentation is good enough. Also, I enjoyed the soundtrack a lot. The mechanics are interesting. The luck mecahnic is perhaps the most novel in that luck is a qunatifiable source much like stamina or mana are in other games. It depleats for each shot that whizzes by your characters, or if you use a special ability granted by poker cards you collect in a scenario and equip to your characters. It is replenished through usable items or from taking damage. Another interesting mechanic is that by using the poker cards obtained as you play, you can create different hands for your characters, granting them different bonuses.
Hard West is by no means perfect. It appears to be short, as I am 14 hours in and have only 2 'scenarios' left. Some menu screens can be laggy, and what personally bothered me was that enemies had an overwatch feature that prevented characters from walking straight up by them, but my characters lack such a feature. Gameplay also proves to be repetative at some points: Play around in the over-map making various decisions, encounter, kill badguys/whatever other objectives, repeat.
The game is very well made especially for being made by a small dev. It is a nice addition into the turn-based tactical strategy genre, which I feel doesn't get enough love. If you can find it on sale, it's a great purchase. Hard West has a lot of potential if the devs want to do more with it, and I think it would make for a pretty cool table-top game system itself.

I'm going to split my review up into segments for order purposes
Story: 9/10
Art (Including environment, sound, music, etc.) 10/10
Gameplay: 4/10
Story: The Story of Alan Wake is highly enjoyable. It is well thought out, and developed fairly well both through the main story elements, as well as the hidden story elements (manuscripts, radio, etc.). I found myself enthralled by the story, especially when it picks up in the last couple episodes. A bit slow at times, and a bit slow to start is the only reason it isn't 10/10. Stick with it and you'll be rewarded
Art: This game is gorgeous for it's release date. The environment is beautiful, the sounds are clear and pleasing (or terrifying, depending) and the soundtrack is second to none. (The Poet and the Muse is amazing). Visually, a very appealing game, one of it's strong points.
Gameplay: The gameplay at the start is fresh and exciting. The combat is innovative, and challenging. Then it stays effectivley the same for 6 Episodes. The combat is spruced up here and there but by and large remains static. At times the game employs some "false difficulty", rather than making the combat different or actually any harder, it just throws hordes of enemies at you to give the illusion of difficulty. That was perhaps the most frustrating part. Towards the end, when it really started getting old I had to take pauses and walk away to avoid breaking a controller.
Verdict: The gameplay gets old, and it can be hard at the end to want to push yourself through, but do so. The story is well worth seeing through to the end. If you're thinking about getting this game: consider the other games you play. If slow developing story and repititive combat aren't outdone by your love of story, maybe avoid this game. But just know, you'll be missing out on an artistic gold mine, and a masterful story.

Alan Wake. What a helluva game. I remember back in 2010 when I was 12, and played it for the first time in my best friend's Xbox 360. I was truly scared-yet amazed at the scope and story of the game.
I've always been a sucker for thrillers, and noires and such. In fact, it is one of the things that shine the most in this game. I love how the levels are presented in a T.V. detective show kind of format, like "In the last episode", or "On the next episode".
I am not going to get into major spoilers, but I am going to give you a little bit of context on the story.
You are Alan Wake, the titular hero of the story. Alan was once a successful and respected writer. However, he was not able to write a single page in 2 years. It's pretty obvious he has writer's bloc. Happens to the best.
Anyways, Alan's wife, Alice, decides to go with his husband to a little town in the middle of nowhere with the intention of reigniting Alan's imagination, and help him deal through his creative crisis. Shortly after arriving, Alan notices things are not how they seem. I fact, Alice disappears, and it's up to you, to figure out what the heck is going on in this town, and where Alice is.
Now that we got that out of the way, let's talk about gameplay. It is truly fun to battle the forces of darkness with a flashlight, a gun, a shotgun, or whatever gun is at your disposal. You can also use flares, flashbangs, anything that can dispose of shadows is good actually. Heck, if you turn the lights on, they'll be gone!
Now, about visuals, I personally enjoy the horror movie feel of it. All dark, moody, without any signs of positive emotions. It really accompanies the mood of the whole story and narrative, but hey, what can you expect from Remedy, the guys that made Max Payne?
About the music, nothing particuarly interesting about it, besides the fact that it's quite good.
Overall, I think Alan Wake is both a great game, and great story on it's own. It's lengthy, it's great, and the story is just awesome.
