Okay, so this game isn't awful, but Virginia has it's problems and you should definitly know what you are buying before you get in to it.
Firstly, it's not a game but more of a movie that you have to click sometimes. There is almost nothing you can do that will influence the game in any way. You are supposed to click on things, but the interaction serves no purpose.
This in and of itself isn't a deal breaker. The story is interesting, or at least has the potential to be so, and it's labled as a walking simulator so I wasn't expecting the most interactive game. All that can be forgiven. I can even forgive the unatural character movement and the fact that most of the people in the game look like Wii avatars. Where this game lost me was it's lack of dialouge.
The creators obviously cared a great deal about the soundtrack and the sound design. The music is amazing, it's true, but there is no speech in the game at all. No voice actors, No dialogue in the whole thing.
That was what made me stop playing this game after about a half an hour. The lack of dialogue was at times just annoying, and at other times frustrating, but mostly it was distracting. There are a lot of tools a storyteller can use to tell a story. Music is important, sure, but words are pretty important, too.

Man, I would never thought this kind of game would appeal to me, but it does.
First the gameplay. It is quite a challenge. You will get killed unless you have the aim of a marine sharpshooter and the reflexes of a cheetah.  It reminds me of a top down version  of Not.A.Hero, even though that game came later. Same premise, you go to different floors of a building and cause a bloodbath in every house. Various masks give you various abilities and unlocks as you progress.
Second: the graphics. Beautiful 1980's style setting with trippy drug-like visions. This is what Vice City would be like if it was on the Game Boy, except it looks a lot better, and probably would play a lot better as well.
Third: the music. I usually don't like 80's music, but the various styles of music on this game is fantastic. Chillwave is one of my favorite genres and some of the songs on this game features some of that.
Overall, I recommend this game if you are looking for a decent challenge. It is not difficult on the degree of Dark Souls but it can be hard if you have a difficult time with reacting in a fast way. As I said before, you will get killed numerous times, especially if you do not incorporate some stealth.

Summary – 7/10 Good game for those who like post apocalypse setting, top down 3rd person point of view, large variety of weapons.  Buy when on sale for under $20.
Pro:
+ Post Apocalypse setting
+ Lots of decision trees, dialog options
+ Multiple ways to complete an objective
+ Interesting story (bringing law and order to a place of total anarchy)
+ Decent number of quests (about 60-70)
+ Nice unique maps
+ Dismemberment, melting on some kill shots
+ Easy to use UI
+ Humor and funny references especially of the 80’s throughout.
Con:
- Lacks the immersiveness of 1st person viewpoint games  (Fallout: New Vegas, Fallout 3)
- Can’t interact with most of the environment.  Almost all building entrances are blocked and using explosives won’t change that.
- Poor AI – just set up an ambush point on a map send out a meat shield to draw the enemies and kill them as they approach.  Works almost every time.
- Explosives so overpowered in combat.  They never miss even if your character doesn’t have a single point in explosives. Give meatshield a ton of STR (which equals HP).  Have enemy mob him.  He runs out then toss grenades.  Battle won. Rinse. Repeat.
- Game maps are fairly linear (except for Titan Canyon)
- Dull weapon/shooting animations (just one animation for all weapons)
- Non realistic skill (Toaster Repair (really!!))
- Poor stat optimization.  Intelligence > all.  Many stats just not important.
- Too many skills focused on just opening containers (open lock, tumbler, alarm, trap, perception) since you have to divide up skills amongst players to max them all quickly it means switching through multiple players just to open a container.  Pretty poor design.
- Every container is either trapped or has an alarm attached to it (or both).
- Few locations (Less than a two dozen maps in the AZ and CA zones)

Step into the shoes of Alan Wake, a best-selling novelist who is going on vacation in hopes to relieve his writer's block. However, Alan has much more to think about other than his novel when his wife mysteriously vanishes, and pages of a manuscript that he doesn't remember writing suddenly begin to appear; ominously outlining events that are about to occur. Alan Wake is brought to us by the developer of Max Payne 1 and 2, Remedy Entertainment, and was initially released in 2010 for the Xbox 360 before finally making its way to PC in 2012.
Things start off normal enough, you're on a ferry with your wife Alice, headed to a remote destination in the forest for your vacation. Your writer's block has been killing your career, you need the escape. You're met by friendly locals who are excited that a big-shot such as yourself will be vacationing near their little town. You stop by a gas station on your way to the cabin that you and Alice have rented, but once you come out of the bathroom things begin to go haywire. However, it's when Alice goes missing at the cabin that things really heat up. She's scared of the dark, so badly that she becomes paralyzed with fear, and now everything is dark; save for what becomes illuminated by your flashlight, and your wife is nowhere to be found.
The storytelling in the game is absolutely fantastic, as Alan's inner monologue is spoken as though it is in book format. The game itself is set-up in a TV show format, where once you reach the next chapter you'll be greeted with a "Last Time on Alan Wake" sequence. The entire experience is like playing through a deranged horror show while listening to a coupling audio book. These unique factors only adds to the eeriness of the game, and they also add a different spin on the horror genre as a whole. For the time of release, the environments are lavishly detailed and come with a thick amount of ambiance such as fog, rain, and lightning. Most of your time will be spent in the dark, with only a flashlight to help guide you from one creepy destination to the next. While most of the baddies look the same, their potential of showing up always keeps you looking over your shoulder to make sure that you're not being chased by their near silent presence.
Equipped initially with only a flashlight and a pistol, you will later find yourself with more diverse guns to battle the onslaught of evil that awaits. Even though Alan Wake is fast-paced, the fact that you never know from which direction, and when, the devious shadow-people will make an appearance keeps tight tension in the air. Combat is simple, you must shine a concentrated flashlight beam on the shadow-people to dissolve their darkness barrier, and then fill them full of bullets. Paranormal entities are abound, and even inanimate objects become possessed and deadly. When you get overwhelmed, flares and flashbangs are your best friend when it comes to keeping these monstrosities at bay. Whatever you do, your ultimate goal is to stay in the light; that's the only place that you're safe in, but well-lit areas are few and far between.
To say that Alan Wake was, and still is, one of the best horror games of the last generation is an understatement. The game was initially a diamond in the rough when it was released on the Xbox 360, though it appears to have garnered the attention it deserves after being released on PC. Graphically, it doesn't even look that dated, it was very far advanced for its time when looking at other games of the same genre and time period, such as F.E.A.R. and Condemned: Criminal Origins. Alan Wake has a flair to it that no other horror title has yet to emulate, duplicate, or even attempt to replicate, it's one of the few games that have been left alone to be uniquely itself. Even six years later, this game stands as one of the horror games that must be played, but not for the price of $32.99 CAD; wait for a summer or holiday sale first.

This turn-based tactical combat game is a unique combination of wild west and demonic themes. There are two phases to gameplay - the overworld phase and the combat phases, and both deliver varying degrees of choice, fun, and satisfaction. Scenarios are comprised of several (around 5) cycles of overworld - combat phases.
The overworld phase requires players to move from location to location in a text based "choose your own adventure" type format that initially feels high-stakes and open ended. While there is a bit of exploring and choice here, and the outcomes can have some interesting impacts on gameplay (and combat phases), players will quickly discover that this phase isn't quite as deep as it at first seemed. Nevertheless, I found it to be fun/engaging and did feel like replaying scenarios to explore a bit more or (ocassionaly) to make different choices.
The combat phase has a few unique aspects (choosing buffs via cards/poker hands; injuries turning into strengths, etc), much of the mechanics are simplified versions of other approaches/systems. Nevertheless, the wild west shoot-out feel kept things fun enough for me to enjoy. I would have greatly appreciated more time developing characters within each scenario.
Overall, this isn't going to blow people away, but it is a satisfying, enjoyable wild west combat affair. Be warned, it has a strong demonic theme (which will probably matter to some people) and is not particularly challenging (which will likely matter to many people).

As a veteran turn-based strategy gamer, I cannot recommend this game.  It does have a number of positives, which I will enumerate at the end.
CRITICAL FLAWS
-- Poor enemy AI --
The enemies seem to lack the ability to use any items other than their primary weapon.  Your characters, in contrast, have two weapons a piece, and up to two usable items.  This makes you a powerhouse compared to EVERYONE else.  More troublesome is the terrible enemy AI.  Turn-Based Strategy means that battles are meant to be tactical challenges.  This is essentially a squad-based, tactics game.  Enemies all act individually, but seem to lack the ability to work together.  I realize that AI programming is complicated, but it is essential for a squad-based tactics game to be challeging.  This game takes the cheap way out by simply increasing enemy firepower and decreasing your hp for higher difficulty settings.  So, if you think that making the enemies tougher by giving them the power to one shot kill your characters makes the game tougher, then you would be correct.  It doesn't make it more enjoyable.  It simply turns the game into a squad-based puzzle game (avoid all shots).  Not my cup of tea.
Big match up at the end of the main scenario line - over in just a couple rounds.  I don't even think any of my characters were hit once.
-- Main Character restarts at each new chapter, so all items, injuries, fate cards, etc. are lost  (this destroys the role playing element) --
I love rpg advancement because it allows attachment to the characters.  Ex.  My bounty hunter gets a mangled hand during a firefight.  Now, with a mangled hand, he can't aim worth anything, so give him a sawed-off shotgun, sneak him in close, and it won't matter.  This sort of thing makes characters develop and change over time - they gain character.  In this game all rpg-esque advancements are reset between scenarios (a couple hours a piece).  No character has any permanency.  Think of it more as Commandos instead of X-Com.
-- Poor proofing & crashes --
I only had a few actual crashes, though there were many lags & slow down.  For a while I had a game-breaking error that was caused by having a gamepad plugged in but not using it. (took a while to figure that one out)  Fate abilities that I had placed on a character would mysteriously not be present in some combats, and other character would be completely rekitted within the same scenario.  Just seemed to lack polish and playtesting.
-- Lack of explanation --
I still don't know what the defense statistic does, and there are less than 6 statistics per character.  Perhaps it reduces the enemy chance to hit me.  Perhaps it reduces my chance of receiving an injury when hit.  Perhaps it increases the effective of cover for that character.  Perhaps it provides a chance of decreasing incoming damage.  It likely does one of those things.  I shall never know which.
Making certain storyline advances in some scenarios prevent completion of side content (with no warning).  Combined with the  lack of ability to save and reload, it means that you make simply miss big chunks of content unless you want to restart the whole scenario from scratch.
Enemies have a radar-looking effect that appear near them if you walk too close.  It means that they get a free shot on you.  Given the "closeness," a hit is almost guaranteed.  This was never brought up during the tutorial.  I permanently lost one of my secondary characters in the first scenario when I "discovered" this mechanic, and was a bit salty about it.  Further it is a poor, jury-rigged mechanic to offset the lack of an overwatch mechanic.  The jury-rigged nature of the mechanic is clear because it only applies to enemy characters (from what I could tell).
-- Poorly implemented mechanics --
This is mostly about "heat" and "daylight" vs. everything else.  Heat is about how suspicious/dangerous your current weapons look.  It has gameplay effect related to subduing enemies, but was otherwise largely ignored.  There was the potential for prefight setups where you have to enter a guarded establishment and must adjust your kit to below a certain heat level to get it.  Never happened in any scenario I played.  It felt like heat was a mechanic that the developer had intended for much more, but then ran out of time/money to implement fully.
Daylight/Night had the same feel.  There are ablilities that are "stronger" in the shadow, but the difference is tactically insignificant.  There is no option to allow your to plan an event during the day or night to get the effect of favorable lighting conditions.  They simply are preset going into each encounter.  Felt like it had potential that wasn't fully implemented.
CRITICAL SUCCESSES (the things they got right)
-- Has a good flavor for the period/setting they try to create --
Lots of dialogue, old west movie style narration, and some graphical flourishes (ex. gunsmoke effect following shooting) all greatly aid immersion.
-- Basic combat mechanics are solid --
Cover based shooting, sight distances, fog of war, actions points, etc.  All tried and true mechanics.  No innovation here, but they apply them well to the setting (except for the poor AI noted above).
-- Music --
I thought that the music was well applied and thematically appropriate.  Some will certainly find it repetitious, though.
OVERALL
There are some fun things about this game, but the overall game lacks sufficient development to be a challenging, immersive experience.

The good way to play this game would be to puzzle out a plan to  the solution in your head first, before executing your plan.
The basic premise is you need to work your way towards having the tiles arranged in a certain order. This requires some level of foresight and some reverse engineering of the solutions, a task which I find quite difficult. You can find yourself to the solution randomly, but the big difficulty is in minimizing the number of moves it takes.
This provides a very difficult puzzle, but the earlier levels do offer a good way to ease you into it. And if you do find yourself burnin through all the levels, note that you're unlikely to run out as there are a lot of them.

Weeellllll, I just finished playing Broken Age. Hmm. First off, it's so beautiful. SO beautiful. I can see why I paid full-price for it after knowing hardly anything and watching the trailer. The game is just as beautiful as the trailer looks, with a whole lot of tiresome monotony thrown in.
Broken Age is split into two acts. Act One has fairly simple puzzles which follow the fun story. Vella and Shay, the two main characters, each inhabit their own world with no knowledge of the other (but you know that's gonna change). Playing either character is possible at any time. In Act Two, Vella and Shay switch worlds, and while each world is expanded on and new characters introduced, the puzzles became so tedious and not-obvoius, I found myself walking around the same places over and over.
The puzzles were tough in a way that didn't feel very stimulating, or creative, or challenging. Just sort of a shiny cute laborious thing to sludge through, with the help of walkthroughs that I very quickly turned to. I really want to make this sound more positive than I am, but I think the best part of the game for me was finishing, haha. Being done brought a feeling of satisfaction and relief that the game itself mostly hadn't.
I did find Vella and Shay both to be interesting characters, largely because they're their own people and don't align so much with gender stereotypes. That said, a lot of other characters are pretty cliche and boring. Like, there are some married parents in Act Two, and the mom's main activity seems to be worrying about her kid, while the dad is gettin' all scientific with the PH balance of a mud puddle and patching holes in a spaceship.
I recommend buying Broken Age on sale, taking lots of screenshots, enjoying Elijah Wood's voice (as Shay), turning to walkthroughs as wanted, and maybe having the snacks you like best nearby. Because this game, like any, is a whole lot better with some nice ridged chips and a towel to wipe the grease.

There's one part of the game where she's like "Oh crap, I should get rid of this bomb before it blows up and kills us all," but the lack of conviction makes it sound more like "Oh crap, I should take out this trash before the kitchen gets smelly and it attracts flies." Heck, Jennifer Lawrence plays a character in this game, and does a good job, why couldn't she have just voiced Vella. WARNING: This is slightly rushed because my steam kept crashing while writing this. Also if you wish to add anything to help this review, please comment, it's greatly welcomed. Thank you.
TL;DR One - This game is fantastic, it reinvigorated my love of gaming. At full price it's worth it, but if you're unsure wait for it to go on sale. Act one is above and beyond amazing, act two is great but sometimes overly challenging. Worth playing till the end.
(PROS) I'll flesh this out more later.
- The art style is so beautiful and unique I could cry. It really makes you feel that you're part of their world.
- The storyline is fantastic, it has twists and turns that even if somewhat expected, will surprise the living hell out of you.
- The characters are crazy and wonky but in all the right ways, I loved the dialogue and listened to every possible option.
- The morals of the story are inspiring, and honestly the reason why I'm writing this, because I see all these recent negative reviews and if the story taught me anything it's to stand up for what's right and don't believe everything you're told.
This game is wonderful, I loved damn near every second of it and I recommend it for everyone. I don't play point and click adventure games but now, I definitely will.
(CONS) Now as I said, I enjoyed almost every second, I do have a few complaints.
- The beginning of Shay's story (He's supposed to be bored but you become bored to), at least for me, was hard to get into but about twenty minutes in it picks back up (I started with Vella and it absolutely captivated me, sucking me into the game. I love her as a character and her side of the game greatly).
- Act two's puzzles can become overly challenging, you may wish to take notes or pictures with your phone, maybe even look up a guide.
- The ending, without spoiling, left too many questions for me but it wasn't an awful ending. I honestly makes me want a sequel.
(My steam crashed again, so I'll cut this short last part short.)
Final notes:
- Took me about eleven hours to complete this game and I listened to almost every last line of dialogue fully.
- I try to play all genres of gaming, but mainly stick to RPGs. Here are some games I love so you know if you like these games too than you might like this game, as I do. Elder Scrolls, Fallout, Borderlands, Fable, Fate, Portal, TF2, Half Life, Shovel Knight, etc, etc.
- I immediately after playing, started texting my closest friends and family about how phenomenal this game was and how they need to play it.
- Buy this game unless you already know you hate point and click adventures and if you do, still consider this game when it's on sale.
- I did use an online guide for two parts where I wasn't sure where to go in Act two.
- I never write game reviews, this is the first game to make me actually feel that I needed to, especially after seeing all the recent negative reviews.
- I got this game on sale with the full Double Fine games, bundle but I literally said to my friend, without knowing the price of this game that I'd pay $30 for it and be satisfied.
- I'm not a fan of point systems on games or anything, so none of that here.
TL;DR Two -
All of this is just my opinion and if you don't agree that is completely fine, my experience is different from yours. This game makes me believe that I can do anything I want, it inspires me and it inspires me to inspire others. I feel that this game is an experience that everyone should have. So please try this game you won't be disappointed (hopefully), maybe it won't have the same effect on you as me, but maybe, just maybe it will. If it does, than you need this.
Thank you for reading my insanely long rant.

Damn solid  multiplayer game. Although the learning curve is pretty tremendous  for what seems to be a simple AVP concept, the reality is that Natural Selection 2 involves requiring strategy that most games do not. Each of the two teams of Aliens and Marines have one commander, a person who assumes a top view of the map and can order his soldiers to go to a certian location, complete an objective, upgrade their armor and weaponry, and build structures to fortify the main base and make their team more powerful. I have found that the community for NS2 is generally helpful to rookies, and most (not all) will give tips and advise to new players struggling with the heavy expectations for a team in the matches that can last upwards of half an hour. Occasionally you witness the gruff veteran who lacks patience for the new recruits, but you can pick up on the game mechanics fairly quickly before they nag at you consistently. The gameplay is solid and balanced, playing as either team is fun and enjoyable. Playing as the vulnerable aliens as you stalk your prey can be exhilierating, but hunting the agile opponets with a pulse rifle can be equally enjoyable. The best game involves high levels of cooperation for all, but when you win, it feels great to have contributed to a team and I think I can say the level of comradery felt between two people is greatest when you squinting in the dimly light power room trying to reconstruct power to get the lights on as knee-high aliens shoot acidic goo at your feet. Fantastic game at any price, and it is gaurenteed to last you quite a while.

Having sunk countless hours into Fallout Shelter, I can say with confidence that the best possible outcome would have been for Fallout 4 to directly port over the mechanics of this game for settlements and, to a certain extent, equiment.  For example, it makes sense that the institute laser rifles would be more powerful than standard ones - they've had centuries to perfect the old tech that most wastelanders can only get through salvage.  Having happiness and settler attributes directly tied to output for various posts would have made the settlements in FO4 so much more dynamic.  There's a lot to like about the design decisions made in Fallout Shelter, and the game has been updated even though the game it's a tie-in for has been out for at least a year, so it's worth more than the price of admission in my humble opinion.
The addition of playable quests, item creation, and side-quests to wasteland exploration has extended the shelf life of this game significantly.  While the action can become repetitive as you reach the upper population limit of your vault (which, in my opinion, should be raised in light of the number of different positions and quest slots for your limited number of dwellers to occupy), there's a 'fish bowl' quality to FS that makes it something easy to waste time on.  The conversations the dwellers have are occasionally amusing - no one expects the Belethor refference the first time - and little nuggets of the classic Fallout black humor bleed through the cartooniness.
If I had one complaint about Fallout Shelter, it would be stability issues.  While the computer port has resolved a number of them, there remain a few times when the game has crashed on my otherwise high-end PC without warning or explaination.   Some optimization, stability fixes, and tweaks to the drag-and-drop mechanic to make it more accurate would be nice.  I'd also like to see some sort of accounting for familial relationships between dwellers added to the game, such a family tree, both because it can get quite confusing  figuring out who will breed with who (relatives can't) and because it always struck me as odd that a retro-futuristic send-up of 50's American society would effectively be comprised entirely of open relationships without any refferences to drama when, say, a dweller cheats on the other parent of their child, even though there are gossipy refferences to this kind of thing in dialogue.  Then again, that might be overthinking the mechanics of a casual game, so your mileage may vary.
Overall, I rate Fallout Shelter a 7/10 - not groundbreaking, but a satisfying time-sink with forgiveable flaws.

While I really enjoyed this game and recommend it, this is one of those games were you should make sure it's the right game for you before spending money on it as it's definitely not for everyone. Despite the massive critical acclaim this game has recieved I never really knew how difficult it was before diving into it. I knew it would be hard, but I wasn't expecting this.
This is one of the most unforgiving shooters I've ever played. One false step can mean death in an instant and the game doesn't wait too long to throw you into this punishing difficulty. That though is where the game really shines for me. It's hard but that makes the game super satisfying to progress through. If you enjoy the adrenaline of playing a fast and brutal game, the satisfaction of killing an annoying enemy, or the high of finally completing a level then you will love this game.
You could look at it like the Super Meat Boy equivalent to the top down shooter genre; really difficult yet short levels meaning that every time you die you think to yourself "this time I think I can make it" and that drives you right through the whole game, despite how many times the game likes to tell you "You are Dead". I think with enough persistance you would eventually beat it but how good you are might make you rage quit and never touch the game again. I personally kept going until I beat the story which took me about 4 hours, that's probably terrible compared to a lot of players, but the game kept me hooked brilliantly.
If however your idea of a good payoff for a difficult game is a satisfying story conclusion then I think you should look somewhere else. I've seen some people praise the story but I find it became such an incomprehensible mess by the end of the game that I started to ignore the story, and the "explanation" at the end for all the events of the game is pathetic. Perhaps that was the point? but that's still a negative in my eyes. Some people seem to be enjoying it though so perhaps you'll see something I don't.
The only other problem I have with the game is that it didn't seem very stable. In the 4 hours it took me to complete the story it crashed on 3 seperate occasions. I checked around and apparently it was due to a recent update shortly before I bought the game that hasn't yet been fixed. There are various work arounds supposedly so you might be ok.
I had a lot of fun with this game and I'll absoultley try the second game, which I also bought along with this one. Do I recommend it at full price though? I bought both games on sale for 3 pounds so I clearly got my moneys worth, but is this game alone worth the full price of 7 pounds? This again I think comes down to personal preference. If this is the kind of game you enjoy, brutal yet satisfying shooters, then I do think it's worth that price, just. If you are a very casual gamer who doesn't like gameplay that'll make you want to pull your hair out then I would try it at sale price, or pass on it.
Overall though a very well designed and original Indie game that I'm glad to have in my library.

Alright, it was hard for me to decide whether or not to recommend this game, but I finally decided. My two main reasons for negative review: the ending and the "gameplay." The combo of these two letdowns is what gets my downvote.
I love a good walking simulator and also a great cinematic game (think Until Dawn type), but this game came up short for me. There are zero choices to make, zero things to do, zero places to go. It basically plays as "left-click for next cutscene." And especially since nothing you do changes the story in any way, the lack of gameplay is unacceptable for me.
Next is the ending. [No spoilers] It's not that I don't understand the ending, it's that there are things that aren't made evident throughout the game and things that remain unresolved still. The townspeople all have these mini story lines at the end, but all the characters look the same to me so it was a little difficult to keep track (better upon second playthrough). Also just the ending doesn't feel like it "wraps up" the narrative.. it just sort of..... Ends.

Short: The best game there is.
Long: This game is a gem hidden from most public by not being from some AAA releases, and probably it keeps being good exactly cause of it. It shows a little more than 400hrs played but that are only the time playing online with steam, i play most of time direct from the 64bit starter that steam doesnt count. So it is easily above 1k hours in reality.
The first thing i can say good about it is that it deliveres excatly what the pictures shows... and MUCH MORE. It is not that kind of game that is deceiving cause of lots of picture of CGs and not actual gameplay. Everything show above is accessible right away and MUCH MUCH more gourgerous images are at your disposal.
The second thing is the community. This game has simple the best community of any game ever. People are helpful, friendly and incredible encouraging you on keep trying and getting better. This should be incredible for real life, for the internetz, its unheard off.
The third, MODS! My god, this game have the simple, easiest, most fantastic, mod support ever. Some of the mods are more complex than the game itself, like Fearam Aerospace Research(which adds a much more realistic aerodinamyc aspect to the game and will make your crafts spin a lot on launch and simple destroy your dreams of spaceplane reentry) or Remote Tech(which adds more realistic comunication network, including ranges, planet blockage, disc antenna targeting and more). The game can room smoothly on most computer or put your video card to pray if you install the visual enhancements mods wich make the planets and atmospheres looks incredible, specially from space! Mods can be completely addictive and you can easily find yourself lost browsing "just one more mod" to add to tha game.
The fourth, GET Kerbal Engineer Redux, technicaly its should be on the mod section, but it is so light, simples and just give you quality of life information that i find it should be already on the main game.
The fifth, the LEARNING CURVE! This game isnt difficult, like many people say, but it has like a 50hrs learning time. It is not the difficult of the gameplay, actually its fairly easy, its the sheer amounth of new information your have to learn and process to play the game. After 500hrs it is pretty easy to go to any planetary body per se, the problem is staying there and building your colony! In a certain way, this game is exactly like a the first half of human life: You start knowing nothing and thinking everything will be easy and you hurt yourself at you very first step! As you put time in this game you get "older", then lauching rockets become a little more complicated cause they need to have purpose! You start to try to do specific things, like going into orbit, docking, going to the mun, minmus, then other planets and moons. After that long teenager and early adult years, you become adult and not the real game begin! You manage your resources, try to estabilish yourself, explore the entire system. Then, at last middle age come and you have more long term goals! Like having family and a home for them, you build your colonies on other worlds and moons and try to get them to become self-suficient. Everything i just said is just a scratch of what this game can deliver.
The last, you will learn a lot of real life physics and astronomy. You will not have a master degree, but you will know much more that some of the people who do have but dont work on this kind of stuff. You will give imagination to your engineering dreams, like building rockets and planes, and after that some ships and even submarines! (There is an aquatic moon on the game). You will learn HOW difficult is to get into orbit and how difficult can be to get from orbit to the moon and back (the is a mod called "realism overhaul" for those wanting to try themself into realscale rockets, planets and solar system, cause the game uses a reduced scale to make launchs more manageable and rockets easier, but dont get me wrong, it is still very challenging). Then you will realise how incredible the mankind was back into the 60s and 70s to be able to do that with much less computer power than we have today. (Just out of curiosity, the aproximations used into the game are far more acurate than the aproximations available to the real apollo astronauts).

This game is far from perfect, but the pros outweigh the cons, and it is definitely worth playing through. You're sure to get over 20 hours of gameplay, so you won't be wasting your money. In fact, I've put in almost 15 hours, and I'm only a little over halfway through the campaigns.
Pros:
+ The atmosphere is incredible and unique: an old west setting plagued by satanic cults and demons. It's almost like H.P. Lovecraft meets the wild west.
+ There are three difficulty options and two special options, permanent injuries and ironman, that can make the game either extremely difficult or mostly casual.
+ Collectible playing cards allow you to customize each character's abilities for each scenario. If you want a super stealthy cannibal, playing cards will allow that. If you would rather make a sniper-like character who can ricochet bullets across the map to hit enemies from behind cover, playing cards will also allow you to do that.
+ The story, although rather simple, is quite engaging. You'll be excited to figure out what fate awaits each character.
+ Combat is easy to learn and solid.
+ Each of the eight scenarios add a new element to the campaign that distinguishes it from all the others. In one campaign, you'll have to cause as much destruction and chaos as possible, while in another campaign, your goal will be to manage a large group of treasure seekers.
Cons:
- There are no manuel saves, even when you're not on ironman mode. This means that you aren't really able to explore your actions without restarting the whole campaign.
- Combat starts off quite fun, but may grow repetetive.
- After each scenario, you lose your playing cards and equipment. Some special pieces of equipment can be bought in a special store in each scenario, however, known as Fate Traders. These pieces of equipment carry over from each campaign.
If you can forgive the cons, this game is definitely worth $10 or $20. And no matter what your opinion on it is, you will not be able to deny that this game is a unique experience in a crazy untamed world.

I backed it on Kickstarter, I'm a huge fan of the Baldur's gate series, Fallout 2 to New Vegas, Diablo, and many other RPGs, and think Wasteland 2 was absolutely terrible.
With 40+ hours of game-time I feel like I have a pretty substantial view on Wasteland 2, and in the end, I  think the devs just don't understand what actually makes a game ***fun***:
* Walking across an entire area cleared of all enemies to get back to the world map is not fun.
* Holding back on my attributes because I might run into some challenge requiring more lockpicking is not fun.
* Being interrupted on the world map for nearly always boring-as-♥♥♥♥ random encounters is not fun. (Seriously though, couldn't you make some unique random encounters that are more than nameless badies, or stop spamming me with encounters when I have a 100% chance of running?)
* Save scumming is not fun. Holy ♥♥♥♥, 50% of my time is spent save scumming. Want to open a safe? Save scum. Want to take apart a weapon and need a certain piece? Save scum. Starting a hard battle and need to hit an enemy with a hard-to-hit headshot? Save scum.
"Oh but just don't save scum and accept the consequences" is the worst excuse I can think of. It is simply human nature to shoot for the best outcome; failing at a percentage based challenge we know we can avoid by save scumming just feels bad. It feels almost equally as ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to waste time trying to get the desired outcome, but still feels better than getting♥♥♥♥♥♥all for your effort by accepting your♥♥♥♥♥♥luck.
New Vegas did this right: If you had the attributes to attempt a challenge it was pass fail. There was no reason to save scum,; save scumming wasn't even an option! Diablo did this right: If you exit the game, you save the game; you aren't even able to save scum! How did the devs mess up this crucial component in 2014?
**Graphics and Camera**
The graphics themselves are only OK. I don't expect them to be ground-breaking on an indie game. With that said, Fallout 1/2 and Baldur's gate still stand the test of time because every background is a literal work of art. Wasteland 2 simply looks, well, OK.
The real issue is that the 3D camera mechanism SUCKS. The compass is constantly off in some unexpected orientation, things are often hidden from view, and the map system is painful at best. The landscape is so bland and monotonous that you can't tell where you are from simply looking around. Even after 40+ hours of game time I still get lost unless constantly looking at the map and re-orienting the compass. Even Baldur's gate, a game made in the late 90's, had user-placable map-markers, and BG 2 had pre-placed markers on top of that so you could tell where the ♥♥♥♥ you were.
On top of the confusing camera and map, there is almost NO quick travel. Why do I have to walk across the entire prison map or Ranger Citadel to get in and out!? How does that enhance my experience? How is that enjoyable? It certainly doesn't make the game any harder, it just wastes more of our time.
**Combat**
Combat is OK; there is some element of strategy, and action point management is mildly interesting. That said . . it could really use more variety. Games like Diablo and the BG series had so much variety with spells and skills. Fallout 3 and New Vegas had the VATS system, stealth, and live combat. Wasteland 2 is just a throwback to Fallout 1/2, which is fine on it's own, but 15+ years later they couldn't think of anything new?
On top of this, the lack of pause and coordination before a fight is maddening. In baldur's gate you could issue tasks to each member of your party to do unique and interesting actions . . you know . . LIKE A REAL AMBUSH!? In wasteland 2, all you can do is shoot the ♥♥♥♥ out of one person. Hell, even fallout 1 and 2 let you go into VATS mode!
When I win a fight in Wasteland 2, I don't feel very GOOD about it. There simply isn't enough strategy to actually make much of a difference in a fight. The real decider of outcome seems to rely on your weapons, and the enemies decisions. If anything, I feel like I should go grind for experience to have a better chance, and that just makes me sad about wasting more time to progress in the game.
**The Attribute System**
Fargo talked all about making characters with specialties but absolutely failed. Getting by with a character who has under 8 intelligence is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because you miss so many skill-based opportunities. None of the other attributes influence your skills, so they are all a depressing mix of combat-stats. Charisma only needs to be high enough to pick up companions, and you're left♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off if you put it too low to include one. It all just feels like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ min-maxing formula: "At least 8 int, at least X charisma for these party members, and whatever mix gets the best AP for the rest of the stats while retaining a reasonable combat initiative. All this tailored to the weapon (higher CI for close-range weapons)".
Because the stats do not influence skills, they all do practically the same thing. Nobody is actually specialized because making a character with too low of AP or combat initiative makes them near useless. Anyone used to a little bit of customization in RPGs will just make everyone a bland average that optimizes as much AP as possible.
**The writing/acting**
Good god, I don't know if it is the writing or the actors, but this♥♥♥♥♥♥is cringe-worthy the whole way through. From the insanely clean live-actors (really? No dirt on a DESERT ranger?) to the how-in-the-♥♥♥♥-am-I-supposed-to-suspend-my-disbelief voice acting, it is just painful. Did anyone actually enjoy the live-action video? Couldn't that money have been spent better elsewhere? Does Vargas talk like any real person you've ever heard?
And finally . .
**Side Quests**
Rails nomad is the only place in all of Arizona that is full of quests you don't need to do to finish the game. All other standalone areas either have only a handful of trivial sidequests. The main areas themselves have many trivial side quests . . but none have any *substance*. The nuke silo is about the only substantial sidequest I can think of, and even that is pretty damn trivial in length. Compare to things like Fallouts 1 - New Vegas or BG, where there are side-quests spanning multiple areas, and MANY areas at least as intricate as Rails Nomad. All the side quests in Wasteland 2 just feel like shallow time-sinks.

I'm one of those who backed the game on Kickstarter three years ago and, being a long time Tim Schafer fan, with a substantial amount of money (and boy, does my now completely worn backer t-shirt look great!).
I hate episodic gaming, so I was really disappointed when I came to know the game would be split in two chapters. I decided to wait until the whole game would be out, which resulted in a LONG wait. Eventually, the game came out and we played it. Was I happy with it? Well, yes and no... If you're wondering whether I recommend the game, the answer is yes. But don't expect the masterpiece that we were all waiting for, considering the names involved.
The two chapters are so different in terms of story and gameplay that you cannot help but talk about them separately: you probably already heard up to the point of nausea of what everybody talked about. Of how more story-rich but incredibly easy the first part was, and how the puzzles were much harder in the second part where they forgot adding some story though. That's completely true, and depending on your inclination towards adventure games you'll most definitely like one of the two parts much more than the other. I personally prefer richer puzzles and so I enjoyed the second part more, gameplay-wise, but I totally agree that the first part was much more interesting in terms of scenarios, characters, dialogues and story. The second part seems to almost completely cast them aside, which is a pity.
Anyway, since this is supposed to be a review on the game as a whole, let's focus instead on what unites the two parts. First of all, the UI: I don't think I ever hated the UI of a point'n'click adventure so much. It was so obviously conceived for touch interfaces that you cannot help but feel deprived of a much richer experience. There is just a single button for everything: no one was expecting the SCUMM verbs, but was a left/right click interface too much to ask for? This results in a much limited experience in terms of user interaction, as watching/using/talking/etc. are all done the same way, and the game decides what to do for you. Apart from that, I'm also not a fan of how the game looks: I guess the cardboard look&feel was specifically conceived like that, but it feels cheap, especially considering the budget. The music, while decent, is quite forgettable as well, which is a stab in the heart if we think Peter McConnel composed it.
At this point you might be wondering: well, if all of this sucked so far, why are you recommending the game? Well, it's still a Tim Schafer game and it feels like it. Dialogues are (most of the times) funny, and, especially in the second part, puzzles are clever and rewarding. The music is often dull but pleasant and, while as explained I'm not a fan of the graphics, there is some art that is really good to look at (the clouds world, for instance).
Just don't expect a masterpiece and you'll enjoy some 12-13 hours of your life.

I liked this game. I think? It's complicated, okay!
Well, it isn't that I can't recommend this game. I would, to certain kinds of people and I know for sure that they are out there, it's just that I wouldn't to the majority out there. But let's get into this because as I said: It's complicated...
Let's talk about the mechanics first.
It's your standart Point'n'Click Adventure. Inventory system's a bit wonky but it does its job. Collect items, drag and drop, solve puzzles. That's about it.
The only new and interesting thing - and the one that drew me to it in the first place - is that you switch between the two main protagonists and experience the world from their points of view. They didn't really do anything with it mechanic-wise until Part 2 though, so up until then it was only a gimmick really. But a nice one. I enjoyed switching between charakters every other puzzle and it helped to paint a better picture of the world and its story, in my opinion.
Oh, story. In theory I should love this game. For me narrative is more key to a great experience than mechanics (a blend between the two being the "perfect game") which is why I enjoy games that do focus on it more than I do "skill-based" ones. Adventure games typically one of the genres that shine in that regard.
And the story to Broken Age is interesting. Well, the ending of Part 1 that is and some of Part 2 up until its rather anticlimatic finish.
All in all it's a story of coming-of-age, paralells and juxtapositions between the protagonists drawn rather well. All characters are likeable, the voice work is well done, the humour keeps your attention but nothing really stands out much.
Looking at the other arts as well, the designs are great and so is the music, the animation does its job and all in all they work together well.
But never before in my life have I found myself so physically tired while playing a game. Not frustrated, not bored, not overjoyed, not laughing - nothing. And that's a pitty because I like this game. It just does everything well but supposedly not well enough for me to really be enjoying it. And even when thinking back about the games I've played in my life this one will probably be forgotten somewhere down the line and to be honest, I'm kind of sad about it.
Well, if you want to give it a try I can't NOT recommend it either. It's a bit pricey for the experience you get out of it, in my opinion, so if you ever catch it on sale and are curious about it, please, do help yourself. And I hope you'll be able to enjoy it more than I have.

Short: The best game there is.
Long: This game is a gem hidden from most public by not being from some AAA releases, and probably it keeps being good exactly cause of it. It shows a little more than 400hrs played but that are only the time playing online with steam, i play most of time direct from the 64bit starter that steam doesnt count. So it is easily above 1k hours in reality.
The first thing i can say good about it is that it deliveres excatly what the pictures shows... and MUCH MORE. It is not that kind of game that is deceiving cause of lots of picture of CGs and not actual gameplay. Everything show above is accessible right away and MUCH MUCH more gourgerous images are at your disposal.
The second thing is the community. This game has simple the best community of any game ever. People are helpful, friendly and incredible encouraging you on keep trying and getting better. This should be incredible for real life, for the internetz, its unheard off.
The third, MODS! My god, this game have the simple, easiest, most fantastic, mod support ever. Some of the mods are more complex than the game itself, like Fearam Aerospace Research(which adds a much more realistic aerodinamyc aspect to the game and will make your crafts spin a lot on launch and simple destroy your dreams of spaceplane reentry) or Remote Tech(which adds more realistic comunication network, including ranges, planet blockage, disc antenna targeting and more). The game can room smoothly on most computer or put your video card to pray if you install the visual enhancements mods wich make the planets and atmospheres looks incredible, specially from space! Mods can be completely addictive and you can easily find yourself lost browsing "just one more mod" to add to tha game.
The fourth, GET Kerbal Engineer Redux, technicaly its should be on the mod section, but it is so light, simples and just give you quality of life information that i find it should be already on the main game.
The fifth, the LEARNING CURVE! This game isnt difficult, like many people say, but it has like a 50hrs learning time. It is not the difficult of the gameplay, actually its fairly easy, its the sheer amounth of new information your have to learn and process to play the game. After 500hrs it is pretty easy to go to any planetary body per se, the problem is staying there and building your colony! In a certain way, this game is exactly like a the first half of human life: You start knowing nothing and thinking everything will be easy and you hurt yourself at you very first step! As you put time in this game you get "older", then lauching rockets become a little more complicated cause they need to have purpose! You start to try to do specific things, like going into orbit, docking, going to the mun, minmus, then other planets and moons. After that long teenager and early adult years, you become adult and not the real game begin! You manage your resources, try to estabilish yourself, explore the entire system. Then, at last middle age come and you have more long term goals! Like having family and a home for them, you build your colonies on other worlds and moons and try to get them to become self-suficient. Everything i just said is just a scratch of what this game can deliver.
The last, you will learn a lot of real life physics and astronomy. You will not have a master degree, but you will know much more that some of the people who do have but dont work on this kind of stuff. You will give imagination to your engineering dreams, like building rockets and planes, and after that some ships and even submarines! (There is an aquatic moon on the game). You will learn HOW difficult is to get into orbit and how difficult can be to get from orbit to the moon and back (the is a mod called "realism overhaul" for those wanting to try themself into realscale rockets, planets and solar system, cause the game uses a reduced scale to make launchs more manageable and rockets easier, but dont get me wrong, it is still very challenging). Then you will realise how incredible the mankind was back into the 60s and 70s to be able to do that with much less computer power than we have today. (Just out of curiosity, the aproximations used into the game are far more acurate than the aproximations available to the real apollo astronauts).
Enjoy this masterpiece, one of the few games i took my time to write a review and i think thats the only one i gave a good review :P

Alright, I've been playing this game for quite a few hours now. I have to say this, if the game runs for you, this is a brilliant story driven game. Am loving the diversity of the jobs one has to undertake to capture a district. The shooting as well as the stealth is fun. Of course, stealth has quite basic options (we're not playing Splinter Cell now.. lol)
The few things I'd like to see in future updates would be the ability to fast travel. There are a few instances where the textures appear blurred. The game crashes every couple hours (every 1-3 hours). The AI should have been much smarter. You could keep whistling and killing a group of 3-4 people from just one spot. I can understand the reaction of the cops and why they only target Lincon Clay in a mob fight at times, but the reaction AI of the peds should have been better as well. Haven't encountered major bugs yet.
Coming to the good part. The story telling & narration is quite awesome. The character introductions are great. You need to really concentrate in the early hours and take in all the major players of the game. Shooting and driving is fun. Love the Mafia style drift driving around the corners. The cops are quite bad♥♥♥♥♥so I'd steer clear of them. Got swamped by 10 at a time in a matter of minutes because I failed to see one pass by during an interrogation.
Well, hope Mafia 3 will keep me coming back for more for at least 1-3 months. Good job 2K

If you like xcom you are probably gonna like this one as well.
Game is deevided into scenarios and after every scenario you lose progress on your characters, which is a bit shame, but it's not really that big of the deal imo.
Scenarios are devided into world map and tactical encounters.
-On world map you travel and basically do the story of the scenario, you make money, buy weapons, consumables and  trinkets
-Tactical encounters are comat which is very similar to xcom. Cover system, % hits, flanking... However, it also brings new mechanic that is luck which you need to use abilities and it makes your character harder to hit.
Though it adds some new stuff, instead of levels you have cards which you can freely put anytime to any character of yours. That gives them certain active abilities, (like golden buller, cannibalism..) which you can use in combat if you have enough luck for it, and pasive abilities which enhance your characters by giving them better stats.
Game doesn't have a lot of cinematics but it has superior voice acting and story telling.
Game is not that hard even when you play on Hard difficulty. I think it's still easier than xcom on hard maybe medium, but you can  allow ironman mod (if a key character dies in sscenario you are done and have to play it again) and combat injuries which give your characters debuffs. You can heal them by visiting medic on the world map or let it heal by itself, but your characters will recieve scars and those enchance some stats, but it also brings some bad stats with it.
Overall I had really a lot of fun with the game. Only the fact that it goes into Old West is actually really fun by itself, because I think there are not enough new interesting western games on the market (hopefully it's gonna get better tho :3) And since the game isn't expensive at all I really recommend you to buy it, it's really worth it if you like Old West, XCOM type of games, Story driven games,...

I bought this game because it looked awesome. I really enjoyed old wild west games, such as desperados, however I have to admit to be seriously underwhelmed by this game. I have only put in 6 hrs but already I feel that my time has been wasted, which is not a good sign.
The game has some really good graphics, and the scenarios are well thought out. I like the way the game mechanics works, so why have I not recommended this game.
Although the story for each scenario is well thought out there is actually very little fighting, before each fight you have to spend a lot of time on a map going from place to place reading text based boxes and this builds up the story. The reason you have to do this is because this is how you purchase weapons, armor/apparel, bombs,healing and character mods. without these you would be seriously under-equipped to complete the fights. Also this is where you find all the gold with which to buy said items. It feels as if the fighting scenarios were developed first and then the developers realised you needed to have a story to link it all together.
For those of you that have played desperados each map added to the story and I think it would've been better if the developers had put more thought into how to develop the story as part of the fight scenes, rather than making the player spend 30+ minutes on text based pop ups  between each fight scene.
I am glad I did not pay full price for this game, and if you have a choice buy something else.

Sights might be a bit rudimentary, but they work; that might bug you but then you open up the options menu and you can fully customize the HUD. It's something of a backhanded compliment, but I'd say that this is really good work done by dedicated students. The shortcomings can be somewhat handwaived as the product of inexperience, while the overall experience is actually pretty fun.
If it's on sale for a dollar or so, as it is at the time of this writing, I'd recommend buying the 4-pack and sending copies to a few open-minded friends. Boot up a quick server, mess around, and don't take it too seriously. I think you'll find that you've had a good time, passed a few hours, and all for less than five dollars.

There was once a pen and paper RPG called Boot Hill, it was created by a company facing obliteration from larger an better organized coporations.  In an attempt at immortality, they offered up their great Western RPG, Boot Hill to the R and D deptartment of an organization called X-COM.  A devoted team of Scientest and Engineers streamlined combat systems and gave the pen and paper product pixels and sound.  But the technology used to do this magic was not fully understood, and a rift formed; and in DOOM like fashion did the forces of Hell seize upon this new X-COM / Boot Hill hybrid, and gave it atmosphere and twisted plots.  And Cthulhu did stir from it's dreaming in agrivation his video games weren't near as kool.  This is a Great piece of work!  mechanics lag every once in a while (if you get the blue spinning wheel of Win thought just wait, the game will catch up), and can be repetitive as any top down squad based stratagy game can be.  But all in all outstanding fun, music, story, and play!

I don't want to go into too much detail here since the story is really where this game shines the most.  Basically, you're a writer with writer's block & you move to a new town to get some insperation.  Then things start to go south real quick.  You start seeing wierd shadows that chase you & people think you're crazy, until they start chasing them as well.   Now you've got to find a way to stop the darkness from taking over the town.
If you've played any 3rd person shooter then this will come naturally for you.  The only difference is you have to weaken the enemies with your flash light before you can actually deal damage to them with your guns.  Light em up & then light them up again.  There are hidden collectables throughout each level that detail more of the game's story.  The game is also presented in episodic fashion but it's done fairly well.  Each chapter begins & ends with an intro & credit sequence like you're watching a TV Mini series.  Other than that the gameplay is pretty straight forward 3rd person action shooting at it's finest.
Overall, the game is enjoyable if a bit short.  There's not really much to it either other than flash light, shoot, repeat.  The best part of the game is the acting & story segments which also happen while shooting things which is what keeps you interested in playing it.  If it was just a shooter without a story it would be fairly mediocre but because the story is so well done it ranks it up a couple more notches.

Alan Wake is a very atmospheric game with elements that I like alot... and then again the game has elements that I dislike a lot. The thing that makes this game is the story - everything between the beginning and the end is worth it for the story.
The most frustrating thing in this game is that you are basically forced to run through it since the shadow enemies keep respawning and respawning. And all I wanted to do is explore the beautiful setting! That's usually a game killer for me - endlessly teleporting enemies - but with this exact game a lot can be forgiven just for the story. And to be fair there are also sections where the enemies do not spawn into existence eternally - once you kill all of them you can explore safely but unfortunately this is not always the case - and it hurts this game a lot.
If you're into exploration then this might not be the ideal choice for a game since even if you ever manage to find a hidden cache somewhere you are punished immediately with a band of shadow enemies who basically steal your loot because you end up using your newly found ammo on them. Towards the end the combat gets really tiring, the same pattern keeps repeating with predictable enemy "ambushes". Regarding the story the last chapter could have been cut short removing some uninspiring combat sections and forwarding the story instead.
With all that said the game is still good. The story manages to turn a gameplay-wise mediocre game into a masterpiece. I also enjoyed the little things a lot - the radio shows, TV shows and posters with some recognizable references. Personally I don't wish to see more of Alan Wake, I hope that after Quantum Break Remedy moves on to something else entirely - but that's just me. I know there are some hardcore Alan Wake fans out there dying to see more of it.

Abstract
Hypothesis is put forward explaining a superpower flash, a shock wave and instant
evaporation of the most part of Chelyabinsk meteor by the emergence of conditions for a low
energy fusion exothermic reaction between Mg and Si nuclei contained in olivine and pyroxene,
which were found in the meteorite. The possible initiators of that reaction are considered. They
are supposed as common for the known experiments of similar type.
Keywords: fireball; explosion; olivine; pyroxene; isotopes; silicon; magnesium; iron; nickel;
chromium; nuclear fusion; LENR
The most mysterious feature of an airborne meteor is its sudden burst in
atmosphere accompanied by a dazzling continuous flash and a power shock wave
with estimated energy reaching several megatonnes of TNT equivalent. These
events happened in the history of mankind several times [1]. Maximum values
have Tunguska phenomenon (10-15 Mt) and Chelyabinsk bolide (0.44 Mt) [2].
The actual data famine in the first case gave rise to assumption about a natural
nuclear fusion reaction in a nucleus of a comet [3,4], which is, however,
inconsistent with our knowledge of the chemical composition of comets and of the
temperature and pressure conditions necessary for initiating this reaction [5]. But
the second case shows that the idea of a natural nuclear reaction is not devoid of
sense by itself and deserves attention.
Meteorite fragments were a persuasive proof that on 02.15.2013 at an altitude
of 23.3 km it was just a meteor of mass about 11,000 tonnes that has exploded,
which was traveling at the moment of its burst at a velocity of 18.6 km/s [2]. It is
unlikely that the meteor lost 9/10 of its initial mass due to ablation in traveling time
of 13 s in atmosphere [6], but even so, about 1000 tonnes of meteor’s substance, to
say the least, instantly evaporated leaving a dense smoky trace in the air, which
was absent before the burst. The assertion that 1000 tonnes of fragments fell down
[6] looks rather doubtful and is obviously based on simple arithmetic.
Thus not for the first time Nature demonstrates us the experiment in which
there happens a powerful burst and instant evaporation of a stone block containing
no explosives. Among all known means only a nuclear explosion is capable to
provide the energy required for that. There is ample evidence for that conclusion.
Just the main features of a nuclear explosion characterize the behavior of
Chelyabinsk meteor. First of all, there is superpower light radiation lasting 5
seconds as an extraordinarily increasing fireball. The radiation did not increase
gradually but appeared suddenly and considerably exceeded heat radiation of
burning gases attending the meteor flight. Approximate total radiated energy of the
fireball was 3.75·1014 J [7]. The flash brightness was so awful that a lot of
eyewitnesses got a tan on their faces even the man who was sitting in the back of
his car. It is well known that light duration of nuclear explosion in seconds is equal
to the cube root of its energy in kilotonnes [8]. From this correlation it is possible
to make the rough estimate of energy as 125 kt that is of the same order of value
with estimated in [2]. The first shock wave came to Chelyabinsk after 177 s , i.e.
the explosion occurred at a distance (measured along an inclined straight line)
about 60 km. If the explosion had happened at a lower height the shock wave force
would have been much greater. There are no valid data about electromagnetic
pulse besides short-time disappearance of mobile communication. There has not
been any radioactive contamination, possibly, not only due to the high-altitude
burst, but mainly because of total absence of unstable reaction products.
So the subject under consideration may appear as follows: at the input: a stone
meteor (chondrite) of an estimated initial mass of 11,000 tonnes traveling at a
velocity of 18.6 km/s; at the output: “pure” nuclear explosion.

Wasteland 2 is defintely a mixed bag. The game has all of classic features of the big post-apocalyptic ARPGs.
The Bad: The combat is good on the whole, but the way battles begin could be a lot better. The battles have an ambush feature, but outside of battle you can't set up an ambush for enemies you see ahead of you. You have two options, have one of your characters shoot at them first, or have all of your characters (which are typically bunch up in a formation I like to call "Please throw a grenade at us") fire simultaneously. The second option usually results in one of your teammates getting a shotgun, or automatic volley, to the back. You can painstakingly set up each of teammates in position ahead of time, but that will usually trigger the battle. As with most games, enemy AI is not great and seldom do they use any sort of tactic other than running headfirst towards the nearest person and attacking. Like the original Fallout series some characters are voiced and some aren't. Nowadays this seems lazy. If TES IV Oblivion can get away with voicing thousands of NPCs with a handful of voice actors, so can this indy studio.
The plethora of jokes and Easter Eggs were a nice addition, but many of them have been used in both Wasteland and all of the Fallout games. They are getting old.
Lastly, the sidequests were really tedious for the most part. Usually it involves getting a quest that leads to a secondary location in BFE, then needing to come back to the original location only to return to the second (or third location) again. Usually without anything interesting happening. I almost joined Matthias and his evil robot army just to wipe out all the Wastelanders that were too lazy to go on their own gopher runs.
The Good: Combat was solid and once you get your squad tuned up and outfitted, you can really wreak havoc on all manner of enemies.
Wasteland 2 gives a lot of playtime for the price. I bought it at full price and got sixty-three hours out of my first and only playthrough. That's a decent deal. Sure, other games have more replay value, but for an indy game sixty-three hours of story, with no repetition, is a good deal. Another bonus, for busy people, is that you can play it once and feel like you did pretty much everything. You don't have to play it again to get a feeling of completion.
Finally, the goats were hilarious.
As far as indy RPGs go, Wasteland 2 was worth the price tag.

Natural Selection 2 is a twist on normal FPS games, integrating the aliens aspect to it.
my personal review? i think the game could be incredibly fun. However, it is extremely stacked in the marine's favor. When a mech walks into the room, there is literally nothing you can do against it except try to get away. when a flamethrower walks into the room, you (as an alien) must run; a human weilding a flamethrower can clear an entire room of enemies within seconds.
Sure, Aliens have some perks. one alien can climb on walls (not all that helpful, since marines have all ranged weapons, except trying to hide). one alien can construct slightly permanent structures (also easily clearable by flmethrowers, grenades, etc). one can fly (thats pretty nice, not gonna lie). one is almost unstoppable if its one on one (however, is extremely vulnerable against more than one enemy). and theres one thats basically a walking tank (an etremely useful idea, but it takes almost the entire match toeanr enough points to use it). However, All these perks aside, all the aliens (for the most part) are melee. not only are they melee, but it takes 4-5 attacks to kill a simple marine (never mind the mechs), whereas it takes MAYBE half a clip from a marine to kill most aliens (on top of the fact that theyre ranged). on top of that, the melee range is so close, that you literally have to be standing on them in order to hit them. this being said, the term "bunny hopping" comes to mind, and is an extremely effective method to avoiding attacks. while these marines are jumping, they can still shoot. so while playing an alien, you not only have to get up close, not only are you weaker, not only are you squishier, but now you have to contended with actually trying to keep up with their jumping.
The only time ive ever seen the aliens win is if their commander is a pro player or if the marines commander is a rookie.
as i said earlier, this game can be incredibly fun. i really enjoy the alien racial aspects. that being said, i have never heard of somebody who enjoys losing every single game they join. i recommed the game, because it IS fun, but if you plan on playing the aliens, be prepared to have about a 1/10 win ratio.
overall score; by yourself its a 6/10 at most. with a team, id give it a 7.5/10

I have mixed feelings on this game.  Underneath it all, I think there is some artistic merit.  The soundtrack is great, although even that had moments that felt a little too derivative.  I never got the sense that the production team didn't have an underlying idea of what they were trying to convey.
The problem, I think, is that you have to "earn" leaving everything for the gamer- in this case "audience" may be more apt- to figure out.  Most of the gameplay is walking from point A to point B (if that) and making one or two clicks.  I'm one of the adventure game-loving, story rich-loving gamers who would be willing to go along with that if the story is strong enough.  Unfortunately, the scenes tend to be so short and so disconnected from any traditional narrative, that it comes together more like a collection of facts than an actual story.  Again, I have no doubt that the clues are all there to put together a satisfactory solution and to understand what the seemingly endless flashbacks or twists mean, or "might" mean.  The problem is that the gamer isn't given sufficient motivation to become invested.  I don't see a "hook" to drag the gamer into the world and actually want to piece everything together.
So while Virginia has some things going for it, I don't think I could actually recommend it to most people.  Still, there is, or could have been, a good game in there somewhere.

It plays like an interactive drama, because it is one. But what sets it apart from other similar games you've played such as Firewatch is that none of the character ever talks -- the whole narrative is told through the actions you take as they're prompted, and the subtle hints given to you throughout the game thus the game requires your constant attention or you'll end up missing a few key details that can prove troublesome to understand certain aspects of the story.
However, just because nobody speaks in the game isn't necessarily a bad thing, it gave way to one of the great soundtracks that you can enjoy in a game which changes dynamically from scene to scene and hints you about the type of scene that's about to come at you and such, not only that but the music in this game was played by City Of Prague Philharmonic Orchestra, and trust me when I say this, they did a really good job with it in this game. For a game that has no audible talking at all, you needed the right type of music to carry it and this did just that.
As for the story, I quite liked it. Without going into spoilers too much but still giving you an idea so you know what you're getting yourself into, it starts as a story about a recently graduated FBI agent, which is the one you play, along with her partner that you're sent to work with -- if you pay close attention to the files given to you, read them swiftly before the animation happens and they're gone, you'll be let in on some of the key elements of the story and can see some part of it coming from a bit away, which isn't necessarily a bad thing as it keeps you hooked to the story. And something to keep in mind is that the game is quite short, only about two hours.
Now here's the kicker, the story that's conveyed through the game is actually based on the official real life records of the events that happened during the summer of 1992 when the FBI undertook an investigation in a small town in Virginia. So, all that you see happen in the game has actually happened in real life too, which is not surprising considering how real the game gets towards the end giving you certain life lessons.
If you guys are into indie titles with the likes of Firewatch and such, you definitely will enjoy this baby as it's cut from the same cloth. The art direction in the game is amazing, I loved the visuals too. I have grown quite fond of indie titles in the past year and been preferring them over AAA titles most of the time too as I have finished quite a few of them and this game is no different.

If there was a middle option between yes/no, I'd pick it here. However, despite how much I love games that go outside the norm, and experiences that focus on a good story, I can't bring myself to recommend this.
I'm also not against cryptic narratives, but Virginia achieves this by giving you 5 seconds to read a key document early on, before cutting away from it. The last third of the game is also an avalanche of absurd stuff which only muddies the waters further. If I have to google for Reddit threads and articles to understand what the heck your game was about, I can't say the narrative worked as far as I'm concerned. Not having dialogue in a game is always an interesting choice, but I don't think it was wise when the story has this many characters and elements for you to try to follow.
While the art direction is great, its technical execution is lackluster. Your character feels really bad to control; there is no deceleration when you stop, and there is a really sharp "bounce back" when you look around. It doesn't help that your field of view is quite limited, though I quite liked the camera-like optical distortion to make the perspective feel more organic, something I wish more games did.
What destroys the little enjoyment I still had of it was the level/interaction design, which is not clear more often than it should be; when the gameplay actions are "minimalistic" like this, what you do ask the player to perform should not be unclear to them.
Ultimately Virginia is the kind of game that may have been overambitious for its budget—it would probably strongly benefit from some kind of "Director's Cut".

KSP embodies everything I want from a videogame. I've played shooters, RPGs, hack/slashers, roguelikes, whatever people hype up nowadays. Sure, they're fun. But after a while, I get bored. Actually, I get bored really quickly with most games these days. But this one is still as fresh as the day I played it at a friend's house years ago. If you're the kind of person who enjoys getting out their creativity in both systematic and (usually) chaotic ways and making things that you're sheepishly proud of (or hey, even legitimately proud of), check this out. The game has a plethora of mods to check out in case sandbox mode ever gets repetitive for you (apart from a few core mechanics/utility mods, I prefer vanilla), and I can promise you that if you want to peep your head into this genre and have ever had the urge to build something crazy and launch it into space, this is the game for you. Have a good one!

If you're not the most patient individual in the world and a master of lateral thinking, get ready to look at walkthroughs.
