Where oh where do I begin in trying to describe this game..? Think Legend of Zelda + Smash TV + a genrous, heaping slathering of fetus-centric humor with some tongue-in-cheek biblical parody (so much tongue, in fact, that your cheeks will probably end up bruised) and an accurate image should begin to emerge. It's an over-head action/shooter (the same visual perspective as seen in the original Legend of Zelda) with a very nifty techno soundtrack and literally hundreds of powerups & gimmicks with randomly generated level maps. No play session is the same as any that came before it. There are several characters to unlock (some more difficult to achieve than others); each with differing combat statistics. Dare I say that this is one of the best indy games I've encountered in a very great while..? I do indeed!
Everyone must be forewarned: This game is HARD!!! Seriously! You're gonna die! ...and often! It's not so bad though. Your frustration will be quite effectively mitigated by the virtually infinite variety produced by the random level layout generation and the massive number of random power-ups and other entertaining items.
My only real complaint is that there is no native gamepad support in this game. If you really need to use a gamepad (as I certainly did), you'll want to get your hands on a program called Xpadder. With this software, you can seamlessly map keyboard keys to the desired gamepad functions. It works perfectly. Once you've gotten it configured to your liking, you won't even be able to tell that the game actually lacks said controller support natively.
Go on! Buy this game right now and do your part to help guide Isaac through his tyrannical mother's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and uterus in order to put a permanent stop her abusive reign of terror! (Yes, you read correctly; the levels feature the inside of Isaac's mother's twisted & rotten nether-regions)... Enjoy!

Either this game is stupid or I am. And I'm not ruling out either.
First off, you're playing an FBI investigator, but it's hardly an investigation game, just to be clear. You're not piecing together clues, and only a handful of the questions you have in the beginning of the game get partial answers by the end. You don't finish the game feeling like you've solved a nagging question; at the end you're more confused than ever, and not in a good "I'll have to dwell on this for the next week" way.
So many story lines are introduced and then dropped completely, amounting to little more than narrative clutter. It seems like the developers were going for a kind of esoteric thriller a la "Memento" but focused on the wrong things. The narrative checks the "misleading" and "confusing" boxes without remembering to put in a good payoff. You trek through the game being pelted with all sorts of red herrings and dream sequences assuming that you're working your way toward a satisfying conclusion, but it never comes.
And this kind of game *needs* a good story. Gameplay is nothing more than walking around a room, finding the *one* thing you can click on, and repeating. I don't mind linear experiences, but there is absolutely no choice involved (or possible) while playing, leading me to wonder why this was made as a game and not a short film or something. And I have absolutely no problem with these kinds of "games without gameplay." Gone Home is still one of my favorite games, period. But with Gone Home, I felt like I was learning as I played, putting together a story myself with puzzle pieces the developer had left scattered around. But the puzzle pieces in this game don't fit together, nor I am sure that there are even enough puzzle pieces to finish a bigger picture.

I am a hard person to please when it comes to games. I have found myself leaning more and more to more tactical based games such as this. This game could have been better, sure, I will not argue with that. There are some glitches and some things that don't entirely make sense, but over all I have enjoyed playing this game a lot. It has taken the lead over other games I've purchased including some of the much larger titles with much larger budgets. The story is involved enough to keep you going and the exploration factor, although not enormous, is enough to keep you going for quit some time outside of the main game questline. There are certain skills in the game that are MUCH MUCH more useful than others. I, for example, haven't put anything into the dialogue skill options. The skill points are just too valuable in other categories and although this can be a curse ... at the same time it keeps you slightly on edge knowing that you have a limited amount of points to spend and once you have spent them that is IT. If you cannot open that lock box or gate or disarm that bomb then YOU either come back later, take the damage, or move on. I do not like all of the followers some of them seem very unuseful aside from pack mules or bullet sponges. The intelligence skill is VERY heavy and you can almost justify maxing out everyone's intelligence in place of other options just for pure fact that the skill points are so darn valuable. I say almost because although it is heavily weighted.... other skills are needed to maximize other areas. For example if you want enough action points to do anything you need to have coordination or strength maybe some minor speed. That being said the attributes should have been ballanced a bit better.
Bottom line: I love the game. It could have been better and I hope that this group continues to improve upon this style and polish on this style of game.  This is, In my opinion, what the fallout series should have continued to be. Don't get me wrong the new one is alright and has its place, but the nostalgia is not as prevalent in the newer fallout title.

Just pass on this. Seriously, it isn't worth the time.
If you were excited like I was that Tim Schafer would be making a game the same calibur as Grim Fandango, this is not it. Instead, go buy
and enjoy the game that Broken Age should have been.
Here's the long version:
Tim Schafer wrote and directed Grim Fandango, which I believe is the best point and click adventure game of all time. I say that with confidence as I've played a huge amount of adventure games (ags anyone?). Schafer, as it turns out, is a horrible project lead. Broken Age was kickstarted for over 3 million dollars which gave players Act 1. Act 1 took me about  2 hours to complete, and was fine. Just fine, it was not a game that should have taken 3 million dollars to complete and other studios have done more with much, much less. After the game released, Double Fine announced they had enough money to complete the project and deliver the abysmal Act 2.
But not everybody really cares about the politics of the game, so here's some extra stuff for the passionate adventure gamer:
The "good":
Might as well start here as there is so little.
Act 1 was okay. The puzzles were fair and made sense, and it did create this idea of some dark story beneath the kid friendly veil. Had Double Fine continued immediately from this point and used their 3 mil to make the entire game, I think it would have been fantastic.
The bad:
While the puzzles in act 1 were fair and made sense, they were very easy. It just didn't take a lot to get through it, leading to the very short 2 hour runtime. Act 1 soaked up all 3 million dollars and was only 2 hours long.
As previously mentioned, Act 1's story was pretty good and gave the sense that there was something much darker in the story than we got from the frilly and colorful aesthetics. For example, at the end Vella's arc:
.
The worst part about the game is act 2. Following the story from act 1, act 2 feels like it was written long after act 1 ended and they never really knew where they were going with the story. In fact, I found this on wikipedia: "In October 2014, producer Greg Rice announced that Schafer had finished writing Act 2 and the game's finale.". But the game released on January 28 of the same year. So after 3 million dollars, and a moderately successful release, Tim Schafer didn't even know how the game would end. And that should tell you all you need to know about how funky act 2 feels.
I won't even bring up the awful wire puzzle later in the game. Others have, and everybody hates it.
So there you have it, it took 3 million dollars to make a mediocre, 2 hour adventure game with a cliffhanger, and the sales from that (probably not 3 million btw) paid for an awful act 2.
Just... just go play Deponia.

I really enjoyed my playthrough of Broken Age. A lot of games nowadays have trouble holding my attention for extended periods of time unless I've already previously invested a lot of time in them. However, when I picked up Broken Age, I fell in love with it right away. It's visual art style as well as its voice talent brought me in, and I stayed for the comical yet engaging storytelling. The characters are also likeable, not two-dimensional but rather have depth to them which adds to the immersion that the game tries to present, especially the game's two protagonists, Shay and Vella. The puzzles did not feel like a chore: they felt challenging yet fair, and when completed, made me feel good about solving them, rather then feeling as though I had lifted a burden off of my shoulders like other games. The puzzles started off simple and later on grew in scale, encompassing (at some points) both of the game's protagnists to solve puzzles, which was an interesting game mechanic in itself. Would definetely recommend, especially to those who have yet to try point and click adventure games.

Broken Age: A classical Point-and-Click Adventure Game that follows the parallel stories of a young man; who is pampered into a disconenting, safe, life, and a young woman; who is under scrutiny by the culture around her for breaking the mold of tradition and refusing to sacrifice herself, rebels against her peers to find victory.
When I first started up the game I was absolutly in love with the Art Style the game used. It is extremely unique, yet harkens back to the childrens books of my childhood. The dual story lines were very intriguing and artfully crafted.
Act 1 was extremely well written and executed, and while the 2nd half of Act 2 seemed a little rushed and not as dense in story as the first act I believe it was fitting. Due to the context of the situation of Act 2 the main characters wouldn't have time, let alone interest in every tiny fiber of their surrounding. The setting of Act 2 requires more urgency than Act 1. Also, Act 2's puzzles where slightly more challenging, which helped with the quick pace, altough was frustrating at times.
Overall I loved this game. The Art is spectacular. The story and characters are rich and satisfying. The subtle humor is heart warming. The deeper messages of various social issues is very intriguing. The design of the game is extremely well executed, which involves one of the most user friendly UI systems I've seen. The music is rich and fitting for each situation.  And the Knife. Oh that Knife.

Ok, so, it's a Myst-ish game, a puzzle/escape/explore game where you navigate through a sequence of pre-rendered vistas (many of which you can pan around to give a semblance of 3d location). The characters are early 3d, the player character resembling an early attempt to 3d-ify the Avatar from the Ultima series.
97% of the game involves looking at static objects and environment, though, which are mostly pretty.
The puzzles are passable, and I manged to make it through much of the game without help. I did get stuck for a rather long time near the beginning because I missed the left-most view of the tables full of stuff in the house near the beginning.
There is one puzzle in the third act that really made me mad, though. At one point where the path is blocked, on turning back you will see an item. It is the item you need, and is not held down by anything, but you
. You need to find or have already stumbled upon a different copy of the item in a different area. That copy of the item can only be found by
to find it in an area that you should have been able to see it from other locations in, but cannot.
The plot is largely forgettable -- get all the pieces of the magic whatsit before the bad guy can -- and backed up by mediocre voice acting and characters with strange names I can't remember a few hours after playing. This is passable, if you're playing for the puzzles, except for the ending. I won't spoil it just in case someone cares, but I'll say that I actually expected a final area to play after the last cutscene and was kind of shocked when the credits rolled.
Yeah, I can't really recommend this to anyone but the most masochistic puzzle-hound who's played every other game in the genre already.
Oh, and you can't play it in anything but fullscreen of 800x600/1024x768, which makes multiple monitor people like me sad.

The game's okay. The story isn't anything stellar, and feels very slow-paced, but the combination of match-3 and RPG makes for an interesting twist on the typical puzzler genre. If you've ever played a Heroes title, it borrows the hero + troops trope of that, but instead of a map for the creatures to battle on, you have a matching system. Match a corresponding color to earn either mana for spells, instant attack damage, or build up an attack with your troops.  The battles in these games become insanely easy 90% of the time, and the only frustrating parts are when you have to clear the board of all matching pieces in the Altar 'minigames' in order to progress the lackluster story. Perhaps if there were achievements or trading cards added to it, I might have enjoyed the experience a little more.
If you want to try something different for a match-3 style of game, pick this up when it's on sale for under $5. Otherwise, save your money.

Long time horror-games fan here, action-horror especially. Have lots of games to compare Alan Wake to. And I have to say the game is just mediocre. Was OK in the beginning, but because negatives piled up with the time and it dragged on for way too long (partially because of "brilliant" idea of developers to hide story details behind collectibles, I care about stories in my games, I couldn't ignore them) I started to dislike it by the end
What was bad:
-in-game ads! Crime in any game, doubly so in horror game, which lives and dies by it's atmosphere. "On a way to finally end it all, destroy the darkness, save your wife? don't forget, this is really, really important! VERIZON!!!"
-Shooting. It is tied to the story, yes, but as feature in a game, imho, it doesn't work that well. Your flashlight is like a laser sight in other games, except worse. You have to keep pointing it to the enemy, waiting till the game decides it wasted enough of your time and let's you deal damage.
-Only 4 weapons - gun, shotgun (2 variants), hunting rifle and flaregun + flares and flashbang grenades, that's it
-Few enemy types. Smaller dudes, bigger dudes, teleporting dudes, crows and poltergeist. Combined with limited weapons variety encounters get stale really fast and don't change in any way from beginning to the end
-random encounters, like in some cheap old JRPG. About 5 (!) seconds after dealing with one group, another appears. Again and again. Combined with previous two points.. you get the picture. This got much better in second half of the game though
-camera, in close areas, especially inside buildings, it really doesn't know what to do, cost me several retries
-unlikable main character. Spoiled whiny diva, gets angry when he has problems with writing then gets angry at Alice for trying to help him. Also, pointing a gun at a sheriff, who just saved him, as answer for offered help? What an asshat!
-story wasn't really engaging, "save the princess" with lots of talking, but nothing to make me care. And when everyone is a character in a book written by Wake, why worry if something happens to them? They aren't real anyway
-Darkness as main antagonist. Just darkness, with some old woman's face, doing it's evil Darknessy things. No amount of cheap jumpscares makes it actually scary or interesting or anything but boring.
-no sense of progression. Comparing with amazing Resident Evil 4 - you could chose the weapon you liked, chose what you wish to upgrade, make it yours (dat Red 9!). Here it's the same weapons all the time, with the game taking them away constantly, just because (for you to find them later casually laying around)
+it looks good, night forest with trees swinging and shadows of the clouds running through. Pretty creepy
+Night Springs stories were cool, until once the game tricked me showing ads instead - bye immersion!
... I think that's it. Other things could be good, but left me disappointed or I got sick of them (combat) so they went to negatives.
What could make it better?
If Wake writes it, and it's a fiction, what stopped him to give himself some supernatural abilities maybe? He could add new ones with time, get better with old ones the more he used them. This could add new ways of dealing with enemies, and add new types of enemies with abilities to match. Why it only has to be possessed people, birds and stuff lying around, reanimated as poltergeist. Is it all "the almighty Darkness" can do?
No random encounters, hell no. Enemies appear from nowhere and disappear into nothing when defeated, only to come back 5 seconds later, leaving you with a sense that they are there only to waste your time and ammunition.
Also, don't start with combat 10 minutes in and then push it almost non-stop till the end - the town is beautiful (with Twin Peaks vibes), spend some time with it. game! Make Alan interact with townsfolk more, build an atmosphere. And then, gradually, with only hints and suspicions at first, go into horror mode.
could add more but it's already a wall of text, nobody will read it all anyway, lol
Overall, I understand why this game could be enjoyable to other people. Depends on how much the stuff I mentioned will bother you. I just couldn't ignore it all in the end. Could have been really good game, but Remedy wasted this opportunity

Simple FPS with instant action, small install size, and a lot of fun.
Pros:
+Not Pay2Win, there are microtransactions, but only for masks and badges
+Netcode is better than most games I've played in the last 5 years.
+Matches are easy to get into, and you can switch your team at any time.
+Respawns are within a few seconds with a 3 second spawn shield.
+Well balanced guns, most have no recoil, the weapon system is almost copy-pasta of CS:GO.
+Super-fast gameplay, so if you're a fan of Quake Arena and Unreal Tournament, this is for you.
Cons:
-Netcode is good, but you get the occasional no-reg, or it may take a second before it regs.
-There are the hackers, and there is no vote-kick system or report feature to compensate.
-Zoom is there, but it's almost not worth using except for guns that have a scope.
-Spawn camping happens a lot, be prepared for that, and hope you don't have a crap team.
-There is an occasional random death glitch when you're next to a spawning player or from certain objects.
-Maps are pretty small (I don't care), and there's no option to vote for the next map.
-I get weird artifacts and lost textures on various maps, although I'm not sure if it's just me.
-There's a bias towards Corps (blue team), as they are much harder to see on some maps than the Mercs (red team).
It has it's ups and downs, but overall, this is a really fun game to just pick up and play for a few hours.  Aside from some lag kills, all you really need to win is some decent skill and decent teammates (and always aim for the head).

Puzzle Kingdoms takes a familiar match-three base and adds a little spin on it to make it feel fresh. Basic gameplay involves pushing tiles onto a grid of blocks, making the rest of the row or coloumn move along by one tile and hopefully making a line of 3. The spin comes from the player-built armies you take into each match.
From swordsmen up to dragons, you can take up to four units into a battle with you, and your opponent does the same. Each unit is “fuelled” by a different colour of tile on the game grid. Clearing a line of three adds one point of fuel to your unit, and combos add more. Once your unit is fully powered up you can unleash their attack on your opponent or wait for other units to be ready to attack which grants additional damage.
The added layer of strategy in building an efficient army changes Puzzle Kingdoms from a well made match-three into something much more interesting. You may have a powerful Green unit, but stacking your army full of only those not only means the other colours go to waste when you match them, but also you need to clear a lot of Green tiles to get any combo bonuses. You also need to pay attention to what colours your opponent is going for so you can try to get those lines yourself and prevent them attacking.
The story is kinda dull. There's a pretty interesting twist in the tail, but little reason to really care about it- so you should grab this for the Puzzle more than the Kingdoms. It's well worth sinking some time into if you can get it cheap.

TL;DR
Should you buy this? No. Not yet.
Although the trailers made me feel like this was going to be some generic "you're a badass, work your way towards it" game, the story is actually compelling and the characters are very interesting.
Sadly though, that's the only reason to get this game so far.
It's like mafia 2, only worse.
Graphically it's all drab and dark, there's no color or ambience like in Mafia 2, although it has some appeal for itself.
Right now just expect minecraft graphics and you might be pleased with what you get; they downgraded the graphics and tried to compensate for it by spamming post processing effects.
You'll see out of place textures, effectes and objects that make the whole thing not feel like 1 world, but more like a world with objects in it placed by the dev.
Also it's worth noticing that the day and night cycle will appear in 2 seconds, literally.
You'll see the sun flying past you on the ground and at least a second later it'll all go dark for nighttime, it's just broken.
I've even had one occasion where it all went pitch black and eventually gained more and more brightness after 5 seconds of waiting, probably also an issue with the day/night cycle.
All in all this is a terrible port, they even had the balls to release it at a 30fps cap, which as now been removed.
Sadly though, it's VERY noticable that the rest of the game hasn't been adjusted accordingly.
You'll get a very poor framerate at a high end PC, resulting in something that looks WORSE than mafia 2.
How, you ask? Mafia 2 is outdated by now, this is a AAA next gen game.
Well it's not any more impressive than Mafia 2 graphically. It's very clear when playing this that this was intended for consoles exclusively; textures are very drawn out and blurrish and one look at the skybox will reveal that it's a stretched out JPEG with no effort in it.
Heck, just look up some footage of a mirror in this game. It's a picture in picture screen with a 10 second delay.
In english; this means if you look in a mirror after walking at it, you'll see yourself about 10 seconds ago.
Wait for another 10 seconds and it might load the picture of you standing closer.
Game is full of bugs, and i do mean full.
As an ArmA fanboy and Early access tester i've never shyed away from bugs, even on a AAA title.
However in this game you'll see at least 50 of them within 30 minutes of playing.
Dead enemies will ragdoll into walls and objects around you, melee kill animations will clip you, your opponent and your camera through walls and objects alike.
Cars will teleport in front of you as a result of the console's intended view distance.
My personal tip; never drive at full speed.
A car will eventually spawn 1cm in front of you standing still and you'll have a deadly crash.
The AI is horrendous.
I'm not sure how scripted the AI in mafia 2 was, but it definitely seemed better than here.
You can basically "sneak" at your enemy, AKA crouch-run at your enemy.
If you react within 5 seconds of him seeing you, you can still press control to slide lincoln into cover at the enemy's feet.
He'll then be like "what's that sound" instead of "why is there a huge♥♥♥♥♥african-american war hero sliding past me", and as a result you can easily press Q to kill him.
As for the cops; they're on the "broken AI" bandwagon.
You can drift diagonally across 4 lanes at an intersection with 2 patrol cars and 4 officers on foot watching you, you'll get a blue marker indicating they're "about" to get alerted, but they won't.
They won't chase you if you speed, they won't chase you if you cut them off in incoming traffic, they won't chase you if you drift like a maniac.
They will, however, immediately pull their weapons and start firing at you if you slightly hit something. The good old bribing and them attempting to arrest you at first is history.
It's mafia 3; it's dumbed down, so don't expect any details like the ones you got in mafia 2.
Stealth is no challenge whatsoever, i'm challenging myself to do the entire playthrough guns blazing, although i'm generally a massive fan of stealth gameplay.
Gameplay and graphics wise it feels like a letdown from mafia 2.
Storywise and characterwise however; it's definitely worth it.
That is if the game gets fixed or deserted and discounted down to 20 bucks.
Don't pick it up for any higher price for now.

This game likes to throw stuff at you:
Knives, axes, barrels, tires, fridges, cars, boats, train carts and trains.
Apart from that, the game throws you a good story, beautiful and creepy (but sometimes trippy) visuals and great music with a side dish of "jumpscares". Worked for me sometimes, but most people won't find them scary. I just don't enjoy horror games/movies, so my heart skipped a few beats here and there. ;_;
The story starts off kinda confusing, but thats the point. Alan is confused, so you should be too. As you progress and find more manuscript pages, the story starts to unwrap itself. I personally enjoyed it.
I genuinely had a hard time of trying to stop playing this. The game really grabs you tight.
The gameplay is really good. There's only two things that kind of bugged me:
Minor things though, no need to worry.
Some people here say that the gameplay is repetitive. Sure, I think it can be and is that, but I enjoyed the good, solid gameplay and it doesn't feel like a chore. I never got the feeling while playing the game, that this is repetitive. The combat situations don't last forever, it's not like in COD, where enemies just keep throwing themselves at you before you move. But technically it's just "point enemies with flashlight, then shoot". For me, that simple gameplay is ok as long as it works flawlessly. And I think Remedy accomplished that in this game. Of course nothing is absolutely perfect, refer to things listed above.
I recommend this game to anyone who likes good stories, mysteries, twilight zone references and third-person shooter gameplay. And doesn't mind a dark, creepy atmosphere and possible tiny jumpscares. (They aren't "real" jumpscares, just that some enemies might want some surprise butt sex with you and jump from a bush towards you.)

Really an excellent game, especially considering the fact that it was put together by an indie developer on a (relatively speaking) shoestring budget. Although I never played the original Wasteland, this felt like a proper homage to Fallout 1 and 2, but with squad-based combat that feels more akin to Fallout Tactics or even XCOM: EU.
Pros: Old school top-down isometric RPG goodness; enjoyable and branching storyline with enough notable break points to encourage multiple playthroughs, whether as hero or villain; a huge variety of largely necessary skills that require smart squad design to cover all your bases; fairly tight turn-based combat; tons of different weapon and mod types; generally well-written dialogue; and (of course) the wonderfully irreverent humor and implicit social commentary that we all know and love.
Cons: Despite the huge variety of weapons, a ton of rebalancing is still needed to make anything other than assault rifles worth using in the higher difficulties; ditto the attribute system, which needs some serious rebalancing love make anything other than high coordination/awareness characters worthwhile; the armor mechanic in relation to energy weapons feels broken and counterintuitive, and even encourages parties to fight naked if they're going up against a ton of robots; quest breakage still seems possible under some circumstances, although most of the time it's just the game failing to telegraph how to progress or conclude any given task (this may be a selling point for some, though); and the overreliance on the (IMO) super stupid toaster repair mechanic to resolve various sidequests.
Bottom line: this is a big, messy, beautiful beast of a game, and one that's well worth your time. Hopefully the devs have enough time and money to rebalance weapons and stats accordingly, but in the meantime there are some pretty decent WL2 Nexus mods that do the job.

Fallout shelter is a fun little game that you play for five to ten minutes at a time that can get pretty challenging at times. A lot will complain about it being a 'pay to win' game, but it isn't; if you're impatient or make stupid decisions, like send your dwellers out into the wasteland with no stimpaks or horde your weapons instead of equipping people, then you'll be tempted to buy lunchboxes and other items. But that's why this is a 5-10 minute session game: you check your vault(s) in the morning, at lunch, after dinner, or whenever you have a few free minutes with nothing to do, fiddle around, and go about your day, including playing other games. There's no need to spend money on this game in order to enjoy it.
There are a few issues that do prevent me from giving this game a better score and will irritate you:
-The cursor isn't precise in some situations, the most common one being needing to place dwellers on the ceiling of the room you assign them instead of in the room itself.
-When combat takes place in some of the rooms, dwellers will stack and stand behind each other, preventing you from clicking on the right person to heal them. This happens rarely, but when it does, you will need to pay to resurrect your dweller what feels unnecessarily.
-About a third of the Mysterious Stranger's spawn locations, namely those with forebround and background areas, are cheap; as in, he's behind a wall or one of your dwellers and unless you dramatically change the angle of your view, you won't see him, even if that room is the only thing you see. You'll get sick of this fast and is something that, like the dwellers stacking in rare combat instances, needs to be patch-fixed so it's less cheatsy BS.
-Click and draging to change perspective is not recommended. Accidentally click on a dweller and you'll end up sending them somewhere you don't want or just unasign them. Also, double-clicking while doing this causes the camera to focus on the person or room you double-clicked, fighting against your manual controls and require you to double-click and let the camera do what it wants before you get control back or else you'll be camera-locked in that one dweller or room.
These are all minor annoyances and irritations that could due to be patch-fixed out or are just part of the game's mechanics and need to be kept in mind when playing. Playing for short lengths of time will keep you from being bothered by them too much or feel tempted to buy anything.
Recommended if you spend a lot of time on your computer, but the iOS version is more convenient and enjoyable.

An absolutely amazing and extremely addictive roguelike that will leave you wanting more and more and more. At least 100 hours in and I can never get enough this is by far one of the best values you can get for your money on this site.
-Graphics
Nothing mind blowing to see here, keep in mind this is an indie title, but the visuals are very sharp and crisp and the hand drawn style is something I think everyone could appreciate. Ed Mcmillen brings his dark imagination alive with cute enemy design with dark tones in a vivid and smooth way. 9/10
-Sound
Another excellent aspect of this game, Danny Baranowsky graces this game with an intoxicating score that never gets old and is always welcomed. The sound effects also nail it with gross tones and excellent notes that bring more life into the game. 10/10
-Controls
One of the few areas I believed needed work. A game that is a pain to play with mouse and keyboard, but feels amazing with controller, just needs mapping attention. I feel like this game deserved some native controller support. Once you get the controller mapped and configured however, it feels like a dream, I highly recommend using an Xbox controller when mapping. 7/10
-Gameplay
A randomly generated dungeon crawler, you'll complete a set number of levels and floors all ending with a boss fight. The level structure for this game as well as item placement and boss encounters are all random, which the only strategy for this game has to come from experience which is completely amazing. You clear rooms, discover treasure, acquire upgrades, fight bosses in the end. Will you make it? Will you get all the way to the end and choke? That's up to you. This is definitely the shining tower in this title which is most important in any game. 10/10
-Replayability
I believe I already used the term "Random" so I really cant stress enough just how impressive and addictive this title is. Everything about this game is random, item placement, loadout possibility, the structure and all is a random dip. 11/10
Overall while no game is perfect, this game comes pretty damn close. 9/10. Buy it if you don't have it, there are no regrets here.

After finishing Wasteland 2, I decided to write a review.

If you LOVED Fallout 2, you'll SORTA LIKE Wasteland 2!
If you've never PLAYED fallout 2 and are interested in Wasteland 2, instead; go buy or at least look at Fallout 2, right here on Steam.
This game kept me entertained for a solid 60 hours.... and then Hollywood... The buggiest land to exist in all video games, ever.
For the most part, the game is a load of fun (just not Hollywood). Great detail, good pathing on almost all maps and the AI is fairly balanced, if not a little clunky at times....
Wasteland 2's dialogue is sometimes some of the funniest stuff I've read in a long time. The random things NPC's say, etc. The storyline is serious and there's no slapstick comedy or anything like that, no poop jok---- well... okay, there are poop jokes but 95% of the game is serious and VERY well written.
The camera, however, is downright awful and the towns interior maps are hard to keep track of without map markers.
It feels rushed. Like this was supposed to be something much longer and bigger.
They call it the spiritual successor to Fallout 2, yet my one playthrough of FO2 on steam yielded around 140 hours ish. This, only 75.
My number one complaint is the ending credits
(what happened to the world after you saved it slideshow)
Even if you complete almost every task in the game, you won't get credit in most cases. The game will go against what you actually did; for example: I made a certain mercenary group become extinct, took over their prison and helped a town they were terrorizing. At end credits, the game had said that the gang I killed were stronger than ever and had never given up that town.

-- 4/10 --
The hours I've put into it make it worth the cost. If you don't have Fallout 2; go buy fallout 2 instead.

I never played WL1 unfortunately, it seems, I had missed out on some good old times. While it was provided with WL2 I can't find myself playing it, I have no history with it so I'd probably just find it frustrating to play (given its age). Anyways...
I dove straight into WL2 having no background of its story aside from it was the idea behind Fallout, or so I've been told. It's exactly what you think it is, a strategy game based in a wasteland. If you loved the play style and strategy of X-COM then you're going to love this one.
Creating your own squad of rejects is a fantastic feature that really give this game a personal touch. That piled atop the countless types of skill sets and passive ability makes the combinations limitless. You start out in a group of scrubs as a sort of Robin Hood squad beating up on those that choose absolute power over all.
The game is combat oriented, obviously, but contains plenty of story elements and dialog to make a well rounded adventure. The combat is a pause-based system, meaning that out of combat you remain in real-time however once you enter combat you're dropped into turn-based. Fights play out depending on your team composition, skills, and most importantly the type of opponent you're facing.
Non-combat related sections are filled with witty dialog and at times strange challenges that require certain skills to surpass.
My pain points are primarily in the chance-of-X percentages, which seem entirely incorrect, many of which are probably quite easy to fix if they choose to do so.
-Critical failures: This causes so much rage it's unreal. Seemingly a 1% chance here feels like 99.9%. WHY...it's a joke.
-Rogue chance: This is most definitely broken, proven when a squad mate with a reduced-to-zero chance went rogue on the FIRST TURN. Even after every turn he went rogue...
-Broken cover seems to be a big problem, obvious walls which should be providing the bonus...don't.
Side notes: I would highly recommend the save/char editor merely as a respec tool. Why this wasn't included as a training feature in the game baffles me. The skills can be confusing for most people and incorrectly allocating points can be a real game breaker.

This is a game in two parts, and unfortunately, I have to review it is such.
I can sum up part one in one word: Brilliant!
Here we have two characters in two seemingly unrelated situations. One has been chosen as a human sacrifice to a monster that has been terrorising the local villages for generations, the other is alone on a deep-space exploration vessel. You, as the player, have to guide these two through their own stories of "escape".
I found the story interesting, and then when the two characters briefly meet, then abruptly change places...
On to part two, and in a word: Disapointing.
After months of waiting, we get this lacklustre, almost generic point-and-click game that relies more on player knowlege than imersion in the story. I got stuck on several puzzles, only to discover that the solution requires finding something AS THE OTHER CHARACTER, totally destroying any immersion that I may have still had, and dumping me into the mode of "player behind the keyboard" instead.
And then, when the final solution required co-ordinating the actions of both characters at the same time, without either character even knowing what the other is doing, well, I guess that's the "Broken" part of Broken Age.
While I would like to recomend this game based on the first part, I just can't. Sorry.

Virginia is a short (clocking in at only about 2 hours of playtime) surreal first person experience with an excellent soundtrack and a unique graphical style.
If you are unfamiliar with the "Walking Simulator" genre be cautioned the genre is very minimalistic with player interaction. Although Virginia's gameplay consists mostly of what is seen in many other walking simulators, i.e. first person "experiences" triggered by the player by simply approaching a person, place, or thing and pressing a button to advance the next series of events, its presentation sets it apart within that genre to be a unique experience, which is in large part due to its unique visuals and the great soundtrack.
Though some have complained the "jumpcut" style of its narrative and scenes can be jarring, I found it pretty refreshing (at first- it did begin to wear on me by the end of the game as well, and I found myself becoming a bit impatient with the game always switching to another scene when I was hoping for a bit more of a linear narrative by the game's conclusion...) The player is often in surreal situations including
, and jumps into and out of vehicle seats. Virginia is an interesting cinematic experience, but the game is little else than that.
The soundtrack -performed by an actual orchestra- is particularly well done. The characters never speak, and instead do exaggerated, sometimes oddly "cartoony-looking" gestures to imply their emotions. This can be immersive from afar, but the closer you get to certain character models their general stylization begins to look a bit too wooden. Still, the game does a good job of depicting emotions between the characters. The game is recommended to run at 30fps as the creators intended, which I don't mind but I didn't bother to swap it to anything else. The graphical options are pretty limited in the game overall, but when viewing the game more as a prolonged, interactive series of events or cutscenes experienced through the first person view, it didn't bother me as much.
I enjoyed the game's locale and style overall, and its soundtrack and the surreal, frequent changes of scene are all pretty captivating for a passive player experience. For better or for worse, Viriginia leans heavily into the fact that it is more a cinematic experience first and a game second, with even the game itself alluding to this inclination in its main menu option to "Resume Feature" when selecting to pick up the game where you left off (as well as having a chapter select screen very reminiscent of a DVD...)
I enjoyed Viriginia for what it was, but I was beginning to lose my patience with some of its nonsense (and at times meandering plot) by the end of the tale.

First off:  MAJOR plot spoilers but no puzzle solutions.  That said, unless you subscribe to this specific theory, the plot doesn't have a whole lot of weight or emotional depth, at least from where I'm viewing it.  It's a silly game and that's absolutely fine.  I bought it because I wanted six or seven hours of mashing every single object I picked up into every single interactable location I came across, and it did indeed give me that, plus some rather ingenious brainteasers (triangle/circle lock puzzle, I'm looking at you).
But.  Um.  So.  There's a weird thing about this.  I played this with a group of people, and we all found it rather silly, and some of the Moon Logic Puzzles are frustrating, but we cheated, because the point was to have fun, and we got about halfway through (I just finished it on my own).
And.... about at the point where we discovered the main character's name was Umang and he looked like a white guy with a vacant stare, and that the "Sacred Rings" looked exactly like a gyroscopic physics toy, we collectively decided to stop taking the game seriously, and we made it our headcanon that he was, in fact, a patient at a mental hosptial, and the other characters were the doctors trying to help him, or other patients, and all these puzzles were little tasks they'd given him to help him reconnect with the physical world and keep him occupied, so he wouldn't hurt himself or others.  It kept the occasional non-intuituve answer from seeming pointless, and as time went by it got more and more fun to point out, you know, "More evidence for the asylum theory!"
They left off on the world of Knockoff Skyrim in the Clouds, and I kept going.  And I kept finding more and more places where the asylum theory fit.  The children left alone after their mother died.  The nonsensical way the puzzles and worlds are connected.  The way the Grain of Life connects to the Stardust.  The fact that everyone who helps you can only help to a certain extent, even though they are supposedly the masters of their realm - one even says, "The rest you will need to do on your own."  The way Umang is pushed over and over and over to journey to these lands, and the way he is eventually pushed to, quite literally, travel to an alternate reality.  And it makes his reaction to that all the more poignant.
(The only wrench in this plan is the Generic Evil Guy (TM) who gloats over his sequel hook/plot device, but I'm ignoring that because it's literally the only thing that stops this interpretation from flying like a paper airplane straight into the back of the teacher's head.  And I haven't played the second one, or the third one if that exists yet, so I dunno, maybe I can make something up.)
Let me put it this way.  On its own, this is a more or less stupid game with a hysterically funny plotline at best and a clunky, boring one at worst.  Whoever came up with the proper nouns in this game should be forced to redraw all the characters as though they actually come from the cultures in which their names originate - for instance, I don't know that many blond white guys from India, and yet Google tells me that is where the name Umang originates.  The graphics are as advertised: from 2007.  The music is on a loop that's not long enough, and the audio transitions and voice acting are about as smooth and skillfully executed as me getting up before noon on a Saturday.  At one point, if you fail to do several things in the correct order, you are treated to a blacksmith wearing some kind of flexible metal (?) staring at you/Umang with what appears to be unrepentant (though restrained) lust (??), and you are allowed to repeat this five-second cutscene as often as you like (???).  I turned all the sound off partway through and substituted in the Pacific Rim soundtrack, which by total chance played "Mako" at exactly the right moment to give the ending cutscene a beautiful, ethereal, almost
feel.
On the other hand. I love what I was able to make of this game.  I love that I can share it with everyone else, and that the narrative was free enough that this is a viable interpretation.  I love the puzzle solving and the fact that for the most part, there was a great balance between the amount of effort I exerted to solve the puzzles (at least, the ones I didn't peek on) and the cutscene, item, new area or plot detail I was rewarded with (this is definitely a game for people who like shiny things).
Overall - if you'd like the game to carry itself and take itself seriously, don't play this, because it's not what you're looking for.  If you'd like to solve some puzzles and maybe laugh a little at the absurdity of what's going on, at least at face value, and then find meaning in your own interpretations - then this is perfect.  I wish you good night, good luck, and a good imagination.

Broken Age is a fun but uneven, oddly paced, hit-or-miss affair. I will still recommend it on the merit is that it tries very hard to do the adventure game genre justice with the unique telling of a story with two separate characters. It also plays with a dream-like aesthetic that is often soft and cuddly that makes up for any faults I found with it. The puzzles also try to recapture the spirit of LucasArts days puzzle solving with some good logical puzzles included, it is a fairly fun experience overall.
Storywise, this one probably wouldn't win any awards, it's lackluster in back story and a lot of the characters' dialogue comes across pretty chill. All the characters are very charming, and I think my favourites are still the hexipals, they're just so cute! Honestly funny moments are too few and far between. Tim Schafer's dialogue and story writing skills unfortunately weren't on full display here, and I grew to miss the wit that usually was to be found in his work.
Some players will find the puzzles too easy in the first act and too challenging in the second act. I personally found myself stuck a few times in the second act, but some friendly hints along the way got me back on track. The logical puzzles are good and they required me to have the pen and paper handy, something I really enjoy doing when solving puzzles.
What I truly appreciated about Broken Age was that Tim tried telling the story in a format that was something different, where the player is the unseen link between two physically separated characters. Some puzzles are solved with both characters seeing clues that aid the opposite character, all without them speaking or saying anything. I wish this idea could have been taken further.
For those who enjoy a good adventure game will certainly enjoy this title and still be pleased by the art, puzzle design and the Schafer style storytelling. Also, with a soft and cuddly aesthetic, it's hard to be displeased with the final product.

This should not have been a game. Despite finding the symbolism ham-fisted and the story at times quite convoluted and unnecessary, simply making this a short film would eliminate my biggest complaint by far.
I'm a fan of walking simulators. Gone Home was the first one to grab me due to it's ability to tell a simple story through exploration. The game wasn't built around the story. Despite the lack of gameplay mechanics, exploration was key to understanding the characters and hence the plot; they work in tangent.
The Stanley Parable, another game that engaged me through a unique implementation of a narration system that reacts to your decisions, similar to Bastion's. It worked on both a gameplay and meta commentary level. You could take it for what it is, enjoy the novelty and humour in someone reflecting on your movement in real time, or you could dig deeper into how the narration comments on player behaviour and game design.
Virginia stands out in that it does neither of these things, nor anything distinctive and remarkable to shape the growing genre like the former games did. It's merely a film stuck behind the constraints of player input, and even though I disliked the substance in this game, if this was an hour long animation I could easily recommend it.
The problem is everything is handed to you. No amount of exploration or decision making (because there is none) will change the outcome of an event or add any new information. There is very literally no reason for player control, made even worse since the crosshair highlights the object in the scene you need to interact with. In another game, say a commentary on the role of an actor and how they parallel a player in a video game (or walking sim in specific), following strict rules set by the director/game designer could absolutely work, but this isn't that.
Virginia is a semi-abstract cop conspiracy story with an overreliance on heavy handed symbolism and quick cuts. The end credits reveal the main inspiration was Thirty Flights of Loving, another game to use a lot of quick cuts. This is what confuses me, because TFoL uses quick cuts with a clear purpose; for stylisation and story development. Virginia uses quick cuts because at heart it wants to be a movie.
In TFoL, there is merit for exploring the levels, as you gain information into what character motivations and more critically the foundation of the plot itself. Since Virginia hands all of this to you, there is no need to explore even if that was an option.
To end with I’d like to highlight that anyone interested in sound used in games should check this out. The sound design is phenomenal, from the diverse soundtrack to the superbly accurate ambient effects, this aspect was the only thing keeping me engaged at all and I’d easily say this is one of my favourite examples of sound used in a video game ever.
Sadly, the rest of the game fails on fundamental levels, and unless you want something to nap to I’d suggest steering clear.

At first glance this is a Myst clone. No doubt about that.  But the differance between Aura and a good adventure game like Myst is that there is immersion and substance to what you're doing and why.  Aura gives you a brief introduction then plops you into its world with no idea what you're supposed to do.  It's another 360 degree panoramic adventure game like Myst III and IV and there's nothing wrong with that.  Where Aura gets it wrong is that there is no logic to some of the puzzles. They're just there for the sake of a puzzle to impede your progress.  There is no dialogue besides the introduction. No lore explaining anything besides the introduction.  You have a desire to get the rings of destiny or some such but while in the game you really don't know why you're doing certain things becasue nothing is explained.
The game does give you hints in the form of a journal which gives you a very 'basic' understanding of how to proceed.  The immersion factor is Aura's biggest weakness.  The background music is just awful. It's a mixture of metal and synthesizers.  For a fantasy adventure game it doesn't fit AT ALL.
For 5 bucks I guess this is worth a buy...only if you're  fan of Myst.  But good luck trying to get immersed in Aura's world.  I didn't enjoy it at all.

If The Witcher was great, then The Witcher 2 is phenomenal. CDProjekt Red out did themselves with this sequal. Everything that made the original great, has been included, and even improved on greatly. The writing is engaging, the characters are vibrant and interesting, the enviroments are varried and incredibly gorgeous, and the story is even bigger than before. With an "import save" feature, everything you've done in the first Witcher has an impact on the narrative and events that you experience in the game. To make a long story short: They've turned this game up to 11. Another notable improvement over the first is the overhauled combat system. Although it has been switched from the "styles" combat, to a more standard 3rd person hack'n'slash system of combat, it feels thousands of times more fluid, and is incredibly satisfying. Not to mention with the addition of much more loot, armors, and steel/silver swords to pick from, it's a much more customizable combat experience than the first was. Incredible game, and if the series improves at the rate is has between the original and this title, I can only imagine what's to come in The Witcher 3.

I DO NOT RECCOMMEND THIS GAME FOR COMPETITIVE PLAY AT ALL IN ITS CURRENT STATE! However, for the first 100 hours this game is absolutely amazing!
I will begin with the bad: After grinding for hours playing most characters, you can unlock competitive game matches in which it is suppose to match your player skill with similar players to play a match with people at roughly your skill level. The problem with this is because the game is a MOBA, some people do not understand that there are roles that if played correctly, greatly enhances a teams ability to win the match. Majority of the matches you will get stuck with people who really have either no idea what they are doing, play like complete crap, or just plain out ignore the team meta/objective to win the match and instead play whoever they want to play/do their own thing.
This is all fine and all, but THE GAME DOES NOT LET YOU MAKE YOUR OWN TEAMS! Therefore if you actaully want to play team vrs team matches, you'll be out of luck. The best you can get is the ability to group up with 1 friend and join a match full of randoms. This is very frustrating as you may get stuck on a really bad losing streak because of "that one guy" on your team who plays a healer as a flanker etc...
I only really mention this as after 100 hours you'll reach a skill level where you are likely always to make first place in casual matches with any hero making the game boring and too easy, but the only alternative is a coin flip competitive match.
THE GAME IS IN BETA, SO THIS IS NOT A DEAL BREAKER IN MY MIND. I just hope they plan to fix it before an offical release.
Now the good:
Free to play: As of this review, the game is a true free to play game meaning all characters and skins can be achieved without having to spend a dime. I even have gotten premium skins from logging in daily to get gems. You'll have access to a good sort of starter characters, and can unlock the other ones by leveling up and earning gold. And the good thing about this game is that it does not have stupid time windows when you unlock a character. Once you unlock a character, you have them to play with for good. You can also buy the founders pack to skip all the grind which is a good option for those with less time and those who would like to support this cool game.
Wide variety of characters: There are four character classes to choose from and a large variety of characters to play from.  The game is great for allowing you to switch up play styles or the mood you feel like playing in. You can play as a full on healer, a crazy damage dealer, an objective tank, or even a person who sneaks up and flanks enemies. The game almost never gets dull even over long play times.
Easy to learn, hard to master: The game is super easy to pick up (unlike dota) and the learning curve is small, but it takes awhile to master heroes abilities and playstyles. And some heroes take much longer than others to master, leaving a lot of challenge in for those who enjoy it.
Lower end pc friendly: While some may bash the game for having "poor graphics" I think they are just fine, and shouldn't be the main focus of the game anyway. After all most people play games to have fun or to compete. The graphics are friendly for those who are on pc's with a little bit dated hardware, so they can still play this game without having massive framerate problems.
Final Thoughts: I really think that if you're looking at this game and even have the slightest interest, that you should go ahead and try it. I orginally didn't think I'd like this game when I gave it a go, but now i have 200+ hours into it already. It is surprisingly really fun.
I am upset that this game is not really competitve as most competitive games are usually completely one sided, but ocassionally you'll actually get a match where its down to the wire. But like i said the game is in beta, and i'm keeping my fingers crossed that they will fix the competitive match making before a full release.
So download the game right now and give it a shot!

This is a great game, though it hasn't aged well. It is still a lot of fun to play: a simpler, more streamlined version of Civilization, without things such as unit promotions and religion... just the essential Civ. It is different enough from newer games to be worth playing, it is not just the same but worse. The old graphics show their age, but in the end are easy to bear. But the user interface... yeah, that is a tough one. If you already are used to old strategy games, you probably can deal with it; but if you are not, figuring out the unintuitive mechanics and the convoluted way of showing and doing things might be a challenge in the beginning and make it hard to enjoy the game itself. If you can get past this barrier, go ahead and give Civ3 a try, but if you want a better experience with a convenient and intuitive UI maybe stick to newer titles.

When I bought Puzzle Kingdoms, it was on a 90% Steam sale and costed me a buck and a half. Unfortunately, money isn't the biggest concern when it comes to a game's actual worth, the real valuable resource we truly pay when playing games is time.
Puzzle Kingdoms is a Bejeweled-like puzzle game with some strategy RPG elements thrown in. Now if you're not farmiliar with those match the shapes kind of games that's been flooding the web for the past several years, you're not missing much. The activity consists of endlessly and effortlessly moving shapes around in one way or another to group them together, and when you do a nice little sound effect plays and the shapes disappear to make room for new ones, manipulating your brain with constant small benefits to drive you to keep playing.
While doing a good job at cloaking itself from the fact, Puzzle Kingdoms is much like those games. The game provides you with "troops" you can buy and use which can attack and deal damage to enemy troops after you have matched the same shape enough times, and later on gives you more kinds of troops and different items which give you slight benefits. At first one may think the game has a neat twist to the formula, but soon enough one will discover that the game is just covering it's one boring mechanic- moving shapes around to group them- with much more distraction and brain manipulations than the other games of it's type, rather than adding any new interesting mechanics.
The game is insultingly easy, giving you a staggering amout of money to endlessly fill up your board with troops while the opposition never attacks you with anything bigger than what you already have. It forces you into painfully slow paced puzzles that makes you roll an invisible dice over and over again until you win, all for the sake of a story that is so obviously ment to manipulate you into giving any context to matching shapes it's laughable. The choices made in this game- the kind of troops you buy and the items you equip- have zero implication egainst an opponent that literally can't beat you as long as you deny him a specific shape to group together.
The game as a whole can pretty much last forever, and that is a pretty big part of the problem- it manipulates you to play it endlessly and effortlessly and in turn do nothing but waste your precious time. If a game does that it should at least have a strong point (Prime examples are Allan Blomquist and Kyle Gabler's "Little Inferno" or Edmund Mcmillen's "AVGM") or have some really solid mechanics to go with it so the player will have to [god forbid] think about the game.
As much the gaming industry wants to dany it, "time spent divided by money spent" is not a healthy way to measure a game's value, because that implies your time is a bad thing you want to throw as much of it away as possible. This game is just not worth your time even if it costed you zero dollars.
Please, do something and play something meaningful and fulfilling with that time, because your time is limited and it is worth much more than this.

A must have action thriller for those fans of psychological and eldritch horror. Not a moment gone by without suspense and constant mystery.
Pros:
-Incredibly rich and detailed world, this is an older title but its eye for detail is out the wazoo
-Episodic narrative that really immerses you with fantastic (and slightly tragic) writing
-Very challenging gameplay
-Creative use of weaponry
Cons:
-Lethargic mobility, and wonky vehicle physics
-The game holds you back quite a few times which could get annoying on a 2nd or 3rd playthrough
-Lip synching could've been better
-The light can be a bit too bright, making it hard to see
A masterfully written and bearing game wrapped within so much mystery that will make you question more well after you've finished it, definitely worth another playthrough (do it on Nightmare, it's not that tough) just to get a full understanding of it all. I really suggest grabbing all of the manuscripts (I mean all of them) so you can really get a sense of how the story developed.
The thrill and combat is near constant, with only a few short beautiful vistas to give you a breather, and you'll definitely be grinding teeth now and then until you fully master it all. My tip, conserve your ammunition! Now I understand that Alan isn't exactly an athlete or action hero, but he sometimes moves in a way that is way too slow, taking his time to do his stuff when you're really pressed for time, it shouldn't be that hard to actually SPRINT instead of running just a bit faster for a bit longer, or hurry up with climbing up ladders or getting in and out of vehicles, which takes me to the next point - they're pretty garbage. They're like jello on ice, so be careful when maneuvering the finnicky cars. You'd best leave them alone altogether if they weren't useful for traversing long and sometimes dangerous lengths, so be warned! The game also tends to interrupt your flow by slowing down time to show incoming enemies or pan the camera to locations that are kind of obvious to get to, it's fine on your first playthrough, but gets quite frustrating on your next ones.
All in all, besides those gripes, I'd have to say this is one of the best horror games I've played yet, and it shows that a game doesn't have to rely on gore or excessive action to tell a great story and really strike a sense of fear and anxiety in you.

I sunk many an hour into the original Puzzle Quest, lured in with its simple match-3 mechanics and addictive leveling system. But after trying to get in to Puzzle Kingdoms twice, I've given up. Both times, I didn't get far enough to see some of the features it has to offer. The problem is that the actual puzzle gameplay is inferior to what other games in this genre bring to the table.
The issues I have with the gameplay are as follows:
- Whereas standard match-3 gameplay requires only a few seconds to scan the board and look for the best move, Puzzle Kingdoms, with its numerous possibilities based on the icons that can slide in and out of gameplay, requires more care. This slows down the game, increasing the amount of time one has to take between moves. Some may like this, but I miss the faster gameplay experience.
- “Dueling” match-3 games can sometimes be unfair based on what drops into play. Even though one knows the first icon that comes into a row or column in Puzzle Kingdoms, the need to only connect three or more (not three-in-a-row) tends to make things especially random. Simple matches often turn into devastating combos that are impossible to predict.
- This game is made for touch-screen controls. If you have one, great. If not, prepare for an awkward “click and drag” fest or the counter-intuitive “click the slide you want to slide the icon in on, not the side you want the icons to move out.” Controller support is non-existent, so don't expect an easy-to-use system like used in puzzle games similar to this one, such as Yoshi's Cookie on the consoles of yore.
This isn't a complete review of what the game has to offer, but it demonstrates how that the secret sauce for puzzle games like Puzzle Quest isn't in the metagame and story (which are what elevates them beyond Bejeweled), but the core puzzle mechanics. And in this case, Puzzle Kingdoms did not fit the bill for me and I have to move on to other gameplay experiences that are more to my liking.

Fallout shelter is a fun little game that you play for five to ten minutes at a time that can get pretty challenging at times. A lot will complain about it being a 'pay to win' game, but it isn't; if you're impatient or make stupid decisions, like send your dwellers out into the wasteland with no stimpaks or horde your weapons instead of equipping people, then you'll be tempted to buy lunchboxes and other items. But that's why this is a 5-10 minute session game: you check your vault(s) in the morning, at lunch, after dinner, or whenever you have a few free minutes with nothing to do, fiddle around, and go about your day, including playing other games. There's no need to spend money on this game in order to enjoy it.
There are a few issues that do prevent me from giving this game a better score and will irritate you:
-The cursor isn't precise in some situations, the most common one being needing to place dwellers on the ceiling of the room you assign them instead of in the room itself.
-When combat takes place in some of the rooms, dwellers will stack and stand behind each other, preventing you from clicking on the right person to heal them. This happens rarely, but when it does, you will need to pay to resurrect your dweller what feels unnecessarily.
-About a third of the Mysterious Stranger's spawn locations, namely those with forebround and background areas, are cheap; as in, he's behind a wall or one of your dwellers and unless you dramatically change the angle of your view, you won't see him, even if that room is the only thing you see. You'll get sick of this fast and is something that, like the dwellers stacking in rare combat instances, needs to be patch-fixed so it's less cheatsy BS.
-Click and draging to change perspective is not recommended. Accidentally click on a dweller and you'll end up sending them somewhere you don't want or just unasign them. Also, double-clicking while doing this causes the camera to focus on the person or room you double-clicked, fighting against your manual controls and require you to double-click and let the camera do what it wants before you get control back or else you'll be camera-locked in that one dweller or room.
These are all minor annoyances and irritations that could due to be patch-fixed out or are just part of the game's mechanics and need to be kept in mind when playing. Playing for short lengths of time will keep you from being bothered by them too much or feel tempted to buy anything.
Recommended if you spend a lot of time on your computer, but the iOS version is more convenient and enjoyable.

To be honest I didn't know this title until it's been out from years and was already on heavy sale. Lucky me. I knew Remedy for their masterpiece, Max Payne, so when I realized Alan Wake was their latest game I took it without further inquiries. And I really believe I was right.
Alan Wake is a third action (and I dare to call it) survival shooter (considered the measured amount of ammos and the weak constitution of the protagonist). You are Alan Wake, a world best seller Writer... Kind of a Stephen King level of Fame. Due to the amount of stress after the writing of the last book Alan is retiring with his beloved Wife Alice in a small mountain town called Bright Falls. When they get to their cabin Alice is abducted by a dark entity and pulled to the depth of Cauldron Lake. Alan will then realize that there's something really odd and dark happening in Bright Falls and their citizens.
The game is structured as a classic third person shooter, but you won't have any mass destruction weapon, nor you won't have any huge amount of ammos. The most interesting concept in the gameplay is the contrast between light and darkness, so when the Takens (citizens possessed by darkness) approach you, you must light them with your torch first in order to get rid of their "protective dark aura" and be able to shoot them and eliminate them. Also there are few street lamps here and there that will give you protection against them (and serve as checkpoint as well). Besides, this game is definitely full of collectibles that will lead to various achievements.

Let's start with the overall setting: the game's very atmospheric. The world is finely crafted and believable and makes the player want to go exploring it further. It's designed like a TV show, and it pays homage to Twin Peaks and other mystery/thriller shows. I also liked the tongue-in-cheek humour in the Twilight Zone parodies and TV talk shows. The characters are memorable and even likeable (except Alan himself IMHO). The characters have a pretty decent voice acting, but horrible lip-syncing. Their mouths are just unnatural and gave me the creeps (purposefully uncanny valley or just inability/laziness?).
The gameplay is smooth and involves a heavy use of light, which adds to the atmosphere nicely. The shadows are impressive. Unfortunately the gameplay repeats itself and you start noticing some patterns. For example, you mostly run through linear paths, fighting enemies every 2 minutes. And at the end of the path there's a calm area and you always drop down into a lower platform, so that you can't go back where you came from. This is an arena, where you have to hold out for a certain time or fight a miniboss. Or your path is suddenly blocked off by some falling debris or something and you have to find another way around. You always see it coming and it gets really tiring after a while. This is my main gripe with the game; it's repetitive.
The game starts slow and picks up the pace around midway through. It kind of keeps you interested throughout, just enough to not make you want to uninstall it before finishing it. But if you're not a patient player, this game might not be worth your while. In the end, you're not missing much. I'm recommending this game for its atmospheric qualities only, the rest is a bit unrewarding. There are a few moments that I'll remember fondly, like the "rock concert" or the part where Sarah and Barry join you. The game has some frustrating moments, but it's never too difficult if you take the time to learn the mechanics.

Let all comparisons to Fallout 1 and/or 2 be retroactively rendered null and void with the same nullification applied to all comparisons henceforth. Simply put: if you are looking for an experience like the original Fallouts, keep looking. This isn't any fraction as good as either of them because it simply isn't good at all.
I can forgive an ENORMOUS quantity of technical faults. Bugs, bland combat, and graphics that were obsolete 10 years ago simply don't phase me if the less tangible aspects of a game are exceptional. These aspects include, in order: writing, character interaction, and world interaction/immersion (coherence, reactivity and a sense of player agency). Fallout 1 and 2 had these in spades and although no game can touch Planescape: Torment's character interaction, I at least never felt like I was running around with faceless, generic AIs for companions.
I should've known by the fact that you create an entire party (versus one player character who represents you) that the most meaningful and elusive elements of an RPG would be missing (the feeling that you're a participant in a world). The difference between Fallout and Wasteland 2 is like the difference between Baldur's Gate 2 and Icewind Dale...except Icewind Dale advertised itself correctly and successfully executed the thing it was trying to do/be.
I don't know if it was laziness or simply a lack of skill that produced this heap of a plot, but it feels like it could be either and/or both. At around the 12 hour mark, I hear the radio transmission about becoming immortal, invulnerable, disease free and beautiful...Combined with the mysterious robotic/synthetic threat, the 'faction' known as Children of the Cathedral and the basic ability to put 2 and 2 together, I deduced that the plot was something to do with turning people into robots. Not unlike Fallout 1's Children of the Cathedral being a front for the Master seeking to turn people into mutants who are long-lived, disease free, stronger, faster, better, whatever. That's so much not unlike it, that it's EXACTLY like it. You can't even call that an homage...because homage doesn't mean 'blatant ripoff'.
And the writing that everyone is showering in praise? Here's a stool - I mean writing - sample from Wasteland 2: "A lone road stretches on. A dry wind whips at your back with the sandy shards from decades of lost hopes and dreams." That's the line of text you get on entering The Prison...which is a former prison now occupied by raiders. So not only is there no visible/audible wind/swirls/eddies/gusts, the other half of the description is hard to connect to a place that housed criminals in the past and present. I'm not sure that I care about the hopes and dreams of murderers...and unwarranted melodrama aside, it's just too lengthy and hard to read...the second sentence should've been broken up into two. Compare this with a description from Fallout 2: "Before you stands Hakunin, the village shaman. He appraises you with his crazy eyes from somewhere in the world only he inhabits." Not only is that less cumbersome/awkward to read, when you actually see and speak to Hakunin, you realize that a more perfect description could not have been penned.
All I have to say about the music is that I can't believe it was done by the same Mark Morgan who composed Fallout 1 and 2's music. It's as if he couldn't find any inspiration in the material for which he was to compose. No surprise there.
The voice work is...serviceable at best and one step shy of laughably bad at worst...but mostly serviceable. I don't know if it was for a lack of space on CDs or for an abundance of sense, but games back in the day RIGHTLY kept voice acting to a minimum. This guaranteed that the voices that were present were of excellent quality. Compare this to the Elderscrolls approach of giving a million characters the same grating voice. Thank christ for the march of technology. There simply isn't a game budget (unless Warren Buffet was involved) to fund quality voice acting for all characters. Wasteland 2 seemed to understand that...but then couldn't cast decent actors for the few voiced characters it had. It also should've voiced fewer characters and hired better actors instead.
That about covers all the non-mechanical stuff. And the mechanical stuff has already been covered by everyone else and yes, it's as awful as they say. 5 different skills for opening things. 3 different skills for talking to people. Did there really have to be separate skills for assault rifles and SMGs? Or for bladed and blunt weapons? The more obscure skills yielded disproportionately better results than the generally useful ones, artificially decreasing the effectiveness of reasonable characters. For instance: Hard safes contained the same crap as easy safes but hard toasters contain useful and unique weapons?!? 4% jam rates translate to 6 characters jamming in a row for two turns??? It costs more action points to clear a jam than to reload?!?!?! I can make headshots but I can't target other body parts for at least SOME tactical depth?!?! Enemies can't do more than charge or stay in place? Characters' faces can't have features in 2015???
I could've forgiven all of that...if only Wasteland 2 gave me a world I could care about with characters that were more than quest dispensers and text that was better than college level. UGH! Even the first major choice you make, going to Ag Center or Highpool, is so poorly and heavy-handedly executed. HERE ARE TWO PLACES THAT NEED RESCUING BUT YOU ONLY HAVE TIME TO SAVE ONE. MAKE A HARD CHOICE AND THEN LISTEN TO THE DRAMA OF THE SCREAMING PEOPLE FROM THE PLACE YOU CHOSE NOT TO GO TO!!! IT'S BRILLIANT AND IMPORTANT AND NOT AT ALL FORCED! In Fallout, there would've been 5 ways to handle it. 2 with different, gruesome outcomes. 2 different neutral outcomes. And 1 where the outcome was unrelated but important and revealed later in the game (like in the Vault City vs Gecko quest arc).
TL;DR Fallout is an experience. Wasteland 2 is just a game. Don't buy this thinking that your Fallout needs have finally been answered. They haven't. Lets just hope Beamdog somehow acquires the Fallout license and remakes Fallout 1 and 2 with added content or makes a Fallout 4...or something...I don't know...I have a Fallout deficiency.
