Hard West is a western-themed, turn-based, episodic RPG with some dark (as in horror) elements in it. There are 8 chapters, within which are several scenarios where there may be combat or puzzles to solve. The puzzles aren't really heavy duty, and the combat (once you get used to the system and weapons) is pretty simple. Concepts of cover apply here; there is also a "setup" real-time phase that allows you to explore and do things if you stay out of sight and not shoot anyone. Once you shoot someone or if they discover you, turn-based combat begins. You also get to collect cards that can boost your stats if you play the right poker hand. All in all:
Pros:
I like the western theme. As far as I know, there aren't any of this genre in a turn-based combat RPG
The narrator, Death, is a nice (albeit common) touch
The audio was authentic sounding (guns firing don't sound like modern guns, for e.g.), though music became a little repetitive after a while
Stats, loot, etc. only carry forward within each chapter, once you complete the chapter, you start fresh. This can also be a con, but I think it keeps the player on their toes
The game has you play the roles of many characters (not just the "hero" character), which is refreshing
The stat boosting cards are a nice feature
Cons
Inventory is too limited. You only get 2 slots for usable items, so there's a lot of effects you don't get to try out, or strategies, unless you keep replaying, but
Given the structure/design of the game, there's limited replay value
The game can be completed in around 20-30 hours
The campaign is fairly linear; there's pretty much just one story arc and one route to follow. Sometimes it feels very scripted
Once you get farther in the game, the load times took a while. You also can't save within the scenario, the game only auto-saves between chapters. This is not a big deal, but I have to mention it
I'm still recommending this game because I think the devs took a risk, and did a decent job with the released product. Although the backstory could be tighter -- why the Stranger appeared, the role of Purgatory, etc. -- the multiple viewpoints and different characters you get to play make up for it. And in the end, the overarching lesson that "bad things sometimes happen to good people" is all too true, and all too tragic.

TOBII 4C EYE TRACKING MINI REVIEW SERIES - Amphora
CORE GAME SCORE 3/5
EYE TRACKING SCORE 3/5 (for immersion)
(NB - I'm not reviewing the whole game, just how well the eye tracking worked FOR ME with Tobii 4C eye tracker e.g. was it well implemnted and did using it add something to the game. Assume if I'm bothering to review the game for it's implementation of eye tracking, I like the core game itself).
* Eye tracking appears to be integrated into the game settings which are accessed in game but are just on / off - basically acts as an in game hint tool / adds to the immersion
* Look around 'extended view' worked but adds little
* The smoke follows your gaze and adds visible / audible hints when you look at an object that you can interact with
* There are also HDR style lighting effects when you look at bright objects
Overall, another intriguing little basic physics puzzle game with fanatastic, shadow puppet art style, you control the smoke (from the Amphora of the title) to interact with objects on screen in a dreamy / fairy tale style series of simple puzzles. The game has a fairly intuitive control scheme using the mouse to control the smoke and in this case the eye tracking adds little to the gameplay (you still basic control it with thew mouse) but the fact the beautifully animated smoke follows your gaze is quite mesmerising. The game feels a little short but I bought it on sale so I'm OK with that.
An enchanting little gem.

It's hard not to compare this to entries in the Myst series, specifically Myst III: Exile and Myst IV: Revelation. This is mostly due to the fact that numerous elements were borrowed from each of those games and made just different enough not to seem as though Streko Graphics had done little more than create a Myst clone.
While this is a perfectly serviceable adventure game, it's not without flaws (some major, some minor depending on how particular the player is).
(A technical aside - some bugs do exist within the game and may likely go unpatched given the age of the title, including a crash to desktop when attempting to delete a save through the in-game menu)
The age of the title means that it hasn't held up well over the years, so all the modern visual comforts and relevant settings that accompany them are absent. No true widescreen support and no option to run windowed being two prime examples. The extent of the video settings go as far as color depth options and a few standard definition resolution choices.
Going hand in hand with that, most of the 3D modeling in the game is standard fare for the time this title was originally released. Some of the characters look absolutely ridiculous at times and move in a rather wooden manner. Something that certainly allows one to appreciate the advances in that technology at present.
As to the plot, what's there is a fraction of a whole. This isn't made clear here on the store page but this is the first part of a series which means the story ends on something of a cliffhanger.
What story that is present isn't all that compelling and lacks depth, especially when it comes to the characters it introduces.
Unfortunately most of the voice acting in the game is substandard, delivered in monotone with no real inflection toward emotion (perhaps best exemplified by the blacksmith character who does nothing but shout in his brief interaction sequence yet still manages not to sound angry while doing it).
Gameplay is typical of the adventure game type - click to navigate a pre-rendered landscape and interact with points of interest. A majority of the puzzles are simple and can be solved without use of a hint system or walkthrough. Only one puzzle in the entire game is randomized, frustratingly to the point where it becomes less a traditional puzzle and more a mini-game of chance as to how many tries it takes before the correct sequence is found.
Don't be fooled entirely by the simplicity though as there are a small number of puzzles that present a challenge in how they can be solved.
The music and sound design are a mixed blessing somewhat. Most of the game's soundtrack consists of pieces of music that have utterly random ambient noises and sound effects dropped within the middle of their loops. This leads to awkward moments at certain points in the game where something like a door knock can be misinterpreted as a cue that a door nearby needs opened.
Likewise there are questionable moments of music used that betray the atmosphere of the game at certain times. Several dramatic stings are completely out of place in the likes of a small mirrored chamber or a well lit, spacious room.
The pre-rendered environments in the game are quite possibly the best done aspect of it. Seeing flecked paint on aging wood or an expanse of snow covered land watched over by a cadre of planets is nothing short of wonderful.
Taking Aura: Fate of the Ages for what it is, would I recommend it? In general, no. While it is not entirely horrible, there are better examples of the adventure game to play (be it Myst or otherwise) that accomplish exactly what this game does (if not more).
However, if you've exhausted the number of adventure games (scarce as they come these days) available to play then Aura: Fate of the Ages is (possibly) worth a few hours of your time. It likely won't climb to the top of your "best of" list but it's definitely not a total failure of the genre either.

Amphora is a short physics based puzzle game with the story following the life of a girl, from infancy to adulthood. It has a beautiful art style and wonderfully enchanting music.
You aren't given any instuctions or hints to solve the puzzles, instead you must look around the enviroment and use this information and your own logic to figure out what the game wants from you. For the most part this was not a particular problem, as after a short bit of time I could figure out what I had to do to get things moving along.
There were, however, one or two puzzles the frustrated me a good deal, because I had figured out what to do but it felt like the placements of the objects and the lines seemed finicky to the point where I essentially had the solution but it was off by just a hair or two.
Despite this annoying aspect, I feel like overall the game was well done and an enjoyable experience because there wasn't much problem with the other puzzles and the visuals and the audio were so aesthetically pleasing that it was hard to dislike the game just for the little trouble it caused.
Given the mostly positive aspects of the game I would reccomend it, but it would probably be better to get on a sale as it is a shorter game (it took me about 4 hours to get all the achievments, which I did through two playthroughs - my second one obviously being much shorter than the first because I knew the solutions).

Virginia is art.
Before you start playing the game you should know, that you shouldn't expect any gameplay. Your actions are limited to a few interactions with certain objects and walking.
Instead this game offers you a 90 minute long David Lynch, Twin Peaks-esque experience and trip that you will certainly not forget for a long while. The soundtrack is absolutely amazing an accompanies the game perfectly.
The story is kept vage enough to keep you speculating and encourage theories but there still is enough for anyone to get the gist.
The way this game is paced is very interesting and innovative. Even in walking sections they use jump cuts as a form of cutting out any down time. The game could have easily been stretched but that wouldn't have made it any better.
Virginia is certainly not for everybody. Even though it makes a strong case on the "games as a form of art discussion", its short (more movie like) run time and the absence of real gameplay may upset some.
If you like Narrative Exploration Games (just a fancy word for Walking Simulator, a term which just gives a wrong impression) like Gone Home or Firewatch you will like this one too, if you do not, than you won't. But espacially for a few Dollars on Sale this is worth a try.

Ultimately, I did not like Virginia.
I have no problem with this genre - 'interactive narrative' or 'walking simulator' - because I enjoyed many other titles such as The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Gone Home, and Thirty Flights of Loving.
The manner of how the story was told in Virginia was the main problem.  Although I didn't have a problem with the jump cuts - Thirty Flights of Loving did this as well - I found the changing of timelines and perspectives to be confusing.  Also, in the last portion of the story, Virginia seemed to show several different endings simultaneously, as if the authors could not agree on how the story should play out.
The lack of dialog was not a problem in itself, but it was difficult to understand the emotions at play in some of the scenes.  It may have helped if the characters had more detailed faces to better convey what they were feeling.  And some of the characters looked too similar, which led to some of the confusion.  Again, if the characters were more distinctive and unique, this may have helped.
On a positive note, the music is fantastic.  Having a full orchestra perform the score was a really nice touch.  The environments are also beautiful.

This is, honestly, one of the best games I've ever played. While the campaign would make Tolkien roll in his grave (Shelob is a
), it's got an amazing story, though parts of it you can kind of see coming. The armor and weapons give you huge customization options to your play style, but be warned, the Nemesis system will make you deviate from your preferred combat style. It will force you into uncomfortable situations that make you a better player. In short, adapt or die. This game has a more open-ended ending than Shadow of Mordor had, with much more end game content and missions like the Slaughter Tribe (if you chose to purchase that DLC) missions to keep you having fun. My personal goal is to install Legendary warchiefs at all my fortresses. A small note on microtransactions: They're not as bad as everyone is letting on. You surely do not need them to complete the game and get the best orcs. You can find a lot of them in the landscape. My personal rating is a 9/10, one point removed for small nitpicky things like odd graphical images, some glitchy combat, and personal story gripes.

What do you do if you really want to make a detective show but you only know how to programme games? You make Virginia of course!
If it wasn't for its unique (if perhaps a little uninteresting) art style, Virginia would be pretty hollow in every regard. There is no issue with wearing your influences on your sleeve, but all of Virginia's attempts to be enigmatic on anything deeper than an artificial level just leave it feeling like a cheap knock-off of Twin Peaks. As a player, I felt next to no engagement with the story. It's just Lynchian cliché after cliché after cliché. It brings nothing new to the table, and in the time it took me to complete it, I could have watched an episode of the show it so desperately wants to be -- that would have at least left me feeling satisfied.
Just watch a walkthrough on YouTube for free -- if it's meant to be "treated as a film," then do exactly that.
If your a fan of fantasy in any shape or form, not playing this game through at least once is a crime.

I'll tell you why you may want to skip over NS2, but let me start on a positive note.
NS2 is a bold step in an industry full of very similar multiplayer experiences. Multiplayer is asymmetrical, with each team featuring multiple classes and vastly different approaches to play between teams. Rounds require the participation of not only individual teammates and their skill, but also the (micro)management skills of a commander, acting in an RTS role. These factors lead to NS2 having not only very deep tactical gameplay, but also a very large skill curve to climb and become immersed in. The results of fully embracing and immersing yourself in these systems can lead to a very fun and utterly different kind of gameplay which is truly one-of-a-kind.
Now I'm going to tell you why you may want to pass on getting this game.
Unless you are prepared to adopt the committed ethic and mindset of a competitive gamer when going in, you're going to have a very rough time; or at least a very inconsistent experience. The difficulty curve is downright brutal. Maps are huge, complex sprawls with a lot of tactical options hidden away in the architecture and terrain placement. They take a lot of time to learn. Gameplay, even for the human side (which you'd think is in more familiar territory for most people) is not too hard to get a handle on at first, but the leap from functional play to consistently effective technique is ENORMOUS. It also does not help that the core community of this game consists of very talented and highly competitive players that one of them alone can stack a team to an almost assured victory.
The other major problem that this game presents for new players is related to its greatest strength - its complexity and essential reliance on communication and teamwork for success. This depth ensures almost DOTA-like skill and tactical moments to shine in league play, but in pub play it is a different story. The reliance of one person, the commander, to basically support the rest of the team to ensure victory can be a huge liability in pub play, as having the wrong guy in the commander chair can spell instant doom for a match - very frustrating when it happens consistently. Unlike a lot of other games, like Battlefield and Team Fortress, in which throwing a lot of like-minded players at common objectives usually results in emergent teamplay, constant voice and text communication is essential to a fun and successful game in NS2. Sometimes you get lucky and have a lot of teammates who communicate effectively and listen to orders from the commander. A lot of the time, this isn't the case, and it's frustrating.
Because of the aforementioned complexity, another problem arises. A small mistake by the commander, or players under him/her can lead to the team's doom in the early stages of the game. Most of the time everything goes smoothly early on and you roll the team, or you lose a battle early on and it's all over.
Anyways, at the end of the day, I'll say this. If you're prepared to immerse yourself in NS2 completely - make it your religion, as you would with a game like DOTA - you're probably going to have a great time with its tactical complexity and heavy reliance on teamwork. If you're not that hardcore, you're going to play an interesting game, with interesting levels, but with an enormous skill curve and a lot of frustration trying to deal with players who seemingly cannot be killed or bested in any way.
Me, I'm not that hardcore. I played the game, it was fun while it was interesting, but after 50 hours I can see some of the complex mechanisms move about and I realize I'm simply not a bad enough dude to become one of those 142 - 2 k/d kinds of players that you'll no doubt run into if you play this game.

I played this a lot before the Steam edition as well. It was one of the best flight sims for its time, only rivaled by X-Plane. Sadly it hasn't gotten much updates since then and this was the last good flight sim ever created by Microsoft.
It has a good variety of scenery, the whole world to explore. What makes this game stand out is that it includes every airport in the world (when it came out) and all the airport codes, gps data and ils frequencies needed to land at every airport just like the real world, it also has a fully voiced atc.
What this game lacks however is controls, the cockpits are more simplified, it doesn't give you all the buttons you need to start an aircraft properly, instead you just hit the ignition switch and your started. But you can download new aircraft's to give you the full realistic cockpits such as PMDG.
Where this game does shine though is the multiplayer which is still active today, with dozens of active servers, some of them with up to 50 players online at once, usually because of Virtual Airlines which uses mods to give the most realistic experience in learning how to be a pilot working for a "clan" of players to earn money and build a fleet of planes.
I got this for $10 on a steam sale which is very well worth it, but if your looking for the absolute best in flight sims you should look for the newest X-Plane 11 which just came out this year.

This game was gifted to me after the summer sale by a Steam angel, and I've been having quite a bit of fun with it. The puzzles themselves are short, which definitely feeds into "just one more turn" syndrome. The music is pretty stellar, and the puzzle mechanic itself is fairly neat and easy to grasp.
However, there are some downsides, but none of them are very severe. The art style is mediocre, the RPG-esque options (on hero level up) are very limited, the story is awful (but who comes to a puzzle game for the story), and the game in general gives you the feeling that it just isn't challenging enough. Compared to other matching games (Bejeweled, or even Puzzle Pirates), there just seems to be very little depth. That being said, this is still a great timesink puzzle in its own right, and I've been finding I leave it open in a window while browsing or watching YouTube and switching back over to run through a puzzle. Definitely a great gift -- I wouldn't say it's worth full price though. Thankfully, it goes on sale reasonably often for very low prices, so just be patient and hop on it the next time it's discounted.

In what seems like forever ago, I was excited for the release of Civ 3. It was the time in my life when I was relentlessly digging into history books, and it would be great to have a game compliment that. Of course, I had already had games that did that such as Age of Empires 2. But a big strategy game that let me do everything? That seemed shiny. A friend let me borrow of Civ 2 so I could at least get a vague idea of what it was like before Civ 3 released, and then, eventually, I got my hands on the game itself.
Ok... this is probably an excess of nostalgia, but I was trying to convey something important here. Namely that I
liked Civ 3 when it came out, and played it for countless hours. It was also the only real time where I actually got involved in modding, since the Civ 3 Scenario editor was super easy to use and making historical scenarios was one of the few fun things I had in those days. I didn't use this screen name back then, but I had another and it was synonymous with creating detailed, but accessible, scenarios about events such as World War I, the Eastern Front of WW2, and more.
Civ 3 also was the only Civ game I really got into. Sure, I played 4 and 5 plenty, but they just didn't suit me as much. Naturally, what I really mean by this is that like Civ 4 and 5, 3 had strategic resources that you needed in order to build certain units. Unlike those later Civ games however, the amount of a resource you had didn't limit the number of units you could build that used those resources. So in my games I ended up with enormous empires with scores of cities, thousands of military units, and also that one time I made over 300 ICBM's. While that might seem absolutely crazy (you do know who is writing this, right? :P), it made everything seem large in scale and made the late-game wars huge endeavors that actually felt like it was a world war rather than just a skirmish over a handful of cities. Civ games since have drastically cut down the number of cities wanted or needed for their games, and with it Civ, to me, lost the "epic" quality that made me like Civ 3 as much as I did. Some might prefer how Civ has changed in this regard, but for me there isn't quite anything like the kinds of global wars or the very real sense of nuclear annihilation that Civ 3 had.
So... yeah this "review" is basically just a nostalgia trip. Humble Bundle was giving this game out for free not so long ago, and so I found Civ 3 reinstalled on my PC close to fifteen years after I first played it. Does it work on Steam? Well, I was able to boot it up and poke around a bit just fine. I have heard that others have had problems with getting this running however, which is kind of funny because Civ 3 was a
stable game in the sense that it almost never crashed.
Giving this a "yes" for all the fun times this game provided me in the distant past. I can't really do otherwise. :3

To be honest I didn't know this title until it's been out from years and was already on heavy sale. Lucky me. I knew Remedy for their masterpiece, Max Payne, so when I realized Alan Wake was their latest game I took it without further inquiries. And I really believe I was right.
Alan Wake is a third action (and I dare to call it) survival shooter (considered the measured amount of ammos and the weak constitution of the protagonist). You are Alan Wake, a world best seller Writer... Kind of a Stephen King level of Fame. Due to the amount of stress after the writing of the last book Alan is retiring with his beloved Wife Alice in a small mountain town called Bright Falls. When they get to their cabin Alice is abducted by a dark entity and pulled to the depth of Cauldron Lake. Alan will then realize that there's something really odd and dark happening in Bright Falls and their citizens.
The game is structured as a classic third person shooter, but you won't have any mass destruction weapon, nor you won't have any huge amount of ammos. The most interesting concept in the gameplay is the contrast between light and darkness, so when the Takens (citizens possessed by darkness) approach you, you must light them with your torch first in order to get rid of their "protective dark aura" and be able to shoot them and eliminate them. Also there are few street lamps here and there that will give you protection against them (and serve as checkpoint as well). Besides, this game is definitely full of collectibles that will lead to various achievements.
Anyways this game It's not about the gameplay (which actually includes funny sections where you can drive a car which can be used to quickly enlight the takens and drive over them B-) ), nor about the graphics, which is nice and always shows beautiful landscapes and ambiences. It's about the story, which is not original but involving. Besides the unexpected end, the story is quite linear and explicative but its strong side is how it gets you involved with the main protagonist and other characters. And this is one of the few times it happened to me, because the game isn't what I'd call revolutionary or innovative yet I'm still playing it, or better, re-playing to attempt a 100% completion which is something I rarely attempt on this kind of games.
The story and the settings are quite dark, almost horror. Almost because you'll never jumpscare nor be afraid or stressed as in other games like, I don't know... Amnesia, maybe? But it's still a great setting anyways. The story doesn't end on its own as there are a couple of DLCs included: "The Signal" and "The Writer" Which follow after the end of the original game (no spoiler about it, as they're strictly bound to the end).

Let's start with the overall setting: the game's very atmospheric. The world is finely crafted and believable and makes the player want to go exploring it further. It's designed like a TV show, and it pays homage to Twin Peaks and other mystery/thriller shows. I also liked the tongue-in-cheek humour in the Twilight Zone parodies and TV talk shows. The characters are memorable and even likeable (except Alan himself IMHO). The characters have a pretty decent voice acting, but horrible lip-syncing. Their mouths are just unnatural and gave me the creeps (purposefully uncanny valley or just inability/laziness?).
The gameplay is smooth and involves a heavy use of light, which adds to the atmosphere nicely. The shadows are impressive. Unfortunately the gameplay repeats itself and you start noticing some patterns. For example, you mostly run through linear paths, fighting enemies every 2 minutes. And at the end of the path there's a calm area and you always drop down into a lower platform, so that you can't go back where you came from. This is an arena, where you have to hold out for a certain time or fight a miniboss. Or your path is suddenly blocked off by some falling debris or something and you have to find another way around. You always see it coming and it gets really tiring after a while. This is my main gripe with the game; it's repetitive.
The game starts slow and picks up the pace around midway through. It kind of keeps you interested throughout, just enough to not make you want to uninstall it before finishing it. But if you're not a patient player, this game might not be worth your while. In the end, you're not missing much. I'm recommending this game for its atmospheric qualities only, the rest is a bit unrewarding. There are a few moments that I'll remember fondly, like the "rock concert" or the part where Sarah and Barry join you. The game has some frustrating moments, but it's never too difficult if you take the time to learn the mechanics.

This is an excellent game. 9/10 easily. Very polished, great tactical gameplay. I seem some similarities to X-Com in that its a top down turn-based strategy game, but it's by no means "a clone."
This game could easily be more than $19.99. If I paid $39.99 for this, I'd feel good about it. I've put about 6-8 hours into it and I'm through 2.5 scenarios. Great combat, weapons, and storyline. The setting / voice acting really adds to it.
Some people bashed it because there isn't a heavy RPG element to the game. But there is.
The game has one of the coolest equipment / skill / combat systems I've seen. There are a multitude of factors that will modify your character. Based on choices you make, you will get certain perks / disadvantages. You will also reveal "cards" - this is how you give characters specific skills. Each character gets a hand of cards they can equip which bestows certain skills / perks to the character for example, being able to consume bodies to gain health. If you combine cards into hands, eg full house, four of a kind, etc. you will get additional attribute modifiers.
Some skills work in sunlight, some work in darkness. For example, there is a card that makes you invisible in shadows / darkness. Very cool strategic element to the gameplay.
Cover game mechanics are excellent, so flanking and tactics will almost always win vs. brute force. It is really the type of game where if you run out in the open, you will likely get one or two shotted.
You can only see enemies if they're in your line of sight or if they make noise. However, lighting can reveal shadows of enemies hiding. Never seen this in a game before.
Your luck rating is how you activate some skills. If someone shoots you and misses, you lose luck. If they hit you, you gain luck. The more luck you have, you can dodge hits (eg, if your luck is low, then you have a higher chance of getting hit). This all happens automatically. So everything you do has a tradeoff - this is pretty much the core concept of the game.
So basically, this game offers almost a dozen modifiers to your playing style at any given moment and has elements that most AAA games don't include.
Some reviews said that the non-combat "game world" seems like it was quickly put together. I agree the first scenario is a little lackluster. However, after an hour or so and especially in the other scenarios, the non-combat gameworld feels very polished. The majority of the storyline happens here including player choices to the story.
Overall, excellent game. Will 100% buy the expansion. Certainly a steal for anyone who likes tactical games like Wasteland, Fallout Tactics, X-Com (though no super weird close-ups) but in a new Western meets The Devil setting.
It's like watching a really good movie which you can modify the way you want.

Well, I'm kind of torn about this game. On one hand it's an excellent game, with a decent story, fun combat, interesting skills to use and well-enough made. But there are a million of annoying things, which don't really ruin the game for me, but bug the hell outta me. The game does have some very good ideas, for example looting enemies is well done; you automatically loot nearby enemies when selecting one, and you can send loot across the party to Rangers who can use the found ammo, medi-kits, etc. Also the conversation system is rather good. You can involve all of your group in a conversation, if you want to (not that it matters who speaks, but gives me an opportunity to roleplay my group). I'm still on my first playthrough, but I've already noticed there are almost always several ways to complete a task. Which is wonderful, not only for replayability's sake, but makes me feel I can do things my way.
But the annoyances? They are aplenty. For example, no group formation. Seriously? The game is even designed so that battles start where the characters stand, so every fight I have to start with all my characters clumped together. And you can't even move through other characters!! Very frustrating. Another big problem with combat is that I can't postpone a characters turn. This is especially annoying when my Ranger gets to act first when combat begins, but she is surrounded by her team mates, and cannot move. This added to the fact that hitting your own teammates by accident seems a little too easy, and it gets frustrating fast. This kinda omissions should have been patched a long time ago, I can find no excuses why they are still in the game.
There are other gripes, also. The logbook for one is next to useless. There are only two sorting options, both of which make very little sense. And in this kind of game, I would expect that I could check the log for all the conversations I've had. But no. You can't even manage the logbook in anyway, except for tagging some tasks. I have a task regarding some objects I found, and after running around for over an hour, I finally checked the quest from the internet, and found out that I can't complete it, because the guy I was supposed to talk to was now dead. But I can't remove the task from the logbook even manually. Adds to frustration.
A big problem is also the enemy AI. There is none, seems like it is artificial stupidity rather than intelligence. Enemies have no tactics or sense of self-preservation. Usually they just rush you and get killed.
So, in closing, the game is rather good, but has a million small problems, which aren't that bad alone, but start to eat you up eventually. Oh, and the humor seems rather forced, most of the jokes left me feeling "meh". I still recommend this, though.
PS: Game of the Year 2014? Gotta to be a joke, Divinity: Original Sin came out the same year. Other than the setting, these two games are very similar, but D:OS is soooo much better made.

You are the protector of a child who grows into a young woman and follow her story. There is no dialogue, only tableaus where the puzzles take place. The music is likewise great.  All in all, neat story, great art, great music. My only real complaint (besides the fact that I want more of this game, but it's only 2 hours, max!) is that the control to create connections between objects is the same as the one to break them, which means if you are trying to erase a very short connection, or in an awkward place, you end up having to restart because the game ends up making a dozen more tiny connections while you're trying to break one. I had to restart levels lots of time because of this.

Virginia is the narrative design equivalent of a tech demo. It's gorgeous and a masterclass in storytelling and characterization through audiovisual cues. There's not a single line of dialog, but you still understand what's going on. There are sudden jump cuts all over the place, but for the most part they make sense and pace the story. Virginia explores all kinds of interesting and unusual tools that other game developers should take note of and incorporate into their own work.
That said, the systems you'll interact with are extremely minimal, and while there are a few cases where I appeared to be presented with a choice between mutually exclusive alternatives, I'm not sure how much those meant in the long run.
If you absolutely need a game to be challenging or whatever, this might not be for you. But it's short and aesthetically really interesting, so if you're curious about experiencing new or unusual or polished narrative techniques that try to adapt cinematograpic and theatrical approaches to the interactive medium, give this a shot.

Broken Age Act 1 was an incredibly beautiful, deeply interesting game with simple but fun mechanics, amazing art style, and a story I couldn't wait to finish and learn more about. It had good writing and voice acting, plus a twist that actually surprised me at the end. I was desperately excited to play Act 2.
Broken Age Act 2 took every plot point set up by Act 1, every character detail and known fact, and threw it in the trash. All the questions I wanted answers to were resolved in throw-away dialogue and boring cop-outs. Plus it introduced a huge new plot point for no reason that tied up no loose ends and just made the whole thing confusing. It felt fake. It felt like a betrayal after how good part 1 was. The puzzles were increased in difficulty for no reason and they were mind-numbingly difficult. The solutions were usually ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It took 9 hours to finish this act (only 4 hours for act 1), with no breaks, and I was playing with a friend! In most cases I'd say my dislike of the ending or plot choices was my own opinion but Double Fine really dropped the ball on this second half.
Would I recommend Act 1? Absolutely. It's still a fun and beautiful game, it's worth playing. I do not recommend Act 2 to anyone. Just stop after you finish the first part and let your imagination do the work for you, I promise it'll be a better ending then what Double Fine gave us.

Whether or not you consider Amphora worth the price (on sale or otherwise) might depend on your tolerance for frustration.
I really wanted to love this game - I've been attracted to the look of it since I first saw it, and finally decided to buy it on sale.  It is stunningly beautiful, and I feel very sorry to give it a thumbs down but it's just too irritating!
I don't mind having to put some thought into a puzzle solution, and it can be a great feeling when you finally get it, but if the physics are unpredictable it just becomes an exercise in frustration.  As an example, in the "fireworks" level I could see what I needed to do after a moment.  But getting it done?  (Potential spoilers.)
I eventually got it done after maybe 25 minutes or so (more through luck than judgement), had a quick go at the following level, and gave up for the night when that one looked to be even more frustration just waiting to happen.
Added to that is the issue mentioned by another reviewer of not being sure what the chains are actually capable of and when they might break, which often seems illogical and just adds to the frustration when you finally get something right and then moving something else breaks that perfect positioning.
Perhaps a tutorial with more information might be helpful here, or at least a couple of levels where learning the tolerances of the chains and objects might be easier and not cause so much irritation.  Figuring out how to play in the beginning was fun, but the difficulty of understanding the apparently-unpredictable physics after a few levels took that fun away.
I'm sorry, developers - you've made an incredibly beautiful game that just isn't very much fun for me, and fun is more important than looks in the end.  Although it was relatively cheap on sale, my funds are too limited to waste right now so I'm afraid I'll be requesting a refund.  :(

Amphora is a physics-based puzzle game which takes its charming visual style from the beauty and tradition of stained glass windows, historically used to tell valiant, heroic or cautionary tales based in either folklore or religion. The game draws on this, with each puzzle expressed as a partially-animated stained glass portrait which you have a certain amount of control over. Each 'puzzle-portrait' is a self-contained story, but put together they weave a loose narrative which you uncover as you progress through each scene - just like a series of stained glass windows will tell a bigger story when read from left to right.
Working out the solution to each puzzle involves nothing more than visually interpreting the story of the scene in front of you. Once you've got it, you'll have a rough idea of both what the game wants and what's required to do it. For example: one very early scene depicts a mother reading a story to a child, a hare and a tortoise which are not moving, and an unbroken starting line. Once you understand that the scene refers to the fable of The Tortoise and The Hare, it becomes very obvious as to how you progress.
Although my review is a thumbs up, however, I am actually on the fence. Amphora definitely does more things right than wrong; its visuals, music and atmosphere are stunning, and during the first two chapters I had a huge amount of fun figuring things out, learning new techniques and uncovering its story. However, towards the end of the game the physics became a bit of an issue, and I found more than once that I'd been stuck for a silly amount of time on puzzles I fully understood but needed to keep resetting (when objects got stuck). I also personally found some scenes very unclear, to the point where I didn't understand what the solution was supposed to be doing even when looking at a guide. The last 20% of the game was extremely unenjoyable in that regard.
Despite the mixed feelings, Amphora is definitely a game I will return to, particularly as I am now far more familiar with the way its mechanics and physics work. It's beautiful, relaxing, extremely family-friendly and tells a simple, pretty story that you can lose yourself in for a short while. If you like the look of it or enjoy a relaxed puzzle game, I'd definitely give it a shot. That being said, the £10 asking price is quite a lot more than I'd ever recommend this game at, so make sure to wait for a sale before investing.

This is another game on the line between recommend or not recommend. Is it worth the $13.99 it usually is? I don't think so. Even with struggling on puzzles I was able to complete the game twice in under five hours... and I left the game running during a break for dinner so it's really even less than that. Now, I don't like to judge a game's worth on it's length, and I've played plenty of short games that I'd happily pay $5, $10, even more for, but this is not one of them, so I recommend catching it on sale when it's only a few dollars. The game isn't just short though, the content is lacking. Aside from a few puzzles that you may struggle with, most of them are simple enough to complete in seconds. The "story" it supposedly tells is disjointed and the few puzzles that will give you problems (and those problems won't be in solving them, but in getting the physics to work on your side) will make you forget the story entirely when you spend 20 minutes trying to throw a fireball at a soldier. On the other hand it is a beautiful game, truly. The stained glass art style is enchanting and the music is pleasant, but whether that's enough to make the game worth it is up to you-- for me, eh, it evened things out.
Overall:
+ art style
+ music
+ concept is fun, in a crayon physics sort of way
+ when it works, it works and will make you smile
- way too short
- fails at telling its story
- most of the puzzles are too easy
- the difficult puzzles are difficult because of uncomfortable physics, with only one or two requiring you to actually figure out a clever solution

Aura is a first-person point & click puzzle/adventure game, similar to the Myst series.  Differences are a 360 degree camera and an inventory where you can pick up and hold items to later be used in puzzles.  Some of the puzzles are quite difficult, either because you're on the lookout for small details which are easy to miss, or they genuinely require some brains to piece together.  Sketches are scribbled in your journal to give you some not-too-obvious hints if you get stumped.
The music, atmosphere and voice acting aren't comparable, but if you enjoyed Myst or Riven there's a decent chance you'll enjoy this game.  I'd say it's a bit easier overall since, unlike either of those games, every single thing you can interact with is key to progressing in one way or another.

Virginia plays like a Thomas Pynchon novel adapted for film by David Lynch, but with women of color as main protagonists. Its plot is decently abstruse without being utterly incomprehensible -- and treading this line without any dialogue is an impressive feat, to say the least. Plot comes through with musical cues and characters' facial expressions and body language. If you expect to have full control over the player character at all times, you'll likely be disappointed, but if you can accept that the game is less of a game than it is a semi-interactive movie, you'll enjoy it. The controls leave something to be desired: it handles like a semi with square wheels at times, but this does not distract too heavily from the experience. Overall, Virginia is a very good game. 8.5/10

A masterpiece of modern medieval fantasy themed rpgs. This game has it all: a game of thrones, a tale of two lovers, kings and their quarrels and most importantly an amazing underlying lore that pulls you in from the start and does not let go until the ride ends with a bang at the end. Every character can be as fleshed out as you want them to be, and some may become more friendly than others depending on your choices. Your decisions will come to haunt you or to help you as the game progresses, because what choices you make have an impact on the game world and npcs will treat you differently. You get the sense that the world changes around you and that there is an urgency to all your actions. In this game you are never safe, be it from hostile foes to swindlers and thieves to deceptive traps set in the world. And the  game does all of this with a masterful score of music and amazing visuals to boot. The only reason for the nine is the fact that it is not quite an open world adventure like that of GTA or Skyrim, but just wait until the Witcher 3!

I originally wrote a review back when this was Orion: Dino Hunt, I'll leave the original review at the bottom.
The developers have come a long way with this, they even admitted it was a disaster at first. But they did something I'm very surprised and pleased with; instead of abandoning this failed game, they reworked it, made it better and sold it cheaper.
It may be just another Unreal wave survival game with little-to-no story, but it is fun to play, especially with friends. The developers have realized that they should just make this game fun more than serious, so you get people running around in Halo Spartan-style armor with lightsabers and cheeseburger hats.
The devs have changed my opinion on this title, it is worth getting this cheap if you can and having some fun running around in this game with your friends.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Yes, I know, shoot dinosaurs in the face with high-tech weaponry, yadda yadda
But that gimmick doesn't last long. All the survival matches have the same format and waves of enemies no matter what the map is. Plus the game has a lot of quirks; the animations feel unrefined, the user interface is very user unfriendly (there's no labels or hover-text to describe what each number or button is for, and some buttons you have to double click quickly or it will only play an annoying select sound), the controls for vehicles feel awkward, and there's plenty of glitches.
I was in a vehicle when I was tossed up onto a rock by a T-Rex, none of the wheels contacted the rock, so I couldn't get down, and the vehicle was at such an angle that whenever I stepped out, I was magically forced back into the vehicle. I had to wait about four waves before my teammates could ram a tank up onto the rock far enough to dislodge me!
This game has an interresting concept (although I can't find a story anywhere for this to make sense), but it's just too clunky and unrefined for it to be a worthwhile game.

What an addictive game! I wasn't expecting much, to be honest, but I installed it, played a bit, and here we are, 25 hours later. Yes, 25 hours for a single playthrough. Okay, yeah, I started over a few times early on, but once I got the hang of it I just kept going. The primary gameplay is match 3, with a slider rather than a swap mechanism. Each kingdom you conquer opens up a tavern and a ruin where you can find new relics, spells and items, and recruit new troops. To do this, you use some of the gold you've gotten in your warmongering, and then play a minigame. Higher level items and troops have a higher gold cost and a tougher minigame to play.
You can customize your newly acquired kingdoms with your chosen hero(s), troops, and relics, and use them in battles against kingdoms that you haven't conquered yet. You can outfit your hero with the items and spells you've gotten. All of these items have a color value and a points value, and each kingdom has either discounts or increased costs for using these items. (Ie, a kingdom might have lower point cost for blue and red items and troops, and higher point cost for red and yellow items and troops. Your hero's total cost is affected by his color and the combination of items and spells he or she has assigned.)
It's relaxing, but it can also be challenging, especially if you have trouble with the recruitment minigames.
Mountain is a very 'zen' game that is nice to have running in the background, and checking in every twenty minutes or so.

This game is by far is my favourite game. The concept of using light to fight darkness sounded so interesting, I just had to try it out. Honestly, it is hard to come up with cons. I believe this to be a brilliant game from a brilliant company.

My opinion could be biased, because I liked the combat, but after reading some other reviews, the combat can interrupt the story a bit. Alan is simply a writer that gets thrown into a mess of darkness and has to defend himself with guns.

I do not recommend this game for the price of $60...

Amphora proved to be more than meets the eye. And judging at first glance it does look colorful and artistic, perhaps to the point at which you might consider it superficial. It features indeed distinct set pieces that have little to no connection with one another. Yet a shallow game it is not. The clever use of smoke and silhouettes reminded me of the shadow play theater prevalent in Southeast Asia and though the game’s very title is of Greco-Roman origins, many scenes within it feature a wide variety of individuals and cultures. With no consistent storyline per se, you might be tempted to think that Amphora’s silent treatment tries to hide its flaws, but I found none other than the slightly high price. It is like many arthouse titles before or after it, a game that may polarize its audience. I personally enjoyed the rather brief experience and saw it as a break from convoluted stories. One thing is certain. It’s less abstract than some of the games it shares similarities with and the puzzles are far from a challenge.

Amphora is a short, but exceedingly beautiful puzzle-game. I bought it solely for its visual design, though the gameplay and overarching story were fitting, welcome additions.
The game operates in a series of interactive, scenes that follow the life events of the nameless female protagonist. In these scenes, you complete anywhere from one to several actions to trigger an event. I had a bit of trouble figuring out the solutions to a few scenes, but overall the puzzle portions are pretty simple. And I say simple, not boring. Later solutions can take a bit of thinking though, a bit of ruminating on what exactly you're trying to do, and what kinds of options you have available to you (you gain a few different skills as the scenes progress). Of course, there's always the "try it and see" approach, but I think most things are better solved by careful observance. There are also multiple ways to complete the scenes.
Overall, the gameplay was fun, and sometimes challenging, but the best part of this game is the stunning visual design. The sound design is also light, but effective.

This game is gorgeous. I can't say I loved the soundtrack as much as I hoped to, since that's something everyone seems to like, but it fit the game nicely.
Essentially you follow a girl through her life, from the time she's a baby until she's married to her husband. There's a war in between, and she ends up helping her husband out in the middle sometime. The whole thing is really well done--I had no trouble following the story, though there were no words.
Each puzzle is a scene from her life. And that's the entire game: scenes from her life. The puzzles are all pretty simple, once you figure out what to do. I think I could replay the entire game in a half hour, maybe less, now that I know what I'm doing. It took me roughly two hours, though, to finish the entire game and get all the achievements.
I have to disagree with the people complaining about the physics. In general, it was fine. There were a couple puzzles toward the end, once I'd become confident in my ability to use the tools given to me, that were a bit rough because of the way things moved, but certainly nothing impossible. I think the most time I spent on any given puzzle was probably ten minutes or so, which is really not too bad.

Virginia is so completely different and you have to be in the right mindset to play this game, or else you won't like it.
The biggest thing to note about this game: there are no voice actors or written narrative. and that is
a bad thing in my opinion. How can you follow the story with no dialogue? Because the game is interactive and has a linear gameplay that lets you fill in the blanks.
The next biggest thing to note is the style: it looks like this is from the early 90s, and that's the point. You are set in a small town investigating as and FBI agent set in the early 90s. It creates a mood different from anything else I've ever played.
Another difference is you play as a woman who is not white. For some reason this enrages people who claim it isn't necessary, or it's pushing some agenda, but how so? If you are angered by the gender and color of the skin of an animated character you play and only see a few times in mirrors in game, then you have serious life issues to sort out and you shouldn't be playing video games to begin with. Also, it is hinted at (I say hinted because there are no words) that your character is gay and has a relationship (short term) with another woman in game. The hints are subtle, but there. Again, what does this matter to people so upset by this?
__________
Given all this, I loved it. It was such a unique game and only takes a couple hours to finish the story. It is bizarre for sure, but that's what makes it good as a stand-alone story.
This is a game for someone looking for a story, not skill or action, and a completely different mode of story-telling.

It's a silent interactive 'movie-game' with a simplistic art style.
After completing
a couple of times I was desperate for more story driven exploration games but couldn't get my fix with the likes of
or
- they just didn't do 'it' for me, then I remembered the weird controversy that surrounded
on its release so finally decided to buy it...I'm glad I did, this game really is unique and stylish.
The game is not for everyone, it has no dialogue or text and you only use one mouse click to interact with the very few items/objects in the environment. The story, and how it's told, is why people love this game. The story is told in a fractured way with you jumping from one scene to another, if you've seen the movie
then you'll get it. It's the kind of game that leads you to believe that you've figured out the story and solved the crime...but you will be wrong. The work of David Lynch and
are a clear inspiration for the ever changing narrative.
You traverse the game locations freely but the game is not open world. You walk at a snail's pace but large sections of the environment are skipped when unnecessary to the overall story - for example; a long and empty corridor, you'll get a few steps in when you'll 'skip' to end like an edit in a film.
The music is amazing, it guides you through the game injecting emotion into situations where the art style limits animation. The music replaces dialogue, in a way, leading the interactions between game characters and is used to express the inner emotions of the protagonist, which as a first person experience, is not exactly easy to portray.
I did get the game in the sale for only £1.74 ($2.25) though, I can say I'd probably be less praising if I paid the full £6.99 for an hour and a half worth of game. I view this as less of a game and more as a story to be experienced, much like a movie, that is driven by an awesome soundtrack.

I tend to like narrative experiences (or just "experiences") as long as they're good. Sadly, Virginia is not good.
The developers tried to create a blend of a game and a movie, but it seems that they lacked understanding of both mediums.
It fails as an interactive experience because of lack of interaction with player. Scenes start and end abruptly, sometimes the player even can't reach the end of a corridor before the game forces him/her into another place. Even if it lets you explore, there isn't much to see or do. The lack of visual clues often makes you pixel-hunt for a thing to interact in order to move story forward. Without much interesting to explore, it can be quite irritating. And more importantly, it feels like you do not matter. There's a set screenplay with very little possible alternations, and you must obediently follow it. I seriously doubt that the developers wanted players to feel this way.
It fails as a movie too. Pacing is all over the place. Especially the editing. The rhythm of changing scenes alters too many times without any sufficient reason. Some scenes feel too short, others feel too long or just unnecessary. The music is quite good, but usually it doesn't quite fit what happens on the screen. And even more importantly, I don't think that the game had to be dialogue-less. Maybe I didn't understand something, but after playing Virginia, it feels like it was just a stylistic choice or a gimmick. Moreover, they didn't even follow it through and included a few texts in the game. It completely destroys any meaning left. Also I didn't care about the story, but maybe it's just me. The most fun part is the last half an hour when it becomes very, very random. It's not good for the narrative I guess because it left more questions than answers and felt generally inconsistent (especially compared to what happened before), but at least it wasn't boring.
I can say however that I enjoyed the visuals, and some scenes were nice (for example, at the bar). But in overall, I can't recommend it. It's definitely not trash and it can has effort put into it, but I think that it didn't come together  in the end, and it's a shame, really. It has a lot of potential and a good style.
Play What Remains of Edith Finch instead. It's of the same genre and of pretty much the same length, but the creators there actually understood how to do interactive experiences.
P.S. I think that the Twin Peaks references felt forced too. Lynch had horse, we will include bull. But again, maybe I'm wrong, maybe I didn't understand the game.

This game is a mix of good, bad, and everything in between.
Pros:
-Orc Killing Simulator
-Tons of variety in the orcs, both initial encounters and how encounters with them changes them.
-Pretty exciting and interesting story (♥♥♥♥ you i liked it)
-Multiple regions with their own pools of captains
Cons:
-Clunky controls that work fairly well 95% of the time, but consistently fail you during the most intense battles.
-Vital UI warnings (like for incoming projectiles or quick time events) occassionally don't appear when they should.
-Player level should be flat out removed. Level restriction has no constructive place in this game whatsoever, especially the insane week long grind it creates once story missions are done.
-Fort Sieges suck, becoming insanely boring if the player does any prior prep work, being sadly repetitive and devoid of special events (in my experience), and otherwise simply just not challenging or interesting the player to any real degree.
-Nemesis system could be a bit better as it feels very random what orcs it decides are special, rarely using ones that gave the player trouble or were interesting for one reason or another.
-Surprising lack of orc names. I know people go through a lot of orcs, but it can't be that hard just to add more names.
-Storylines feel a little scattered at times, broken up into too many individual story missions.
-Entire first act is basically one long drawn-out tutorial.
Mixed:
-Gear is kind of cool and adds variety to how your character is built, but its always very short lived as gear is constantly out leveled by new, higher level gear. Legendary gear is too difficult to get, simply not worth the time and effort it takes to get.
-Pit fights are pretty fun to watch, but are soiled by the repetitiveness of their attacks, how clunky their fight is, how unbalanced some attacks are, how cringey the fight is when a captain becomes afraid, and how its pre-determined who should win and makes that supposed winner deal massive damage compared to the other orc.
tl;dr:
Its basically the first game just better (although the controls need serious polish). This is really great in its own right and alone makes it worth recommending, however theres really nothing outside of the orc killing that doesn't need serious polish. It feels like this game needed another year of development to fix up the quality of pretty much everything. No feature that I didn't list under the pro's is one that makes the game better or that the game would be any worse if removed.
7/10

I generally pass up F2P shooters (besides TF2, of course), but this one caught my eye. I started playing it for a little over half an hour and I was instantly enjoying it. The game is pretty much a mix of Counterstrike and any other interchangeable shooter. When you spawn, you have roughly 25 seconds to buy a new weapon to replace the handgun that you start with. You get this treatment every time you respawn. You can only have one gun, however, which is a downside that I'm sure will be changed somewhere in the near future. There is a selection of other handguns, SMGs, LMGs (heavy rifles), assault and sniper rifles, and shotguns that you can choose from. To buy them you use in-game cash that is earned by getting kills (you start with 2000 and get 100-300 on every kill) and the most expensive weapon is a little over $6000, if I remember correctly. There is a knife function (default key F), but it can be a bit difficult to get close enough to the enemy's hitbox to hit them. If you do hit them, it is a one-hit kill that is completely uncounterable, unlike Battlefield where knife attacks can be countered against. It's good if you want to♥♥♥♥♥♥people off by way of knife rush, but it's not completely impossible to avoid because of the difficulty of getting to the enemy.
Overall, I'd give WARMODE a 6-7/10. Definitely recommended to try at least once.

It's a waiting/eugenics simulator. It's free. It's a lot of fun at the beginning but quickly loses steam as things seriously slow down during middle game, and picks up again as you're entering late game. You do not need to pay to win in this game, and there really isn't a winning condition to begin with. You mostly spend cash to speed through the game, which I wouldn't personally recommend. It is far more satisfying to earn your way to the top.
The graphics and sounds are minimalistic but charming, and the game is really good at rewarding your actions. The only real downside to FOS is that it has no multiplayer component, not the micro-transactions, which I think is a huge oversight and would have added far more re-playability to the game. There are also some questionable gameplay decisions, and there are frustrations when dealing with dweller combat in the vault and some disasters (radscorpions), but it's nothing you won't be able to deal with if you're adequately prepared.
Many players find enjoyment by conducting social experiments. For example, is your vault only populated by women and all the men are sent into the wasteland? Or maybe your vault has everyone named Jerry? Maybe all the kids born into the vault have to go through a rite of passage in the wasteland or die trying? You can decide all of that, and I highly recommend that you do. FOS is all about making your own fun, so be creative. For added bonus, try survival mode. It's actually pretty easy if you know what you're doing, even if you're completely new to FOS.
A few tips right off the bat: The game is based around several key concepts, and if you don't want to get completely destroyed by rad roaches or fires, make sure you aren't upgrading your rooms unless your dwellers are all armed and in their 30s. This is critically important by the time radscorpions start showing up (60 and 35 population for normal and survival). Keep you overall dweller level down if you don't want to be minced by deathclaws (60 and 35 pop). SPECIAL stats only matter for manning rooms and exploring the wasteland, and questing to a lesser extent.
Endurance should be your number one priority, since health in FOS is only determined at level up and does not work retroactively with endurance. Endurance does stack past 10, so you want to level up with the best endurance gear you have to get the most health possible.
As a bonus tip for survival mode, you can avoid disasters by isolating rooms in a checkerboard-like pattern, since everything but radscorpions cannot travel past dirt tiles. This won't work past 35, when the radscorpions show up, so I suggest being well-armed and well-trained after that point, and then hitting nuclear reactors as fast as possible. The rest you can read about online, if you desire to know more about the inner workings of the game.

And even stranger is that Alen is finding pages of events that have yet to happen. Alen must now figure out the truth of Bright Falls and save his Wife.
Put simply the Story isn´t really anything that original in that it sounds like a simple prince must save the princess thing. But the thing is that theres actually a lot more to it. If only I could say the same about the characters. In that there not that interesting at all, the only characters name that I remember by heart is Alan Wake´s. For obvious reasons.
Visuals/Graphics:
Put simply there stunning. The game looks amazing from walking in the forest to running in the town. and because the game has such an emphasis on light, the lighting effects are probably the best I´v ever seen. Simply look at gameplay videos if you don´t belive me. I f I had to knock 1 thing though, It´s that the faces are very stiff, And almost robotic.
Gameplay:
this is actually a bit of a mixed bag. In that it´s actually atmospheric just walking in the woods collecting pages and watching things on the TV´s in the level. but the combat while fun at first just gets really repetative after so long. which is a shame because the combat system is really good and fluid, as well as beliveable. But it´s just wasted on a rinse and repeat rutine. fighting the afore mencioned shadowed up towns people. you first have to shine your flashlight on them to get rid of the shadows, and afterwards shoot them down. There is also flare guns in the levels that act like grenade launchers but there far and few, so use wisely. The biggest problem is that the enemies here are not really scary. At all. so thers no tencion. AT ALL. maybe the first few times but it dosn´t take long to become boring. Maybe because when you get down to it as Zero Punctuacion said in his SH Downpour review: There really just dudes. Yeah dudes covered in shadows but still dudes. I mean that can work like it did with Condemmed, but it just didn´t here. The simple formula is: Dodge, shine light, shoot, kill, repeat with every now and then there´s a change of Dodge, shine light, dodge, shine light again , now shoot, kill. and whenever theres 3 or more enemy´s just use a flare gun and use the simple formula on the survivors and your fine. In all honestly it feals wasted. but the combat aside the game is still fun to explore and like I said the combat is fun the first few goes.
Overall:
It´s a good game. It´s decent. That´s really all there is to it. If it´s a horror game you want you won´t find it here. although I can appreciate the homages to the horror genre, and it really does have it´s creepy moments. Mostly thanks to it´s amazing atmosphere. but I really can´t bring myself to call it a great game. just a good one.

This great little game is broken up into several "scenes," and each scene advances the storyline. In each scene, the player must figure out what must be accomplished or completed before that scene is complete - it dissolves and then a new one loads. Each scene has its own color scheme - reds and oranges or greens and blues or shades of yellow - with simple 2-D figures in them. There aren't any directions, so you have to figure out what you're expected to do in most sections, although there are one or two that give you visual cues.
The name of the game comes from a small stained-glass-looking jar appearing in each scene that a generates a colored smoke effect that moves and swirls as you move the mouse. I have played this game about 15 times at this point, and I keep playing it, despite the fact that there isn't much challenge to figuring out the scenes anymore, because of the gorgeous graphics and mesmerizing sound. Sometimes I just sit and watch the smoke twist and unfurl and zen out listening to the music. How many games have you played that are THAT visually and aurally interesting?

Roguelike games have always been a somewhat niche genre. The majority of gamers shy away from these bizarre games that can take months on end to finish with 99% of all attempts ending in abject failure. BoI reminds us what makes these games so appealing. Variation. With nearly 200 different powerups, a huge pool of monsters complete with unlockable harder upgrades, cutesy graphics, funky music  and a twisted story, BoI has enough to keep you going for the rest of your life. With the Wrath of the Lamb DLC adding even more stuff to explore you might as well sell your soul to the devil and spend your next life playing this too.
Every attempt to complete even Isaac's basic story mode will seem like a fresh new game and by the time you realise that this game is waaaaaay bigger than it lets on you'll start to wonder if you'll ever manage to experience everything this game has to offer. In terms of content it's one of the best value for money games Steam has available and if you're lucky, one day, you'll be able to tell your grandkids about that one time you actually made it to the end...
Prepare to lose months of your life.

I'll start by singing the praises of the one and only positive to this game, with that being the presentation. The art-style stands out from the crowd and is striking, and the music suits the game perfectly. The score produced by the Prague Philarmonic Orchestra (I think that's the orchestra I saw in the opening credits) is genuinely fantastic. One of, if not the best, scores I've ever heard in an indie game.
As for the 'game' itself. Meh. Infact, this is below meh. Having adored Gone Home, and having recently played the fantastic Edith Finch, this game has maybe 1/10 of the charm but lacks any of the gameplay or story that these two had.
The plot is wafer-thin. The writers went to the Steven Moffat school of setting up lots of mysteries and choosing to let the viewer decide the outcome, in their head, not on the screen. For a game based around a number of mysteries, this is a huge no no.
Secondly, playing this game feels like being an actor in a play where the plot is withheld from you, a play with no dialogue and just pages and pages of stage directions. The way this game plays out in front of you is baffling, confusing, and leaves you feeling lost. Unlike Gone Home, there is no chance to explore your surroundings or nearby objects to flesh out the plot, as the game rips control away from you seemingly every 5 seconds with some very harsh jumpcuts. Compounding the issue of the sudden jumpcuts is the lack of dialogue. If the game is going to constantly rip control away from you there needs to be some dialogue as sometimes there just isn't enough time to figure out what the scene is trying to show you. You try to observe your surroundings or nearby objects, but the next scene is instantly presented before you had a chance to get any context. This style of presentation would have worked with dialogue. I wanted to explore this game scene-by-scene, but I was just a passenger rather than the driver. A good 'walking simulator', like Gone Home or Edith Finch, lets you be the protagonist. With Virginia, I may as well have just watched a YouTube Let's Play.

Broken Age is a fantastic callback to the golden age of Point and Click adventures. It brings back the Whimsy of Monkey Island nad the Outlandish themes of Day of the tentacle.  Interesting characters, including the background creatures with no voice. It keeps you entertained and interested the whole way, with just enough difficulty to the puzzles to make sure you don't breeze through it. Just like every other game I've encountered from Double Fine, it is excellent, polished, and something I will strongly recommend.

You drive one of seven 1980s Russian trucks on one of five 1000mx1000m freeroam maps, to uncloak the map, to unlock other trucks, to bring lumber from "lumber" to "objective", to scout one of several routes for doing so, and to winch out all your trucks that got stuck while trying to do the former.
You may point out that to bring lumber of A to B is no real challenge, and if you think of other trucking sims like Euro truck Simulator 2, it isn't (there isn't even a game economy), but the challenge is in getting there because the terrain fights dirty (I paid my dues to the pun union, so shut up). You need to fight the mud every step of the way, and the smaller your truck and the heavier your load, the more difficult it gets. There are ruts in the dirt, your trucks will leave ruts in the dirt, you will get stuck in mud, in boggy soil (it's ok if you go fast, but as soon as you slow down...), in loose soil, on rocks, and in the rivers, lakes and puddles (don't go in to deep, the water has it in for you as well). You will tip over and spill your load, then winch yourself back upright and pick the logs up with a crane. You will repair and refuel yourself and others. You will slip off a rough log bridge carrying a heavy load. You will snag on tree stumps and logs. You will bump against trees and waltz over them.
It's you and your truck against the terrain.
If you think that's boring, don't buy.

I've been following Tim Schafer since the first time I played Psychonauts, and I am always interested in his stuff.  So I picked this game up as soon as I heard it existed.
When I played the first chapter of Broken Age, it seemed like it was setting up a lot of thematic elements and mysteries for the second part.  We've got two young people on the cusp of adulthood, questioning the way things have always been, being lied to their whole lives...  There are many different forces and people influencing the way they see the world, and they're finally breaking away and beginning to question those things.
In an attempt to avoid spoiling much...  The second act kind of drops the ball on all those ideas.  It takes the thematic elements and makes them literal, and introduces concepts out of nowhere to explain preexisting plots and wrap up the story.  The puzzles also seemed less cohesive in this act.
Like, I'd recommend it -- but it wasn't a religious video gaming experience or anything.
SPOILERS FOLLOW
My biggest beef with this game is that there are all these unfortunate, sexist subtextual narratives that stem from a minigame in the first act: Shay has some kind of outrageous intuitive "mateworthy" radar that makes him, I don't know, uniquely capable of selecting the most appropriate women for procreating???  And then Malik or Malichi or whatever his name is in the second act is straight up implying that all the women sacrificed in the feast aren't MERELY BEING CAPTURED/DEVOURED, no, they are being used to provide genetic material to the super human race -- and then either exhausting their bodies to the point of death, or literally just being killed in the process of extracting the aforementioned genetic material.
I cannot believe the epilogue implied everyone was supposed to have made peace after the end of the game.  Like, how else was anyone meant to interpret that?

Puzzle Kingdoms is a boring extremely repetitive grind with poor art design, generic music and sound finished off with a high price tag.
What limited gameplay there is plays out with a grid of symbols where the player and their opponent taking turns shifting one of the rows or columns in an attempt to get 3 or more of the same symbol next to each other in an attempt to store up points so that they can attack each other in a way similar to games like Hearthstone or Magic the Gathering. While this sounds like it could be an interesting idea. By the time you have done your 2nd battle and realize that every single one will be the exact same just with a few numbers changing it quickly loses all appeal.
There is also an overworld that serves as a hub between battle zones and allows you to choose to grind even more by fighting previous battles again if the game is not enough of a grind for you. You can play still more rounds of the game with slightly modified goals like match x number of each symbol type or clear all symbols within x turns to get different poorly drawn items and solders which behave the same as the ones you start with except for a few numbers being different.
It is clear that just as little thought and care as was put into gameplay was also put in to the rest of it. The writing shows a lack of proofreading. Including messages like “If their (000,240,60,255}Colors match” showing up in the TUTORIAL and a story with both the content and writing quality of a 13 year old’s school project. The music is as bland as it comes as it comes as are the sound effects which is made worse by constantly hearing the same things over and over. What few effects there are during battles are simple and as barebones as can be while still existing.
One look at the $15 list price as of writing this combined with what is a small and simple game from a decade ago plus adding nothing of value on its own this game is not worth the purchase.

Firstly, I have to say that when the act 1 came out, I wasn't really impressed. Sure, the graphics style and atmosphere are unique, but honestly, I was expecting something else. . Like act 1, act 2 is good, too.
Now, the main thing that really made this game, apart from being a really ok game, for me is the documentary series. Since it is now available in Steam, I really encourage to buy the game with the documentary - or go watch it on youtube, if it is still available there.
