First see the store page for details.  NS2 blends FPS/RTS into a very unique experience; almost every single game will be different and this game has massive replayability; if you want to get a general idea about how it works, you could look up NS2HD on youtube.
Generally, these things things should considered before you buy NS2 so that you will truely enjoy it:
- Teamplay. This game primarily focuses on it, and if you're lone-wolf you'll not get the full experience out of this game
- Communication; it goes hand in hand with teamplay - consider buying a microphone and talking to your team - communication is a key to success in this game
- Complexity; unlike many FPS, this game is rather complex - after all you're playing a game with RTS elements, so don't expect it to learn it in a day; make sure to watch some of the tutorials and you'll get the hang of it
- Competitiveness; due to the steep learning curve and that it takes a lot of skill to become good, this game is pretty much anti-casual - it will take serveral hundred hours to master it; however, you can always help your team - not very good at FPS? You can always play commander (RTS) or take a supportive role (such as builder/healer alien "gorge", or build/repair on marines)
- Decent Gaming Rig: quite sadly, you should have a recent gaming rig to enjoy this game. A good high end CPU (like recent gen Intel 4770k) plus an a decent grafics card will ensure this game run smoothly on your computer. Don't expect this to run well without meeting the requirements.
- Replayability; even though there are only 8 offical maps in this game at the point of writing, the replayability is extremly high. Almost every match will be different, as it revolves about your team and your commanders work. And if you get tired, you can always play a custom map or a mod... which leads to:
- Moddability; with most of it being written lua, it's quite possible to mod the game; if you are more a user then modder, you can simply run one of the mods from the workshop or look for servers running gameplay mods (such as Combat, which is more of a pure FPS without the commander)
However, there are some twirks with this game, balance might not be completly perfect, some technical issues [lag compensation, loading times and performance], and some other occasional bugs, but it still gets patched every now and then  with bugs and balance being addressed.
In any case, for 23€ it's already too cheap for a decent game like this, and for 5,75€ on sale, it's just a steal, go buy it!

When this game was first announced on Kickstarted I was overjoyed to throw my money down in the hopes that something great came of it, and I was not disappointed. There were some bugs and concerns when I fired up the game day 1, but for the next 72 hours of glorious exploration, combat, and dialogue I was hooked. It becomes necessary to run away from random encounters so as to not inflate your playtime for battles that offer very little to the story.

If you are a fan of tactical RPG's and are in need of a well written story in a bleak and desolate environment I would recommend you pick this game up.

TL:DR buy Fallout 1&2 and play those instead; they are similar, superior games and cost a fraction of the price.
I backed this on kickstarter and was very enthusiastic about playing the finished product.  I loved all the old Interplay games back in the day, and I thought that a modern remake of Wasteland that stayed faithful to old-school RPGs couldn't possibly go wrong.
It's a real shame that Wasteland 2 turned out to be such a slog. The 'tactical' combat is basic and repetitive, with no tactics beyond making sure you have your best weapons equipped, and focusing fire on each enemy until they are dead. This game is supposedly the spiritual successor to the early Fallouts but the combat is actually a step backwards from them. No aimed shot limb cripples, torso-shredding burst fire crits, stuns, knockdowns, or anything beyond hitting and subtracting hitpoints - headshots are available but they just take a bigger chunk of HP. There is a half-hearted cover mechanic but if you don't use it, it doesn't matter. Even when levelling up later in the game and getting better armour and weapons the combat is still the same grind.
Levels are certainly sprawling, but are mostly full of monotonous fights and heavily trapped/locked boxes (that usually turn out to be full of jokey 'flavour' junk items). Fight, help locals, move plot forward a bit, travel to next area. Not necessarily a bad formula but it is the same over and over, coupled with the incredibly dull combat. Text pops up for dialogue and to describe things happening but it appears in a tiny box at the corner of the screen which can't display much of it at once - which seems bizarre when there is so much reading to be done, and very little voice acting.
The setting is interesting and the plot isn't bad, with some genuine laughs and memorable characters to encounter. But when they come wrapped up in such an unpolished, uninspiring package with such ancient production values, it's very difficult to appreciate them.

Roguelike games have always been a somewhat niche genre. The majority of gamers shy away from these bizarre games that can take months on end to finish with 99% of all attempts ending in abject failure. BoI reminds us what makes these games so appealing. Variation. With nearly 200 different powerups, a huge pool of monsters complete with unlockable harder upgrades, cutesy graphics, funky music  and a twisted story, BoI has enough to keep you going for the rest of your life. With the Wrath of the Lamb DLC adding even more stuff to explore you might as well sell your soul to the devil and spend your next life playing this too.
Every attempt to complete even Isaac's basic story mode will seem like a fresh new game and by the time you realise that this game is waaaaaay bigger than it lets on you'll start to wonder if you'll ever manage to experience everything this game has to offer. In terms of content it's one of the best value for money games Steam has available and if you're lucky, one day, you'll be able to tell your grandkids about that one time you actually made it to the end...
Prepare to lose months of your life.

Remember the 90's?... When turn-based combat was king....with the original jagged alliance or the original x-com, we used to be given Action Points, and we could "spend" em how we liked. Run, throw a grenade then disappear around a corner at a run with the last of your points. That caused you to calculate quickly if you had enough points to do what you wanted. That,in turn, made character stats and abilities relevent to the gameplay in a big way.
The "new", dumbed down form of turn based combat found in this game and others like Wastelands 2 need to be taken out back and shot. In my oppinion this style of turn based combart is damaging to this wonderful genre, and does not show its glory or potential in the modern age.

Amphora is one of those tiny little masterpieces that you
are out there, but you only get to hear about it by accident. And my, what a happy accident this is!
A game of love, sorrow and perseverance, Amphora is a stunning art piece by a two-man studio called Moondrop. From the very first scene, I found myself completely immersed within its stained glass visuals and hauntingly beautiful music.  There is no text, speech or even a tutorial. You learn about the game, its story and its mechanics by simply exploring the lovely scene in front of you. That might sound a bit troubling, but in practice it works wonderfully.
Even though some of the puzzles are quite easy, I recommend taking it slow. Try to look beyond the puzzle and explore the scenery, otherwise you'll easily miss out on the story.
Overall, Amphora has been one of my favourite gaming experiences in 2015 so far. I have a feeling Moondrop is another Supergiant in the making. Time will tell...

tldr; great game for the price
Take XCOM, add in a occultic western plot and you get Wild West.  Great game for the price, I got about 18 hours of play in at $20 USD and that was doing all the scenarios on Normal once.  If you are a completionist and want to get all of the unlocks (which does have gameplay impacts), you could spend another 20-30 hours playing the scenarios multiple times.
The story is well written and it's interesting to see the scenarios weave together with the main characters.  The game allows you to choose a few different paths to take to learn it all so everyone's experience will likely be slightly different as they go through it.  The map mode allows some choice/consequence actions to take place adding more variability in how the story plays out overall.
I only played on Normal so I can't speak to the other difficulties but overall it wasn't too difficult with a little bit of strategy.  The AI was pretty dumb in many cases allowing me to take advantage of positioning often.  The best example would be them ending their turns in a small area where I had range through a window.  I was able to kill 3-4 guys that way over 5-10 turns as they refused to take advantage of their numbers and kept ending their turns right where I shot their buddy after a move or two.
I also enjoyed the card upgrade system and the different types of guns available; the progression was quite noticable during gameplay and they allow for quite a bit of customization for each of the characters you can control.

The Binding of Isaac, what can I say it's a fun game, and the random generator makes sure that  game can be easy or just hell. Especially if you also have the DLC wrath of the lamb, that adds new bosses, new enemies, new items and trinkets and not one but two extra floors after the womb, so instead of going down in sheol, you can now go to the cathedral and after that and you have a certain trinket on.  You can go down and beat the final boss of Wrath of The Lamb, that and much more. The control scheme is easy to use WASD keys to move, the arrow keys or mouse to shoot tears or whatever your tears has been replaced with, the E key to lay down bombs, the Q key to use tarot cards and pills and finally the spacebar key to use your activated item or all the items that are not passive.
The premise is as follows, Isaac lives alone with his mother, one day when the mom watches christian television, a mysterious voice tells Isaac's mother that he is god, and Isaac has become corrupted by sin. He makes her remove Isaac's stuff and throw Isaac inside his room. He then demands that for her to show her devotion to him, she has to sacrifice Isaac. Isaac's mother grabs a buther's knife from the kitchen. Isaac sees this through a crack in his door, he scrambles in panic for a way of escape, he finds a trapdoor and jumps down into the dephts below.
Again to make sure the game doesn't become stall, you can play as seven different characters each with different stats and everyone has at least one item, except Isaac which you have to unlock first.
The game also features references from Edmund Macmillens other games, like Meat Boy, C.H.A.D, Larry Jr, Gish, Steven and many more. Warning if you do not like religious references in your game at all, this game is not for you, and parents shouldn't buy this game for their children and if they do don't say I didn't warn you. The Binding of Isaac gets 8/10. For being an entertaining game, that you can play while still having background noise and for it's simple yet challenging gameplay.

The puzzle are really simple and mostly straight forward, just use the tools that you have in order to solve the complications that the characters are facing, and as an entity where you can create connections, you'll unlock different and stronger type of connections as you progress, to help you finish later levels, so this kept the puzzle solving interesting and with low redundancy. Although one could argue that the mix of story and gameplay alone keeps the game interesting on its own.
The whole game is charming, with how your journey is helping other people's journey in their best and worst times, through puzzle solving, and you do it in a way that actually interacts with the progression of the story, as mentioned above, and it would be great if more puzzle games, or games in general, made it so you interact with the story through gameplay like this game, because it's refreshing and barely any game use this technique. But yea, the game is great to look at, heartwarming to experience, and fun to play-through.

Amphora, developed by Moondrop, is a puzzle story game where you will be assisting a girl throughout her life to see what all her life has in store for her. You will be playing the part of a mist/smoke that has a sphere of influence. Inside this sphere you will be able to influence objects in many different ways.
Graphically we are talking about a very unique and pleasing looking game. Everything is either in silhouette or in stain glass. The people and the objects follow that decor, and I have to say that it looks sharp. As stated before you are going to be going through a tale of a girl as she grows so you will have plenty of different levels, with all different looking mechanics to try to navigate through.
There is no voice acting, but that's not the point of the game, this game is set to teach you through action. There is, however, a very soothing soundtrack that will follow you throughout your gaming that keeps you calm even when there are frustrating parts to the game.
The controls are pretty straight forward and they all revolve around your mouse. You will be utilizing both mouse buttons to perform actions, and depending on what you are trying to do you will find many different potential solutions, hopefully one of them will get you through the level.
So this was one of those games that I heard about through another game's advertising, and I thought, man that looks like a unique game. So I had to try it, and when I did I sailed through about 30% of the game without even breaking a sweat, and then I hit a wall, a big one. Unfortunately this is one of those games that basically gives you the keys to the kingdom and then fades into the background, which is great because you have free reign to try several different things within your sphere of influence, but it did grate on me that there wasn't going to be a very intuitive way of completing the stage, or so I thought. I did break down and watch a YouTube video and had an immediate face palm moment. So I think I can safely tell you that there is definitely some challenging levels that will make you think outside the box, but not outside the sphere of influence ;)
This is definitely a game for those who are more interested in unique puzzles, and enjoys the soft flowing melodies. Throughout my playing of this game for reviewing purposes I have to say that even when I hit an obstacle the overall feel relaxed me, and with that I would like to give this game an 8.3 out of 10.

A very good game from a small studio.
I recommend it for players who like westerns and/or tactical turn based combat.
Game has 8 different scenarios, which are connected by story. Each scenario has different mechanic on the map (sometimes to lead exploration expedition, sometimes you mine gold, sometimes you just want to kill and burn and cause chaos) and few tactical missions.
In each scenario you manage a group of up to 4 characters who do not level up, but as you play and find loot and ability cards you can customize characters to your liking. Although ability cards are given at random and as soom as much better than others, each time you play your characters will have to be customized differently.
Tactical turn based combat is simillar to XCOM, but since cover also reduces damage greatly, the focus is much much more on flanking oponents or using unique ricochete mechanic which allow one of your team-mates to fire and bounce bullet from metal objects like bells, buckets etc to hit oponents behind cover.
All that in a devilish mood of western and six-shooters.

I just didn't see what the appeal was. However I was happily proven wrong. Duck Game is a insanely fun and frantic game. While the game does feature a single player arcade mode. With weapons and strategies flipping and changing constantly as you go through the 50 levels. That might be a small room with grenades. A forest area with four sets of Knight's armor. However as multiplayer is the primary draw here. It's something to keep in mind. If your looking for a good way to blow off steam with friends or online. Duck Game is great choice for a party game. This game's story has actually surprised me. I thought that it would be something like an absurd gore-y homour-ey western about demons and zombies, but instead it appeared as a serious tragedy with high emotional impact.
Other than that, it is a pretty solid tactical game about a squad of different units with different skills, who move twice per turn and shoot each other. There are, however, some little things, which renew your image of a typical tactical game - for example, final probability of getting shot is not random - there is a scale of "Luck", which depletes when your enemy missed and fills when you get shot. So there won't be any kind of situation, in which some unaccessible unit will snipe others from long range with 0% chance to get hit, and that's good. Also, gameplay on a world map differs in different campaigns - some campaigns will make you collect food, so you won't starve, and other will give you mysterious powers, which you may use to your advantage. This is also pretty cool.
Well, I guess that I would like to recommend this game to anyone, who like turn-based tactical games, westerns and great storylines. Other people are also invited to buy this game, but preferably when it's on sale - there is a chance that some gameplay basics can be seen as tedious and repetetive.
For myself, however, I would like to praise this game and say that I liked it very much.

Civ III is an apogee of the former "Civilization" games focus. Why play it now, when Civ V is tuned,fixed, updated so many times - and even price looks fine for almost every pocket? Well, it's all for that focus I'm talking about.
First three of Civilozation games were taking the player back at the dawn of the known history- and to help to notice the flow of time,there was some borderlines across that mighty river of the so-called "4th dimension". Starting with the Civ V this process of moving through timeline were "smoothed", to the point where player gliding from the start to the end of the game without any noticable delay. I'm not saying that's bad- I like Civ V myself, but sometimes you don't want simple transfer from A to B, from the stone to electricage, you want to see cornerstones to each specific era. And with that, Civ V is giving you the better experience.
All that i said in the previous passage,is arguable,of course. But here is another trait of Civ III which was intentionally cutted off ( in favor of balance, of course) , the size of armies and all warfare business.
With all complexity of the game mechanics in the Civ V,armed conquests there looking as they performed 20-30 people at best. In Civ III,we have totally another scale. So,when I want to win a game of Civilization by Assault strategy, I start Civ III.
The third volume of Civilization is dated, but still deep,still challenging, still holding the billion of possitibilities to build your nation. Make your Way. So I'll mark the game as 9?10, not ideal, but so much enjoyable! :)

Puzzle Kingdoms is a fairly poor Bejeweled clone with a metagame tacked on. You do "conquer" new lands but it's really just series of Bejeweled games. You do find new items and artifacts but it requires you to play through series of Bejeweled games. You do cast spells to improve your Bejeweled games and there is strategy involved but what it all comes down to, is just grind.

Wait, I never recommended this game?
Okay… Let’s fix that.
This game is weird because it’s the anti-bastion. While bastion showers you with whimsy, wonder, and wild, this game takes you to a darker place…
And you will love every second of it.
It takes you into the earth, where you will eventually traverse some unspeakable places. The point is you go to these paces to escape your mother’s wrath, as she’s trying to kill you. You will have to do battle with her unborn children, screaming abominations that smell your innocents and purity and wish to rend you to pieces for it. You can only fight back by hitting them with your bitter tears.
It gets better through. You will have the opportunity to become more powerful as you delve deeper into the abyss. You will find artifacts, and they will strengthen you while robbing you of some of your purity. When this adventure starts you will be a mere babe, but by the end you will be indistinguishable from that which hunts you…if you want to survive, like they have for so long. By the time you get to the lower most floors, IF you get to the lower most floors, you may even begin to wonder if under all that bile, rotting flesh, and tears, if there’s a soul anymore.
If you fail, you can always try again. But you will have to start all over, pure and innocent. This is a rouge like after all.
Maybe you will become like me. I have been reincarnated over a hundred times. Starting out pure and bright like a full moon, only later to eclipse my virgin body and mind with vile darkness! I have slain my mother over sixty times, and each time leaves me filling more fulfilled than the last!
Maybe we will encounter each other. You will know me by my ivory crown of children’s teeth. You will know me by the fires burning in the back of my empty eye sockets. You will know me by the void on my face, deeper than any pit and blacker than any darkness. When you see these things you will know that the end has come, for you, everything you have known, and everything you would have known.
PS: Wrath of the lamb is cool too. You should download it after the game gets boring, as there’s plenty of stuff to do before then.

Overall Amphora has a deep story to tell, and does so in an unconventional way. The stained glass, art style and hauntingly, beautiful music are the strength of the game, but sadly are not supported well enough by the gameplay. While the mechanics are interesting, the puzzles never really challenge the player, and feel like they were the last thing on the developers mind. I really enjoyed my time in the world of Amphora, and give it 7 out of 10.
Designed by Moondrop, a two person Norwegian developer, Amphora is a physics puzzle game, with a strong narrative. The main story of Amphora follows a girl as she grows from a baby to a young woman, meets a partner, and then struggles through the challenges of war. The story is beautifully portrayed through the speechless and text-less imagery of the game, with perfectly paced and balanced music, supporting it every step of the way.
Moondrop aimed to portray their tale through a shadow theatre style, and with the striking colour schemes used, have made an outstanding visual experience. The music used through this touching tale is a cross culture mix and is a pleasure to listen to.
The main puzzle mechanics of Amphora are simple. The player is able to move objects within a certain area, and utilise various chains for hanging objects, pushing and pulling objects and for adding weight to lever systems. These base mechanics all work in well with the general physics of the game world, but sadly I found the puzzles all too often lacked depth.
In fact, I got so deep into my puzzle solving mind frame, that I started to smash through levels too quickly and missed large chunks of story all together. Don't get me wrong the puzzle mechanics are clever, but the developers missed opportunities to overlay multiple mechanics or really utilise the physics system.
I recommend taking your time with this game. Stop at the start of each level and soak up the ambience and think about what the scene is saying to you, before diving in and solving the puzzle. I used this approach on my second play through and found it to be far more rewarding. The playtime of this title may be a little short for some gamers, at only a touch over an hour, but after completing this game I wasn't disappointed.

I've never played the original Wasteland so I had no particular expectations about this game.
I hold Fallout 1 and 2 in high regard and I can say that Wasteland 2 is what I would have wanted a different Fallout 3 to have been. A PC-centric isometric turn-based cRPG through and through; detailed stat sheets, lots of options, lots of skill and much room for exploration. This game has a learning curve, it doesn't hold your hand in the way many modern AAA RPGs do. It's also long. Very long. Depending on how thoughrough you are with side quests and exploration it may take between 40-60 hours to complete. The many choices you have in the game does offer replayability, but the gameplay is quite combat-oriented.
But it also has some problems though:
1) Pacing. This game requires a lot of patience. It takes a while before the story gets off the ground. The skill checks eat up time as well. I needed to take a break from the game about half-way through (I found some of the areas midways somewhat uinteresting and the combat was becoming repetitive) and then come back to it again after a couple of months. However the second half of the game feels better. I almost think it would have been better if the developers had cut some of the content to make the game more focused.
2) Armor system. This is just badly designed. Armor comes with a armor threshold. Weapons come with armor penetration. If weapon penetration exceeds armor threshold then armor does nothing. And it so happens that most enemies you encounter use weapons with armor penetration that just about match the best armor you can get in that part of the game. And later in the game more enemies use energy weapons which deal increased damage to high armor ratings. Thus you find yourself in situations late game were your armor is either detrimental or useless. This really calls for a major balance rehaul patch.
3) Graphics and animation. This game would have looked good ten years ago. The animations are fairly rough and stiff at times. Many backgrounds are nice, but the overall impression is very mediocre.
But these issues should not deter you if you're into long and involved turn-based cRPGs.

This game reminds me of the old-school X-Com games with it's hidden enemy movements and percent-to-hit chances.  Couple that with some good ole-fashioned western demonic possession and you've got a great game.  The difficulty ramps up nicely, and the fact that your actions (such as whether to slaughter an entire household of cleaning staff) will actually impact your game later (merchants tend to not like to sell to cold-blooded murderers...who knew?)  I also really like the whole playing card deck, where you can allocate up to 5 cards to each character, and those cards give different stat bonuses...and, if you happen to put together an actual poker hand (from the lowliest single pair to a straight flush) you gain even more benefits.
I can't really find much about the game that I don't like (although, much like X-Com, I get real tired of starting a mission over when one of my characters dies, 'cause once he's dead, he's dead...no respawns after combat here).
Pick this game up if you're a fan of turn-based, squad level tactical combat and you like demon-possessed bandits :)

I love this game! Amphora is not your standard point and click adventure / puzzle. It tells the story in a very interesting way - a series of mini games / puzzles. Each scene can be looked at as on its own, or as a part of a bigger story, that is slowly revealed in front of the eyes of the player. A story of a little girl ... growing up... falling in love ... aaand I'll stop spoiling ;)
The game doesn't hold your hand or teaches you how to play - it starts with a couple of simple scenes, where you're left alone to figure out, what actually the goal is, what you can and can't do. You are playing some kind of invisible entity, that's watching over this girl as she grows up, able to move stuff around within the reaching distance of the magical amphora. I guess the game does help you a little bit, by telling you how you can rotate the objects you "hold" in your ghostly hand, but that's about it. When a new puzzle / scene is presented to you, you need to observe, discover what part of the story this can be, figure out what needs to happen and make it happen. Sounds simpler, that it is, and I guess that could be somewhat irritating for people new to the puzzle adventure genre, but I felt right at home. Took me some time to get used to the mechanics and understanding, what exactly the mechanics are, but I guess that's just part of the puzzle.
Here is what happens : You start the game and dive into the beautiful world of this "1001 nights-themed" shadow theater, you listen to the amazing music and your heart opens, the game touches your heart with it's story, and a strong bond occurs - you're in love with the game. Can only recommend the experience!

Amphora isn’t quite what I expected when I finished the first couple of levels. Not that that’s a bad thing, on the contrary, but its narrative consists of solving separate puzzles that tie everything together. So the story is told by showing you bits and pieces of the bigger story but it never relies on using audio, or text. It’s all up to you how you want to interpret the story, even if some of it is crystal clear.
Behind the gorgeous graphics lies a game that reminded me a bit of WarioWare Inc. The gameplay consists of rotating and connecting items in a specific way in order to get the results you need. Never are you given an objective. Again, there are times when you’ll know exactly what to do, and other times it will take you several minutes before you realize exactly what the game’s asking from you. Discovering how to solve these ‘harder’ puzzles gives you a sense of accomplishment, which is good, but in a way it’s also kind of bad. Not letting the players know what’s expected from them might annoy or frustrate people who aren’t as experienced with playing (puzzle) games as others might be and I’m not afraid to admit that there were times where I became annoyed because the objectives weren’t entirely clear. It also felt a bit like it was a way to artificially lengthen the story, which is already quite short at about 2-3 hours of playtime (I didn’t find this a problem personally, but I know some people might appreciate a game (a little) less because of it). In any case, a small on-screen hint would suffice and help players in need and I think it could easily be implemented by the developer. But that’s up to them, of course, and it’s only a small flaw/complaint from my side.
As I said the game plays a bit like WarioWare Inc. That’s because the puzzles feel like mini-games, minus the time limit. You usually have to interact with the scenery and objects to solve a puzzle, so in one level you might have to guide fireworks into the air by positioning tables, while in another one you have to pull a ship to the shore using a block of ice and a specific tool (just don’t ask me what it’s called). It’s all pretty fun. That is, until you hit a level where you’re having a hard time using the physics to your advantage. There was one level where it was perfectly clear what I had to do (save a girl from drowning) and yet, because of the physics, it became a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to accomplish. The game could be a little more forgiving in this department. I also reached a point in the game - just a few levels later - where the game just infinitely rotated every object I picked up. There was no way to finish the level so I had to restart the game (after which the problem was solved). I might be nitpicking here, but a game this small shouldn’t have too many bugs or glitches I think.
Now, it seems I didn’t enjoy it because so far pretty much all I’ve been doing is complaining, but trust me, I really do like the game. The puzzles usually make sense and it’s generally fun to complete a level. And I was intrigued by the way it was telling me its story. It’s certainly different than many other games, and I mean that in a good way. It’s unique and beautiful and people should take note, which brings me to the following: the graphics.
And God, these graphics are absolutely gorgeous. It has an Arabian, dreamy, atmosphere where everything in the foreground is silhouetted with only a few parts here and there that are shown as what looks like stained glass. It’s an amazing effect and it looks just beautiful in motion. The background is shown in full color, with gradients and it makes the whole game look perfect. Amazing work was done here, the developers can be really proud of this aspect.
The animations could use a little work. Again, this is also partly thanks to the physics (the level with the rabbits is a good example here), and it’s nothing distracting but definitely noticeable.
The voice acting consists of little sound bites that are simple but get the job done and the music is subtle but relaxing, and feels very natural in a way that you don’t really notice it while playing.
Amphora is a game that puzzle fans will absolutely love, thanks to the lovely visuals, but even frequent, senior puzzlers might find a couple of the game’s puzzles hard to solve. This is not because the puzzles themselves are hard, because they aren’t, but because the game lacks direction and too often you’re left wondering what to do. If you can look past that then there’s a charming game to be found here. In that case this game is an absolute must. In all other cases I would still recommend it, but some of you might want to wait for a sale. Because it’s pretty good, but nothing revolutionary.

Hard West describes itself as “A Weird West Tactical with world map exploration, a hint of adventure and a drop of RPG.”Which is a pretty good description of this Turn Based Tactical shooter set in the "Weird West".
I found out about this game when I was watching a video on YouTube about "The Most Under Appreciated Games of 2015" and I would have to agree this game is very under appreciated. I was able to buy it on sale on steam and I got every penny back 100 fold in hours of enjoyment.
Essentially, you play different "scenarios" with different characters. In these "scenarios" you explore the Hard West map making decisions and discoveries that can lead to big turn based gun battles. Through all of this a new story is told and as you play all the different "scenarios" you come to understand how the Hard West became horrifically cursed and tainted with evil.
Overall, I loved it. It was unique, challenging and kept me playing. However, like all games it had a few things that could be better.
Keeping in theme with the game there is a lot good, some bad and a little ugly with Hard West, in my opinion and here it is:
THE GOOD:
- Combat is solid, you sweat every turn and the AI is smart
- Your decisions matter. Decisions you make in the world play can help or harm and really cant be reversed. In combat getting hit hurts and character deaths have impact. Also, you can not just save in order to re-load and avoid your mistakes
-Luck Points are unique aspect of the game that make combat more nerve wracking and/or rewarding
-  Unique environment and style that is maintained through the whole game
- Interesting (but simple) stories. "Scenarios" feel like a module series in a classic pen and paper RPG
- It does a good job of rewarding your for characters for selling their soul, the powers truly tempt you
- While graphics are not "cutting edge" the game art is great
- Perks and weapons are fun to discover and use
The Bad:
- While you really think about your choices in the World Map Exploration, it is a tad lacking and feels more like you are choosing your own adventure than making big strategic decisions
- While the combat is solid, it can get redundant after you have played a few of the scenarios especially cause the characters can all use the same guns and perks
- Stealth, is a little hard to grasp initially y and when you do understand it, it is kind of dumb
The Ugly:
- When in the world map I would often have crashes when switching to my character inventory, this made me lose some weapons and perks. Which is frustrating considering you can not really save your game and you work hard for all your gear.
All in all, if you like tactical turn based games and you want a unique setting, I say get Hard West. Personally, I hope they make more Hard West games,   I think there is lots more they could do with this world.

This could easily be a very good game, but unfortunately it is only a good game. My biggest problem is that I found the difference between hard and normal mode too big. Normal mode was too easy and boring, I finished most fights with everyone being at max HP, but hard mode was too hard, I restarted a mission at least seven times, but still could not complete it. Finally I got enough doing the same thing again and again, so I went back to normal mode. I think the best would be if you could have at least 1-2 more points in a mission where you could go back, if you fail. At least you should be able to restart after the setup phase (it was pretty annoying doing the setup phase again and again).
PROS:
- really good tactical possibilities, the fight is almost fully deterministic, so you can carefully plan the turn.
- the luck system is a great idea, and I think it works pretty well.
- despite other people, I like that the game is split to chapters. So if I liked one, I can try it again in harder difficulty.
- the cards are a very interesting idea, I enjoyed optimizing the layout.
- good atmosphere (especially the music and voice)
- covers reduce damage, so no more unavoidable death from some extremely lucky enemy (how I hated that in XCOM).
CONS:
- difficulty levels are too rough, there should be something between normal and hard
- no save during mission. I understand that the devs wanted the player to face the consequence of their acts, but currently you cannot continue a mission if you had to suspend, for example if something IRL prevents you to play on. Also the game has some bugs, which I can accept, but if I have to restart a 1 hour mission because of the bug, then that is not fun.
- bad optimization: the game freezes many times (even during menu manipulations)
- the UI just feels bad, several things are hard to see. For example on the card screen I can hardly tell which cards are assigned to a char, if I want to create a flush for example.
- the adventure part (or whatever it is between missions) feels repetitive and boring (probably only me, I bought this game for the fight)
- some abilities are not balanced
EDIT: It turned out that on the mission where I failed hard mode I was fighting with two waves of enemies at the same time, which I supposed to kill separately. So my comment about hard mode being too hard is no longer valid.

Fantastic Shooter with RTS elements. This game belongs in any serious competitive gamers library.
Team work is key in this game and there's a bit of a learning curve, but winning is extremely rewarding. Unknown Worlds has nearly perfected the asymmetrical balance of the maps and the two teams, whos play style is radically different from the other. Marines work better as a well coordinated unit, straying off by yourself is a surefire way to get yourself killed. Aliens use guerilla warfare and chaos to confuse and overcome their enemies.
You'll fight to gain ground and push the opposing team back until you can take out their commander/hive, who gives the teams orders through an overhead RTS-style view of the map, seeing is troops in real time. Some of the most intense moments happens when swarms of aliens cut the power to a room. The lights flicker and the room goes black. Marines switch on their flashlights frantically and aliens lurk in dark corners with their night vision, waiting for the right moment to strike.
You won't want to miss this game.

When the wife of the best-selling writer Alan Wake disappears on their vacation, his search turns up pages from a thriller he doesn’t even remember writing. A Dark Presence stalks the small town of Bright Falls, pushing Wake to the brink of sanity in his fight to unravel the mystery and save his love.
Presented in the style of a TV series, Alan Wake features the trademark Remedy storytelling and pulse-pounding action sequences. As players dive deeper and deeper into the mystery, they’ll face overwhelming odds, plot twists, and cliffhangers. It’s only by mastering the Fight With Light combat mechanic that they can stay one step ahead of the darkness that spreads across Bright Falls.
With the body of an action game and the mind of a psychological thriller, Alan Wake’s intense atmosphere, deep and multilayered story, and exceptionally tense combat sequences provide players with an entertaining and original gaming experience

Even if you don't want to "play" the game, it has great atmospheric sounds to keep on in the background while you do other things.  The game has an interesting visual style and can only be described as oddly fascinating.

An excellent flight simulator that has unmatched realism and user friendliness.

If you have any interest in flight, get this game. You can't go wrong with purchasing a classic.

Simply put, Alan Wake plays like a Stephen King novel turned into a TV miniseries turned into a videogame. This is intentional by Remedy and this narrative complexity is one of the game’s strengths.
Remedy has woven a very complex story into Alan Wake and that’s really half of the reason to play this game. The main story, told in episodes like a TV series, is about Alan piecing together what’s happened in his missing week while the ever-present darkness corrupts the townspeople and relentlessly pursues him. However during that missing week, Alan apparently wrote a pre-cognitive novel about the very events that are happening to him, because as you play you keep finding manuscript pages that he wrote and that describe everything that subsequently happens to him. These are a lot of fun to hunt out and collect because they explain the rather fragmented story and make you feel just as desperate and paranoid as Alan—groping in the dark for answers, desperate that the next chapter page will reveal the truth he needs.
Blood and gore are so downplayed in Alan Wake as to be next to nonexistent. There are no chainsaw wielding psychopaths or bloodthirsty monsters—just the creeping darkness, and the unsettling things it does to the citizens of Bright Falls. People go missing in the woods and nobody sees this as unusual; later, when you’re lost in the woods, these missing people come after you, shrouded in oily shadows and out to gut you with whatever bladed implement they have handy.
Alan is a writer, not a warrior, but he has his trusty flashlight and an assortment of small arms to beat back the Taken, as the infected townspeople are called. First you must aim Alan’s light at an enemy and boost its output to burn away the darkness, and then finish off the Taken with a few shots from your pistol or shotgun. It might sound repetitive but with multiple Taken emerging from the shadows and your flashlight dwindling, it can get pretty hectic as you juggle reloading your tiny snub-nose and popping fresh batteries into your light, all while running away from and dodging attacks. Later on you can get better lights and weapons, including flares to give you breathing room and flash bang grenades to clear an area, but ammo is usually scarce and you must balance exploration with your limited reserves.
Everything in the PC version is essentially the same as the Xbox 360 version. Alan Wake is one of the best converted, least buggy PC ports I have played in a long time. The quirky characters and stark daylight sequences might temporarily pull you out of the terror, but the memories of wandering around in the woods, hounded by eldritch shadows, will haunt your nightmares for months to come.

I've been playing Fallout 2 since I first bought it new in 98' and never got the chance to ever play Wasteland, although I was aware of it and its profound influence. I picked up this game as soon as I could afford it and have fallen in love with isometric turn based combat all over again.
I first played this on my off the shelf HP desktop with just a factory AMD A8-6500 using integrated Radeon 8570D graphics. This game played well with decent performance in all situations without measuring FPS on low settings. I since have added a GTX 750 Ti and can play the game maxed out and it is running over 60fps in all situations. So with my A8 barely on par with an Intel i3, anyone can pretty much enjoy this game on low end systems.
Graphics: 10/10, it is beautiful and is what you would expect from a Fallout type universe.
Combat: 10/10, some nice features that remind me of FO Tactics, familiar and easy to grasp.

A major tip for new players: Make sure when building your squad you incorporate certain skills. This is not like Fallout games where you could master all skills throughout the game such as demolitions, lockpick, traps etc. This game forces you to equip characters with these skills or they simply will not be able to be utilized at all until you have a character possesing that particular skill. So if you start your squad and nobody has lockpicking skill, you will not be able to lockpick any doors at all until you acquire someone that does have the skill.
If you like Fallout or the genre, you will not be dissapointed! Price has consistently dropped over last few months, I paid full price and would again.

Well... I went all the way from loving this game into hating it and then to accepting it and finally to like it. So, it turned out that:
1. This is NOT a Fallout1/2. It's more like Fallout Tactics with FO 1/2-ish endings.
2. You can solve most of your problems 2 ways: using speech or lockpicking skills. Or both.
3. Devs thought "We will make 3 kinds of speech and 3 kinds of lockpicking skills. It will create so many choices". Well, actually no, it's still 2 ways.
4. Assault rifles are most useful weapons in the world. All other weapons are not worth your skillpoints.
5. Melee specialists will do nothing first half of the game except getting hurt all the time. During second half they should learn how to use assault rifles.
6. Throwing weapons do not require a skill. Even monkey could throw a grenade, right?
7. You can never tell from the view of your team which armor they are wearing. Cause stockings with garment are more important in the wasteland then power armor, right?
8. Energy weapons do very little damage to unarmored enemies. Please read this line again to understand the level of absurd.
9. Main story quest deviated very little from "the search for GECK". Actually you'll look for 2 types of chemicals.
10. You can dig all the graves in the world. No one cares.
I could go on with this list, but I think you get the picture by now. Not to mention clumsy 3d-models with ugly skin and absolutely unnecessary sims-like character editor (can give you nightmares). It's mostly poor choice of engine. But if you like a good tactics with turn-based combat in a postapocalyptic setting - you'll buy this game. It will punish you in order to make you start another playthrough. And you'll learn to accept it "as is". Like I did.

The characters feel more like passive obstacles and dialogue dispensers rather than the kind of interesting people you met in the likes of Grim Fandango, with the result that the world and characters feel like they're just background for characters to wander through rather than particularly interesting in themselves.

Virginia is a single-player first-person thriller.
The game takes place in the last days of summer 1992, the player takes control of Anne Tarver, a graduate FBI special agent assigned to her first case. You investigate the disappearance of a young boy. As a rookie detective, you get a experienced partner, Maria Halperin. Tarver's superiors instruct you to keep a watchful eye on her...
The special aspect of Virginia is that in the whole game no word is spoken at all. Instead of dialogue, the story in Virginia is told through the physical performances of its characters.
There is not much interaction, you can collect some objects but more or less it fits to the walking simulator categorie.
The game needs something around two hours to be finished.
The music is wonderful and fits perfectly to the atmosphere of the game.
Virginia manages to tell a deeply engaging story about friendship, loyalty, betrayal and identity, without using a single word of dialogue.
From my point of view Virginia was a great experience and was worth its price.

Haven't played through this game since it launched, but I figured I'd roll back around to provide some thoughts on it.
First of all, if you're a fan of coherent plots with coherent endings, you probably will not appreciate this game. It's Twin Peaks-esque not just in the aesthetic, but in the subtle surreality of the storyline as well. It's a storyline that's intentionally, not incidentally, confusing - as is the case with most good mysteries.
Of course, people are much less likely to accept a confusing ending than a confusing plot. And I agree that the ending of this game is more of a NON-ending in the sense that it does nothing to tie up loose ends, or answer questions that were likely stirred up at earlier points.
I'd argue, however, that the game doesn't really set itself up for a clear ending at all. It's a series of snapshots in the protagonist's life more than anything, characterized by the social and interpersonal conflicts that crop up along the way. Though bewildering things (such as the repeating image of the bison) do appear and do leave you with questions, they serve primarily as symbols for the player to interpret, rather than solid plot points that'll somehow all be connected in the end. Needless to say, the game reached a point where I just stopped expecting a conclusive ending altogether. And I still pressed on with interest.
Beyond that? Well, visually, it's a beautiful game. Furthermore, don't let the strange, "indie" art style lead you to believe that there are no cinematic scenes or expressive characters - in fact, given the complete absence of dialogue, it's a story told entirely through "pure cinema" (i.e., telling by showing). May take you a bit of getting used to, but it suits the game just fine. (Twin Peaks fans will thoroughly enjoy the soundtrack, too.)
Overall, there's nothing
bad about this game. It all comes down to taste, and how much tolerance you have for a David Lynch-style surrealistic story that doesn't wrap things up in a shiny gift ribbon when it's over. If you're like me and just felt that the ending came a little...abrubtly, hit the discussion boards! To rephrase what I said earlier, the game leaves you a lot to interpret, so it's a great one to sit with if you enjoy doing that with media.

I have not fully completed the game yet, i have fully captured 6 districts and given 2 to each of the team which i think has given me a great setup. I have also fully maxed out all rackets and collected all the things to collect in these 6 districts. So i have a good feel for how this game plays.

-Shooting starts off sloppy and improves as you upgrade which i loved, so you can't headshot everyone so easily to begin with.
-CQC animations are fun and brutal kills making enemies afraid is a great touch and very useful to take out 2 guys stood toghether
-Story is very gripping as with all the mafia games
-Great details like white only shops in certain areas, fast/slow police reponse times depending on the area. And lots more just like that
-50 hours and not fully completed yet, great value for a game of this price.
Cons:
-Crashing although rare do happen, 50 hours and roughly 5 crashes.
-Lighting is not great at times, my fix for this is to change the brightness settings at times when it got to bad, either the glare is way to bright so you turn it down or the darkness is way to dark so you have to turn it back up! Gets annoying.
-The Map seems to bug out allot when going under bridges or over them or inside a building and then back out.
Overall - I love it, it is as good if not better than mafia 1/2 which i loved. On launch it was capped at 30 fps so it has allot of bad reviews already but personally i thought it looked great then, since the patch it looks amazing and runs smooth. Duck Game is a very special game.  It's a game designed for everyone, but especially crafted for anyone who grew up in the Couch Multiplayer era, specifically Sega Genesis fans.  It's a game with simple mechanics and an endless supply of frantic over the top fun.
The rules are simple, first to 10 match victories wins!  Matches generally last about 10-30 seconds, after which the next one starts up almost immediately on a randomly selected map.  The rhythm of the game is almost never broken up, keeping a quick and exciting pace throughout.  There's an ungodly amount of weapons, each with their own variety and mechanics.  You'll find everything from Derringers, to Shotguns, to Nerf Guns, to Mooninite Lasers!
Although the main draw of this game is easily the Multiplayer, the Single-Player challenges offer you a chance to train your skills through a series of modes.  These challenges give you major insights into lesser known mechanics of the game, which can give you that little edge in combat.  Through winning challenges you get Tickets, which you can spend not only to buy hats, but also GAMEPLAY MODIFIERS for multiplayer!
Did I mention there's a dedicated Quack Button? That can be pressed at any time. Seriously. It's the best thing ever.
So grab this game, grab some friends, grab some RPGs, and let the feathers fly!

This review is (also) for FSX SE with "FlyInside FSX Pro" and Oculus Rift support. See below.
Simulator basics: FSX does a good job in simulating aviation. It's hard to consider it as a "game", and according to the comments, some people seem to be confused about this. It's a simulator, and as such it does many things very well, except maybe "quick and easy fun dogfight shooting" and up-to-date graphics.
I especially like the following features: First among all, aviation (not just flying) is simulated -- air traffic control leads you to your glideslope, ground operators supervise taxiing, all with actual voices and flexible reactions to your situation. Then, all important navigation aspects for instrument flight rules are covered (VOR,NDB,DME,ILS etc). Next, the airplanes have working fly-by-wire systems (e.g. the Airbus 321 goes "TO/GA" when stalling) and the autopilot systems are functional -- but sometimes also a bit buggy, sadly. The flight models seem okay -- as not being a pilot I can hardly say how good they are actually, but common sense seems to be that they're not that bad, and landscapes and airports, even small airstrips, all around the world are covered. The graphics is not ultra-realistic (quite bad some times when being very low), but it's acceptable for the purpose.
So, if you want to learn about the details of airplane flying, navigation, communication and procedures, this is a relatively cheap entry point in comparison to other simulators (which have their advantages and disadvantages). If you want some arcade action, this is simply the wrong genre. Don't buy it then.
Now to Oculus Rift / VR support: With the FlyInside extension (currently around $30), you can sit in your cockpit and enjoy flying in VR. That works pretty well, but has some requirements. First, get some flight equipment, like a decent joystick with lots of configuarable buttons and a throttle. I use a Saitek X52 pro and it works well. Remember: Keyboard, Mouse and external flight instruments (Saitek offers some) become invisible with a headset on. ;) Second, take a lot of time to configure everything to suit your needs.
FlyInside also allows you to handle cockpit buttons and knobs by looking at them (you get a cursor like in Oculus Home) and you can assign an action-button to select things. This is okay for some parts of the cockpit (toggles and switches), not so good for tuners and knobs where you need to set a value, especially when you need to be quick. So, your joystick really should have some "scroll wheels", turning knobs, sliders and stuff to get things comfortable.
Additionally, you can handle things with touch controllers, but believe me, in the current state of FlyInside you probably don't wanna do this. Not all buttons react as expected, hitting them with a gesture is difficult and you loose some fine control over virtual throttles, yokes or sticks.
When it comes to menus or additional windows (ATC, GPS, etc), FlyInside has a very good concept: They "capture" those windows from the screen and put them as moveable/resizeable 3d panes into your virtual cockpit. You can use the eye curser and select things just like with your mouse. You can also use FSX's main menu (the white one when you launch FSX), as FlyInside pauses the sim and shows your desktop as a 3d screen in VR on demand. By that, you never have to take of the VR goggles.
If you have a VR headset, I can highly recommend FSX+FlyInside. Works very well, and being "in a cockpit" is much more fun than sitting in front of a monitor that just displays a cockpit.

Alan Wake, this game kept me coming back to it over and over again.
Despite its older graphics, it still holds stunning scenery and an unforgettable atmosphere that, at times, will creep you out to the very core. The story itself is intriguing and the narration is well written. The soundtrack is great, especially when listening to the radio broadcasts. I found that simply enjoying the scenery whilst listening to the radio really built up different emotional atmospheres throughout the game.

Stunning scenery and strong characters make Alan Wake a standout in the horror-action genre.
Alan is a Stephen King-ish novelist dealing with writer's block and a deadline from his publisher, so he and his wife Alice take a vacation trip to a remote town nestled in the misty mountains of the Pacific Northwest. Alas, even though his muse awakens (heh heh), his newfound writing has a vicioius dark side that he must now conquer.
As a third-person shooter, the controls are intuitive and quick. You can switch between shotgun, pistol, flare gun, and flash bang in less than a second (a much needed fraction of time when surrounded by advancing shadow creatures). The gameplay does get a bit repetitive -- go to this place, kick on the generator to ward off the dark, go to this other place -- but the gorgeous surroundings are never boring, and Wake's continuing voiceover narrative contributes much to the foreboding mood. Plus, the pages of the manuscript you find along the way tell their own story, and serve as both foreshadowing and much-needed breaks from the action. In a game about a writer, it's nice to actually read some of his work.
The story is the real reason to play this. I would have been done with this game after 3 hours if not for it drawing me in with beautifully choreographed cut scenes, clever dialogue, and believable if dramatic characterization. Alice feels like a real person, so Alan's quest to rescue her from the Darkness which holds her hostage never feels like a "your princess is in another castle" situation. It's high-stakes, emotional drama. As a husband myself, I'd love to think that I would similarly dash forth and take on the evil hordes to rescue my wife. But who knows? ;)
All in all, Alan Wake boasts great TPS dynamics and characters worth rooting for, all set against breath-stealing imagery in a story with twists windier than a clock.

Alan Wake is one of those games that really surprised me of how good atmosphere can really be!
It's about a writer dude that comes to Bright Falls with his wife to get rid of his writers blockage and to get some hot wifey action on a lake in a boat (but they never tell you that)..
Ofcourse,♥♥♥♥♥♥hit the fan and some misterios, unexplained events happen, his wife is missing, everyone think he killed her, but few townsfolk actually have some hints on what is going on there.. As the story develops, you learn about similar events that happen before and about Alan's troublesome past..
Game is action/adventure survival, in third person view that doesn't have that much adventure puzzles in it, it's more of enjoying the story as it builds up from chapter to chapter with great cut scenes that are directly in the game..
Sometimes you really can't tell if Alan is crazy, imagining things or things he is going through are actually real! Game is divided in 6 chapters and 2 special features that furter explains the story behind Bright Falls and bla bla spoilers..
PRO
- incredible atmosphere, heavily influenced by Twilight Zone, one of the best TV psychological horror show..
- Graphics and scenery, game is spread over a town Bright Falls, mountain, cabin on the lake, roads, many awesome places, a lodge, old sawmill, farm etc.
- gameplay is smooth and enticing, story is very well paced and delivered and for once, there are not many logical errors..
- sounds and music are very good made, music get little wilder when you fight enemies, and all that clasic♥♥♥♥♥♥hehe
- weapons and stuff are very well made, there are few clasic weapons like pistol, shotty, flare gun, flares, and as you play, you really don't need much to think about saving ammo, there are plenty (until you play on hard or nightmare mode :)
CONS
- controls are somewhat "slow" i.e. Alan needs few steps to stop or slow down, which is actually realistic but it can be problem when he doesn't stop when you want him to,
- field of view, to my liking, is somewhat to close to main character, so you can't really "see" what is behind you.
SHOULD I PLAY IT?
Yeah, especially if you are into psychological horor games and liked to watch twilight zone (NOT SAGA), or any kind of survival game like Silent Hill (all of them :) especially SH2!, in some degree Resident Evil (first 3 parts, rest of them didn't quite fell good on me)..
Something that really made this game excellent in my mind is as you "approach" the ending of the game, events get really weird/crazy with very good subcontext about whole plot, with many details that gives you small hints about Alan psyche and people around him (his wife, best friend,..)
Anyway, it's 4 years since this game is out, and I played it just now, and it's still a MUST PLAY!

Recommended for newbies; Not recommended for today's expectations.
I'm not qualified to write this, but I feel that in terms of experience, this is the benchmark the flight sim market minimally ought to follow. I have some hundreds of hours on FSX before owning the Steam copy, and I find that FSX comes off as cheap but relevant and working, however is quickly becoming a failing "gold" standard.
FSX is beginner-friendly, but also at least meets some needs of experienced sim/IRL pilots without burning a hole in wallets. There's a good reason why this software is what got many aviation enthusiasts into the hobby, and that is accessability.
The controls are responsive, while flight models and physics are alright offline. Although not recommended, the mouse/keyboard control scheme works. As of this writing, I'm using a X360 controller which work great with FSX, while saving up for a full Saitek set up that I hope will be a great investment. (Bleeping Flying Spaghetti Monster, those rudder pedals are expensive!)
If you don't mind outdated netcode and multiplayer support, you might still find some fun in multiplayer. Don't be surprised finding passenger aircrafts somehow hovering above an airport. That seem to occur every now and then.
That being said, if you *really* don't mind some immersion being broken, FSX is overall a good
realistic flight sim, minus the same boring landscapes covering almost the whole Earth. At least the aerodome locations are accurate. If you have some budget to spare, go ahead and purchase some of the scenary DLCs.
It's a shame that FSX does not age well with improving hardware. After more than a decade since its inception, we have found that its performance did not scale along. The same loading/caching/occlusion isssues still remain. There are some occasional stutters and awful crashes (both plane and software lol). Some planes still have oversized hitboxes!
Conclusion:
Budget and fair flight sim for noobs. Good enough for practise runs but expect diminishing returns.

Whilst the art direction of this game is to be lauded, along with the cinema quality orchestral score, this game hit a sour note with me in that I get that it's trying to be a game equivalent of a film with obvious references to Silence of the Lambs/Twin Peaks - fine, I get that - but no dialogue? How does that compare?
You watch an episode of Twin Peaks without any dialogue and tell me if you like it or not - I would hope that you would furrow your brow and ask "Why?" Why indeed to the makers of Virginia Variable State did you not have any dialogue - which is the essence of every great story - in this game?
The other major problem as far as I'm concerned relates to the total lack of choices, meanful or otherwise, to make in the game - it's just walking (really slowly) for point A to B, holding down the left mouse button, and watching a cutscene or jump cutting to another scene. If you're going to make a game why not utilise the one major advantage games have over other art forms: Interactivity? And no - looking around and walking from A to B is not interactivity in my mind - if a monkey can do it it's not interactive enough.
Getting on to that point of cuts - I've read a reviewer (might have been PC Gamer) who gushed over how clever the cuts are and as a film-maker I can tell you that they are not. In film the significance of a cut follows a basic theory of montage (look up Eisenstein) like a jump cut being a used to show another angle in the same time/place, or a slow dissolve signifying time passing. Virginia is haphazard at best with its cutting and there were several points where I found myself saying "What? Now? Ermm, why?" or "That needed a slow dissolve not a jump cut". If you're going to borrow something from film at least do it right.
Overall I followed this game with baited breath before it released and I was really looking forward to a game version of Twin Peaks (which I loved) and whilst this feels like a non-dialogue homage to Twin Peaks, it also feels like a total missed opportunity and the lack of dialogue/decisions smacks of the designers being too lazy to implement these two crucial things rather than any revelationary game direction.
TL;DR: Great art direction/music, terribly lacking dialogue or desicions, with haphazard (not thought out) cutting.

I understand that Virginia is meant to be a metaphor about the choices you make in life and how they affect you and those around you. Nice game with interesting mechanics via the Luck attribute. I'm still getting to grips with the ability cards/deck and how they combine to give additional bonuses but I like what I've seen so far (just finished the game on easy setting). These two mechanics lend a very strategic layer to the tactical squad based combat. You could build a character with high luck values and some "expensive" abilities that chew through luck to turn him/her into a demonic juggernaut, or into a character that spams out prayers/buffs every few turns to make them shoot the wings off a fly from half way across the map. Due to the random supply of cards you can't munchkin/twink your way through the game, at least not in the early parts of each scenario until you have a larger card stash.
I was somewhat puzzled by the "metagame" in each scenario as the mechanic changed in each scenario with no real explanation in the game itself (the manual had some info). In one scenario I need to recruit servants, keep them fed and healthy in order to secure certain positions or to do certain tasks, in another scenario I needed to mine gold by myself (no servants), in another scenario I had to manage my premonition power to avoid tactical disadvantages later in the scenario or to secure advantages later in the scenario. These changing mechanics in each scenario  were interesting, but puzzling at the start with some as it was not clear how best to use them or when they should be saved/stored.
All in all I like the game, in particular the squad/tactical combat parts. A Kickstarter/crowd-funding success in my opinion :-)

Got all the way to Duna after having been to the Mun half a dozen times and Minmus twice. Building mechanics are unique and fun. You won't find anything like it in any other game. You'll spend twice the time in the Spaceplane Hangar learning to make a plane that can actually take off (smh).

You need to plan your trajectory ahead of time. Plan your route. Plan this, plan that. And for the love of Kerbol don't forget your heat shield.

The first reaction to seeing Duck Game in action tends to be a prolonged “WTF!?”. The second reaction is equally as entertaining. Once the shock settles, a near permanent smile sets on your face and the faces of those watching and you can hear genuine excitement in those whoops and shouts of delight as you annihilate your opponents to the oh so sweet quack, quack, quacking of the winner. I am not going to beat about the bush here. This game is silly. This game is fun. This game could very easily be THE multiplayer video-game of 2015.
Released previously on what many consider the now defunct Ouya, Duck Game hits windows Steam harder than Donald Duck does English. Featuring a 2 and 4 player local couch co-op, single player challenge modes and for this new release a 2 to 4 player online battle also. With over 50 pre-built levels and over 50 weapons of various hilarity inducing carnage plus a built in level creator the game offers much to keep the gamer interested. It doesn’t really matter though as this game is so much fun to play you never really get fed up of a set level.
It plays fast and furious, slick and silly, and whilst the gameplay may not venture above running around a 2D platform, picking up weapons, throwing grenades and causing general mayhem, it perfects the genre. It looks fantastic with its ‘old skool’ retro-gaming feel and sounds like you are back in those 80s arcades that many of us grew up with and many others wish they had too.
This is Indie gaming done proper. A small idea turned on edgeways, a dash of laughter, perfect controls and fluid gameplay. The Dev, Landon Podbielski will hopefully rake in the kind of money that would make Scrooge McDuck blush and it’s publishers, Adult Swim Games, should court Landon until he comes up with more of these gems. I really do have a hard time criticising this game but in an effort to come across as balanced and not an utter fanboy… No, sorry, I just cannot fault it. Sure, you can lose in the very first second but even then it is still fun to watch the ensuing slaughter. With practice those insta deaths tail away into memory and you find yourself being a little more cautious as you start thinking tactfully and stop running hell for leather over the edge. Running like a mad dog straight for your opponent with a live grenade that will take you both out though, well that never get’s old.
Despite the obvious violence at play here the whole thing is one big cartoon of jetpacking Ducks and because of this some of you may wish to try the game yourself before assuming it will be ok for the younger generation, the only problem with this is that you are unlikely to want to give it back once you played it too. For those of you who take the plunge, you will not be disappointed. From the very first time you jump in the game, to the moment at the end where the mock sports commentator runs through a quick review of those special highlights and we see who was the most popular and therefore wins prizes, you will be hooked.
Oh yes, whilst having your fun, be sure to check out the party mode and stock up your favourite tipple. If you follow the party rules, one, and most likely all of you will end up extremely dizzy at the end of it all.

Overall the game is fun but I still have a few gripes with it. While it is fun and well designed enough, some characters (namely, ones you have to unlock) feel so much more powerful than others, whether it's a bad balance of damage resistance and DPS, or even an undebatably more powerful ult, the game just feels all around unbalanced at the moment.(Like seriously, to the point of one character's ult just slightly increasing their damage for literally three shots to another's giving them more health and fully automatic rocket launchers and gattling guns for maybe 30 seconds) Also, the fact that no matter which mode you choose, the game makes you play against AI and doesn't tell you is honestly boring. It's like the developers don't trust new players to be good enough at shooters to play against other players. And finally, my biggest complaint of all. I know people constantly say this already but let's be honest, the amount of ideas this game has stolen from Overwatch with no attempt to hide it is just shameful. They can say they were inspired by TF2 all they want but it's incredibly obvious how lazy the design in this game was. Whether it's from the character's appearance or from their gameplay, they're usually lifted straight from Overwatch. We've got:
-The sniper with a rifle that turns into a submachine gun when unscoped, that also carries mines and some sort of tool for climbing (Teleporter/grappling hook)
-The dwarf with a giant beard and a shotgun that builds turrets
-The edgy demon guy that looks like the grim reaper
-An asian man with a bow (That also literally has the same first person animations as Hanzo, seriously look up some screenshots)
-Someone in a mech that has gattling guns on each arm
-A large animal with a shotgun and a hook
-A man in a large suit of armor with a giant blue shield that charges as an attack
-The grizzled, gruff veteran with an assault rifle that sprints and uses explosives as abilities
-The explosives expert whose ult takes control of a large rolling explosive
-The guy with a jetpack and a rocket launcher
And it just goes on and on, on top of how obviously stolen the designs are the characters just have no personality to them, despite their kind of unique designs they all just look cliche and uninspired, like from a game you'd see someone playing in the background in a movie
But, if you can't afford Overwatch and want a decent shooter to waste time with, it's still not that terrible

Now for the gameplay.
Honestly, it's not bad. This game is often compared with overwatch, and I can see why. Most of the classes are pretty balanced, and the only one I've almost ripped my♥♥♥♥♥♥off against is a support class who can pretty much double everyone's health near him, and go invulnerable if he's ever targeted.
While I haven't run into a paywall yet, You do start off with like 5 or 6 classes, which is rather nice, but there's like 40 total that you can purchase using money in-game. There's also quests, which you unlock at "Player rank 7", which I would assume you can also get this currency through. Did I mention each "Character" has it's own ranking, which you can gain exp for? I have no clue what it's meant for, as I haven't noticed a buff, but you get "Chests" (which are kinda like loot boxes but without having to use Real Money to open them), which allows you to get Cards (Which can alter playstyle) or decorative things. Duplicates of cards are auto-turned into this substance I can only describe as "Elixer", which you can use to buy other decorative stuff or cards.
I've only unlocked 2 modes so far, Payload and "objective-payload", Payload is one team trying to push while another stops the payload, and "Objective-Payload" is a race to the objective. When you get the objective bar full, you get one "Gamepoint", and have the opportunity to get (I believe 2) more by delivering it to the enemy base. Of course, if the defense team manages to hold off the payload, they get one point as well.
The cards system is pretty seamless, though there are some annoying spammy/op combinations, it allows you to focus on certain aspects of a character. For example, you can do extra damage after you "roll" on cassie, or buff her knockback shot. It's rather hard to describe this, as I haven't used it much my self, but it's pretty nfity.
Now, one thing that feels very unique to this game is the in-match "Credit System". All characters get Credits passivly, and you start with a specified amount. You can earn more by fulfilling your character's role, so a front liner would get more by objective-pushing, and a support would get more by healing. So far I've only played front liners, so I can't describe how balanced support credit generation is., but front-liner seems pretty balanced, though I pretty much always use the same perks with 1 or 2 deviations depending on character.
I'll cover the other stuff if I get around to it when I play more of the game.

I've just quit the last playthrough after firing over 50 shots at a demon that wouldn't move or fire back at 53% hit chance, and missing every time. It doesn't take a genius to know that missing 50 out of 50 shots at a 53% hit chance is pretty unlikely. I could shoot at him but not hit him despite what the percentage said, and he wouldn't move or fire back. I finally went closer and spotted his shadow but could not fire at him despite him being out in the open, the option was greyed out. The next round he charged and one-shotted me. Not very staisfying.
Clearly this needs work, which is a shame because it's a great idea, but with the combat mechanics so unreliable at this stage I won't be playing it until they patch. I like challenging and dangerous games, but only if the mechanics are clear, reliable, and not bugged.

To sum it up: Virginia is short, beautifully designed, esthetically intense. Go for it.

I had a blast! Virginia is along the lines of the X-Files - a sci-fi drama interactive story set in late summer 1992 in the titular Virginia. The story and editing have a slow, but steady pacing, and the score is outstanding. The animation is pretty limited and feels more like stop motion at 30 FPS. It gives it a childhood charm, though not quite to the extent of Stranger Things. It did get a little long for me at times, but during those times (since your movement is locked like if you are in a car or elevator) you are forced to think about the mystery and look around at details. If it was a bit shorter, I would be more driven to do repeat playthroughs. I definitely recommend it if you like visual storytelling (no dialogue) and sci-fi (or is it sci-fi?) mysteries.
Virginia is very fun, and the story just pulls you in. I sat down one night, and beat the whole game in one sitting.
