Duck Game is a very special game.  It's a game designed for everyone, but especially crafted for anyone who grew up in the Couch Multiplayer era, specifically Sega Genesis fans.  It's a game with simple mechanics and an endless supply of frantic over the top fun.
The rules are simple, first to 10 match victories wins!  Matches generally last about 10-30 seconds, after which the next one starts up almost immediately on a randomly selected map.  The rhythm of the game is almost never broken up, keeping a quick and exciting pace throughout.  There's an ungodly amount of weapons, each with their own variety and mechanics.  You'll find everything from Derringers, to Shotguns, to Nerf Guns, to Mooninite Lasers!
Although the main draw of this game is easily the Multiplayer, the Single-Player challenges offer you a chance to train your skills through a series of modes.  These challenges give you major insights into lesser known mechanics of the game, which can give you that little edge in combat.  Through winning challenges you get Tickets, which you can spend not only to buy hats, but also GAMEPLAY MODIFIERS for multiplayer!
Did I mention there's a dedicated Quack Button? That can be pressed at any time. Seriously. It's the best thing ever.
So grab this game, grab some friends, grab some RPGs, and let the feathers fly!

After 26 hours: meh. It's not bad. It's just not good.
Performance: for me, personally, it's fine. It looks OK; water is very well done, some sunsets / rises look really good, lighting is solid without being anything new or exciting. Excessive glare from some lighting is annoying, but tolerable. The whole 30fps thing was a non-issue for me, so I'll stay out of that debate.
Story: starts well, (actually, started really well); deteriorates quickly until you soon realise you're playing Saints Row San Andreas Assassin's Creed 11: The Quest for More Money. This is a shameless cash grab, that becomes 'Drive to marked point, turn off irritating pop-up 'tip', kill everything conveniently marked in red, drive away' - which is really sad. It lacks innovation, polish and passion; it's just a rehash of every other 'open world' game you've played in the last several years. Frankly, I'm waiting for zombies to arrive: it's that derivative.
Music is really good, if you like 60's / 70's tunes, you'll be in heaven here. GREAT soundtrack. Not enough to redeem it, though, but really goes to show just how good this setting could've been.
It's just so... joyless. It's paint by numbers, without Bob Ross's soothing tones. It's just... bleh.
Case in point: physically wire-tapping a phone box marks enemies, magazines and electronic items on your map. Really? This is the level of design and innovation in AAA games now? Rehashing a mechanic that makes no diegetic sense for the simple sake of convenience.
Grab it on sale. Maybe. If you're bored. Really bored.

The game that people denounce it "Free-to-play/Poor man's Overwatch," is actually pretty dang good!
Honestly, the only similarity to that game that I see is just the fact that you play as more than one hero/champion/class from different areas around its own world. That's honestly it. Besides, as much as the characters in Overwatch are more popular and well known, the characters in this game show up a lot of fun character personalities that remind me of how I was drawn into Team Fortress 2. The characters don't have the greatest personalities, and sometimes a bit more over-the-top than what I'm used to, but they know who they are and it doesn't make me cringe, nor does it make feel slightly annoyed by trying to be more "diverse and outgoing" rather than being fun. In fact, some of the one liners, like Fernando's "Not the FAAAAAACCCEEEE!!!" makes me laugh especially when it comes out of nowhere.
I love how the game and the gameplay follows more of a TF2 route, allowing you to have different weapon upgrades to give you and your team an advantage, or allowing different costumes if you want to be silly. Viktor, and Fernando, are honestly the best characters to be if you are a beginnner and want to have an easy start on the game just like how Scout, Soldier, and Pyro are easy starters in TF2. The game modes are the ones you normally expect from a Team Based multiplayer game like Siege (Control Points), and Payload. But the Survival and PvE modes are wonderful to play if you want to try something different.
The art style for this game is perfect for the setting it takes place in. It may be in a sci-fi setting, but the areas the maps take place in are lush and beautiful with a different setting every match you play, and I enjoy how the game itself is short, sweet, and to the point. "Paladins: Champions of the Realm," A game about different champions from different parts of the world teaming up with, and against, each other in a set of epic battles together. Overwatch might have its different "Heroes," but I'm not waiting months on months for a new video that tells a little story, or a comic that shows the everyday life of one of the characters. Paladins also doesn't overwhelm me with a clout of heroes with the inability for me to choose who's the best hero to help especially during its intense matches like how Overwatch does.
If Overwatch wanted to grab me with their story, they should have included a proper story mode to play, rather than try shove it down my throat by showing me videos that don't really add up. Team Fortress 2 may have that similar issue, but where TF2 works is because you can look at the characters at a glance and see they're retro-styled military men who at times, get contracts to seize, collect, destroy, fight, and get into situations similar to those found in cartoons of the 30s to the 90s. Not to mention that because of the freedom that game has for people to create their own shorts basically shows that the TF2 world of the "Valve Universe" is bound to have any kind of story. Gotham City Imposters is another good example of a short, sweet story because it's just people from two sides of Gotham, both pretending to be their idols, Batman and Joker, and having an all-out brawl when Batman's busy. There's no need for an overarching story, just a fun premise with fun gameplay and I'm sold. Paladins, if it ever goes a similar route as TF2, is open to a series of fun adventures without the need to pander.
The only thing I do wish for the game is more maps to be on and more modes to play, as well as allowing the gaming community make the game as fun and inventive like TF2 by featuring custom maps, or allowing mods that change up the game every once in a while.
The only slight gripe I have with Paladins is setting up your account with Hi-Rez Studios, and how it's not entirely connected with Steam, but that's just a nitpick really. I would also complain about unlocking rewards or the games own treasure chests, but that falls under the same feeling of having an account mixed in with buying in-game content, and you could say that for ANY game.
Overall, I recommend this game as well as enjoy it for what it is. If people say Paladins shouldn't exist, then honestly, Overwatch shouldn't even exist either. We need more Team-Based games like this, and TF2 shouldn't be left as the only popular game that does so.  I believe Paladins is its own success story that just needs the love and support to make it possible. Is it BETTER than the previously mentioned games? In my opinion, it matches up there with them but does balance things a bit better than those games. Besides, if I DID have $60+ to buy Overwatch on PC or Consoles, I'd be spending my money elsewhere honestly or donate to this game to help the devs improve on it. I won't entirely dismiss Overwatch, but I'm not grabbed into it like everyone's been doing so for the past year.

I know people constantly say this already but let's be honest, the amount of ideas this game has stolen from Overwatch with no attempt to hide it is just shameful. They can say they were inspired by TF2 all they want but it's incredibly obvious how lazy the design in this game was. Whether it's from the character's appearance or from their gameplay, they're usually lifted straight from Overwatch. We've got:

Before we start the review on the content of the game, let's review the login/launcher.
One- Don't use Gmail, it says it works, It doesn't. You have to log into the game again in game after you launch the game from the launcher, except it doesn't give you a username or password for a Hi-rez account. I got around this by using forgot username and forgot password. It gave me a auto-generated username, that wasn't even close to my gmail username, which was "U027981832". I have no clue what the password was they autogenerated either before I reset it, which by the way, is a terrible system since it gives you a temp password rather than allowing you to change it.
Now, this part is more at the fault of Hi-Rez, But I couldn't for the life of me find a way to change Username or Password in Hi-Rez's account website. I'll attempt to submit a ticket later for it.
Two- I would also like to say this is at the fault of Hi-Rez, I created another account on a different email the "Normal Way". I couldn't log into Hi-Rez or Paladins, when I attempted to recover username, it sent me the username that I was using to attempt to recover my password, but when I attempted to recover password, it simply said "Failed". It also said "Failed" when I tried to log in with the username and password I set, and attempting to create a new account on the same email did not work. Hi-Rez's accounts are literal garbage, and Probably 2 hours of my time are simply sitting in the launcher attempting to fix the♥♥♥♥♥♥
For those wondering, I am currently using the Temporary password and RNG username from the gmail account, it's janky as ♥♥♥♥, but It works... Sometimes.  If Hi-Rez doesn't fix this♥♥♥♥♥♥though, I can't really recommend this game too heavily, as it is a pain the♥♥♥♥♥
Now for the gameplay.
Honestly, it's not bad. This game is often compared with overwatch, and I can see why. Most of the classes are pretty balanced, and the only one I've almost ripped my♥♥♥♥♥♥off against is a support class who can pretty much double everyone's health near him, and go invulnerable if he's ever targeted.
While I haven't run into a paywall yet, You do start off with like 5 or 6 classes, which is rather nice, but there's like 40 total that you can purchase using money in-game. There's also quests, which you unlock at "Player rank 7", which I would assume you can also get this currency through. Did I mention each "Character" has it's own ranking, which you can gain exp for? I have no clue what it's meant for, as I haven't noticed a buff, but you get "Chests" (which are kinda like loot boxes but without having to use Real Money to open them), which allows you to get Cards (Which can alter playstyle) or decorative things. Duplicates of cards are auto-turned into this substance I can only describe as "Elixer", which you can use to buy other decorative stuff or cards.
I've only unlocked 2 modes so far, Payload and "objective-payload", Payload is one team trying to push while another stops the payload, and "Objective-Payload" is a race to the objective. When you get the objective bar full, you get one "Gamepoint", and have the opportunity to get (I believe 2) more by delivering it to the enemy base. Of course, if the defense team manages to hold off the payload, they get one point as well.
The cards system is pretty seamless, though there are some annoying spammy/op combinations, it allows you to focus on certain aspects of a character. For example, you can do extra damage after you "roll" on cassie, or buff her knockback shot. It's rather hard to describe this, as I haven't used it much my self, but it's pretty nfity.
Now, one thing that feels very unique to this game is the in-match "Credit System". All characters get Credits passivly, and you start with a specified amount. You can earn more by fulfilling your character's role, so a front liner would get more by objective-pushing, and a support would get more by healing. So far I've only played front liners, so I can't describe how balanced support credit generation is., but front-liner seems pretty balanced, though I pretty much always use the same perks with 1 or 2 deviations depending on character.
I'll cover the other stuff if I get around to it when I play more of the game.

Verdict:
I can recommend buying this game at a discount like right now.
Problem with microtransactions:
The game has the possibilty to buy ingame stuff via microtransactions and is therefore excluded by other reviewers. I, personally, just recommend not to spend further money on the game, since the offers in the store only give you a slight advantage in the beginning. For there is no big advantage to people that invest more money in the game, i dont turn down the game automatically, though I think that games at a full price of 60€ should neither have microtransactions nor dlcs to pay for.
What is new/different? What is it like?
- Compared with its predecessor the game has better graphics and better controls, though the options to personalize your commands in the PC version are limited and especially with the game menu feel like a bad console port.
- The gameplay itself is quite similar to the predecessor in its 2nd part: you are to build an army to conquer forts. This is quite fun in my oppinion, because you try to compose the best teams possible in early as in late gameplay and there are some events which make it quite problematic to keep a good team together.
- the general structure of captains with personal traits - good or bad - has been retained and improved, your opponents and followers got more "personality" which sometimes is helpful, sometimes not.
- There is a lot of loot to be collected of slain captains, of bought boxes or campaign rewards, with different levels, abilities, rarity and perks. Therefore you got a lot of optimization possibilities according to your playstyle.
- Contrary to the predecessor, the main character does not gain experience by killing grunts. you gain experience by killing captains and completing quests in campaign and online mode. The maximum level is at 60.
- With quests completed and levels gained, the character advances it its abilities which can be unlocked with skillpoints (I however am at level 60 and still missing one skillpoint, but thats another story). Here, too, is room for customization of your gaming style.
- unused, double or minor quality items can be sold for an ingame currency which can be used to buy stuff at the ingame shop.
Campaign:
- There is a campaign, consisting of four acts, which introduce you into the story and open new game modes for you like online vendetta missions and npc and online conquests as you progress. I liked the campaign with its turns and twists in the storytelling and also completed all other side quests. This has taken some evenings with around 100 hours of gameplay, though I took a good amount of time to do quests, develop my armies etc.
-The campaign has as a big disadvantage in a lengthy series of fort defences in act 4, where you have to defend your hard-won forts against intruders and the number of battles is very high and repetitive and dont seem to end. It feels merely like a cheap way to longen the campaign. Therefore I am not so happy that some eternal defence mode has been added to the game as a new feature, though i am able to ignore it, since it is not part of the campaign anymore.
- I had fun playing the campaign, but working through the long line of defences in act 4 wasnt so much motivating.
online conquests and vendettas
- I tried to avoid the online content, because I didnt want to sign the conditions you are forced into by WB. To my oppinion they want access to too much data and one youtuber pointed out that you might be banned or sued in the future for using game mods, for they secure their property rights with the conditions you are forced to sign for playing online conquests and vendettas.
- I was really annoyed (to avoid stronger words) by that contract window always popping up when i started or closed the game to just continue my missions. I accepted the conditions only by fault and didnt find a possibility to revert my confirmation
- Thus I got accicently access to online vendettas and conquests: In these gamemodes, you enter the game of another player, though not playing with him, just entering his world with his opponents, leaving your gaming world behind for the time of the mission
- In online vendettas, you enter another player's world helping him to kill a captain that had killed this other player before.
- In online conquests, you try to conquer a fort of another player with you attack army and its unlocked abilities in your assault squad (there abilities are bought with ingame currency). The faster you are, the better is your reward. you can gain loot boxes and spoils of war (of which you need to collect 1000 to get a loot box which contains orcs and some training abilities for your followers).
- Online conquests are challenging, because higher level opponents have stronger defenders which may kill orc captains in your assault squad. Captains of the assault squad lost in an online conquest are lost in your game, too, so you may need to grind, buy new heroes after losses in online conquests.
- The game itself is designed to do these online missions, because they allow a bit of variation and thrill, even if the task to conquer a fortress mainly is repetitive, because your opponents have different defences and different orc-captains with other traits that my require different strategies or approaches. expecially staying in a certain time frame to get better loot (7 minutes for gold, 5 fire more for silver rating, fort longer approaches: silver rating)
All in all, doing online missions - though i got there by accicent - is fun and seems to be the design for endgame gameplay.
Ingame-Store ("Market"):
- the ingame-store probably is one of the most controversial features.  My personal experiences with the shop didnt lead to the principal rejection of the game, though I dont like expensive games that want to be AAA-titles to be designed as cash cows to further milk their player base with an ingame shop and future dlcs. This is just greed.
- this ingame shop is not very useful, though.
- yes you can buy boxes with loot or with orc followers, but you also can get good stuff and followers by just playing and advancing in the game.
- spending further real money on the game seemed utterly useless to me. You can buy gold coins to buy boxes of the highest quality (mithril) in the shop with real money, there a possibility to gain gold coins by completing daily quests - so you need some patience and playing, but not to spend real money.
- up to now I bought two mithril war boxes with grant 4 legendary followers with the gold earned in daily tasks. The Problem: I got some followers with some traits that made them completely uesless to me. If there is a trait that makes my legendary follower to become dazed or flee in terror from the battlefield, the follower is of no use to me. I got a lot of those legendary followers with useless traits so i dont see any use at all in investing much money in it.
- Progressing in the game, you gain a lot of ingame currency. With this currency (myrian or so) you can buy silver boxes in the ingame-shop that may also contain loot or followers of a highter quality. I also got legendary gear or a follower  from those boxes, but the drop rate is low, you mostly get rare and epic stuff which is quite good in the beginning  and sometimes in the endgame, too.
- For 1500 Myrian are quickly earned. Silver warchests containts two orc followers and sometimes very good traits, that can be improved with trainingorders found in some boxes aswell. These could be a quick replacement for your assault armies, though it also is possible to dominate and force orcs into your service - like in the predecessor - and collect/gain followers while playing the game.
- In total: I dislike Ingame-Shops where you can be ripped of by high priced offers that influence gameplay (-> pay to win). In this case, I cant see a big advantage to the shop, so i dont reject the game for just having one.
To my oppinion, it is a game that is enjoyable.

Virginia isn't a game. It's an artistic experiment, a minimally interactive computer program telling a story with visual techniques one typically sees in cinema. And the story isn't *really* about an FBI investigation, and it isn't *really* about the relationship between the two agents (one of whose perspective the player takes). The actual story is about you, the player, trying to figure out what you think (or feel) about the game.
It's a surreal, 2-hour (if at that) experience that may elicit, at most, an emotional response, as its handsome, plaintive music score pleads for your understanding and acceptance of an inscrutable enigma.
As a game/film score enthusiast, I found Virginia's music worth the price of admission.

It’s few and far between that a story-driven game can get by without the use of narrative. It takes a unique style and precise direction to communicate a cohesive story, and is even more challenging the more complex the story becomes. Virginia does a fantastic job of building not only a strong set of characters, but an entire world of nostalgic police noir.
Virginia is a walking simulator, simply put. You take on the role of Anne Tarver, a FBI Special Agent placed on her first case. You spend most of the game with your new partner, Maria Halperin, attempting to find a missing boy. During this time, your superiors have you investigate your new partner. Both the case and investigation lead down a dark trail that force Tarver into moral dilemmas that take a toll on her mental health.
The Good
Virginia’s take on progression is more akin to classic cinema than it is to a video game. The mise-en-scène is finely detailed to leave almost no room for excess material. Even the smallest of rooms in this game have every object placed in way that gives the player insight into the life of each character. The home of Halperin has a sense of impulsive clutter the same as her office and her style of investigating. The movement of your character almost feels stilted in a reflection of Tarver herself. A person who follows the rules and does what she’s told.
The cuts between scenes also lend to the emotion and progression of each scene. Sharp cuts are placed to progress you down a barren hallway, climb a set of stairs or drive down a long highway. Other scenes dissolve or fade in reflection of the mood which can fluctuate drastically one moment to the next. The noir style of the game makes sure the suspense rarely never lets up.
At the forefront of this game is the outstanding soundtrack. Masterfully composed by Lyndon Holland and performed by the City of Prague Philharmonic Orchestra. The music is a driving force that emphasizes the emotion of each scene in a way that makes you forget that not a single word was spoken.
The Bad
The cuts help progress one scene to the next, but some of those scenes have a tendency to linger just past the point of uncomfortable. The game hits awkward pauses. You may find yourself annoyingly looking around the area, unable to move, thinking you missed an object you were supposed to interact with in order to move on when suddenly there is a jump cut to another scene.
The linear story can also leave you wanting. There is a lack of freedom in Virginia’s beautifully rendered world that will makes you hope for more of something it just won’t give you.
The Annoying
The sluggish movement creates a bit of a drudge at times. It always feels as though you are moving at half the speed a normal person normally would or even should. This makes the game draw out a little longer than it should. The length of the game, which comes in at a little less than two hours, could have cut some scenes short and placed the time at right around one and a half hours. Just about the same of a short feature film, which is what it aspires to be.
Virginia is a deep story told in a unique way that should not be overlooked. With a strong soundtrack and timeless, intriguing story Virginia is definitely a game that again lends itself to the idea that videogames truly are art.
Cost
For only $10 on Steam, this is a game worth buying and a developer worth supporting.

Virginia is an on-rails narrative that is driven entirely by vignettes and players interacting with the environment exactly how the narrator intends. For those seeking agency/choice as an option and being disappointed by the lack thereof, you're trying to get orange juice from an onion. Agency is not a mechanic in this game, though it is a topic the game deals with and explores pretty directly with a massive "what if" sequence that presents the choice you'd have to make if agency *was* a mechanic in this game. But here's the thing, the game isn't trying to ask you what *you* would do in this situation, it's what *this character* would do. The player's choice on how the narrative turns out doesn't matter by the fact this game doesn't want to be trite about its character's moral dilemma. Whether you agree with it or not is still something that can be made into a discussion. The game also presents a pretty hefty conundrum at the end dealing with duty and pressures to fight against the weight of generational mistakes that's enough of a moral grey to keep you thinking about it for a while.
It's a pretty great short story if you love X-Files or Lynch. Expecting something that requires dexterity, puzzle solving, or anything other than your attention and active engagement is doing a disservice to the narrative.

Alan Wake is a good example of a game that has a great story, yet falls flat in the gameplay department. The story is interesting and different, feeling like a Steven King novel at times. The atmosphere is fantastic with moody environments and good graphics considering when it released.
Gameplay on the other hand is a whole different story. The gameplay for the first half is decent, but it seems that when the developers thought of new ways for the story to go they ran out of ways to vary the gameplay. You max out weapons and discover all enemy types by about halfway through the game. After that point the game just throws more of the same enemies at you. I wouldnt mind it so much but there is a limited number of character models in the game and more often then not you will fight repeats of previous fights over and over again. Weapons are ok, but you will find yourself using the same ability combinations over and over again. Get the picture?
Regardless of the shortcomings this game has in the gameplay department, if you are a fan of the "walking simulator" genre I would recommend this game. It has a great atmosphere and plot that almost make you forget its flaws.

First of all, I'm really glad my friend convinced me to get this game. It was well worth it and has something strangely addictive about it.
Now lets talk about the details:
- Graphics: The game looks stunning. The engine may have some flaws and its not 100% detailed but all in all it looks very convincing (which to me, is was matters most) and atmospheric.
- Physics: Simply amazing. The mud-simulation is groudbreaking. Also very notable (and not mentioned as often) is the water simulation. Water currents are simulated. Water applies force to your vehicles in a very realistical way and you can even roughly estimate the depth of the water by looking at the way the ripples form on the surface.
- Sound: Can't complain about it, the vehicles sound good. You even get to hear a knocking sound from your engine when the vehicle is heavily damaged. Environmental sounds are also pretty nice and create a convincing in-the-woods atmosphere.
- Controls (driving): Takes a bit to get used to but overall they're pretty solid. The controls with a gamepad are also quite ok, however only the keyboard controls can be modified at the moment.
- Camera: I agree with the others here that the camera movement feels very weird at first. Give it some time though and you'll get used to it. The system isn't so bad after all, though I assume that it was mainly built for use with a gamepad (with which it works pretty well).
- Gameplay: I guess this comes down to personal preference. Spintires is quite challenging and you will only enjoy it if you like those challenges and if you enjoy fighting against the mud and overall harsh terrain. If you do however, you'll find that the game can be incredibly addictive.
- Learning curve: Pretty steep to be honest. I agree that some sort of tutorial or a map that starts out with easy terrain would be needed. If you're not at least roughly familiar with driving in mud, you'd better learn it fast because that will be your first challenge.
ps.: I suggest starting on the "coast" map, that one is rather forgiving.
- Multiplayer: Working together with a friend makes things alot easier and can be quite entertaining when something goes wrong. I'm surprised how well suited this game is for coop !
ps.: At time of wirting, steam isn't really the best place to buy this. Look around and you can get it significantly cheaper.

Not bad, but not graet either.
I'm going to talk about the issues, so you know what you are getting going in  (Patch 1.3)
The 'Luck' mechanic:
Bad. It's an interesting idea but given the way the campaign is set out, the enemies you encoutner and the fact that luck doesn't regenerate by itself, means that if you get shot at two or three times, means you barely get to use any of your abilities. I'm not sure if this is the way it's supposed to work. I like the way that luck works in regard to hits and to-hit, but keying abilities to amounts of luck seems a bad idea and in my experience it doesn't work. Would have been better if abilities were on a number-of-turns cooldown based on how powerful each ability is. It's strange that some abilities have both a luck cost and a cooldown.
Enemy overwatch: This is never explained, but some enemies in some situations will ahve a red ring around them where if you cross into that ring the enemy will fire at you. You don't get that ability on your own posse. This can be really annoying if the enemy happens to run into a room with only one entrance and where they can't be seen from the outside.
The campaign: The exploration part of the campaign is equal thirds interesting, boring, and awkward. They tried a lot of different ideas and each part of the campaign plays differently. Introducing mechanics that exist just for that campaign's exploration. The problem is that most of these mechanics are just awkward and boring and don't add anything more than tedium to the game.
Good Stuff:
Ricochet: this ability is a lot of fun, but often you find that either you don't have a line of sight to a ricochet object or there's only one object. Still, it's a lot of fun to chain ricochet off a bell, anvil, washing tub, bucket, another anvil, and hit a guy behind full cover that you can't see directly.
Interesting Ideas:
Poker hands bonuses on deck construction. It could have been much better - more cards, persistent cards between campaigns, cards that you could improve in some way.
Randomised event outcomes: This sort of works as well, although it's never really explained which events are random.
Doesn't really work for me:
Most of the exploration stuff just doesn't work for me, nor does the quirky variety of guns. Ultimately there are just 3 things you're looking for  - damage, damage against full cover, and magazine size. Most weapons deal a maximum of 1 damage against someone in full cover, unless you flank them.
It feels like a lot of ideas were sort of tried here, as if the developers werent sure what would or wouldn't work, but it leads to a very inconsistent and confusing feel to the game, and often just adds awkwardness to the experience.
Still, it's a good enough game and it's set in the wild wild west, which is awesome.

Let me start by saying this: Even though I downvoted it, I'm actively still playing it once and a while. It's really not THAT bad.
That said, I still had to downvote it. The actual mechanics of the game itself are very well done, the maps are fun and the gameplay is always interesting. The game itself is actually very well designed, the major problem I have is the lag. It's a very simple game, and since you buy your guns CSGo style in the beginning of a round, the "leveling up" afterwards has literally no function. There are no perks, no long-lasting effects that you can have on your account. Which, honestly, I kind of like. It's always fair, then.
That being said, the entire server system is terrible. I live in the US, and none of the US servers are open. Sometimes you'll join a game and it will immediately kick you for no reason. About half the time the lag is intermittant and will mess up your kills/get you killed. Other notible downsides which contribute to all this, is the amount of cheaters and spawn killing. The concept of "safe spawn" Isn't even considered, and you can literally watch people fall to the ground and murder them repeatedly (as I have done). Many people uses hacks and cheats and the game seemingly has no way or care to actually filter them all out.
Still, at the end of the day, it is a really fun game if you can actually find a server where there are no cheaters/spawnkillers/lag. It's just a matter of finding that server, which may be a harder process than you would want to expect. But hey, you know what? It's free. I'd suggest downloading it and trying it for yourself.

You can be the commander of your own army or you can BE the army in this game.
While the story is nothing to rave about what's there isn't bad, the gameplay and the now famous nemisis system is where you will devote countless hours to forging your army or become death itself and reak fear among those who oppose you. I feel like there was a difficulty increase from the first game as I can often find myself in situations where retreat is necessary and this good as I never felt overpowered even when going back to lesser leveled areas where sheer numbers is enough to deplete even a hardened rangers health.
The addition of Orc tribes and classes was a massive improvement in terms of varity in the game. Its very pleasing to see all of the diverse Orcs in the world and the fact the area can completely change depending on the tribe of the Orc as overlord. Just another enhancement from the first game where the world felt not so much boring as it did monotonous.
The games collectables and side missions don't feel like a daunting task to retrieve/complete however they are there and they don't feel like a chore to me most of the time.
A often overlooked strong point is th voice acting and dialog between all characters, be it in the cutscenes or orc interactions. While the orc lines will inevitablly overlap you do get a real sense that each charactr is unique from their dialog alone, and you will get the ocasional laugh from the smart and cheesy humour.
Overall as a big fan of Shadow of Mordor I can say that I was not dissapointed with the sequel however I can't help but feel like something is missing, but I can't quite figure out what it is. Either way I still plan on playing this game far into the future.

I should note, that this game takes time. First 4-6 hours i wondered what's so good about it, but later it was impossible for me to stop playing, so if you're having problems with the game just try to force yourself through couple of first quests. I promise you, it gets better.
Pros:
+ nice and versatile story. There are several different outcomes of the main quest and each is interesting in it's own way
+ gameplay is good. It's turn-based and mostly depends on your positioning, gear and your character's skills
+ visuals are fine. Sure they're not stunning, it's not Crysis, but it'll do
+ tons of cool side-quests and ways of completing them. You can go in guns blazing or take a more subtle approach(es). Each choise has it's own advantages and good sides, but it's up to you to decide what to do.
+ interesting characters. Not all of them, of course, but mostly characters (aswell as the story) are written very good with a nice slice of humor.
+ exploration is really rewarding. Game encourages you to go where you're not supposed to (like radiation clouds and other places, where you might find shrines or cache)
+ lots of weapons, clothes, equipment and other stuff
+ tons of fun easter eggs and references
+ is generally fun to play once you get a hang of it
Cons:
- sometime it feels like the game overstays it's welcome
- some quests and their alternative ways are really not so obvious. Some people might like it that way though
- it's really easy to screw up your character (try to pick 3-5 skills for each character and only level up those. Otherwise your char will be a mess)
- it's slow. Because of turn-based gameplay and lots of walking-there-doing-that some basic quests take lots of time.

Wasteland 2, oh Wasteland 2. I had more than a handful of bugs happen to me. I fought with the camera nearly the entire time of my play through. I understand why some people didn't like it. I felt frustration and almost stopped playing more times than I can remember, but boy does this game have charm. I played in Seasoned difficulty, it was painful but I was careless.
If you are looking for another Fallout in the traditional form, this comes the closest. There are a few things I wish I knew from the beginning, things the game doesn't explain. The further you go into the game, the more these are revealed, and yet there are even more unexplained things scattered around the wastes. Things I couldn't figure out. Things no one has. I was a cat thrown into a laser disco. In the brief flashes of light between the waves of shadow, you were sure you saw the grin of a dog. Then the shadows come back, and the figures move, and behind all the masks are things moving to the groove of some unheard music. You know there are other cats around somewhere. But the shadows continue to dance, and it looks like one is following a laser though maybe it is not. And you don't know who is who, and what they want, but you know the only way out is through the crowd and the shadows, or you could just follow the lasers. Though in between the lights, and in between the macabre dance, a few beautiful notes licked at the edges of your perception. You could tell something beautiful was around the corner, and you weren't sure where it was going or where you were coming in but you had to find out, you had to let yourself be engulfed in the dance.
The Wasteland dance.

TL;DR
Short, confusing, but oddly satisfying movie-like experience that Virginia offers is very original and interesting.
This one is very confusing. It's set in a small town and follows gradute FBI agent Anne Tarver who's assigned very interesting case to investigate. Story takes a weird turn midway and it almost seems impossible to catch what's completely going on. Due to game having zero dialogue or monologue for that matter, different interpretations and experiences of the story may lead to different opinions.

Crafted with beautiful visuals and an amazing audio and soundtrack, Virginia plays out like an interactive movie. You're expected to do a certain action and there's no 'freedom' to roam or explore on your own. Game presents itself like a movie and it does that rather well albeit with weaker story execution.

Interesting artstyle, solid optimisation offering 30/60 and uncapped FPS with apsolutely fabulous soundtrack will take you on an interesting and rather complex trip.

Game while offers something somewhat unique in terms of movie-like experience, its vague story leaves a lot of unanswered questions that are never properly filled. If you are looking for a short, but alluring experience that will most likely leave you confused and hanging by a thread, feel free to pick this up. Otherwise, wait for a deeper discount.

For all the Lynch fans out there: this is NOT the game for you. This game fails at nearly anything it tries to accomplish. Let’s take for example the story which is at points so dumb, that you can’t take the overly complicated parts seriously. The characters also have little to none facial expressions in a story driven game with no dialog, when there was clearly the intention to make you emotionally committed.  I really haven’t cared at all about any protagonist in this game. But for me the worst part was the music which was so annoying, that I really wanted the game to end even faster (It took me 1.6 h to finish the game) It is as cliché as it can get for a classical score, which wouldn’t be that bad considering it was recorded with a real orchestra, but it plays through the whole game, where it should only be 5 minutes long.
Over all I have to say that I didn’t understand a hell of a lot, and this is the one point where I think the game accomplishes what it tried to achieve, but I couldn’t care less about what is going on. I currently have played the game INSIDE, where (beside it having real gameplay) the story is also cryptic and non-dialogic, but so much more powerfully told. VIRGINIA on the other hand lures you with a hidden, supposedly meaningful message, when there is nothing really happening that keeps you interested enough, so you don’t want to know it anyway.

Dark, Disturbing, and at times makes you drop your jaw. It can be a bit lackluster, but the reason is for you to play the levels in order, and do a lot of research to understand the lore. I understand some people think its much more rewarding discovering for yourself. Then again you don't entirely have to play the levels in order to make sense of the story. ---Gameplay---
Unlike Hotline Miami 2's absolutely trash level design, and absolutely unfair AI, this game actually gives you some breathing room, and a fair chance. Melee characters are absolutely possible, in nearly every level, there are some levels that are definetly harder with melee characters. But in this game its remotely possible, as in Hotline Miami 2, if the game actually let you play a melee character, the level design almost counter-acted any player decision forcing you to do this routine.
'Fire bullet, everyone walks through door to spot you, fire weapon as they come charging through door'. Repeat as many times as needed. I had to in nearly every level, because it was my only option.

Sometimes levels restrict player choice, but not as much in Hotline Miami 2. The levels are short, give you breathing room, and let you plan out what you are going to do. The levels are fair, and are lovingly designed.

Sometimes quite annoying, but all in all like nearly everything in this game. It's not as bad as it is in Hotline Miami 2. Jesus 'as it is in', try saying that ten times fast.

The only thing that Hotline Miami 2, has better than the first game. Hotline Miami's music is more limited repeats more often, but it didn't bother me to much. Its not like every level has the same song.

For some reason much more smoother animations are in the first Hotline Miami, but like the second game the pixel art isn't to confusing. I wasn't left scratching my head at any objects, wondering what I just looked at. The pixel art is well done.

I highly reccomend this game, far more that that of the second game. I never finished the second game, and I doubt I ever will. Great story, great level design and gameplay mechanics, enemy AI is pretty fair and believable, Music is great as always, and pixel art is top notch.

is a game that is everything and nothing, all at once.
There are undeniably great things about this game; the thing that comes to mind for many here is the phenomenal score, and with good reason: if this was a movie, this score would be Oscar-nominated in an instant. It's not the only notable thing about the game, however: The visuals are lovely, with just the right balance between detailed and minimalist, and the atmosphere is simmering with a welcome sense of mystery. On top of that, the art direction brims with realism and life, and an ambiguous and hallucinatory late-game section dazzles in both pacing and imagery.
Unfortunately, the rest of the game doesn't really live up to the polished elements around it. The plot intrigues, but ultimately falls flat because of its refusal to flesh out any of the events or characters that surround it..... The game takes a gamble with its lack of dialouge, and it's a choice that never quite works in its favor; all of the character arcs get reduced to a cycle of trying to guesstimate whatever the hell is going on with them. The lack of any lines whatsoever also means that the game entirely lacks the wit it sorely needs to make itself sustainable. It ends up feeling like
without color, or
without dialogue:
On top of that, there's the feeling that even for a so-called 'walking simulator' there's a near-complete lack of interactivity; I felt like I did more in one runthrough of
than I did in two playthroughs of this game. This sort of thing wouldn't be an issue if the story surrounding it was better, or if the player character had more of a role in advancing the plot, but neither of those are the case. And then there's the whole motion sickness problem: Even for someone who can ride a ton of rollercoasters in a row without feeling sick, I couldn't help but feel my stomach turn noticably during both of my playthroughs of the game. (Thankfully, I didn't throw up either time, but it still was enough to be a frequent annoyance during the game.) Upping the sensitivity helped, but I didn't find anything helpful besides that in the game's settings to fix the problem properly.
Even with these significant problems, however, I still give
a definite, if very slight, reccomendation. If you don't like walking simulators much, then stay away completely. Know this, however: This is a game that has had an undeniable amount of effort into it. It has a style all its own, even as it frequently references the works that inspired it. It is not one of the random, shoddily made crapfests that seem to splat onto the Steam store everyday. It is a worth a look for fans of this genre, if for nothing else but to analyze what it does, good and bad. And I am still, actually, kind of glad that I gave money to developers that took a real chance on something and did their damndest to try and make it work.
Even if
is often too slight and lacks the polish to leave the mark that games like
and
did, one thing is undeniable: As much as it is everything and nothing, it is most definitely
. In a gaming world full of people who are too afraid to take a chance, it's refreshing a group of people really stand up and try to make something different, even if the end result has almost as many lingering misses as it does genuine hits.

As a "walking simulator" or "adventure-game-lite," Virginia's ~2 hours is worth the $10. I've paid more to see worse movies. That said, it's not for everyone; though the environments are artistic and beautiful (they remind me of Alone in the Dark), there isn't really much to do except exist in them until you find the right thing to click. At times, it becomes a pixel hunt.
For me, the game did establish an emotional connection, and I felt for the characters as the storyline progressed. I'm not sure my patience would've lasted much beyond the two hours though.
My big beef with Virginia is that I wish it'd found it's own heart. The Twin Peaks influence is heavy-handed. The game's authors seem to revel in showing symbols that are essentially un-interuptable by the player. This is fine of course - who knows why there's a dwarf talking backwards in Twin Peaks - but the strangeness feels more like window dressing. Like there was a quota and they just kept adding strange things until it "felt" good enough. I would've rather focused on the relationships in the game. Moments like sitting on a water tower, looking over the lights of the small town as the sunsets, drinking a beer; because these are rooted in reality and it's something we can all relate to, they're stronger than discovering a bird that disappears whenever you pick it up. The Twin Peaks-y-ness decays and distracts from the game's real strengths.
The music is strong too, ast least until you think, "I've heard this before," and you recall that Virginia's primary composition is one note off from Hans Zimmer's Interstellar score. I was fine with the band in the bar playing a deriviative of the Twin Peaks theme; but almost wholesale ripping another well-known score is poor taste.
All told, the game is worth $10 and two hours of your time, but as a person who likes watching the game as a medium grow more potent and impactful, I wish the designers had forged their own path more and riffed less, in almost every aspect. What's the non-attributable quote? "Good artists copy, great artists steal?"
Virginia's designers must have taken that to heart because too much is stolen here.
They need to be able to separate "style" from "invention;" the visual art of the game - that's a style. The quick cuts and flashbacks - that's style. Borrow as much style as you can. But when the symbols and the musical themes are stolen; they're doing themselves and their game players a disservice.

A very good puzzle game.
Puzzles involve sliding jewels on a board so that all jewels of the same color touch. If you cover certain specific positions in the board, you get stars and possibly a coin. Stars unlock special levels and you can use coins to show solutions in levels you find dificult. As you progress through the game, new elements are introduced in the levels.
Levels are not timed and there's no movement counter either. You can solve the levels at your own pace. As you solve the special levels, you get mementos that tell a story.
I found the game leaning towards the easy side. Even if some levels have many elements, there are not that many paths available and a solution shows itself.
PROS:
- Well created logic puzzles.
- No timer. No looking for the best solution.
- Undo function allows you to quickly go back to previous positions.
- Good length for the price.
CONS:
- The game uses a 3D engine and is not as optimized as it should be. The loading time is not short and a couple of times the game refused to start. Not a big problem but you have to be patient at times.
- The music is not bad but there are few tracks so it gets repetitive. It can be disabled.
- No way to quickly reset a level.

A real review.
The missing tag for Alan Wake in it's discription is 'story driven'. Alan Wake is a story driven game. There are many good things about this game but it is the story that will compel you to finish it.
The horror aspect is mixed into the gameplay and it works at the start as you nervously walk through a forest at night with the feeling you are being chased by axe weilding country folk. As the story progesses you will master the combat style of duelwielding a flash light and a gun to kill the 'darkness'. Once mastered you find yourself collecting heaps of ammo, flares, flashbangs etc, so much so that no matter what object the 'darkness' chooses to posses you will have more than enough to defend yourself and loosing some of that horror in the process.
The gameplay is different than anything else i have played which straight away makes it fun. Visually, the world you are in is beautiful, dark, dangerous and mysterious. The sound is also very good. The game has a great atmosphere. But...
The cutscenes and story are so so so much better than the level design and gameplay that you will reach a cutscene, learn more of this increasingly interesting and captivating story, you will be all excited to find out more when Alan somehow manages to fall back into a forest. A dark forest. You finally get to the next cutscene, awesome, more story but then Alan slips and falls into the forest. Cutscene, forest, cutscene, another ****ing forest. That is how i felt playing this game by the end. I was racing through the level to get to the next part in the story. The horror gameplay really takes a back seat maybe half way through the game.
But the story is that good that you will want to keep playing. One last thing, there is one type of enemy that you come across , little spoiler...
It is so annoying, runs super fast so you cant shine your flashlight on it until it attacks you. It runs all around so you dont know from which direction will it jump out of the darkness, sounds scary but it isn't. It takes so long to try attack you that you have to stand there for a few minutes waiting. It's frustrating. You will know this enemy as soon as you see him. If he takes too long to attck you just run to the next checkpoint and he will dissapear. Really stupid character.
All in all, if you want an action game with non repetitve gameplay this game is NOT for you! If you want something different with a great story this game IS FOR YOU!
I liked it accept for that one type of enemy, so stupid, shouldn't be in the game.

Also, a game about a bestselling writer that includes excerpts from his books should really hire a fiction author to write the book text. The book excerpts in Alan Wake are remarkably flat and unappealing. Even widely panned authors like Dan Brown at least put some kind of descriptive verve into their prose. Alan Wake's book excerpts read like they were written by, well, someone who usually writes cut scenes and dialogue trees for video games. That's a different skill set than horror fiction. Collecting pages of Alan Wake's book should have been a major story driver; instead it was just a drag.
The painful combat system and the 'reward' of collecting pages of dry prose from Wake's book made for a one-two punch that knocked me right out of the game, on two platforms.

I don't agree with the idea of microtransactions. I think that they should be relegated to having no affect on gameplay, if not outright removed from gaming. Thankfully I can say that Shadow of War does at least find a middleground. People were worried during the pre-order period, but after release we can see that any unlocked content from loot crates are not only easily unlockable throughout normal gameplay, but do not outpace gameplay to the point of making it trivial. XP boosters are plentiful, but they mainly affect only ranking leaderboards, and any enemies will scale effectively with your Character level.
As for the gameplay itself, Shadow of War delivers on the promises of more of what the orriginal gave. The Nemesis system has been expanded beyond just appearance. Tribes and classes offer a twist to the fighting style of each ork, and is being added upon with further downloadable content. The character abilities have been refined, and those along with gear allow for great customisation of playstyle. Playable maps have been made larger, and more varied from Gondorian City to lush plains, to tundra, craggy caves and volcanic wastes.

After playing Super meat boy, I started looking out for new games by the same developer. Edmund Mcmillen’s wonderfully strange imagination is an interesting thing to explore through his games, that’s for sure.
This game was not a disappointment. At first, I had no idea what to expect, the trailer was very strange but a tad intriguing. When I came across it there was next to no information about the game and the mechanics of it on the store page and back then there was no costumer reviews to go off of. Admittedly I never actually brought it to give it a go off of the information I was given, I ended up with it from a bundle and it’s the only reason I really played it. Although I wish I had taken the leap to try it because it is well worth it.
Binding of Isaac is a randomly generated dungeon crawler, one I have heard to be described as Zelda-like you’re a young boy running from his demented mother. Who has been blinded by her hard-core Christianity and believes that the voice of god has spoken to her and told her to murder her son to prove her loyalty. So a very interesting concept, indeed.
A short cut scene plays on start-up, which expands on what I just described, you find yourself wandering through randomly generated dungeon floors, fighting monsters, picking up loot and items as you go along that changes how you fight, gives you different abilities and drastically changes Isaac’s image. At the end of each floor, you fight a boss, and move on down to the next floor. It being harder than before, with a bigger space to explore and more enemies to defeat.
There’s a large range of items to collect that when found for the first time is added to the “things I found” section in the main menu, so a lovely bit of collecting there to entice those OCD minded like myself, There’s new characters to unlock which vary in stats, challenges to complete and even some DLC that can extend your gameplay.
You are given one life and one life only. You can find hearts to heal, but once you are dead, that’s it, you start all over again. So throughout the whole game and especially when nearing the end, it starts to put a little pressure on and gets that heart rate going. I’m not one to be good under pressure so it gets me every time. I FINALLY managed to complete the game a few times over, again, admittedly, only after I gained some “top tips” from my way-to-good-at-games brother. There have been people that have completed the game 10 times over and still not gotten bored. I think that the randomly generated dungeon element to it keeps its replay ability intact. If it were to replay the same levels over and over when you died, the game would be a lot different and no doubt a lot less popular.
I have heard from friends that it is quite hard to complete without “doing your research” on the wiki or seeking tips from those nerdy minded like my brother who managed to figure all of it out themselves. I on the other hand find that kind of thing enjoyable, because it beats you every time and you work and research and try to understand the game more to finally get to that ending. I can quite honestly say that the first time I reached the end, my heart has never beaten that loud or that fast in a long time. And that sense of accomplishment you get from finishing a game, is a on a much higher scale when you work to complete this one.
The music is great, it fits the setting perfectly and is great to listen to. Rarely have I actually wanted to download a game’s soundtrack, I can give most soundtracks a thumbs up but not often do I actually want to listen to game music outside of gaming.
The art, as per usual in Edmunds games, is amazing. And I hear they are also looking to remake the game to have a more “retro” look, with possible multiplayer features. Which should be very interesting. For those interested you can look up “Binding of Isaac: Rebirth”.
All in all, it is a great indie game, which is both fun and challenging. Definitely worth trying, I am not usually the dungeon crawler type, but this game is a lot of fun. The only fault that I had with this game, which has bothered me quite a few times now, is that I have lost my save for no reason. The game is listed as having ‘Steam Cloud’ features, but it definitely doesn't work. I haven't uninstalled the game, I haven't touched it. But recently I hopped on and seen all the progress that I had made was gone. And for a game that has no real save points or ongoing plot to keep up with, your stats, unlocked characters and collection of things you have found is pretty much all you have. I was pretty upset to see it had vanished and it’s something I felt I needed to warn people about.
TL;DR : Awesome music, fun and engaging game with a slightly 'twisted' side to it. It's a challenge to reach the end and you can definitely end up putting a lot of hours into this. Addictive and awesome all around.

This is a game made to be as confusing as possible. There is absolutley zero dialogue. Initially, this intrigued me, because a story told visually could be done well. This wasn't. The low-poly art style (another feature which isnt bad on it's own, but was terrible here) didn't convey enough detail for me to understand the story BEFORE it went off the rails. Which it does. Alien conspiracy? Acid trip? Dreams? I think all three happen, but who knows. It's a plot as convoluted as your first time watching Interstellar, except your vision is 20/100 (no glasses) and your volume is muted. You keep waiting for it to be good, and it never does. The developers tried to undertake a lot of ambitious ideas (art style, lack of dialogue, involved story) and that effort is the only thing I give them kudos for.
On top of the unenjoyable premise, this game also suffers perfomance issues. Irregular mouse acceleration can be a drag on any game, but in a point-and-click pixel-hunt, it is a nightmare. The game also intentionally features cinematic cuts. Sometimes these almost make the game bearable to follow, but when it cuts from in a car, to standing outside the car, to walking on a sidewalk, to looking at a door, to seeing the door close behind you, I have to ask myself if my computer is having a seizure, or if some director is just really into sloppy scene editing.
TL;DR: I bought this game at 75% off and still feel ripped off. I've half a mind to request a refund but after looking online, it seems that this game's director is happy that a lot of people hate it.

Virginia doesn’t shy away from taking risks and trying original ideas, complemented by beautiful art design, fantastic music, and some of the most outstanding visual storytelling I’ve seen in a game. But unfortunately the game ultimately fails to deliver an enjoyable experience.
The biggest failing is the game wants to be watched, not played. It's a game of “click hotspot to progress the story”. Interaction is limited to walking around a room and looking for a single hotspot to click, clicking a series of objects in turn from a set position to play a sequence of animations, or in some cases simply waiting in place with nothing to do until the camera cuts to the next scene. This doesn't exactly make for interesting gameplay and became tedious very quickly. I couldn’t help but feel that I would much rather be watching this as a short film without the “interruptions” that were the limited gameplay. Indeed it felt a lot like watching a video and having it pause every few seconds to buffer until I clicked to continue playback.
It’s a shame, because everything else about Virginia is wonderful, and though I have given this a thumbs down, I would still recommend it to anyone interested in storytelling in games (especially other developers). The game is an outstanding example of how to tell a story visually and without a single word spoken. It’s compelling, mysterious, engaging, and moving. And although it devolves into a confused and overcomplicated mess towards the end, it’s worth playing just as a study into visual storytelling alone.
As a games developer myself I’m glad I played this and would recommend other devs do too. But I can’t recommend it as a consumer product.

Grandpa's Table is a beautifully crafted puzzle game.  The classical music accompanies the game in a wonderful way and has a soothing and relaxing effect.
It is never too difficult that you start to feel overwhelmed or frustrated. Yet, each new puzzle is a challenge. As soon as you start to get the hang of one puzzle type, another is introduced. If you get stuck you have options to help, moves can be reversed starting from your first move or where you believe you made the mistake, or if you are completely stuck you may use tokens from previous solved puzzles to solve the puzzle for you.
The basic concept of the puzzles is reminiscent of other sliding tile/sphere puzzles; however, it is so well done that it gives an original feel. I would recommend Grandpa's Table to any fan of games such as Quell, Sokoban or the classic Wooden Labyrinth games.
In addition, the game was made/developed in Ubuntu Linux with Blender, Gimp, Inkscape, libGDX and the Universal Tween Engine :-) . So, as a Linux user it's a must buy to support the dev!

I'm not an unconditional of puzzle games myself, though I enjoy good ones every now and then. With its very rich atmosphere, skillfully designed puzzles and timely introduced gameplay elements, Grandpa's Table is definitely one of the puzzle games that I enjoy playing for a while and going back to when I feel like.
The very atmospheric main menu says long on the overall quality of the game and perfectionism of its (charming, judging by the credits) two developers. Drinking some in-game coffee while playing with light effects on a georgeous 3D wooden table is just a blast - even better when also drinking real-life coffee and listening to Grandpa's Table's awesome music.
Gameplay wise, it's just great. There is some good difficulty for people who are got at puzzles, but it's not overly hard and people who don't want too great a challenge can also easily skip some puzzles, or solve them without grabbing all stars if they're not OCD'ed like I am. New gameplay are added little by little as you play, which makes every set of level quite interesting, and makes you want to go forward through this
level set (5 level sets with - presumably, I haven't unlocked them all yet - 30 levels each). There's enough to play with for a few months depending on your pace, and for this price and overall quality, it's a must have.

Also, a game about a bestselling writer that includes excerpts from his books should really hire a fiction author to write the book text. The book excerpts in Alan Wake are remarkably flat and unappealing. Even widely panned authors like Dan Brown at least put some kind of descriptive verve into their prose. Alan Wake's book excerpts read like they were written by, well, someone who usually writes cut scenes and dialogue trees for video games. That's a different skill set than horror fiction. Collecting pages of Alan Wake's book should have been a major story driver; instead it was just a drag.
The painful combat system and the 'reward' of collecting pages of dry prose from Wake's book made for a one-two punch that knocked me right out of the game, on two platforms.

It's okay, but not as good as I remembered its first release on Xbox 360. The below is spoiler-free:
The extra DLC chapters help embed the intended meaning of the ending without expanding upon it, which makes it fizzle out a bit - with remixed levels as sort of a novelty. It held my interest a lot more than the spinoff "American Nightmare" which tried to mix things up marginally by having deserts instead of forests, but you can basically stop at the 'true' ending of Episode 6 of this original since the story and gameplay don't have much to offer after that.
The plot teases a few loose ends, because it's 'mysterious' and 'fits the genre', but it means that the ending doesn't really give a satisfying payoff for all the self-proclaimed weirdness that's gone on in the story. It's not lazy writing, but it's a bit (intentionally?) messy - and the focus is kept more on the story than the characters - to a fault.
If you really really like the genre enough (like I did/do) then sure, go nuts for some hard-boiled narration and a lot of excuses to fight wave after wave of bad guys in dark forests. There's a lot of extra content like commentary and easter eggs and fricking scavenger hunts for the 100% completionists out there - and you can see how many hours of my time this game occupied without reaching OCD levels of absorption in the story like the developers intended.
Remedy, creators of the original Max Payne but not its superior sequel, have all the right ingredients for making the exact games I want to play (badass stories with bits of action to break things up) and I'll probably be a sucker for Quantum Break nomatter what, but I can't... *openly* recommend Alan Wake, at least not for everyone.

Edit: Some notes after a lot of game time.
- You will go nuts fighting the controls. You can use both mouse and keyboard, but when you try to use them at the same time - zooming out with the mouse and moving up with the keyboard, or the reverse etc - the game "snaps" you back resulting in lost time and killed dwellers during incidents (like deathclaw attacks that get a lot more frequent).

"Broken Age" is an adventure game that lets you dive into the adventures of Shay and Vella - two young people who live their lives without a connection to each other. Shay lives in his own, colourful spaceship run by his mother and Vella lives in a bakery town that prepares for the traditional "maidens feast". Unfortunately Vella is one of the maidens to be sacrificed to the hideous monster Mog Chotrha. But she is unwilling to bow down to senseless traditions while Shay is unwilling to play childish games practicly as a prisoner every day. But big events will offer them new perspectives and tasks...
In "Broken Age" you pretty much solve puzzles the old school way (like in the classic LucasArts adventures or in "Simon the Sorcerer"): you talk to people in order to squeeze out information, you collect items, you explore environments and objects and you figure out specific patterns for puzzle solutions. And when I mean "old school way" then I also mean that the puzzles are far from easy. Sure, some are quite obvious but many others are very hard to figure out and some also demand perfect timing. This makes the game challenging and thanks to its length it will keep you entertained and occupied for a couple of hours (personally I needed about 16 to 17 hours in total). But prepare for a few frustrating moments as some puzzles demand you to think around a few corners to figure out a possible solution.
The gameplay is easy - point and click. Also you can switch between Shay and Vella anytime (which reminded me of "Day of the Tentacle" where you switch between three people).
But what about the story? Personally I think it's very fine. I dig the characters and the environments they're in. I just couldn't quite get the evil plan from the villains. I won't spoil it here but let's just say that I think this could all sound more logical.
Also I really like that this game obviously spoofs cults and superstition, the ways people are made to believe stupid things in order to enrich a leader or to establish rituals that do nothing than silence one's conscience (and hurt others).
There's a lot of humour in the game and it gave me a few good laughs wether it's due to absurd dialogues or to funny visuals and animations but the jokes never felt flat.
I wanna say about the graphics that they are just beautiful to look at. Pure eye candy! This all looks like a hand-painted, colourful story book (only with moving, talking people). I enjoyed the visuals and also the animations to the end.
The soundtrack is very likeable, too. I bought it as a DLC on Steam and don't regret it. Different but fitting tunes and styles give the game another awesome touch.
The voices were very well selected, in my opinion. Elijah Wood voices Shay, Masasa Moyo (who I know best as Sarah from "Team America") voices Vella and both do a great job in giving these characters their personality. But the other voice actors and actresses are great as well.
The most criticized part of "Broken Age" is the second act (of three). Many people complain that the story feels half-done or just not good enough. Personally, I don't quite get what the deal here is. I enjoyed the second act as I did the first one. What disappointed me was the ending that felt too sudden and short.
In the end, can I recommend "Broken Age"? Absolutely.
If you love solving puzzles and playing (old school) adventures then this is certainly for you. Give it a chance!
In my opinion it's not the best adventure game ever but at least one of the best and most beautiful in the last few years.

This game feels in many ways and with ample reason like a gracious throwback to the golden era of classic LucasArts adventure games of the 90's, while giving it a light evolutive nudge in the right direction. Simplified interface, slick execution, dynamic cameras and hi-resolution art all contribute to making it feel contemporary without compromise.
Imaginative art and characters evolve in an intriguing story that is best explored without any previous exposition. I deliberately shielded myself from all spoilers before playing and this resulted in a most pleasurable and strangest experience, without preconceived notions.
Creativity and originality abound in all the worlds you'll visit. The game does an excellent job of nudging the player in the right direction with its own positively peculiar logic, or at least hinting at what to do next, even in situations that couldn't possibly have their equivalent here on Earth. It is mostly a matter of figuring out how to do things rather than guessing at what the game is expecting from the player, except in a few rare occasions when a walkthrough did come handy.
There is no wrong choice, no way to die or fail, and almost every line of dialogue is funny, sometimes hilarious, or at least worth hearing. This sets the perfect tone for easy going discovery and lets the player enjoy the ride without worries. Some of the plot twists aren't fully surprising but there is a good lot of them that were pleasantly unexpected.
The cast has been superbly selected to give every character complete credibility, despite the innocence or stupidity of some. I wish some of them had been better explored, some clichés avoided, and without spoiling the end it could certainly have been improved. The game does not take itself seriously but is generally nonetheless credible, except in the last bits and tacky conclusion.
While I did have a clear preference for Vella's world and her part of the story (and her overall personality), Shay's also features its load of welcome distinct elements. The latter did have that weird bit of discomfort hanging all over it though, almost from the onset, like a lingering feeling that all is not right and that this protagonist is just weird and unable, which initially made me wish they'd done this part slightly differently.
The game does have a few grating elements that become a bother in several instances. The bottom UI sometimes really gets in the way, especially when hot spots are located close to the inventory corner. The game does feature some silly puzzles despite the inherent logic that drives the majority of the rest. Switching characters is never made necessary until the second act and initially feels underused, whereas it could have been a central feature (Day of the Tentacle and
are excellent examples). Some going back and forth becomes very tedious especially at the end (the rewiring bits drove me nuts!) and unfortunately left a bitter taste that tainted my enjoyment.
Overall Broken Age is still a clear winner for anyone with a bit of nostalgia for good old LucasArts and Sierra titles. Its few wrong steps and shortcomings manage not to get in the way of its fun setting and narrative. It is refreshing to see classic adventure gaming take the spotlight once again, even if one should not expect them to regain their crown as a leading genre.

I bought wastland 2 while it was in beta. I loved the game from the start, and actually wanted to support Brian Fargo.
It was a great experince playing the beta to the finished verison. Of course any major patch would break your saves, but it's that type of game where you want to restart a few times anyway, more so to play with your Characters stats.
I will say a lot of people have wrote about the game not being very tatical. There is some truth to that, there aren't too many cases where you can strage your characters for a fight, most encounters are just a straight up♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥contest. A couple of hours just exploring the wasteland and looting will turn you into one tough ranger.
In the start of the game it seemed like there would be a lot of choices that would directly effect the game. Basically there is only one major choice to be made in the game and really only effects which character your going to pick up as a side kick.
Some of the weapons don't hold much value, such as rocket launchers. Generally before you can use one the baddies are  on top of you already, or it's just not worth using. But it's interesting that you do have to have  players who are better with riffles than lazer weapons, which is part of the tatical portion of the game. Basically each Character should be very well rounded with two different weapons, more so till about 30 hours into the game. You can't have everyone using the same ammo.
Half the game takes place in AZ and the other half in CA. CA is interesting because things just get very strange. In any post nuclear war game youe expect raiders and mutant frogs, but crazy nuns? I wish the AZ portion of the game had more of the odd ball encounters you ran in during CA. The Characters in CA are more interesting as well as the plot.
What I don't understand is the water movement system. In the first half the game you need to refill your canteens which isn't a big deal. In the second half, the concept just stops. It's minor, I'm not sure why I'm even bringing it up but it seemed like a major portion of the game but slowly got scaled back.
I had a lot of fun with this game, like fallout you play for the story and the ride, not so much the end result. It does have a lot of replayability, but as I said I played it from beta which meant I had several restarts. It does let you import your characters that you have progressed through out the game when you finish.
A lot of the skills overlap, and there is more than one way to open a door generally.
I paid 60 dollars for the game and got a little over 230 hours of pure enjoyment of the game, it was worth every penny. I just hope they make a wasteland 3 or a DLC to the game.
One thing they should add is being able to make your own rangers at your base even after you started. I think that would be a fun concept.

I was one of the people who backed this game on Kickstarter years ago. I like point-and-click puzzle games for their stories, and Double Fine has done some other games that I've loved.
Broken Age was... disappointing. The review would have been rather glowing if I'd written it when we were still waiting for the second act to be released. But with the release of the conclusion of the game, it feels... lazy? The first act introduces two interesting storylines with colorful, interesting landscapes (Or, sort-of landscapes) to explore. True to P&C adventure games, you meet all manner of interesting, quirky people, and get to ask them all manner of interesting, quirky questions.
The second act offers... very little. For the most part you're revisiting the areas you saw before, but with the other character. Dialog options seem less varied and numerous, and puzzles begin to feel more like legwork than puzzles (Get X item that's on the opposite side of the game and bring it back to me).
The ending feels sort of lackluster, but it may simply be that it's a letdown after the outright grueling back-and-forth grind of setting things up required for completing the final puzzle.
