It's hard to say how I feel about this game, but I'll start with breaking it down by Act since that's what everyone else does. I put a TLDR on the bottom. I put this game as recommend because if it goes on sale, buy it. Otherwise, just wait for one.
Act 1 was incredible, the characters were great, the art style and incredible voice acting drew me in really quickly. The puzzles were all incredible, I really felt like the puzzles were a fair challenge but it wasn't stupid difficult. I enjoyed all the characters, I loved how some of the puzzles even made fun of some basic adventure game tropes. The writing was amazing, each character delivered funny lines and I love most of it. Each setting and character was unique in it's own way and very different from each other. And the writing really helped build up towards that amazing ending.
Act 2, everything falls apart, there are so many glaring plot holes, all the characters and setting that I said are interesting, I hope you liked those cause it hasn't changed as the second act didn't introduce us to any new settings at all. But also, all the characters from the first act, didn't feel as well written as before. As I said, I loved many of the characters and they each made me laugh in a fun way. But in the second act, I'm not sure if it's cause I got sick of them, or they just weren't funny. The puzzles also were not delivered as well as the first act. You could find yourself stuck on a puzzle for 20-30 minutes and the game gives you no hints of it's solution. Just to help you out if you already have this game, the robots that need to be wired, the solution is in the other characters play through. This puzzle in particular just broke all immersion for me. Shay would have no idea how to wire this robot, but once Vella finds out how to wire it, suddenly Shay knows? That makes no sense. That's not the only plothole in the game but the rest of them have spoilers. But one thing I can say, there's this conversation near the end that you can have with another character, and it's very clear this conversation is supposed to be the exposition drop of the game. And yet it tells you almost NOTHING about what is going on or why. Also, this game gives you, in my opinion one of the worst endings after a puzzle that makes no sense! The ending sealed the deal for me on how bad the second act is.
Conclusion: By the end of Act 1, I had such high hopes, I was one of the first people to go to everyone I know and sing praises of the first act, it was so well done and designed that I was extremely hopeful for the second act. But then the second act just feels like it was done by a completely different team, they put some extreme rush on it due to deadlines or whatever.
TL:DR, Act 1 is great, Act 2 sucks. Buy the game on sale, play the first half. Uninstall before the second half and just make up your own story, because honestly, it'll probably be better.

My favorite Civilization title of all time. This game may be old, but I find it's graphics are just right for the genre and it does not have the cartoony look that some later titles are sometimes guilty of. Being an older title, the AI isn't always the smartest and will struggle to perform certain tasks like sea-based invasions. A huge problem with this game is its infamous RNG which has led to powerful units being killed by weaker unit (i.e. spearman kills tank). However, just play without "preserve random seed" enabled and you can just save before each battle and reload quickly to get a better result if you feel you have been cheated. Other features missing include advanced diplomacy beyond war and trade and revolutions occuring in pre-established empires (a feature lacking from most unmodded Civ titles).
The thing that makes this game my favorite Civ is the availablity of mods to customize this game to your heart's content. You can play out just about any scenario you can think of. Although a lot of files were lost when civfanatics changed a while back, there is still plenty of diverse content available. I would highly recommend the WorldWide mod for anyone looking for a much expanded version of the game. Whether you want to make small changes like add in one or two units or a custom civ, or install total conversions and scenarios, the tutorials online make it very easy to add such things in.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys Civilization and other empire-building RTS games.

Virginia is full of interesting choices in terms of direction. Be it the fact that the story is told without a word, which is pretty bold considering it's a "detective" (well more like drama actually) story. Or this idea of having ellipsis cutting player's movement or investigation to juxtapose another place, object, scene or element of the story. And I must say that for all those decisions and the visual style, it's a nice try.
Unfortunately, I don't think it pays off really well...at all. For it's short length, Virginia never really hits hard and the less than two hours I spent on completing the story felt more like four hours because of how bored I got mid-way. The story is told in an interesting but not refined and mastered way. The ellipsis more often than never just cut the mood and transition abruptly to nothing particularly interesting in regards of what the player was doing beforehands. Though it's not the focus of the plot, the story never resolves the case, and the other part, the main piece, is honestly kind of deja-vu. And the game uses a lot of symbolism, some directly borrowed from Twin Peaks, and never uses it really cleverly.
TL;DR
If I had to summarize, I would say that Virginia is the "The Cell" of videogames. It often feels like style went before substance, and that the level of polish and competency is not used to tell a good story, but more to experiment. And that can be find. But it just felt flat for me...

A twinstick shooter/roguelike hybrid, The Binding Of Isaac combines a tough but mostly fair difficulty with near-infinite replay value. Each playthrough lasts only an hour or two (assuming you don't die early on), but the procedurally generated levels, enemies, and item spawns make each one unique. The sheer amount of content is also impressive: I've sunk over 115 hours into the game as of this writing, and there's still a good bit more I haven't unlocked or discovered yet.
TBOI has an old school mindset to it, in that there are tons of different enemies and powerups, but the game does not spell out for you the best way to take on the enemies or make use of the powers, or sometimes even what the powers do. This might sound off-putting, but I find it provides for a highly satisfying sensation of skill progression as you work these things out for yourself. Over time, you will even begin making tactical decisions about when to skip a powerup that doesn't work well with your current build.
The Wrath Of The Lamb DLC is also heartily recommended, which provides a huge increase to the number of powerups in the game, a new character to unlock, and an entirely new class of pickup, all of which make for even more build possibilities; special challenges that unlock new powerups upon completion; a plethora of new enemies, bosses, and level permutations; and even a brand new level at the endgame.
In the interest of full disclosure, the game does have a number of bugs and glitches, including a rather annoying bug regarding unlocks that can result in 4 specific ones being removed from your save history, making you have to unlock them all over again. Very few of these bugs are gamebreaking though, and the few that do cause you to have to cancel your current playthrough are extremely rare (I've never encountered one in all my playtime). Reading the wiki page on bugs, and keeping a spare copy of your most recent so.sol file (which records your unlocks and settings), will help you avoid nearly all of them, and those that can't be avoided tend to be completely trivial at worst, so I would strongly advise you to not let these few minor annoyances dissuade you from picking up one of the best values for the money you can possibly find on Steam.

!!!SOME MINOR SPOILERS ALERT!!!
Well, this is how it starts: Lincoln Clay returns from Vietnam, gets back to his family. He helps his father (not real one) to deal with his problems, kills some Haitians, robs a bank for local mafia boss. Then mafia boss kills Lincoln's father and (brother?) with hands of your heist crew members. All these missions are great, you feel that Mafia atmosphere around, lots of details, really good cutscenes and acting. You feel attached to characters. This is great intro, not cliche bullsh*t with revenge for characters you met 5 minutes ago and dont even remember their names. You play this intro for hour or so, but then you realise this was just an intro to the actual game, and the game itself should be even better, right?
Actual game turns out to be cheap grinding openworld sh*t. I realised that when i captured 3rd district in town, and my actions were all the same:
1. You come to guy who can help you to capture district.
2. He tells you where to find a snitch, who you can interrogate.
3. Snitch tells you locations of places you can hit to damage property of local district boss.
4. You come to this places and kill everyone/destroy something. (By the way, interrogation missions are the same as this step).
5. Repeat step 4 until boss of the property comes out, and kill him. Yeah, and boss comes out in a same place you have trashed already, so you have to trash it again. I did 3 districts, no exceptions for that. And yes, you do this step same way as step 4 again.
So after 3 districts I have 6 more to go and I realised that the game is already boring and repetitive. I still dont understand how from these beautiful intro missions game instantly turned into grinding piece of sh*t. You basically do one mission with little variations over and over again and even story missions between this district grinding (which are killings of the district bosses) are pretty much the same.
I knew, that the game will be openworlded, and I know what to expect from this kind of games. I like Shadow of Mordor and Batman: Arkham Something series, and i thought Mafia 3 will be same solid openworld expirience, where you do same things but it is not boring because realization of game mechanics is really good.
Game mechanics in Mafia 3 are not good. The game has dumbest AI I saw in years. Stealth mechanics are pure trash (thanks a lot to AI). You can run around stealthy in crowded place, killing guards one by one scaring the f*ck out of civilians, yet their screams and panic will not alert nearby guards at all. To kill everyone stealthy you need only 2 buttons: D-Pad Left (whistle) and B (takedown). You stand behind cover luring brainless enemies right in your hands and kill them without any trouble.
Shooting in this game feels good, but AI is still dumb so they like to leave cover and run to their deaths. I've been playing on Hard difficulty, and i had problems in shootouts only when there were really a lot of enemies. They run to you from different directions, throw molotovs and can kill you in 3-4 hits on Hard, but if their number is less than 6, they are doomed. And yes, I play with a gamepad, so if you play with KB&M you can multiply this number by 10.
And few words about graphics. Lets compare it to GTA. Mafia always had better graphics than GTA of same (+-2) release year. It looked really mature in comparison with "casual" and not serious GTA. Mafia had a lot of highly detailed interiors, "movie-like" characters and animation. Mafia 3 looks... meh. Nice enough, but meh. GTA 5 that released 2.5 years ago still looks way better, more detailed and has more fps on max settings (I have i5-3570K, GTX 1070, 16 GB RAM and 2560x1440p monitor). The only graphics part that feels like real step forward is cutscenes. They were great in previous Mafias but in this one they are even better. And you've probably seen videos like Mafia 3 vs Mafia 1 where you see how every little detail that worked in Mafia 1 doesnt exist in Mafia 3, so I will not talk about it in detail.
So, my final rating is 5/10. If you remove title Mafia 3 and Vito from the game you will not find anything remotely close to previous Mafia games. I will continue playing and if by some miracle game will return to missions like in intro, I will be really happy. But I doubt this will happen, and it would be really frustrating anyway to dig through this sh*t missions to play some golden ones.
And sorry for my bad english, btw.

Game Name: Alan Wake
Game Overall Score: 10/10
Alan wake is an amazing horror survival game made by Remedy Entertainment. The game starts off with you being a successful writer and taking a trip with your wife to Bright falls to relax from novel writing. The game has a very unique story and interesting combat system, although it is repetitive since there are few enemy types in the game. It’s a fairly straight forward game, point your flashlight at the enemy, wait for its darkness shield to disappear and then fire away with one of your weapons (Revolver, Shotgun, Flare gun, etc.) until its destroyed. I also like how the game is not too futuristic or advanced, but more of an old-fashioned kind of a game. Nowadays most of the games that are produced and sold are way to futuristic, which makes the production of old-fashioned games rarer. The performance and quality are very realistic and makes you feel that you’re in the game. I also like how there are secret chests and supplies lying around which gives you more to explore in the game. Also the game has fairly easy keying binds and controls for the player.
I would recommend this game to people that are looking for an old-fashioned, third-person, survival, and horror game. But the game in my option, lacks enemy diversity. But the mysterious story of Alan wake makes up for lack of enemy diversity.
But I like the way they closed the story, because it has potential idea for DLCs or other games.
Fun Fact: The Remedy team spent a lot of time in the pacific northwest, collecting reference photos and getting a sense of the geography and climate in the areas. The art director and the rest of the team drove about 2,000 miles around Astoria, North Bend, and outside of Seattle for almost two weeks gathering information for the creation of this game.

Grandpa's Table.  Man does that bring back memories.  I remember my grandpa's favorite game was about how his little friend under the table had accidentally eaten poison and I had to squeeze his neck until he threw up.  We played that so many times, and as many lives I saved I should get some sort of medal.
That's not a lot like this Grandpa's Table though.  My time with this game has not involved any elderly genitalia, or even washing everything up “so the bad guys can't find out”.  I've seen this game compared to Quell, and that seems accurate.  You slide colored bits around until they line up in specific ways, thereby winning the game.  The puzzles get more and more devious, until you think they were designed by the Bilderberg Group.
Suffice it to say, Grandpa's Table has many secrets, and you won't even have to spend years in therapy to reveal them.  Two thumbs up.

People should know by now that early access games are a gamble for buyers, I mean come on, if you didn't know that then you have no business to complain after you made the purchase. So if you are reading this and you don't have much experience with Early Access games(which I would find odd) then know that you should watch some videos and do some research before you buy, and of course read the reviews with your own tastes in mind.
-Now there are a couple of set backs with this game at the moment, which I am sure will be fixed, like the camera view. You don't have full control of the camera, which can be a bit annoying, but as far as I know that is the main set back besides the modding not being fully integrated really (steam workshops would be nice).

So yeah, I got this game directly from the dev team thanks to a friend's input.
This review won't be simple gloryfying, though :)
First thing first - GT has AMAZING main menu! It's actually an interactive old desk with things like radio (sound on/off, next track), options, level select, flags (language change) and credits. It works beautifully, creates surprisingly nostalgic aura all around, and made me stay in for longer time than I had planned.
The gameplay is more common. Sure, I like the logic puzzles as much as the next guy, but don't expect groundbreaking inventions in this particular area. Nevertheless, it's still job well done and can make you think while beating subsequent levels. Achievement system is quite thoughtful as well. All in all - a solid system with properly working mechanics.
And one more thing - this game has a story! Not something you'd expect from a piece of puzzles, but a pleasant add-on nonetheless. The nostalgic aura I mentioned bringing one's own memories is one thing, but the game explores this theme quite thoughtfully. Remember the main menu is shaped like a desk? Well, there's a drawer in it, where you collect pieces of the past, a group of memorablia if you will. Things like notes, shirt buttons, everything that could hold a warm feeling and be connected to things we've experienced. Those pieces form a bigger picture, which deepens your own understanding of memories and maybe even brings some of them back. Truly remarkable feat that makes this game unique.
If there's one thing I'd brag about - it's music. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy the sound of piano, reminds me much of The Sims 1 build mode. It's getting repetitive soon enough, though, and the game really could use a few more tracks. Also, volume controlled in-game would be most welcome, since there's only an on/off option. Still, it's nothing you can't fix from outside the game.
All in all, Grandpa's Table is a very enjoyable experience in this particular genre that I'd recommend wholeheartedly.

The Witcher 2 is an interesting beast.  On one hand, it manages to be quite possibly the best written and acted game ever made.  On the other, it is filled with numerous flaws and glitches that are still present after numerous patches.
The story in the game is fantastic, and it has some of the most real characters I've ever seen in a game.  The voice acting is superb almost without exception, even with the minor characters.  It really is the game's main strength, and if CD Projekt can keep that same level of quality while improving the aspects of the game that are lacking, The Witcher 3 will be damn near impossible for anyone else to beat.
The game also sets a standard for graphics, setting a benchmark like Crysis did while still managing to run well on slower systems.  The graphics are still quite good even on medium, just as long as you disable the sharpening filter through the ini, as it gives the game horrendous aliasing and sharpening halos.  I honestly don't even know why they included that feature because it only makes the game look worse.  In some areas the effect is turned up to about 500% making it look beyond terrible.
As for the gameplay, this is where the game is lacking.  The controls are rather unresponsive with actions often taking up to a second to execute, and it becomes even worse during combat.  The game provides frequent extreme difficulty spikes in battles and often starts them with you being hit before it will let you block.  A good number of the battles can essentially only be beaten by executing a very specific tactic near perfectly so it quickly devolves into trial and error.  This may have been alleviated with a working dodge ability but the combat roll doesn't actually prevent you from getting hit by enemies attacking where you started the roll from.  Some fights are extremely frustrating and since the game is largely linear, it isn't an option to level up and try again later.  It's really unfortunate since a well designed combat system would put this game miles above others in the genre.
Despite that, I do enjoy the game's unique systems, making being a witcher like nothing else you've ever played.  The skills, alchemy, magic, even the stat systems are all quite unique and seem well thought out, though the flat damage reduction for armor could really use some balancing.
I really want to recommend this game, but at the same time I want to save others the frustration of all those painful fights throughout the game.  You'll have to decide for yourself if the quality of the story is worth it.

This game boasts a basic Match "Gem" setup that many low-cost games have now. It has wonderful artwork, terrible mechanics, and a story that can be tweaked and played through in 25 - 40 minutes.
* Steam Capsules & Potions fall so slow, that it is repeatedly possible to clear 75% of the board at once and have to wait; getting killed in the process for other capsules to fall.
* The animation is non-existant in between scenarios, making this more of a stop motion picture than a game.
* A specific encounter glazes the screen over with frost so you cannot see what you are doing. On low-resolution or small screens; you have to squint really hard to see what goes where, on top of having certain capsules frozen.
* The final boss fight is a bit easy, if you use a specific
's Special ability, making it feel like the point was moot you had to go through the cronies in the first place.
* The game has no resolution settings. You are stuck playing it at a very small screen.
* In terms of effect to damage, steam capsules really do pay off asthetically. The animation for the enemy battles are sweet.
* There is just something about destroying a mechanical spider I enjoy. Adding this to the pros.
* The combat is quick-paced; to the extent you die because you look away from the screen.
* Reminds me of old flash games made back in 2000; bringing a feeling of nostalgia.
I can't say this game is a gem of a find, not even for it's low price. It's low budget, lackluster in it's actual gameplay mechanics, and unbalanced to the point it eats away at you. But if you want to give it a go, I say try it, though don't say I didn't warn you.

Secondly, your mouse has to be in the EXACT correct position before clicking, otherwise it won't render. Even 0.01mm off will cause it not to work. Let me start from basics, I didn’t like the game. Mechanics is not intuitive, if it was 2014 game I wouldn’t say anything but it is supposed to be new… dragging objects you want to use instead of clicking and hoping you’ll hit just the right spot, moving back and forward to pick up the same item that is used in two scenes, map that requires 3 clicks before you can move to desired area, simply annoying.
The description of the game says “unbelievable investigation” but I only got bored and confused. The makers were trying to put it all into one story, mysterious murders, occultism, elites lives, ghosts, visions, portals…. And because of that it felt random and illogical.
“Stunning hidden object scenes”, well, maybe, but that doesn’t justify using each scene twice (!) simply by changing the list of objects we are searching for.
Alternate day and night scenes…. Let’s be clear, it could be interesting, but the main character finds his grandfather’s watch, discovers it can change daytime to nighttime and just accepts it, naturally this type of things happen all the time, I don’t know why was I surprised. He also doesn’t use it when it could be very useful, just in two scenes.
“Variety of minigames and enigmas”, that one is true. Unfortunately, variety means “oddity” and you spend more time trying to figure out what they want from you than actually solving it.
“Intriguing characters at the heart of a quest into the underground world”, possibly, but none of them got introduced properly so you will not have a chance to be intrigued. And when it comes to the underground. Cut scenes with the character walking through underground tunnels, arrrgh! I’m pretty sure it is there (multiple times) just to make the game seem longer than it actually is and to irritate the players.
The game is around 2 hours long but it feels much longer, not in a good way. When I finished I was happy to find out there is no bonus chapter.
To summarize, I do not recommend the game for the above reasons, if it was older game, I could forgive some of the drawbacks. The short list of pros doesn’t balance the long list of cons.

Wasteland 2 is unfortunately a booring game. Four critical flaws make it so.
First, it doesen't really capture the post-apocalyptic feel. The sounds aren't haunting and lonely enough, the people you meet doesen't have character enough, the narrative doesen't emphasise it enough, and the world is more absurd than gritty.
Second, the story doesen't grip me. It's bland and seems uninspired, more like a backdrop for laying down lead than anything else. It fails to motivate me, making leveling and shooting the only motivation to keep playing.
Thirdly, because the game fails to convey the feel and story of the wasteland, each new area is just a hub for more generic tasks. Exploring in this game just mean finding another safe to crack, another lock to fiddle with and another bandit to shoot. In other words, exprloring is booring.
Fourth, the leveling is also booring. The formula is too easy, has too little crunch, too little character and feels kinda pointless. Once you figure out that the only thing that matters from character creation is action points, initiative and skillpoints, you realize that the best party consist  of 4 clones, with some small ajustments to one of them to make sure you have good range of sight. There is almost no correlation between stats and skill, meaning you can pin any skill on any character with the same effect. This is ok if you don't want to make character building a focus, but it also removes character building as a motivation to play on. Further, this game reward not spending your skillpoints until you really need them, which kills the excitement of gaining a new level.
In contrast, Fallout 1 and 2 was the opposite in all of the above, and it's what made them shine imo.

I've truly enjoyed this game.
Some quick pros:
1)Although tactical parts are mostly similar, each campaign has a slightly different feel to it which makes things seem fresh.
2)Dynamic and fluid/moving combat because of the following:
-Enemies get free shots if you move within a certain range if your character is in view at the start of turn. On the other  hand, if your character starts turn out of sight then you can get as close as you want.
-Cover affects both hit chance and damage.
These encourage you to constantly maneuver your characters in small groups and flank enemies from multiple directions.
3) Gunshots and blood are satisfying.
4) You play multiple sides, which is an interesting narrative choice.
Some quick shortcomings:
1) Some systems aren't explained well on the campaign map.
2) The hit/miss conditional on luck system, while interesting in concept with no randomness involved at all, can be somewhat unreasonable, depending on your perspective, and easily played. For example think of a situation where same three people shoot at one enemy. The enemy has 8 health 60 luck left, your group has 4 damage (35%)/ 5 damage (50%) / 3 damage (90%). The only shot sequence that would kill the enemy is 4/5/3 (assuming they gain 50 luck when hit), and any other sequence of shots will leave the enemy alive.
When it is impossible to kill an enemy in one turn no matter the order if your highest damage shot has low percentage, and you want it to hit, drain luck first with weaker shots. It will be a sure hit.
Manipulating enemy luck differently according to different situations simply by changing the shooting order can make situations drastically easier (in my opinion--some might say it is tactical).
One might argue that since you don't know the starting luck of enemies, it does not matter. However most of the time the remaining luck is simply identified within a sufficient band for manipulation.
3) Once a character has the JINX passive ability, you can drain most of the enemies' luck during setup stage to zero if you want.
4) When you reload or restart tactical battles some bonuses seem to disappear. (not sure about other stuff but HP often decreases)

Sadly, I went in with high hopes in this game.
I mean: a TBS game with RPG elements, on a "western with occult" theme and a well-drawn atmosphere/UI? What could possibly go wrong?
With only a few minutes in, I have seen what made this game so apart from other good tbs:
-no game saving during the scenario: which means long, weird strategies where you have to begin again when you need to replay or situations where you actually have to replay the whole scenario to do something, tragically, you lose everything from one scenario to another;
-the obvious defensive tactics: I mean, you cannot defend, overwatch (duh!) or make complex strategies with your turns, just attacking when your time comes;
-weird AI: I mean, usually in TBSs, we have the conscious AI that do not throw themselves in an attempt for self-preservation. However, not in this game, you don't. They usually run across the map, on the open, just trying to flank the hell out of you with one hit kills. Quite frustrating indeed, considering their numbers and weird situations.
-rpg elements: well, the story have strange, unnecessary parts and you usually expect your decisions to matter. Not this time, though. Temporary allies, text progression and desperate meaningless warnings.
Despite that, if you are curious and have frustration-denial abilities, it does have some nice art and UI, interesting mechanics (luck-defense, card-perks and cover making) and great maps/scenarios to fight in.
(Maybe the next one! Instant refund.)

I am only 10 hours in and I am already beyond addicted! The kickstarter guys did NOT phone this game in (unlike another kickstarter game I won't mention *cough* *Shadowrun Returns* *cough*).
This is the kind of game that will make you long for a return to actual RPGs and will remind you of why you fell in love with the genre in the first place.
The character generation is so in depth! You have your basic stat setup (Str, Spd, etc) but all 7 of the core attributes work beautifully together. But where the game really shines is with the plethora of skills that you can choose from. You get four "core" characters and can recruit up to three more in game. I really like the 7 member squad, I don't like it when games limit you to only 4 or 5 members.
I also am really impressed with how well the designers worked in making all of the skills actually useful and not just the combat skills. There are plenty of traps, locks, safes, alarms, and more that will make it essential to have a well rounded team with all of the proper skills to effectively get the most out of every environment you visit. Additionally where many games fail when it comes to "dialouge" skills--there are three in this game--and each one offers some very nice perks.
The setting is nice, but does not offer much of anything new to the whole post-apocalyptic setting found in many games today (I do concede that the original game--to my understanding--spearheaded this type of game though). But it is still a fairly well written story. Also, I admit I don't know how often this will happen in the game, I have already came across a choice that has acutal in game everlasting consequences. So that's always fun.
This game can be hard and unforgiving, but in a good challenging way. So if you are a veteran of this genre of game you will not be disappointed. If you are a rookie but are tired of the cookie cutter action "RPGs" and would like to try something different, then at 30 bucks this might be the game for you. I will warn the rooks out there that there may be somewhat of a learning curve, but once you get past that you will finally see what all of the fuss from us older gamers is about.

After 50+ hours into the game, it started feeling like doing homework. 69 hours in, I had a blinding flash of the obvious: I was not required to continue playing. How liberating!
It had its points. The combat mechanics were kind of fun. The post-nuclear America setting is always a good time. Some of the subplots were clever. The weapon-smithing was very satisfying.
But the downsides were inescapable:
* Some of your NPCs are fun, but your main characters are pretty much ciphers. Not very engaging.
* The skill system is an annoyance. It is less about making interesting tradeoffs than making sure that you have someone maxed out in each of the 4 different "opening things" skills. It is less about looking forward the neat things that you get to do when you go up a level, than that you get to keep pace with the boxes that are inexplicably getting harder to open.
* OMG, running back and forth across the map all the time. When I have to have a book sitting next to my computer to occupy myself during your game, there is a problem.
* The characters and key items don't stand out well. You're constantly hitting the "highlight all" button, spinning around and trying to see if there is some bit of scenery that you're supposed to be interacting with.
* It has an encumbrance mechanic. And if that wasn't enough: for many items it won't be clear when you'll find someone who needs it. So you have the choice of carrying it around all the time, or stowing it, finding the person who needs it, running across the g-- d--- map. Again.
If you want an isometric tactical game, play the new xcom. If you want that + engaging plot, grab Shadowrun Dragonfall.

This game is awesome.  You drive around the deep wilderness in old russian trucks (some of which are very large), carry a ton of logs across the region, and get stuck or run out of fuel.  Rescue yourself with another truck.
My favorite moment was when I was far away from the garage.  I was towing a small jeep behind a large truck, and crossing a narrow bridge (over a ~4 meter ditch).  The big truck slipped off the edge of the bridge, fell in the ditch, rolled on it's side, and stalled.
I drove the jeep across the bridge, positioned myself behind a tree, and attached the winch to the big truck.  It groaned, and the tree bent backward, but nothing moved.  I jot the gas (tires spinning) and the winch. and the big truck just barely slid down the side of the ditch, and rolled upright.
I got in the big truck, started it up, engaged the diff lock and all-wheel drive, and floored it towards the end of the ditch.  I made it near the top, hit the handbrake, and winched myself out.
I drove around the edge of the ditch, put the jeep into tow, and adventured on.  Epic.

Playing this game is storytelling at its very best.
Great visuals, great sounds, well narrated cut scenes and a well working atmosphear (intentional misspelling). The storyline moves along nicely with some not too hard enemies that appear logical and relevant to the story. The thriller and slight horror elements are excellent!
Since I play more for the story and experience than the die hard combat challenge, I played on easy level which seem like a well balanced trade off.
There is little freedom of choice to take alternate routes but it doesn't feel like it matters.
There were times when I got stuck, usually combat situations, but it did not last long enough for me to get discouraged, so this is a very well balanced game on every level, something which is harder to design than one might think.
It took me good 20 hours to complete the story and although I am not one to repeat and play on a harder level, I can see why some would want to do that. I will always look back at the Alan Wake adventure with fondness and memories of great times!
Don't forget to play the two included DLC's which are found under episodes, they are both great and continues the story from the main game!

Yet another Double Fine masterpiece: a fantastic story and setting with equally excellent voice acting and visuals and great dialogue. The gameplay is the classic point and click adventure style where you have to talk to people, find and combine items in a particular order to advance the plot by resolving various situations the game presents you with. There is a twist here where there are two characters whose stories are linked and run in parallel, both coming from very different backgrounds and you can switch between the two, also enabling you to find hints to solve one's puzzles in the other's world (although how they exchange information is never clearly explained there are some hints in some of the implied actions). The characters are great although Vella (the girl in the story) is overwhelmingly stronger out of the two. You travel from scenic location to scenic location while solving a deep mystery in a world that is a mix of fantasy and a degree of modernism without being directly contemporary. There's a minority of people complaining about some obtuse puzzles and backtracking but I did not find anything here that is any worse than other great classics of the genre (I've played almost all of them) and although a hint system would have been nice, the puzzles are generally feasible. Seriously though, do not let the minority of complainers (less than a third of the 2000+ reviews on Steam) whose reviews somehow got voted as most helpful thanks to people never seeing and voting for the positive reviews in the other tabs distract you from this great adventure game, it is something to be experienced.

Steam Heroes is a Match 3 puzzle game that unfortunately fails to deliver. It consists of a story mode which, as others have stated, takes ~40 minutes to complete and is pretty meh. The game then proclaims that this was meant to act as a tutorial and that the now unlocked 'Steam Heroes' mode is the real game.. but this is just the ability to choose from the same 12 bosses you just defeated. There is a significant jump in difficulty with these - a decent amount of my play time has been an exercise in frustration trying to defeat Baron Von Smog. Which brings me to my main gripe (aside from the horrendoes controls) and that's the claim that there's more strategy involved in Steam Heroes than other Match 3 games...
The basic idea is that different colour/steam matches will power your different heroes (tank, heals, dps) and also do direct healing or damage. But there isn't a whole lot of time to employ this, especially in Steam Heroes mode, where taking a moment to find a match you want could actually cost you - the most strategy you can really employ, other than furiously matching things that might be detrimental to you depending on the boss, is picking which special is going to serve you best if you happen to trigger one.
So, while you could get a reasonable amount of time out of this game if you wanted, it's really not the most fun you could be having. And really, once you've defeated the bosses twice there's no real incentive to come back. Also, either the ranking doesn't work or I'm the only person to have bothered with Steam Heroes mode. :P
Sadly I feel there is potential here, but it's wasted on sub-standard.. everything. There are better games out there. Glad I got this in a crate,

Wow. Let me tell you, this game rivals Mass Effect 2 for masterful combination of storytelling and gameplay. This game is based off of a series of books if you didn't know, so that should say something about the strength of its plot, but that doesn't mean it falls short in its gameplay. Combat is fun and extremely varied. Being a witcher, you have access to 5 "signs", or spells, which all do different things. The combination of your signs with sword-swinging constantly vary the combat. In addition, each enemy in the game has a specific style to take it out easiest. You can find that out on your own, or by killing enough of the them you are rewarded with knowledge which about the enemy which you read to better prepare yourself for the next encounter. Leveling up awards you a skillpoint which you can spend in one of four trees which are summarized as follows: general (skills you need for the other trees, and it's a small tree), magic, sword, and alchemy. I personally didn't touch the alchemy tree, but focused on the sword and magic trees. With a modular plotline and varied combat, this game has a fairly large replay value. My only problem with the game is that I was a little lost in terms of story the entire time because it doesn't do a good job explaining it in the beginning (I was completely lost on background). However, a little researching set me straight. I would very highly recommend this game to anybody who asks.

Only 7 hours into this game and already hooked.
XCOM style move & shoot tactical combat & cover system is at the core of this game.  The focus on movement, flanking and cover make this system one of the best ideas form recent turn-based games.  The 'scenarios' are each mini-campaigns complete with a world map to explore and several scripted battles.
What you get in Hard West, that you don't really get in a lot of these tactical games is a great story.  Hard West is a gripping series of interconnected stories set in a Steampunk wild west with a bit of Lovecraftian horror tossed in for good measure.
Customisation options are there for your characters and have a lot of flavour to them.  Perks are obtained by slotting playing cards, each with unique passive and active bonusses.  These can be arranged into sets constituted form classic poker hands.
If the game has a drawback, I guess the lack of legacy.  I found that once I got invested in a character, they died or the scenarios finished.  That said, the changing cast of characters is part of the charm.

Superb blend of supernatural/demonic themes and Wild West tactical gunplay. What impressed me the most is the unique way the story is told and new areas are revelead based on the decisions you make. Battles are solid, turn-based firefights made interesting with the hugely customizable skill system: equippable playing cards yield direct bonuses and extra effects by carrying a poker hand. Weapons and items add an extra layer to this customization and are also upgradable if you look in the right places. Cover and luck systems are great: choose almost anything to duck behind/under and take your shot, shattering windows along the way and if you miss, it's not a total loss becaue you'll detract from your target's luck which is needed to activate powerful and interesting skills.
True to it's name, Hard West is a tough tale set in the unforgiving wilderness of the Wild West. In the opening scene, your mother is lost to bandits. Left with low hope and little choice, your father ropes you into the dangerous gold mining trade from which you struggle to eek out a living. Opportunities belie misfotrune at every turn; caves collapse upon discovering their riches and working relationships become
soured when your new friend is captured. With prospects hitting rock bottom, your father succumbs to a suspicious offering from a mysterious stranger: an amulet that will cure bad luck and heal your woes. Unforuntately, your woes are not at an end and the amulet forever curses the owner to bring bad luck wherever they wander. Burdened with a poisonous aura of misery and the guilt of his decision, your father exits your life.
Hard West's story begins like a sombre western, except it includes all of the action they promise but usually fail to deliver on. Soon enough, clues begin to drop to suggest that this is not your typical wild west world and you begin to get the feeling that something big is gonna go down. The fantastically voice-acted narrator is suddenly revealed to be Death himself, the mysterious stranger no longer shows up on foot but instead materializes out of thin air and it's not long before you're battling horned demons and cannibalizing the corpses of your assailants (not a mandatory activity). It's an effective transition from ordinary to supernatural that makes for a refreshing backdrop to this tactical RPG.
What surprised and impressed me the most is the way in which the story is told. While visiting areas on the overworld map, text-based branching dialogue options will open up various opportunities and potentially reveal new places. Narration flows seamlessly from cutscenes into map exploration and battles, which helps to tie them all together nicely into a singular storytelling device. Once again living up to it's name,
is littered with tough choices that have far-reaching or sometimes immediately impactful consequences. Curious promises will be made in return for your help, risks will surround the paths to riches and pursuing the local myths and legends is a trepidatious endeavour with unpredictable outcomes. Your morality and trust will be called into question as you are presented with these hard choices and you'll have to carefully consider whether you want to play the role of a selfish, profit-driven individual or a selfless, helpful character. It's a hugely interactive method of storytelling that deeply involves the player and the decisions they make.
Evident from the outset is the attention to detail Creative Forge Games have applied throughout the game. Check out the first screenshot: how's that for a snazzy main menu with all the animated bells and whistles? Battle maps extend beyond threadable ground to include a multitude of extra buildings and scenery, which is nice to see while you're scouting around for enemies. Almost every wall, piece of wood and object lying around can be used or turned into cover. Shotgun shells and rounds of ammunition shatter windows and send glass in every direction. The user interface is also highly-detailed with decorative silver flourishes surrounding every button and piece of canvas.
Let's talk action. Encounters are turn-based, tactical firefights which see you choosing an area to take cover behind and line up your shot from. That giant boulder may offer you full cover but will consume all of your action points reaching it whereas the nearby barrel will offer half cover and leave you with enough AP to take a shot. Skills add new layers of depth to this would-be familiar system: pray for random bonuses, ricochet shots off obstacles, reduce all friends and foes to 1 HP and much, much more. These skills are obtained as rewards, in the form of playing cards. Sacrificing the skills and passive bonuses of individual cards can be beneficial, because special bonuses are obtainable by equipping a set of cards whose combined face value amounts to a poker hand. Combine this tinkering with a wide range of weapons, relics and items and you're in character customization heaven. I personally loved the level of customization this allows, especially given that the skills are tied only to cards and are therefore completely interchangeable amongst characters.
Death is permanent in Hard West; if a character dies in battle, they're gone. However, most extra party members are fleeting due to the fact that the story moves on between chapters. Mess up once and you'll have to restart or move on without them. After making a few rash decisions myself, I was left with only 1 party member to take on the next mission: a siege against a high-profile criminal and a mob of his best shooters. Herein lies the beauty of the skill and exploration systems. While wandering around the map for the best equipment I could find, one store owner had a new dialogue option: he offered to add an extra barrel to my double-barreled shotgun. Yes please. Talking to him again, he offered to add a 4th.
I also now had a large deck of cards to choose my skills from, since my other members had bit the dust. I won't talk about the combination used because it was one of the highlights of the game for me and I don't want to spoil it. Suffice to say, I was transformed into a supernatural, quad barrel shotgun wielding force to be reckoned with that went on to kick some serious♥♥♥♥♥ It still wasn't easy, but boy was it glorious. I found playing around with the skills, stats and weapons and then using them to successfully enact your own strategies and theories on the battlefield to be hugely entertaining.
Gameplay is challenging but always fair. Positioning yourself effectively is paramount if you want your shot to have a high chance to hit. Missing is never a total loss though, because you will detract from the enemy's luck instead, which is needed to use skills. Taking a hit from an enemy adds to your own luck and brings you closer to activating powerful skills that can really help to level the odds. Even when I had to restart a battle, I wasn't cursing the decisions I made but instead found myself excitedly looking forward to trying out new strategies and skill/item combinations. There are so many other good ideas and little secrets knocking about in this game too copious to cover here, but they await any pilgrim who ventures out into the Hard West.

Although I understand a lot of complaints about the technical aspects of the game, I'm not fully on board with hating it because of these.
First, my specs for some context:
I let Geforce Experience configure my video settings and it's running everything at max settings (I run a single 1080p monitor). The game has played very well for me, even before the FPS update that happened the day after release. Although I saw a very small handful of weird floating objects and somewhat janky collision detection problems, overall it's run very well and those glitchy things are NOT hindering my game play. Personally I've always found stuff like that funny. WIth the FPS update I haven't noticed a single FPS drop from 60FPS, and when it was running at 30FPS before the update it simply never happened.
The game is great looking, I've noticed a very small handful of texture popping problems but nothing obscene. The loading times are a little longer than I'd expect but not severe. The complaints about 720p upscaling, although valid, are only noticeable at 1440p or 4k, I imagine.
The biggest technical problem I can side with is the lack of challenge from enemies. The AI is pretty dumb. That said, I'm choosing to ignore it because I feel like the southern rednecks I'm slamming forehead first into the ground should be dumb.
...is fantastic. Every character I've seen has been well rounded (once you give it time for exposition to happen). I've LOVED how the voice acting and face motion capture has played out so well with every character I've seen so far. These characters feel real. This is the first open world game in a long time that I'm not skipping cutscenes. No character is cut and dry good or bad, everyone's living in a grey area of morality.
Lincoln is probably my favorite (non-played created) protagonist I've gotten to play since Corvo, but for wildly different reasons. I'm a 30 year old white guy, born in New England, and I moved to the South when I was a kid. I've seen the crap that black people have had to live through first hand, and the pure horror represented in Mafia 3 is not a stretch considering the history of this region. I was worried that the strong overtones of racism would be difficult, but during the opening playable scene where I get to slam a racist piece of trash's head into a hot furance ... I knew I'd be ok. I usually play games like this somewhat passive. Lots of non-lethal take downs, minimize how much killing I do, etc. Mafia 3? Lincoln's got a license to knife every racist PoS that crosses his path.
The biggest problem I have with the story is, at least as far as I am, I'm not sure how the game is approaching sexism yet. Two of the collectable items in the game are Playboy magazines and "tasteful" naked women art. When viewing your collected items you're basically just staring at boobs. There are a number of strip clubs and bordellos where naked women are dancing. So far in the game I haven't seen much commentary about it... You're shutting down the bordellos, sure, but there's a bar down the road with another stripper on stage right next to the door. I'm not sure if the developers are putting this stuff in the game as a, "yup, this was another thing of the era and we're acknowledging that" or a cheap way to get some T'n'A in the game. I'm choosing to see it as a way to say, "This racism? Yeah, not the only problem back then," but unless by the end I see some hard pressed, "seriously aren't these people gross?" I might not be able to.
If you don't like this game because of your hard stance on PC ports or your accepted requirements for PC gaming, I can understand that. However, I do think many people are blowing it out of proportion. It's not as bad as many reviews are making it out to be. There have been worse (from a technical point of view), and will be even worse, games that are otherwise loved by PC gamers. Read the technical complaints with a grain of salt: How many of these people are on lower end spec'd machines? How many people with great rigs didn't build it right, have faulty hardware, have a mess of software/driver problems, etc, etc? Are these problems you'll have, too? How many people are choosing to pile onto these problems for other reasons?
I don't see many people actually hating the story for the wrong reasons. Some people will find the extreme racism represented here as difficult to handle, and I understand that. It's heavy, and really hard to disassociate from. That said, this is part of OUR American history and ignoring it because it makes you uncomfortable is wrong. If you're like me (stereotypical white guy that's trying to not be such a privileged piece of crap), play it. Understand what's happening, acknowledge it, and learn that it's not OK.
I don't want to get all SJW on here, but I'm worried that some complaining is coming from a place of hate. There has been a lot of blatant racism throughout American media in the last couple of years. I'm hoping people play this game to learn about what an entire race of people have experienced for decades, and learn from it. I'm not saying Mafia 3 discusses the issues flawlessly, but it does it in a much better manner than we're getting from other forms of media.
It's got a great story, I feel like I'm learning to acknowledge the hate people have been forced to grin and bear far more than I have in the past, and it's just pretty. There's a lot of fun to be had, but approach it as a learning experience, too.

So there are two or three significant drawbacks to this game. The first, and most pronounced is its skill check system, with its critical failures and long load times making trying to pick a lock or open a safe an exercise in the worst type of RNG hell. Secondly, the game goes a bit overboard with the number of skills, to the point where something like speech has three seperate skills, and the clarity of how attributes translate to derived stats could be improved. Lastly, there are a handful of sections (Rail Nomads in part, but mostly the interminable Canyon of Titan) that are drawn out exercises in slowly walking back and forth that switch the plot to a snails pace.
All that said, while Wasteland 2 can often feel like a game that does not give a damn if you're having fun with it, when it shines, and when you've finally gotten a hang on creating and developing your  squad of rangers (or evolving the scant few NPC recruits who aren't garbage) you'll really find a game that can be a real blast. There are few delights like getting into combat and having the ranger squad work like a well oiled led-spewing machine. Better still is flicking through character creation options until you've put together a suitable distitnctive four-man-band of Desert rangers, as there's a fair ammount  of room to put an imaginative stamp on your team.
Its got its warts, but it deserves its spot as one of the standout trinity of kickstarter CRPGs, even if the ride to the finish can be bumpy at times. If you haven't yet, check out the Director's Cut. Do youself a favor and find a build guide online (for the love of all that's good in this world, find a build guide), but check it out.

Flight Simulator X (more commonly known as FSX by it’s users) was Microsofts’ latest offering in their long line of Flight Sim software.  Despite it being the latest, FSX is now over ten years old with it’s original European version having been released on October 13 2006. Since it’s inception, FSX has seen two Service Pack updates (known as SP1 and SP2) and an the ‘Acceleration’ Expansion.  In 2014, Microsoft signed a licencsing deal with Dovetail Games who then took over development of the software.
Once Dovetail Games received the licence in 2014, they wasted little time in identifying an opportunity to increase the gaming audience of FSX and, later that year, released it Steam as FSX:Steam Edition, incorporating both of the service pack updates and the Accerleration Expansion.
As far as gameplay and graphics quality go, it’s a software that’s now ten years old and, to an extent, that should give you an idea of what you’re likely to experience when you load up and take your first flight into the unknown.  There are other, newer, flight simulator products out there that carry much higher quality graphics and therefore offer a better ‘immersion’ into the experience.  But on the flip-side of that statement, FSX:SE does provide a relatively inexpensive way to get into flight simming.
Gameplay itself in FSX is, by and large, still as competent now as it was at release.  Stock aircraft that come with the software are plenty varied (everything from passenger airlines and prop craft to gliders and helicopters) and adequate to get going.  If you're new to flight simulators, a large and detailed range of lessons are available to help you understand basic flight dynamics and how to use the systems in the range of offered aircraft.  There’s also a wide range of ‘missions’ that you can undertake, which range from simple take-off, fly for 15 minutes and land missions to racing P-51 Mustangs and performing oil rig transports.
Where FSX really noses ahead of the crowd in terms of it’s competitors are the huge range of freeware and payware addons that are available.  There are so many addons, downloads and expansions out there that you will literally need two lifetimes to try absolutely everything.  I’ve heard, more than once, my fellow virtual airline colleagues who use Prepar3D or X-Plane state that they aren’t able to access a particular aircraft model because no one has developed it.  If variety is the spice of life, then FSX is very, very spicy!
On a technical note, some areas of FSX have been plagued with issues resulting in software crashes and Out of Memory (OOM) problems and I've heard a number of my simming friends compain of such issues, even with high end rigs.  However, this can sometimes be related to the number and variety of addons that are added to the software, rather than the software itself.
Pros:
- Relatively inexpensive compared to other flight sims
- Insanely wide range of potential addons (free and payware)
- Good introductory lessons for those new to flying
Cons:
- Standard graphics are a little dated (can be improved with addons)
- Has been known to crash and have OOM errors more than we'd probably like
- Can be system resource intensive

Viriginia is a loosely put together tale with interesting themes, that ultimately falls flat due to lack of focus and a case of overcomplication. The game hides a classic 90s psychological thriller with overt references to Twin Peaks and The X-files in a mess of timelines, dreams and allegorical symbolism. On the surface, the story is a tangled web of details and unfinished sentences, leaving the player to put it together.
The problem is that the game is just trying much too hard to cram it all together for the two hour duration of the game, with the gameplay not really being as such, as Virginia is more of a visual novel rather then a Gone Home. You spend little time using mechanics to progress, instead just walking to pre-determined scripting points and pressing the button to be taken to the next scene.
To me, it seems clear that this is a game plagued by a long and ardous development cycle where too many writers wanted to have their say and tell their story - it lacks a goal. The themes of social justice and racism never go beyond, again, surface-level, and instead seems comfortable leaving any type of point or discussion up to the player.
While I can't recommend this to a buyer in general, not even story-game/walking simulator fans, I can suggest you give it a shot if you really like to figure things out yourself and don't mind filling in endless plot holes with your own interpretation. I just can't help to think how fantastic this game would have been if it just focused on the main case in the story, while allowing character development to progress much slower to allow more nuance and details in the overarching themes.
As it's released, Virginia is a TV-show crammed together in a panic over the course of two hours instead of a season, and I recommend you spend your time on Gone Home or Firewatch instead of this.

Game name: Alan Wake
Game score: 10/10
Reviewed by: Wolf
Alan Wake is a psychological horror survival game produced by Remedy Games in 2010. The game follows writer Alan Wake, who becomes trapped in his dreams pursued by the antagonist "The Darkness" who turns people basically into pawns of an evil force. Your main goal is to find and save your wife, Alice Wake, who is presumed taken by The Darkness.  The DLC, The Signal and The Writer, respectively, continue the story of Alan being trapped in his dreams, and further expands the story on how he defeats The Darkness.
In The Signal DLC, you travel through memories of the past game (main story) uncovering clues to how to wake up from your dream. With Barry to accompany you, he guides you through the area with both motivation and moral support (such a good guy Barry is).
In The Writer DLC, you finally uncover the truth about Barry, as well as uncover the reason your dreaming. Zane is there to guide you as like the main story, and helps you defeat The Darkness and wake up from your dream.
Alan Wake is an episodic story, meaning it's told in episodes rather than all at once, kind of like how TellTale styles their games.
Mouse 1 - Shoot
Mouse - Look
WASD - Move
Q - Reload flashlight
E - Pick up objects/use
R - Reload gun
F - Focus
Tab - Toggle view (which side displayed in 3rd person)
1,2,3,4,5 - Cycle weapons
Being a horror game, Alan Wake is filled with jump scare sounds (at least for me) such as when a Taken jumps out and attacks it's pretty sudden at times and can scare some people. Some of the cutscenes also have jumpworthy sounds when transitioning, not going to spoil where it's at because that would ruin basically the whole story.
Another thing to note is the music. Each episode ending features music which in my opinion is perfect for the game. It's not disrupting in any way, and perfectly fits the atmosphere of the game. It's mostly Indie Rock, but very fitting with the game and mood, so it fits in well with everything.
So most people may not know this going into this game, but doing research will point out this game took over 5 years to develop. Being that this game was released in 2010, the graphics are still unbelieveable to this day, prividing both very scenic background areas, and also amazing cutscenes. Now, they may not be "Unreal Engine: real life vs video game" standards, but literally, I loved them, and got quite a few worthy of posting screenshots out of them.
Honestly, the game was very easy. At points I did struggle (died a lot because I honestly wasn't thinking, just attacking, especially at points where I just needed to run to a Safe Haven and Taken were infinitely spawning because of it), but in the end I realized how easy the enemies were and how easy it was to progress through the levels.
Albeit, I did play on normal difficulty the whole time (Nightmare I still have to do for the rest of the achievements) but I've read it's the same as normal, just less ammo, which is perfectly fine, there's way too much ammo in the game as it is. Think of Nightmare mode as hard difficulty, since they removed hard mode and there is a gap between normal and nightmare.
Remedy, ♥♥♥♥ Microsoft and find a new producer/publisher. They aren't biting and your fans NEED Alan Wake 2.

Wow. Let me tell you, this game rivals Mass Effect 2 for masterful combination of storytelling and gameplay. Combat is fun and extremely varied. Being a witcher, you have access to 5 "signs", or spells, which all do different things. You can find that out on your own, or by killing enough of the them you are rewarded with knowledge which about the enemy which you read to better prepare yourself for the next encounter. Leveling up awards you a skillpoint which you can spend in one of four trees which are summarized as follows: general (skills you need for the other trees, and it's a small tree), magic, sword, and alchemy. I personally didn't touch the alchemy tree, but focused on the sword and magic trees. With a modular plotline and varied combat, this game has a fairly large replay value. My only problem with the game is that I was a little lost in terms of story the entire time because it doesn't do a good job explaining it in the beginning (I was completely lost on background). However, a little researching set me straight. I would very highly recommend this game to anybody who asks.

I like the attempts at novelty on the tried and true sudoku formula. The nomiko variant is initially interesting but isn't actually much different, once you get used to it. You always solve puzzles in the exact same way.
I also like the fact that you only  need to solve certain squares to advance a level -- since a Sudoku puzzle always starts off at maximum difficulty and get easier as you go, this is a clever way of avoiding the tedious last third, where you're just filling in obvious cells.
This title has a real lack of polish, though. There's no background music, and a number of technical errors mar what could have easily been a fun timewaster. There's not a quick/easy way to input 'possible' values. You have to click on the pencil to toggle this on/off each time. Playing on paper or the Nintendo DS is a markedly better experience.
You're probably better off just googling "play sudoku" and going with whatever HTML5 bs pops up.

Natural Selection 2 is an independent (indie) crowdfunded multiplayer game from before the time of game crowdfunding at kickstarter.
It is based on the the most played, non-commercial, Half-Life mod Natural Selection, which is a masterpiece!
The two key features of NS are:
1. Asymmetric teams!
The aliens have several completely different, specialised classes, all of whom mainly rely on melee combat. To their aid the aliens have a wide variety of movement abilities and possibilities.
The marines play like a regular FPS and are defined by their equipment.
2. The game is at the same time an RTS!
One player on each team takes the role of commander with all the traditional RTS elements, as top-down view of the map together with building placement, technology research, expansion and resource collection - from resource points spread out on the map which need to be controlled!
As much as I can talk about the incredible depth of gameplay of NS1, this standalone sequel has gone a slightly different path, mostly for the worse. Nevertheless, this is one of the very few unique games out there with very deep and entertaining gameplay!
For people who want to challenge the best, there is a big and very welcoming competitive/pro community!
On the whole, NS2 (and NS1! requires HL1) is absolutely recommended to anyone who likes multiplayer first person shooters and wants something MUCH more than soldier vs soldier deathmatch!
Practical considerations:
1. Having a microphone is a big plus as a soldier and a lack thereof is a big minus when being commander.
2. You need a good gaming computer to play this game enjoyably. The developer Unknown Worlds is continuously working on improving performance.
Of the current generation, a midrange Haswell gaming CPU together with a midrange AMD 200-series or nVidia 700-series GPU.
Of the previous generation, a midrange Ivy-Bridge gaming CPU together with a midrange AMD 7000-series or nVidia 600-series GPU.
Of the next-previous generation, a top range Sandy-Bridge gaming CPU together with a  top range AMD 6000-series or nVidia 500-series GPU.

If you're thinking, "This looks like a budget version of Puzzle Quest," it's not. The "story mode" takes about 35 minutes to play through, consists only of battles against 12 marginally different opponents (no map or choices to make), and when you're done even says explicitly that the story mode was "designed as a tutorial, and designed to be easy to complete." The "real game" is the "hero mode", where you just pick one of those 12 opponents and play against them, trying to get a high score.
And how is that game? There's really very little strategy in this "puzzle strategy game." It's real-time, and moves quickly enough that there's no time to plan moves. Even if there were, the visual effects (including even the basic effects from your own matches) obscure the board and get in the way. That bit about "not every match is a good one" really only applies to the last of the 12 opponents. Basically, it comes down to spamming as many matches as you can, and occasionally hitting the 1-3 keys to activate special abilities. It also suffers from a pet peeve of mine in match-3 games: As far as I can tell, you don't get the "4-match" bonus (whatever that might be) from a T-match, so if you see a T setup, you may be better off taking the straight 4 than full T-match of 5.

Although I understand a lot of complaints about the technical aspects of the game, I'm not fully on board with hating it because of these.
First, my specs for some context:
I let Geforce Experience configure my video settings and it's running everything at max settings (I run a single 1080p monitor). The game has played very well for me, even before the FPS update that happened the day after release. Although I saw a very small handful of weird floating objects and somewhat janky collision detection problems, overall it's run very well and those glitchy things are NOT hindering my game play. Personally I've always found stuff like that funny. WIth the FPS update I haven't noticed a single FPS drop from 60FPS, and when it was running at 30FPS before the update it simply never happened.
The game is great looking, I've noticed a very small handful of texture popping problems but nothing obscene. The loading times are a little longer than I'd expect but not severe. The complaints about 720p upscaling, although valid, are only noticeable at 1440p or 4k, I imagine.
The biggest technical problem I can side with is the lack of challenge from enemies. The AI is pretty dumb. That said, I'm choosing to ignore it because I feel like the southern rednecks I'm slamming forehead first into the ground should be dumb.
...is fantastic. Every character I've seen has been well rounded (once you give it time for exposition to happen). I've LOVED how the voice acting and face motion capture has played out so well with every character I've seen so far. These characters feel real. This is the first open world game in a long time that I'm not skipping cutscenes. No character is cut and dry good or bad, everyone's living in a grey area of morality.
Lincoln is probably my favorite (non-played created) protagonist I've gotten to play since Corvo, but for wildly different reasons. I'm a 30 year old white guy, born in New England, and I moved to the South when I was a kid. I've seen the crap that black people have had to live through first hand, and the pure horror represented in Mafia 3 is not a stretch considering the history of this region. I was worried that the strong overtones of racism would be difficult, but during the opening playable scene where I get to slam a racist piece of trash's head into a hot furance ... I knew I'd be ok. I usually play games like this somewhat passive. Lots of non-lethal take downs, minimize how much killing I do, etc. Mafia 3? Lincoln's got a license to knife every racist PoS that crosses his path.
The biggest problem I have with the story is, at least as far as I am, I'm not sure how the game is approaching sexism yet. Two of the collectable items in the game are Playboy magazines and "tasteful" naked women art. When viewing your collected items you're basically just staring at boobs. There are a number of strip clubs and bordellos where naked women are dancing. So far in the game I haven't seen much commentary about it... You're shutting down the bordellos, sure, but there's a bar down the road with another stripper on stage right next to the door. I'm not sure if the developers are putting this stuff in the game as a, "yup, this was another thing of the era and we're acknowledging that" or a cheap way to get some T'n'A in the game. I'm choosing to see it as a way to say, "This racism? Yeah, not the only problem back then," but unless by the end I see some hard pressed, "seriously aren't these people gross?" I might not be able to.
If you don't like this game because of your hard stance on PC ports or your accepted requirements for PC gaming, I can understand that. However, I do think many people are blowing it out of proportion. It's not as bad as many reviews are making it out to be. There have been worse (from a technical point of view), and will be even worse, games that are otherwise loved by PC gamers. Read the technical complaints with a grain of salt: How many of these people are on lower end spec'd machines? How many people with great rigs didn't build it right, have faulty hardware, have a mess of software/driver problems, etc, etc? Are these problems you'll have, too? How many people are choosing to pile onto these problems for other reasons?
I don't see many people actually hating the story for the wrong reasons. Some people will find the extreme racism represented here as difficult to handle, and I understand that. It's heavy, and really hard to disassociate from. That said, this is part of OUR American history and ignoring it because it makes you uncomfortable is wrong. If you're like me (stereotypical white guy that's trying to not be such a privileged piece of crap), play it. Understand what's happening, acknowledge it, and learn that it's not OK.
I don't want to get all SJW on here, but I'm worried that some complaining is coming from a place of hate. There has been a lot of blatant racism throughout American media in the last couple of years. I'm hoping people play this game to learn about what an entire race of people have experienced for decades, and learn from it. I'm not saying Mafia 3 discusses the issues flawlessly, but it does it in a much better manner than we're getting from other forms of media.
It's got a great story, I feel like I'm learning to acknowledge the hate people have been forced to grin and bear far more than I have in the past, and it's just pretty. There's a lot of fun to be had, but approach it as a learning experience, too.

So, after playing the first scenario, a few things to note:
-The comments about the story feeling a little disjointed are somewhat accurate.  After each scenario, the game sends you back to the main menu as though you'd just finnished a chapter in a book, but the next chapter wasn't out yet.
-The combat is straight out of XCom/Jagged Alliance.  That's not a critisism as much as it is an observation.  If you don't like those types of games, you won't like this one.
-Even though it seems like there are different approaches to reach the objective for a map, so far they just boil down to "kill any and everything that moves".  That may change further along in the story, but the only "stealth" mission I did still ended up forcing me to gun down all the bad guys to escape.
-Characters come and go pretty much on a whim.  Fortunately you don't lose any equipment as the character dumps their gear in your inventory pool when they bail, but anticipating an upcoming battle only to end up having to go in a gun down with nothing to say about it is kinda rough.
-Difficulty options and ironman modes add replayability.
Overall, the game seems solid and decently put together.  Yeah, one gun looks like the next but ultimately, if you see a guy with a rifle, he's got a rifle.  If that rifle has a scope, it's a sniper rifle.  Pepperboxes have their own look as do revolvers and shotguns.  It would be nice if everything had its' own unique image, but there aren't any surprises.
All said and done, Hard West is a very functional tactical strategy game set squarely in an old west setting with a supernatural spin.  First impressions give it a solid 7/10.

As for the XCOM and Jagged Alliance comparisons, Hard West really is it's own game.  While it is turn based, its combat system is simpler then XCOM's and much less sophisticated then the one found in Jagged Alliance 2.  That said, the game doesn't suffer for this.  Combat is fun, tense, and always seems fair.
I played it on an older system (Dell XPS 420) and it ran smoothly.  There were temporary hangs in the inventory screen and I ran into one mission that did not end when the trigger should have occured.  I was able to work around this without any issue.
So, solid game.  Fun, not terribly difficult (on normal), entertaining, and very interesting.  I look forward to see what the developers do next.
