TL/DR below:  Getting-stuck-in-the-mud simulator.  8.5/10
In some ways this game may not be considered "complete" - but the important question for me is this: is it fun?  (Is it worth my $30?)  My experience thus far has yielded a definite "yes."  The only "objective" is to pick up logs on one side of the map, and deliver them to another.  Sounds simple, doesn't it?  Even on "casual" mode - this is far more challenging than I thought, and in the best possible way.  If you enjoy carefully navigating heavy vehicles through terrain they have little to no business being on, this game is for you.
More specifically:
Vehicles:  There are a decent variety, and each has a different feel and driving style.  By default, each has different equipment that serves a different function, though many are customizable and each to a different degree.  Mainly, there is the cargo function, and support functions.  Get your favorite truck stuck in the mud or flip it over making a bad turn?  Whip out the heavy slow one and wench it out!  Smash it into a boulder?  Bring in the repair vehicle.  Run out of fuel?  There's a tanker for that.  Just feel like exploring in something faster?  Go find the little jeep thing stuck in the woods.
Driving Mechanic:  Weight plays a huge role in the feel of driving, and once your vehicle is loaded-up, every few yards of movement become a strategic series of decisions.  Should I brave that pile of large rocks or try wading through that pool of uncertain depth?  Is your vehicle sure-footed on 8 wheels but slow as father time - or is it fast as a rabbit but top-heavy like a bobbing-bird?  Seriously - getting stuck in the mud has never been this fun.  The driving feels mostly realistic - certainly enough to suspend my disbelief, and make me feel like I'm really piloting many tons of metal, rubber, and wood through a slimy river-bed.
Graphics / Physics:  This is a beautiful game.  Muddy, swampy, sloshy, beautiful.  Not only is the level of graphical detail very impressive, but the physics and voxel deformation match it in kind.  Tires smoosh under the weight of cargo and deform over rocks.  Mud squishes out of the way of your tires and splatters all over your cabin in higly convincing fashion - and it even slowly dries over time.  Water reacts absurdly well to disturbance and current - this might be the most convincing 3d water I've ever seen in a game.  It isn't perfect - but it's still the best I've ever seen.  As mentioned above, the driving and physics thereof are not perfect, but they are better than most when it comes to off-road - and I've never played a game before this one that accurately portrays the feeling of getting bogged-down in wet river-mud.  Seriously.  This is very convincing gloopyness, and the splatter of mud and splash of water are of higher quality than you're likely to see anywhere else.
Gameplay:  This is really all about the experience of driving these machines in this environment - that is: big heavy trucks over packed-dirt, wet grass, rivers and puddles, and of course - mud.  Lots of mud.  There is an objective in each map, and near as I can tell it's always the same - but as I said, that doesn't make it a simple task.  There are also "cloaking points" - which are basically an alternative to "fog of war" that obscure the map, as well as garages and vehicles to discover - and in hardcore mode - to repair, refuel, and reclaim.  Each map is hours of fun.
That said - my one gripe on the current version of this game is that starting a different map will overwrite the save from another - so until you finish a map, it's best to stick with the one, as you can continue after quitting the game.  However, the developers have explicitly stated this will change in the next update - so hey!  If this sounds like a dealbreaker to an otherwise awesome experience, put this on your wishlist and check back later.  You might want to check the free tech-demo on their website to get an idea what this is like - that's what I did.  I bought the game at full price, and I am not at all disappointed - $30 very well spent, in my opinon.  The technology in the full game has been pushed a lot farther: every aspect feels better, more polished, and more realistic - but the demo will at least give you a feel for whether you will enjoy this style of driving or not.

My favorite part of KSP is that you learn something every time you fail, and you usually only fail because of your own incompetence. At almost 1000 hours I'm still learning new things all the time. I'd put this in the same category of "buy it now, you won't be sorry" as The Witcher 3 and Mount and Blade: Warband. This is my favorite gift for students.
I'd recommend that new players start in Career mode on easy to get the hang of things. Career is essentially a tutorial, giving you new parts as you progress through the tech tree.
Pros:
- Build custom rockets, see if they fly.
- Learn to streamline and build more efficiently.
- Learn about orbital mechanics, space flight, and physics in general.
- Interface is intuitive and easy to pick up. I had a class of teenagers that had never played get to orbit in about an hour. Tutorial videos are not required, just don't be afraid to revert when you crash and burn.
- Mods for pretty much everything.
Cons:
- Poorly designed rockets can be frustrating. Conventional logic says "add more rockets", whereas "build more efficiently" is generally the better choice.
- Key information about your rocket is not easy to get without mods. Highly recommend getting Kerbal Engineer to provide detailed info on your craft.
- Some instability when heavily modded. Playing with 10-15 mods active I can usually go 4-8 hours per session without issues. Just save often - there is a quick save and persistent save.

I made the mistake of believing the "Incredibly deep story!" reviews. "Virginia" tries way too hard to pay homage to David Lynch and forgets that funky visual metaphors aren't enough... engaging characters, an interesting plot, and effective pacing are what gives the funkiness punch. There's nothing "deep" about this story unless you choose to infer a novel's worth of unjustified conjecture from psychoanalyzing the clichéd dream sequences.
Beyond the story, the "interactive" portions of the narrative are merely annoyances and do nothing to engage the player or serve as dramatic edits/cuts. Maybe this could be effective as a VR movie experience that avoids "gameplay" all together... but the story is so thin, emotion is so lacking, and the metaphors are so heavy handed that I doubt even VR could distract you long enough.
I’ll wrap up by saying that I might have enjoyed "Virginia" more if I hadn't just been kicked in the gut by "Firewatch’s" all emotion, minimal story approach... but probably not. Then again, my “Firewatch” love will probably be enough to disqualify my opinion for some. :P

I came relatively late to the KSP party, joining just after release 1.0. I had a friend who had been telling me to try it out, and eventually acted on his suggestion.
KSP is utterly superb. I can't really say anything more than that.
It is, at its heart, a Aeronautical/Space Simulation game. A planetary system is available for your exploration, along hundreds of different parts, engines, capsules and many other associated parts with which to build your rockets.
Couple this with a wicked sense of humour, an unexhaustible supply of little men and green women to send to distant planets (or to be blown to kingdom come on main engine start) and a modding community that is second to none and you have one of the greatest games in existence.
This combines into an experience like no other, where you can be tearing your hair out but yet keep coming back for more. It has generated an entire sub culture online, Elon Musk is rumoured to play - hell, even NASA has had involvement with a mod that is now included in the base game! The sense of achievement to be gained from landing on the moon, flying a Shuttle or just surviving re-entry is the sweetest reward.
Just experience it, and you won't regret it.

No room for an intro with this damn word limit, so let's dive right in!
Design: 8/10
If you're familiar with point and click games, the gameplay of Broken Age is standard fare, and you don't need to read the rest of this paragraph. For those not in the know, I'll explain how it goes. You interact with the world by, you guessed it, pointing and clicking. There will be things in the environment that you can interact with, and you can see what they are by hovering over them with your mouse, and then click on them to interact. You also collect items throughout the game, which you'll need to use together and with parts of the environment in order to solve the puzzles. You'll also talk to characters, choosing from dialogue options.
Now that we know how it works, how does Broken Age do? Quite well, as it would happen. As I go through this, please note that the game was released in two acts, and I'll be talking about them separately sometimes.
Difficulty is the biggest misstep in the entire game, though the fact that it isn't too bad serves as a testament to the overall quality of the game. The first act is quite easy, I didn't have to look up anything, which is a good thing. However, I felt that the first act was too easy, that it could have had harder puzzles. Double Fine heard this feedback and went a little overboard on act 2. It was as hard as a lot of old school point and clicks, and I had to look up a number of puzzles. I feel that act 2 was worse than 1 in difficulty, because it really broke up my pace getting stuck and having to look stuff up so often. The difficulty balance was a pretty big issue for me, and I think only the best point and click gamers could have gotten through act 2 without some major frustration. Ideally, the whole game would have been a little harder than act 1, but not so hard that we had to look things up a lot.
Speaking of puzzles, I want to talk about the design of them, leaving the factor of difficulty out. Most puzzles were good, with a few great, highly memorable ones, and a few that I wasn't so crazy about. All the puzzles with the tree were awesome, certainly high points in the game in terms of creativity and humor. The puzzles I didn't like were all in the second act, specifically the hexipal and knot puzzles, which were too confusing and irritating for me.
Story: 9/10
Easily the high point of the game. Now, I'm usually going on about how design and gameplay are the most important things in games, and that's true, for most games. But adventure games are different, the story is a central part of the experience, and is almost or even as important as the gameplay. Tim Schafer wants his games to be a seamless fusion of interactivity and story. Though he hasn't gotten there yet, Broken Age does it better than most. First we're going to look at how good the overall plot is, and then characters.
You need to know that Broken Age follows two different characters in separate locations, who don't communicate with each other. The opening of the game shows both characters, Shay and Vella, both 14, sleeping. You click on whichever one you want to start with to get going, but you can switch any time you want. In act 1, you don't need to switch between them, you can play through one and then the other if you want, but in act 2 you need to switch.
Shay lives on a spaceship, with computers that call themselves his mom and dad. He's stuck in a brutally boring routine of 3 gross meals a day and fake missions, the same four over and over again. Shay's goal is to break free of his monotonous prison and go on real adventures. Vella lives in a village called Sugar Bunting, where she has been chosen to be offered up to a horrible monster, Mog Chothra, as part of the generational maidens feast. Being sacrificed is seen as a great honor, but Vella doesn't think so, and determines to kill Mog Chothra instead.
The plot is really fun and compelling, one of the best in memory. The ending to act 1 is one of the best twists in gaming; seriously, it's amazing. The reason I don't award this section a perfect 10/10, though, is because some of the big questions don't have totally satisfying answers. It's not a huge problem, and some things make more sense as you keep going, but it's enough to keep this from story-telling perfection.
The world that we find ourselves in in Broken Age is well-fleshed-out, and so fun and full of life. We don't see a huge number of different locations throughout the game, but those we do visit are spectacular. While it would be nice to have this world explored more, I'm left very satisfied with it. Most of the environments from act 1 are revisited in act 2, but they have interesting changes to them, and I won't tell you how, but you explore them from very different perspectives. All in all, the varied and beautiful world of Broken Age is one of the most fun, beautiful places I've visited in a game in a long time.
Every character in Broken Age is good, no part is wasted. Other developers could take a page from Double Fine in how to populate a world with great characters. Of course some characters are better than others, but none are very weak, and there are quite a few standout personalities. The voice acting is top-notch, not just from big names like Elijah Wood and Jack Black, but also from the unknowns like Masasa Moyo, who voices Vella. There are some ridiculously funny characters such as Knife, a sadistic talking knife who loves cutting anything and everything. The yarn pals and hexipals are also super-cute and -silly characters. Oh, and we can't forget Curtis, the lumberjack who thinks trees are talking to him. My biggest complaint in this department is the man who voices Alex, he really didn't do a lot of the lines justice. We knew Tim Schafer was a hilarious writer, but Broken Age brings his writing to new heights.
Graphics: 8/10
There are a lot of different art styles out there, but there's nothing like what you'll find in this game. The art has so much charm and personality, it's so beautiful, and it's fun. If an art style can be fun, this is. I can remember one instance, very brief, in act 1 where there was a little bit that didn't look quite as polished, but aside from that, the art here is absolutely superb. After playing Nintendo games that tend to have a certain look, or pixel art games, or gritty western games, or even other Double Fine games, it's impossible to describe how I felt about the art of Broken Age except as refreshed. It's like tasting a flavor you've never tasted before, or feeling a wonderful new texture. It's simply wonderful and refreshing. The art of Broken Age is great, and adds another layer of fun and charm onto an already charming and fun game.
Music: 9/10
The music for Broken Age was conducted by prolific and talented video game composer Peter McConnell, who composed for many LucasArts adventure games, most Double Fine games, and the Sly Cooper series. His brilliant score is given what it truly deserves by being fully performed by the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra. The result is a soundtrack that is swimming with life, with a quirky and fun personality to match that of the art and characters. This isn't the kind of music that gets stuck in your head, but it's a majestic piece of work which contributes more to the atmosphere and feeling of Broken Age than most games achieve.
Conclusion:
Broken Age is an infusion of new life into a genre that's been largely dormant for over fifteen years. The graphics are great, the music is amazing, the story and characters funny and exciting, and the gameplay, while not overcoming the faults of yesteryear, is still great. If you like point and click games, try this one. If you don't, Broken Age doesn't bring the genre to the mainstream, but it is one of the best point and clicks out there. Long live the point and click!

Pros:
-Well enough executed turn based combat in the style of x-com.
-Interesting mechanics such as the luck system and altering/using the environment depending on your loadout.
-Atmosphere. It does a great job of establishing a "weird horror" vibe and the setting of the Old West is one that isn't overdone. It builds and holds tension well.
-Locations between missions add a lot to the story and setting. The choices they provide are fun. If you've ever played the "Arkham Horror" board game, they're very much like the location cards you would draw.
-The music is fantastic and moody.
-The art fits very well.
-Scenario-style campaign is good for starting and finishing a sub-story in a single session.
-$20 price tag, if not on sale for less.
Cons:
-The interface could use a bit more polish. I would like a hoykey to confirm actions instead of clicking "Confirm". I might be missing something, though.
-Occasional interface delay noticed after playing for a few hours. Resolved by closing and re-opening the game.
-I found quite a few typographical errors while playing the game. They're easy enough to overlook, but made me occasionally pause to make sure I wasn't just reading the passage incorrectly.
This is a definite pick up for anyone with a love for horror, turn-based combat or the Old West. It's not perfect, but for $20, you don't want to miss this one. Especially if you're looking for something to pass the time until X-Com 2.

I loved it!  I've enjoyed several other classic point-and-clicks: Monkey Island I and II, Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis, Day of the Tentacle, and Full Throttle, and I think this one makes a fresh and interesting contribution to that library.  The art and music direction is fantastic, the voice acting is great, and the humor is done well.  Minor things bothered me in the final puzzle sequence (mostly the music), but overall I liked the game a great deal.  The puzzles in Act I are fairly easy, so most of my enjoyment came from watching the story unfold and interacting with the characters.  In Act II the difficulty increases a bit, which I appreciated.  Online walkthroughs are easy to find, but of course I recommend playing without them as much as possible if you actually want to enjoy hitting those "Aha!" moments when you solve particularly challenging puzzles.
The "Double Fine Adventure" documentary series online is also fun to watch if you're interested in the blood, sweat, tears, and laughter that goes into video game production.

Note to other reviewers: The game HAS an alternative overwatch system, "reaction fire". Your units never use it because the enemy AI never moves into the zone which triggers it, because that would be dumb. You CAN run up to an enemy for point blank blasting by starting your move out of their line of sight. If they don't see you coming they can't use reaction fire (And the red circle won't appear). A full overwatch as in XCOM would break the other mechanics of THIS game. This is not XCOM. (XCOM2 February, YAY!)
++ Tightly designed turn based combat, fixed damage, high mobility. Very satisfying when you get under its skin. Favourite tactic: Charging into point blank range with a group of enemies and using the Barrage or Chain-Kill skills to shoot them all down at once. Do it right and you have 100% chance of success thanks to the "point blank" aim bonus. I've seen several reviews that say you can't do this.
++ Deterministic chance-to-hit. 75% chance to hit doesn't mean random, it means it will cost 75 luck to dodge the shot - or the target takes fixed damage and gains luck points. It's really elegant and drives lots of new tactics. The only randomness is that you don't know how much luck the enemy has. - Note: This is how I understand it, please someone correct me if I'm wrong.
++ Linux support. I haven't used it much because the Linux version doesn't work with my Steam controller but massive thumbs up for Linux support!
++ Western setting, fantastic. Love the art style.
++ Budget price.
-- No saving in missions - major oversight. It needs to auto save every turn and save on quit. I always play Ironman so doubly important.
-- Not so keen on the magical, weird, demonic, satanic elements. Just a personal preference but more pure western stuff please.
-- Game is too easy on Medium Ironman. I'm about to start my Hard Ironman run so I may have to retract this line.
-- Small, squinty fonts are hard work on even a really big tv+couch.
Conclusion: Love the game, everyone should buy it and support it, and try harder to understand the actual mechanics instead of moaning without understanding. It doesn't have the depth or longevity of an XCOM but it's not priced like an XCOM either.

Wasteland 2 is basically Fallout / Fallout 2, but you control a team instead of one person (companions still exist, called recruits here).  It was made by Brian Fargo, the guy who listed his name as the creator for those games, along with a few other relevant names to make by my definition a great team of developers for this kind of project such as Liz Danforth and Chris Avellone, among others.  The combat plays like a cross between Fallout / Fallout 2 and X-Com:  Enemy Unknown, and the non-combat feels just like Fallout / Fallout 2, as well.  W2's story context is in the game itself scattered throughout books and dialogue, so there is no requirement to play the original Wasteland to appreciate this game.  The soundtrack is great with the exception of the GOD AWFUL ending theme song, the art direction is as expected for a post-apocalyptic game, and the game is quite long for modern single-player game standards.  That last point is generally a good thing in my opinion, but I think that W2 exceeds that sweet spot of game length to promote replayability to the point where many players would not be making an effort to play through a second time any time soon after finishing W2.
Some faults:
-This game is full of bugs and inconsistencies, to the point where one would think that this game is still in beta due to how it is such a central part of the gameplay experience.  These bugs and inconsistencies will never get fixed, so be aware that you are playing a game which feels as though it did not really undergo any quality control between the ending of the beta and when the live, "complete" game launched.
-In inconsistencies, there are many white-named items which indicate importance, but have no purpose whatsoever and are just mislabelled junk items.
-Another important thing to consider with said inconsistencies is that the description for all energy weapons is backwards.  Using the Meson Cannon as an example, it says that it has an armour threshold of 3, and that its threshold damage multipliers are 0.4x damage above 3 armour on the target, 0.9x at 3 armour, and 2.2x below 3 armour.  This indicates that energy weapons do more damage to lower-armour targets.  All energy weapons are listed in this format, and all of them are listed WRONG in this way; the skill description itself tells you correctly that energy weapons do less damage to unarmoured targets, but the weapons say the opposite.  You end up doing 2.2x damage with the Meson Cannon to targets with above 3 armour and 0.4x damage to targets below 3 armour, and so on for every energy weapon.
-Pistols, sub-machine guns, and shotguns are pretty worthless because of their range.  I believe that the highest range I saw was 21 metres with mods to extend the range as far as possible, whereas I had assault rifles often over 40 metres, and sniper rifles over 50 metres.  This makes a HUGE difference in combat efficacy.  Melee as a main combat discipline is also worthless for the same reason, but it works well enough if the enemies get close enough to you where you do not have to go to them to use melee.
-Portraits are reused HEAVILY, to the point where supposedly meaningful NPCs end up sharing the same portraits with nobodies from the wastes.  It seems really lazy imo to only make a small handful of portraits and recycle them; not using any at all would have been a better choice than reusing the same several.
-The proper endings, like with the endings for the Fallout games, is the phoned-in slideshow which cheapened the efforts put forth to complete the game.
All in all, this is a great game in spite of its problems, and I highly recommend it if you enjoyed the original Fallout games.  The devs like to tout that someone once called it "game of the year," but let us be honest here:  unless that year is 1996 or prior, it most likely will not be the best game of any given year that you play it.

Welcome to the glorious wastes of Arizona with nothing but old school RPG turn based combat and a plethora of cross roads to travel. This was a game I had been watching from the early beta days but decided against diving straight in and waiting for the "final" version of the game to come out. On that note before continuing, I use the term "final" very loosely.
The first half of the game is fantastic. Hands down one of the most enjoyable games I've played in a while. Refreshing real choices with actual consequences. Multiple choices and decisions to be made at every corner ranging from simple attire, to devastating lesser of two evil choices that affect the rest of the game and years to come following. Great character creation allowing role-players to enjoy a world the can fully immerse themselves in. This and so much more awaits you.
On the opposite side of the review this game is not without short comings and issues. The second half of the game is anything but complete. More than ever this is a game that you save often for and making 100+ individual save files. Major quest lines are riddled with bugs and plot holes the size of the grand canyon can be found more frequently than not. While I still enjoyed the vague idea of the second half of the game, it was a disappointment after how amazing the first half was. Another big issue was balancing. Take this bit of advice. Sniper rifles/ assault rifles/ shotguns and energy weapons are the only good guns in the game. The rest are terrible.
If you enjoy turn based RPGs and an apocalyptic theme this game is for you, while I may have listed some off putting downsides especially for the second half it is still worth playing. The first half of the game does such a great job and the curiosity you will have to see how things turn out will help you through the issues of the second half. I finished this game 100% including a run on the higher difficulty in 158 hours. Well worth the money. 8.5/10

Review after 9 hours. I do not plan to continue. And the review mostly focuses on the negatives.
Mafia III had a rough start with the 30FPS lock which can make alot of people get negative feelings toward a game and see bad because they're looking for it. But I really like to keep an open and positive mind on a game unless it forces me to stop, Mafia III did that.
The story and setting in this game can be a reason to play it, from what I've seen the story is quite good with interesting characters, but the story won't save a game because its a game and not a movie. The setting is of course what makes a Mafia game and its nice to see a 1960's world with all of its amazing music. Too bad that the game was advertised as having this amazing New Bordeaux city but for me, it kinda feel's boring and unmemorable.
That brings me nicely into the open wold gameplay... unless after 9 hours I havent unlocked the "real game", its terrible. You can not get a haircut, can't at least change clothes, you can't even customize cars or even store them, there are set few cars you can call after you've unlocked them by progressing through the story. All the open world does is let's you pick which order you want do complete your objectives. Mafia II literally had more "open world stuff" than Mafia III. Mafia II suffered from not being open world, Mafia III I don't think would suffer if it was linear. Mafia III could have been something interesting, it has such a potential for a GTA-like, open world game but set in 60's, but it feels very much like just another "generic open world game" with no soul. Gameplay and world feel stiff and with terrible physics and with repetetive open world tasks you need to do. I'd love to have a world I feel like I live in like Mafia II, not the generic open world game world with nothing to do in.
What else we got... gunplay is quite nice, driving is much more arcadey than mafia 2 and I'm personally not into that, I liked the realism of slower and heavier old cars. Stealth is fine... quite a nice addition where you can chose if you want to stab everyone or go guns blazing, both work and are pretty much equally as fun so when stealth goes wrong, shooting is still an option. And stealth would be great if not for the absoluteley awful AI that will not see you when you stand in front of them (trying to play into racism that black people are harder to spot in the dark or what?), or when you LITERALLY STAB SOMEONE IN FRONT OF THEM,
Aside from the 30fps lock, the graphics look fine... as long as its not daylight
The reflections in this game are garbage and day lightning makes me ill, shaders break sometimes. Really, games that are pre-alpha can look better than Mafia III and thats complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I paid for a AAA game and not early acess. In other situations its quite alright, the facial animations for an example are really nice.
Then theres other stuff, the glitches that you can find everywhere,
The extreme lack of polish this game is really pushies it over the line into hate territory for me. While playing you constantly run into a new bug every few minutes and it gets really distracting, like someone poking you once being alright but poking you once every minute would make you go crazy. I could have have rated it "ok", as buy for a lower price when it comes and play this game that doens't really feel like Mafia II but a kind of generic open world game. But all this lack of polish and abundance of glitches, bugs and all other annoyances push me to say. Don't get it.
Its my opinion, I'd play it if it was some sub at least 20euro game after all of the glitches are fixed. Right now I only wish I could refund...

Alan Wake would of been a marvelous addition to the stealth genre.  Combined with the fabulous landscapes of the mountainous Pacific Northwest and the arresting drama, moving quietly around the mountains and woods of an eerie remote town would seem to meld like needle and thread.  Remedy, listed as the developer and the publisher and of Max Payne fame but not much else, thought otherwise.
Alan Wake is brilliantly atmospheric.  A compelling yet subservient Stephen King  penned horror yarn narrated by our protagonist, enveloping the player into his plight.  A story told by progression and environmentally produced manuscript pages that fill in the backstory.   Alan Wake the game is a missed opportunity.  A famous person once said "He who bemoans the lack of opportunity, forgets that small doors many times open up into large rooms.".  Alan Wake is a well realized world of small rooms that never open up into the game-play that this game so richly deserves.
As the manuscript plays out before our very eyes, a character utters the words "Like a really bad movie. Who wrote this crap anyway".  The combat in Alan Wake is misplaced, the combat is criminally designed.  Repetitively placed bullet sponge Taken as they're called, evil, are dispatched by our clunky controlled writer turned Rambo, Alan Wake.  Armed and weaponized with only enough ammo to make the game petulantly annoying we blast our way shining light upon the dark and dodging evil as if evil were rapid fans eager to strip us from our dignity.
This is Alan Wake, the game, the whole game and it never deviates.  Occasionally a few good looking environmental set pieces challenge, but these like the game as a whole can be annoying and not always well executed, presuming that the player knows what is about to happen and should play out the script, except the player's rehearsal is failure, initially not privy to any script and winds up not properly anticipating and failing scenario after scenario such as staying attached to an object for example or not jumping until a grate is dynamically set to 45 degrees ensuring that a jump can be executed in a run sequence.
Besides manuscript pages the game has a number of collectibles.  Many can only be obtained through some deviation of your intended path, some exploration required if you will.  Though found, they are not recorded until you reach the next checkpoint.  The game makes the egregious error of punishing such exploration by removing any collectibles you've discovered upon your failure.  The game will restart at the last checkpoint as if nothing has happened.  Exploration and the collection of an object may have no quantitative effect of reaching the next checkpoint.  Don't demand exploration of already explored areas.  Design that wastes time, removes immersion, ultimately stilts the task at hand and actively discourages the very exploring the game was designed for.
Alan Wake, for only it's story, was saved from early termination and towards the end I thought I was not going to finish the game.  Bored, desensitized from over used enemy and combat mechanics I just about made it over the finish line.  The developers expose a console command to anyone who wants to "customize" the game.  -developermenu will allow you unlimited ammo, flares and grenades.  Enough essentially to make the game somewhat less but not completely annoying.

Natural Selection 2 is a Multiplayer team-based First Person Shooter & mixed Strategy game, with an awesome twist. One team are Human Marines "Frontiersmen" and the other are Alien Lifeforms "Kharaa", each team featuring a completely asymmetrical way of playing against the other, making the gameplay very diverse and versatile, yet very balanced. The marines, mainly relying on ranged weapons technology like rifles, shotguns etc VS the aliens that will ambush lonely unsuspecting marines by jumping down from dark corners in the ceilings in dark hallways or flying past scared marines chewing on their legs or exposing them to lethal toxins like poisonous gas.
NS1 was a mod from 2002 developed until 2007 for the GoldSRC (Half-Life) engine which was very popular #1 HL
, and in the last few years, a few original key people formed the company Unknown Worlds Entertainment to work on NS2 to become real, a sequel on its own engine with more than 150,000 owners and thousands of daily players, AAA-quality, released Nov 2012, and still being supported and developed with many updates each month even one year later. The developers won't abandon this game like many other developers do. The game has an awesome community not only noticable in-game, some of which helped crowdfund the developement of the game before it was even Beta-released; or contributing huge amounts of cash to help funding further huge updates to the game like massive new maps, new features lifeforms and revolutionary changes etc etc etc.
The game is played in servers with player numbers ranging from 2 - ~32 players, however my sweet spot is around 16-20 players. (Note some n00b admins run some 32p servers on ancient server hardware causing bad experiences, beware)
Each team has one player as the commander giving giving the game an amazing RTS addition, whom anyone can choose to be.
Even after several hundred of hours you won't get bored or tired of the game. It only gets more and more fun the more immersed you get. The tension and fun of this game is 100% guaranteed Addictive! =)

On the audio front, the licensed soundtrack choices, especially at the end of each chapter, were amazing. The entire episodic format was a nice touch, both for said tunes and for how it played into reinforcing Alan's role as an author. Having boss fights in the game felt a bit peculiar, but most of them are simple enough to figure out with few to no obliterations while attempting them. I kind of hate farming equipment forever now, though.
Definitely pick this one up, especially if you're a fan of stuff like The Outer Limits, The Twilight Zone, or the more subtly menacing works in Edgar Allan Poe's bibliography.

Couple this with a wicked sense of humour, an unexhaustible supply of little men and green women to send to distant planets (or to be blown to kingdom come on main engine start) and a modding community that is second to none and you have one of the greatest games in existence.
This combines into an experience like no other, where you can be tearing your hair out but yet keep coming back for more. It has generated an entire sub culture online, Elon Musk is rumoured to play - hell, even NASA has had involvement with a mod that is now included in the base game! The sense of achievement to be gained from landing on the moon, flying a Shuttle or just surviving re-entry is the sweetest reward.
Just experience it, and you won't regret it.

A decent game with a lot of good ideas and a lot of not so good implementation. If you like XCOM and want to try something that's roughly similar, Hard West
be for you. I wish I could give it a neutral review.
- The setting is really interesting. Wild West + demons. Why not.
- Some really nice ideas, like the luck resource and abilities/bonuses granted by cards and card combinations.
- It's fun for a while. Gets old fast once you know how to combine cards and abuse the weak AI.
- The AI is not great. It will kill you when you make a mistake, but if you stay in cover and play carefully, it's pretty hopeless.
- There's no overwatch. It works surprisingly well with how the game is set up, but it might be a huge deal for some people.
- There's (basically) no RNG, even though the game shows % to hit. Missing just depletes target's luck resource, once you get hit you gain some luck back. Basically it's just another form of armor (that can also be used as a resource for abilities).
- The way the game is set up is weird. You play short "episodes" of 3-4 battles, then lose all progress even if you use the same characters.
Overall: good effort, alright game with a lot of issues, in my opinion only for people who like turn-based tactics and don't mind some huge changes from the typical rules.

What a gem of a game. It exudes charm, humor, and lightness in only the way Tim Schafer and crew know how to do it. On top of that the art is brilliant, the voice acting top notch, the script clever and hilarious, and so many fun little easter eggs all over the place. I spent a good portion of the game just talking to everyone and combining every kind of item just to hear the knee-jerk responses. Double Fine are some of the best comic writers in the entertainment biz, games or otherwise.
The only downsides are those typical of point and click games. Some objects really do blend in with the background too well, you'll do lots of backtracking, various puzzles need to be solved in very specific order, etc. I must admit I did have to use a guide later in the game as some of the puzzle solutions were just not obvious enough after lots of back and forth trying out many different things. I can't really fault the developers for this, as I think these sorts of games do need to have some tougher puzzles, not everything can be elementary. Certainly nowhere near as perplexing and complicated as some of Machinarium's puzzles.
I can't recommend it enough!!

Very fun first person shooter/real time strategy game crossover. The objective is to destroy all enemy bases.
It is Aliens vs. Marines, each side has unique controls, weapons, and strategies.
Each player has a first person view, and each team has 1 commander who has a top down view like a real time strategy game, directing the players on the field and giving them support and supplies when needed.
A person should first understand the game and all units and structures, learn basic strategy, and play the game for a week or so before attempting to play as the commander.
A mic silent game of Natural selection 2 is not a good thing. A player should always speak up if they want an upgrade from the commander, or see an opening for an attack. Do not stay silent and assume your commander or other players see what you see. The more information you share with your team, the better.
I have seen countless matches where a team has control of almost all of the map, but end up losing, because they think that they've already won and don't need to communicate anymore. Slowly, the enemy team just wins all the fights and takes back the entire map.
This game also has good mod support, with some nice alternative game types, including one similar to gungame from counterstrike, where you simply try to destroy the enemy base, and you get upgrades and get better lifeforms through spending points. You get those points by killing enemies.
This game has a learning curve, you can't just jump in and start winning. It will take a lot of practice before you become good.
If you were thinking about buying it, you should definitely go for it. If you stick to the game past the learning curve, you will have loads of fun.
Plus, the developers are still supporting it with free, very frequent updates, with new content such as new units and weapons, bug fixes and better optimization.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the dark and gritty Western, Turn Based Strategy game Hard West. Hard West was released by Developer CreativeForge Games and Publisher Gambitious Digital Entertainment.
(NOTE: This game was NOT reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher, it was a game I purchased for my own account)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Solid Western take on the Turn-Based Strategy style. More than just "XCOM" in the Wild West.
4/5 and worth the $20
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
Hard West is, at first glance, just another take on the Turn Based Strategy genre that has seen an uptick since the popularity of XCOM: Enemy Unknown. Don't sell this game short though, it is it's own beast for sure. This is a western with a twist! It's dark. I mean, demon-dark. There is GREAT story going on here. The gameplay is superb. It's Turn-Based Strategy, but there are some great mechanics in play as well. One being the "Card" system. Each charterer can carry cards (Essentially, you'd like to build a poker hand) that add to your perks. The perks can boost attributes during the Combat scenes. The visuals are grand and the sounds are great as well. This score is fantastic. I am really excited to play this one and very happy about it. In between battles you explore the area and mine for gold, learn more about the town and story, have your choices make for consequences, etc. There is a lot to do here and it seems as if there may be multiple stories/endings to pursue as well. Fans of Turn Based Strategies and Westerns are going to simply LOVE it. A western gem for the genre. 4/5 and loving it. Spend your $20 without regrets.
Happy Gaming!

My relationship with this game is like a Hollywood RoCo: At first I hated it, then later realized that I actually love it and want to have its baby.
Just to be clear: This is a great game.
But (there it is, you knew it was coming) it has a few shortcomings.
At the tactical level, the supernatural aspect of the game feels like a coat of paint, not a core element. The weird west could be way weirder, especially when I desire demon exorcism and witchcraft along with my shotgun and dynamite.
The fact that the enemy have reaction fire and you don't seems a bit unfair; this is obviously a rules bandage applied to discourage players from certain tactics the designers don't like or felt would diminish the experience.
It is narrated (in English anyway) by the most boring-sounding voice in the world; make sure you have a huge cuppa coffe to sip before each mission, or you might fall asleep and miss the whole thing.
It's pretty linear, so replayability is based on cranking up the difficulty, rinse and repeat.
My biggest criticism, though, is that there's simply not enough of it. Devs, get to work on some expansions!
Ideally, I'd love to see an instant-action skirmish mode: Let the player assemble a squad of characters s/he's unlocked, then have the game assign a map (there are plenty to choose from) and an appropriate cadre of enemies for some fun one-off bloodshed.
Here's the report card:
Graphics: A
Sound: B
Strategy: C
Tactics: B
Fun factor: A
Bang-for-the-buck: A

Great game that takes a little while to get going. The amount of customization available combined with some early missions that don't hold your hand can make for a frustrating first dozen or so hours, especially when you inevitably have some bad luck with misses and weapon jams.
You can either power through the learning curve through guess-and-check, trying and failing, and figuring out ways to survive in the wastes with a party that likely has some glaring flaws; or you can read up in advance and meticulously plan out a balanced party that will be able to meet anything that stands in its way. I did the latter, and took great joy in always having the right skills available for whatever job was at hand, being able to afford the best weapons, and becoming quite powerful in combat.
But I imagine that sounds painfully boring to some, so I'd be remiss not to say that the opposite experience would have been great too: scrounging for spare ammo, surviving combat by the skin of your teeth, likely losing some of your initial characters permanently, and having to come up with creative and often non-ideal solutions to problems that your party lacks the skills to solve.
The point is that Wasteland 2 is robust enough to support whatever kind of experience you want to have. I never found myself growing tired of combat, the game's story is perfectly serviceable (though the smaller stories are more effective and cohesive than the larger one), and there's well over 50 hours of material to keep you interested. If you don't like turn-based strategy or post-apocalyptic settings, that's probably a deal-breaker; but otherwise, I'd wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone.

In Hotline Miami you play in a top-down perspective, with the camera nearly always focused on the player. The goal is to kill all enemies on a "stage" before you can either advance through the level or get to the next stage.
This isn't as easy as it sounds, as your character can't take much more than a sneeze in your general direction. The enemies are pretty difficult, though they die in one or two hits. The game also presents several questions to players that make them rethink their actions and the mystery surrounding the story makes it all the more tantalsing to beat chapter after chapter.
The game is extremely creative, and everything feels insanely polished, and the game looks good, for a top-down 8-bit shooter.
All in all, pretty good game. I reccoment it highly.

A lot of the negative reviews come from the same issue: There is no gameplay. And they're right, this is a textbook Walking Simulator. I think Virginia was a beautifully well told story but that's all it is. No puzzles, no dialogue options, no dialogue at all.
I personally love this genre. People have been asking why isn't this just a movie, if the player has zero input other than movement? But the appeal of these Walking Sims are that YOU are the main character. It's much easier to empathize and get invested in her story, because it's happening to YOU. Not some character on screen. And the lack of dialogue lets you implant your own conversations and reactions and thoughts from your character. That really get you inside her head.
The downside of the presentation, is that a few story elements were lost on me. Things I didn't realize or understand until reading up on it, but that's obviously going to vary per person. There's a lot of Lynch inspired surrealism here that's meant to be left to the player.
Final Thoughts: This was a great, beautiful little story. One that I'm very glad I bought. But it's 100% dependent on story. The fact that they're even able to tell such a understandable story without a single line of dialouge is hugely impressive

I've had this game in my library for quite a while, not having thought too much about it and only dabbling in trying it out... until recently.
This game is unusual... and phenomenal. It's really easy to overlook this title with its non-descript visuals, obtuse lack of instructions and seeming resemblance to any other doujin shooter. But make no mistake this is an exceptionally original title, particularly for the genre.
It borrows many concepts from a variety of shooters but what makes in unique is its system which treats lives and bombs as one and the same. To be clear, when you bomb you lose a life. Your bombs are your lives. The game translates as "human bomb" which is apt as this is the core mechanic.
The way it all works is ingenious. You would think that it's a flawed system but actually it's very difficult to master and extremely well balaned. For the most part you want to save your lives (bombs) until you get into a sub-boss or boss which  then requires careful adminisration of doing a suicide bomb. You can't just bomb any time. You have to wait until the meter fills up (which only happens after a while and often many successfull bullet dodges). Then, when you have a bomb armed it is ofen equally diffiuclt to navigate through the bullet maze in order to deploy it. How do you deploy it? By INTENTIONALLY RAMMING YOUR SHIP INTO THE ENEMY!
The fact that this works at all means it can only be the work of a madman and a genious.
After each level you buy more lives/bombs with the gems you earned (earnings which are maximzed  by cancelling bullets in the explosions of shot-down enemies). You can spend your earnings on buying different types of ships, which all have different strengths and weaknesses, as well as special attacks via each ships mana meter. There's a lot of creativity involved in choosing the types of ships you want to carry into the next level to better deal with the bullet patterns and enemies you'll face.
By the second level you could easily have 30 lives/bombs and yet lose them all by the 2nd level's boss. Again, it takes planning and skill to deploy the bombs, else you just lose a life (getting hit by a bullet doesn't deploy the bomb).
I could go on about how original it all feels in spite of its unassuming appearance.
Do yourself a favor and read a guide on how to play the game and/or watch some youtube superplays/1cc's and watch the game open up and surprise you no matter how many shooters you've played before.

The entire episodic format was a nice touch, both for said tunes and for how it played into reinforcing Alan's role as an author. Having boss fights in the game felt a bit peculiar, but most of them are simple enough to figure out with few to no obliterations while attempting them. This game showed so much promise. The first act was mostly a lot of fun, I really enjoyed the story, and I was excited to see what was going to happen next. The game felt really polished and relatively well-designed, with only some minor annoyances.
But the second act completely negated all the good from the first. It felt poorly designed, poorly executed, and like they just rushed it to market rather than properly designing the puzzles or worrying about the story.
Rather than explaining any of the things I was excited to find out, the second half just introduced major plot holes that were then either entirely ignored or quite poorly explained. And, most damning for a game, the gameplay and puzzles were increasingly frustrating, not fun, and arbitrarily difficult to figure out. Random and entirely unconnected things needed to be done in a certain order; there were things I needed to do that the character would in no way have knowledge about; and the puzzles were so poorly explained that I sometimes couldn't even figure out what the problem was that I was trying to solve (meaning that I had no hope of solving it).
The only way I could finish act 2 was by following a detailed walkthrough -- something I usually try to avoid -- and even with the walkthrough to guide me, one of the final puzzles was so poorly designed that it took me over an hour just to figure out how the puzzle even worked. Guessing correctly at the solution didn't ease my frustration since it's a puzzle that needs to be solved in different ways several times.
I would generally recommend the first half, but I would definitively NOT recommend the second half. Stay away! It was not worth the frustration. This game has so much promise -- I really wanted to like it! -- but was too poorly designed and executed to me to recommend it.

Natural Selection 2 is not your average Call of Duty or Battlefield game, and that's a good thing -- because different is good. You can play as either the humans or the aliens, and the aliens have some very unique gameplay, including flying and crawling on walls/ceilings. The team leader sees the game from an RTS-perspective, while everyone else plays the game from a first-person shooter perspective. You cannot win the day by charging off by yourself with guns blazing; teamwork and communication are essential.
You develop your base of operations, and then you and your teammates can have access to more powerful equipment or alien species. Aliens can get large, mammoth-like beasts, while humans can get access to weaponized mechs. Team strategies will win the day in the end, so communicate well and follow the lead of others until you know what you're doing.
As a new player, I had no problems getting into the game and feeling welcomed. I was never criticized or judged, though I can't guarantee your experience.

Hitogata Happa is a game that is completely different from the other Gundemonium games, opting for the traditional top down view and focusing itself as a prequel. But is this a suicidal concept?
Hitogata Happa, for whatever reason, plays very differently from the other Gundemonium titles. Using the more widely used top down view, Hitogata Happa's main gimmick is in its name. Roughly translating to "humanoid explosion," Hitogata Happa features the ability to crash your playable character into an enemy to create a powerful explosion that is almost necessary for completing the game. To offset this questionable sacrifice, your playable characters are an army of non-sentient dolls created by your BFF and partner in revolution, Kreutzer. Your dolls are 100% expendable, and you get more after finishing each campaign mission, so you can stockpile. In addition to having lots of them, you also have a variety of dolls to choose from, with all of them doing different things. You'll, of course, need all of this because this game is hard. Like, really hard. Harder then the other Gundemoniums, at the least. Bosses have time limits, enemies are quick to the draw and cover the screen with bullets very fast, even on normal difficulty, and things go downhill really quick unless you're good at dodging or erasing bullets (You can do that!).
Probably the most "updated" graphics of any Gundemonium game besides Recollection, Hitogata Happa looks alright, but definitely loses a bit due to the same color palette being used on every enemy (This is mostly done as the enemy faction, the Genoremasody Reich, are suppose to look similar and very factorialized, justifying the color palette). The game also has a bit of color loss, mostly due to the game's darker approach in story. It does make up for these lackluster colors with its intriquite weavings and patterns that you see all over the game, from the marking on the AoE of your suicide bomb attack, to the text on the mission complete screen.
Nothing particularly bad. Good ol' Potato friendly gaming.
As per the Hitogata Happa way, the Soundtrack is a bit more different, going for a more elegant approach with tons of organ, piano, and fiddle/violin abuse. It's good, but not what you're used to if you've listened to the other two soundtracks. Still, it's kickass in it's own way, especially the true-final-boss track. Really good stuff from Woofles, who takes DM Ashura's place in the soundtrack department this time.

You are pretty much a glass cannon no matter your build and if you stand in the open you loose.  Careful movement and placement are a huge part of the outcomes of the battles.  j
On the mechanics side, the luck system is a nice resource management system, the cards add a lot to combat and making hards for buffs is a nice bonus to make it more complex.  They could add the whole deck to make it better, once you get so far it does get repetetive.
The downsides are there as well.  Inbetween fights is not the best, the stories were good but it got bland. Hotline Miami is a grotesque and surreal top down shooter that has become a staple of indie gaming. The protagonist of the game is a nameless man in a letterman jacket who is called to random Russian mob houses in Miami, Florida to go on spree killings. The various animals masks you can unlock and use on different levels grant you different abilities such as the Tony mask which makes your punches lethal, or the Rasmus masks which highlights secrets to be found on levels.
Hotline Miami can be appreciated for both its artistic and pragmatic merits. The gameplay is extremely addicting and you could spend many hours trying to get an A+ on all of the levels. The game’s soundtrack is also stellar. The hair on the back of your neck will stand up as you plow through Russian mob thugs whilst listening to the electronic masterpieces of such artists as Scattle, Perturbator, and M.O.O.N.
Overall, Hotline Miami is one of of the greatest indie games to ever be created, and it is the kind of game everyone should play. This is a game that will not disappoint. I’d recommend this game to anyone who hasn't already played it.

First up, I thoroughly recommend this game.  It's an old school isometric RPG, and it's excellent.
It has it's flaws, but overall they don't undermine the experience, the worst I could say about this game is that there are some balance issues, and there are elements of the game that feel rough and unfinished.
I think it suffers from kickstarter-itis .. where a developer seeks a budget on the KS platform, achieves or exceeds it, then works to that budget.  Back in the day, a company would outlay their own capital and not make money until the product was released, now kickstarter covers development and profit goes into someone's bank account.
The problem with this (understandable) model is that there's not a lot of room for stretch and polish.  You either wildly exceed the kickstarter or you don't - and if you do, let's face it, there's probably a bit more of a 'loose' approach with project management and a higher budget for chicken chow mein.
I think there are functional elements of the game that should have been deeper, and there are story-telling elements that fell onto the 'nice to have but not essential' list and got cut.
Incidentally, I haven't finished the game yet, I'm about 75% through (I think).
Here's my view on the Good/Bad
Good:
- graphics and theme are nice
- world map and random encounters makes you feel 'there'
- radio chatter from different factions is immersive
- background lore (the rangers, their character, their personalities) .. all good
- combat: for the most part is satisfying and tactical
- story: although contrived in places, overall the storytelling pulls you in and holds your interest
- conversations and character writing is good for the most part (but also a missed opportunity)
Bad:
- weapon balance has some very bad decisions, energy weapons in particular range from OP in some situations to useless in others.  I say balance, but I don't really care too much about balance, what bothers me is some of the weapons are balanced is .. well, not logical and doesn't fit into a consistent and realistic universe
- Skills & Attributes: for me a real missed opportunity, they disconnect.  Example, Charisma doesnt effect conversations.  Seriously.  There's no randomness or discreet skill impact on conversations, just gatekeeper skills hardarse/intimidation, smartarse/logic, kissarse/charm .. and those skills are just numbers.  Likewise the balance of stats and skills is not really intuitive and clever in it's design, I guess in a way the game suffers from being compared to Fallout 2 in that regard.
- Contrived/Illogical writing:  there are some key points where the writing is a bit .. contrived.  No matter what you do, it's pre-ordained that the outcome will lead you from A->B->C, doesnt matter if you're evil or good.  If I were to analogise with pen&paper roleplaying, it's basically having a GM who can't 'think on their feet' .. the underarching story should be invisible, it should feel like you have total freedom and YOU (the player) are calling the shots .. instead, there are a few key points in the story writing where you feel more than a bit led by the nose (worse, there are some points where you only have a couple of options and those options don't allow for wide variations in character, one specific example you have 3 options to respond to a challenge from your CO, and each of them forces you to lie.
Overall, I give the game a solid 8.5 / 10 golden jabberoos.

At the current state of this game, I would not recommend it.
I loved Mafia 2, and happily (and blindly) bought Mafia 3... What a mistake!
First of all, scenario-wise, I hoped we would be able to go save our dumb but dear cousin... Mmmmh nope. Instead of that, we get a politically-oriented game with no link to Mafia 2. If I want politics, I watch the news. When I play a game, I want to play a game and have fun, not get my brain washed or whatever!
Second, my God the game feels sluggish and clumsy! This is unbelievable for a late 2016 game. The character is heavy to move (at least it feels like it), the aim cursor moves in a weird slow way... And I'm not even talking about the ennemies who walk in a non-natural and rigid way... The game feels horrible. The driving is weird too, plus they didn't even bother adding semi-realistic car damage or anything: each time you hit a car (even at high speed), worst case scenario: the hit car jumps a bit and falls on its wheels. In any case, the driver always goes on like nothing happened. What the hell is that?! It this year 2005 or what? And even then, GTA was already supporting targetted car damage for years. And Carmageddon too for that matter. And probably plenty other games.
Adding stealth mechanics is a good idea. But it would have been better to do it right.
First, you can't one-hit melee from behind a cover unless you use a specific key to "really" be behind a cover. Well. Anyway. Also, whenever you take-down a cop, automatically all cops get angry and know where you are. They shouldn't! It renders a stealth take-down useless! Plus, these cops don't drop their weapons... Holy cow! Weird bug that prevents you from grabbing ammo or guns.
The game won't remember that you parked a car. Actually this is the same bug you can encounter in Far Cry 4: when you move only 50 meters away from something, it "unloads" (disappears and does not reappear if you come back, even without delay). In Mafia 3 it's the cars. And it's boring. Because you have to break into a new car each time, which means people will call the police, etc. Boring.
It would have been great to have some freedom of action. Like exploring some neighbourhoods and kill enemy gang members (like in Saints Row), and expand your territory this way (of course with some high profile enemies restricted to scenario-only missions). But nope. Sure you can go into a shop and punch the owner and take (with no animation or specific UI notification whatsoever) the money in the cash register. But that's it. You can do nothing more.
Last but not least. Bugs. There are plenty. It's boring. Please fix the bugs!
And what's this "edge calibration" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ft? Because of your sheet-y system, the game doesn't take the whole screen because your rectangle wasn't properly centered and there was no way to slide it, only expand/shrink it... Well done!
The 60's theme is nicely done. However what on Earth is this futuristic GUI that you dared put on top of it?! It breaks the immersion!
Well, now you know: do not buy this game. At least not in its current state.

text: Honestly, having anticipated this game for about a year, my expectations were pretty high.  This game has a lot going for it, and for the most part it's beautiful.  That said, there are some issues.  While I like the style of the gameplay, it's a bit buggy (understandable seeing as it's a pretty new game).  but there were also some really terrible design choices made durring development.  For example, there's no meaningful implementation of a manual transmission.  The shift lever operated with the mouse is pretty neat, but overall it doesn't do a whole lot and doesn't add much challenge to driving.  (even if you select forward with the shift lever, you can use reverse by pressing the brake (S or LT)).  In addition, I was quite disappointed by the crane controls.  They are very abstract and cumbersome, just a feeble attempt to simplify what could have been very good, realistic controls.  As of current time, I no longer have a computer that can handle the game's high system requirements, so some of these items may have been improved upon, but until I see myself that the game has been fixed, I cannot recommend this game.  It's a really clever game, and I give the Devs at Oovee 10/10 for style, but minus several million for good thinking.  When I get a new computer I'll be playing it some more, and when I do I'll update this review if anything changes.

OK, So i am editing this after a long hiatus from the game. I have played this game more than most other people.
I tried to introduce some new players to the game recently, and i don't believe either were sold on the game, with the main complaints being : "its hard to aim the guns cause the targets move so fast and are so small." and "its hard to understand the strategy in the game, cause its so complicated."
One experience which really led me to the conclusion that the strategy is hard to grasp, is the frequency with which i was the only one on my team who realised we had just lost, or won a game.
My opinion is that they released this game too early, at a time where to get decent FPS during combat a PC of ridiculous spec was required, most people had a bad time playing the game at this point.
These days, it is well optimised and running on machines that didn't exist when it was released, it is an incredibly smooth play, i get a buttery smooth 144fps.
Because this game was released in an unfinished state, MAJOR changes were made to the game after its release, which completely destroyed any chance the game had. The addition of gorge tunnels was particularly irritating to me personally (as it made the teams less diverse).
There were other major changes, i have to admit i wasn't a fan of this chopping and changing, because i have put so much time and energy into maximising the efficiency of my strategy, only to have to start over from scratch on the next update.
This, was what eventually led me to leave the game, near the introduction of gorge tunnels.
After a couple of years break from the game, i have come back. The game is well optimised now, the combat is snappy and enjoyable, the strategy hasn't been messed with. I could play this game, if there were enough other people playing it!
This is a VERY GOOD GAME, I don't think there is a skill ceiling for the strategy and combat, if there is, i haven't reached it !
This game trains your aim, hearing, and combat sense. After playing in this game, go and play counterstrike and see how much easier the aiming seems.
If you like games where you have to have incredible aim, and a deep understanding of strategy, this game is for you!
Oh, and also get a microphone, or don't buy the game :)

Being one the people who got this game gifted after the second act came out, I think I can give it a look that isn't sullied by backer's disctontent. So let's go and try to do it.
The game starts off great - you got 2 pretty different characters in rather different settings going on about their rather unusual daily lives. The world is bizzare, characters are colorful and voice acting is great, music score while nothing spectacular does compliment the tone of adventure very well, so it really drags you in for the first 1 or 2 hours. At that stage puzzles are almost trivial and you spend more time listening to dialog and exploring the world, rather than getting frustrated filling out charts and solving equasions, it feels like you playing a lighthearted interactive movie more than playing a game.
After about 4 or so hours in, with a bit of twist at the end, 1st act of the game ends and unfortunately what follows it up is one big mess. Act 2 is pretty much a dissapointment in a variety of ways - you meet next to none new characters, 95% of the locations you will visit are rehashes of the old ones, the plot unravels itself but leaves holes and doesn't really give a satisfying ending to the story. One important thing to notice about second act is the difficulty of puzzles - it racks up in a big way, so much, you would be excused to think devs have tried making second act feel longer by making you spend majority of the time scratching your head. Main strengths of the game so far: characters, dialog, bizzare setting, fade out at this stage in favour of trying to figure out what's the trick behind another wiring puzzle. It really kills the mood of the whole story and leaves a sour taste in a mouth.
At the end I feel troubled recommending this game, for even though I still managed to squeeze some fun out of it, I also didn't have to spend any money, which made me far less judgmental. Since it doesn't really doesn't have interesting satisfying puzzles, or at least a decent enough ending to the story, I urge you to purchase this product at your own discretion, for it can really get your hopes up only to crash them down and leave you feeling dissapointed.

I wanted to like this game, I really did. It had so much going for it; a big budget, a beautiful art style, and fantastic voice acting, but ultimately all of that was squandered on the creation of a mediocre game.
Act one was great in my opinion; the puzzles weren't too hard, the plot was compelling, and it showed a truly masterful control of the creation of suspense and intrigue. All of that was thrown out of the window on the second act though, which smacked of rushed laziness on the developer's part. There were no new environments, huge plot holes were introduced, and the old intrigue was shuffled out and shot in a dark alley.
I also had a lot of technical trouble with this game, with random crashes and super long load times. I don't know if it's my PC, or poor optimisation on the game's part, but every time the screen changed (the screen changes a LOT!) it would take 15 seconds to load. With it taking the character one second to cross a room, then fifteen seconds to load the next room, one second to cross it, fifteen to load the next one etc, I would estimate that 40-50% of my total gametime was spent staring at a black screen, and by the end of it I just didn't care anymore.
TL;DR: The second act only served to ruin the best parts from the first. Not a game I would recommend to friends unless it's on a deep sale and bundled with the very necessary walkthrough.

You'll either hate it or love it - as such, it's a game about duality and how seemingly unrelated paths through crazy circumstances lead to one point.
While I was not a backer for the original Kickstarter campaign (I didn't start backing games on that site until last year), I did follow their journey through the DoubleFine Adventure via epsidoes released every so often on YouTube, and let me tell you - it's a whole other experience watching a game being made, and THEN playing it. In short: it was an intimate experience, and I have much better understanding as a gamer about how the other side of the coin operates.
I played Broken Age all the way through in one sitting - due to the anticipation from fans, I felt it was most appropriate to play it that way since serveral people complained about the "broken" experience where they whizzed through Act 1, then waited, waited, waited, got impatient, then brute-forced Act 2. If your experience was like that, I'm sorry you feel hatred towards this game, but your particular experience casued your particular reaction. The game, while it may feel unevenly paced, is still an enjoyable game in what many modern gamers consider to be "A dying genre". Adventure games are here to stay, as long as people play them, classics, remakes, or modern ones, it makes no difference.
The art direction is great, the music is excellent, the animation (while not Disney calibur), fits the artwork appropriately and tolerable. The mechanics are as-expected for a Point-and-Click adventure, along with controller support (if that's your thing). The story is interesting enough to keep you moving ahead, even if some puzzles are frustrating until you look up hints or draw a diagram on a post-it or two (like I did for that Hexpals wiring puzzle) - it only makes you more satisfied once you finish. Depending on your first playthrough, you may or may not want to do it again to snag all of the achievements (for you Perfectionists/Completionists/Achievement Hunters out there).
Overall, if you love the magic of Double Fine games, if you love Adventure games, if you like games that try to do something different and pray somebody will appreciate it, play this game. Whether you come to love it or hate it, at least acknowledge the money, the hard work, and most of all, the love that Tim Schafer and friends put into the game.
It's worth the experience.

Hard West is a western themed story based tactical RPG, which combat reminiscent of XCOM: Enemy Unknown (2012). Scroll down for my impressions on the game, or you can watch the video if  you prefer:
The tactical layer of Hard West has a unique setup phase which involves sneaking around and sometimes subduing foes to prevent them from raising alarm for a few turns. I thought it was a fun and thematic addition to the gameplay.
Combat in Hard West feels similar to XCOM: Enemy Unknown because of the cover system, but it works a bit differently. Cover both reduces the accuracy of incoming shots, and decreases damage taken. Hard West also has a unique character attribute called Luck which reduces a character's chance to get hit, but each time an enemy misses them, they lose some Luck. Each time they are hit, their Luck replenishes. These two things combined result in a game where units in full cover are incredibly time-consuming to kill. Flanking is too dominant a strategy, which leads to invariant gameplay that quickly gets old.
Hard West's character system has a cool poker theme to it. Each character has card slots, and each card has a passive bonus, plus a unique passive or active ability. Creating poker hands in these card slots gives the character a unique special bonus. For example, four of a kind grants a bonus to aim. I like the system, but didn't find much use for the active abilities.
The game also has an overworld map which allows you to travel between areas. Each location gives a small dialogue popup with a few options. Sometimes these are basic things like trading at a store, or asking for information, but on occasion you get to make choices with meaningful gameplay consequences.
The narrative of Hard West is told through cutscenes, text, and a voiced narrator. The main story line is about exacting brutal revenge, which is perfect fit for a western setting. I think the plot is structured well, but the characters are weak. There's not much that demonstrates each character's personality. That being said, Hard West absolutely nails the setting. The themed game mechanics, the sounds, and the visuals all  come together to make the game feel like something special. The religious horror aspects are interesting too, although the actual demons were introduced a little abruptly.
Overall, Hard West is a very polished game that has some unique ideas and a stellar atmosphere, but I found the combat lacking in the variation and depth that I had hoped for.

Definitely a game worth experiencing. Nuclear Throne lets you learn, test and adapt to interesting environments that are littered with a variety of weapons, all on top of plenty of abilities/characters that create different playstyles to experiment with that help keep things fresh. For a while at least.
From my experience, my favorite rogue-likes are the ones where the game promotes leveling-up in skill and mechanical knowledge gradually between runs. You’ll be progressively learning what’s good and also what works well for you and Nuclear Throne does a good job of satisfying that idea.
This game is a full rogue-like, meaning that dying and loosing whatever awesomeness you had going can be frustrating. A series of bad runs/start-offs can also lead to spending quite a while just trying to get out of the first/second zone again. Furthermore, getting overwhelmed in new, far-off area and dying because of a lack of knowledge does steadily become defeating as reaching new areas gets longer. The fact it takes so long just to get one attempt at learning a new area after trying to get the previous levels more consistently beaten means that new information, the blood of rogue-likes, becomes scarcer. This is usually what turns me away from rougher rogue-like after a bit. You can only die so many times on level 1, while you want to be learning level 4, before you just have to cut your losses.
I’ve got somewhat of an addictive completionist’s mindset. In fact, collecting everything and looking up guides to save time has often gotten in the way of enjoying games. Having to set Nuclear Throne, and games like it, down in frustration and feeling like run after run with no progress was a waste of my time is a disappointing way to end the majority of my time with such a solid game.
From what I’ve seen/googled, Nuclear Throne has a whole host of secrets, challenges and unlockable ready to keep devoted players appetized. There are plenty of resources that have tips and other help to either get you started or help you advance if you think you need a boost.
Whether or not you have the drive to try and break wherever your personal-best-barrier develops and begin to dig deep into this game will vary player to player. Still, the game is engaging and worth checking out. Remember that knowing when you’ve had your fun can help save your relationship with this game.
