While I loved games like Grim Fandango and Monkey Island,  I have to say this game combines great story telling, heartwarming animation, user-experience and puzzle design in way that simply surpasses the former greats.
I seem to have a different opinion than many, and that is likely due to the fact that I played Act 1&2 together.  Waiting several months and then playing in mostly the same settings I suppose could be disappointing, but if played together actually makes the game feel seamless and natural, and in fact the story is as well thought-out as it is whimsical.
I think the same is true with puzzle difficulty: the puzzles progressively get harder over the course of Act 1&2, which makes sense.  Yes, there are times when I got stuck, but that just made figuring them out satisfying. I think one or two puzzles required a pencil and paper (or memorization) in Act 2, which crossed the line for some people.  I would say: 1. the puzzles make sense (enough for an adventure game), and 2. the game is liberal with clues, and 3. no puzzles "require" help online.
Kudos to the developers and all involved.  I think there are many stories left to be told in this universe, and I hope we get to see them someday.

Hard West is a very cool low budget game. The gameplay is fun and addictive, the story is really stylish and original in its own way. The soundtrack is fantastic, however there is not that many tracks, which can make it feel repetitive at times.
You will not find any spaghetti western stuff in this game, so the overall feel is somewhere between the Call of Juarez series and the good ol' Blood by Monolith. This gives the game a very mature and violently depressive theme, which is unfortunately rarely seen in modern games.
A lot of people in the reviews section are salty at the lack of saves, however this is actually one of the best decisions taken by the developer, as your every decision on both global and battle maps really means something and you actually feel like taking the risks.
Some of the game flaws include the lack of balance (some card combinations are completely broken and getting them earlier in the campaign allows you to completely faceroll your way through, such as shadow regeneration+equalizer), having basically only 1 type of enemy (if you do not consider generic dude with shotgun, demon dude with shotgun, Mexican dude with shotgun and Indian dude with shotgun as different enemy types), the overall low budget feeling such as reusing the same 3D models and sounds for different people and weapons. However, it is kind of amazing how 2D portrait of a guy and his generic description provided in text or by the narrator is enough to make each one you meet totally unique and badass, while AAA games keep failing to do that even with full voice-over (Sup Bethesda!).
Overall, if you enjoy playing turn based games, reading a lot of text and games having their own charm, Hard West is going to become one of the biggest surprises of 2015.

This game is XCOM meets Fallout. It has the dark humour and post-apocalyptic setting of the Fallout series, with the punishing, perma-death combat of the XCOM series.
The graphics aren't amazing, but they're adequate for the game style. The music is atmospheric, the writing is fun, and the voice acting is hit-or-miss.
The gameplay is great for people who like this sort of turn-based squad combat. All the usual elements are here: objects in the environment provide cover, hits are percent-based, and actions cost AP to execute, which replenishes each turn.
My only real complaint is the navigation on the overworld map, which seems like a cop-out from making an interesting overworld. Whenever you aren't in an encounter area (random encounter, dungeon, town), your party is represented as a marker on a huge map of the American Southwest, which will slowly move toward your destination in the way Indiana Jones travels-- a line drawn on the map.
It's fun to create characters, and the combat is challenging but rewarding.
Well worth the purchase price.

Take the other negative rewievs in here with a grain of salt. Most of them got tripped up by disregarding the above paragraph. Some either haven't played the original one on their phones, or are unfamiliar with these kind of games. A small number got scorned by discovering that the microtransactions are bound to a vault / save, which means that any penny spent on a file that got a Game Over is GONE. Which reminds me, the "RNGeesus" in this game is seriously bipolar. To roguelike levels, even. Like I mentioned above, a Lv.1 pencilnecked dude in dirty clothes and a flimsy revolver steamrolled through lots of Yao Guais (mutant ghoulish BEARS) and even a freaking Deathclaw (carnivorous, bipedal Jackson lizards with claws forcefully evolved to the point they can tear through titanium plates EASILY. Obviously, an endgame-level creature) with just enough Health to even go through two Raider parties (bandits with Mad Max-like gears and rabid attitude) back home. While a Lv.6 brutish dweller, with naturally high Strength and Endurance, with a sturdy Combat Armor, a gatling gun, and even a companion dog, got clocked by the first Mole Rat he found five minutes into the wastelands. Soooo... Yeah. Expect the game to treat you like a tabletop GM easing your mind into some fortune just to humiliate your proteges in the most laughable fashion possible at times.

Wasteland 2 is a party based RPG set in a post nuclear war USA. The player controls a squad of Desert Rangers, whose mission is to protect civilians and maintain law and order, but now an army of robots want to wipe out Humanity, and its up to the Rangers to stop them. I never played the original Wasteland, but I'm a massive fan of RPGs, and I certainly found alot to enjoy in this game.
Combat is turn based on a square grid, with each action such as moving, firing, reloading and healing costing ability points, similar to Xcom or Shadowrun. Its very tactical, and you also have to pay attention to factors like cover, line of sight, weapon range and friendly fire. The maximum party size is seven, four of which are created by the player, and the others have to be recruited as you progress through quests.
There is a wide variety of abilities to put points into when levelling up. You can use several different types of guns and melee weapons, but also non-combat skills including lockpicking, safecracking, computer hacking, trap disarming, machinery repair and more. These skills are very useful because many quests can be completed in multiple ways, by finding alternate routes to enter a building or unlocking extra dialogue options.
The story is really good and there are lots of interesting characters and groups. From drug gangs to slavers and religious fanatics, there's always somebody more crazy in the next town. Many quests involve a conflict between two or more factions and the player has freedom to choose who to support, but you'll rarely find an obvious "good guys" faction, more often its a case of "which is the lesser evil?". Dialogue is mostly text based, with only the major characters being voiced, but its all well written with lots of dark humour.
I didn't encounter any game breaking bugs, but occasionally I thought certain quest progressions could have been better. Like the time I drank from a water well, got infected with a disease, and used a normal inventory item to cure myself. Later I found the town's doctor, who asked me to investigate why the people were getting sick. I didn't have any option to say "dude, its your well". The only way to progress the quest was to travel to another town to find a special microscope so the doctor could check out some samples, and discover what I already knew several hours of gameplay earlier.
I also didn't like that inactive companions didn't seem to gain XP. One of my earliest recruits was kind of annoying, constantly complaining about literally everything, so I wanted to ditch him. But every new recruit I found after that was several levels lower, and I didn't want to be weaker in combat, so I was stuck with him.
Except for those complaints, Wasteland 2 is a really great game, and I definitely recommend it to RPG fans, although genre newcomers would be better off starting with something less complex. It took me 68 hours to finish and I didn't complete every side quest, which is excellent value for money at full price.

The story is enthralling, and you feel like you are capable in the beginning.  As you progress, find weapons, level up, you see how it has a direct impact on your success. However, there are many ways to tackle problems, so you are never helpless or out of options.  Every quest I've encountered has clear requirements and satisfying endings.
You may be jarred by the rough character models at the beginning on character creation, but know that the game is not played at that close of a view.  They look sharp from the normal game camera, and graphics overall are good.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys Baldur's Gate, X-Com, Divinity Original Sin, and the like.

Well, I recommend the game, but it isn't without it's problems.
The story was interesting and the roleplaying was good.  I felt some situations were set up as gotchas, where the obvious choice inadvertently made you a child murderer or shafted you in some way farther down the chain.  That being said, despite a few "Oh ♥♥♥♥ off" moments, overall it was a positive gaming experience, perhaps made better for the unknown ramifications of your choices (however much I don't like gotchas).  Several quests chains possessed weird bugs that made accessing the 'best' path counter-intuitive or impossible to achieve, which was annoying after putting in the time and legwork to get those results.
The tactical combat was good, but the pre-battle set up was lacking in interesting choices.  Long range characters were the best, because they can fire at enemies to start a combat, where medium or close range characters could not.  In fact, trying to set those characters up strategically would often cause the enemy to start the battle and get to go first, ruining the 'advantage' of setting up in the first place.  In the end it just made more sense to run up to within long range, crouch the party, and open fire with snipers.
When I finished the game I wasn't inspired to play through it again, and I'm not sure that's a shame.

Wasteland 2 - a game that completly flew under my radar til it was discounted on the last Steamsale. Having played all FallOuts up til New Vegas with the Exception of Tactics I was genuinly interested how this game would work out. That and I'm a huge nerd over CRPGs, still considering Baldur's Gate II the best RPG ever developed.
The game is played from an Isometric perspective, with a typewriter on the right side describing the locations and subtitles. This game has ALOT of reading, so when you are no fan of that you should take that into consideration. Only a few important characters are voiced and your PCs are  mute all the time (Sadly we can not make our own basic voicelines like in Baldur's Gate, but hey atleast we can use our own portraits). You traverse the locations in realtime while the Worldmap has a water limitation and combat is turnbased. It is pretty much reminscent of FallOut 1&2 before the series became what is today. You travel through Arizona visiting the different locations and working towards your way to uncover a sinister plot.
The game was made in the Unity-Engine and is certainly not the prettiest one, but it does the job and all locations are unique and memorable. The sounddesign is well done and paired with the games music it can feel downright creepy at times, the perfect feeling for a post-apocalyptic game.
All in All if you liked the old Fallout-titles or you are intrested in CRPGs Wasteland 2 is definatly worth a look, even if it can feel downright clunky sometimes yet it was modernized in the right way and I will definatly see forward to a 3rd installment

Short review: Virginia is awful, truly awful.
Long review: Virginia is the newest in a long line of so-called "walking simulators" - games that barely qualify as such. I'm going to assume that the reader is familiar with this emergent form of gameplay so that I can cut to the chase. Virginia does not make a single attempt to justify its choice of medium. Interaction is completely linear - the concept of choice does not exist. Other walking simulators, to use the infamous Gone Home as an example, often have supplementary material littered throughout the game to help flesh out the world and immerse the player. The player can either rush through the game, or take things slowly and examine their environment. Corridors in Virginia are completely empty, and thus all the player can do is walk from point A to point B (is this the truest form of walking simulator?). Without any interaction or exploration possible, there is no reason for Virginia to be a video game. I'll take it a step farther, it actively tries NOT to be a video game at times, completely preventing the player from moving the camera or heavily restricting its use.
If Virginia's not a game, we'll have to look at it as a film. Virginia never gives the viewer a reason to care about its characters or what is happening on-screen, but expects them to anyway. At one point the protagonist is flipping through archived documents and really exciting music is playing and it really feels like this is supposed to be some incredible earth-shattering revelation but it all feels so empty and that's just the way the whole thing feels. The lack of dialogue simply does not work in a setting like this, and it prevents any meaningful characterization from happening. It almost seems like this decision was an afterthought after the devs were unable to find any decent voice actors, but this is just speculation on my part. The empty rooms and silence by the characters create a powerful one-two punch of apathy in the viewer, and turn what should have been a relatively straightforward plot into one that can be hard to decipher at times.
The plot in Virginia is nothing special and in the end doesn't really have anything new or important to say. This isn't to say that every film needs to have some sort of message, but I cannot think of a single unifying theme present throughout Virginia. It's simply a series of events that happen without purpose, and purpose is the key word here because Virginia does not have one and no matter how long I think I cannot justify its existence. I cannot see the Twin Peaks comparison outside of the character that looks suspiciously like Agent Cooper - (at least the first part of) the series had a clear purpose, and the characters themselves were charming enough to care about. I cannot see this as a character study akin to Mulholland Drive - again, it's just so empty and the lack of dialogue does not work at all (maybe this is just a way of saying that the protagonist is mentally handicapped).
Technically, too, Virginia is a mess. This is of course subjective, but the art style is extremely ugly in its strange blockiness and simplistic lighting. Less subjective is how mechanical a lot of the movements appear - a character will suddenly start moving a hand without any sort of build-up, and sometimes they'll completely stop moving at all. Having such unrealistic movement in a work that already doesn't feel very immersive only further detracts from the experience.
As game or film, Virginia fails on all fronts. Whatever you do, do not buy this game, even ironically. If you are looking for a "so bad it's good" experience I can point you to several similar games (personally out of 2016's releases I've enjoyed That Dragon, Cancer) that you and your friends may find entertaining. Games have the potential to hold serious artistic merit, but those like Virginia make no effort to carve out their own path, instead opting to take the lazy way out and attempting to copy film. The more I write about this game the more I hate it, and I hope that everyone involved in its creation got a good spanking when it was all over.

Broken Age was the very first project I backed on Kickstarter. As such, it will always have a special place in my heart. It also revived my interest in adventure games, which I didn't think possible in my old, jaded age, but it's a consequence of the game that will stay with me long after the game itself is finished, which is an impressive feat.
The first act is a love song to 2D adventure games. There are tropes that play out like you'd expect and others turned totally upside down. It's fun and light-hearted and whimsical. You won't find another voice cast including the likes of Jack Black and Wil Wheaton in an adventure game any time soon. It's funny, and at times, poignant.
Sadly, the second half doesn't follow nearly as strongly. The puzzles are more obtuse. The writing is more matter-of-fact, and a lot of the situations, artwork, and even puzzles get heavily re-used. In some cases this allows for a creative twist on things, but in others it stinks of laziness. Personally I think the issue is that the success of the Kickstarter and Act I gave Double Fine some room to maneuver, so they got distracted: they made several new games such as Massive Chalice and remastered some old adventure titles in between the releases of the acts. The second act feels like it's a necessary conclusion to the story, but one that they rushed through creating rather than taking the time and care needed to make it something truely memorable.
My other complaint is with the achievements. Most of the time I feel that achievements are neutral - you would've done the requirement for it anyway - or positive because they force you to play the game in a new or interesting or challenging way. But here the achievements are almost all neutral or negative - actively detracting from the experience. First, they were only included for Act I
Act II was released, which forces another run through just to get credit for things already completed. Furthermore, some of the achievements require you to get something right
. For me, this is the worst kind of achievement because it discourages experimentation and encourages relying on guides. It's exacerbated by the fact that there is no chapter select, despite the natural break point in the middle and the forums shouting for some kind of way to jump into Act II when it came out.
Finally, there is a speed run achievement. Simply put: it has no place here. An adventure game is the not the kind of game where you want to skip all the cutscenes and dialogue and use a guide for all the puzzles. That's like purposefully ignoring all the best parts. It's stupid. Some people have theorized it's only there because Xbox Live requires games to have leaderboards. It's just speculation, but if it's true it's awful reasoning and it's fustrating that they kept it included in the desktop version, where there are no leaderboards. And to top it off, because of the included manual save feature the speed run is not even challenging, since you can just save when you only complete a section in the optimal time. So it's an achievement that is a worthless chore requiring no skill that forces you to skip past the best parts of the game. I can't imagine what they were thinking.
Broken Age has some beautiful moments and engrossing puzzles set in a unique world. It can't carry the magic all the way through, but it doesn't have to for it to be a game worth playing.

Nuclear Throne is a fast-paced, twin-stick shooter, roguelike, and bullet hell game. If they don't snowball, runs will usually take 10 to 15 minutes max, but if you're good enough at the game they can go much longer. At around 70 hours, I'm edging towards this point, so if you like the genre(s) you will get your money's worth.
There are many different playable characters whose unique abilites really change the flow of the game and also a plethora of guns to choose from. This gives the opportunity for you to try tons of playstyles.
In general, you're rewarded for striking the right balance between aggressive and too aggressive as you duck and weave through the bullets clouding your screen. The further you progress towards the end-game, the more the game becomes about dodging bullets as opposed to, well, shooting things. In some respects, being able to aim well is almost less important than being able to dodge.
Unfortunately, there is a lot in the game that requires an understanding of mechanics which aren't very well-laid out, though if you don't mind, you can always look on the well-documented wiki (which also does a good job of hiding spoilers). You can learn almost everything through trial and error, though this may be needlessly frustrating and grindy for some.
Some people are curious about playing this game with a controller versus a mouse and keyboard. I personally feel like it's much more responsive with a mouse and keyboard, but others may feel differently. Perhaps I don't care to use a controller since I turn off any auto-aim. If you don't own a controller, you can certainly play the game fine with a mouse and keyboard in my opinion.
For such a well-made and enjoyable game, it is sad that it doesn't have online multiplayer ... except it does because an amazing person who goes by Yellow Afterlife reverse-engineered the game and implemented netplay into it and even added the support for mods. This mod goes by the name "Nuclear Throne Together" and is a must if you have friends who own the game. The game gets even more chaotic, but also even more fun with more people.

Overall I really did enjoy the game and honestly I believe it is worth picking up.
The story of the game is something you would expect from King or Coontz. You are a writer. A writer with a writers block - sounds familiar? You go on holiday with your wife and something starts happening. Strange darkness attacks you and you start living out a story written by you that you don't remember writing. Oh - and there is some lake that the native americans living in the area called gate to hell or something like that. At this point I really thought I'm going to despise the story. But oddly enough after a rough start I really did like it and felt it wasn't all that bad.
The strong part for the game are the visuals which are very nicely done. The scenery is pretty nice, and the lighting effects which are pretty important part of the story are very well made as well. Locations at the beginning tend to be bland - forest, forest and nothing interesting. But later on they do change and are quite nicely designed.
The main part of the game is trying to find your wife and beat the darkness. You do this by following the story and fighting people possessed by the darkness. You kill them by shining your flash light on them long enough so they become vulnerable at which point you can safely unload your gun and finally kill them. And you pretty much do that all through the game with just a couple of guns - revolver, shotgun, hunting rifle and assorted helpers like flares or flash grenades. It does get repetitive after a while but not to a point that you hate the whole fighting. And I must admit that I did got scared once or twice - though mostly the game is not really that scary. But has a very consistent atmosphere and you generally feel quite nice when the sun rises.
There are also a couple of elements involving driving a car - but these could have been surely skipped as they're pretty dreadful.
Voice acting and animation is of very nice quality so watching cut scenes is quite pleasant.
Overall after a week beginning the game provides good fun up till the very last part which seems a bit dull and you have to push through it. Luckily it's not long enough too leave a bad impression on the game. I had fun. I really enjoyed it. If you like story driven action games along the lines of resident evil or alone in the dark there is little fear you will not like this game.

Oh wow... I finished Wasteland 2 and it took me over 70 hours. At any point it didn't feel a waste of time.
How have I been missing the genre. I'm talking about old-school CRPGs with turn-based combat and that really feel almost like P&PRPG:s. The gamer really plays a role. For me, 90's was the golden age of gaming, spawning CRPGs like Baldur's Gate series, Planescape: Torment and the first two Fallouts.
I was worried if Wasteland 2 would be too hard for me. In the nineties I used to play a lot PC games, but as I've gotten older, I don't invest so much time for the gaming anymore. Also, today's video games are more easier and I though I'd be spoiled. But I was wrong! Yes, Wasteland 2 is challenging, also pretty frustrating at time to time, but it is also so compelling that I want to play it more and try harder. The difficulty is spot on.
The game is fugly. I mean the game world graphics. It looks like something from the early 2000's when the 3D graphics were still awkward as hell. On the character portraits and all the drawn 2D stuff are decent and cool. I personally don't care much about the graphics, though. The audio is good. I especially love the ambient (Fallout-ish) soundtrack by Mark Morgan. It really sets the mood for exploring the vast desert wasteland and the ruins of the past world. Also the voice acting is well executed.
Combat is a major part of the game. People have complained that it is not tactical enough. I don't know about that, I don't care. When I bought Wasteland 2, I was buying an RPG not a tactical strategy game. So, I like the turn-based combat as it is. Well, addition to the headshot, more targeted shots would've been nice, but you can't always get everything.
I liked the main and side quests. There seemed to be several ways to deal with everything and the player's choices really have effects in the Wasteland. The story and dialogue was well written. There is a lot of text to read, but I don't mind that. You like reading a lot of text or you don't — its' really just a matter of taste. I do understand gamers that just want to ”play the game, not read a book”, but I enjoyed reading the dialogue and all kinds of item descriptions and little jokes here and there. The game is immersive as hell and it just sucked me inside its world.
Wasteland 2 is not perfect, but it truly is a great game. I hadn't enjoyed playing a new videogame this much for many, many years.

Before I played Virginia, I wasn't really sure what to do with my evening. I wanted to watch something, to passively consume, but couldn't find a movie that would hold my fleeting attention. I considered picking up a controller and trying to engross myself in a game, but nothing took my fancy. Then I saw Virginia in my library, unplayed, and thought I'd see whether that would scratch both itches.
Long story short, it really did.
Takes as purely a game, it falls several hundred feet short of being noteworthy. There is no real gameplay of which to speak; if you're in a corridor, for example, there are no doors you can open just to see inside, no boxes you can check for clues or collectibles. You can walk around occasionally, but it's mostly just "Press A to Continue"
As a story, it has some flaws too. I don't think the writers wanted to create a game like The Wolf Among Us, or anything similar. Rather, this is much more of an indie arthouse-style film, with liberal use of cinematography and tropes like the feared "dream-sequence" to cast doubt on the factual events, even as the credits roll.
Why then did I enjoy it so much? Because despite all of these problems, it still delivered a beautiful-looking, novel and engrossing experience, with an interesting first and second act, and a score so cinematic you can't help but engage.
Furthermore, the above-mentioned narrative choices leave a lasting impression, with doubts and questions about the outcome of the plot swirling. To my mind, that only adds to the enjoyment.
It's £7. Sit with a friend or a partner, and play this for the 1-2 hours it takes, rather than staring at Netflix (again). I guarantee, you'll want to talk about it after.

]
There’s something to be said for being bold and creative when it comes to video game development; be it mechanics, what is expected of player input, visual style, storytelling and so on. This of course often leads into the trap of being called ‘hipster bait’ or ‘art house garbage’ if these creative angles end up being too far straying from the ‘typical’ game design path, though that’s an argument in itself depending on who you ask. That said, Virginia ends up being one of those cases where the liberties with being too creative ends up kneecapping itself to the point of feeling obnoxious and too smart for its own good - I can certainly imagine this wasn’t the developers intent, but Virginia’s desire to be clever and bizarre makes me hold utter contempt against it, especially when it runs flashbacks into the ground assuming that the player has the memory of a goldfish or transitioning between scenes that make little to no sense. It’s been a long time since I’ve played something this inadvertently atrocious, which is an incredible shame despite some of its aspects actually working.
The elephants in the room that will likely turn off some is the lack of any dialogue or player control. To address the former, the animation and information supplied visually achieves its goals well enough in communicating what characters are going through during interactions - Facial expressions and subtle movements go a long way. Player control however is extremely limited; when the game is advertised as a cinematic experience, understand that you’re not playing this for fun or getting success or fail states from your input. Excluding limited instances where you can divert the path to find collectibles or small events for worthless achievements, the game practically plays itself once you walk Anna, the protagonist, to a point and are prompted to click to proceed the scene. You can look around during these cinematic events, but often times there isn’t anything to see other than what’s directly in front of you, and even if you try to examine your surroundings, the scene will often transition elsewhere without your consent, leading to missed information if any happens to be there - For example at the very beginning, Anna (a member of the FBI and the player character) is handed a file regarding her partner whom she is meant to investigate during a missing person case. Before I could finish reading it, the scene leapt elsewhere and I was lost on why Anna’s partner needed to be investigated at all.
These transitions are initially jarring at first, but they grow to be expected as they help keep the game moving even if it means robbing the player of information. However, the use of flashbacks feels almost insulting at times, cutting back to memories that had occurred twenty or so minutes earlier as if the audience hadn’t seen these moments for hours on end - The game is just under two hours long, so needing to remind the player of something so recent is needless and arguably rude. These transitions work as the art style lends itself nicely, being something of a visual shock as Virginia has a full, ranged color palette that makes effective use of shading - The game may resemble a cartoon, but its color and tones cement it in reality (despite later plot elements), making it a prime candidate for spamming the screenshot button since the lack of a HUD means that there are loads upon loads of fantastic scenes to snap. The visuals are only rivaled by that of Virginia’s soundtrack, which I dare say could its own when stacked against other evocative film scores. The orchestrated music excels when it makes itself known, putting heavier impact on events transpiring near the finale or being an eerie companion in the earlier acts. Virginia looks good and sounds good, but then we get to the critical deal breaker that made me loathe it in the first place: The story.
The initial plot involves FBI investigators Anna and Maria going to the town of Kingdom to investigate a missing person, with a side element of Anna needing to investigate Maria for suspicious activity that could harm the bureau. The story puts a greater focus on uncovering Maria’s secrets, but both of these are generally shelved when Anna has to go through her hallucinogenic, time-hopping and body-swapping dream sequences. I wish I was kidding. As a means of separating chapters, Anna will have these vivid and bizarre dream sequences that occasionally muddle themselves into the real world. These dreams serve little purpose other than to confuse you and perhaps(?) give clues as to where Anna should look for her next clue even if the game plays itself for you in terms of direction. Eventually the game devolves into a series of events where reality is nigh-impossible to decipher; transitions jumping around rapidly, viewing the world through the eyes of another character only to jump cut and be watching that character from a different angle. Or when Anna apparently can leap through time, going years ahead in her career or back in time to events experienced by the other characters. Or when she’s suddenly a member of a cult, or staring down a buffalo at a gas station or when aliens get into the mix somehow - Now imagine all of this coming at you rapidly with no explanation or clarification whatsoever, other than Anna is absolutely losing her mind via drug trip. The climax and conclusion to Virginia is so deranged, weird and infuriatingly nonsensical that I grew physical angry, and don’t get me started on the ending that manages to be a series of empty resolutions where nothing truly is resolved, more brushed aside and ‘left to interpretation’.
Virginia tried to do something unique, creative and well intended as a storytelling game, however it’s the fact that it takes so many weird twists and turns with nary explaining an ounce of itself that makes the game come across as pompous and ‘too smart’ for those not able to deduct its hidden meanings. Analyze and break it down all you want, Virginia tries to get away with being weird because it has a legitimately interesting tale to tell based in reality, but that’s being masked with supernatural events and a muddled timeline, and none of it works in any way whatsoever when combined - More specifically, mashed together in shoddy fashion. If the game focused entirely on its mystery thriller angle and ditched the frustrating weirdness, Virginia’s two hour game length would’ve been much more enjoyable, especially with its lack of dialogue and sole use of visual communication. This has been one of the worst things I’ve had to sit through in a long time, and under no circumstances can I recommend it, even if you, the reader, have gotten a tickle of morbid curiosity. Virginia tries to be weird for the sake of being weird, not that it has any point, purpose or idea to get across come the credits roll - It’s a shame such great art and music is lost on this nonsensical, obnoxious excuse for a storytelling game.
